summary: A guide to behavioral interviews: build and tell high-signal stories, answer the essential questions, and show nine competencies at your target level.

unitSummaries.Chapter 1: A three-pillar plan for preparing behavioral interviews: build a story bank, make stories strong, and match them to company values.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: How companies detect fit and level from signals: scope, contribution, impact and difficulty, and how to calibrate and research what a company values.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: The High-Signal Storytelling pyramid: how to tell stories that carry signal rather than noise, and how to build one.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: How to answer the questions every interview asks: introductions, proud projects, why this company, your questions, weaknesses and why you are leaving.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: What taking initiative means, the signals and red flags interviewers look for, and example stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: What delivering means, the signals and red flags interviewers look for, and example stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: What problem solving and deep diving mean, the signals and red flags interviewers look for, and example stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 8: What earning trust and handling conflict mean, the signals and red flags interviewers look for, and example stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 9: What learning and growth mean, the signals and red flags interviewers look for, and example stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 10: What customer and user focus mean, the signals and red flags interviewers look for, and example stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 11: What innovation means versus optimization, the signals and red flags interviewers look for, and example stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 12: What developing others means, including mentoring people you do not manage, with signals, red flags and stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 13: What strategic leadership and thinking big mean, the signals and red flags interviewers look for, and example stories by level.
unitSummaries.Chapter 14: How to prepare, hold a real conversation, handle the unexpected and follow up so your stories land on the day.
unitSummaries.Reading the book as a whole: Put the preparation steps, story pyramid and competency signals together for a real interview.

concepts.title: Stories make your skill visible
concepts.question: Why can strong experience still fail to win an offer?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Technical strength is only part of what a company evaluates. Behavioral interviews are where you also have to prove, through stories, what the technical rounds do not show.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author says even strong experience can be overlooked when it is not communicated clearly. A poorly delivered story makes you seem unqualified, not because the skills are missing but because the interviewer never saw them.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Each answer is the only evidence the interviewer gets, so it has to show what you did and what came of it. (Our reading: judge a draft story by what a stranger could learn from it.)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: An interviewer who has actually seen the skills you have.

card.rule: Skills the interviewer never sees cannot count in your favour.
card.limits: Clear delivery reveals real experience; it does not replace it. The book later insists that every story be true.

media.alt: A smiling man in a sweater gestures openly beside a board listing four interview types; the first three have check marks, while the last, behavioral interviews, has a question mark and an underline.

concepts.title: Rehearse real stories, do not cram
concepts.question: What kind of preparation helps you speak with ease when the interview comes?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Prepare as you would rehearse an important presentation, not train for a marathon: turn real experiences into concise stories and practise them until they feel natural.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author calls the common approach backwards: waiting until the day before, scrambling for project details and writing large dense paragraphs full of corporate speak. The results are forgotten details, meandering monologues and answers too vague to judge.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Short stories built from real events, prepared ahead of time and practised. You need focused preparation, not months of work.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Being confident, clear and authentic when it matters.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.text: Dense written paragraphs that are hard to memorize and hide your contribution.

card.rule: Build short, real stories early and practise them until they feel natural.
card.limits: Early preparation is the ideal, but the book says the roadmap adapts to any timeline, from months to an interview next week.

concepts.title: How the book is built
concepts.question: What does each of the book's three parts do, and in what order do they build?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The book has three parts: Part I, The Framework; Part II, The Competencies; and a closing section, Nailing the Interview, with an afterword on using the skills across a career.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Part I teaches you to identify, structure and deliver behavioral stories and shows what companies evaluate, ending with the essential questions every company asks. Part II covers the specific behaviors companies assess, from problem-solving and delivery to leadership and innovation. The closing section covers delivery and the unexpected.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Learn the method in Part I, use Part II as a reference for the competencies your target company cares about, then finish with delivery techniques. (Our reading: this is the order the chapter implies, not a fixed rule.)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories that are ready to deliver, so you can turn to the other parts of the interview process.

card.rule: Learn the method in Part I, look up competencies in Part II, polish delivery at the end.
card.limits: This is only a preview of the structure. The pillars, not the parts, make up the preparation plan that follows.

concepts.title: The three pillars of preparation
concepts.question: Which three areas does preparation have to cover, and why must all three be strong?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Prepare in three areas: Building Your Stories, Ensuring Story Strength and Matching Company Values.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author says the three work together. Great experiences are not enough if you cannot deliver them, stories pitched below your target level will not earn that level, and an employer's values cannot be ignored. To get an offer, all three must be strong.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Building: turn raw experiences into clear, structured stories. Strength: show the right competencies at the level of your target role. Matching: learn what the target company cares about and make the stories speak to it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: An offer at the level you want, from a company where your stories fit.

card.example: The author's own contrast: junior-level stories do not get you senior-level offers, however well you tell them.
card.rule: Strengthen all three pillars; strength in one does not make up for weakness in another.
card.limits: The pillars are parts of one plan, not alternatives to choose between. Our reading: how much time each needs depends on where you start.

concepts.title: How many stories you need
concepts.question: Which three factors decide how many stories your bank needs?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Size your story bank from three factors: the questions everyone faces, your target company's values and the level you are interviewing for.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Every company asks similar general questions, so you always need stories for Tell me about yourself, a project you are proud of, and why this company or role. Different companies value different competencies, so the target company determines which ones matter.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Prepare 3-4 stories for the essential questions, which also cover weaknesses, failures and challenges. Add 4-10 stories for company-specific needs. Your level then changes which competencies are essential and how many to cover.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A bank sized to the interview you actually face.

card.rule: Count stories from three sources: the essential questions, the company's values and your level.
card.limits: The ranges are the author's guidance, and your target company may value different or additional competencies than a general list suggests.

concepts.title: Company type shapes the competencies
concepts.question: Which competencies should you prioritise for a startup, a large tech company or a traditional enterprise?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Let the type of company guide which competencies you prepare first. The author's lists are starting points for research, not fixed rules.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: According to the author, startups and high-growth companies emphasize speed and autonomy, large tech companies value scale and collaboration, and traditional enterprises value stability and process.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Startups, at a minimum: Initiative, Delivery, Innovation and Learning. Large tech: Problem Solving, Cross-team Leadership, and Trust and Conflict as the core. Traditional enterprises: start with Delivery, Trust, Customer Focus and Developing Others.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories aimed at what this kind of company rewards.

card.rule: Start from the competencies that suit the company's type, then research the specific company.
card.limits: Your target company may value different or additional competencies than its type suggests, so the lists are only a place to begin.

concepts.title: Level sets how many competencies
concepts.question: How many competencies should you cover at entry, mid and senior level, and which are essential?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Let your target level decide how many competencies you cover and which ones are essential.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Higher levels are expected to show wider impact. According to the author, senior candidates must show Strategic Leadership and Developing Others to demonstrate organizational impact, and Innovation to show they can drive technical direction.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Entry level (4-6): Problem Solving, Delivery and Learning, plus one or two that match the culture. Mid-level (5-7): add Initiative and Trust and Conflict, and Customer Focus or Innovation by role. Senior and beyond (7-10): the senior set above plus everything the culture values.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A set of stories that reads like the work of someone at the target level.

card.rule: Cover more competencies, with wider impact, as your target level rises.
card.limits: The ranges are guidance. Company culture can still add a competency at any level, such as Initiative for a startup.

concepts.title: Mine projects for story-worthy moments
concepts.question: Why should you look for moments inside projects instead of treating each project as one story?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Treat each significant project as a source of several stories: every moment where you made a real difference is its own story.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: According to the author, most people list their projects and then force-fit them to whatever question arrives, which leaves value on the table. A half-year project holds several behavioral moments, each about a different competency.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Look inside a project for separate moments, such as a decision you pushed through, a rescue, a disagreement you settled or a colleague you developed. Each is a complete, standalone story, not another version of one project story.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Wide competency coverage from a small number of experiences.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.text: Forcing one whole-project story onto every question that comes up.

card.example: The author's half-year database migration yields five stories: a case for migrating against skeptical leaders, a team split over strategy, a new zero-downtime approach, a lead engineer quitting, and a junior engineer mentored.
card.rule: Find the separate moments inside a project; each one is its own story.
card.limits: Only moments where you made a real difference count. A project is not a source of stories only because it was long.

media.alt: A vertical timeline of one project with five dated markers, from week two to month five, each linked to a rounded box naming a separate moment: scaling limits found, a conflict over approach, an innovation, restructured work, and mentoring a junior engineer.

concepts.title: Four steps to a story bank
concepts.question: What are the steps for building a story bank from your experiences?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Build the bank in four steps: gather significant experiences, find the story-worthy moments in each, use Part II as a reference, then develop each moment as its own story.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A story covers one moment, so the number you get depends on how many key moments happened, not on how long the project took. A complex multi-month project might give three or four stories; a two-week critical incident might give one.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Start with recent significant work. Look for a direction-changing decision, a problem others could not crack, a group you brought to agreement, delivery despite an obstacle, a lesson that changed how you work, or a step beyond your role. Give brief context, then zero in on one challenge, decision or outcome.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A bank of single-moment stories you can draw on for any question.

card.rule: Gather experiences, find the moments, check Part II, then write each moment as its own story.
card.limits: Part II shows what strong moments look like per competency. Our reading: borrow the shape of those examples, not their content, because your stories must be your own.

concepts.title: Four dimensions every story signals
concepts.question: Which four dimensions does every story signal, and how do they help place you at a level?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Every story signals four dimensions to an interviewer: Scope, Contribution, Impact and Difficulty. Your portfolio should reach your target level across several of them.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author says recruiters and interviewers use these signals to decide both whether to hire you and at what level. Reaching the target level on several dimensions, in different situations, shows you can work at that level.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Scope: how broad the work was and your role, from one function to a whole feature to systems across teams. Contribution: what you did, in 'I' terms, apart from the team. Impact: results with numbers and how you created them. Difficulty: complexity, ambiguity, new approaches and trade-offs.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: An interviewer who can place you at your target level.

card.rule: Make each story show its scope, your contribution, its impact and its difficulty.
card.limits: Attribution must stay honest: the line between what you did and what the team accomplished has to be clear, so 'I' covers only your own work.

concepts.title: Research the values, find the gaps
concepts.question: How do you learn what a company values and see where your stories fall short?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Learn how your target company expresses its values, then map your stories against them to find the gaps.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: According to the author, knowing the competency categories is not enough. You must understand how a specific company expresses those values and make sure your stories speak that language.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Go beyond the career-page bullets: read employee blogs, watch tech talks, study interview guides and notice how the company describes successful people and which behaviors it rewards. Then compare your stories with those values.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories that speak the language of the company you are applying to.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.text: Trusting the careers page alone, or assuming the company type tells you everything.

card.example: A company stresses thinking big, but your stories show only incremental improvements: that is a gap. Another stresses learning from failure, and you have only successes: another gap.
card.rule: Research how the company shows its values, then check each against your stories.
card.limits: Our reading: a gap is only as reliable as the research behind it. Thin research gives a misleading map.

concepts.title: Fill gaps with real material
concepts.question: How can you fill a gap in your stories without inventing anything?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Close a gap with real material: dig for overlooked experiences, or reframe an existing story to stress a different aspect.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The goal, according to the author, is to find real examples that show your values match the company's.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Dig: check a side project for an innovation story, or a production incident for a story of learning from failure. Reframe: retell a project you already have, moving the emphasis to what the company values.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Genuine evidence of fit.

card.rule: Fill a gap by digging for real experiences or reframing real ones.
card.limits: Reframing changes emphasis, not facts. Our reading: if no real example exists even after digging, the honest result is a gap, not an invented story.

concepts.title: True stories, honest fit
concepts.question: Why must every story be true, and what should you do if your values clash with the company's?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Tell only true stories about real experiences, and do not fake alignment with values you do not share.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: According to the author, showing that your values match theirs raises your chances and, if you accept an offer, your enjoyment of the role. Fabrications get exposed, with consequences from immediate rejection to career-ending termination.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Use the book's techniques to find and present your genuine accomplishments clearly. If your values genuinely clash with the company's, keep looking rather than pretend.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A role where both you and the employer fit.

card.rule: Present real accomplishments clearly, and if the values truly clash, keep looking.
card.limits: Honesty does not mean understating. The techniques exist to present genuine accomplishments clearly.

concepts.title: Pick your route by situation
concepts.question: Which route through the book fits your timeline and situation?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Choose your route through the book from your situation. It is built both for reading straight through and for quick reference.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Your situation and timeline decide the best approach. With little time you cannot do everything, but you can still build a solid foundation.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Interview next week: Chapters 3 and 4 first, then skim the Part II chapters closest to your target, then Chapter 14 on delivery. Several companies at once: work through Part I in order, use Part II as a reference for each company's values, and note which stories suit which company type.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Planning ahead: read straight through and complete all three pillars to build a comprehensive bank. Assessing your readiness: start with Chapter 2, sample Part II stories at your target level and ask whether you can tell similar ones with comparable scope and impact.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A preparation route that fits the time you have.

card.rule: Match your route to your timeline: a short one for next week, the full one when planning ahead.
card.limits: The routes are the author's suggestions. Our reading: they overlap, so combine them when your situation straddles two.

concepts.title: The two questions behind every offer
concepts.question: What two things do companies use behavioral interviews to decide about you?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Behavioral interviews answer two questions: do you fit both the role and the company, and, if you do, at what level will you be most effective?

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Technical skill alone cannot decide offers. If it did, everyone who solved the coding and system design problems would get the same result.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Each story you tell is read twice: once for fit with this role and this company, once for the level it shows. Our reading: choose stories with both readings in mind.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: An offer at the appropriate level. A wrong read on fit means rejection whatever your skills; a wrong read on level means down-leveling or rejection as underqualified.

card.rule: Prepare each story to answer both questions: does this person fit, and at what level?
card.limits: Our reading: the two questions describe how stories are judged. They do not say which stories to pick, which the later sections cover.

media.alt: Two men sit across a table. The interviewer holds a steaming mug, with two thought bubbles above him asking whether the candidate fits and at what level. The candidate sits calmly with hands clasped.

concepts.title: Role fit and company fit
concepts.question: What is the difference between fitting a role and fitting a company?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Beyond technical skill, behavioral interviews check two kinds of fit. Role fit is about the position; company fit is about the organization around it.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The same technical skills can face very different demands. A backend role at a fast-growing startup asks for different capabilities than a backend role at an established enterprise.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Role fit: can you handle this position's specific challenges and working conditions? Company fit: do your working style, decision-making and values match how the company gets things done?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Hires who can work well in the actual position and setting, not only candidates who look good on paper.

card.rule: Ask two things of any target job: what does this position demand, and how does this company work?
card.limits: Company fit goes beyond surface-level culture. The book does not say any one answer is better; a fit is relative to the particular role and company.

concepts.title: How fit shows up as signals
concepts.question: Since nobody can ask whether you fit, what do interviewers read to find out?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Companies cannot ask outright whether you would fit, so they look for signals of alignment or misalignment in the stories you tell.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: No candidate would answer such a question with a no, so the question itself would reveal nothing.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Role-fit signals come from how you describe handling situations like the role's: ambiguity, cross-team coordination, rapid iteration. Company-fit signals come from the choices you made and how you describe them, matched to values such as bias for action, customer obsession or radical transparency.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A way for the company to see your alignment, and for you to show it, without anyone asking the direct question.

card.rule: Choose stories whose situations and choices match what the role and the company's values call for.
card.limits: A signal is only read against the particular company's own values, so one story can look strong at one company and weak at another.

concepts.title: Mis-fit: independence versus collaboration
concepts.question: How can a story about working alone, or about working with the group, count against you?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Companies differ on independence and collaboration: some want people who take a problem, run with it and return with a solution, others expect you to bring the team along at every step.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The same behavior reads as ownership at one company and as a warning sign at another, so a talented candidate can still be rejected.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: If every story is solo work, consensus-driven companies worry you will steamroll people or make choices that will not stick. If every story involves checking with the group first, ownership-minded companies wonder whether you can decide without a meeting.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories that show the working pattern your target company wants, instead of a one-sided pattern that raises doubt.

card.rule: Match your stories to the company's pattern of working alone or together, and avoid a one-sided set.
card.limits: The warning applies to a pattern across all your stories. Neither pattern is wrong in itself; it is wrong for a particular company.

concepts.title: Mis-fit: speed, thoroughness and the quality bar
concepts.question: How do companies differ on speed versus thoroughness, and on excellence versus pragmatism?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Two linked tensions can separate you from a company: speed versus thoroughness, and excellence versus pragmatism.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Startups often need rapid experimentation, shipping early versions and iterating on feedback, while healthcare and finance companies need careful validation before any release.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Some organizations gladly spend extra weeks on clean architecture. Others want a working solution on deadline even if cleanup comes later. Focusing on perfect code fails at deadline-driven companies; accepting technical debt everywhere fails where critical infrastructure is maintained.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories that show the pace and the quality bar the target company expects.

card.rule: Show the pace and quality bar of the company you are interviewing with.
card.limits: Our reading: these are tendencies by type of company, not rules. A team inside any company may set its own pace and quality bar.

concepts.title: Mis-fit: innovation versus stability
concepts.question: When do stories about changing things, or about keeping them as they are, hurt a candidate?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Roles differ on innovation versus stability: some need new solutions and challenges to existing approaches, others need people to maintain and optimize proven systems.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A team's work decides which habit it values, so the same record reads as creative at one place and unsettling at another.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: If you say you are constantly reinventing established processes, teams that value stability will not see you as a fit.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories that show the balance of creating and maintaining the target team asks for.

card.rule: Show change where the team wants change and care for proven systems where it wants stability.
card.limits: Our reading: this is about the balance in your stories. Few teams want only one of the two.

concepts.title: Mis-fit: direct versus diplomatic
concepts.question: How does the way you describe disagreement match, or clash with, a company's communication culture?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Cultures differ on communication: some prize radical candor and want you to say exactly what you think, others value maintaining harmony and face-saving.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A style that signals honesty in one culture signals harshness in another.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: If you are too blunt, you will not fit well at a relationship-focused company. Stories about how you handled disagreement show where on this range you sit.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A communication style that matches the culture you hope to join.

card.rule: Describe disagreements in a way that suits the company's direct or diplomatic culture.
card.limits: Our reading: the book gives two poles. Most people sit somewhere between, and a story can show both frankness and care.

concepts.title: Mis-fit: data versus intuition
concepts.question: How do companies differ on the evidence they want behind decisions?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Companies differ on evidence: data-driven cultures need data to justify every decision, while others trust experienced judgment and move on gut feel.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Each culture rewards the habits that match how it decides, so the stories that impress differ.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Showing that you decide on instinct does not impress analytical companies. Stories at those companies should show what data you gathered and how it shaped the decision.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Decision stories shaped for the culture's evidence standard.

card.rule: Match how much data your decision stories show to how much evidence the company expects.
card.limits: Our reading: the evidence standard is a matter of degree; most companies want both some data and some judgment.

concepts.title: Mis-fit: specialist versus generalist
concepts.question: Does a company want deep expertise in one area or comfort across many?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Large companies often want deep experts who master one domain; smaller companies need people comfortable wearing multiple hats.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Our reading: a large company can split work into narrow specialties, while a small one has fewer people and each must cover more ground.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Know which sort of company you are walking into. Lead with stories of depth in one domain for the first, and stories of covering several kinds of work for the second.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories whose depth or breadth matches how the company divides its work.

card.rule: Match the depth or breadth in your stories to the size and structure of the company.
card.limits: Our reading: size is only a rough guide. Some large teams want breadth, and some small ones need one expert.

concepts.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
concepts.title: The four dimensions of level
concepts.question: Which four things do interviewers read in every story to place your level?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Companies assess your level through four dimensions that appear in every story: scope, contribution, impact and difficulty.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Each dimension reveals a different aspect of your capability, and together they show where you operate most effectively.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Scope: how many people your work affected. Contribution: what you did, not what happened around you. Impact: what changed for the better. Difficulty: the complexity, constraints and trade-offs you handled.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A reading of your level from stories, so that you get an offer at the right level.

card.rule: Check every story against scope, contribution, impact and difficulty before using it.
card.limits: Our reading: the four dimensions are a way to read a story, not a scorecard the interviewer must follow. Stories of the same level can be strong on different dimensions.

concepts.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
concepts.title: Scope: how far your work reaches
concepts.question: How does the reach of your work move up through the levels?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Scope measures the number of people on your team and, as you advance, outward to those whose work your actions affected. More people affected means a higher level on this dimension.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Levels grow outward: first your own work, then your team, then neighbouring teams, then the wider organization.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Entry: your own productivity, starting to help teammates. Mid: aspects of your team and how it operates. Senior: your whole team, with influence reaching at least one other team. Staff: at least two teams directly, with influence on the wider division or organization. Principal: many teams or large parts of the organization.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Showing the reach of your work at the level you are targeting.

card.rule: State how many people and teams your work actually affected, and match it to your target level.
card.limits: Scope counts people whose work you affected, not the size of the audience; it is one dimension of four.

concepts.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
concepts.title: Contribution: what you did, in I and we
concepts.question: What did you personally do, and how does that rise with level?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Contribution is what you did, not what happened around you. Be precise about the line between I and we, because companies expect rising leadership and ownership as you advance.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A team result tells interviewers little unless they can see your own part in it, which is what places your level.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Entry: you execute assigned work and start to own small pieces. Mid: you own complete solutions from problem to implementation. Senior: you lead initiatives that need coordination, even when requirements are unclear. Staff: you lead cross-team initiatives and set technical direction. Principal: you create organizational capabilities and often define the problem first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Showing the right amount of ownership and leadership for your target level.

card.rule: Say what you personally decided and did, and match the amount of ownership to your target level.
card.limits: Precision about I and we does not mean hiding the team; the point is that your part is clear. Contribution is one of four dimensions.

concepts.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
concepts.title: Impact: what changed for the better
concepts.question: What result should a story show, and how does it grow with level?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Impact is what changed for the better because of your work. Companies want results worth the investment, so strong stories put numbers on the impact and connect technical wins to business or user outcomes.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A bare description of work does not show whether it mattered; a measured result does.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Entry: your own productivity improves and you start to help the team. Mid: team effectiveness improves in specific areas, and you can quantify it. Senior: you transform how your team works and begin to affect others, including product outcomes and costs. Staff: several teams improve and the effect ties to business metrics. Principal: organizational capability and strategic change.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Evidence that your work was worth doing, at the level you are targeting.

card.rule: Put a number on the result and tie it to a business or user outcome.
card.limits: Our reading: not every result can be measured exactly, but a stated estimate still helps. Impact is judged with the other three dimensions.

concepts.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
concepts.title: Difficulty: how hard the problems were
concepts.question: What makes a story hard enough to count, and how does difficulty rise with level?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Difficulty reflects the complexity of the problems you tackled, the constraints you faced and the trade-offs you managed. Easy problems with big impact are less impressive than hard problems solved well.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: How hard the problem was shows what you can handle, apart from how large the result was.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Entry: straightforward problems within established patterns. Mid: more moving parts and less obvious solutions. Senior: constraints and decisions with team-level architectural effect. Staff: competing trade-offs across teams. Principal: fundamental trade-offs, novel problems and no clear solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Showing problems of the right hardness for your target level.

card.rule: Choose stories whose obstacles, constraints and trade-offs match your target level.
card.limits: A hard problem with no result is a weak story; difficulty works with the other three dimensions.

concepts.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
concepts.title: Level as a pattern across dimensions
concepts.question: How do the five levels differ across the four dimensions?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Levels run in order: entry, mid, senior, staff, principal. Each is read as a pattern across all four dimensions, not one.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Each step up widens reach, ownership, results and difficulty together.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Scope widens from yourself to many teams. Contribution moves from executing assigned work to creating organizational capability. Impact moves from personal productivity to business outcomes. Difficulty moves from straightforward problems to novel ones.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Placing a story on the ladder and seeing what a step up would require.

card.rule: Judge a story's level by the whole pattern across the four dimensions.
card.limits: Our reading: the dimensions need not match exactly. The book says stories of mixed levels are normal.

media.alt: A staircase of five steps rising left to right, each labelled with a level and its main job: entry executes small pieces, mid owns full solutions, senior leads team work, staff drives cross-team impact, principal shapes organization-wide systems. A cartoon man runs up the steps.

concepts.title: Comparing adjacent levels
concepts.question: How should you use the sample stories for each level?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The sample stories at each level are not templates. Use them to compare adjacent levels and notice what changes between a mid-level story and a senior one.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The same types of accomplishments look different at each level, and the change shows in the four dimensions.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Lay a mid-level story beside a senior one and check each dimension: who is affected, what you personally did, what improved and how hard it was.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A sense for the difference between levels, so you can tell where your own stories sit.

card.rule: Compare your story with the levels on either side and note what changes on each dimension.
card.limits: The stories are samples and not scripts. Copying them would not be your story.

concepts.title: Entry and mid-level stories side by side
concepts.question: What changes between an entry-level story and a mid-level one?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Read the entry and mid-level samples together: entry-level work is mostly your own, with a clear small measure, while mid-level work reshapes how the team operates.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Entry samples touch your own work and a few teammates, such as scripts for a testing task or a fix for an on-call rotation. Mid samples cover a whole workflow or set of services your team owns.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Entry: you write scripts, document a process, or trace and fix a root cause. Mid: you design, implement and roll out a workflow, balancing competing needs such as speed with reliability, and you start to influence a neighbouring team.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A model for judging where your own stories sit between the two levels.

card.rule: Entry stories fix your own or a few teammates' work; mid stories own a complete solution for the team.
card.limits: These are samples, not templates, and the lines between levels are soft: a strong entry story can show early reach beyond one's own work.

concepts.title: What senior-level stories look like
concepts.question: What do the senior-level sample stories have in common?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Senior-level stories transform how your whole team works and start to reach other teams, with you leading adoption rather than only building.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Senior scope is the whole team plus influence on at least one other, and senior contribution is leading initiatives that need coordination.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The samples share a shape: the author drove the vision or the design, won buy-in from other teams, and led adoption. Difficulty comes from different team needs, governance and architectural choices.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Telling stories in the way that signals senior scope and ownership.

card.rule: Senior stories show you leading adoption across your team and beyond, through buy-in and architectural decisions.
card.limits: A senior story does not need every dimension at its peak. The book says mixed levels are normal.

concepts.title: Staff and principal stories
concepts.question: How do staff-level and principal-level stories differ from senior ones?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Staff stories turn on trade-offs among several teams with different needs. Principal stories turn on organization-wide capability, executive alignment and problems with no clear solution.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Staff scope is at least two teams, and principal scope is many teams or large parts of the organization, so the difficulty moves from team trade-offs to organizational ones.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Staff samples: observability standards across three backend teams, an API design framework for five product teams, and deployment infrastructure for about forty engineers. Principal samples: an engineering strategy for AI infrastructure, a data privacy program and a technical fellowship.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recognizing the upper levels so you do not claim them without evidence.

card.rule: Staff stories resolve trade-offs between teams; principal stories change how the whole organization works.
card.limits: Our reading: the samples are illustrations. Few engineers will have a principal story, and the book does not require one.

concepts.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
concepts.title: Scoring your own stories
concepts.question: How can you check which level a prepared story actually shows?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Take your prepared stories and score each one against the scoring guide, to see whether it matches your target level.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Most candidates either undersell their accomplishments or overstate their contributions, and scoring helps you find the more accurate middle ground.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: For each story, compare the four dimensions with the guide: entry is individual and straightforward; mid covers team aspects and owned solutions; senior is the whole team plus one or two others; staff is two or three or more teams directly; principal is company-wide.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A clear picture of how your stories sit against your target level.

card.rule: Score each story on all four dimensions against the level guide before you decide to use it.
card.limits: Scoring is a self-check. Our reading: it is useful only if you are honest, and an outside reader can help.

media.alt: A blank scoring table with columns for story topic, scope, contribution, impact, difficulty and overall level, each with a guiding question. One worked row, about repairing a deployment process, rates scope mid, contribution senior, impact mid, difficulty mid or senior, and overall mid-senior. Two empty rows follow.

concepts.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
concepts.title: Reading your scores as a set
concepts.question: What should you do once your stories are scored?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Read the scores as a set. Stories clustered below your target mean you need stronger examples, a better account of their scope and impact, or a different target level.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: You do not need every story at your target level, but you need enough of them to show you can consistently operate there.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: If your stories show mixed levels, which is normal, make sure at least two or three sit solidly at your target level, and lead with those.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A set of stories that shows your target level consistently, without overreach.

card.rule: Make sure at least two or three stories sit solidly at your target level, and lead with them.
card.limits: Our reading: the count of two or three is the book's rule of thumb, not a guarantee.

concepts.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
concepts.title: Fixing a weak dimension
concepts.question: If your stories are weak on one dimension, what kind of story should you look for?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: When your stories are weak on one dimension, look for examples that strengthen exactly that dimension.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Each dimension is read separately, so a gap on one can hold back an otherwise good story set.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Weak on scope: find work that affected multiple parties. Weak on impact: find stories with quantified business outcomes. Weak on difficulty: choose challenges that suit your level. Weak on contribution: find stories where you can name your own decisions and actions.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A story set with no obvious gap in any dimension.

card.rule: Name the weakest dimension and choose stories that are strong in just that one.
card.limits: Our reading: you can only fix a gap with real stories you have. The book does not suggest inventing them.

concepts.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
concepts.title: Choosing emphasis without fabricating
concepts.question: How far may you tailor your stories to a company without making things up?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: You are selecting which real experiences to share and which aspects to emphasize. You are not inventing stories.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: If you pretend to have experiences you lack, follow-up questions will expose it and you will be rejected, or worse, you will be hired into a role you cannot do.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Tailor your emphasis to what each role values, not your underlying experiences. If your experiences do not match what a company values, that is useful information: this may not be the role, you may need to gain experience first, or you may need a different culture.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Truthful, persuasive stories, and good decisions about which roles to pursue.

card.rule: Choose and emphasize real experience for the audience; never invent it.
card.limits: Emphasis is bounded by the facts of the story. It is persuasion in the book's sense, but not deception.

concepts.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
concepts.title: Stories pitched below the target level
concepts.question: Which patterns of stories lead to down-leveling when you interview for a higher level?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Two mismatches can lead to down-leveling or rejection: junior stories for senior roles, and mid-level stories for staff roles.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Interviewers read the level your stories show, and the role asks for a higher level of leadership.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: A senior role needs team leadership, so stories of individual task completion fall short. A staff role needs cross-team leadership, so stories of single-team ownership fall short.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories pitched at the level the role requires.

card.rule: For a higher-level role, bring stories that show the leadership that level needs.
card.limits: Our reading: a good story set can still include lower-level stories as support.

concepts.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
concepts.title: Claiming scope you did not earn
concepts.question: Why does stretching your role in a story damage you rather than help?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Do not claim scope you did not earn: say exactly which part you built, designed or decided.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Interviewers probe the details, and an overstated claim destroys your credibility instantly.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: If you built one service inside a larger platform rebuild, say that you built that service, not that you led the whole rebuild. Name the real boundary of your part.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Credibility, so that the real strengths of your story are believed.

card.rule: State the exact boundary of what you owned, decided and built.
card.limits: Our reading: accuracy does not mean modesty. Claim fully what you did, and no more.

concepts.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
concepts.title: Impact without difficulty, difficulty without impact
concepts.question: Why do important but easy work, and hard but pointless work, both read as weak?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A story needs both a meaningful result and real difficulty. Important but easy work, and hard work with no purpose, both read as weak evidence of level.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Easy work does not show problem-solving, and complexity without purpose hints at over-engineering and raises red flags.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: For senior roles, show constraints and architectural decisions, not only important checklist items. For complex work, explain why existing solutions would not work or what business problem it solved.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stories that pair a worthwhile result with a hard problem.

card.rule: Pair a meaningful result with a genuinely hard problem, and explain the purpose of complexity.
card.limits: Our reading: the balance depends on level. An easy but useful story can be fine for an entry-level role.

concepts.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
concepts.title: Unclear contribution: the trouble with we
concepts.question: What goes wrong when every sentence of a story says we?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Using we throughout makes it impossible to assess your level: make clear who decided, who did the work and who handled the problems.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: If your role is unclear, interviewers cannot tell whether you drove the work or simply took part.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Use I where the action was yours, and name team actions separately. Keep the team in the story, but let your decisions and actions stand out.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A story whose contribution can be read, so that your level can be judged.

card.rule: Separate what you decided and did from what the team did.
card.limits: Our reading: I is not better than we everywhere. Replace we only where you were the one who acted.

concepts.title: Start with your recruiter
concepts.question: Why is your recruiter the first place to look for what a company values?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Start your research with your recruiter, who is your best source of insider information.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Recruiters want you to succeed because their performance is based on the number of accepted offers from candidates they put forward. They also have prep materials and know the interviewers' focus areas.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Ask directly what you should know about the company's current challenges, which competencies matter most for the role, and whether they can share interview prep materials.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Knowing what the company evaluates before you choose your stories.

card.rule: Ask your recruiter about challenges, key competencies and prep materials.
card.limits: Our reading: a recruiter may not be able to share everything, and what they share is a guide, not a guarantee.

media.alt: A tree diagram headed by researching what companies value, with four branches, each with an icon: ask your recruiter, mine public information, look for patterns in online discussions, and talk to current employees.

concepts.title: Mining public information
concepts.question: Where can public sources show what a company values?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Public material shows what a company values. Words repeated in job postings tell you what matters, and what a company publishes shows what it celebrates.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Repeated words are there for a reason: a posting that stresses fast-paced signals something different from one that stresses compliance.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Look at engineering blogs for wins and problems celebrated, tech talks for the topics presented, and release patterns for pace. Technology choices help too: newer frameworks suggest a focus on innovation, proven technologies a preference for stability.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A picture of the company's priorities, even without insider help.

card.rule: Read what the company publishes and repeats; its choices show its priorities.
card.limits: Our reading: public material is curated by the company, so treat it as evidence to cross-check, not proof.

concepts.title: Patterns online and voices inside
concepts.question: How do you separate real signals from noise in reviews, and what should you ask insiders?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Look for patterns across many posts and ask current employees specific questions, to learn which behaviors the company actually rewards.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Single rants are noise, but a theme repeated by several people is a signal. Current employees tell truths the company website never would.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: On review sites, ignore individual rants and note what people complain about and praise across posts. Praise for autonomy suggests trust in people to decide. With employees, skip surface questions about culture and ask what earns promotion, what draws negative feedback, how disagreement is settled and what surprised them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Knowing the behaviors the company really rewards, beyond its slogans.

card.rule: Trust patterns, not single posts, and ask insiders specific questions.
card.limits: Our reading: review sites over-represent strong opinions, and one employee's view is one view.

concepts.title: Putting fit, level and research together
concepts.question: How do fit, level and research combine into choosing and telling your stories?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Fit and level together decide whether you get an offer and whether it sets you up for success. Research tells you which of your stories to emphasize.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Understanding fit shows which experiences connect with what the company values; understanding level lets you position them. Neither environment is inherently better, since different environments reward different approaches.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Use research to choose stories. If they prize speed, emphasize shipping quickly and iterating; if technical depth, diving into root causes; if collaboration, cross-team work. Frame each story at your true level.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: The right offer at the right level at the right company.

card.rule: Pick stories that match the company's values, and frame them at your true level.
card.limits: Our reading: this chapter helps you choose and frame stories; it does not replace the experience those stories describe.

concepts.title: Behavioral stories, not project stories
concepts.question: Which parts of my story show how I behaved, and which only describe what was happening around me?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Tell the interviewer how you behaved (what you thought, decided and did), not the history of the project.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the interviewer see how you would act on the kinds of challenges their own company faces.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, behavioral questions test how you met deadlines, investigated problems, made decisions, influenced people and created impact. When you explain the whole situation first, your behaviors end up tangled with company, team and technology detail, and the interviewer cannot tell what you did from what happened around you.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A candidate asked about a hard deadline spends two minutes on the history of the product and the team's tooling, and mentions the scope cut she chose only at the very end. The stronger version opens with her decision and what she did next.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick one story you plan to tell and underline the sentences that describe your own thinking or action.

card.rule: Tell the interviewer how you behaved (what you thought, decided and did), not the history of the project.
card.limits: Some background is needed for a decision to make sense, so the rule trims context rather than banning it. That project stories lose offers is the author's observation from experience, not a measured result.

concepts.title: What project stories cost you
concepts.question: What can go wrong for a capable candidate who tells a linear, project-style story?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat a linear project-style answer as a risk to your offer and your level, not as a safe default.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure your real abilities and judgment reach the interviewer's notes.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author names two costs. Strong candidates fail to win offers when their problem-solving stays hidden inside the story. Experienced people get placed at a lower level when proof of their judgment is buried under project details. Either way, ability that is not visible in the answer cannot count in the decision.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A senior analyst walks through a reporting rebuild month by month. The interviewer's notes end up reading 'worked on reporting migration', with no sign of the trade-off calls she made, so the panel sees a mid-level contributor.

card.rule: Treat a linear project-style answer as a risk to your offer and your level, not as a safe default.
card.limits: This is the author's account of consequences; the chapter gives no figures for how often it happens. Other things also affect level, so a better structure raises your chances without guaranteeing an offer.

concepts.title: What a good story structure must do
concepts.question: What five jobs should a story structure do for you within a 45-minute interview?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Judge any story structure by five jobs: easy notes, behaviors upfront, quick to set up, flexible to follow-ups, and impact inside the story.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Fit several stories into a short interview while giving the interviewer exactly what they need to evaluate you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author points to a hard limit: about 45 minutes for several questions answered through different stories. Five minutes of context on one story costs you room to show what you can do on the rest. A structure that is quick to set up, notes-friendly and flexible leaves time for the conversation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A product designer has 45 minutes and five questions. She spends five minutes on background for her first story, and by the fourth question has to rush a story that would have shown her best work.

card.rule: Judge any story structure by five jobs: easy notes, behaviors upfront, quick to set up, flexible to follow-ups, and impact inside the story.
card.limits: The five jobs are the author's criteria, not a standard test. A structure can meet them on paper and still fail if the story chosen does not show the competency asked about.

concepts.title: The three layers of the pyramid
concepts.question: What are the three layers of a story pyramid, and which ones do I prepare to say?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Build each answer in three layers (a headline, a behavioral core and a base) and prepare the first two to say while keeping the base ready for follow-ups.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give the interviewer a story they can follow and note, with depth available wherever they choose to probe.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The headline matches the one-line summary an interviewer writes after your first answer. The behavioral core matches the bullet points about what you did and achieved. The base matches the follow-up exploration, where they probe a thread. Because the layers mirror the notes, the interviewer does not have to dig for your actions.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A support agent is asked about a recurring refund error. Her headline names the cause she found and the fix. Her core gives three moments of noticing, deciding and acting. Her base holds the refund policy history and the tools she rejected, ready if asked.

card.rule: Build each answer in three layers (a headline, a behavioral core and a base) and prepare the first two to say while keeping the base ready for follow-ups.
card.limits: The pyramid is the author's own framework, not an industry standard. It organises what you prepare; it cannot choose a story that fits the question.

media.alt: A triangle split into three layers under a storytelling title. The top is a one-sentence headline summary, the middle holds two or three key actions as the behavioral core, and the wide base is prepared detail available on request. A man works at a laptop beside it.

concepts.title: Giving up perfect chronology
concepts.question: What does the pyramid cost me, and why does the author think the cost is acceptable?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Accept that you will not tell events in strict time order, and give the exact timeline only when the interviewer asks.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the interviewer's attention on your capabilities rather than on a record of the project.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author's reason is that interviewers are evaluating you, not documenting project and team history. They need to understand what you can do, not every twist of what happened. If they want the exact order of events, they will ask; if they do not, you can assume they got what they needed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An emergency-room nurse is asked about a staffing crisis. She skips the sequence of shift changes, opens with the triage decision she made, and gives the sequence only after a panel member asks how the evening unfolded.

card.rule: Accept that you will not tell events in strict time order, and give the exact timeline only when the interviewer asks.
card.limits: Our reading: where listeners need the order of events to follow a decision, keep a brief sequence. The author's trade is aimed at evaluation interviews, and the chapter says to compress timelines unless duration matters to the story.

concepts.title: The headline at the peak
concepts.question: What should the single opening sentence of my story say, and what is it for?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Open with one sentence that holds your whole story, written so the interviewer could note it almost word for word.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Have the interviewer record the gist of your story the moment you start.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author describes the headline as reverse-engineering the interviewer's notes. It confirms you understood the question and previews your specific contribution. Because it names the problem, your key action and the result in one breath, the listener knows what the story is about before the details arrive.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Asked about unclear requirements, a wedding planner opens: 'I found that the venue's rules, not the guests, caused our seating chaos, and I rewrote the plan so the room worked with no complaints.' The panel can note that line almost as spoken.

card.rule: Open with one sentence that holds your whole story, written so the interviewer could note it almost word for word.
card.limits: A headline only previews; it cannot replace the core. Our reading: promise in it only what the rest of the story then shows.

concepts.title: Offering a choice of headlines
concepts.question: When several of my stories could answer the question, how can I let the interviewer choose?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When more than one story fits, offer two short headlines and ask which is more relevant.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the interviewer steer toward what they are evaluating while showing you have prepared several strong examples.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each option works as a miniature headline, so the interviewer has enough information to choose the one that matches what they are assessing. The author notes that this puts the interviewer in control and also shows you have many strong examples.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Asked about handling a sudden change, a restaurant manager says: 'I have two examples. One is when a supplier failed an hour before service and I rebuilt the menu on the spot. The other is when I redesigned our booking process after a policy change. Which is more relevant?'

card.rule: When more than one story fits, offer two short headlines and ask which is more relevant.
card.limits: Our reading: offer a choice only when more than one story truly fits. With one clear story, just tell it, and two options with vague labels leave the interviewer unable to choose.

concepts.title: Headline as preview, then pause
concepts.question: What does the headline leave out, and what should I do right after saying it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep the headline a preview of what you did that mattered, not a summary of context, then pause briefly before moving into the core.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give the interviewer a moment to take in your direction and redirect you if you chose the wrong story.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A headline that describes the company or team gives the listener nothing about your contribution. The pause is a chance for the interviewer to react if the story is not what they wanted. If they say nothing, you carry on to the behavioral core.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A retail buyer says: 'I cut returns on our winter range by finding the size guide was wrong, and fixed it.' She pauses. The interviewer nods, so she begins her first key moment.

card.rule: Keep the headline a preview of what you did that mattered, not a summary of context, then pause briefly before moving into the core.
card.limits: The pause is brief. Silence that drags on gives the interviewer an extra duty to fill it, which is our reading and not a claim the chapter makes.

concepts.title: The behavioral core: key moments
concepts.question: What goes in the middle layer, and how many moments should it hold?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Fill the core with two or three key moments that show your thinking and your actions, with their impact included.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show how you think and act, so the interviewer has complete evidence to evaluate.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Companies want to evaluate how you think and act, not which projects or technologies you have touched. Two or three moments are enough to give a complete picture. Putting impact and metrics inside each moment, rather than at the end, gives the interviewer all the key information in one place.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Asked about improving a failing onboarding flow, a UX researcher tells three moments: spotting that drop-off clustered at one screen, choosing to test a shorter form against redesign, and the sign-up rate that followed.

card.rule: Fill the core with two or three key moments that show your thinking and your actions, with their impact included.
card.limits: The core cannot fix a story with no real decisions in it. Two or three moments is the author's guidance, and a very small project may only yield one or two moments.

concepts.title: What belongs in the core, and what is missing
concepts.question: If I read my draft core aloud, what should I find in it and what should be absent?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check a draft by what it holds: reasoning, investigation, decisions and results should be there; company history, org charts, tool stories and meeting accounts should be absent.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show how you worked, not only what you worked on.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author's sample core is full of what you did: an observation, the reasoning, the way you investigated, the discovery, learning, a solution and a measurable impact. What it leaves out is company history, team structure, the tech stack, meeting discussions and what others tried first.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A pharmacist's draft about cutting dispensing errors has her noticing one shelf layout caused most mix-ups, testing a relabelling, and showing a drop in errors. It omits the chain's history, who sat on the committee and why the pharmacy chose its software.

card.rule: Check a draft by what it holds: reasoning, investigation, decisions and results should be there; company history, org charts, tool stories and meeting accounts should be absent.
card.limits: Our reading: absent does not mean forbidden. Anything left out is held in the base until it is asked for, and a missing detail can be added when it explains a decision.

concepts.title: The base: prepared depth
concepts.question: What do I keep ready but unsaid, and what would happen if I said it all upfront?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Prepare technical detail, team dynamics, extra context, alternatives considered and deeper lessons, and share them only when asked.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Follow the interviewer's lead naturally instead of guessing what to include upfront.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The base holds everything you might need for follow-ups. Keeping it ready means you are not forced to guess which detail will interest this interviewer. Keeping it unsaid means the core stays focused on your behaviors. Neither half works without the other.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A warehouse supervisor prepares her base for a layout-change story: why the old layout failed, which two alternatives she rejected, how the night crew reacted and what she would change now. None of it is said until a question calls for it.

card.rule: Prepare technical detail, team dynamics, extra context, alternatives considered and deeper lessons, and share them only when asked.
card.limits: Preparing the base does not mean memorising answers; the author later says to prepare categories so you respond naturally. A base can also be too thin if you never rehearse it aloud.

concepts.title: Different interviewers, different probes
concepts.question: How do different interviewers explore the base, and how should I prepare for each?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Prepare base material for several kinds of interviewer, and answer the question you are asked instead of guessing which one you face.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be able to satisfy a technical interviewer, a manager and a senior leader with the same story.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author gives three sample probes about one story. A technical interviewer asks about the specific cause. A manager asks how you got buy-in for a change. A senior leader asks how you made sure users were undisturbed and data safe. A prepared base lets you answer each as it comes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After a story about replacing a clinic's booking process, one panelist asks which technical limits shaped her choice, another how she won over reluctant receptionists, and a director how she protected patients' records.

card.rule: Prepare base material for several kinds of interviewer, and answer the question you are asked instead of guessing which one you face.
card.limits: The three probes are examples, not a complete list. The author notes that Part II adds follow-up patterns for each competency, so the base grows with the type of story.

concepts.title: Where STAR goes wrong
concepts.question: Why does the author think STAR's equal treatment of its four parts weakens a story?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not give every STAR part equal time, and do not invent a Task when you acted on your own initiative.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach your actions quickly, so the interviewer does not have to join context to behavior for you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) weights all four parts the same. People then spend too long on Situation and Task, which are context, and arrive at Action with the clock running down. A forced Task also makes you look passive, as if you act only when assigned, and senior work rarely arrives as assigned tasks.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A teaching assistant spotted that late marking was hurting weaker students and acted without being asked. Squeezing in an invented 'task' of being asked to fix marking would make her seem to wait for instructions.

card.rule: Do not give every STAR part equal time, and do not invent a Task when you acted on your own initiative.
card.limits: The author calls STAR and CARL 'not wrong approaches'. The complaint is about the anti-patterns they invite, so a candidate who keeps Situation and Task short and finds a real task is not breaking the rule.

concepts.title: Where CARL goes wrong
concepts.question: What does CARL change from STAR, and what trap does its mandatory Learning create?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Add a learning only when you have a real one; do not close every story with a forced lesson.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep your endings honest, so impact and results are not crowded out by generic insight.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: CARL (Context, Action, Result, Learning) drops Task and adds Learning, which improves on STAR. The trap is making Learning compulsory. A forced lesson tends to sound generic, and sometimes the impact and the metrics matter more than anything learned.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A new graduate who ran a small survey closes with 'I learned that communication is important'. A stronger ending gives the response rate she reached and what the survey changed.

card.rule: Add a learning only when you have a real one; do not close every story with a forced lesson.
card.limits: The author does not say learnings are unimportant; deeper lessons stay ready in the base. The rule is aimed at forcing a lesson where none is genuine.

concepts.title: Converting STAR stories into the pyramid
concepts.question: Where does each part of a STAR story go when I rebuild it as a pyramid?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Rebuild each STAR story by moving its parts: highlights to the headline, Action expanded in the core, Situation and Task shrunk, Result into the core, Learning to the base.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reuse the stories you already have instead of starting over.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The headline pulls the most important parts of Situation, Action and Result. The two-minute core expands Action by adding your thoughts and decisions, and Result moves into it instead of waiting at the end. Situation and Task shrink, and Learning is held ready in the base.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A recruiter's STAR story about filling hard roles runs: hospital context, her task of filling twelve posts, her actions, then a lesson. As a pyramid: a one-line headline, a core on her sourcing choices with results, and the lesson saved for a question.

card.rule: Rebuild each STAR story by moving its parts: highlights to the headline, Action expanded in the core, Situation and Task shrunk, Result into the core, Learning to the base.
card.limits: Our reading: conversion is a rewrite, not a relabel. If the old story has no real decisions in its Action, expanding Action will not rescue it.

concepts.title: Signal and noise
concepts.question: In a behavioral story, what counts as signal, and what counts as noise?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make your core heavy on signal (evidence of how you behaved) and keep out noise, which is anything that lengthens the story without showing how you work.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make your abilities easy to see, so nothing hides them in the interviewer's notes.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Signal is evidence of your behaviors: how you investigated, how you read the situation, why you decided what you did, what you did and what impact you created. Noise creeps in when base-layer detail is pulled into the core. It feels helpful, but it buries the signals under unnecessary information.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A bakery supervisor asked about cutting waste talks for a minute about the bakery's founding and its supplier contracts. The two sentences about how she tracked unsold loaves by hour and moved the baking schedule are the signal, and they are now hard to find.

card.rule: Make your core heavy on signal (evidence of how you behaved) and keep out noise, which is anything that lengthens the story without showing how you work.
card.limits: Noise is judged against the question, so a detail can be signal in one story and noise in another. Our reading: the same fact about team size may be signal if the story is about leading it.

media.alt: A balance scale. The signal pan on the left lists five items: how you figured things out, your decisions, your specific actions, how you worked with others, and your results. The noise pan on the right lists company context, teammate context, over-explained technology choices, and excessive detail.

concepts.title: Five kinds of signal
