Put signal, meaning evidence of how you behaved, in the core, and keep noise, meaning context that only lengthens the story, in the base. An old STAR story converts by moving its highlights to the headline, expanding the action and keeping the learning in reserve.
card.example: Our illustration: a clinic manager's moment is finding why no-shows spiked. Headline: the cause she found and the fix. Core: how she noticed, what she decided, what she did and the result. Base: the old booking tool, the options she rejected and how staff reacted.
card.rule: Take one moment per story, then build it as headline, core and base, keeping signal in the core and detail in reserve.
card.limits: The chain organises what you say; it cannot strengthen a thin moment. Our reading: if a moment holds no real decision, look for a better moment before polishing.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Flags that cost you credibility
concepts.question: What do the recurring flags about exaggeration, blame and a vague 'we' have in common?

paragraphs: Some flags come back in several chapters. Lying or exaggerating and a vague account of your own part appear early, in Chapters 2 and 3, and blaming others returns in Chapters 3, 6 and 8. Chapter 14 adds a rule that stories must be true, because deep follow-up questions expose invention.

Our reading of what they share: each stops the interviewer trusting or assessing what you personally did. Exaggeration damages credibility, blame suggests you do not own outcomes, and a vague 'we' hides your contribution. The authors explain each flag separately; the common thread is our summary.
card.example: Our illustration: 'The vendor missed every deadline, so we slipped' blames and hides her part. 'The vendor's delay put our launch at risk; I re-sequenced our tasks and agreed a smaller first release' names what she controlled and did.
card.rule: Tell each story through what you personally did and controlled, truthfully sized, and name your own part when things went wrong.
card.limits: Context matters, and the rule is about what a story claims. Our reading: it does not ban describing a hard situation, only turning it into an excuse.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Short answers and pyramid stories
concepts.question: Which essential questions get a short direct answer, and which get a full pyramid story?

paragraphs: Chapter 4's questions are not all handled alike. The personal essentials, such as tell me about yourself, why this company and why you left, call for brief, direct answers, because they draw little behavioral evidence and few follow-ups.

The project question (proudest, most complex or most challenging) is the exception. It is answered with the Chapter 3 pyramid: a headline that says why the project mattered, a core of about two minutes, then a stop so the interviewer can pull you into the base. Across the three variants, only the headline changes much; the core stays largely the same.
card.example: Our illustration: Lina is asked why she left and answers in about forty seconds, neutral and forward-looking. Ten minutes later she is asked about the project she is proudest of and opens with a headline, gives a two-minute core and stops.
card.rule: Match the form to the question: brief and direct for the personal essentials, the pyramid for the project question.
card.limits: Short does not mean vague. Our reading: each brief answer still needs specifics, and the authors' timings are guides, not stopwatch limits.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Critical, strong and supporting signals
concepts.question: How do the nine competency chapters rank their signals, and how should that shape a story?

paragraphs: Each of the nine competency chapters (Chapters 5 to 13) sorts the signals interviewers look for into three tiers: critical, strong and supporting. Most chapters name one critical signal. Two chapters, Taking Initiative and Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict, name two.

The tiers show where to put weight. Build the story around the critical signal first, and let the strong and supporting signals add to it. Our reading: a story that is strong on the critical tier is better than one that touches every signal thinly. Each chapter then lists the patterns that damage or weaken the same stories.
card.example: Our illustration: for a delivery question Tomas picks a launch where a dependency broke and requirements changed. His core shows the blocker, the workaround and the on-time release, then one trade-off he made and an early warning he raised.
card.rule: Identify the competency's critical signal, build the story to show it first, and add the lower tiers as the evidence allows.
card.limits: The chapters rank signals; they do not require all of them. Our reading: the ranking does not tell you which competency a company values most.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Stories that look like a competency
concepts.question: How do you stop a story from passing as a competency it does not actually prove?

paragraphs: Competencies sit close together, so a story can look like one and prove another. The chapters separate them with a deciding question. Who chose the problem: initiative. How deep was the search for the cause: problem-solving. Did working software reach users despite obstacles: delivery. Did you invent a new method: innovation.

Several red flags are look-alikes: hard work on assigned tasks passed off as initiative (Chapter 5), optimization passed off as innovation (Chapter 11) and local optimization passed off as strategy (Chapter 13). Our reading: the three share a pattern, real effort labelled with a competency it does not show.
card.example: Our illustration: a candidate calls a 30 percent speed-up of a report innovation. It is valuable work, but it used a known technique. Told as problem-solving or delivery it fits; told as innovation it raises the red flag.
card.rule: Before naming the competency, ask the question that separates it from its neighbours, and choose the story that answers it.
card.limits: The pairs overlap in practice, so the labels guide emphasis. Our reading: one story can honestly serve two competencies if you tell the part that proves each.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: End on a concrete result
concepts.question: Why do so many chapters warn against stories that stop before a concrete result?

paragraphs: Impact is one of the four dimensions, and it asks for results with numbers and an account of how your actions created them. The competency chapters repeat the point as warnings: effort without outcome in delivery, depth without impact in problem-solving, innovation without adoption, vision without implementation, and vague relationship outcomes in trust.

Each warning says the same thing about a different competency: the interviewer needs to hear what changed, and for whom, because of you. Our reading: closing a story on the concrete result, not the idea or the effort, is one habit that answers all five warnings.
card.example: Our illustration: instead of 'we improved the relationship with the data team', Omar says 'we now hold a short sync every Monday, and late schema changes fell from about six a month to one'.
card.rule: End every story on a specific result: what shipped, who used it, what changed and how you know.
card.limits: Rough figures are fine; false precision is not. Our reading: a result may be small, or the lesson of a failed attempt, as long as it is concrete and true.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Prepared, not scripted
concepts.question: How does the structure you prepare turn into a natural conversation in the room?

paragraphs: The whole system is structure underneath and conversation on top. The pillars, the story bank, the pyramid and the signals are what you prepare. The authors say your stories should be the start of a conversation, not a memorized monologue.

The pyramid works at every scale. A story has a headline and a core. The project question has a headline and a core. A follow-up gets a one-sentence answer first, then more only if the interviewer wants it. Key points stay fixed as waypoints, while wording and order between them can change.
True stories make this possible, because deep follow-ups probe your exact role, decisions and outcomes, and a true account survives wherever the conversation goes.
card.example: Our illustration: Zoe prepares a headline, three key points and a landing. The interviewer interrupts about testing. She answers fully, checks it landed, then returns to her next key point. A later follow-up gets one sentence first, and more only when asked.
card.rule: Prepare the structure thoroughly, then deliver it as a conversation: fixed key points, flexible wording, depth on request.
card.limits: Our reading: flexibility is not improvisation, since a story with no prepared key points has no foundation. Tools such as check-ins also become a performance if applied mechanically.

questions.q: A candidate matches a job description almost perfectly yet fails the behavioral interviews. Which explanation does the book's opening favour?
options: The interviewers tested a different role than the one advertised
The skills were real, but the interviewer never got to see them
Strong technical experience counts for little in behavioral rounds
The candidate answered too quickly for the panel to follow
optionExplain: Role mismatch is a reasonable guess, but the opening blames what the interviewer saw, not the role.
Right: the author says the problem is not missing skills but that the interviewer never saw them.
Plausible, yet the book says technical competence matters; it is only part of the picture.
Pace can hurt an answer, but the opening names visibility of skills as the issue.
questions.explain: The opening claims a poorly told story hides real skills. The card next sets out the idea.
questions.rule: Hidden skills do not help you.

questions.q: A poorly delivered story can make you seem ____ even when you have the skills.
questions.explain: The author's point is that the skills may exist but were never visible to the interviewer.
questions.rule: Visibility, not just ability, shapes the verdict.

questions.q: Leo led his team's checkout redesign. Asked about it, he says it went fine and the team did great. What is the main problem?
options: He has not named the tools the team used
He sounds too confident for a behavioral round
The interviewer still has no view of what he delivered or contributed
He should have waited for the interviewer to ask a follow-up before describing the team's role
optionExplain: Tools can add detail, but the gap here is evidence of his own results, not a tool list.
Confidence is not the issue; the answer is vague, not boastful.
Right: a vague answer leaves the interviewer unable to see what he achieved, which is the failure the author describes.
Waiting for a prompt keeps the answer vague; the story must carry its own evidence.
questions.explain: Leo may have done excellent work, but his answer shows none of it. The interviewer can only assess what the story reveals.
questions.rule: Make the story show what you did and achieved.

questions.q: Which candidate's reasoning conflicts with the book's opening?
options: I have the skills, so how I tell my stories will not change what the interviewer concludes
My story has to make my results visible, since the interviewer knows only what I choose to show
Technical rounds are one part of the evaluation, and my stories have to carry the rest
A poorly told story can hide real skills from the person judging it
optionExplain: Right: this ignores the author's warning that delivery decides whether skills are seen.
This matches the book: results have to be shown in the story.
This matches the book: technical competence is only part of the evaluation.
This matches the book: poor delivery can hide skills.
questions.explain: The first claim treats skill as self-evident. The author argues the opposite: untold skill is invisible.
questions.rule: Skill that is not communicated is not assessed.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a candidate who meets a job's technical requirements will be judged on the technical rounds alone.
questions.explain: The author says technical competence is only part of what companies evaluate; behavioral interviews assess more.
questions.rule: Technical fit is necessary here, not sufficient.

questions.q: A designer has strong portfolio pieces and expects the behavioral round to be a formality. According to the author, what else will it check?
options: Whether she can recite the specifications of each portfolio piece from memory under pressure
Whether her design taste matches the interviewers' own preferences
How long she held each of her previous job titles in turn
Whether she can deliver results, work well with others and operate at the needed level
optionExplain: Recall of specifications is detail, not the qualities behavioral interviews look for.
Taste may matter elsewhere, but the book does not frame behavioral rounds this way.
Titles and tenure are facts, not the behaviors the stories must show.
Right: the author says behavioral interviews are where you show you can deliver results, work effectively with others and operate at the needed level.
questions.explain: A strong portfolio covers the craft; the behavioral round is where the rest has to be shown through stories.
questions.rule: Behavioral rounds test results, teamwork and level.
questions.teaches: Behavioral interviews are where you show you can deliver results, work effectively with others and operate at the level the company needs.

questions.q: Two weeks before a behavioral interview, which plan seems most likely to help you speak well?
options: Write one long, detailed paragraph for each project, then memorize it word for word
Wait until the final evening, then review everything at once
Turn real experiences into short stories and practise them until natural
Prepare only for the technical rounds and improvise the rest
optionExplain: Scripts feel safe, but long paragraphs are hard to memorize and tend to sound like corporate speak.
Cramming feels efficient, yet the author calls it the backwards approach.
Right: concise stories from real experience, practised, are what the author recommends.
Technical prep matters, but behavioral answers need their own preparation.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows the author's reasoning.
questions.rule: Short real stories, practised early.

questions.q: The author says to think of preparing less like training for a marathon and more like rehearsing for an important ____.
questions.explain: A presentation is rehearsed from real material until it comes out naturally; a marathon needs months of conditioning.
questions.rule: Rehearse a presentation, do not train for a marathon.

questions.q: The night before, Meera writes a dense 400-word paragraph for each project. What outcome does the author warn about?
options: Hard-to-memorize text that leads to forgotten details and meandering answers
A confident delivery, because every detail has been written down and learned in advance
A better offer, because long answers show depth
No effect, because interviewers judge only technical skill
optionExplain: Right: the author links dense, jargon-filled paragraphs and last-minute scrambling to forgotten details and meandering monologues.
Writing everything down feels thorough, but dense text is hard to deliver.
Length can look like depth, yet the author says it conceals contributions.
The book says behavioral answers matter; it does not limit judgment to technical skill.
questions.explain: Meera repeats the pattern the author calls backwards: late, dense and hard to remember.
questions.rule: Dense scripts written late fail under pressure.

questions.q: Which statement matches the author's picture of preparing for behavioral interviews?
options: A marathon: months of steady training build stamina
A cram session: concentrate the effort in the days shortly before
A recital: memorize a polished script word for word
A rehearsal: practise real stories until they feel natural
optionExplain: The author rejects the marathon image: months of work are not needed.
Cramming is the approach the author calls backwards.
A recital sounds like rehearsal, but the author wants natural delivery from real stories, not a memorized script.
Right: rehearsing for a presentation is the author's own comparison.
questions.explain: The author contrasts rehearsal with marathon training and cramming alike. The recital also fails, because natural delivery is the aim.
questions.rule: Rehearse for naturalness, not for recital.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, with an interview next week you should skip the roadmap and wait until you have months to prepare.
questions.explain: The author says that whether you have months or an interview next week, you can adapt the roadmap to your timeline.
questions.rule: The roadmap adapts to the time you have.

questions.q: Ravi built a set of prepared stories for one company. A second interview is scheduled at another firm. What does the author expect?
options: The same effort again, because every company needs entirely new stories
Much less effort, because the preparation he did carries over
No effort at all, since prepared stories fit any employer unchanged
More effort, because a second interview is harder than the first
optionExplain: It feels natural to start over, but the author says earlier work pays off.
Right: the author says that once you have prepared, future interviews take much less effort.
This overstates it; later pillars still ask you to match company values.
Nothing in the book says later interviews are harder.
questions.explain: Stories built from real experience are reusable assets, so the second round starts from a base rather than from nothing.
questions.rule: Preparation done once lowers the cost of later interviews.
questions.teaches: Once you have prepared, future interviews take much less effort.

questions.q: A book on behavioral interviews has a framework part and a competencies part. Where would you expect story structure to be taught?
options: In the framework part, before specific competencies are covered
In the competencies part, introduced one competency at a time with examples
In the closing section on delivery techniques
In the afterword about careers beyond interviews
optionExplain: Right: structure is a general method, so it comes first, in Part I.
Competency chapters give examples, but they assume you already know how to structure a story.
Delivery comes later and builds on a finished story.
The afterword looks past the interview itself.
questions.explain: A general method usually comes before its applications. The card next gives the book's layout.
questions.rule: Method first, applications after.

questions.q: Match each part of the book to what it covers.
pairs: How to identify, structure and deliver behavioral stories
The specific behaviors companies typically assess
Delivery techniques and handling the unexpected
questions.explain: Part I is the method, Part II the competencies, and the closing section delivery and surprises.
questions.rule: Framework, then competencies, then delivery.

questions.q: Ines has an interview in two days and fears being interrupted mid-story. Which part of the book addresses delivery and the unexpected?
options: Part I, in the essential questions
Part II, in the competency chapters
The closing section, Nailing the Interview
The afterword on applying skills across a career
optionExplain: Part I ends with essential questions, which concern what to prepare, not delivery under pressure.
Part II concerns the behaviors companies assess, not handling interruptions.
Right: the closing section covers delivery techniques and how to handle the unexpected.
The afterword looks at using these skills across a career, not at a live interview.
questions.explain: Delivery techniques and the unexpected belong to the closing section.
questions.rule: Delivery help lives in the closing section.

questions.q: Sort each need by where the book answers it.

items.t: Learning how to give a story an effective structure
Finding out what companies evaluate
Preparing for Tell me about yourself
Studying what strong problem-solving behavior looks like
Checking what leadership behavior companies typically assess
Reading about innovation as a competency

questions.explain: Part I covers the method and the essential questions every company asks. Part II covers each competency, such as problem-solving, leadership and innovation.
questions.rule: Part I is how; Part II is which behaviors.

questions.q: Which statement about the book's structure is wrong?
options: Part I teaches how to identify, structure and deliver behavioral stories, and what companies evaluate
Part II covers the specific behaviors that companies typically assess
Part I opens with the competencies, and the essential questions come last in Part II
The closing section covers delivery techniques and handling the unexpected
optionExplain: This is accurate for Part I.
This is accurate for Part II.
Right: this is wrong. Part I ends with the essential questions, and Part II holds the competencies.
This is accurate for the closing section.
questions.explain: The essential questions close Part I; the competencies are Part II's subject.
questions.rule: Part I ends with the essential questions.

questions.q: Dee wants to see how a startup and an enterprise judge learning stories differently. Where does the book place that kind of guidance?
options: In the Part I chapter on essential questions
In the matching Part II chapter, through its cultural variations
In the afterword on applying these skills over a career
In the closing section, which covers only delivery techniques and the unexpected
optionExplain: Essential questions are the ones every company asks, so they are not company-specific.
Right: each Part II chapter includes level-appropriate examples and cultural variations.
The afterword looks at later career use, not at company differences in judging stories.
The closing section concerns delivery, not how companies weigh competencies.
questions.explain: Learning is one of the competencies, so its chapter in Part II is where level and company-culture differences are shown.
questions.rule: Competency chapters hold the level and culture detail.
questions.teaches: Each Part II chapter includes level-appropriate examples and cultural variations.

questions.q: You have excellent experiences and tell them well. Which gap could still cost you the offer you want?
options: Having so many experiences that choosing among them becomes difficult
Telling your stories in a conversational tone rather than a formal register
Practising your stories ahead of time instead of improvising them on the day
Stories pitched below the role's level, or ignoring what the company values
optionExplain: A large pool is an advantage; the real risk lies in how the stories fit the target.
Tone is a matter of style; the author worries about level and values, not formality.
Practice is what the author recommends, so it cannot be the gap.
Right: a level mismatch or ignoring the employer's values can sink well-told stories.
questions.explain: Experience and delivery are two pillars of three. The card next names all three.
questions.rule: Experience and delivery are not the whole plan.

questions.q: Match each pillar of preparation to what it asks of you.
pairs: Turn raw experiences into clear, effective stories
Show the right competencies at your target level
Make stories speak to what the company cares about
questions.explain: Building is about the stories themselves, Strength about their level, Matching about the employer.
questions.rule: Build, strengthen, match.

questions.q: Sort each action by the pillar it mainly serves.

items.t: Swapping a story about fixing one bug for one about owning a whole feature, for a senior role
Reading a company's engineering blog to see how it talks about customers
Checking that your stories show scope and impact that fit a mid-level role
Retelling a project to stress the priorities a company says it rewards
Dropping a junior-level story from your set for a senior role
Noticing that a company's interview guide praises speed and autonomy

questions.explain: Strength is about fit to the level of the role; Matching is about fit to the employer's stated and observed priorities.
questions.rule: Strength fits the level; Matching fits the employer.

questions.q: Fatima tells her stories brilliantly and decides the other two pillars matter less. What does the author's roadmap say?
options: She is right: delivery skill makes up for a weak fit to the level
All three pillars must be strong; brilliant delivery cannot fix a level or values mismatch
She is partly right, because company values matter only at startups and small, fast companies
She should drop the first pillar and put her effort into the other two
optionExplain: It is tempting to think skill in telling compensates, but the author says no amount of good telling fixes the wrong level.
Right: the author says to get an offer all three pillars need to be strong.
The book gives startups as one example of company differences; it does not limit values to them.
Building stories is the base of the plan, so dropping it undermines the other two.
questions.explain: Fatima has one pillar. The plan treats the three as working together, so a weakness in any one can cost the offer.
questions.rule: All three pillars have to hold.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, excellent delivery can turn junior-level stories into a senior-level offer.
questions.explain: The author says junior-level stories do not get you senior-level offers, no matter how well you tell them.
questions.rule: Delivery cannot raise the level of a story.

questions.q: Tomas's stories celebrate moving fast without sign-off. He applies to a large, process-driven firm. Which pillar is most at risk?
options: Building Your Stories: the stories lack clear structure
Ensuring Story Strength: moving fast signals a junior level
Matching Company Values: the stories were shaped for a different kind of employer
None of them: strong stories that are well told fit every employer in the same way
optionExplain: Speed says nothing about structure; the stories could be perfectly clear.
Moving quickly is not a sign of low level; scope and impact decide that.
Right: the fit to the employer's priorities is what is at risk here.
This ignores the third pillar, which exists because employers differ.
questions.explain: The stories may be well built and at the right level yet still miss the priorities of a company that prizes process.
questions.rule: Check each story against the employer, not just the level.
questions.teaches: A story that impresses a startup might fall flat at an enterprise company.

questions.q: Roughly how many stories does the book say you need for the general questions every company asks?
options: One or two stories
Three or four stories
Six to eight stories
Ten to twelve stories in total
optionExplain: One or two would leave you without a story for some of the standard questions.
Right: the book gives 3-4 stories for the essential questions.
This is closer to what the company-specific stories need, not the general ones.
Ten to twelve is more than the book asks for the general questions.
questions.explain: The essential questions repeat across companies, so a small set covers them. The card next adds the other two factors.
questions.rule: Three or four stories cover the essential questions.

questions.q: Match each factor to what it does to your story count.
pairs: Changes which competencies are essential and how many to cover
questions.explain: The first two factors have ranges; the level adjusts which competencies count and how many.
questions.rule: Essential, company, level.

questions.q: Sort each interview question by the group of stories it belongs to.

items.t: Tell me about yourself
Why do you want this role?
Describe a project you are proud of
Tell me about a time you mentored a junior colleague
Tell me about a time you put a customer first
Tell me about a time you invented a new approach

questions.explain: The three under 'Essential questions' are general questions that nearly every company asks. The three under 'Company-specific competencies' target particular competencies that a given company may or may not weigh.
questions.rule: General questions are essential; competency questions depend on the company.

questions.q: Mia's research shows her target company values different competencies than she assumed. What happens to her stories?
options: Her essential-question stories stay; her company-specific stories change
All her stories must be rewritten, because values change every answer
She needs fewer essential stories, because the company asks fewer general questions
Nothing changes, because competencies do not depend on the company
optionExplain: Right: every company asks similar general questions, while the company decides which competencies matter.
The general questions are the same everywhere, so those stories do not need a rewrite.
The company does not change which general questions get asked.
The book says the target company determines which competencies matter most.
questions.explain: The essential stories are company-independent. The company-specific group is where new research makes a difference.
questions.rule: Changing the company changes only the company-specific group.

questions.q: Which claim contradicts the book's guidance on story count?
options: The general questions every company asks need 3-4 stories
Your target company's values affect how many extra stories you need
The same number of stories suits every candidate at every company
Your level changes how many competencies you should cover
optionExplain: This matches the book's range for the essential questions.
This matches the book: the company determines which competencies matter.
Right: the book makes the count depend on three factors, so no single number fits everyone.
This matches the book: the level shapes how many competencies you need.
questions.explain: Three factors set the count, so it differs from person to person.
questions.rule: The count depends on the interview, not a fixed number.

questions.q: Dani is a senior engineer at a strong-culture company; Lee is entry level at a 30-person firm. Which pairing fits the book?
options: Both need the same number, because the essential questions dominate the whole bank
Dani needs only a few, because seniority replaces breadth
Lee needs every competency, because small firms ask about everything
Dani may need stories for all the competencies; Lee may focus on only a few
optionExplain: The essential questions are shared, but the company-specific and level factors still differ.
Seniority adds expectations rather than removing breadth, according to the author.
Smaller companies are the case where an entry-level candidate may only need a few.
Right: the author says senior candidates at companies with strong cultures may need all the competencies, entry-level candidates at smaller companies a few.
questions.explain: Level and company culture together stretch or shrink the company-specific group.
questions.rule: Strong cultures and senior roles widen the bank.
questions.teaches: Senior candidates interviewing at companies with strong cultures may need stories for all nine competencies, whereas entry-level candidates at smaller companies might only have to focus on a few.

questions.q: Which pair of themes would you expect a fast-growing startup to prize most?
options: Stability and process
Scale and collaboration
Speed and autonomy
Hierarchy and approvals
optionExplain: Stability and process describe a settled organization, not a fast-growing one.
Scale and collaboration fit larger companies better.
Right: the author says startups emphasize speed and autonomy.
Approval chains slow a startup, so they are an unlikely theme.
questions.explain: Small, fast-growing firms rely on people who move quickly on their own. The card next gives the book's three company types.
questions.rule: Startups prize speed and autonomy.

questions.q: Match each company type to what it emphasizes.
questions.explain: Each type's emphasis shapes which competencies matter first.
questions.rule: Type points to values; values point to competencies.

questions.q: Aiko applies to a 15-person high-growth startup. Which competency set matches the book's minimum focus?
options: Strategic Leadership, Developing Others, Customer Focus and Trust
Initiative, Delivery, Innovation and Learning
Problem Solving, Cross-team Leadership, and Trust and Conflict
Delivery, Trust, Customer Focus and Developing Others
optionExplain: These lean toward organization-wide impact, a theme for senior roles and large companies.
Right: this is the minimum list the book gives for startups and high-growth companies.
This is the core list for large tech companies.
This is the starting list for traditional enterprises.
questions.explain: Speed and autonomy translate into initiative, delivery, innovation and learning.
questions.rule: Startups: Initiative, Delivery, Innovation, Learning.

questions.q: Sort each competency by whose starting list in the book names it.

items.t: Initiative
Innovation
Learning
Trust
Customer Focus
Developing Others

questions.explain: Startups start with initiative, innovation and learning (plus delivery). Enterprises start with trust, customer focus and developing others (plus delivery).
questions.rule: Different company types start from different lists.

questions.q: Which reading of the book's competency lists is wrong?
options: They are examples that give you a place to start researching
A startup may also value Customer Focus or specific technical knowledge, so check for them
Large tech companies may add Strategic Leadership for senior roles
A startup needs nothing beyond its four listed competencies, so more research is wasted
optionExplain: The author presents them exactly this way.
The author tells you to research whether startups also value these.
The author lists it as a common addition for senior roles at large tech companies.
Right: the lists are starting points, and the author says your target may value different or additional competencies.
questions.explain: Treating a starting list as complete is the mistake. Research adds to it.
questions.rule: Lists start the research; they do not end it.

questions.q: Marco is a senior engineer at a large tech firm. Beyond the three core competencies, what extra ones does the book suggest?
options: Strategic Leadership, Innovation and Developing Others
Initiative, Learning and Delivery
Customer Focus, Delivery and Trust
None: seniority changes the level of stories, not the competencies
optionExplain: Right: many large tech companies also emphasize these, especially for more senior roles.
These lean toward the startup list, which is a different company type.
These lean toward the enterprise list, which is a different company type.
The book says senior roles add competencies as well as raising the level.
questions.explain: Level and company type combine: a senior role at a large tech company adds to the core list.
questions.rule: Seniority adds competencies to the type's core.
questions.teaches: Many large tech companies also emphasize Strategic Leadership, Innovation and Developing Others, especially for more senior roles.

questions.q: A new graduate and a principal engineer both prepare. Whose story bank does the book expect to cover more competencies?
options: The new graduate's, because they have more to prove to the interviewers
Both the same, since the competencies are fixed
The principal engineer's, because senior roles cover more ground
Neither, since count depends only on the company
optionExplain: A graduate's bank is narrower, since fewer competencies are expected at entry level.
The book gives different ranges for different levels.
Right: the book gives 7-10 competencies for senior level against 4-6 at entry level.
Company culture matters, but the level also changes the count.
questions.explain: Seniority widens what is expected. The card next lays out the three ranges.
questions.rule: More senior means a wider set.

questions.q: Match each level to the number of competencies the book suggests.
questions.explain: The ranges overlap but rise with level.

questions.q: Noor is mid-level and has stories for Problem Solving, Delivery and Learning. What does the book say to add?
options: Strategic Leadership and Developing Others, to show organizational impact
Initiative, and Trust and Conflict, to show independence and team handling
Innovation only, since the entry-level core is already enough for a mid-level role
Nothing: a mid-level set is identical to an entry-level set
optionExplain: Those are the senior-level musts, not the mid-level additions.
Right: mid-level builds on the entry foundation with these two.
Innovation can join at mid-level by role, but the book names two other additions first.
The book sets a wider range for mid-level than for entry level.
questions.explain: Mid-level adds independence (Initiative) and team dynamics (Trust and Conflict) to the entry foundation.
questions.rule: Mid-level adds Initiative and Trust and Conflict.

questions.q: Pia is entry level and applying to a startup. Beyond the entry core, what does the book suggest adding?
options: One or two that match the culture, such as Initiative
Strategic Leadership, to show organizational impact
Developing Others, because every level needs it
Nothing, because the core three are all an entry-level set holds
optionExplain: Right: the book says to add one or two others matching the culture, such as Initiative for startups.
Strategic Leadership is a senior-level requirement.
Developing Others is listed for senior level, not as an entry-level addition.
The book explicitly adds one or two for culture.
questions.explain: Level sets the core, and company culture adds to it, even at entry level.
questions.rule: Culture can add to the level's core.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, senior candidates should prepare fewer competencies than entry-level candidates.
questions.explain: The book gives senior level and beyond the largest range, 7-10, against 4-6 at entry level.
questions.rule: Senior sets are wider, not narrower.

questions.q: Raj has 12 planned stories and little time. His list spans essential questions, company competencies and level. What does the book suggest?
options: Cut the essential questions, since the company's values matter more
Memorize all twelve word for word instead of building more
Build stories that serve all three factors at once, then fill gaps for the company
Prepare only the stories that match the level and leave the other two factors aside
optionExplain: The essential questions are asked everywhere, so dropping them is risky.
Memorizing adds no coverage, and the book prefers natural delivery.
Right: the factors overlap, so one strong story can serve several, and gaps are filled afterwards.
Level is one factor of three; ignoring the others leaves gaps.
questions.explain: Overlap lets a small set of well-chosen stories cover the three factors together.
questions.rule: Choose stories that do triple duty.
questions.teaches: The factors overlap: a single strong story can answer an essential question, cover several competencies the target company values and show the scope expected at your level.

questions.q: A candidate has done three large projects. How many distinct stories could they have?
options: Three, one for each project they completed
As many as the moments in which they made a real difference
One, since interviews ask only for the best project
Ten, which is the standard size that every story bank should reach
optionExplain: One per project feels tidy, but it leaves moments unused.
Right: the count follows the moments, not the projects.
Interviews ask many different questions, so one story would be stretched thin.
The book gives no fixed number like this; the count depends on factors and moments.
questions.explain: Large projects hold several moments. The card next shows the author's view.
questions.rule: Count moments, not projects.

questions.q: Each ____ within a project where you made a real difference is its own story.
questions.explain: The author's unit of a story is the moment, not the project.
questions.rule: One moment, one story.

questions.q: Sort each approach by whether it mines moments or force-fits a project.

items.t: Listing a story for each decision point in a six-month app redesign
Preparing one redesign story to answer every question
Treating a rescued launch and a mentoring episode in one project as two stories
Writing the full project history, then fitting it to whatever is asked
Presenting five moments of a project as five versions of one story
Naming the competency that each separate moment shows

questions.explain: The author wants separate stories for separate moments. Fitting one whole project to every question is the approach the author says leaves value on the table.
questions.rule: Split the project; do not stretch it.

questions.q: A support lead's three-month rollout held three moments: a data gap caught, a squad clash settled, a new hire trained. How many stories?
options: One rollout story, because it was a single project from start to finish
Two, because only the clash and the training involved other people
Three, one for each separate moment where she made a difference
None, until the rollout has been judged a success or failure
optionExplain: One project does not mean one story; the author splits a project into its moments.
Involving others is not the test; each moment of real difference counts.
Right: each moment is a complete, standalone story.
The author does not make stories wait for a verdict on the whole project.
questions.explain: Each moment is a different challenge or decision, so each can answer different questions.
questions.rule: Each separate moment is a story.

questions.q: Dev says his one big project can only ever give one story. What is wrong with that view?
options: A project can hold several moments where he made a difference, each its own story
Nothing, because the stories drawn from one project would end up repeating each other
He should split it by calendar month instead of by moments
He should add a second project and tell both as a single story
optionExplain: Right: the author says one project contains several stories.
Repeating is a worry, but the decisions highlighted make each story different.
Calendar slices are not the test; the moments are what matter.
Merging projects makes the story longer, not stronger.
questions.explain: Dev is treating the project as the unit. The unit is the moment, and a big project holds several.
questions.rule: Split by moments, not by projects or months.

questions.q: Ana tells two stories from one product launch and repeats the team size in both. Is that a problem?
options: Yes: the two are really one story and should be merged
Yes: any detail repeated across stories should be removed
Yes: she should keep only the launch's strongest story and drop the weaker second one
No: shared context is fine because the decision each story highlights differs
optionExplain: Different moments still make different stories, even in one project.
Some context is needed in each story so the listener can follow.
Dropping a story loses coverage the second moment could provide.
Right: context such as scope or team size can repeat, while the decisions highlighted make each story feel different.
questions.explain: Background is shared; the challenge and decision are not. The latter is what the interviewer remembers.
questions.rule: Repeat context, vary the decision.
questions.teaches: Contextual details such as technical scope or team size may appear in several stories from one project, but the decisions you highlight make each story feel different.

questions.q: Starting a story bank from scratch, what should you gather first?
options: Answers to the questions interviewers might ask
A list of the competencies the company values
Significant recent experiences such as major projects and role changes
Polished opening lines for each of the stories you expect to tell in the interview
optionExplain: Drafting answers first starts from questions instead of your real material.
Competency lists help later, but stories come from your experience.
Right: the book starts with significant experiences from recent work.
Openings come after you know what stories you have.
questions.explain: Stories need raw material. The card next lists the four steps in order.
questions.rule: Start from your experiences.

questions.q: Put the book's four steps for building a story bank in order.
items: Start with significant experiences from recent work
Identify the story-worthy moments within each experience
Use Part II as a reference for what strong moments look like
Develop each moment as its own story
questions.explain: The steps move from raw experience, to moments, to reference examples, to finished stories.
questions.rule: Experiences, moments, reference, stories.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is a story-worthy moment of the kind the book lists.

items.t: Convincing a split group to back one approach
Fixing a problem several colleagues had given up on
Filing the same weekly report as usual
Taking on a duty well outside your defined role
Attending a recurring status meeting
Finishing a routine task that met no obstacles

questions.explain: The book lists decisions, hard problems, building agreement, delivering despite obstacles, lessons learned and stepping beyond your role. Our reading: routine work with no decision or obstacle is not on the list.
questions.rule: Look for decisions, obstacles and stretches.

questions.q: Compare a two-week outage response with a nine-month platform rewrite. How does the book say the number of stories is decided?
options: The rewrite gives nine times as many, since the number of stories follows the months
Each gives exactly one story, since each is one project
The outage gives none, because it was too short to hold a story
It depends on how many key moments each held, not how long it lasted
optionExplain: Duration looks like a fair measure, but the author says the count does not depend on how long the project took.
One per project is the approach the book moves away from.
A short event can hold a strong moment; the book says a two-week incident may give one story.
Right: the count follows the key moments.
questions.explain: A short incident can be a rich single story, while a long project may hold a few moments.
questions.rule: Moments, not duration, set the count.

questions.q: A candidate opens her story with three minutes of project history. What does step four of the book's process advise instead?
options: Keep the history, since background shows the whole picture
Give brief project context, then zero in on the challenge, decision or outcome
Skip context entirely, since each moment should be able to stand completely alone
Move the history to the end, after the result has been told
optionExplain: A full history buries the moment that makes the story worth telling.
Right: brief context, then a close focus on the specific moment.
Context is needed so the listener understands the stakes; the book says to give brief context.
Reordering the history does not fix its length.
questions.explain: The moment is the story. Context supports it and should stay brief.
questions.rule: Brief context, tight focus.

questions.q: Hal memorized his story word for word. The interviewer interrupts with a follow-up. What does the author's view imply?
options: Hal should finish the memorized version in full, then answer the interviewer's question
Hal should restart the story from the beginning to keep it intact
Hal should adapt, since a story is the start of a conversation and not a monologue
Hal should ask to hold follow-ups until the story is complete
optionExplain: Finishing first ignores the interviewer's interest, which the author says to follow.
Restarting wastes time and repeats what was already heard.
Right: the stories should be the start of a conversation, adapted to follow-ups and to the interviewer's interest.
Postponing follow-ups treats the interview as a recital.
questions.explain: A story is a way into discussion. Adapting to the interviewer's questions is part of the skill.
questions.rule: Treat a story as the start of a conversation.
questions.teaches: Stories should be the start of a conversation, not a memorized monologue: adapt them to follow-up questions and to the interviewer's interest.

questions.q: An interviewer hears a story about reorganizing a team's deployment process. What can they judge from it?
options: Only which tools and technologies the candidate chose during the whole reorganization effort
Only how likeable the candidate seems when speaking warmly about the team
Only whether other teams adopted the new process once it was finished
How broad the work was, what the candidate did, what resulted and how hard it was
optionExplain: Tools are one detail, but the interviewer also reads the size, role, result and difficulty.
Warmth may help, yet the stories are also read as evidence of what you did and achieved.
Adoption by others could be part of impact, but it is only one of several signals.
Right: the author says a story signals scope, contribution, impact and difficulty.
questions.explain: A single story carries several signals at once. The card next names the four.
questions.rule: One story, four signals.

questions.q: Match each dimension to what it covers.
pairs: The breadth of your work and your role in it
What you did, apart from what happened around you
The results and value, ideally with numbers
The complexity of the problems and decisions
questions.explain: Scope is about size, Contribution about you, Impact about outcomes, Difficulty about the challenge.
questions.rule: Scope, Contribution, Impact, Difficulty.

questions.q: Elif describes her whole project with 'we'. Which dimension does that blur most?
options: Scope, because the size of the launch is hidden
Impact, because no results are given
Contribution, because what she personally did is hidden
Difficulty, because the trade-offs she weighed are hidden from the listener
optionExplain: Scope is about breadth and role; 'we' can hide role, but the sharper loss is her own actions.
Impact is about results; the pronoun does not remove them.
Right: the author says to use 'I' for your own work so the line between you and the team is visible.
Difficulty concerns complexity, which wording with 'we' does not remove.
questions.explain: Contribution is the line between you and the team. Using 'we' for everything erases it.
questions.rule: Use 'I' for your own part.

questions.q: Which sentence adds Impact most directly?
options: I redesigned the search index with a team of six over three months
Search latency fell from 800 to 200 milliseconds, and I can show how my changes caused it
I worked through unclear requirements and weighed three possible index designs with the team
I owned the entire search feature rather than only one function inside it
optionExplain: This gives size and timeline, which speak to scope.
Right: it gives a measured result and links it to the candidate's own actions.
This speaks to difficulty: ambiguity and trade-offs.
This speaks to scope: owning a whole feature.
questions.explain: Impact is a result with numbers and a link back to what you did. The other sentences show scope or difficulty.
questions.rule: Impact is a result tied to your action.

questions.q: Sort each description by the dimension it mainly signals.

items.t: Owning a whole feature rather than one function
Working through significant ambiguity
Transforming systems across several teams
Weighing trade-offs between two designs and explaining the choice
Creating a new approach instead of following an established pattern
Improving a single function

questions.explain: Scope is how far the work reaches. Difficulty is how hard the problem and the decisions were.
questions.rule: Scope is reach; Difficulty is hardness.

questions.q: Sana claims she led a migration that eight engineers built together. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: using 'I' is exactly what the book asks for
She should say 'we' throughout, to stay modest
She should drop Contribution from her story altogether and talk only about the Impact it had
Contribution should show what she did, with a clear line between her work and the team's
optionExplain: The book asks for 'I' about your own work, not for a claim on the whole effort.
Saying 'we' throughout hides what she did, which the interviewer needs to see.
Dropping Contribution leaves the interviewer unable to tell who did what.
Right: the line between your part and the team's has to be clear and honest.
questions.explain: 'I' is for your own work. Claiming the team's work blurs the very line Contribution exists to draw.
questions.rule: Draw the line between you and the team.

questions.q: A hospital IT candidate says her scheduling fix improved things. Which statement would the book count as Impact?
options: The fix replaced the old scheduling module and used three different programming languages in total
Her manager praised the fix in her annual review, which she was pleased with
The fix was released on schedule, after several rounds of testing and review
Clinic booking time fell by a third, freeing hours for each team and improving patient flow
optionExplain: This describes the work and its complexity, not a result.
Praise is an opinion, not a measured effect of the work.
Timeliness is delivery, not the value created.
Right: a measured change in team productivity or business outcomes, tied to the fix, is impact.
questions.explain: Impact is the value the work created, with figures where possible, rather than a description of the work.
questions.rule: Count the change the work caused.
questions.teaches: Impact can be shown through effects on team productivity, product metrics or business outcomes, with numbers and an explanation of how your actions created them.

questions.q: You want to learn what your target company really values. Which approach would the author favour?
options: Memorize the value bullets on the company's career page
Assume the company type tells you everything you need
Read employee blogs, watch tech talks and study interview guides
Ask friends which stories worked for them at the other companies they interviewed with
optionExplain: The author tells you to go beyond the career-page bullets.
Company type is a starting point; the author says categories alone are not enough.
Right: these sources show how the company actually describes and rewards behavior.
Other companies' interviews do not show this company's values.
questions.explain: The author wants evidence of how people at the company talk and what they reward.
questions.rule: Look past the bullets.

questions.q: Which sources does the author tell you to use when researching a company's values? Select all that apply.
options: Employee blogs
Tech talks
The company's interview guides
The career page's bullet points alone
The company's share-price history
optionExplain: Right: employee writing shows how people describe their work.
Right: talks show what the company teaches and celebrates.
Right: interview guides show what the company assesses.
The author says to go beyond the career page bullets.
Share price says nothing about the behaviors the company values.
questions.explain: The recommended sources reveal behavior and language; the bare career page does not.
questions.rule: Blogs, talks and interview guides.

questions.q: A company prizes ownership at every level. All of Mina's stories show her carrying out her manager's plans. What does the method call this?
options: A strength, because following plans shows reliability
A gap between her stories and the company's values
A level problem, because her stories are junior
A delivery problem, because she tells them poorly
optionExplain: Reliability is useful, but it does not answer the value the company stresses.
Right: mapping her stories against the stated value reveals a gap.
Level is a separate pillar; the mismatch here is with the company's stated value.
Nothing suggests poor telling; the content is what misses.
questions.explain: Comparing stories with the value shows what is missing: examples of taking ownership.
questions.rule: Map stories against values to see gaps.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it is a gap in the book's sense.

items.t: The company values learning from failure; the candidate has only success stories
The company values thinking big; every story shows small incremental fixes
The company values speed; the candidate's stories show quick delivery
The company values collaboration; the candidate has three team stories
The company values customer focus; the candidate has stories on user feedback
The company values ownership; every story shows only following instructions

questions.explain: A gap exists when a known value has no matching story. Where a story already shows the value, there is nothing to fill.
questions.rule: A gap is a known value with no story.

questions.q: Jun reads only the career-page bullets and decides he knows what customer obsession means. What does the author say?
options: Go beyond the bullets and ask what the phrase means in practice
Nothing: official bullets are the most reliable source of values
Ask the recruiter to define the phrase before writing any story
Drop the phrase and use generic stories that suit every employer
optionExplain: Right: the author says to go beyond bullets and find out what such phrases mean in practice.
The author warns against stopping at the career page.
Recruiters may help, but the author points to blogs, talks and interview guides.
Generic stories ignore the company's own language, which the pillar asks you to speak.
questions.explain: A slogan is not a behavior. Jun needs to see what the company rewards.
questions.rule: Ask what the phrase means in practice.

questions.q: Lena hears a firm praise polite relentlessness. What should she do with the phrase?
options: Repeat it in her answers to show that she has studied the firm and its language closely
Treat it as marketing language and ignore it
Find a story about being polite, since the phrase names a trait
Work out what it means in practice from the behaviors the firm rewards
optionExplain: Echoing the words without the behavior behind them shows little.
The author tells you to take such phrases seriously and ask what they mean in practice.
Politeness is only half of the phrase, and a trait is not yet a behavior.
Right: understand the phrase through examples of rewarded behavior, then find stories that match.
questions.explain: Value phrases are shorthand. Their meaning shows up in what people are praised and promoted for.
questions.rule: Translate the slogan into behavior.
questions.teaches: Value phrases such as polite relentlessness or customer obsession matter only once you know what they mean in practice.

questions.q: A company prizes learning from failure, and your stories are all successes. What is the best first move?
options: Look back through past work, such as incidents, for a real lesson from failure
Invent a failure that sounds instructive and rehearse it until it feels like a real memory
Tell the interviewer that you have not failed at anything in your work
Take a success story and describe it as a failure to match the value
optionExplain: Right: the author suggests looking at overlooked experiences, such as a production incident.
Inventing a story is what the author warns against.
That answer leaves the gap open and sounds evasive.
Relabeling a success misstates what happened.
questions.explain: A real overlooked experience closes the gap honestly. The card next shows two ways of doing it.
questions.rule: Look for real material first.

questions.q: The author says to check that side project, because there might be an ____ story in it.
questions.explain: Side projects are an example of overlooked experience that can fill a gap.
questions.rule: Overlooked work can hold the missing story.

questions.q: Jo's database speed-up story stresses technical depth. The firm is product-led and prizes customer impact. What does the book suggest?
options: Replace it with a new story from a different project
Add invented customer quotes to make it sound relevant
Cut the technical detail entirely, whatever the interviewer asks
Reframe it to highlight the customer impact it had
optionExplain: A new story may help, but the same work can already carry the right emphasis.
Invented quotes are fabrication, which the book rules out.
Dropping detail removes evidence, and the interviewer may still ask for it.
Right: the same project can stress customer impact when that is what the company values.
questions.explain: Reframing shifts the emphasis to the part of the true story the company cares about.
questions.rule: Same facts, different emphasis.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it digs deeper or reframes.

items.t: Re-examining a side project for an innovation example
Retelling a launch story to stress customer impact instead of technical depth
Reviewing a past outage for a lesson you learned
Telling the same migration story with technical depth in front
Scanning old projects for forgotten but relevant experience
Foregrounding the customer outcome of a performance fix

questions.explain: Digging finds experience you had overlooked. Reframing changes the emphasis of an experience you already have.
questions.rule: Dig for new material; reframe the old.

questions.q: Mika reframes her project by changing what happened to fit the company's values. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: reframing means adjusting details to suit the audience
She should reframe by deleting the real challenge from the story
Reframing changes the emphasis, not what actually happened
She should dig for a new story and never reframe at all
optionExplain: Adjusting details turns a reframe into a fabrication.
Deleting the challenge removes the part that shows the skill.
Right: reframing highlights a different aspect of a true story.
The book offers reframing as a legitimate option next to digging.
questions.explain: The facts stay fixed; only the aspect you highlight moves.
questions.rule: Reframe the emphasis, never the facts.

questions.q: An agency designer has one brand-refresh project. One employer prizes craft depth; another prizes community impact. What should she do?
options: Invent a second project so that each employer hears a story built specially for them
Tell the same true project with a different emphasis for each employer
Use one fixed version everywhere to stay consistent
Skip the project and talk only about her skills in general terms
optionExplain: Inventing a project breaks the book's rule of true stories.
Right: the same project can emphasize different aspects depending on how you tell it.
A fixed version cannot adjust to what each employer cares about.
Skills in general terms leave out evidence, which is what interviewers need.
questions.explain: One real project can serve two audiences when the emphasis shifts to what each values.
questions.rule: One true project, several emphases.
questions.teaches: The same project can emphasize technical depth or customer impact depending on how you tell it.

questions.q: Your real stories feel unimpressive next to what others might claim. Which approach would the book endorse?
options: Embellish them slightly, since interviewers expect a certain polish
Invent a larger story that fits the role you are applying for
Present your real accomplishments well, using the book's techniques
Avoid stories altogether and answer every question in general terms instead
optionExplain: Small embellishments feel harmless, yet the author asks you to resist them.
Invention is the step the author warns can end careers.
Right: the techniques exist to present genuine accomplishments clearly.
General answers leave the interviewer without evidence.
questions.explain: The book assumes every story is true and asks you to present it well. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Present the real thing well.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, fabrications get exposed, and the consequences range from immediate rejection to career-ending termination.
questions.explain: The author warns that invented stories do not last and can cost a candidate dearly.
questions.rule: Fabrication carries severe risk.

questions.q: Kim finds that her values genuinely clash with a firm's. What does the author advise?
options: Fake the fit, since skills matter more than values
Keep looking, since both she and the firm would be better off
Take the offer and hope that the culture changes over time to suit her
Reframe her stories until the clash seems to disappear
optionExplain: Faking fit is what the author says not to do.
Right: the author says that if the values genuinely clash, you would both be better off if you kept looking.
Hoping for change leaves her in a role she may not enjoy.
Reframing adjusts emphasis; it cannot remove a genuine clash.
questions.explain: The aim of matching values is a real fit. A genuine clash means this is not the right role.
questions.rule: A real clash means look elsewhere.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it reframes a true story or fabricates.

items.t: Stressing the customer side of a true project for a customer-focused firm
Adding a metric you did not reach, to match a numbers-driven culture
Putting the technical depth of a real project in front for an engineering-led firm
Claiming a teammate's work as your own to fill a gap
Implying a job title you did not hold
Choosing the real incident that best shows learning from failure

questions.explain: Reframing chooses and emphasizes among true facts. Fabricating adds or borrows facts that are not yours.
questions.rule: Choose among true facts; do not add false ones.

questions.q: A candidate fakes alignment with a company's values and gets the offer. What does the author's reasoning predict?
options: Greater enjoyment, because the company's culture will soon come to suit them well
No downside, since an accepted offer settles the matter for good
A fair test of the company's culture and of their own fit
A role they are less likely to enjoy, at an employer where they do not fit
optionExplain: Cultures rarely adapt to one new hire, and the author does not suggest it will.
The author links fit to enjoyment of the role, so there is a cost.
A pretended fit tests nothing, because the company never sees the real candidate.
Right: the author says values that genuinely clash leave both sides better off apart.
questions.explain: Matching values is supposed to reveal a real fit. Faking it hides the information both sides need.
questions.rule: Faked fit produces a bad match.

questions.q: Ola feels her stories are modest next to her peers' and is tempted to inflate one. What does the book say?
options: Inflate a small detail; the risk is low if it is minor
Replace the modest story with an invented dramatic one
Resist the urge and present her genuine accomplishment well
Withdraw from interviewing until her record is more impressive
optionExplain: Even small inflation breaks the rule of true stories.
Invention carries the severe risks the author lists.
Right: the author says to resist the urge and use the techniques to present real accomplishments.
The book does not tell candidates to wait; it tells them to present what they have.
questions.explain: The temptation to embellish is real, and the author's answer is to resist it and work on presenting the true story.
questions.rule: When tempted to embellish, present the real story better.
questions.teaches: The urge to embellish or invent is strongest when you feel your real stories are not impressive enough, and the author's advice is to resist it.

questions.q: You have an interview in a week. Where would you expect the book to send you first?
options: Straight through from Chapter 1 to the end, without skipping anything
The chapters on story structure and the essential questions
The afterword about applying these skills across a career
Every competency chapter in order, one after another
optionExplain: Reading everything takes time you do not have in a week.
Right: the book sends you first to Chapter 3 on storytelling and Chapter 4 on the essential questions.
The afterword looks past the interview itself.
Reading every competency chapter is too much for one week.
questions.explain: With little time, the highest-value chapters come first. The card next sets out each route.
questions.rule: Short time means a short route.

questions.q: Match each situation to the route the book suggests.
pairs: Chapters 3 and 4 first, then skim relevant competency chapters
Part I in order, then Part II as a reference by company
Read straight through and complete all three pillars
Start with Chapter 2, then sample Part II stories at your level
questions.explain: Each route trades time for depth in a different way.
questions.rule: Time decides the route.

questions.q: Omar interviews at three companies with different cultures this month. Which route fits?
options: Work through Part I in order, then use Part II as a reference for each company
Read only Chapters 3 and 4, then stop, since they hold everything that is needed
Skip Part I and read all of Part II once, treating every company alike
Pick a single company, prepare for it fully and ignore the other two
optionExplain: Right: this is the book's route for actively interviewing with several companies.
Chapters 3 and 4 are the next-week route, which gives up depth Omar can afford.
Skipping Part I removes the framework, and companies are not alike.
The book gives a way to cover several companies, so dropping two is unnecessary.
questions.explain: Several companies call for the full framework plus company-specific use of the competencies.
questions.rule: Several companies: Part I, then Part II by company.

questions.q: Dana has an interview next week and plans to read every chapter in order. What does the book suggest instead?
options: Nothing: thoroughness beats focus when time is short, so read everything in order
Read only Part II, since the competencies are what matter
Postpone the interview until she can finish the book
Focus on Chapters 3 and 4 first, then skim the most relevant competency chapters
optionExplain: The author acknowledges you will not have time for everything.
Part II alone leaves out the story framework and essential questions.
The book offers a route for short timelines, so postponing is unnecessary.
Right: this is the book's route for an interview next week.
questions.explain: A short timeline calls for a short route. Reading everything in order is the route for planning ahead.
questions.rule: Short timeline, short route.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, if you cannot tell similar stories at your target level, you will know where to focus your preparation.
questions.explain: Sampling Part II stories and comparing them with your own is a readiness check. A shortfall points to the area to work on.
questions.rule: Use sampling to find your gaps.

questions.q: Tam is junior with a final-round interview in three days at a bank. Which part of Part II should she read?
options: Every section of every competency chapter, from the start
Only the sections on cultural variations, since those cover company differences
The chapters closest to her target, focusing on example stories at her level
None of it, because Part I is enough for a short timeline
optionExplain: The book says you will not have time for everything.
Cultural sections help, but the book's advice is about example stories at your level.
Right: with little time, skim the relevant chapters and focus on examples at your own level.
The next-week route still includes skimming relevant Part II chapters.
questions.explain: The short route keeps Part II selective: relevant chapters, and the stories at the reader's level.
questions.rule: Skim selectively, at your own level.
questions.teaches: On the short route, focus on the example stories at your level in the most relevant Part II chapters instead of reading every section.

questions.q: A strong coder is turned down after the behavioral rounds. Which reason is the most plausible?
options: The interviewers judged the person would not fit the role or the company
The behavioral rounds exist only to check the coding skills a second time
Strong coders are placed at the lowest level to be safe
The behavioral rounds only test whether the person is pleasant in conversation
optionExplain: Right: a poor fit can lead to rejection even when the skills are strong.
It is tempting because both rounds involve skill, but behavioral rounds look at something else.
Placing is about level, and it is not a blanket rule for strong coders.
Likability may help, but the interview is built to judge fit and level, not charm.
questions.explain: Companies use behavioral interviews to judge fit and level, so strong skills can still end in rejection. The card next sets out the two questions.
questions.rule: Prepare each story to answer both questions: does this person fit, and at what level?

questions.q: Companies use behavioral interviews to judge whether you fit and at what ____ you would work most effectively.
questions.explain: The second question is about level: where you would be most effective once you fit.
questions.rule: Fit first, then level.

questions.q: Priya is offered a post one level below the one she applied for. Which question did the company answer differently from her?
options: Whether she can write working code at all
Whether she is willing to relocate for the role
At what level she would be most effective
Whether she fits the role in principle
optionExplain: Coding ability is judged mostly in technical rounds and was presumably not the issue here.
Relocation is a practical matter, not one of the two questions the chapter names.
Right: down-leveling is what happens when the company reads your level differently.
A fit problem would more likely lead to rejection than to a lower offer.
questions.explain: Getting the level wrong leads to down-leveling or, when the gap is larger, rejection for being underqualified.
questions.rule: A lower offer points to the level question.

questions.q: True or false: according to the book, a candidate who fits the role well can still be down-leveled if the stories signal the wrong level.
questions.explain: Fit and level are separate questions. Good fit does not protect you from a mismatched level.
questions.rule: Fit and level are judged separately.

questions.q: A candidate says: my coding and design rounds were excellent, so the behavioral round cannot change the result. What is wrong with this?
options: The behavioral round matters only if the technical scores happen to be tied
Fit is judged separately, so a poor fit can mean rejection despite skill
Behavioral rounds replace the technical ones whenever those go badly
Technical results count toward the level but never toward whether she fits
optionExplain: Tie-breaking sounds like a sensible job for it, but the chapter says a poor fit can mean rejection whatever your skills.
Right: the chapter says that if you get the fit wrong you are rejected regardless of your skills.
It is tempting to think a bad technical result gets rescued, but the behavioral rounds add judgments rather than replacing the technical ones.
Skill does inform level, but the chapter makes fit a separate question that can end the process on its own.
questions.explain: Fit is a separate judgment and can end the process even after excellent technical results.
questions.rule: Prepare each story to answer both questions: does this person fit, and at what level?

questions.q: A candidate for a software tester job impresses in every behavioral round but cannot show the core technical skills. What does the chapter's logic suggest?
options: Strong fit signals will outweigh the missing skills
The company will hire at a lower level to compensate
The company will treat the technical gap as a level issue
The behavioral results do not rescue the application
optionExplain: The chapter treats technical capability as the first requirement, not something fit can buy back.
Down-leveling is about misjudged level, not a missing core skill.
Level is judged from stories after the skills are shown; it is not a way to absorb a skill gap.
Right: the book says that without core technical capability nothing else matters.
questions.explain: The two questions sit on top of technical capability, which is assessed mostly in the technical parts of the interview.
questions.teaches: Technical skill is assessed mostly in the technical rounds, and without core technical capability nothing else matters.
questions.rule: Prepare each story to answer both questions: does this person fit, and at what level?

questions.q: Two applicants have identical technical skills. Which extra thing would a company most want to know before hiring one?
options: Whether either applicant has already used the company's own product at home
Whether the position and the company's ways would suit each of them
Whether either applicant has spent more years working in the industry overall
Whether either applicant gives more confident answers across the interviews
optionExplain: Familiarity with the product may help a little, but it says nothing about working conditions or style.
Right: companies look at how the person would handle this position and how they work in this environment.
Years can matter for level, but they say nothing about whether the person fits this setting.
Confidence is not what fit is about; fit is about how you work and decide.
questions.explain: Skills alone do not predict success, so companies look at fit with the position and with the organization. The card names both.
questions.rule: Ask two things of any target job: what does this position demand, and how does this company work?

questions.q: Match each kind of fit with the question it asks.
pairs: Can you handle the specific challenges and conditions of this position?
Do your style, decisions and values match how the company gets things done?
Can you do the core technical work, judged in coding or design rounds?
questions.explain: Technical skill is judged mostly in the technical rounds. Role fit and company fit are the two extra kinds of fit the behavioral rounds look at.
questions.rule: Role fit is the job; company fit is the environment.
