questions.q: Sort each question an interviewer might be asking into role fit or company fit.

items.t: Can she cope with the constant ambiguity of this platform position?
Will he handle the daily cross-team coordination this job involves?
Can she manage the on-call conditions that come with this position?
Does his habit of deciding alone match how this firm reaches decisions?
Do her values line up with how this organization gets things done?
Does his working style suit the setting the whole company operates in?

questions.explain: Role fit concerns the demands and conditions of the position. Company fit concerns the organization's way of working and values.
questions.rule: Ask two things of any target job: what does this position demand, and how does this company work?

questions.q: A manager worries that an applicant who codes well may struggle with the conditions of this particular position. Which concern is that?
options: A technical skills gap
A company fit concern
A level concern
A role fit concern
optionExplain: The worry is explicitly that the coding is fine, so it is not a skills gap.
Company fit would be about style and values matching the organization overall.
Level concerns scope, contribution, impact and difficulty, not working conditions.
Right: working conditions and challenges of the specific position are role fit.
questions.explain: Role fit is about the position's challenges and conditions, separate from skill and from the company's wider way of working.
questions.rule: Ask two things of any target job: what does this position demand, and how does this company work?

questions.q: A candidate says company fit means only liking the office perks and the slogans. What does the book say that contradicts this?
options: Company fit goes beyond surface culture to working style, decisions and values
Company fit is judged only through the coding rounds, so culture does not matter
Company fit is the same thing as role fit, so the two need no separate checks
Company fit cannot be known before you are hired, so interviews cannot test it
optionExplain: Right: it is about how you work, decide and what you value in relation to how the company operates.
The book assigns fit to the behavioral side of the interview, not the coding rounds.
The book treats role fit and company fit as two different questions.
Fit is assessed during the interview through signals in your stories, so it can be judged in advance.
questions.explain: Company fit is about working style, decision-making and values matching how the company gets things done.
questions.rule: Ask two things of any target job: what does this position demand, and how does this company work?

questions.q: A design studio found that applicants with top portfolios often struggled after joining. Which lesson matches why tech companies added fit questions?
options: Great portfolios are unreliable evidence of skill, so studios should stop reading them
Studios should hire only people who already know someone on the staff
Talent alone does not guarantee that people work well in the environment
Fit questions replace skill checks once a studio has been caught out
optionExplain: The issue was not that the skill was fake; it was what happened after the hire.
Hiring only through connections is not what the book describes.
Right: the book says companies hired smart people who could not work effectively in their environment.
Fit adds to skill checks; it does not replace them.
questions.explain: Fit assessment grew out of hiring mistakes made on skill alone.
questions.teaches: Companies added fit questions after learning the hard way that smart hires sometimes could not work effectively in their environment.
questions.rule: Ask two things of any target job: what does this position demand, and how does this company work?

questions.q: Interviewers cannot ask you whether you would fit the company. How do they most likely find out?
options: From how you describe your past work and the choices you made
From the salary you ask for when the offer stage begins
From how quickly you answer each question that you are asked
From the names of the companies you listed on your resume
optionExplain: Right: the way you tell your stories gives clues to alignment.
Salary may matter to an offer but says little about how you work.
Speed of answering is not tied to how you work in the role.
Employer names say little about how you behaved in a particular situation.
questions.explain: Fit is judged indirectly, from signals in stories. The card next shows which signals matter.
questions.rule: Choose stories whose situations and choices match what the role and the company's values call for.

questions.q: Match each signal with where it comes from.
pairs: How you describe handling situations like the role's
The choices you made and how you describe them
Would you fit here? Nobody would answer no
questions.explain: Interviewers read stories because the direct question gives them nothing.
questions.rule: Signals come from stories, not from claims.

questions.q: A role involves coordinating across several teams. Which story detail would send the strongest role-fit signal?
options: Finishing a solo task well ahead of schedule and with very little review
Learning a new programming language over a weekend for a side project
Aligning three teams with clashing deadlines around one release plan
Receiving praise for a very polished slide deck at the quarterly review
optionExplain: It shows speed, but not the cross-team situation the role requires.
It shows learning, which is not the situation the role describes.
Right: it shows the person handling the organizational complexity the role involves.
Polish does not show coordination across teams.
questions.explain: Role-fit signals appear when the story's situation resembles the situations the role requires.
questions.rule: Choose stories whose situations and choices match what the role and the company's values call for.

questions.q: True or false: if a role needs rapid iteration, stories about one release polished for months send a weak role-fit signal.
questions.explain: The situation described does not match the shipping-and-adjusting the role requires, so the signal is weak. Role-fit signals work in both directions.
questions.rule: Mismatched situations weaken the signal.

questions.q: A candidate plans to open with: I am a great fit for this company. Why does this miss how fit is judged?
options: Interviewers prefer humble openings, so a claim of fit sounds boastful
A direct claim is not evidence; fit is read from what the stories show
Fit is decided before the interview begins, so the opening changes little
Fit can be shown only in the technical rounds, not in behavioral ones
optionExplain: Humility is not the issue; the claim cannot be checked.
Right: companies look for signals in what you did and chose, not in a statement.
The chapter says fit is assessed through signals in stories during the interview.
The chapter places fit signals in behavioral stories.
questions.explain: Companies cannot take a claim of fit as evidence, so they look for signals in what you did.
questions.rule: Choose stories whose situations and choices match what the role and the company's values call for.

questions.q: A hospital with a quality-first culture and a fast-response clinic hear the same story of a nurse manager spending weeks perfecting a protocol. What follows?
options: Both read it as the same quality signal, because the story is identical
Both read it as slowness, because three weeks is long at any company
Only the clinic treats it as a fit signal, since hospitals ignore stories
The hospital may read care for quality while the clinic reads delay
optionExplain: The book says one story can send different signals to different companies.
A quality-first culture would not read it only as slowness.
Both audiences read signals; the readings differ.
Right: this matches the book's point that the same story is read against each company's values.
questions.explain: The same story is interpreted against each company's values.
questions.teaches: The book's example: three weeks spent perfecting a solution may show attention to quality at one company and analysis paralysis at another; moving fast and fixing later shows good judgment at a growth startup but recklessness at an established healthcare company.
questions.rule: Choose stories whose situations and choices match what the role and the company's values call for.

questions.q: A candidate's every story starts with: I went off and built it by myself. Who is most likely to worry?
options: A company that prizes individual ownership
A consensus-driven company
A startup that needs quick builders
A company with no view on teamwork
optionExplain: Ownership-minded companies would welcome this pattern.
Right: it may suggest the person will steamroll others or make choices that will not stick.
Quick builders working alone may be welcome at such a place.
Most companies have a view on how decisions get made.
questions.explain: Solo stories help at some companies and hurt at others. The card names the two sides.
questions.rule: Match your stories to the company's pattern of working alone or together, and avoid a one-sided set.

questions.q: Companies that prize individual ownership may wonder whether a candidate who checks with the group first can make a decision without a ____.
questions.explain: Over-collaborative stories raise the doubt that the candidate cannot decide without a meeting.
questions.rule: A one-sided pattern raises doubt.

questions.q: Sort each story pattern by the kind of company it would most worry.

items.t: I designed and shipped the whole feature alone while the team was busy
Before any code, I got every team member to approve each step
I chose the database myself and told the team afterwards
Each time I hit a snag, I paused until the group had weighed in
Every project I describe, I worked alone from start to finish
I circulated a proposal for every decision and waited for agreement

questions.explain: Solo, decide-alone stories worry consensus-driven companies; wait-for-the-group stories worry companies that prize individual ownership.
questions.rule: Match your stories to the company's pattern of working alone or together, and avoid a one-sided set.

questions.q: True or false: according to the book, a behavior that is positive at one company can signal a poor fit at another.
questions.explain: The chapter's point about mis-fits is that the same behaviors can be positive at one company and a warning sign at another.
questions.rule: Fit depends on the company.

questions.q: A candidate reasons that group buy-in is valued everywhere, so waiting for consensus in every story is safe. What is wrong?
options: Buy-in matters only at the final stage of a project, not earlier
Consensus is valued at no company that hires engineers
Interviewers cannot tell how a person decides from stories
Companies that prize individual ownership may doubt she can decide alone
optionExplain: The chapter does not tie buy-in to a stage of the project.
Consensus-driven companies do value it, so this goes too far.
Stories show how a person decides; that is what is read.
Right: such companies may wonder whether she can decide without a meeting.
questions.explain: Waiting for the group in every story is a one-sided pattern too.
questions.rule: Match your stories to the company's pattern of working alone or together, and avoid a one-sided set.

questions.q: A research lab expects scientists to pick a problem and run with it. Which decision style does the book's pairing suggest goes with this?
options: Making calls on your own
Waiting for group approval at each step
Avoiding decisions
Letting managers decide
optionExplain: Right: companies that want solo work also tend to want individual calls.
That is the style the book pairs with collaborative work.
The book pairs work style with decision style, not with avoiding decisions.
Leaving it to managers is not the pairing the book describes.
questions.explain: Work style and decision style tend to go together.
questions.teaches: Independence versus collaboration covers both how you work and how you decide: companies that want you to work solo tend to want you to make calls alone, and collaborative ones want group buy-in on decisions.
questions.rule: Match your stories to the company's pattern of working alone or together, and avoid a one-sided set.

questions.q: Which company is most likely to value a story of shipping an early version and improving it from user feedback?
options: A bank that validates each release at length before it ships
A hospital software team that applies strict checks to every change
A fast-growing startup that runs rapid experiments on its product
A firm that maintains critical infrastructure for other businesses
optionExplain: Banks usually need careful validation before releasing.
Healthcare settings usually require careful validation.
Right: startups often need rapid experimentation and iteration.
Critical infrastructure tends to demand a high bar for quality.
questions.explain: Companies differ on how fast they want work shipped. The card shows both sides.
questions.rule: Show the pace and quality bar of the company you are interviewing with.

questions.q: Match each company type with what it tends to want.
pairs: Ship early versions and iterate on feedback
A working solution on time even if cleanup follows
questions.explain: Each type rewards a different balance of speed and thoroughness.
questions.rule: Pace and bar differ by company.

questions.q: A developer tells a team facing a release in two weeks about six weeks spent perfecting an architecture. What do interviewers likely read?
options: A fit problem for a company that works to deadlines
A strong fit with pragmatism, because the work was thorough
A strong sign of seniority at companies of every kind
Nothing about fit, since architecture is a technical matter
optionExplain: Right: focusing on perfect code fails at deadline-driven companies.
The story shows the opposite of shipping on deadline.
Seniority is not automatically shown by long perfecting; the company's bar matters.
The story says a lot about how the person trades speed against quality.
questions.explain: Perfection that ignores the deadline reads as a mis-fit where deadlines rule.
questions.rule: Show the pace and quality bar of the company you are interviewing with.

questions.q: True or false: according to the book's logic, quickly shipping an unpolished fix is a strong story for a payments company that validates every release.
questions.explain: Finance companies require careful validation before any release, so this story signals a mismatch with their pace. The same story helps at a startup.
questions.rule: The same speed story helps at a startup and hurts where validation comes first.

questions.q: A candidate decides to lead every interview with the story of her cleanest architecture. What does the book say is wrong?
options: Clean architecture is not valued by any employer in the industry
Architecture stories belong in the technical rounds and nowhere else
It is risky where deadlines rule and working solutions are wanted
Interviewers dislike detail, so any specific story will count against her
optionExplain: Some organizations happily spend weeks on it, so this goes too far.
The chapter uses such stories as behavioral evidence.
Right: perfect code fails at deadline-driven companies.
Detail is not the problem; the fit with the company's bar is.
questions.explain: Leading with the same story everywhere ignores that companies set different bars.
questions.rule: Show the pace and quality bar of the company you are interviewing with.

questions.q: A mobile game studio and a fire-safety equipment maker both hear a candidate's story of shipping quickly and fixing issues later. Which pairing matches the book's logic?
options: A worry at the studio and good judgment at the equipment maker
Good judgment at the studio and a worry at the equipment maker
A worry at both, since fixing issues later is careless anywhere
Good judgment at both, since shipping quickly is always a strength
optionExplain: This reverses the logic: safety-critical makers need careful validation.
Right: the book says ship-it-and-fix-it stories can terrify a medical device company while fitting a growth startup.
A game studio iterating fast is the kind of place that welcomes it.
A safety-critical maker needs careful validation before release.
questions.explain: The same behavior reads differently where mistakes are costly.
questions.teaches: Stories about methodical testing might bore a startup, while ship-it-and-fix-it examples could terrify a medical device company.
questions.rule: Show the pace and quality bar of the company you are interviewing with.

questions.q: A candidate says: I rewrote our release process three times last year because I kept finding a better way. Which team is most likely to be uneasy?
options: A team seeking creative problem-solving
A team that lets members choose tools
A team new to the company
A team that values stability
optionExplain: They might welcome the creativity.
Nothing in the story concerns tool choice.
A new team is not the subject of the story.
Right: constant reinvention of established processes worries teams that value stability.
questions.explain: Reinvention helps in some teams and worries others. The card shows both.
questions.rule: Show change where the team wants change and care for proven systems where it wants stability.

questions.q: Some roles require creating new solutions, while others need you to maintain and ____ proven systems.
questions.explain: Stability roles centre on maintaining and optimizing what already works.
questions.rule: Know whether the team creates or maintains.

questions.q: Sort each role description by what it needs most.

items.t: The team is asked to challenge how things have always been done
The role is to keep a proven ledger system running and tune it
The job is to create new solutions to open problems
The team wants someone to optimize established systems
The posting asks for people who question existing approaches
The group protects well-tested processes that customers rely on

questions.explain: Innovation roles centre on new solutions and challenging approaches; stability roles on maintaining and optimizing proven systems.
questions.rule: Show change where the team wants change and care for proven systems where it wants stability.

questions.q: A candidate tells only of tuning proven systems and keeping them reliable. Which team will find this most compelling?
options: A team that is seeking creative problem-solving for new products
A team that values stability and the upkeep of proven systems
A team inventing a brand-new product line from scratch
A team that has no systems of its own to maintain yet
optionExplain: That team may find the stories too safe.
Right: it matches maintaining and optimizing proven systems.
That team wants new solutions, not maintenance.
There is nothing proven to maintain in such a team.
questions.explain: Maintenance stories fit where proven systems are valued.
questions.rule: Show change where the team wants change and care for proven systems where it wants stability.

questions.q: A candidate says reinventing processes shows initiative, so it goes into every interview. What is wrong?
options: Initiative is not valued by any team, so the story adds nothing
Interviewers do not ask about processes, so it is wasted effort
Process stories suit startups only and fail at larger companies
Teams that value stability will not see a constant reinventor as a fit
optionExplain: Some teams value creating new solutions, so this overshoots.
Interviewers use stories about work, including processes.
The book does not limit these stories to startups.
Right: constant reinvention of established processes signals a poor fit for stability-minded teams.
questions.explain: A trait that is a strength in one setting is a flag in another.
questions.rule: Show change where the team wants change and care for proven systems where it wants stability.

questions.q: A product studio hiring for creative problem-solving hears only stories where the candidate followed established patterns. What does the book predict?
options: The studio will be disappointed
The studio will be impressed by reliability
The studio will ignore the stories
The studio will assume the candidate invents too much
optionExplain: Right: stories showing you only follow existing patterns disappoint teams seeking creative problem-solving.
That reliability suits stability-minded teams.
Interviewers read stories as signals, so they will not ignore them.
That is the worry for stability teams, not creative ones.
questions.explain: The mismatch runs in both directions.
questions.teaches: Stories that show you only follow existing patterns will disappoint teams that look for creative problem-solving.
questions.rule: Show change where the team wants change and care for proven systems where it wants stability.

questions.q: A candidate proudly describes telling a senior colleague, in front of the group, that the plan was wrong. Which company is most likely to be uncomfortable?
options: A company that prizes radical candor in all its meetings
A company that wants quick answers to its questions
A relationship-focused company that values harmony and tact
A company with a flat structure and few levels of management
optionExplain: That culture would welcome the directness.
Speed of answers is not what the story shows.
Right: too blunt a style does not fit well at a relationship-focused company.
Structure is not the issue; the manner is.
questions.explain: Bluntness is valued in some cultures and unwelcome in others. The card next sets out both sides.
questions.rule: Describe disagreements in a way that suits the company's direct or diplomatic culture.

questions.q: Match each culture with what it values.
pairs: A candidate who is too blunt fits poorly
questions.explain: The contrast is between frankness and harmony.
questions.rule: Frank or diplomatic: know the culture.

questions.q: At a radical-candor company, which account of handling a disagreement fits best?
options: I told her directly the design was flawed and explained why
I hinted that other options might exist and left her to find the flaw
I waited a few weeks and raised it privately
I avoided the topic to keep the mood positive
optionExplain: Right: it says exactly what you think.
That softens the message.
Delay and privacy fit a harmony culture better.
That avoids the disagreement entirely.
questions.explain: Radical candor is shown by saying exactly what you think.
questions.rule: Describe disagreements in a way that suits the company's direct or diplomatic culture.

questions.q: True or false: a very blunt candidate is expected to fit well at a relationship-focused company.
questions.explain: The book says too blunt a style will not fit well there.
questions.rule: Too blunt: poor fit at relationship-focused companies.

questions.q: A candidate reasons: directness is honesty, and honesty is welcome at every company, so I will describe my bluntest moments. What is wrong?
options: Honesty is unwelcome at relationship-focused companies in any form
Interviewers want stories without any conflict in them
Harmony-focused cultures may read bluntness as a poor fit
Directness is valued at startups only and is a risk elsewhere
optionExplain: That overstates; the issue is bluntness and face-saving, not honesty.
The chapter does not say conflict stories are unwelcome.
Right: cultures that value harmony may read too much bluntness as poor fit.
The chapter ties it to culture, not to company age.
questions.explain: Culture decides whether directness is a strength.
questions.rule: Describe disagreements in a way that suits the company's direct or diplomatic culture.

questions.q: A candidate softens feedback every time until no one loses face. According to the book, which workplace is a poor match?
options: A culture built on maintaining harmony between people
A culture that prizes saying exactly what you think
A culture with only a few meetings each week
A culture with long working hours during launches
optionExplain: That is the culture where this style fits.
Right: not being direct enough does not suit companies that value disagree and commit.
Meetings are not the contrast.
Hours are not the contrast.
questions.explain: The mismatch runs both ways.
questions.teaches: A candidate who is not direct enough will not enjoy working at a company that values disagree and commit.
questions.rule: Describe disagreements in a way that suits the company's direct or diplomatic culture.

questions.q: Which description best fits a data-driven culture?
options: Experienced judgment settles most choices
Decisions are made by seniority
Decisions are made quickly with no discussion
Data is required to justify decisions
optionExplain: That is the culture trusting experienced judgment.
Seniority is not what defines data-driven culture.
Speed is not the defining feature.
Right: data-driven cultures require data to justify every decision.
questions.explain: The two cultures differ in what counts as a good reason. The card next describes both.
questions.rule: Match how much data your decision stories show to how much evidence the company expects.

questions.q: Match each culture with how it decides.
pairs: Requires data to justify every decision
Trusts experienced judgment and moves on gut feel
Instinct story at an analytical company
questions.explain: Evidence standards differ between companies.
questions.rule: Evidence expectations differ.

questions.q: A candidate explains how she cut a feature at an analytics-minded fintech. Which version would fit best?
options: It felt unused to me, so I took it out in the next release
Three months of usage numbers showed few people used it, so I removed it
Senior colleagues told me to drop it, so I removed it
I ran a quick poll in the hallway and followed the result
optionExplain: That is a gut-feel story for a company that wants data.
Right: it shows a decision based on data.
That is deference, not evidence.
A hallway poll is weak evidence for such a company.
questions.explain: Analytical cultures want to see data behind the decision.
questions.rule: Match how much data your decision stories show to how much evidence the company expects.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate who decides mainly on instinct is expected to impress an analytical, data-driven company.
questions.explain: The book says showing instinct-based decisions does not impress analytical companies.
questions.rule: Instinct stories do not impress analytical companies.

questions.q: A candidate decides to mention a heavy testing process for every choice to look rigorous at all companies. What is the risk?
options: Rigor is not valued by any employer, so the process wastes effort
Interviewers dislike tests and see them as a sign of weak ability
Heavy testing signals low impact on the business as a whole
Companies that trust judgment may see heavy testing as a poor fit
optionExplain: Data-driven companies value it.
Interviewers care about fit, not a dislike of tests.
Impact is a different dimension.
Right: where judgment is trusted, heavy testing can read as a mismatch.
questions.explain: Rigor reads differently by culture.
questions.rule: Match how much data your decision stories show to how much evidence the company expects.

questions.q: A candidate tells a judgment-trusting studio he ran three A/B tests to choose a button color. What does the book predict?
options: It could get him struck off the list of that company
It will earn him extra credit for being so thorough
It will count as a strong impact story for the role
It will be read as a sign of openness and transparency
optionExplain: Right: the book says this can get you struck off the list of a company that values experienced judgment.
That credit fits data-driven companies.
It is a decision-style story, not an impact one.
No sharing of information is shown.
questions.explain: Measurement for a trivial choice can read as a mismatch.
questions.teaches: Telling a company that values experienced judgment that you ran three A/B tests to choose a button color can get you struck off their list.
questions.rule: Match how much data your decision stories show to how much evidence the company expects.

questions.q: A candidate has spent ten years mastering one database system. Which company is most likely to value this most?
options: A five-person company where everyone covers many tasks
A company wanting someone to cover design, support and deployment
A large company wanting deep experts in a single domain
A company that has not decided on a database yet
optionExplain: Small teams usually want breadth, so depth in one system matters less there.
That describes someone comfortable wearing multiple hats.
Right: large companies often want deep experts who master one domain.
Such a company is not the one the book links to expert depth.
questions.explain: Depth is prized at some companies and breadth at others. The card shows which.
questions.rule: Match the depth or breadth in your stories to the size and structure of the company.

questions.q: Smaller companies need people who are comfortable wearing multiple ____.
questions.explain: Wearing multiple hats means covering several kinds of work, which smaller companies need.
questions.rule: Small companies need breadth.

questions.q: A candidate interviews at a five-person startup. Which story should she lead with?
options: How she picked up design, support and deployment during a launch
Two years as the only person tuning one query planner
A long account of mastering one framework in great detail
A deep dive into one algorithm that she optimized at length
optionExplain: Right: it shows comfort with many hats, which smaller companies need.
That shows depth in one narrow area, which a tiny team may not need.
This is depth rather than breadth, so it suits large companies better.
This is also depth, not the breadth a small team needs.
questions.explain: At a small company, show breadth.
questions.rule: Match the depth or breadth in your stories to the size and structure of the company.

questions.q: True or false: stories of covering many kinds of work are expected to be the strongest evidence for a role at a large company that wants deep experts.
questions.explain: Large companies often want deep experts who master one domain, so breadth stories are not the strongest evidence there.
questions.rule: Large companies often want depth.

questions.q: A candidate thinks generalists are the safer profile and hides her deep expertise in every interview. What does the book suggest is wrong?
options: Expertise is valued at small companies only, never at large ones
Generalists are not wanted anywhere in the industry
Large companies often want deep experts, so hiding it can hurt
Interviews do not cover expertise, so there is nothing to hide
optionExplain: The book says the reverse for small companies, which need many hats.
Smaller companies need exactly that comfort with multiple hats.
Right: large companies often want deep experts who master one domain.
Interviews are where depth and breadth are shown through stories.
questions.explain: Neither profile is safe everywhere; it depends on the company.
questions.rule: Match the depth or breadth in your stories to the size and structure of the company.

questions.q: A highly talented candidate is turned down by a small agency that needs people to cover many tasks, then hired by a large firm as a deep expert. What does this illustrate?
options: The agency misjudged her skills, which were never in doubt
The same profile can fit one organization and not another
Large firms accept weaker candidates than small agencies do
Experts are rejected by every small agency that interviews them
optionExplain: Skill was not the issue; fit was.
Right: the same behaviors can be positive at one company and a poor fit at another.
Nothing in the scenario suggests a weaker bar at the large firm.
The scenario does not support a claim that broad.
questions.explain: Fit depends on the company, not only on the person.
questions.teaches: Even a talented candidate is sometimes rejected for poor fit, because the same behaviors are positive at one company and signal poor fit at another.
questions.rule: Match the depth or breadth in your stories to the size and structure of the company.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: An interviewer places the level of a story about faster deployments. Which set of things does the book say they weigh?
options: Job title, years of experience, team size and company name
Technology used, project length, language and number of commits
Confidence, brevity, humor and polish
Scope, contribution, impact and difficulty
optionExplain: Titles and tenure describe a career, not a single story.
These are details of the work, not signs of level.
Delivery matters, but these are not what level is read from.
Right: these are the four dimensions in every story.
questions.explain: Level comes from four dimensions in the story itself. The card names them.
questions.rule: Check every story against scope, contribution, impact and difficulty before using it.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Match each dimension with what it shows.
pairs: How many people your work affected
What you did, not what happened around you
What changed for the better because of your work
The complexity, constraints and trade-offs you managed
questions.explain: Each dimension shows a different aspect of capability.
questions.rule: Four dimensions, four different questions.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Match each statement from a story with the dimension it mainly speaks to.
pairs: Two neighbouring teams adopted the new process
I wrote the migration plan and ran the cutover
Support tickets about billing fell by a third
The old system had competing owners and no documentation
questions.explain: Adoption by other teams shows reach, the migration plan and cutover show your actions, fewer tickets are a result, and competing owners are a constraint.
questions.rule: Check every story against scope, contribution, impact and difficulty before using it.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A tool was used by twelve teams but changed little for any of them. Which dimension is strong and which is weak?
options: Impact is strong and scope is weak
Scope is strong and impact is weak
Contribution is strong and difficulty is weak
All four dimensions are strong
optionExplain: The reverse: reach is wide, so scope is not the weak dimension.
Right: wide use shows reach, but little changed for them.
The facts given do not say anything about what the person did or how hard it was.
Little changed for the users, so impact cannot be strong.
questions.explain: Scope counts reach; impact counts what improved.
questions.rule: Check every story against scope, contribution, impact and difficulty before using it.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: True or false: a candidate who picks stories only for their impressive numbers has read the story the way interviewers read level.
questions.explain: Level is read from scope, contribution, impact and difficulty together, so numbers alone, which speak only to impact, are not enough.
questions.rule: A story with one strong dimension does not place a level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A teacher's story: her new reading routine was used by her own class and two colleagues' classes. Which dimension says how widely it reached?
options: Contribution
Impact
Difficulty
Scope
optionExplain: Contribution is about what she did, not who was reached.
Impact is what improved for them, not how many were reached.
Difficulty is the complexity she faced.
Right: scope measures how many people your work affected.
questions.explain: The four dimensions work in any field, not only engineering.
questions.teaches: The book describes each of the four dimensions at five levels, in order: entry, mid, senior, staff and principal.
questions.rule: Check every story against scope, contribution, impact and difficulty before using it.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A developer's script saved her own time and helped three teammates. At which level does this scope usually sit?
options: Entry
Principal
Staff
Senior
optionExplain: Right: entry scope is your own productivity plus starting to help teammates.
Principal scope reaches many teams, not three teammates.
Staff scope reaches at least two teams.
Senior scope covers a whole team and reaches beyond it.
questions.explain: Scope grows with the number of people affected. The card shows the steps.
questions.rule: State how many people and teams your work actually affected, and match it to your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Put these scope descriptions in order, lowest level to highest.
items: Your own productivity and a few teammates
Aspects of your team and how it operates
Your whole team and influence reaching one other team
At least two teams directly
Many teams or large parts of the organization
questions.explain: Scope widens from yourself to a few teammates, part of the team, the whole team plus one more, two teams, and finally many teams.
questions.rule: Scope widens outward.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A candidate's runbook change is used by her whole team, and one neighbouring team adopted it. Which level of scope does this match?
options: Entry
Mid
Senior
Principal
optionExplain: Entry scope is her own work and a few teammates.
Mid scope is parts of the team, not the whole team.
Right: the whole team plus influence on one other team is senior scope.
Principal scope reaches many teams.
questions.explain: Whole team plus a neighbour is senior scope.
questions.rule: State how many people and teams your work actually affected, and match it to your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: True or false: if the runbook change directly changed how three teams work and began to influence the wider division, its scope would still be senior.
questions.explain: At least two teams directly, with wider influence beginning, is staff scope. Senior scope reaches at most one other team.
questions.rule: Reach across two or more teams is staff scope.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A candidate counts two million users of her feature as senior-level scope. What is wrong, according to the book's definition?
options: Scope counts colleagues and teams whose work changed, not users
Scope counts only users above one million, so her feature qualifies
Scope ignores teams and counts only the size of the audience
Scope is measured in lines of code that the person has written
optionExplain: Right: scope is about colleagues and teams whose work your actions affected.
No such threshold appears in the book.
Teams are the main unit of scope.
Lines of code are not part of the definition.
questions.explain: Count whose work you changed, not how many people see the product.
questions.rule: State how many people and teams your work actually affected, and match it to your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A staff engineer's technical strategy changes how her team works and now guides how product and design partners plan. What does the book say about staff-level influence?
options: It stays within engineering at every level of seniority
It is limited to her own team and its immediate partners
It extends into product, design and program management
It applies to people managers and not to individual contributors
optionExplain: The book says it reaches beyond engineering.
Staff scope is at least two teams.
Right: staff influence extends beyond engineering into product, design and program management.
The book describes engineers at these levels, not only managers.
questions.explain: Higher levels reach across functions.
questions.teaches: At staff level, influence extends beyond engineering into product, design and program management, and at principal level it reaches business strategy alongside product, design, program and business leadership.
questions.rule: State how many people and teams your work actually affected, and match it to your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A candidate says: we shipped the new search. What would an interviewer most want to learn next?
options: How the team celebrated after the launch went live
Which parts she personally did and decided
How many people worked at the company overall
Which older search tool the new one replaced
optionExplain: Celebration says nothing about her own part.
Right: contribution is about what you did, not what happened around you.
Company size does not show her part.
The earlier tool is background; it does not show what she did.
questions.explain: Level depends on your own part. The card explains the line between I and we.
questions.rule: Say what you personally decided and did, and match the amount of ownership to your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Match each level with its contribution pattern.
pairs: Executes assigned work and starts to own small pieces
Owns complete solutions from problem to implementation
Leads initiatives needing coordination, even when requirements are unclear
Leads cross-team initiatives and sets technical direction
Creates organizational capabilities and defines the problem first
questions.explain: Each step adds scope of ownership: from pieces, to whole solutions, to initiatives, to cross-team direction, to organizational capability.
questions.rule: Contribution grows from executing to creating.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Dana found why reports were slow, designed the fix, built it, checked it worked and explained her reasoning to teammates. Which level of contribution is that?
options: Entry
Senior
Staff
Mid
optionExplain: Entry is executing work assigned by others.
Senior leadership involves coordination and unclear requirements.
Staff leads across teams.
Right: owning a complete solution from problem to implementation, and helping others understand it, is mid.
questions.explain: Owning a whole solution is mid-level contribution.
questions.rule: Say what you personally decided and did, and match the amount of ownership to your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: True or false: if Dana had only implemented a fix that someone else designed, the story would show mid-level contribution.
questions.explain: Implementing solutions designed by others is entry-level contribution. Mid-level means owning the solution from problem to implementation.
questions.rule: Who designed the work changes the level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A candidate counts everything her project achieved as her own contribution. What is wrong?
options: Contribution counts the meetings that she attended during the project
Contribution is limited to what she did, not what happened around her
Contribution is the same thing as impact, so the numbers cover it
Contribution cannot be described in an interview, only inferred
optionExplain: Meetings are not the measure.
Right: contribution is what you did, not what happened around you.
Impact is a separate dimension.
Interviewers read it from what you say you did.
questions.explain: Claim your own part, no more and no less.
questions.rule: Say what you personally decided and did, and match the amount of ownership to your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A head cook designs a new prep process that others carry out, coaches junior cooks through hard dishes and answers for the quality of the kitchen's output. Which level does the pattern match?
options: Entry
Mid
Principal
Senior
optionExplain: Entry executes assigned work.
Mid owns solutions but is not described as architecting for others.
Principal creates organizational capabilities.
Right: architecting solutions implemented by others, mentoring and ensuring quality for many people is senior.
questions.explain: Senior contribution includes designing for others to build.
questions.teaches: Senior contribution includes driving technical decisions, mentoring others through complex problems, architecting solutions for others to implement, and ensuring quality outcomes for many people.
questions.rule: Say what you personally decided and did, and match the amount of ownership to your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Which description of a result is strongest?
options: Checkout errors fell from five percent to one percent, saving about three thousand orders a month
Performance improved a great deal once my work was released to every customer last spring
Everyone on the team and in the wider company was happy with the new checkout flow
The checkout flow was rebuilt from scratch using the latest tools and frameworks available
optionExplain: Right: it puts numbers on the result and ties it to an outcome.
A large claim with no figures is hard to check.
Satisfaction is not measured here.
This describes the work, not what changed.
questions.explain: Strong impact has numbers and an outcome. The card shows how this grows.
questions.rule: Put a number on the result and tie it to a business or user outcome.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Strong stories put ____ on the impact and connect technical wins to business or user outcomes.
questions.explain: Quantifying the result is the book's advice for strong stories.
questions.rule: Quantify the result.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Sort each result by the level of impact it fits best.

items.t: Cut test time for the services my team owns
Built a data platform that dozens of teams rely on
Wrote a tool that saves my team hours each sprint
Unblocked a company-wide launch no single team could solve
Removed a recurring class of bugs in my own area
Set up an approach whose benefits keep compounding across the company

questions.explain: Mid-level impact improves team effectiveness in specific areas. Principal-level impact is organizational and strategic.
questions.rule: Put a number on the result and tie it to a business or user outcome.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: What if a mid-level story gives no figures at all for its result?
options: It will be easy to place at the right level without any figures
It will automatically score higher for being short and clean
It will be harder to judge, since there is little to weigh
It will be counted as an entry-level story by default
optionExplain: Without numbers, interviewers have little to go on.
Missing figures do not raise a story.
Right: strong stories quantify impact and connect it to outcomes.
Level is not set by whether figures are missing.
questions.explain: Without numbers the result is hard to weigh.
questions.rule: Put a number on the result and tie it to a business or user outcome.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A candidate describes impact as: I built a caching layer with the newest technology. What is missing?
options: What changed for the better as a result
Nothing, since new technology is the impact
The names of the team
A longer technical description
optionExplain: Right: impact is what changed, ideally with numbers and an outcome.
Using new technology describes the work, not the result.
Names do not show the result.
More technical detail does not state what improved.
questions.explain: Impact is the result, not the method.
questions.rule: Put a number on the result and tie it to a business or user outcome.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A logistics lead's routing change cut late deliveries across four depots. Which figure would tie this multi-team work to a business outcome, according to the book?
options: Lines of code written
Number of meetings held
Customer retention
Hours the lead worked
optionExplain: That counts effort, not results.
That counts activity.
Right: staff-level impact is tied to business metrics like revenue, customer retention or time-to-market.
That counts effort, not results.
questions.explain: Higher levels connect results to the business.
questions.teaches: Staff-level impact can be tied to business metrics such as revenue, customer retention and time-to-market.
questions.rule: Put a number on the result and tie it to a business or user outcome.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Which problem shows the most difficulty?
options: Adding a field to a form by following an existing pattern
Balancing conflicting needs of several teams in one shared design
Reading unfamiliar code for a day to fix a small, clear bug
Writing a status report for the team at the end of each week
optionExplain: This follows an established pattern.
Right: competing needs and trade-offs signal greater difficulty.
This is a straightforward debugging task with clear next steps.
This is routine work.
questions.explain: Difficulty rises with complexity, constraints and trade-offs. The card next shows how it grows by level.
questions.rule: Choose stories whose obstacles, constraints and trade-offs match your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Match each level with its difficulty pattern.
pairs: More moving parts and less obvious solutions
Fundamental trade-offs and problems with no clear solution
questions.explain: Difficulty moves from clear paths to ambiguous ones without precedent.
questions.rule: Difficulty grows from clear problems to novel ones.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Which story best shows senior-level difficulty?
options: I followed our template to add one more report for the team
I mediated among three product lines whose best designs differ
I fixed a vague bug that had several moving parts behind it
I chose a messaging design for my team's services under a vendor limit
optionExplain: That is an established pattern, so it is entry-level.
Competing trade-offs across teams are staff-level.
A vague bug with several moving parts is mid-level.
Right: constraints, competing concerns and an architectural decision for the team are senior difficulty.
questions.explain: Senior difficulty is constraints and architectural decisions.
questions.rule: Choose stories whose obstacles, constraints and trade-offs match your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A story delivered a big benefit through an easy, straightforward change. Which dimension is weaker?
options: Impact
Difficulty
Scope
Contribution
optionExplain: The benefit was big, so impact is strong.
Right: a straightforward change shows low difficulty, however large the benefit.
The facts say nothing on scope.
The facts say nothing on contribution.
questions.explain: Big results do not make a problem hard.
questions.rule: Choose stories whose obstacles, constraints and trade-offs match your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: True or false: a candidate is right to argue that a big impact proves the problem she solved was hard.
questions.explain: Easy problems can have big impacts, and the book says these are less impressive than hard problems solved well. Difficulty and impact are separate dimensions.
questions.rule: Impact and difficulty are separate.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Three hospital wards each need a different discharge process, and the best design for each differs. Which description matches the book's staff-level difficulty?
options: Learning the hospital's software during the first month of work
Fixing one confusing form that staff had complained about
Writing the weekly report on admissions for the managers
Getting wards to agree when the best design differs for each
optionExplain: That is entry-level difficulty.
That is a simple fix.
That is routine work.
Right: staff difficulty includes getting teams to agree when the technically optimal solution differs for each.
questions.explain: Staff difficulty involves conflicts between teams.
questions.teaches: Staff-level difficulty includes getting teams to agree when the technically optimal solution differs for each of them, and making architectural decisions that must work across diverse contexts.
questions.rule: Choose stories whose obstacles, constraints and trade-offs match your target level.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Which order of levels is correct, lowest to highest?
options: Entry, mid, senior, staff, principal
Entry, mid, staff, senior, principal
Entry, senior, mid, staff, principal
Mid, entry, senior, staff, principal
optionExplain: Right: entry, mid, senior, staff, principal.
Staff comes after senior.
Mid comes before senior.
Entry is the lowest.
questions.explain: The ladder has five levels. The card names them in order.
questions.rule: Judge a story's level by the whole pattern across the four dimensions.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: The five levels from lowest are entry, mid, senior, staff and ____.
questions.explain: Principal is the highest of the five levels.
questions.rule: Five levels, entry to principal.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: Sort each pattern by the level it describes.

items.t: Helped a few teammates by fixing slowdowns
Established ways of working across dozens of teams
Executed assigned work and began owning small pieces
Defined the problem before solving it in an ambiguous setting
Solved straightforward problems, asking for help when needed
Handled novel problems that needed executive buy-in

questions.explain: The entry pattern is personal and straightforward. The principal pattern is organizational and ambiguous.
questions.rule: Judge a story's level by the whole pattern across the four dimensions.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: True or false: according to the book, a story's level is judged on a single dimension such as impact.
questions.explain: The book reads level through four dimensions together.
questions.rule: Read all four dimensions.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A candidate thinks moving up a level only means bigger numbers in the same kind of story. What does the pattern across dimensions show?
options: Nothing changes except the numbers, which get bigger at each level
Only the difficulty changes, while the other dimensions stay put
The kind of ownership and the kind of problem change as well
Only the scope changes, while the rest of the story stays put
optionExplain: The book describes changes in all four dimensions.
Scope, contribution and impact change too.
Right: ownership, ambiguity and trade-offs change as well as the numbers.
Contribution, impact and difficulty change along with scope.
questions.explain: A step up changes the kind of work.
questions.rule: Judge a story's level by the whole pattern across the four dimensions.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A club ranks organizers by reach: own tasks, the club, several clubs, a region. An organizer whose scheme directly changes two clubs and starts to influence the region matches which level of scope?
options: Staff
Mid
Senior
Principal
optionExplain: Right: at least two teams directly, with wider influence, is staff.
Mid scope is parts of a team.
Senior is the whole team and one other.
Principal scope is many teams.
questions.explain: Reach across two groups with wider influence is staff scope.
questions.teaches: Staff scope means directly affecting at least two teams while beginning to influence the wider division or organization; principal scope covers many teams or how large parts of the organization operate.
questions.rule: Judge a story's level by the whole pattern across the four dimensions.

questions.q: How should you use sample stories at each level?
options: Copy the closest one and replace the names with your own
Memorize them so that you can repeat them in interviews
Compare adjacent levels and notice what changes between them
Skip them and rely on your job titles to show your level
optionExplain: The book says they are not templates.
They are not scripts to repeat.
Right: the aim is to develop a sense of what changes between levels.
Titles do not show level.
questions.explain: The samples train your eye. The card explains how.
questions.rule: Compare your story with the levels on either side and note what changes on each dimension.

questions.q: True or false: the book's sample stories are templates to copy.
questions.explain: The book says they are not templates but a way to sense the difference between levels.
questions.rule: Compare, do not copy.

questions.q: Mira owned the redesign of her team's testing process, and one other team later copied it. What should she check when comparing with adjacent levels?
options: Whether her story is long enough to cover all four dimensions
Whether it reached beyond her team and whether she led the adoption
Whether her job title matches the level of the role she wants
Whether the other team that copied it liked working with her
optionExplain: Length is not a dimension.
Right: reach beyond the team and leading adoption are senior markers.
Titles do not decide level.
Likability is not a dimension.
questions.explain: Check scope and contribution against the next level.
questions.rule: Compare your story with the levels on either side and note what changes on each dimension.

questions.q: A mid-level story whose adoption you led across other teams starts to approach the ____ pattern.
questions.explain: Reach beyond the team plus leading adoption is the senior pattern, so added reach and leadership move a story up.
questions.rule: Added reach and leadership move a story up.

questions.q: A candidate copies the book's staff-level story, changing only company names. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because published stories are free for anyone to reuse
Staff-level stories are too brief to fill an interview answer
Staff-level stories contain too many numbers for anyone to memorise
The samples are not templates, so the story would not be hers
optionExplain: The book says the samples are not templates; the story would not be hers.
Length is not the problem the book raises.
Numbers are not the problem; the stories are samples for comparing levels.
Right: the stories are for learning what changes between levels, not for copying.
questions.explain: Use samples for learning, not copying.
questions.rule: Compare your story with the levels on either side and note what changes on each dimension.

questions.q: Alice reorganized her own cooking station; Ben redesigned prep flow for four kitchens with different equipment. The same type of accomplishment, but what separates them?
options: Which of them cooks faster during a busy service
Breadth of reach and the trade-offs between kitchens
The length of the menu that each kitchen serves
The number of recipes each of them has written
optionExplain: Speed is not the dimension.
Right: scope and difficulty differ, which is what changes between levels.
Menu length is unrelated.
Recipe counts do not show level.
questions.explain: Same task, different level.
questions.teaches: In the book, deployment work appears at mid level as a team's workflow, and at staff level as about forty engineers across four teams with different needs, including monoliths and microservices.
questions.rule: Compare your story with the levels on either side and note what changes on each dimension.

questions.q: Which story is the most typical entry-level story?
options: Redesigning, building and rolling out the team's whole deployment workflow
Owning the error-handling strategy across all of the team's services
Designing a performance-testing framework for every backend service
Writing scripts that speed up a testing chore for me and a few teammates
optionExplain: Owning a full workflow from design to rollout is a mid-level pattern.
Owning a strategy across the team's services is mid-level ownership.
A framework for all of a team's services is mid-level scope.
Right: entry work centres on your own tasks and a few teammates.
questions.explain: Entry stories stay close to your own work. The card compares them with mid-level ones.
questions.rule: Entry stories fix your own or a few teammates' work; mid stories own a complete solution for the team.

questions.q: True or false: in the book's samples, entry-level stories mainly affect the person's own work and a few teammates.
questions.explain: Entry-level scope is your own productivity and starting to help teammates.
questions.rule: Entry scope is personal.

questions.q: Sort each story by the level it most likely shows.

items.t: Wrote a script that sped up my own report checks and a colleague's
Redesigned how my team releases and rolled it out across the services we own
Traced a flaky alarm through unfamiliar code and fixed it with testing
Built a validation tool for the team, balancing coverage against runtime
Documented our setup steps with my manager's review
Owned a new alerting approach across all five services my team runs

questions.explain: Entry stories are about your own tasks or helping a few teammates. Mid stories own a complete solution that affects how the team works.
questions.rule: Entry stories fix your own or a few teammates' work; mid stories own a complete solution for the team.

questions.q: Which detail best separates a mid-level story from an entry-level one?
options: Owning a complete solution that reshapes how the team works
Using a longer list of tools in the project overall
Spending more weeks on the project than a colleague did
Having a teammate review the final result before release
optionExplain: Right: mid-level contribution is owning solutions from problem to implementation.
Tool lists do not set level; the pattern across four dimensions does.
Duration does not set level; ownership and reach matter.
Review by another person is common at every level.
questions.explain: Ownership of a whole solution marks mid-level.
questions.rule: Entry stories fix your own or a few teammates' work; mid stories own a complete solution for the team.

questions.q: A candidate calls a change she made only to her own script, saving herself ten minutes, a mid-level redesign. What stops it from reading as mid-level?
options: It is too short to be a story that an interviewer could judge
It mentions no tools, which a mid-level story must name
It affects only her own work, which is entry-level scope
It happened on a weekday, outside the team's normal cycle
optionExplain: Length is not the issue; the reach is.
The tools are not what sets the level.
Right: mid-level work affects aspects of the team, not only the individual.
Timing is unrelated to level.
questions.explain: Match the claim to the real reach.
questions.rule: Entry stories fix your own or a few teammates' work; mid stories own a complete solution for the team.

questions.q: A barista wrote a quick-start guide that got new hires working in two days. Which result would match the book's entry-level documentation sample?
options: The guide became a template that other locations copied
The guide won an industry award for its design
The guide was rewritten by the owner before release
The guide replaced all of the training for new staff
optionExplain: Right: in the sample, the docs became the template other teams copied.
The sample does not mention awards.
The sample does not mention rewrites by an owner.
The sample does not say it replaced training.
questions.explain: Even entry-level stories can show reach.
questions.teaches: In the book's entry-level documentation sample, new hires were productive in two days instead of a week, and the documents became the template that other teams copied.
questions.rule: Entry stories fix your own or a few teammates' work; mid stories own a complete solution for the team.

questions.q: Which set of verbs best marks a senior-level story?
options: Followed the plan, fixed the bug, documented the steps
Watched the rollout, reported the numbers, thanked the team
Drove the vision, built buy-in, led adoption
Reviewed the code, approved the change, closed the ticket
optionExplain: That is the executing pattern of entry-level work.
These describe observation and not leading.
Right: senior stories show driving direction and leading adoption.
These are routine review actions at any level.
questions.explain: Senior stories show leadership across teams. The card describes the shape.
questions.rule: Senior stories show you leading adoption across your team and beyond, through buy-in and architectural decisions.

questions.q: In the senior samples, the author does not only build the solution but also leads ____ of it across other teams.
questions.explain: Leading adoption is a mark of senior contribution in the samples.
questions.rule: Senior leads adoption.

questions.q: Which story shows senior scope and contribution?
options: Built a feature alone, with sign-off from the manager at the end
Led rollout of shared tokens for her team and two others
Fixed a handful of small bugs in her own area of the code
Wrote tests for her own module ahead of the next release
optionExplain: A solo feature is below senior scope.
Right: whole team plus influence on others, with leadership and buy-in.
Small bugs in her own area are entry-level.
A module of her own is a personal scope.
questions.explain: Reach plus leading adoption is senior.
questions.rule: Senior stories show you leading adoption across your team and beyond, through buy-in and architectural decisions.

questions.q: True or false: if a shared-library project were used only by her own team, built without consulting anyone, it would still show the senior pattern of scope and buy-in.
questions.explain: Without reach beyond the team and buy-in from others, it resembles the mid-level pattern, because senior stories show influence on other teams and leading adoption.
questions.rule: Reach and buy-in lift a story to senior.

questions.q: A candidate's senior story gives all its difficulty as: I wrote the code. What is missing for senior-level difficulty?
options: Nothing, since writing complex code is hard enough to count
A longer list of the tools and frameworks that were used
More detail about how many lines of code were written
Constraints, stakeholder balancing and architectural decisions
optionExplain: Writing code alone does not show senior-level difficulty.
Tools do not show difficulty.
Code volume does not show difficulty.
Right: senior difficulty includes constraints and decisions with team-level architectural effect.
questions.explain: Senior difficulty is about constraints and decisions.
questions.rule: Senior stories show you leading adoption across your team and beyond, through buy-in and architectural decisions.

questions.q: A senior baker standardizes recipes across three shops. Which outcome pattern matches the book's senior-level library sample?
options: Higher personal speed for the baker who set the standard
Less duplicated effort, more consistency and faster new work
A bigger kitchen in the main shop with more equipment in it
A longer menu offered across all three of the shops together
optionExplain: That would be entry-level impact.
Right: the sample reports less duplicate code, more consistency and faster feature work.
That is not an outcome in the sample.
That is not an outcome in the sample.
questions.explain: Senior impact shows team-wide gains.
questions.teaches: In the book's shared component library sample, feature work that used to take three sprints started finishing in two, alongside less duplicate code and more visual consistency.
questions.rule: Senior stories show you leading adoption across your team and beyond, through buy-in and architectural decisions.

questions.q: What most separates a principal story from a staff story?
options: The principal story uses more tools than the staff story
The principal story is longer than the staff story is
The principal story names more people than the staff story
Organization-wide capability and executive alignment on unclear problems
optionExplain: Tool count does not set level.
Length does not set level.
Naming people does not set level.
Right: principal difficulty involves fundamental trade-offs and novel problems.
questions.explain: Principal work changes the organization. The card compares the two levels.
questions.rule: Staff stories resolve trade-offs between teams; principal stories change how the whole organization works.

questions.q: Match each sample story with the trade-off at its centre.
pairs: Product speed versus compliance at scale
Program overhead versus value with no clear return metrics
questions.explain: Each sample story is defined by a trade-off between competing needs.
questions.rule: Higher levels are defined by trade-offs.

questions.q: Sort each story by the level it most likely shows.

items.t: Agreed a shared logging format across four teams with clashing needs
Set a company-wide strategy for a machine-learning platform with executive alignment over quarters
Built a reference implementation that five product teams adopted
Created a career program for engineers with no clear measure of return
Coordinated a migration across three teams' services
Balanced legal requirements against product speed across the whole organization

questions.explain: Staff stories resolve trade-offs among a few teams. Principal stories set organization-wide direction under constraints with no clear precedent.
questions.rule: Staff stories resolve trade-offs between teams; principal stories change how the whole organization works.

questions.q: What if a staff-level project needed executive alignment across the company over several quarters?
options: It would read more like a principal-level project
It would stay a staff-level project with no change in level
It would drop to a senior-level project instead
It would read as an entry-level project overall
optionExplain: Right: executive alignment and multi-quarter organization-wide rollout are principal markers.
Staff difficulty is trade-offs across teams, without company-wide alignment.
More alignment does not lower the level.
Entry is far below.
questions.explain: Executive alignment marks principal difficulty.
questions.rule: Staff stories resolve trade-offs between teams; principal stories change how the whole organization works.

questions.q: A candidate pitches a company-wide strategy, but every stakeholder was on her own team. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since strategy is always company-wide
Strategy cannot be told in a story
The reach does not match the claimed level
Stakeholders should be removed
optionExplain: Strategy does not show scope on its own.
Strategy can be told as a story.
Right: principal stories involve many teams or large parts of the organization.
Stakeholders are part of difficulty.
questions.explain: Claims must match the reach.
questions.rule: Staff stories resolve trade-offs between teams; principal stories change how the whole organization works.

questions.q: A hospital rolls out a data-sharing policy across clinical and legal departments. Which difficulty matches the book's principal data-privacy sample?
options: Balancing speed and compliance, with executive alignment on trade-offs
Learning the new forms that the departments will start to use
Fixing a single login bug in the clinical records system
Writing the weekly status report for the department heads
optionExplain: Right: the sample balances product velocity with compliance and needs executive alignment.
That is entry-level difficulty.
That is small and local.
That is routine.
questions.explain: Principal difficulty crosses functions.
questions.teaches: In the book's data privacy sample, the difficulty was managing legal requirements across product and legal teams, balancing product velocity with compliance at scale, and gaining executive alignment on trade-offs between features and privacy.
questions.rule: Staff stories resolve trade-offs between teams; principal stories change how the whole organization works.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: According to the book, what is the common mistake candidates make about their own stories?
options: They tell too many of their stories in each interview they attend
They use too many numbers when they describe the results of work
They undersell their accomplishments or overstate their contributions
They avoid mentioning any teammates in the stories that they tell
optionExplain: The book does not name this mistake.
The book encourages numbers.
Right: most either undersell or overstate.
The book warns against hiding your specific part, not against naming teammates.
questions.explain: Candidates misjudge their level. The card shows how to score.
questions.rule: Score each story on all four dimensions against the level guide before you decide to use it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: True or false: the book says most candidates either undersell their accomplishments or overstate their contributions.
questions.explain: This is why it recommends scoring stories against the guide.
questions.rule: Score stories honestly.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A story: she led an initiative with her whole team and two other teams, mentored colleagues, and transformed the team's practice under real constraints. Which level does the guide point to?
options: Entry
Senior
Mid
Principal
optionExplain: Entry is individual and straightforward.
Right: the whole team plus one or two others, with leading and mentoring, is senior.
Mid covers aspects of the team.
Principal is company-wide.
questions.explain: Whole team plus one or two others is senior.
questions.rule: Score each story on all four dimensions against the level guide before you decide to use it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: If the same story involved four teams directly with competing stakeholder priorities, the guide would point toward ____ level.
questions.explain: Two or three or more teams directly, cross-team leadership and competing priorities describe staff level, not senior.
questions.rule: More teams and competing priorities move a story to staff.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate scores a story only on its impact numbers and calls it staff-level. What is wrong?
options: Impact numbers cannot be scored against any guide
Staff stories have no numbers to score, so impact is moot
Scoring is done by interviewers and not by candidates
All four dimensions need to fit the level, not one
optionExplain: Impact can be scored.
Staff stories tie to business metrics.
The book asks you to score your own stories.
Right: the guide covers scope, contribution, impact and difficulty.
questions.explain: Score all four.
questions.rule: Score each story on all four dimensions against the level guide before you decide to use it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A hospital manager creates a new patient-flow approach across the whole hospital, first finding the real problem. In the guide, which contribution description fits?
options: Executing assigned tasks handed over by her manager
Strategic leadership, and defining the problem first
Owning one small piece of a much larger project
Guiding a few teammates through a routine task
optionExplain: That is entry-level.
Right: principal contribution defines problems before solving them and leads strategy alongside partners.
That is entry-level.
That is mid-level.
questions.explain: Principal work defines the problem first.
questions.teaches: In the scoring guide, principal level means company-wide scope, strategic leadership alongside product, design and business partners, organizational capabilities measured in business outcomes, novel problems without established patterns, and defining problems before solving them.
questions.rule: Score each story on all four dimensions against the level guide before you decide to use it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Most of your stories sit below the level you are targeting. Which response does the book suggest?
options: Reword them with more senior-sounding verbs and bigger claims
Remove the numbers so the gap to the target is less obvious
Apply at the same level and hope the interviewers are generous
Find stronger examples, tell scope and impact better, or revisit the target
optionExplain: That claims more than the stories show.
The book values numbers in stories.
The mismatch will show in interviews.
Right: these are the options the book lists.
questions.explain: Clustering below target needs action. The card lists the options.
questions.rule: Make sure at least two or three stories sit solidly at your target level, and lead with them.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: If your stories show mixed levels, make sure you have at least two or three stories solidly at your ____ level.
questions.explain: Mixed levels are normal, but a few stories must sit at the level you aim for.
questions.rule: A few stories at target.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Sam targets a senior role and has two senior-level stories and two mid-level ones. What should Sam do?
options: Lead with the senior stories and keep the mid-level ones as support
Hide the senior stories until the interviewers ask for them
Retell the mid-level stories so that they sound senior
Withdraw the application because the set is mixed
optionExplain: Right: lead with those at the target level.
That wastes the strongest stories.
That overstates the contribution.
He has enough stories at the target.
questions.explain: Lead with the strongest fit.
questions.rule: Make sure at least two or three stories sit solidly at your target level, and lead with them.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: True or false: if most of your stories cluster below your target level, the book suggests you may consider whether you are targeting the right level.
