questions.explain: One of the options the book gives is reconsidering the target level.
questions.rule: Consider the target.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate reasons that mixed levels are normal, so none of her stories need to be at the target level. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since a mixed set can contain any mix
Every one of the stories must sit at the target level
At least two or three must sit solidly at the target level
Stories at lower levels are forbidden in an interview
optionExplain: Mixed is normal, but a few must reach the target.
The book says not every story has to be at target.
Right: she needs enough stories at the target to show consistency.
Lower-level support stories are fine.
questions.explain: Mixed is fine; none at target is not.
questions.rule: Make sure at least two or three stories sit solidly at your target level, and lead with them.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Lena targets a senior role. Which set of stories would the book accept?
options: A strong senior story, a solid mid-level story and another senior story
Three mid-level stories told with senior-level framing
Only mid-level stories, together with senior-sounding job titles
No stories at all, only claims about what she can do
optionExplain: Right: a strong senior story followed by a solid mid-level story is fine.
The book rejects mid-level stories dressed as senior.
Titles do not change the stories.
Claims need stories as evidence.
questions.explain: Framing cannot replace level.
questions.teaches: The book says a strong senior story followed by a solid mid-level story is fine, but three mid-level stories with senior-level framing is not.
questions.rule: Make sure at least two or three stories sit solidly at your target level, and lead with them.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Your story has strong results, but you cannot say what you personally decided. Which dimension is weak, and what do you look for?
options: Impact, and stories with bigger numbers in them
Scope, and stories that involved more teams
Contribution, and stories that show your own decisions
Difficulty, and stories that used more tools
optionExplain: The results are strong, so impact is not the gap.
The gap is about her own part, not the team count.
Right: contribution is about what you personally did.
Tools are not a measure of difficulty.
questions.explain: Each dimension has its own remedy. The card lists them.
questions.rule: Name the weakest dimension and choose stories that are strong in just that one.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Match each weak dimension with the kind of story to look for.
pairs: Your specific decisions and actions, not team outcomes
Challenges suited to your target level
questions.explain: Each remedy targets the weakness directly.
questions.rule: Fix the dimension that is weak.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Her stories are well told and hard, but each affected only her own tasks. Which remedy does the book give?
options: Add more numbers to each of the stories she has
Find examples where her work affected multiple parties
Pick harder technical problems to talk about
Describe her own decisions in greater detail
optionExplain: That fixes impact.
Right: weak scope is fixed by work that affected others.
That fixes difficulty.
That fixes contribution.
questions.explain: Match the remedy to the gap.
questions.rule: Name the weakest dimension and choose stories that are strong in just that one.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: What if she picks stories that affected several parties but still reports no figures?
options: The scope gap remains because several parties are involved
The difficulty gap remains because the work is still easy
No gap remains because one fix covers the others
The impact gap remains and needs quantified business outcomes
optionExplain: Scope has been addressed.
Nothing in the facts concerns difficulty.
Impact is still unquantified.
Right: missing numbers leave impact weak.
questions.explain: Fixing one gap does not fix another.
questions.rule: Name the weakest dimension and choose stories that are strong in just that one.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: True or false: for weak difficulty, a candidate should pick her hardest technical story whatever her target level is.
questions.explain: The book says to choose examples with challenges appropriate to your level, so the hardest story is not automatically the best fit.
questions.rule: Choose difficulty that fits the level.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate aims for staff-level roles and has stories about overcoming obstacles and complexity. What does the book say difficulty should show for staff and above?
options: Obstacles and complexity
Fundamental trade-offs
Constraints and architectural decisions
Learning new tools
optionExplain: That fits mid-level.
Right: fundamental trade-offs are the book's expectation for staff and above.
That fits senior-level.
That fits entry-level.
questions.explain: Difficulty must match the target.
questions.teaches: For weak difficulty, the book suggests obstacles and complexity for mid level, constraints and architectural decisions for senior, and fundamental trade-offs for staff and above.
questions.rule: Name the weakest dimension and choose stories that are strong in just that one.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: How may you adapt your stories to a company's values, according to the book?
options: Add experiences you wish you had to match the role
Use the same story and wording for every company
Refuse to adjust anything, whatever the audience values
Choose which real experiences to share and what to emphasize
optionExplain: Invented experiences are exposed by follow-up questions.
Companies value different things, so the same story may read differently.
The book says tailoring emphasis is expected.
Right: selection and emphasis, never fabrication.
questions.explain: Tailoring is selection and emphasis. The card explains the limit.
questions.rule: Choose and emphasize real experience for the audience; never invent it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: True or false: the book says pretending to have experiences you do not have can get you rejected when follow-up questions reveal the truth.
questions.explain: It also warns that you could be hired into a role you cannot do.
questions.rule: Do not fabricate.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Sort each action by whether it is selecting and emphasizing real experience or fabricating.

items.t: Leading with the cross-team side of a project for a collaborative company
Describing a project you only watched as one you led
Choosing the fastest-delivered project for a speed-focused company
Inventing a metric you never measured
Stressing user research in a story for a customer-focused firm
Claiming credit for a design you were not part of

questions.explain: The items under 'Selecting and emphasizing' choose true facts to highlight. The items under 'Fabricating' state things that did not happen.
questions.rule: Choose and emphasize real experience for the audience; never invent it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: What if your real experiences do not match what a company values?
options: It is useful information about whether the role suits you
You should invent matching experiences to close the gap
The interviewers will ignore the gap when they decide
You should drop all your stories and start again
optionExplain: Right: the book says it may mean the wrong role, a need to gain experience, or a different culture.
That is fabrication.
They will notice the mismatch.
That would not help.
questions.explain: A mismatch is information, not a reason to invent.
questions.rule: Choose and emphasize real experience for the audience; never invent it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate invents a leadership story because the role asks for leadership. What is the risk?
options: None, since interviewers rarely ask follow-up questions about stories
The story will be too short to impress the interviewers who hear it
Follow-ups will expose it, or she may be hired into a role she cannot do
Leadership cannot be shown through stories of any kind in an interview
optionExplain: Interviewers probe.
Length is not the problem.
Right: those are the two risks the book names.
Stories show leadership.
questions.explain: Fabrication fails twice.
questions.rule: Choose and emphasize real experience for the audience; never invent it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A librarian's catalogue overhaul cut search time, involved three branches and finished in a month. For a speed-focused employer, which truthful emphasis fits?
options: The speed of delivery
The number of books
The color of the cards
The branch locations
optionExplain: Right: delivery speed is a true aspect that suits that employer.
Not what the employer values.
Irrelevant.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: Emphasis follows what the audience values.
questions.teaches: The book notes that one project, such as an API redesign, can be told to stress technical depth, customer impact, cross-team coordination or fast delivery, and all four could be accurate.
questions.rule: Choose and emphasize real experience for the audience; never invent it.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate for a senior role describes only finishing individual tasks. What risk does the book name?
options: A quick promotion to the level she asked for
No effect, since level is set by the title
Down-leveling or rejection, as the book describes
Extra interviews, but no change in the offer
optionExplain: That does not follow.
Level mismatch matters.
Right: the book names down-leveling or rejection.
No such effect is named.
questions.explain: Mismatched stories lower the level you are offered. The card next names the two patterns.
questions.rule: For a higher-level role, bring stories that show the leadership that level needs.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Match each mismatch pattern with what is missing.
pairs: Can lead to down-leveling or rejection
questions.explain: The fix is stories at the leadership level the role needs.
questions.rule: Match the leadership the role needs.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate for a staff role says: I owned my team's monitoring dashboards, and the neighbouring team copied them. Which pattern is this?
options: Claiming unearned scope for work she did not do
Mid-level stories for staff roles
Junior stories for senior roles
All difficulty, no impact in the work
optionExplain: Nothing claims more than happened.
Right: single-team ownership with one other team adopting it is a mid-level story.
This is above entry level.
Impact is present.
questions.explain: Single-team ownership is not staff-level.
questions.rule: For a higher-level role, bring stories that show the leadership that level needs.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: True or false: for a staff-level role, a story about owning one team's work that one other team adopted signals staff-level ownership.
questions.explain: Staff roles require cross-team leadership, and single-team ownership is the mid-level pattern.
questions.rule: Staff needs cross-team leadership.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate for a senior role says only: I cut query time from three seconds to 200 milliseconds. What would make it senior-level?
options: Repeating the numbers and the date on which the change went live
Adding more tool names to show the technical range of the work
Saying how hard the work was, without adding any further detail
Showing how she shaped the team's approach, taught others and added monitoring
optionExplain: More of the same is still individual.
Tools do not make a story senior.
A claim without evidence is weak.
Right: the book names influence, teaching and monitoring.
questions.explain: Senior stories show influence on others.
questions.rule: For a higher-level role, bring stories that show the leadership that level needs.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A school IT lead owned her own school's timetable system, which one other school adopted. For a district-wide role, what does the book ask for?
options: Adding more timetable features to the system
Showing consensus across several teams or systems that others use alone
Mentioning how long she has worked at the school
Staying with single-school ownership and polishing the story
optionExplain: More features does not show cross-team leadership.
Right: building consensus across teams or creating systems that other teams use alone.
Tenure does not show it.
That is the mismatch.
questions.explain: Cross-team leadership means shared systems.
questions.teaches: For staff roles, the book asks for stories of building consensus across multiple teams or creating systems that let other teams solve similar problems without your help.
questions.rule: For a higher-level role, bring stories that show the leadership that level needs.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate built one service inside a large platform rebuild. Which description would hold up best under follow-up questions?
options: I led the platform rebuild, since my service was part of it and the project succeeded
I rebuilt the platform, including a service that I built myself and shipped on time
I owned the platform design and delivery, working closely with several other engineers
I built one service in a larger rebuild, and I can say which decisions were mine
optionExplain: It turns membership in a successful project into leadership of it, which follow-up questions will test.
It stretches one service into the whole platform, a claim that the details will not support.
Ownership of design and delivery is a large claim, and working closely with others does not make it hers.
Right: it names the real boundary of her part and she can defend every detail.
questions.explain: Credibility rests on claims that survive probing. The card shows how to state the boundary of your part.
questions.rule: State the exact boundary of what you owned, decided and built.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Interviewers will ____, and overstated claims will destroy your credibility instantly.
questions.explain: Follow-up probing is why overstated claims fail.
questions.rule: Interviewers probe the details.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it is an accurate scope claim or unearned scope.

items.t: I wrote the payment module, one of five owned by different people
I redesigned the whole checkout flow, though I only restyled the buttons
I designed the data model for my team's service and reviewed two peers' versions
I led the company migration, where I moved my own team's repositories
I ran the on-call rotation for my team of six
I chose the cloud strategy, which my director had already decided

questions.explain: Accurate claims name the true extent of the part. Unearned ones attach the whole effort to a smaller part.
questions.rule: State the exact boundary of what you owned, decided and built.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: True or false: if a candidate overstates her scope, interviewers' follow-up questions are likely to expose it.
questions.explain: The book warns that interviewers will probe, and overstated claims destroy credibility instantly.
questions.rule: Probing exposes overstated claims.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate reasons: the project succeeded, so I may say I led it. What is wrong with this?
options: Success belongs to the team, and a claim to have led it must match her own part
Projects that succeed should be described in the passive voice to avoid sounding boastful
Leadership claims are allowed only for people with a manager title, whatever the work
Interviewers discount any story that mentions a team result at all
optionExplain: Right: leading is a claim about what she did, and the team's success does not turn into it.
The book asks for precision about your part, not for the passive voice.
The book ties leadership to what you did, not to a title.
Team results are fine to mention; the book asks you to separate your part from them.
questions.explain: Credit follows what you did.
questions.rule: State the exact boundary of what you owned, decided and built.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: One of twelve crew coordinators says she redesigned the whole project plan, though the lead made the key decisions. What should she say instead?
options: I helped with the plan, which is why the project went well overall for everyone
I redesigned the plan with the other eleven coordinators and the lead together
I planned the schedule for my crew; the lead made the project-wide decisions
I managed the project plan because my crew's schedule was part of the plan
optionExplain: It is vague and takes credit for the project's result without stating her part.
It spreads a design she did not do across everyone, which still overstates her role.
Right: it states her real part and leaves the project-wide decisions to the lead.
It claims management of the whole plan from one crew's schedule.
questions.explain: Name the real boundary of your part.
questions.teaches: The book's second example of unearned scope is saying you redesigned the service architecture when you designed one of twelve services and a principal engineer made the architectural decisions.
questions.rule: State the exact boundary of what you owned, decided and built.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: I added an off-the-shelf login library to our app, protecting fifty thousand users. For a senior role, what is the weakness of this story?
options: It is a significant outcome, but the work was a straightforward implementation
Security work is outside what a behavioral interview covers, whatever the numbers say
Fifty thousand users is too few to count as impact at any level
Using an existing library shows poor judgment, because candidates should build their own
optionExplain: Right: it has impact but shows little difficulty.
Behavioral stories can cover any technical area; the issue is the balance of the story.
The number is a strength; the weakness lies elsewhere.
Reusing a library is often sound judgment; building your own is not a virtue in itself.
questions.explain: A story needs both parts. The card names the two imbalances.
questions.rule: Pair a meaningful result with a genuinely hard problem, and explain the purpose of complexity.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Match each imbalance with what the story lacks.
pairs: A purpose: why existing options failed or what problem it solved
Reads as a red flag of over-engineering
questions.explain: Each imbalance leaves one side of the story empty.
questions.rule: A story needs both a result and a hard problem.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate spent four months building a custom message queue but does not say why existing queues would not do. What should she add?
options: A deeper tour of the queue's internals, so that her engineering skill is evident
A longer timeline of the four months, to show how persistent she was
Why existing queues could not do the job, or what problem the build solved
A list of the technologies used, so that the technical depth is easy to see
optionExplain: More internals add complexity but still no purpose.
Persistence is not a reason for the build.
Right: the book says to explain why existing solutions would not work or what the work solved.
A list of technologies repeats the work without explaining the need.
questions.explain: Explain why the complexity was needed.
questions.rule: Pair a meaningful result with a genuinely hard problem, and explain the purpose of complexity.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Which story is the clearest case of all impact, no difficulty?
options: Spending months on a bespoke compiler that no team ever adopted
Flipping one setting that fixed checkout for a million customers
Leading a vague project with no clear goal or measurable outcome
Rewriting a module in a new language to see how it feels
optionExplain: That is the opposite case: effort with no outcome.
Right: a large benefit from a trivial change.
A vague project with no outcome is closer to neither dimension.
That is exploration with no stated result.
questions.explain: Check both dimensions separately.
questions.rule: Pair a meaningful result with a genuinely hard problem, and explain the purpose of complexity.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: True or false: a candidate is right to say any important piece of work demonstrates senior-level problem solving.
questions.explain: Important but straightforward work does not show the constraints and decisions senior roles look for.
questions.rule: Importance is not difficulty.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A hospital IT officer says: I installed a security update on all three hundred workstations. How would the book read this story?
options: Strong senior evidence, since protecting three hundred machines is high stakes
Hard work with no impact, which hints at over-engineering
Unclear contribution, because the officer does not say who did the installing
Important work, but a routine implementation with little difficulty
optionExplain: High stakes alone do not make the work hard.
The update had a clear purpose, so it is not over-engineering.
The officer says what she did, so the contribution is clear.
Right: like the book's important-but-easy example, it lacks constraints and decisions.
questions.explain: Important does not mean difficult.
questions.teaches: The book's example is adding SSL certificates to API endpoints, improving security for 100,000 users: important, but a straightforward implementation, not a difficult one.
questions.rule: Pair a meaningful result with a genuinely hard problem, and explain the purpose of complexity.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate uses we for every step of her story. What can the interviewer not judge?
options: Whether the project finished on time and within budget
Whether she drove the work or only took part in it
Whether the team was large enough to justify the project
Whether the technology she used was current enough for the role
optionExplain: Completion and budget can be stated with we just as well.
Right: her own part is hidden behind the group.
Team size is not what we hides.
Technology can be named with we just as well.
questions.explain: Contribution needs an I. The card explains how to separate it.
questions.rule: Separate what you decided and did from what the team did.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Using we throughout makes it impossible to assess your ____.
questions.explain: Level depends on contribution, and we hides it.
questions.rule: Make your part visible.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: Which rewrite of the line we cut onboarding time by half best shows contribution?
options: We all worked hard as a team, and onboarding time was cut by half
Onboarding improved by half thanks to the team's efforts and good planning
Onboarding time was cut by half after the new process was introduced to everyone
I interviewed new hires and wrote the guide; the team rolled it out and time halved
optionExplain: It still gives no personal part.
It credits the team and says nothing about what she did.
The passive voice hides everyone, including her.
Right: it separates her decisions and writing from the team's rollout.
questions.explain: Show your part and the team's part.
questions.rule: Separate what you decided and did from what the team did.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: True or false: replacing we with I for every action, including those the team took, solves the problem.
questions.explain: Contribution is what you did. Claiming team actions as your own would swap one problem for another, unearned credit.
questions.rule: Use I only where it was you.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate thinks we sounds modest, so it is the safest word for every story. What does it cost her?
options: Interviewers cannot tell what she did, so they cannot place her level
Interviewers read the modesty as low confidence and mark down her style
Interviewers assume she did the whole project alone and probe all of it
Interviewers prefer team players, so it costs her nothing at any level
optionExplain: Right: with no visible part, her level cannot be judged.
The problem is missing information, not tone.
Overclaiming is the risk of I, not of we.
Teamwork is valued, but the interviewer still needs to see her part.
questions.explain: Modesty that hides your part costs you.
questions.rule: Separate what you decided and did from what the team did.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: A candidate says: we moved the clinic to digital records and cut paperwork by eighty percent. Which follow-up questions would the book's reasoning have an interviewer ask?
options: How many patients the clinic served and how large its staff was
Which records software was chosen and how much it cost to license
Who made the decision, who did the work and who handled the problems
Whether the clinic planned to expand and where it is located
optionExplain: These describe the clinic, not her part.
These describe the product, not her part.
Right: these questions separate her part from the group's.
These describe the clinic's plans, not her part.
questions.explain: Interviewers ask who did what.
questions.teaches: The book's example is we migrated to Kubernetes and we reduced deployment time by 90 percent, and it asks who made the decision, who did the work and who handled the problems.
questions.rule: Separate what you decided and did from what the team did.

questions.q: Why might a recruiter be a useful source of insider information for a candidate?
options: They gain when candidates they put forward accept their offers
They write the interview questions themselves and can reveal every one
They are rewarded for rejecting weaker candidates, so they know what fails
They sit in on every round to coach candidates as they go along
optionExplain: Right: their performance depends on accepted offers, so they want candidates to succeed.
Recruiters know the focus areas but do not usually write every question.
The book says their performance is tied to accepted offers, not to rejections.
The book does not describe recruiters attending rounds.
questions.explain: Recruiters have a reason to help. The card shows what to ask.
questions.rule: Ask your recruiter about challenges, key competencies and prep materials.

questions.q: Match each question to your recruiter with what it asks about.
pairs: What should I know about this company's current challenges?
The company's current priorities and problems
What competencies matter most for this role?
Can you share any interview prep materials?
Documents on format, priorities and competencies
questions.explain: Each question draws out different insider information.
questions.rule: Ask specific questions.

questions.q: Maya has a call with her recruiter. Which request gets her the most useful insider information?
options: Is this a good place to work, and do people seem happy there?
How soon will I hear back, and who will conduct the first round?
Which competencies matter most here, and is there any prep material?
What salary range is typical, and can an offer be negotiated later?
optionExplain: It asks for an opinion and not for what is evaluated.
It covers logistics, which does not reveal what the company values.
Right: it asks for the competencies and materials the recruiter actually holds.
Pay is useful but does not show which stories to emphasize.
questions.explain: Specific questions get specific answers.
questions.rule: Ask your recruiter about challenges, key competencies and prep materials.

questions.q: True or false: if you ask your recruiter for interview prep materials, they may have documents about interview format, team priorities or competencies.
questions.explain: The book says many recruiters have such documents, which is why asking directly is worthwhile.
questions.rule: Ask, because the documents may exist.

questions.q: A candidate skips the recruiter, treating them as a gatekeeper to avoid. What does the book say she loses?
options: A guaranteed offer, since recruiters decide whom to hire in the end
Her best source of insider information, from an ally
The chance to negotiate pay, which only recruiters ever handle
Nothing, since recruiters know little about the interview content
optionExplain: Recruiters do not decide hiring on their own.
Right: the book calls the recruiter her best source of insider information, and they want her to succeed.
Pay is not the point the book makes.
The book says recruiters know the interviewers' focus areas.
questions.explain: Treat the recruiter as an ally.
questions.rule: Ask your recruiter about challenges, key competencies and prep materials.

questions.q: A candidate for a bank receives a prep document with sample questions. What should she infer?
options: They are decoys, so she should ignore them and prepare in general
They apply to other roles, so she should ask for different ones
They are the only questions asked, so other preparation is wasted
They are likely to be asked, so she should prepare stories for them
optionExplain: The book says the opposite about such examples.
Nothing in the document suggests another role.
That goes too far: examples are likely, not exclusive.
Right: example questions in prep materials have a high likelihood of being asked.
questions.explain: Prep questions point to interview questions.
questions.teaches: Questions used as examples in a recruiter's prep materials have a high likelihood of being asked in the interviews.
questions.rule: Ask your recruiter about challenges, key competencies and prep materials.

questions.q: A job posting repeats the phrase fast-paced several times. What does that most likely signal?
options: The company has no firm deadlines and prefers a slow pace
Speed of execution matters to the company
The company values careful validation above everything else
The posting was written carelessly and says little about priorities
optionExplain: Repeated stress on pace suggests the opposite.
Right: repeated words tell you what matters.
A compliance emphasis would use different words.
Repetition is deliberate, not careless.
questions.explain: Repetition is a signal. The card lists where else to look.
questions.rule: Read what the company publishes and repeats; its choices show its priorities.

questions.q: Match each public source with what it can reveal.
pairs: Which wins and problems they celebrate
Topics such as speed, scale or innovation
Newer frameworks suggest innovation, proven ones stability
questions.explain: Each source gives a different clue about priorities.
questions.rule: Different sources show different priorities.

questions.q: A company's engineers speak mostly about how fast they ship. Which story should a candidate emphasize?
options: One where she spent a year perfecting a rewrite before any release
One where she ran an exhaustive review before every change
One where she worked on a single module without releasing anything
One where she shipped an early version and iterated on feedback
optionExplain: That contradicts the pace the company celebrates.
Exhaustive review slows shipping.
Releasing nothing shows no pace at all.
Right: it matches the pace the company celebrates.
questions.explain: Match stories to published priorities.
questions.rule: Read what the company publishes and repeats; its choices show its priorities.

questions.q: True or false: relying on proven technologies indicates a preference for stability.
questions.explain: The book says newer frameworks suggest innovation, whereas proven technologies indicate a preference for stability.
questions.rule: Technology choices show priorities.

questions.q: A company has no engineering blog, so a candidate concludes there is nothing to learn. What is wrong?
options: Such companies still leave traces, such as release patterns and tech choices
A missing blog shows the company hides its priorities, so research is pointless
Blogs are the only public source, so she must rely on guesses
Release patterns and technology choices are private and cannot be seen
optionExplain: Right: the book says even companies without blogs leave traces.
A missing blog is not proof of secrecy, and other clues remain.
Blogs are one source among several.
Both can be observed from outside.
questions.explain: No blog does not mean no clues.
questions.rule: Read what the company publishes and repeats; its choices show its priorities.

questions.q: A company publishes detailed write-ups of its own outages. What does the book infer from this?
options: It probably avoids responsibility by blaming outside causes
It probably values speed over reliability, since outages are frequent
It probably values learning from failure
It probably has weak operations, since it admits outages
optionExplain: Detailed write-ups show the opposite of blame-shifting.
Publishing outages does not show a preference for speed.
Right: detailed postmortems show a value on learning from failure.
The book reads openness as a strength.
questions.explain: What a company publishes shows its culture.
questions.teaches: Companies that publish detailed postmortems show they value learning from failure; open sourcing developer tools suggests they value community, and making internal tools public suggests transparency.
questions.rule: Read what the company publishes and repeats; its choices show its priorities.

questions.q: You read one furious review and several calm ones that mention lots of process. What should you take away?
options: Heavy process may be a real pattern worth weighing
The furious review is the most honest and should decide it
Reviews are unreliable, so none should be read
The calm reviews are paid promotions and can be ignored
optionExplain: Right: a theme repeated by several people is a signal.
A single rant is noise, however loud.
Patterns across posts are valuable even when single posts are not.
Nothing suggests the calm reviews are paid.
questions.explain: Patterns matter more than outliers. The card next shows what to look for.
questions.rule: Trust patterns, not single posts, and ask insiders specific questions.

questions.q: Ignore individual rants; look for ____ across multiple posts.
questions.explain: Several people mentioning the same thing is the signal.
questions.rule: Look for patterns.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether to treat it as a pattern or as noise.

items.t: Six reviews over a year mention no work-life balance
One post that insults the CEO
Many employees praise autonomy
A single reviewer unhappy about one Tuesday lunch
Several posts describe long approval chains
One angry post about a rejected promotion

questions.explain: A theme repeated by several independent voices is a pattern; a single complaint is noise.
questions.rule: Trust patterns, not single posts, and ask insiders specific questions.

questions.q: Many reviews praise autonomy. What does that suggest about the behavior the company rewards?
options: Waiting for formal approval before each change is made
Sharing every draft with the whole group before acting
Making decisions without checking in at every step
Following the manager's instructions to the letter
optionExplain: That is the opposite of autonomy.
That describes a consensus-driven habit.
Right: praise for autonomy suggests trust to decide without checking in.
That describes close direction, the opposite of autonomy.
questions.explain: Praise shows what is rewarded.
questions.rule: Trust patterns, not single posts, and ask insiders specific questions.

questions.q: A candidate asks a current employee about the company culture in general terms. What does the book advise instead?
options: Ask only about pay and benefits, since culture cannot be described
Ask what earns promotion or draws negative feedback
Ask about the company's slogans so she can repeat them back to staff
Avoid asking employees, since they are not allowed to talk to candidates
optionExplain: Culture can be described through specific behaviors.
Right: skip surface questions and ask about specific behaviors.
Slogans are the surface-level material the book wants her to get past.
The book recommends talking to employees.
questions.explain: Ask specific questions.
questions.rule: Trust patterns, not single posts, and ask insiders specific questions.

questions.q: Why might a candidate ask employees instead of relying on a company's values page?
options: Values pages are usually inaccurate, so employees correct every line of them
Employees write the interview questions and can reveal them in advance
Values pages are legal documents, so they say nothing about behavior
Employees can say what a value such as ownership really means day to day
optionExplain: The book does not say values pages are inaccurate throughout.
Nothing in the book says employees write the questions.
Values pages are not legal documents; they just stay general.
Right: they tell truths the website never would.
questions.explain: Insiders translate slogans into behavior.
questions.teaches: Employees may tell you that customer obsession really means checking usage data before writing code, or that ownership means being available to resolve production issues at two in the morning.
questions.rule: Trust patterns, not single posts, and ask insiders specific questions.

questions.q: A small company wants someone who ships fast alone; an enterprise wants someone who builds consensus. Which is the better environment, according to the book?
options: The small company, because speed always wins in the end
Neither is better; they reward different approaches
The enterprise, because consensus is the safer route
Whichever offers the higher salary to the new hire
optionExplain: The book does not rank the environments.
Right: they are simply different environments.
The book does not rank the environments.
Salary is not what the book says decides it.
questions.explain: Environments differ; the aim is a match. The card next ties the chapter together.
questions.rule: Pick stories that match the company's values, and frame them at your true level.

questions.q: Match each piece of understanding with what it does for you.
pairs: Shows which experiences connect with what the company values
Lets you position your stories appropriately
questions.explain: Each piece helps you choose and frame stories.
questions.rule: Fit chooses, level frames, research guides.

questions.q: Research shows a company prizes digging into root causes. Which story should a candidate emphasize?
options: One where she shipped the earliest version in a single week
One where she delivered mostly alone with little team input
One where she copied an established pattern without questioning it
One where she dug into a failure to find its root cause
optionExplain: That speaks to speed, not depth.
That speaks to independence, not depth.
That shows following, not diving deep.
Right: it matches what they value.
questions.explain: Emphasize what they value.
questions.rule: Pick stories that match the company's values, and frame them at your true level.

questions.q: True or false: according to the book, misjudging your level can mean rejection for overreaching or down-leveling for not communicating your capabilities.
questions.explain: Get the level wrong and you are either rejected for overreaching or down-leveled for underselling.
questions.rule: Level mistakes cost you.

questions.q: A candidate treats getting any offer as the goal and accepts a role that mismatches her values. What does the book say the goal is?
options: The right offer at the right level at the right company
The highest title offered, since titles can be moved later
The quickest offer, because delay signals doubt
Any offer, since fit can be learned afterwards
optionExplain: Right: the book names the right offer at the right level at the right company.
Title is not what the book names.
Speed is not the goal.
The book warns against taking just any offer.
questions.explain: Aim for the right offer.
questions.rule: Pick stories that match the company's values, and frame them at your true level.

questions.q: A candidate finds every source describes constant late-night firefighting, which she does not want. What does the book suggest?
options: Pretend to love it, because interviewers expect it
Ignore the research, since sources are unreliable
Perhaps she does not need to pursue that role
Apply anyway and decide after the offer
optionExplain: That is fabrication, which the book warns against.
Research is meant to inform the decision.
Right: research also helps decide whether the company is right for you.
The book suggests knowing before accepting.
questions.explain: Research can screen roles out.
questions.teaches: If research shows that a company values behaviors you do not naturally demonstrate or do not want to develop, the book says perhaps you do not need to pursue that role.
questions.rule: Pick stories that match the company's values, and frame them at your true level.

questions.q: An interviewer asks how you handled a tight deadline. What should most of your answer be about?
questions.explain: Companies ask behavioral questions to learn how you act when facing their kind of challenge, so your behaviors are the content. The card next shows why.
options: How the product line grew and why the team picked its tools years earlier
Who was on the team, how it was organised and what each member owned
What you noticed, decided and did to get the work finished in time
How the project ran from the first kickoff meeting through to the launch day
optionExplain: It feels like helpful background, but it describes the setting rather than your behavior.
Team structure can matter later, but it does not show what you did about the deadline.
Right: the question is behavioral, so your own thinking and actions are the evidence.
A full timeline feels complete, but it spreads your own choices thin among events.
questions.rule: Tell the interviewer how you behaved (what you thought, decided and did), not the history of the project.

questions.q: Behavioral questions ask how you ____ when facing challenges like those at the company.
questions.explain: Interviewers want to know how you have behaved in the same types of challenge that exist at their company, not what the project was.
questions.rule: Your behavior is the evidence.

questions.q: A candidate is asked about influencing a doubtful colleague. Which opening best follows the rule?
questions.explain: The right opening starts with a noticed fact, a decision and an action. The other three open with setting, which the interviewer did not ask about.
questions.rule: Start from your own actions, not the setting.
options: I saw she doubted the plan, so I asked what worried her, then ran a small trial to answer it
Our company had recently reorganised into three squads, and her squad owned the billing module
The project started in spring after a long budget review that involved several senior managers
The tool we used was chosen over two rivals because of its licence terms and support plan
optionExplain: Right: it leads with what the candidate noticed, decided and did.
This is organisational background; it says nothing yet about what the candidate did.
This is project history that delays the first behavior.
A tool choice is project detail, and it is not the behavior the question asks for.

questions.q: Sort each sentence from a store manager's answer: does it show her behavior, or only the surroundings?
questions.explain: Noticing, deciding and measuring are her behaviors. The retail park, the software history and the headcount are setting.
questions.rule: Behaviors go in the story; surroundings wait to be asked for.

items.t: I noticed the Saturday queue peaked at noon, so I moved two staff to the tills then
I decided against extra hires because the peak lasted only an hour
The shop sits in a retail park built in the nineties
Head office had changed the rota software the year before
I measured queue time for three weeks and showed the numbers to my area manager
Our team had eleven part-timers and two full-timers

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, if you recount events exactly as they happened, evidence of your judgment can get buried under project details.
questions.explain: The author warns that recounting events in order buries judgment under detail, which can cost a candidate a level.
questions.rule: Detail hides judgment.

questions.q: A teacher is asked about handling a difficult parent. According to the author, why does she tell the story the natural way?
questions.explain: The pull toward context comes from wanting the listener to appreciate the difficulty. The rule asks you to resist it and let your actions show the difficulty.
questions.rule: Resist the urge to prove difficulty with context.
questions.teaches: The natural pull to tell project stories comes from wanting the listener to understand how hard the situation was, which is why the context floods in first.
options: Interviewers ask for the full chronology of any story and mark candidates down without it
A longer account helps the interviewer remember the teacher among many candidates
Describing the school and its history shows loyalty to the previous employer
She wants the interviewer to grasp how hard the situation was, so she explains it all first
optionExplain: The author says the opposite: interviewers evaluate you and can ask for details if they want them.
The author argues extra detail makes the interviewer's job harder, not easier.
The book offers no such reason; the instinct is about conveying difficulty.
Right: the author says the instinct is to explain the full situation so they see the difficulty.

questions.q: A skilled candidate gets a lower-level offer than expected after interviewing. What is one reason the author gives?
questions.explain: Hidden judgment is the author's explanation for downlevelling. The card next sets out both costs.
options: The candidate gave too many headline sentences and too few project details
The evidence of sound judgment was buried under project details
The interviewer disliked candidates who prepare their stories in advance
The candidate spoke too briefly about the company and its history
optionExplain: It is the reverse: too much project detail, not too much headline, hides the evidence.
Right: this is the reason the author gives for being placed at a lower level.
The author recommends preparing, so this is not the cause given.
More company history is described as noise, not as a fix.
questions.rule: Treat a linear project-style answer as a risk to your offer and your level, not as a safe default.

questions.q: The author says strong candidates can fail to get offers if their ____ abilities stay hidden in their stories.
questions.explain: The chapter says strong candidates fail to get offers if their problem-solving abilities remain hidden.
questions.rule: Hidden ability cannot count.

questions.q: A data scientist has strong judgment but plans a month-by-month story. What is the most likely consequence, according to the author?
questions.explain: Burying judgment under a timeline risks the lower-level outcome the author describes. The other options invent consequences the chapter does not give.
questions.rule: Visible behavior, visible level.
options: Her story will come across as more honest because it is complete
Her judgment may go unnoticed, and she may be placed below her real level
The interviewer will ask her to repeat it with more technical detail
She will be asked fewer follow-up questions, so the interview will be easier
optionExplain: Completeness is not the author's measure; visibility of behaviors is.
Right: it matches the downlevelling cost the author describes.
No such outcome is described; the worry is that evidence is missed.
The chapter does not claim this; fewer signals may simply leave a weaker impression.

questions.q: Which two outcomes does the author link to telling a project-based story instead of a behavioral one?
questions.explain: The chapter ties project stories to lost offers and lower levels. Repeated questions and metric overload are not mentioned.
questions.rule: Hidden evidence costs offers and level.
options: Interviewers may ask for a second round of the same question
Candidates may be rejected for having too many metrics
Strong candidates may fail to receive an offer
Experienced people may be placed at a lower level
optionExplain: No such outcome appears in the chapter.
The chapter asks you to include metrics, so this is not a cost.
The author says problem-solving that stays hidden can cost the offer.
The author says buried judgment can lead to downlevelling.

questions.q: True or false: If a candidate swaps a chronological telling for one that puts behaviors first, the author expects the interviewer to find the candidate's contributions easier to spot.
questions.explain: The framework exists so that contributions are impossible to miss; moving behaviors forward is how it does that.
questions.rule: Put behaviors where they cannot be missed.

questions.q: A nurse manager plans to memorise her whole ward story word for word, so nothing is left out. What does the author warn about?
questions.explain: The author says lengthy memorised narratives can fall apart when you are under pressure, and offers layers that adapt naturally instead.
questions.rule: Prepare layers, not scripts.
questions.teaches: The author says memorising lengthy narratives is fragile under pressure; building stories in clear layers also makes preparation simpler.
options: Memorising makes the story sound too short to carry real signal
Interviewers mark down any candidate who prepares in advance
A memorised story cannot include numbers about results
A long memorised narrative can fall apart under pressure
optionExplain: Length is not the author's complaint; fragility under pressure is.
The author wants you to prepare, in layers.
Nothing in the chapter says memorising blocks metrics; the worry is brittleness.
Right: the author prefers layers that adapt to wherever the conversation goes.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the jobs the author gives for a good story structure?
questions.explain: Chronology is the one thing the author trades away. The card next lists the five jobs.
options: Walking through events in exact time order so nothing is skipped
Making it easy for the interviewer to capture key points in notes
Putting key behaviors upfront so they are neither missed nor misunderstood
Taking little time to set up, so conversation can go where the interviewer wishes
optionExplain: Right: the author accepts giving up perfect chronology, so this is not a job.
This is a listed job: structure should make note-taking easy.
This is a listed job: behaviors come upfront and clear.
This is a listed job: it should be quick to establish.
questions.rule: Judge any story structure by five jobs: easy notes, behaviors upfront, quick to set up, flexible to follow-ups, and impact inside the story.

questions.q: A good structure includes impact and results as part of the narrative, not saved for the very ____.
questions.explain: The list says impact and results belong inside the narrative rather than being kept for the end.
questions.rule: Impact goes inside the story.

questions.q: A candidate's opening spends four of her ten minutes on setting. Which job does this fail first?
questions.explain: Setup that takes 40 percent of the time is a failure of speed first. The other jobs may suffer as a result.
questions.rule: Short setup keeps room for conversation.
options: Making key points easy for the interviewer to capture in notes
Adapting to different interviewer interests while keeping its shape
Taking a short time to establish, leaving room for conversation
Placing the impact inside the narrative, not after it
optionExplain: Notes may suffer too, but the most direct failure is time spent before any behavior.
Adaptability is a separate job; the main problem here is the clock.
Right: long setup eats the time that should remain for the conversation.
Impact placement is a separate job and not what long setup breaks.

questions.q: Sort each description: does it match one of the five jobs of a good structure, or is it not on the list?
questions.explain: Notes, upfront behaviors, flexibility, quick setup and early impact are the listed jobs. Full chronology and company history are not.
questions.rule: Five jobs, none of them chronology.

items.t: Lets the interviewer capture key points for their notes
Covers every event of the project in order
Still works when the interviewer asks about an unexpected topic
Shows impact as part of the story, not only at the close
Lets you give the history of your employer
Delivers key actions upfront and clearly

questions.q: A sales rep has only 20 minutes for three stories in a screening call. What does the author's time reasoning suggest?
questions.explain: Our reading: the 45-minute argument scales down. Short setup protects the stories still to come.
questions.rule: The shorter the slot, the shorter the setup.
options: Give fuller context for each story, since a short call needs extra clarity
Tell only one story and skip the others, to avoid rushing
Skip the results, since they are the easiest part to ask about later
Keep setup short, since time spent on context is time lost on the other stories
optionExplain: A shorter slot makes long setup costlier, not more useful.
The aim is to cover several stories, not to drop them.
Impact belongs inside the narrative rather than being dropped.
Right: our reading is that the same time argument applies, with more force, in a shorter slot.

questions.q: A panel member writes only a few lines per candidate story. What does that suggest about how to shape a story?
questions.explain: Interviewers keep key points, not transcripts, so a story should make those points easy to capture.
questions.rule: Shape the story for the notes.
questions.teaches: Interviewers do not transcribe a story word for word; they capture the key points in their notes.
options: Say every detail twice so none is missed in the notes
Make its key points easy to lift into a few lines
Speak slowly enough that the interviewer can write down each word
Leave the main result out so the interviewer must ask for it
optionExplain: Repetition lengthens the story; the interviewer already keeps only the key points.
Right: interviewers capture key points rather than transcribing every word.
The author says interviewers do not transcribe every word.
Key results are what they want written down, so hiding them works against you.

questions.q: Which part of a prepared story should you keep ready but not volunteer, because the interviewer decides whether to explore it?
questions.explain: Depth is held back; the summary and key moments are told. The card next names all three layers.
options: The one-sentence summary of what you did and why it mattered, since it frames the story
The two or three key moments that show your actions
Supporting depth, such as alternatives you weighed and wider team dynamics
The measurable outcome that your actions produced
optionExplain: This opens the story, so it is always spoken.
These moments carry the evidence, so they are told unprompted.
Right: depth for follow-ups stays available but unspoken until asked.
Results belong inside the story you tell, not held back.
questions.rule: Build each answer in three layers (a headline, a behavioral core and a base) and prepare the first two to say while keeping the base ready for follow-ups.

questions.q: Match each pyramid layer to what it holds.
questions.explain: The headline is the summary, the core is the evidence of your behaviors, and the base is the depth you keep ready.
questions.rule: Summary, evidence, depth.
pairs: A one-sentence summary of your whole story
Two or three key moments of your thinking and action

questions.q: A hiring manager asks how the candidate got approval to change the live system. Which layer supplies the answer?
questions.explain: A probing follow-up draws on the base. The headline and core have already been told.
questions.rule: Follow-ups draw from the base.
options: The base, since approval details are follow-up depth
The headline, since every question should be answered with it again
The core, which must be retold in full for every question
A new fourth layer built from scratch
optionExplain: Right: stakeholder handling is classic base material, available when asked.
The headline is delivered once at the start; it does not answer follow-ups.
The core is told once; a probing question draws from the base.
The pyramid has three layers; the third is built in response to questions.

questions.q: Sort each item: is it told unprompted in the first two layers, or kept in the base?
questions.explain: The first two layers carry the summary, the key moments and the outcome. Alternatives, wider structure and deeper background wait in the base.
questions.rule: Say the evidence; hold the depth.
groups: Told in the headline or core

items.t: A one-line summary of the problem, my action and why it mattered
The two or three moments where I decided and acted
The other designs I considered and why I set them aside
How the wider organisation was structured around the project
The measurable outcome of my actions
Extra background on why the problem arose in the first place

questions.q: An interviewer cares most about how a candidate got others on board. What changes in the pyramid?
questions.explain: Different interviewers explore different parts of the base, and the structure flexes without the first two layers changing.
questions.rule: The base flexes; the top stays.
options: The headline and core stay as prepared; the interviewer's question draws different material from the base
The candidate must replace the headline with a new one about stakeholders, then rebuild the core around the manager's question
The whole pyramid collapses, since it was built for technical questions
The candidate should repeat the core slowly with added team background
optionExplain: Right: the first two layers stay and the base adapts.
The headline is already given; the follow-up shifts which base material is used.
The design adapts to different interviewer interests without falling apart.
Repeating the core does not answer the new question; the base does.

questions.q: A mobile developer's headline plus core takes twelve minutes. What does the pyramid design suggest went wrong?
questions.explain: The headline and core together form a focused narrative of about two minutes. Twelve minutes suggests base detail was pulled forward.
questions.rule: Two layers, about two minutes.
questions.teaches: The headline and behavioral core together form a focused narrative of roughly two minutes, after which the conversation goes where the interviewer wants.
options: Too little context up front, so the story was stretched to fill the time
The headline was too short to carry the whole story on its own
Base detail crept into the core, which should be about two minutes
The interviewer said too little to steer the story toward the details
optionExplain: Context is what usually bloats a story; extra context is the likelier cause.
A short headline is the design; the bloat is in the core.
Right: the top two layers should be short, with depth held for follow-ups.
The structure asks for a focused core whatever the interviewer does.

questions.q: True or false: In a behavioral interview, a candidate who skips telling events in strict time order is bound to lose marks.
questions.explain: The author accepts this trade: interviewers are judging your capabilities, not recording history. The card next explains the reasoning.
questions.rule: Accept that you will not tell events in strict time order, and give the exact timeline only when the interviewer asks.

questions.q: The author says interviewers are evaluating you, not documenting project and team ____.
questions.explain: The chapter says interviewers are evaluating you, not documenting project and team history.
questions.rule: You are being evaluated, not minuted.

questions.q: A candidate finishes the pyramid. The interviewer moves on without asking about timeline or background. What does the author say to assume?
questions.explain: No follow-up means the interviewer judged the evidence sufficient. If they want detail, they will ask.
questions.rule: Detail comes on request.
options: They missed the story and want it repeated in order
They received what they needed to evaluate you
They were bored, so you should add background
They need an apology for leaving out the chronology
optionExplain: Silence is not a request; if they want the timeline, they ask.
Right: if they do not ask for details, you can assume they got what they needed.
Nothing in the chapter treats silence as boredom, and added background would add noise.
The author calls the trade fine; nothing needs apologising for.

questions.q: A panel member asks the candidate to walk through how events unfolded. What fits the author's approach?
questions.explain: The pyramid defers chronology; it does not forbid it. A request turns that detail into signal for this interviewer.
questions.rule: Defer chronology, never refuse it.
options: Refuse, because chronology is noise in every case
Repeat the headline and wait for another question
Switch to a different story to avoid timelines
Give the sequence, since they have now asked for it
optionExplain: Noise means detail nobody asked for; here it is requested.
A direct request for the sequence deserves an answer.
Switching dodges the request, and nothing in the chapter suggests it.
Right: the author's trade leaves room for the timeline when requested.

questions.q: Sort each item: does the pyramid give it up, or keep it?
questions.explain: The pyramid gives up strict chronology and full history. It keeps the behaviors, the impact and the flexibility.
questions.rule: Trade history for signal.

items.t: Strict beginning-to-end order of events
A full history of the team and project
Your behaviors told clearly
Impact placed inside the narrative
The ability to adapt to follow-up topics
Every twist of what happened

questions.q: A teacher has told her short story. How might she avoid being blindsided by what the interviewer asks next?
questions.explain: The author says to prepare for common follow-up categories, covered later in the chapter and throughout Part II, so no direction takes you by surprise.
questions.rule: Prepare categories, not scripts.
questions.teaches: The author suggests preparing for common follow-up categories (covered later in the chapter and in Part II) so that you are not blindsided wherever the conversation goes.
options: Memorise the story's full timeline in case it is requested
Include all the likely follow-up answers inside the first telling, so nothing has to be added later
Prepare for the common follow-up categories, so any direction feels familiar
Choose only stories that have no follow-up questions
optionExplain: Memorising the whole timeline is the heavy preparation the approach avoids.
That pulls base material forward and buries the signals.
Right: preparing for common follow-up categories is how the author suggests being ready.
Interviewers choose follow-ups, so that cannot be arranged.

questions.q: Which opening sentence is most likely to be written down almost word for word by an interviewer?
questions.explain: A good headline gives the interviewer a specific line to note. The card next shows how.
options: I found the orders slowed because of one report query, and I rewrote it so checkout ran twice as fast
So this was at my last company, which sells software to schools, and I joined about two years in
I want to tell you about a project that had a lot of moving parts and many different teams
I am quite a hands-on person who enjoys solving whatever problems come my way
optionExplain: Right: it names the problem, the action and the result in a sentence a note-taker can lift.
This is background about the employer, not what you did.
It promises a story but says nothing specific for the notes.
A trait statement gives the interviewer nothing concrete to record.
questions.rule: Open with one sentence that holds your whole story, written so the interviewer could note it almost word for word.

questions.q: The goal is for the interviewer to write down your opening sentence almost ____.
questions.explain: The aim is a headline concrete enough to be written down almost verbatim.
questions.rule: Write the line they would note.

questions.q: A graphic designer is asked about a time she changed her mind. Which headline follows the rule?
questions.explain: The strong headline names the decision and its result. The others offer background, vagueness or company detail.
questions.rule: Headline equals problem, action, result.
options: Let me tell you about my background in design, where I have worked for about eight years now
Let me tell you about a client project that was quite challenging for everyone on the team
Let me tell you about the brand agency I worked at and how it picks its clients each year
Let me tell you about dropping my favourite logo after tests showed it confused buyers; sign-ups rose
optionExplain: It describes a career, not the story that answers the question.
It is vague about what the designer did or achieved.
It is company context, which the headline should leave out.
Right: it carries the situation, the decision and the result in one sentence.

questions.q: Which two jobs does the author give a headline?
questions.explain: A headline confirms the question and previews your contribution. Company background and step lists do not belong.
questions.rule: Confirm the question, preview the contribution.
options: It previews your specific contribution
It confirms you understood the question
It lists every step of the project in order
It summarises the company and team background
optionExplain: The headline tells the interviewer what you did that mattered.
The author lists this as a core function of the headline.
The headline is one sentence; the steps belong to the core.
The author says the headline is not a summary of context.

questions.q: True or false: If the interviewer knows a story's destination from the headline, they can focus on how you got there rather than wondering where you are going.
questions.explain: This is the author's account of signposting: knowing your destination lets the listener follow the route.
questions.rule: Name the destination first.

questions.q: A coach writes headline guidance for athletes asked about a comeback. What term does the author use for telling listeners where the story is heading?
questions.explain: Signposting is the author's name for previewing a story's direction, which helps the listener follow along.
questions.rule: Signpost the destination.
questions.teaches: Previewing where a story is going is called signposting; it lets the interviewer focus on how you got to the result instead of wondering where you are heading.
options: Anchoring, which fixes the interviewer's view of the company
Signposting, which lets listeners follow how you got there
Framing, which controls how the question is worded
Padding, which fills time before the core begins
optionExplain: Anchoring is not the author's term, and the aim is not about the company.
Right: the author names this signposting and says it helps the interviewer follow your narrative.
Framing is not used here, and the candidate does not control the question.
Padding is what the headline avoids; the headline works hard in a few seconds.

questions.q: Two of your prepared stories could answer the question asked. What is a good way to proceed?
questions.explain: Letting the interviewer choose uses your preparation and keeps them in control. The card next explains the format.
options: Tell the longer story, since it must have more evidence in it
Briefly describe both and let the interviewer pick the one they prefer
Tell both stories in full, one after the other, to be safe
Say neither fits and ask for a different question
optionExplain: Length is not a reason to choose; relevance to the question matters.
Right: offering options puts the interviewer in control of the direction.
Two full tellings use up time and bury signals.
That throws away good material and may look unprepared.
questions.rule: When more than one story fits, offer two short headlines and ask which is more relevant.

questions.q: After offering two headlines, you ask the interviewer which of the two is more ____ to what they are assessing.
questions.explain: The author's example ends with the question of which is more relevant.
questions.rule: Ask which is more relevant.

questions.q: A paramedic can answer a question on prioritising with two stories. Which is the best way to offer them?
questions.explain: Good options are short previews of what you did, followed by a question. The others lack previews or the invitation to choose.
questions.rule: Preview two, then ask.
options: I have lots of stories about prioritising from several roles, so ask me anything you like about my career and I will pick
I have two examples, but I will tell the first one because it is my best
I have two examples; the first happened in March and the second the following spring
I have two examples: triaging four patients at a crash scene, or reordering our shift handover. Which is more relevant?
optionExplain: Vague and unfocused; it gives the interviewer nothing to choose from.
This takes the choice away from the interviewer.
Dates do not tell the interviewer what each story is about.
Right: each option previews the action in a few words, and the choice is handed over.

questions.q: Sort each offer: does it follow the options rule, or break it?
questions.explain: A good offer is two informative previews plus a question. Bare labels, long lists and one story in full do not give a useful choice.
questions.rule: Informative previews, then a choice.

items.t: Two one-line previews of different actions, then a question about which fits
Two story names such as 'the migration' and 'the outage' with no detail
Four stories read out as a list with no question
Two previews that each name a problem and an action, then asking which is better
Telling one story in full and mentioning another exists
Offering a choice because both stories truly answer the question

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, offering headline options shows the interviewer that you have many strong examples.
questions.explain: The author says a choice shows you have many strong examples, as well as handing the interviewer control.
questions.rule: A choice signals preparation.

questions.q: A teacher is asked about leadership. She has one clear story that fits and one weak one. What does the book's offering advice suggest?
questions.explain: Our reading: the offer is for genuine options. The author's example gives each option enough information for the interviewer to choose what they are evaluating, so an option with nothing to choose by adds no value.
questions.rule: Offer genuine options with enough detail.
questions.teaches: Each option must give enough information for the interviewer to choose by what they are evaluating, so an option works like a mini headline rather than a bare label.
options: Tell the clear story, since the offer is meant for when several stories could answer
Offer both anyway, so the panel sees how many she has
Offer no story and ask the panel what they want to hear
Tell both stories in a row, starting with the weak one as a warm-up before the clear one
optionExplain: Right: our reading is that the choice format fits several good matches, not one.
A weak option dilutes the offer and may waste the panel's choice.
The question is already clear; a specific story answers it.
Telling the weak story adds noise and uses up time.

questions.q: After you speak your opening sentence, what is a good next move?
questions.explain: A short pause both lets the headline sink in and lets the interviewer redirect. The card next gives the reasoning.
options: Keep talking at once so the story has momentum and no gaps
Ask whether the interviewer is satisfied with your general background before moving to the details
Pause briefly so the interviewer can react, then continue if they do not redirect
Repeat the sentence in different words to make sure it lands
optionExplain: It gives the interviewer no chance to redirect you early.
That moves the topic away from the story you just previewed.
Right: it leaves room for the interviewer to say it is not what they sought.
Repetition adds nothing; the pause gives the sentence room to land.
questions.rule: Keep the headline a preview of what you did that mattered, not a summary of context, then pause briefly before moving into the core.

questions.q: Your headline is not a summary of the project context or your company; it previews what you did that ____.
questions.explain: The headline is a preview of what you did that mattered.
questions.rule: Preview what mattered.

questions.q: A bank analyst is asked about a data error. Which headline follows the rule?
questions.explain: The correct headline previews action and result. The others describe the setting.
questions.rule: Preview the contribution.
options: Our bank is a mid-sized lender with branches in four regions and a large analytics group
Our reporting team had recently expanded and was running several new systems side by side
The data error was complicated and had been a recurring problem for quite some time before I arrived, so I had a lot to untangle
I traced the misreported balances to a rounding step in one overnight job and corrected it, so reports matched the ledger
optionExplain: This is company context, not what she did.
Team and system context says nothing about her contribution.
It adds drama but no action or result.
Right: it previews what she did and the result.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, if the interviewer does not respond to your headline, you can continue to the behavioral core.
questions.explain: The author says that if they do not respond, you continue.
questions.rule: Silence means go on.

questions.q: After a headline about fixing an outage, an interviewer says, 'Actually, I wanted an example of influencing others.' What does the pause allow?
questions.explain: A pause earns its place when it catches a mismatch early. You can then pivot to a better fit.
questions.rule: The pause saves time.
options: Continuing with the outage story in case they change their mind
Switching to a story that matches what they asked for
Reading out the whole outage story as a courtesy
Asking them to restate their question in writing
optionExplain: Pressing on ignores the signal the pause was meant to collect.
Right: the pause gave them the chance to redirect before you invested time.
That spends the time the pause was meant to save.
It is an unusual request and not what the pause is for.

questions.q: A coach tells job seekers how long a headline should take to say. What does the chapter give as the time to confirm, preview and create interest?
questions.explain: A headline is brief by design. Ten to fifteen seconds is enough to confirm the question, preview your contribution and create interest.
questions.rule: A headline takes seconds.
questions.teaches: A headline should take only about 10 to 15 seconds to confirm you understood, preview your contribution and create interest.
options: About 2 minutes
About 45 seconds, about the length of a short paragraph of speech
About 10 to 15 seconds
About 5 minutes
optionExplain: That is the length of headline plus core together, not the headline alone.
Too long for a single sentence; the chapter's figure is shorter.
Right: the chapter gives 10 to 15 seconds for the headline.
Five minutes is the amount of context the chapter warns against.

questions.q: How many key moments does the author suggest sharing in the middle layer of a story?
questions.explain: Two or three moments is the guidance. The card next explains what each should show.
options: Two or three, each showing something
One, to keep the story as short as possible
Five or six, so no action is left out
As many as the project had, in order
optionExplain: Right: enough to give a complete picture without losing focus.
One moment may be too little evidence to judge from.
That many dilutes the focus and moves the core toward a full history.
A complete event list is the project-history approach the framework avoids.
questions.rule: Fill the core with two or three key moments that show your thinking and your actions, with their impact included.

questions.q: The core is where you show your behaviors by describing your specific ____ and actions.
questions.explain: The core describes your specific thoughts and actions.
questions.rule: Core equals thoughts plus actions.

questions.q: A logistics planner is drafting the core of a story about cutting late deliveries. Which draft follows the rule?
questions.explain: A good core has a few moments, each with action and impact. The wrong drafts are a list, company context and a claim.
questions.rule: A few moments, each with impact.
options: Two moments: she spotted late deliveries clustered on one route and rerouted it, cutting lateness by a third
Eleven steps in date order, from the first complaint to the final report
A description of the courier firm's size, fleet and regions, then a line on the result and a note on her title
One sentence saying she is a strong planner who delivers on time
optionExplain: Right: it shows noticing, acting and impact in a small number of moments.
A long event list becomes project history and dilutes the focus.
Company description is context, and impact is tacked on at the end.
A claim about herself shows no behavior to evaluate.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate keeps all of her results for a final minute after the core, so the actions can stand alone. This follows the author's advice.
