questions.explain: The author puts impact and metrics inside the core, as part of each moment, so the picture is complete.
questions.rule: Impact belongs inside the story.

questions.q: A candidate's core has six moments of equal weight. What does the author predict?
questions.explain: The author says more than three key points dilute the focus. The idea is to choose the strongest.
questions.rule: Choose the strongest few.
options: The interviewer will be more convinced because of the volume of detail
The interviewer will skip the headline because the core is so long
The focus is diluted, so the strongest evidence is harder to spot
The candidate will be asked to restart with the base layer instead
optionExplain: Volume is not the aim; more points weaken focus.
No such effect is described; the problem is dilution.
Right: more than three points dilute the focus.
Nothing in the chapter describes a restart rule.

questions.q: A carpenter explains each key moment in her core. What pattern does the author give for describing a single moment?
questions.explain: Each moment follows a simple pattern: minimal context, thought or decision, action and result.
questions.rule: Context, thought, action, result.
questions.teaches: Each key moment follows a simple pattern: minimal context, your thought process or decision, your action, and what resulted.
options: Full background, then the team's debate, then the final decision by the manager, then the result
Minimal context, then her thought process or decision, then her action, then what resulted
The tools used, then the materials, then the schedule, then the invoice
A lesson learned, then the situation, then a general principle
optionExplain: Team debate and a manager's decision move away from her own behavior.
Right: the four-part pattern for one moment.
A list of project items does not show her thinking or choices.
Starting with a lesson reverses the order and drops the action.

questions.q: Which kind of detail is best left out of a story's behavioral core?
questions.explain: The core keeps your reasoning and results; company history is the clearest detail to cut. The card next lists what is present and missing.
options: How you noticed the problem in the first place
The number that shows what changed after your fix, such as time saved
How you tested your idea before rolling it out
A history of the company and how it came to build the product
optionExplain: Noticing is a thought-process step, which is signal.
Measurable impact belongs in the core.
Your investigation method shows how you work.
Right: company history is background that hides your behavior.
questions.rule: Check a draft by what it holds: reasoning, investigation, decisions and results should be there; company history, org charts, tool stories and meeting accounts should be absent.

questions.q: Match each story element to what it counts as in a behavioral core.
questions.explain: Observations and results are signal. Company structure and others' earlier attempts are left out of the core.
questions.rule: Behavior in, surroundings out.
pairs: The measurable result of your fix
Setting: left out of the core
Others' history: left out of the core

questions.q: A candidate's draft mentions the tech stack, the team size and a weekly status meeting. Which edit follows the rule?
questions.explain: Cut the setting and keep the decision and result. The others add noise or push signal late.
questions.rule: Cut setting, keep decisions.
options: Keep all three and add the company history for completeness
Replace the result with a description of how the team felt about the long project
Cut those three, and keep the part where she decided on a fix and measured its effect
Move the fix to the very end, after the meeting details
optionExplain: More setting adds noise rather than signal.
Feelings of the team do not show her behavior.
Right: the three details are setting; her decision and measurement are the core.
Delaying the action pushes signal behind noise.

questions.q: Sort each sentence from a draft: does it belong in a behavioral core, or was it pulled in from elsewhere?
questions.explain: Noticing, investigating and a measured result are core. Founding history, meeting length and others' earlier attempts are left out.
questions.rule: What I did stays; what happened around me goes.

items.t: I noticed the delays hit only one customer group, so I doubted a network cause
The company was founded by two former bankers eleven years ago
I added timing logs and found the real delay was in a single query
The weekly planning meeting ran for ninety minutes on Tuesdays
Processing fell from eight seconds to under one
Before me, a contractor had tried adding retries

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a core with no company history, team structure or tech stack can still let the interviewer judge your ability.
questions.explain: The author says those items are not needed; what separates strong from weak responses is the focus on behaviors.
questions.rule: Focus on behaviors.

questions.q: A librarian's sample core includes a line about studying a new subject and consulting an expert. Is that a mistake?
questions.explain: The sample core's list of what is present includes learning. Brief mention of consulting experts shows how the person worked.
questions.rule: Learning and teamwork can be signal.
questions.teaches: A short line about learning and working with experts belongs in the core when it was part of what you did; the sample counts learning among its present items.
options: No, because learning and working with experts are part of what she did
Yes, because the core must hold only observation and results, not anything about learning
Yes, because any mention of other people is company detail
No, but only when the expert is a senior manager
optionExplain: Right: the author's sample counts learning and collaboration among the present items.
The sample core also includes learning and working with others.
Naming a helper is different from describing the org chart.
Seniority of the expert is not a condition in the sample.

questions.q: You have extra detail on how you chose between two designs. When should you share it?
questions.explain: Alternatives are base material, kept ready until the interviewer asks. The card next explains why.
options: At the start, so the interviewer knows you are thorough
Never, since interviewers dislike hearing about rejected ideas
Only in your headline, so the whole story rests on it
When the interviewer asks about alternatives or trade-offs
optionExplain: Volunteering it up front hides the main story.
Alternatives are part of what the base is for.
A headline previews your main contribution, not a trade-off.
Right: it is ready, and a question calls it up.
questions.rule: Prepare technical detail, team dynamics, extra context, alternatives considered and deeper lessons, and share them only when asked.

questions.q: The base holds details you should prepare but not ____ up front.
questions.explain: The base is for follow-ups and not for volunteering.
questions.rule: Prepare it; do not volunteer it.

questions.q: A customer-success lead has finished her core and is asked why she did not roll out to every client at once. Where does her answer come from?
questions.explain: Alternatives and trade-offs live in the base. The interviewer's question calls it up.
questions.rule: Follow-up questions open the base.
options: The headline, which she repeats in more detail and extends with new facts
The base, where she holds the alternatives she weighed
A new story with a different set of facts
The core, which she tells again from the start
optionExplain: The headline is a preview; it does not hold trade-offs.
Right: a question about options she considered draws on the base.
Switching stories wastes the prepared layer.
Retelling the core does not answer the question about alternatives.

questions.q: Sort each item: base material to keep ready, or something that belongs in the core?
questions.explain: The base holds technical detail, wider team dynamics, alternatives and deeper lessons. The core holds your decisions and results.
questions.rule: Core: what I did and got. Base: the rest.

items.t: Implementation details of the technical fix
The result of my actions in numbers
How the wider team's dynamics shaped the project
Which alternative designs I weighed
My decision at the key point and why I took it
The deeper lesson I took away years later

questions.q: A candidate pulls base details into her core, hoping to be helpful. What does the author say will happen?
questions.explain: Pulling base details into the core is how noise enters. Signals get buried under unnecessary information.
questions.rule: Base detail in the core is noise.
options: The interviewer will see how thorough she is and rate her higher
Her behavioral signals get buried under unnecessary information
The interviewer will skip her headline because the core is complete
Her follow-up answers will gain more weight because they came earlier
optionExplain: The author says more context does not help; it buries signal.
Right: the author calls this how noise enters a story.
The effect described is burying signal, not skipping the headline.
Earlier delivery of base material does not add weight to later answers.

questions.q: A chef is asked how she redesigned her kitchen workflow, and she holds a lot of detail. How should she deliver it?
questions.explain: Technical depth is given in layers: the most relevant detail first, then a pause to see whether more is wanted.
questions.rule: Layer the depth.
questions.teaches: Give technical detail in neat layers: start with the most relevant detail, pause, and offer to go deeper if the interviewer seems to want more.
options: Give every detail she has in one go, in the order it happened, so nothing needs to be asked
Give one sentence, then change the subject to avoid going deeper
Recite a memorised answer in full, however the question is worded
Start with the most relevant detail, then pause to see if the interviewer wants more
optionExplain: That dumps the whole base at once and buries what matters.
Changing the subject leaves the question unanswered.
A fixed recital ignores what this interviewer asked.
Right: detail goes out in neat layers, and the interviewer's interest decides the depth.

questions.q: Three people interview you about one story. Why might their follow-up questions differ?
questions.explain: People probe what their role cares about. The card next gives three examples.
options: Each explores the part of your story that matters to their role
Each had a different version of the story told to them
Each is checking that your first telling stays the same each time
They are following a script that forces them to ask different things
optionExplain: Right: different interviewers probe different parts of the base.
You told one story; the difference is in what they explore.
The author says nothing about consistency checks as the reason.
The author describes interest tied to role, not a fixed script.
questions.rule: Prepare base material for several kinds of interviewer, and answer the question you are asked instead of guessing which one you face.

questions.q: Match each interviewer to the follow-up the author gives.
questions.explain: The author pairs technical detail with a technical interviewer, buy-in with a manager and safeguarding users and data with a senior leader.
questions.rule: Match the probe to the person.
pairs: What was the specific issue with the cause?
How did you get buy-in for the change?
How did you protect users and their data?

questions.q: A hiring manager asks a candidate how she convinced the finance team to fund her plan. Which base area does she draw on?
questions.explain: A question about winning support from finance is about working with others, not technical depth.
questions.rule: Identify the kind of question.
options: Technical detail, such as the code of the solution
Scale and metrics, such as throughput figures
Working with others, such as stakeholder buy-in
Failure and recovery, such as an earlier setback
optionExplain: The question is about persuading people, not code.
Numbers may help, but the question asks about persuasion.
Right: gaining support from another team is the collaboration category.
Nothing in the question asks about a failure.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate decides to prepare only for technical follow-ups because her story was technical. This matches the author's advice.
questions.explain: The author's three probes show that a technical story can draw technical, managerial and leadership questions.
questions.rule: Prepare for several interviewers.

questions.q: A candidate's story is followed by three different interviewers. If she prepared a rich base, what is likely?
questions.explain: The headline and core stay; the base supplies different answers to different probes.
questions.rule: One story, many probes.
options: She must rewrite the whole story for each interviewer
She must ask each interviewer what they want before starting
She must give the same answer to all of them to seem consistent
She can answer each probe without changing her headline or core
optionExplain: Rewriting defeats the purpose of a base.
The pyramid lets her start, then follow their lead.
Consistency of facts is not the same as identical answers; each probe differs.
Right: the base flexes while the top two layers stay the same.

questions.q: A candidate for a senior post wants to know why interviewers' probes differ. What does the chapter give as the cause?
questions.explain: The chapter says different interviewers explore different parts of the base depending on what matters for the roles they are aiming to fill.
questions.rule: Probes follow the role.
questions.teaches: Interviewers explore different parts of your base depending on what matters for the roles they are trying to fill.
options: Interviewers are told to ask random questions to test composure
Each interviewer explores what matters for the roles they are aiming to fill
Interviewers look for faults in stories told by senior candidates, who are held to a higher standard
Interviewers try to stretch the interview to fill the time
optionExplain: Nothing in the chapter suggests random probing.
Right: the chapter ties probes to what the interviewer's role needs.
The chapter does not say that senior candidates are probed for faults.
Filling time is not a reason the chapter gives.

questions.q: What is one weakness of the STAR format, according to the author?
questions.explain: STAR's equal weighting pushes candidates to over-explain context. The card next shows the details.
options: It leaves out the Result, so impact is never mentioned
It requires telling events out of order, which confuses listeners and hides the result
It treats all four parts equally, so people spend too long on context
It forbids using numbers in the story at any stage
optionExplain: STAR includes Result; the problem is the balance of time.
STAR is usually told in order; confusion is not the author's complaint.
Right: Situation and Task are context, yet get as much time as Action.
STAR has no such ban.
questions.rule: Do not give every STAR part equal time, and do not invent a Task when you acted on your own initiative.

questions.q: The author says Situation and Task are context rather than your ____.
questions.explain: The author says Situation and Task are really context, while Action shows your behaviors.
questions.rule: Situation and Task are context.

questions.q: A candidate noticed a recurring support error and started a fix nobody had asked for. Why would forcing a Task into STAR hurt her?
questions.explain: A made-up assignment turns an initiative story into a passive one. The honest version shows she saw the problem herself.
questions.rule: Do not invent an assignment.
options: It would make her seem to act only when assigned, which is untrue and passive
It would make her story too short to count as evidence, since the missing detail cannot be replaced
It would hide her result, which STAR does not allow
It would show too much initiative for a junior role
optionExplain: Right: the author says forcing a task can make you appear passive.
Forcing a task adds words rather than removing them.
The issue is the invented task, not the result.
The author says initiative beyond assigned work is a strength.

questions.q: Sort each statement: is it a criticism of STAR the author makes, or not?
questions.explain: The author's complaints are equal weighting, over-long context, the forced Task and its poor fit for senior roles. Missing results and brevity are not on the list.
questions.rule: Equal weight, forced Task.

items.t: All components are treated as equally important
People spend too much time on Situation and Task
It leaves candidates unable to talk about results
Not every story has a clear assigned task
It is too short to fill a two-minute answer
Senior work does not come as assigned tasks

questions.q: A staff-level candidate with no assigned tasks forces a STAR Task into her story. What does the author predict?
questions.explain: For senior roles and above, the author says tasks are rarely assigned, so forcing one misrepresents how the candidate works.
questions.rule: Fit the format to the work.
options: She may seem passive, since senior work does not come as assigned tasks
She will seem more organised and professional, because the format is complete and familiar
She will gain time, because Task is the shortest STAR part
She will be moved up a level for using a recognised format
optionExplain: Right: the forced Task clashes with how senior work is done.
The author sees the forced Task as a weakness.
The author's concern is wasted time on context, not saved time.
Nothing in the chapter links STAR use to promotion.

questions.q: A coach says STAR is a wrong approach and should be dropped. How does the author describe STAR and CARL?
questions.explain: The author is balanced: STAR and CARL are not wrong approaches, but they can lead to anti-patterns that weaken stories.
questions.rule: Useful, with traps.
questions.teaches: The author calls STAR and CARL helpful frameworks that are not wrong, while noting they often lead to anti-patterns that weaken stories.
options: As flawed methods that have misled countless candidates over many years of use
As formats that suit only entry-level candidates
As approaches that help many people but can lead to anti-patterns
As formats that interviewers ask candidates to use
optionExplain: The author says they have helped countless people.
The author's criticism includes senior roles but not that limit.
Right: the author says they are not wrong, but can weaken stories.
No such interviewer instruction appears in the chapter.

questions.q: A story ends with, 'I learned that talking to partners is important.' What is the likely problem, according to the author?
questions.explain: A generic lesson tacked on to every story weakens it. The card next explains where the trap comes from.
options: It is too specific for an interviewer to follow
It is a forced, generic insight that adds nothing specific
It shows too little respect for the partners involved
It places the result after the lesson, which breaks the order
optionExplain: The sentence is generic, not too specific.
Right: the author warns about forced or generic insights.
Respect for partners is not the issue.
Order is not the issue; the vagueness is.
questions.rule: Add a learning only when you have a real one; do not close every story with a forced lesson.

questions.q: CARL improves on STAR by dropping Task and adding ____.
questions.explain: CARL stands for Context, Action, Result, Learning, dropping STAR's Task.
questions.rule: CARL swaps Task for Learning.

questions.q: An intern's project was small and produced a clear 30 percent time saving, but no profound insight. How should she end her story?
questions.explain: Impact is the stronger ending here. A forced lesson would sound generic.
questions.rule: Honest ending beats a forced one.
options: With an invented lesson, because every story needs one
With a general principle about teamwork, to show maturity
With an apology that the project taught her little
With the time saving, as the impact is the strongest part
optionExplain: The author warns against forced learnings.
A general principle would be the generic insight the author warns about.
Apologising draws attention to a weakness for no reason.
Right: sometimes impact and metrics matter more than learning.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate says CARL is flawed because it keeps the Task from STAR. This matches the author's critique.
questions.explain: CARL drops Task. The author's issue with CARL is the mandatory Learning.
questions.rule: CARL drops Task; Learning is the trap.

questions.q: A candidate inserts a lesson at the end of every story, whether real or not. What does the author predict?
questions.explain: Making learning compulsory leads to forced or generic insight, as in the author's own example.
questions.rule: No forced lessons.
options: Each story will be shorter, because the lessons replace the results
Interviewers will reward the consistency of the format
Some insights will sound forced or generic
The lessons will move into the headline automatically
optionExplain: Nothing in the chapter says the lesson replaces the result.
The author sees consistency here as a weakness.
Right: a mandatory learning produces forced or generic lines.
Nothing in the chapter describes lessons moving to the headline.

questions.q: A career coach asks which candidates are least likely to have a profound lesson from each project. Who does the author name?
questions.explain: The author's point is that learning is not always the right ending, and entry-level candidates may not have profound ones from each project.
questions.rule: Learning must be real.
questions.teaches: Entry-level candidates may not draw profound learnings from every project, so a mandatory Learning step can force empty insights.
options: Entry-level candidates, who may not draw deep learnings from every project
Principal-level candidates, who have seen so much that they no longer learn from projects
Candidates who skipped the headline in their story
Candidates working in teams of more than ten people
optionExplain: Right: the author says entry-level candidates may not experience profound learnings every time.
The author does not say senior people learn less.
The headline is unrelated to whether a lesson exists.
Team size is not tied to learning in the chapter.

questions.q: You rebuild a STAR story as a pyramid. Which part do you expand the most?
questions.explain: Action is the part that shows your behavior, so it grows. The card next shows where the other parts go.
options: Situation, so the listener has all the background
Task, so the assignment is perfectly clear
Learning, so every story ends with a lesson
Action, with your thoughts and decisions
optionExplain: Situation is context, which shrinks.
Task is context too, and may not exist at all.
Learning moves to the base rather than growing.
Right: Action carries your behaviors, so it grows.
questions.rule: Rebuild each STAR story by moving its parts: highlights to the headline, Action expanded in the core, Situation and Task shrunk, Result into the core, Learning to the base.

questions.q: In the pyramid, Learning moves to your ____.
questions.explain: Learning moves to the base, ready if you are asked.
questions.rule: Learning goes to the base.

questions.q: A candidate's STAR story spends three minutes on Situation and Task. How should she convert it?
questions.explain: The conversion shrinks Situation and Task and grows Action. Result moves into the core.
questions.rule: Shrink context, grow action.
options: Delete Action, since the interviewer already knows what she did
Shrink them to a line of context and expand Action with her decisions
Keep Result as a separate section at the end, as in STAR
Keep all the context but add a headline in front of it
optionExplain: Action is the heart of the core.
Right: context shrinks and Action grows.
Result belongs inside the core in the pyramid.
That leaves the long setup that the pyramid removes.

questions.q: Sort each element of a STAR story: does it grow or stay in the spoken story, or shrink and move to the base?
questions.explain: Action and Result carry the evidence and stay in the spoken story, and the headline draws on the highlights. Situation, Task and Learning shrink or wait in the base.
questions.rule: Grow action; shrink context; shelve learning.
groups: Grows or stays in the spoken story
Shrinks or waits in the base

items.t: Action, with your thoughts and decisions added
Result, folded into the core
Situation, cut to a line of context
Task, minimised by default
Learning, held ready for a question
The highlights of Situation, Action and Result in the headline

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, once you convert a STAR story, Situation and Task are gone for good.
questions.explain: They are minimised by default, but can be fleshed out in your base if needed.
questions.rule: Minimised, not deleted.

questions.q: A baker has a prepared CARL story: Context, Action, Result, Learning. Using the author's STAR conversion, which move fits best?
questions.explain: Our reading: the author gives the conversion for STAR, and the same moves carry over to CARL. Expand Action, put Result in the core, minimise Context and hold Learning in the base. Situation and Task can be fleshed out in the base if needed.
questions.rule: Reuse, don't restart.
questions.teaches: Situation and Task are minimised by default, but they can be fleshed out in your base if an interviewer needs them.
options: Invent a Task so it fits STAR, then convert it using the author's steps
Build the headline from the key parts, expand Action, keep Result in the core and Learning in the base
Tell all four parts at equal length so that nothing is missed or skipped over
Put Learning into the headline so that it is not forgotten by the interviewer
optionExplain: Not needed: the author says forcing a task onto a story can make you look passive.
Right: our reading is that the same moves apply to CARL stories.
Equal treatment is the fault the author found in STAR.
The headline pulls from Situation, Action and Result; Learning moves to the base.

questions.q: In a behavioral interview story, which detail is a signal rather than noise?
questions.explain: Signals show how you worked; the other options describe the surroundings. The card next defines both terms.
options: How the company's product line expanded over the previous five years
Who was on the team and how long each of them had been there
Why the original architect chose the tools that were in place
How you worked out the cause of the problem and why you chose your fix
optionExplain: This is company background and does not show how you work.
Team background is context, and it only matters if it is central to the story.
Someone else's decision is not evidence of your own behavior.
Right: your reasoning and decisions are the evidence interviewers need.
questions.rule: Make your core heavy on signal (evidence of how you behaved) and keep out noise, which is anything that lengthens the story without showing how you work.

questions.q: Noise is everything else that makes your story longer without showing how you actually ____.
questions.explain: Noise lengthens the story without showing how you actually work.
questions.rule: Noise adds length without evidence.

questions.q: A paramedic's draft story has four sentences. Which one is signal?
questions.explain: The signal sentence has her observing, deciding and acting. The others are background or events around her.
questions.rule: Ask whether it shows my behavior.
options: I saw the delays came from our handover form, so I tested a shorter one for two weeks
Our service covers three counties and has been running for over forty years
We had recently moved from paper records to a new tablet system in all vehicles across the region
There were several meetings about the delays before anyone proposed anything
optionExplain: Right: it shows what she noticed, decided and did.
Service history is background that does not show her behavior, so it is noise.
A system change may be context, but it shows nothing she did.
Meetings describe what happened around her, not what she did.

questions.q: Sort each detail from a sample story: signal for the interviewer, or noise that hides the signals?
questions.explain: Prototyping, results and investigation are signals. Company pivots, team composition and timeline detail are noise unless central.
questions.rule: Signal shows what I did; noise shows what surrounded me.

items.t: I decided to prototype it over a weekend to test the idea quickly
The firm had pivoted from consumer products to business customers the year before
My change cut costs by about forty percent
Our team included three seniors, two mid-levels and four juniors
I noticed errors appeared only at lunchtime and checked whether load was the cause
The project began in January and the first meeting was in February

questions.q: A candidate adds company background to her core, thinking it helps the interviewer understand. What does the author expect?
questions.explain: The author notes you might think more context helps, but it buries signals under unnecessary information.
questions.rule: More context can mean less signal.
options: The interviewer appreciates the fuller picture and rates her higher
The interviewer ignores the extra context and notes only her actions
The extra context buries her signals instead of helping
The extra context makes the follow-up questions easier to answer
optionExplain: The author argues the opposite: extra context does not help.
The context does harm by hiding signals, not just by being ignored.
Right: the author says more context actually buries signals under unnecessary information.
Follow-ups draw on the base; volunteering it earlier does not help.

questions.q: A hiring panel member says they note a candidate's signals down and bring them up later. When does the author say this happens?
questions.explain: Interviewers are trained to write your signals down and bring them up during the debrief when hiring decisions are made, which is why unrecorded detail does not count.
questions.rule: Only recorded signal counts.
questions.teaches: Interviewers are trained to write your signals down and bring them up in the debrief where hiring decisions are made, so only what they record can count for you.
options: In a reference call, after the candidate has already received an offer
In the first minute, before the candidate has described any actions
In a feedback email to the candidate, soon after the interview ends
In the debrief, when hiring decisions are being made
optionExplain: Reference checks are a separate step in the chapter's red-flag list, not where signals are discussed.
Signals come from what the candidate says, so they are not available yet.
The chapter does not describe feedback emails.
Right: interviewers are trained to write signals down and use them in the debrief.

questions.q: Which sentence shows the signal 'decision-making' rather than a plain action?
questions.explain: A decision signal contains the options and the reason for the pick. The card next names all five signals.
options: I built the cheaper fix in two days and shipped it to all clinics
I chose the cheaper fix over the rebuild because demand would not grow for a year
I presented the result to the board and received their congratulations on a job well done
I reduced waiting times from forty minutes to fifteen across the site
optionExplain: This reports an action and its speed, not a choice between options.
Right: it names a choice and the reason behind it.
This is a presentation and reaction, not a decision with a reason.
This is a result, which is a different kind of signal.
questions.rule: Check that your story shows how you figured things out, how you decided, what you did, how you worked with others and what resulted.

questions.q: Match each signal type to a sentence from a sample story.
questions.explain: Each sentence shows a different kind of signal: investigation, a choice with a reason, collaboration and outcome.
questions.rule: Five kinds, one checklist.
pairs: I noticed errors only at lunchtime and checked load first
I chose a redesign because growth would repeat the issue
I wrote a migration plan the backend team could follow on their schedule
Processing fell from thirty seconds to two

questions.q: A candidate's draft has her noticing, deciding and acting, but nothing about others or results. What should she add?
questions.explain: The draft needs collaboration and impact signals. The other options add noise.
questions.rule: Fill the missing signal kinds.
options: A longer account of the company's history to place the story in context
More detail on the tools she used, to prove technical depth
How she worked with others and the measurable result of her work
A summary of the project timeline to show how long it took
optionExplain: Company history is noise, not one of the five signals.
Tool detail is not one of the five signals.
Right: these are the two signal kinds her draft lacks.
A timeline is noise unless duration matters.

questions.q: Sort each sentence: is it a signal about the candidate, or a statement about the setting?
questions.explain: Signals describe the candidate's own noticing, planning, building and results. Platform design, company size and general unhappiness are setting.
questions.rule: Is the sentence about me or about it?

items.t: I built a prototype over the weekend to test the approach
The platform used separate services for payments and shipping
I knew the other team would resist, so I offered a gradual plan
The company had around two hundred employees at the time
My change cut infrastructure costs by forty percent
Customers were unhappy about slow loading in general

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, if a story shows only results and no sign of how you figured things out, the interviewer still gets the data points they need to evaluate you.
questions.explain: The author lists five kinds of signal the interviewer needs; a story with only results lacks the thinking and decision signals.
questions.rule: Several kinds of signal are needed.

questions.q: A coach reviews a decision signal: 'I chose the redesign because our growth rate would hit the same problem by Q3.' What makes it strong?
questions.explain: The author's decision example names a quick fix and a redesign, then the evidence for choosing the redesign.
questions.rule: Decision means options plus reasons.
questions.teaches: A strong decision signal names the alternatives you weighed and the evidence behind your choice, as in the example of choosing a redesign because growth would repeat the problem by Q3.
options: It names the options and the evidence behind the choice
It uses a date, and dates always make a decision sound credible
It avoids saying the quick fix was ever considered, keeping it short
It credits the whole team, which shows humility above all
optionExplain: Right: the author's example weighs a quick fix against a redesign and gives a reason from growth data.
The date is part of the evidence, but the strength comes from options plus reasons.
Naming the option not taken is part of what makes it a decision signal.
The sentence is about the candidate's choice, not team credit.

questions.q: A candidate says, 'The firm began as a family printing business and grew through three mergers.' What kind of noise is this?
questions.explain: Company history is the first noise type. The card next lists all four.
options: Too much company context
Excessive team detail
An over-explained technology decision
A drawn-out timeline
optionExplain: Right: it is company history that does not show her behavior.
No team members are described in this sentence.
The sentence does not mention any technology choice.
There is no month-by-month sequence in this line.
questions.rule: Cut company backstory, staffing details, long explanations of technology choices and month-by-month timelines unless they are central to the story.

questions.q: Match each example sentence to the noise type it shows.
questions.explain: Each sentence shows one noise type: company context, team detail, technology reasoning or a stretched timeline.
questions.rule: Name the noise to cut it.
pairs: We began as a small agency and then pivoted to enterprise clients
We had three seniors, two mid-levels and four juniors, plus a new hire
We picked React over Vue for its community and hiring pool
In January we noticed it, in February we met, in March we formed teams

questions.q: A nurse practitioner's story includes which ward each colleague worked on and each colleague's start date. What should she do?
questions.explain: The staffing detail is noise unless it explains her decision. The right move is to cut it.
questions.rule: Cut team detail unless central.
options: Keep it, because it proves she knows her colleagues well and takes an interest in them
Move it into the headline to save time later
Remove the staffing detail unless it is central to her story
Keep the start dates but remove the wards, to shorten it
optionExplain: Knowing colleagues is not the evidence the interviewer needs.
A headline carries the contribution, not staffing detail.
Right: excessive team detail is noise unless central.
Both are staffing detail, and shortening it half-way leaves the noise in.

questions.q: Sort each detail: noise to cut, or a case where the exception 'central to the story' applies?
questions.explain: Details are kept when they drive the decisions or the point of the story. Otherwise they are noise.
questions.rule: Central means it explains my choices.

items.t: A story about leading after the tech lead left; the departure shaped every decision
A story about fixing a bug; the team's size and when each person joined
A story about persistence; the problem took fourteen months to solve
A story about a payment fix; a long account of why the team chose its database
A story about a quick fix; a month-by-month list of meetings
A story about adapting; the whole team changed because of a merger

questions.q: A candidate explains in depth why her team chose one database over another, though her story is about a performance fix. What happens to the story?
questions.explain: An over-explained choice adds length and pushes her own decisions back. If the choice showed her judgment, the author allows it.
questions.rule: Explain a choice only if it shows my judgment.
options: The interviewer treats the choice as her best signal of judgment, since it is the most detailed part
The reasoning behind the tool choice pushes her own decisions further back
The story gets shorter because the tool choice is quickly done
The interviewer stops asking follow-up questions about tools
optionExplain: It would count only if the tool choice demonstrated her judgment.
Right: over-explained technology decisions delay and dilute the behavior.
A long explanation lengthens the story.
Nothing in the chapter links the explanation to fewer questions.

questions.q: A coach asks when naming a technology without defending it is enough. What does the author say?
questions.explain: The author says: unless the technology choice demonstrates your judgment, just mention what you used.
questions.rule: Name it; defend it only if it shows judgment.
questions.teaches: Mention what technology you used without defending it, unless the choice itself demonstrates your judgment.
options: When the technology is common, since common choices need no reasons
When the interviewer has already named the same technology
When the technology was chosen by someone else on the team
Unless the choice shows your judgment, mention what you used and move on
optionExplain: Commonness is not the author's test; showing judgment is.
The chapter does not make it depend on the interviewer's knowledge.
Who chose it is not the test; whether it shows your judgment is.
Right: this is the author's rule for technology decisions.

questions.q: Which question gives the best quick test of whether a detail belongs in your core?
questions.explain: The notes test is the author's filter. The card next explains why it works.
options: Is this detail true and could I prove it if asked?
Did this detail happen early in the project timeline?
Would the interviewer write this in their notes?
Does this detail make the story sound more impressive?
optionExplain: Truth is necessary, but true details can still be noise.
Timing does not decide whether a detail is signal.
Right: details that never reach the notes rarely matter in the debrief.
Impressiveness is not the filter; relevance to the evaluation is.
questions.rule: Test each detail by asking whether an interviewer would write it in their notes; if not, treat it as noise.

questions.q: If a detail will not make it to the interviewer's notes or the ____ discussion, it is noise.
questions.explain: The author ties the test to the debrief discussion where hiring is decided.
questions.rule: No note, no debrief.

questions.q: A candidate considers adding a remark that every engineer on the team used the same editor. What does the notes test say?
questions.explain: No interviewer would write this down, so the test marks it as noise.
questions.rule: Cut what no one would note.
options: Cut it, since no interviewer would write it down
Keep it, since it shows the team was well organised
Keep it, since it is short and costs almost no time
Move it to the headline, where it will get noticed
optionExplain: Right: it would not appear in their notes or the debrief.
Team uniformity is not behavior the interviewer would record.
Short noise is still noise; it also invites questions off the point.
A headline previews your contribution, not tooling.

questions.q: Sort each line by whether an interviewer would likely record it, as in the author's note examples.
questions.explain: Interviewers note the root cause, delivery under pressure and the outcome. They skip the framework, the reasons staff left, and the meeting schedule.
questions.rule: Notes capture behavior and results.

items.t: Candidate found the root cause through systematic investigation
Candidate's firm used one front-end framework
Candidate delivered despite significant attrition in critical roles
Senior staff left for better pay elsewhere
Candidate improved throughput tenfold
The team met every Tuesday at ten

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a detail that would not reach the interviewer's notes will probably not come up in the debrief or change the outcome.
questions.explain: The author reasons that unrecorded details do not make it into the debrief discussion where the decision is made.
questions.rule: Unnoted means unweighed.

questions.q: A team lost two senior engineers to higher pay elsewhere. Which sentence would a candidate's interviewer be likelier to discuss in the debrief?
questions.explain: The author's example contrasts delivering despite attrition, which would be discussed, with the reason people left, which would not.
questions.rule: Frame events as what I delivered.
questions.teaches: The same event can be signal or noise depending on framing: delivering despite attrition would be discussed in a debrief, while the pay reasons behind the departures would not.
options: Two senior engineers left because the company could not match market pay offers
The departures hurt morale and several of us felt the leadership had let us down
Senior engineers leaving was a pattern at the firm and had happened in earlier years
We shipped the migration on schedule despite losing two senior engineers mid-project
optionExplain: This explains why people left, which is not about her behavior.
This is a complaint about leadership and feelings, not her actions.
This describes company history rather than anything she did.
Right: it frames the event as what she delivered despite the loss.

questions.q: How should you handle background that helps explain one of your decisions?
questions.explain: Context belongs where it explains a choice. The card next shows a pair of versions.
options: Give all of it at the start, so the listener is prepared
Give it at the point where the decision needs it, in a line or two
Leave it out completely, even if the decision is then unclear to the interviewer who hears it
Save it for the closing sentence, as a summary of the project
optionExplain: Front-loading delays the point and buries signals.
Right: just-in-time context supports the decision without delaying it.
The rule is about timing, not about removing context a decision needs.
Context after the decision cannot help explain it.
questions.rule: Give context only at the moment it explains a decision, and let everything else wait for follow-up questions.

questions.q: Instead of front-loading context, provide only the information a listener needs, exactly when it is ____ to understand your decisions.
questions.explain: The author says to provide context exactly when it is needed.
questions.rule: Context on demand.

questions.q: A candidate's story about a failed checkout opens with the shop's history and an overview of its software. How should she start?
questions.explain: Start at the problem and attach only the context that helps. The other options keep the front-loading.
questions.rule: Start at the problem.
options: By describing the shop's history first, then its software, then the failure, so the listener has the whole picture
By stating that checkout failed on the sale day, then explaining only the load that caused it
By listing every service in the system, so the cause is easy to find later
By saying the failure was complicated and asking what the interviewer wants to know
optionExplain: That is the same front-loaded order she has now.
Right: it starts at the problem and gives load context where it explains the cause.
A full service list is noise before the cause is known.
She would be handing back a question she should answer herself.

questions.q: Two versions of the same story: A opens with 90 seconds of company background, B opens with the failure and names the tool when it matters. What does the author say about B?
questions.explain: Same facts, different order and selection. The second version puts signal first.
questions.rule: Same facts, better order.
options: It is weaker because it never names the company, the team or the dates involved in the event
It is too short to count as a behavioral answer
It is equally strong, since the facts are the same
It gives context only where it helps the interviewer understand the decision
optionExplain: Naming the company is not what makes a story strong.
Its brevity is the point, not a flaw.
The author says the second version is better because of how it handles context.
Right: this is the high-signal version in the author's pair.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, context you leave out of the story can still be given later if the interviewer asks for it.
questions.explain: The author says everything else can wait for follow-up questions, so the interviewer can ask for it.
questions.rule: Left out, not lost.

questions.q: In the author's pair, a questionable technology choice appears. How does the better version treat it?
questions.explain: The author notes the questionable technology is reframed from a judgment statement into an action taken.
questions.rule: Turn judgments into actions.
questions.teaches: A criticism of a past technology choice is better reframed as an action you took, for example starting a separate effort to investigate a migration.
options: It turns a judgment about the technology into an action, such as starting a migration effort
It explains at length why the technology was a poor choice and how it came to be adopted
It leaves out any mention of the technology, even the part involved in the fix
It blames the architect who chose the technology and says it caused the trouble
optionExplain: Right: the author reframes the criticism as an action.
That would be the judgment statement the author avoids.
The better version names the database that is relevant to the fix.
Blaming is a red flag in the next section.

questions.q: A candidate says, 'I worked alone for three weeks to think this through.' How does the author see it?
questions.explain: The same sentence can land differently by company. The card next explains red flags.
options: It is a red flag at every company, because teamwork matters everywhere
It is a strong signal at every company, because it shows commitment
It can show focus at one company and be a concern at another
It is neutral everywhere, since interviewers ignore working style
optionExplain: The author says the sentence can be positive where individual contribution is valued.
The author says it can raise concerns where collaboration is stressed.
Right: context decides whether it is a signal or a red flag.
The author explicitly links the sentence to company values.
questions.rule: Avoid storytelling patterns that raise doubts about your judgment, accountability or self-awareness, and read each one against the company you are speaking to.

questions.q: Red flags are patterns that make interviewers question whether they should ____ you at all.
questions.explain: The author defines red flags as patterns that make interviewers question whether to hire you.
questions.rule: A red flag questions the hire.

questions.q: A candidate for a company that stresses collaboration plans to say she worked alone for a month. What should she consider?
questions.explain: A collaboration-focused company may read the sentence as a concern. Rewording or switching stories deals with it.
questions.rule: Read the story against the company.
options: Keeping it unchanged, because working alone always shows strength and independence to any company
Adding more company history to explain why she was alone
Saying that she never works with others, to be consistent
Rewording to show how she kept the team informed, or choosing a different story
optionExplain: The author warns that context can turn it into a flag.
More history adds noise rather than fixing the concern.
That would deepen the concern at such a company.
Right: the sentence may raise concerns where collaboration is valued.

questions.q: Which two concerns does the author say red flags raise?
questions.explain: The author names judgment, accountability and self-awareness as the three concerns.
questions.rule: Judgment, accountability, self-awareness.
options: Your age and experience
Your accountability
Your judgment
Your preferred programming language
optionExplain: These are not among the concerns the author lists.
Red flags raise concerns about accountability.
Red flags raise concerns about judgment.
The author does not tie red flags to language preference.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a sentence that signals strength at one company will signal strength at every company.
questions.explain: The author says context matters and gives the example of working alone for three weeks.
questions.rule: Context shifts meaning.

questions.q: A candidate asks where to find red flags specific to each competency, such as leadership. What does the chapter say?
questions.explain: The chapter's list covers general patterns for any interview, and Part II adds competency-specific red flags.
questions.rule: General here, specific in Part II.
questions.teaches: This chapter lists general red flags for any interview; Part II covers the red flags specific to each competency.
options: They are listed in the same section of this chapter
Part II covers competency-specific red flags in each chapter
They are the same for every competency, so one list is enough
They are covered in the appendix of the book
optionExplain: This section lists the general patterns only.
Right: this chapter lists general patterns and defers specifics to Part II.
The author separates general patterns from competency-specific ones.
The chapter points to Part II, not an appendix.

questions.q: A candidate was one of twenty engineers on a project. Which sentence is the safest to say in an interview?
questions.explain: An honest role plus a real contribution protects credibility. The card next gives the author's reasons.
options: I led a team of twenty engineers through the whole project
I managed the day-to-day work of the whole team with little oversight
I was a member of a twenty-person team, and I owned the backend design
I was effectively the technical lead, though the title belonged to someone else
optionExplain: This turns membership into leadership, the kind of inflation the author warns about.
It implies a management role she did not have.
Right: it states her real role and her specific contribution.
A hedged claim still overstates her role and invites a check.
questions.rule: Do not claim a role, a result or a number bigger than the truth, however small the gap seems.

questions.q: Inflating a modest 20 percent gain into a fivefold gain can end your candidacy if it is ____.
questions.explain: The author warns that even small lies can end a candidacy if discovered.
questions.rule: Small lies can end offers.

questions.q: A candidate recalls a speed-up as somewhere between 30 and 40 percent. What is the honest way to state it?
questions.explain: A rough figure that honestly matches memory is fine. Inflating to impress is the problem.
questions.rule: Round honestly, never inflate.
options: About a third faster, which is what I recall
Fifty percent faster, since it sounds stronger and no one will check
Forty percent faster, the top of the range, since it is still possible
Doubled in speed, because the real number is hard to recall
optionExplain: Right: a rough figure that matches memory does not inflate anything.
Rounding up to impress is inflation, and the author says details can be checked.
Choosing the top of the range leans toward inflation.
Doubling is far outside her recollection.

questions.q: Sort each statement: honest claim, or exaggeration the author warns about?
questions.explain: Exaggerations turn membership into leadership, or inflate figures. Honest claims name the true role and rough but faithful numbers.
questions.rule: State the real role and the real figure.

items.t: I led a team of 20, though I was one of 20 peers
I was one of 20 engineers and I designed the backend
Latency improved by about 20 percent, as I remember it
Latency improved by 5x, when it was 20 percent
I was involved in the migration, and I wrote the data mapping
I single-handedly rebuilt the platform, though four people helped

questions.q: A candidate pads one metric and the interviewer, who knows the previous company, spots it. What happens, according to the author?
questions.explain: Credibility is shared across the whole story. A caught exaggeration puts the whole candidacy in doubt.
questions.rule: One inflated number taints the rest.
options: Her credibility can be destroyed, putting the whole candidacy at risk
The interviewer discounts only the padded metric and trusts the rest
The interviewer asks her to resubmit her numbers in writing
The interviewer notes it as a minor point for the debrief
optionExplain: Right: the author says even small lies can end the candidacy.
The author says credibility is destroyed, not just one figure.
The chapter does not describe such a request.
The author treats it as potentially candidacy-ending.

questions.q: A recruiter asks how interviewers can know about a candidate's old workplace. What does the author say they do?
questions.explain: The author notes interviewers will often know more about your previous company than you expect, and they check references.
questions.rule: Assume it can be checked.
questions.teaches: Interviewers check references and often know more about your previous company than you expect, which is why small exaggerations get found.
options: They rely only on the candidate's word, which is why lies are tempting
They compare each story to a database of company results
They check references, and often know more about the company than you expect
They ask the candidate to sign a statement that the claims are true
optionExplain: The chapter says interviewers verify things.
The chapter does not describe such a database.
Right: the chapter names reference checks and prior knowledge.
The chapter does not mention signed statements.

questions.q: A project slipped because another team delivered late. Which sentence is the best way to tell the interviewer?
questions.explain: Facts about an obstacle can stay; fault-finding should not. The card next explains how interviewers read blame.
options: The other team missed their deadline and put the whole project at risk, which delayed our testing
The inputs arrived two weeks late, so I re-planned the work to start testing early
The project failed because our partners were unreliable, as usual
I could not have done more, since the delay was entirely outside my control
optionExplain: This puts the cause on another team and says nothing of her response.
Right: it states the fact and moves to her response.
This blames and generalises about partners.
It disowns any response; a sentence about what she did is stronger.
questions.rule: Describe an obstacle by what you did about it, not by whom you hold at fault.

questions.q: Blaming others shows that you ____ problems rather than finding ways to succeed despite obstacles.
questions.explain: The author says blame shows you externalize problems.
questions.rule: Blame externalizes.

questions.q: A candidate wants to explain that unclear requirements slowed her. Which sentence follows the advice?
questions.explain: The right sentence spends its second half on her action. The others assign fault.
questions.rule: Obstacle, then my response.
options: The product manager gave us unclear requirements and did not return my messages
Unclear requirements are the main reason projects fail, and mine was no exception to that pattern, so it was out of my hands
Everyone on the team struggled because nobody had written proper requirements
The requirements were unclear at the start, so I wrote them down and checked each with the owner
optionExplain: It names the manager as the cause and gives no action.
A general complaint puts the cause outside her control.
A group complaint shows no response from her.
Right: it describes the obstacle and her own action.

questions.q: Sort each sentence: describes an obstacle with a response, or blames someone?
questions.explain: Good sentences state the obstacle briefly and spend their weight on a response. Blaming sentences assign fault.
questions.rule: Spend the sentence on my action.

items.t: The partner API changed, so I added a compatibility layer to keep us moving
The project failed because our PMs wrote unclear requirements
The other team did not deliver their part on time, which sank us
Requirements shifted weekly, so I started logging each change and confirming it in writing
Our vendor kept missing deadlines and made our job impossible
Data access came late, so I built a small sample to start validating early

questions.q: A candidate blames her old product managers throughout a story, and the claims are all accurate. How will the interviewer likely react?
questions.explain: The author says even if true, blaming shows you externalize problems and raises the worry about their own teams.
questions.rule: True blame is still a flag.
options: They will accept the account because it is accurate
They will conclude her old employer was poorly run and sympathise
They may worry she will blame their teams when things go wrong
They will ask for names to check her claims with the managers
optionExplain: The author says accuracy does not remove the concern.
Sympathy is not what the author predicts.
Right: this is the author's stated worry, even when the claim is true.
The chapter does not describe such a check as the reaction.

questions.q: In a failure story, the chapter says to focus on what you could control. What does it add about the role of others in the problem?
questions.explain: In the failure and recovery section the author says to stay centered on what you could control and learned, even when others contributed to the problem.
questions.rule: Own your part.
questions.teaches: In a failure story, keep it on what you could control and what you learned, even when others contributed to the problem.
options: Even when others contributed, keep the story on your actions and what you learned
When others contributed, name their teams so the interviewer knows the facts
When others contributed, skip the story and choose a success instead
When others contributed, ask the interviewer whether blame is acceptable
optionExplain: Right: the failure section says to avoid blaming or defensiveness even when others contributed.
Naming them as the cause is the blaming the author advises against.
The chapter wants failures discussed, because recovery reveals problem-solving.
The chapter gives a direct instruction, not a question to ask.

questions.q: Which description of a team project best helps an interviewer evaluate you?
questions.explain: Specific separation of roles lets the interviewer evaluate her. The card next explains the suspicion vague wording causes.
options: We built the whole system together and everyone pitched in
I was heavily involved in many parts of the project
The team delivered a strong result, thanks to great collaboration
I designed the data model while a teammate built the front end
optionExplain: The interviewer cannot tell what she did.
'Involved' can cover anything from leading to watching.
It credits the group without showing her part.
Right: it separates her work from her teammate's.
questions.rule: Say exactly what you did and what your teammates did, instead of hiding behind a vague 'we' or 'I was involved in'.

questions.q: Be specific: 'I designed the backend while a teammate built the ____.'
questions.explain: The author's model sentence ends with a teammate building the UI.
questions.rule: I did this; they did that.

questions.q: A candidate says, 'We improved onboarding and sign-ups went up.' How should she rework it for her core?
questions.explain: The good version states her own actions, names a colleague's part and gives the result.
questions.rule: Name my part and theirs.
options: We improved onboarding together, and I was a core part of it throughout
I ran the user tests and rewrote the first screen; a colleague handled the email series; sign-ups rose by a fifth
Our team improved onboarding over the quarter, and I contributed to the effort in many ways, including testing and reviews
I improved onboarding, and sign-ups went up as a result of my work alone
optionExplain: It still hides what she did behind 'we' and 'core part'.
Right: it states her part, credits a colleague and gives a result.
'Contributed in many ways' is as vague as 'involved'.
It claims everything and may be read as taking credit for others' work.

questions.q: Which two doubts does the author say vague contribution can raise?
questions.explain: The author's two doubts are credit-claiming and passivity.
questions.rule: Vague wording invites two doubts.
options: That you are too modest and may be underselling yourself in every interview you give
That you are claiming credit for others' work, or were only a passive participant
That you disagree with your team and prefer to work apart from it
That you are too technical and may struggle to explain things to others
optionExplain: Modesty is not the concern the author gives.
Right: both doubts come from not stating what you did.
The chapter's doubts concern credit and passivity.
Technical depth is not the doubt raised.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, using 'we' for every part of a story is a safe way to avoid sounding boastful.
questions.explain: The author says 'we' throughout raises suspicion about credit and passivity.
questions.rule: 'We' throughout is a flag.

questions.q: The chapter's structuring advice for a key point tells you how to speak about your own work. What is it?
questions.explain: The structuring section says to use 'I' when describing your work and to be precise about your contribution versus what others handled.
questions.rule: 'I' for my work, names for theirs.
questions.teaches: When structuring a key point, use 'I' rather than 'we' for your own work and be precise about your contribution versus what others handled.
options: Use 'we' for shared successes and 'I' only for problems you caused, so credit is spread fairly
Use the team's name for every action, so the group gets the credit
Avoid naming teammates so the interviewer focuses on you
Use 'I' instead of 'we' and be precise about your contribution versus what others handled
optionExplain: The chapter gives no such split.
That is the vagueness the author warns about.
The chapter asks you to be precise about what others handled too.
Right: this is the instruction for the action part of a key point.

questions.q: A candidate says, 'I deployed the fix straight to production without testing because we were late.' How will an interviewer likely hear this?
questions.explain: Initiative does not cancel the judgment problem. The card next gives the author's examples.
options: As initiative that also reveals poor judgment about risk
As clear evidence of an ability to work under pressure
As a neutral detail, since the fix worked in the end
As a sign she follows instructions from her manager
optionExplain: Right: the author says such stories show initiative but concerning decision-making.
The author warns the pressure does not excuse the shortcut.
The outcome does not remove the concern about judgment.
Nothing in the story shows following instructions.
questions.rule: Do not present risky shortcuts or the skipping of team processes as achievements.

questions.q: Telling a story where you skipped required code reviews suggests you may be difficult to work with and ignore your team's ____.
questions.explain: The author says dismissing processes suggests ignoring team practices.
questions.rule: Do not brag about skipping process.

questions.q: A candidate wants to tell a story about a late-night hotfix. Which version avoids the flag?
questions.explain: The safe version keeps testing, review and rollback. The others show the shortcuts the author flags.
questions.rule: Show speed with safeguards.
options: I pushed the fix straight to production at midnight because there was no time for review, and I watched the logs afterwards
I turned off the alerts for a night so nothing would distract me while I fixed it
I tested the fix on a copy overnight, got a quick review from a teammate, then deployed with a rollback ready
I skipped the review because the reviewers usually only find formatting issues
optionExplain: It repeats the author's poor-judgment example.
Switching off alerts is a version of the author's error-reporting example.
Right: she meets time pressure while keeping safeguards.
It repeats the author's dismissing-process example.

questions.q: Sort each story detail: reveals sound judgment, or fits the author's poor-judgment or process flags?
questions.explain: Flags are the shortcuts that remove safeguards. Sound judgment keeps safeguards in proportion to the risk.
questions.rule: Keep the safeguards.

items.t: I silenced all error alerts because most of them were false alarms
I filtered the noisy alerts, kept the critical ones and reviewed the filter with the team
I skipped code review because teammates only find nits
I asked for a fast-track review, because the deadline was real
I released without testing as we were running late
I tested the risky part only, and had a rollback ready

questions.q: A candidate's story shows initiative but ends with her bypassing a team practice. What note might the interviewer write?
questions.explain: The author says the story suggests difficulty working with others and ignoring team practices.
questions.rule: Process-skipping signals poor teamwork.
options: It shows she will bring useful new methods to the team
It shows she values speed, which fits any fast-moving team that wants results quickly
It shows she is independent and needs less management
It suggests she may be hard to work with and ignore team practices
optionExplain: The author reads this as a concern, not a benefit.
Context matters, but the author does not give this reading.
That reading is not the one the author gives.
Right: this is the interpretation the author gives for dismissing processes.

questions.q: A candidate argues that her untested production push shows the initiative interviewers like. How does the author weigh that?
questions.explain: The author grants the stories might show initiative but says they reveal concerning decision-making that could create bigger problems.
questions.rule: Initiative does not cancel poor judgment.
questions.teaches: Such stories might show initiative, but they reveal concerning decision-making that could create bigger problems; initiative does not cancel the concern.
options: It shows initiative, which outweighs any concern about process in a fast company
It may show initiative, but it reveals decision-making that could create bigger problems
It shows nothing at all, since interviewers ignore stories about urgent fixes
It shows initiative only if the fix worked, in which case the risk is forgotten
optionExplain: The author does not let initiative outweigh the judgment concern.
Right: initiative does not cancel the concern about judgment.
The author says the story is read, and read as a concern.
The author does not make the flag depend on the outcome.

questions.q: A candidate edited another team's tool without asking, and they were upset. How should she tell the story?
questions.explain: Self-awareness means naming your misstep and your repair. The card next explains the author's two flags.
options: Present the edit as a rescue the other team failed to appreciate
Skip the story entirely, because any admission of error is a red flag
Admit she should have involved them, and say what she did to repair it
Mention that the other team was disorganised, to explain her action
optionExplain: That casts her as the hero and shows the lack of awareness the author names.
The author wants honest handling, not a story with no faults at all.
Right: it shows self-awareness and accountability.
Criticising the team repeats the blaming flag.
questions.rule: Own your part when you were in the wrong, and keep complaints to a minimum even while describing hard conditions.

questions.q: Constant negativity is a flag because interviewers picture you saying the same about their company in six ____.
questions.explain: The author says interviewers imagine hearing the same complaints about their company in six months.
questions.rule: Complaints travel with you.

questions.q: A candidate describes an old job: 'The codebase was a disaster, my teammates were incompetent, the requirements made no sense.' What is the best fix?
questions.explain: Keep difficulty brief and neutral and use most of the story for actions.
questions.rule: Brief fact, then action.
options: State the challenge neutrally, then spend the story on what she did about it
Keep the complaints but add a joke so they sound less serious
List the problems in order of severity so the interviewer sees how bad it was
Say nothing about the difficulty at all, so the story sounds smooth
optionExplain: Right: it removes the complaint and moves to her actions.
Humour does not change that the content is negative throughout.
A ranked list of problems is still complaining.
The author says honest challenges can be described; only constant negativity is the flag.

questions.q: Sort each statement: shows accountability and self-awareness, or fits the flags of hero-casting or complaining?
questions.explain: Awareness and accountability name the lapse and the repair. Flags cast the speaker as hero or complain throughout.
questions.rule: Own the lapse, skip the sneer.

items.t: I fixed their system without asking, and they were upset; I should have talked first
I fixed their system overnight and could not understand why they were upset
The codebase was a disaster and my teammates were incompetent
The codebase had little documentation, so I started documenting as I learned it
After the misunderstanding, I apologised and agreed a review step with them
Everything about that team was a mess and nobody listened to me

questions.q: A candidate completes a story as the hero when she was in the wrong. What might the interviewer write in their notes?
questions.explain: The author lists notes such as 'Doesn't take accountability' as the result of these patterns.
questions.rule: Flags become damaging notes.
options: Doesn't take accountability
Shows strong initiative and confidence
Communicates in a clear, structured way
Has a clear sense of the role's scope
optionExplain: Right: this is one of the author's sample notes.
The author's samples are negative; this one is not among them.
That might be said of the pyramid, not of the hero-casting.
Nothing in the flag suggests this note.

questions.q: The author says certain notes can end offers. Which set of notes does the chapter list?
questions.explain: The author closes the red-flag list by naming notes such as these, and says they kill offers.
questions.rule: Flags become notes; notes decide.
questions.teaches: Red-flag patterns lead to notes like 'Doesn't take accountability', 'Might not work well with our team' and 'Shows questionable judgment', and the author says those notes kill offers.
options: Spoke too quickly; used too few examples; gave a short headline
Talked about metrics; named teammates; kept to two minutes
Doesn't take accountability; might not work well with our team; shows questionable judgment
Asked too many questions; described the company in great detail; seemed nervous throughout the answer
optionExplain: These are not in the chapter's list.
These are positive behaviors in the chapter.
Right: these three notes come from the chapter's red-flag discussion.
None of these are the chapter's sample notes.

questions.q: Which sentence best describes a hard manager in an interview?
questions.explain: Facts rather than labels show maturity. The card next gives both moves.
options: My manager was a micromanaging nightmare who never trusted anyone
My manager wanted daily written updates, which took time from delivery on a tight deadline
My manager was fine, and everything went very smoothly for us
My manager was probably under pressure from above, so I never questioned it and adapted
optionExplain: A harsh label and an absolute are emotional, not factual.
Right: it states observable facts without a label.
It denies the difficulty, which the author says is not the aim.
Guessing at motives and doing nothing hides the facts and her response.
questions.rule: Describe difficult people and decisions as observable facts, and acknowledge that other people had reasons for their view.

questions.q: Instead of emotions, focus on ____ when you describe a difficult situation.
questions.explain: The author's first technique is facts, not emotions.
questions.rule: Facts, not emotions.

questions.q: A candidate wants to explain a disagreement about shipping speed versus quality. Which sentence follows the advice?
questions.explain: A balanced sentence names both positions and her own view.
questions.rule: Acknowledge the other side.
options: The team only cared about speed and refused to listen to anyone's concerns about quality, so I let it go
I was right about quality, and the rest of the team eventually accepted it
The team and I disagreed, but I will not say who was right out of respect
The team prioritised speed and I worried about quality; both views had merit, and I suggested a middle path
optionExplain: It dismisses the other side and casts them as unreasonable.
It presents only her view and a win.
It avoids stating any facts or her own view, leaving nothing to evaluate.
Right: it acknowledges both sides and states her view.

questions.q: Sort each sentence: factual and balanced, or emotional and one-sided?
questions.explain: Factual sentences describe behavior and trade-offs. Labels, absolutes and one-sided claims are emotional.
questions.rule: Describe, do not label.

items.t: My manager was a micromanaging nightmare
My manager preferred daily check-ins and detailed reports during a tight deadline
They only cared about shipping fast and ignored quality
The team prioritised shipping; I was concerned about technical debt; both had merit
The requirements were pure chaos and nobody cared
The requirements changed weekly, which made planning hard

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, describing a hard situation objectively, rather than with emotional labels, is a form of lying.
questions.explain: The author says: you are not lying, you are describing the situation objectively.
questions.rule: Objective is honest.

questions.q: A candidate has described a broken codebase factually. What should most of the rest of the story cover?
questions.explain: After a matter-of-fact statement of the challenge, the author says the story should move quickly to what you did and what came of it.
questions.rule: Both views, plus my own.
options: Further evidence of how poorly the previous team had worked
Her own actions and their results, after naming the challenge matter-of-factly
A balanced account of what each earlier developer might have intended
Lessons for the company about how to prevent such codebases
optionExplain: Dwelling on the problem is what the author warns against; the facts are stated once, briefly.
Right: the author says the majority of the story should focus on actions and results.
Acknowledging other views helps with people, but the story's weight still belongs to the candidate's own actions.
Advice to the company shifts attention away from the candidate's own contribution.
questions.teaches: State the challenge matter-of-factly, then move quickly to how you handled it: most of the story should be your actions and their results, not the problems.

questions.q: A candidate inherited a messy codebase. Which telling follows the author's advice?
questions.explain: The right telling spends most of its time on her response. The card next gives the three moves.
options: State briefly that it was messy, then describe the tests she wrote and the result
Describe the mess in detail first, so the interviewer sees how bad the codebase was before any action
Say nobody else would touch the code, so her work needed no further explanation
Spend most of the answer on who left the code in that state
optionExplain: Right: short challenge, then actions and results.
The author says to keep the negative brief.
It avoids saying what she did.
That dwells on blame rather than her response.
questions.rule: Spend most of the story on what you controlled and did, include the learning only where it is real, and state the challenge briefly.

questions.q: Keep it brief: state the challenge matter-of-factly, then move quickly to how you ____ it.
questions.explain: The author says to move quickly to how you handled it.
questions.rule: Brief problem, long response.
