optionExplain: Right: it signals desperation and suggests she would take any role.
This shows effort and specifics.
This links research to experience.
This states an interest tied to the work.
questions.explain: Interviewers want to see that you want this role specifically. The card next lists the pitfalls.
questions.rule: Show you want this role.

questions.q: True or false: Mentioning perks such as free food, remote work or a shorter commute strengthens the answer to why this company.
questions.explain: The authors list perks as a pitfall because they focus on what you gain and not on the work.
questions.rule: Perks signal the wrong motive.

questions.q: Which answer avoids the pitfalls?
options: This would be a great learning opportunity for me, and I would grow a lot
The job description says you need someone to build services, which I can do
You are a leader in your field, and everyone I know wants to work here
Your hybrid-design post matches a project I led, and I would like to apply that
optionExplain: It says only what she would gain, which marks her as a taker.
It recites the posting back to the interviewer.
It is the generic praise the authors warn about.
Right: it is specific and shows what she would contribute.
questions.explain: Specific research plus contribution avoids the listed pitfalls.
questions.rule: Specific and two-sided.

questions.q: Sort each answer fragment: does it fall into a listed pitfall or not?

items.t: Everyone wants to work here and you are changing the world
Your remote policy and free lunches are what drew me
I would take any role you can offer me
I noticed your Android app handles offline mode differently from iOS
I led a similar optimization, so your scale challenge is one I know
I'd like to bring that experience and learn from your team too

questions.explain: The three under 'Pitfall' flatter, focus on perks, or signal desperation. The three under 'Fine' are specific, tie to experience, and offer mutual value.
questions.rule: Specific and mutual is fine.

questions.q: A candidate says only: this would be a great learning opportunity for me. What will the interviewer likely conclude?
options: That she is modest and takes feedback well in her work
That she is a taker who has not said what she would add
That she is highly motivated by the company's mission statement
That she has done thorough research on the role and team
optionExplain: Modesty is not what the answer signals; it signals one-sidedness.
Right: the authors say such an answer marks you as a taker rather than a contributor.
A mission link would be specific, and this is not.
A thorough researcher would cite something concrete.
questions.explain: A one-sided answer shows what you want to get but not what you offer.
questions.rule: Show what you bring as well as gain.

questions.q: A candidate plans to ask the interviewer what is great about working there. What do the authors say about such a question?
options: They are ideal, because they show enthusiasm and let the interviewer talk freely
They are fine for hiring managers but not for recruiters or HR staff
They are acceptable if they are followed by a question about pay
They draw marketing answers, so ask specific questions that surface insight
optionExplain: Enthusiasm is good, but the question draws a stock reply.
The problem is the kind of answer it produces, whoever is asked.
Adding pay questions makes it worse.
Right: the authors list this as a pitfall for exactly that reason.
questions.explain: The authors warn that asking questions that will only get positive answers from Marketing reveals nothing, and recommend questions that surface real insights.
questions.rule: Ask for real insight.
questions.teaches: Questions such as what is great about working here only draw answers straight from Marketing; ask specific questions that surface real insights.

questions.q: True or false: Interviewers cannot tell the difference between real curiosity and enthusiasm that is put on.
questions.explain: They often can, which is why a question you actually want answered works better. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Genuine interest shows.

questions.q: Real curiosity is obvious, and so is ____ enthusiasm.
questions.explain: The authors make this contrast to explain why you should ask what you actually want to know.
questions.rule: Forced enthusiasm shows.

questions.q: A candidate used the product and wonders why a feature works as it does. Which question best shows curiosity?
options: What is the best thing about working on this feature for you personally?
Is this feature built this way due to a technical constraint or to user feedback?
Does the company plan to do more with this feature in the future?
How do you think this feature compares to a competitor's version of it?
optionExplain: It invites a stock reply and does not show her own observation.
Right: it comes from her own observation and asks about reasoning.
It is a speculative question about future plans.
It asks for an opinion without showing her research.
questions.explain: A question rooted in your own observation sounds genuine.
questions.rule: Ask what you really wonder.

questions.q: Which of these candidate remarks sounds more forced?
options: I noticed your startup time dropped and wondered how you measured it
I read your post on baseline profiles and tried a similar approach
I'm absolutely thrilled and honored by this incredible opportunity
Your offline mode works differently on Android, and I'd like to know why
optionExplain: This is a specific observation and a real question.
This refers to a specific read and an attempt to apply it.
Right: it states strong feeling without any specifics.
This is an informed question based on use.
questions.explain: Enthusiasm shown through specifics is more convincing than declared enthusiasm.
questions.rule: Show interest through specifics.

questions.q: True or false: If a candidate has no real curiosity about the company's work, her enthusiasm is likely to come across as forced.
questions.explain: The authors say forced enthusiasm is as obvious as real curiosity.
questions.rule: Fake interest shows.

questions.q: A candidate discusses a technical decision of the company's and wants to show deeper understanding. What does the authors' advice add?
options: Show that she understands the business context behind technical decisions
Avoid the business side, since interviewers want only technical remarks here
Quote the company's revenue figures to show she has read the annual report
Suggest that the company's decision was wrong to show independent judgement
optionExplain: Right: the authors say decisions make more sense when business constraints are understood.
The authors tell you to link technical and business context.
Quoting figures is not the same as understanding the constraints.
Criticizing without understanding the constraints undermines the effect.
questions.explain: The authors advise showing you understand the company's business context, because technical decisions make more sense when you know the business constraints.
questions.rule: Link technical choices to business constraints.
questions.teaches: Show that you understand their business context: technical decisions make more sense when you understand the business constraints behind them.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: At the end of a long interview, the interviewer asks if you have any questions. You feel the conversation covered everything. What is best?
options: Ask a thoughtful question prompted by your research into the team
Say no, so that the interview can end on time and everyone can leave
Ask how you did, since that is the most useful thing to know right now
Repeat a question that the interviewer has already answered earlier on
optionExplain: Right: the authors say never to decline and always to have thoughtful questions ready.
Declining feels courteous, but it passes up a critical opportunity.
Asking how you did signals anxiety and is one of the questions to avoid.
Repeating a question shows you were not listening.
questions.explain: The closing question is an opportunity, not a formality. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Always have questions.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, answering no, I think you've covered everything is a good way to finish an interview.
questions.explain: The authors say never to answer this way; always have thoughtful questions ready.
questions.rule: Never decline the opportunity.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wants to use her closing questions to decide whether she would accept an offer. What should she ask?
options: Only polite questions that cannot embarrass anyone or cause any trouble
Only questions she already knows the answers to, to appear well prepared
Real questions about the work whose honest answers would sway her
Only questions about how impressed the interviewer was with her answers
optionExplain: Polite but empty questions produce stock answers and no insight.
Asking what you already know wastes the chance to learn.
Right: real questions bring honest answers that help her decide.
Fishing for feedback signals insecurity and gives her no useful information.
questions.explain: Questions let you evaluate the company, so they should be questions you actually want answered.
questions.rule: Ask what you want to know.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Sort each benefit: does the authors' reasoning give it, or not?
groups: The authors do not give this benefit

items.t: It shows the interviewers you are serious about the role
It signals that you are evaluating them as well
Real questions get honest answers that help you decide
It guarantees that you will receive an offer
It lets you skip the earlier parts of the interview
It shows the interviewers that you are an expert in their field

questions.explain: The authors tie the questions to seriousness, mutual evaluation and honest answers. They do not promise an offer or replace the interview.
questions.rule: Questions signal interest and give information.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: True or false: A candidate who has done thorough research for why this company will find good closing questions easier to come up with.
questions.explain: The authors say the research naturally generates questions, so the work does double duty.
questions.rule: Research feeds questions.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate has no questions left after the interview because they were all answered. How can she prepare so that this does not happen?
options: She should cut her research short, since research only creates more questions
She should use the questions her research produced, plus some extras
She should ask the same questions in every interview regardless of the interviewer
She should wait for the interviewer to suggest some topics when they come up
optionExplain: The authors say research is what produces good questions.
Right: research generates questions, and reserves cover the ones that get answered.
The same questions for everyone ignore who is listening.
Waiting leaves her unprepared, which is what the authors warn against.
questions.explain: The authors say the research you did for why this company will naturally generate questions, so you should use them.
questions.rule: Reuse your research as questions.
questions.teaches: The research you did for why this company will naturally generate questions, so use it.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: You will meet a recruiter, an engineer on the team, and a product manager. How should you prepare your questions?
options: Prepare one set of questions and ask the same ones of each person
Ask all three about salary, so you can compare their answers
Ask only the engineer, since the other two cannot answer anything useful
Prepare different questions suited to what each person knows
optionExplain: The same questions waste each person's special knowledge.
Compensation is for the recruiter, and asking the others looks perk-driven.
Recruiters and product managers can tell you a lot, about different things.
Right: each role can speak to different things.
questions.explain: The right question depends on who is in front of you. The card next sorts them.
questions.rule: Fit the question to the person.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Match each interviewer to the kind of question suited to them.
pairs: What the work is really like day to day
Collaboration and how engineering fits in
questions.explain: The authors give each of the four groups a distinct set of topics based on what they know.
questions.rule: Four audiences, four sets.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wants to know whether the engineering team and product team actually work as partners. Whom should she ask?
options: The recruiter, who manages the process and sets expectations about pay
A product manager or designer, who can describe the collaboration
The hiring manager, but only after receiving the offer in writing
No one, because such things cannot be found out before joining
optionExplain: Recruiters know process, not the working relationships.
Right: cross-functional partners can speak to collaboration.
Waiting for an offer wastes the chance to decide with the facts.
Cross-functional interviewers are exactly who can describe it.
questions.explain: Cross-functional partners are the best source on how engineering works with other groups.
questions.rule: Ask the person who can know.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Sort each question: is it well matched to the interviewer named, or mismatched?

items.t: Asking a recruiter what the timeline for a decision is
Asking an engineer how technical decisions are made on the team
Asking a product manager how the team prioritizes features
Asking an engineer on the team about salary range and vacation
Asking a product manager about the details of the benefits package
Asking a recruiter how the team handles technical debt day to day

questions.explain: Matched questions go to the person who knows. Pay and benefits go to recruiters, and daily technical life goes to people who do the work.
questions.rule: Ask the one who knows.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: True or false: If a candidate asks a team member about benefits, the team member may conclude she cares more about perks than work.
questions.explain: The authors give this as the reason to save compensation and benefits questions for recruiters.
questions.rule: Perk questions to teammates misfire.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate's interview loop includes a data scientist. Which group of interviewers does she belong to, and what is she best placed to answer?
options: A technical team member, best placed to describe the codebase and its tools
A recruiter, best placed to describe the salary range and the interview process
A hiring manager, best placed to describe the team's direction and its priorities
A cross-functional partner, best placed to describe how teams collaborate
optionExplain: A data scientist outside the engineering team is not one of its members.
Recruiters handle process and pay, not collaboration.
A hiring manager sets direction for the team, which is a different role.
Right: the authors list product managers, designers and data scientists as cross-functional partners.
questions.explain: The authors group product managers, designers and data scientists as cross-functional partners, who can tell you about collaboration and how engineering fits into the wider organization.
questions.rule: Know who the partners are.
questions.teaches: Cross-functional partners are product managers, designers and data scientists, who can tell you about collaboration and how engineering fits into the broader organization.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: You want to know the salary range and the vacation policy. Whom should you ask?
options: The recruiter, who handles compensation and benefits questions
The engineer on the team, who knows the working conditions best
The hiring manager, in the first minute of the first conversation
Any interviewer, since the answer will be the same from each of them
optionExplain: Right: recruiters are the right place for pay and benefits.
An engineer is likely to think you care more about perks than work.
Leading with pay in the first minute makes the same impression.
Different roles are suited to different topics.
questions.explain: Topics belong with the people who handle them. The card next lists the recruiter's list.
questions.rule: Pay goes to the recruiter.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Save your questions about compensation, benefits, vacation and process logistics for the ____.
questions.explain: The authors direct these topics to recruiters or HR.
questions.rule: Recruiters handle pay and process.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: After a coding interview, an engineer asks if you have questions. A candidate wants to know about the signing bonus. What should she do?
options: Ask the engineer about the bonus, since he may well know the number
Ask the engineer for the recruiter's private phone number to call
Save it for the recruiter and ask the engineer about the work
Say she has no questions to avoid raising an awkward topic here
optionExplain: The engineer may think she is more interested in perks than the job.
That does not help her get an answer and is intrusive.
Right: she saves pay for the recruiter and uses the engineer's time on the work.
Having no questions wastes the chance to learn about the work.
questions.explain: The right question to the wrong person can do harm.
questions.rule: Right question, right person.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Sort each question by who should be asked it.

items.t: What is the salary range for this role?
What does the interview process look like from here?
Can you tell me more about the benefits package?
How are technical decisions made on the team?
How often do you ship features versus address technical debt?
What tools or processes do you wish you could change?

questions.explain: Pay, benefits and process go to the recruiter. Questions about the working reality go to people who do the work.
questions.rule: Process to recruiters; practice to practitioners.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: True or false: A candidate who keeps pay and benefits questions for the recruiter will not need to raise them with the team.
questions.explain: The recruiter conversation covers them, so the team conversations can stay on the work.
questions.rule: Topics have a home.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: With a recruiter, a candidate wants to learn how success is judged and how the team is organised. Which questions suit that?
options: How do you feel about the engineers' current code quality overall?
What do you think the team's biggest weakness is these days?
How is performance evaluated, and what is the team structure?
Why do you think the previous person left the role last year?
optionExplain: That asks for a personal opinion a recruiter may not hold.
A recruiter is not placed to assess the team's weaknesses.
Right: the authors include performance evaluation and team structure among recruiter questions.
That is a question about the individual, and a recruiter may not know.
questions.explain: Besides process, timeline, benefits and salary range, the authors list how performance is evaluated and what the team structure looks like.
questions.rule: Recruiters can explain structure and evaluation.
questions.teaches: Recruiter questions also include how performance is evaluated and what the team structure looks like.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: You meet an engineer who would be your teammate. Which question will tell you the most about daily life on the team?
options: How often do you ship features versus address debt?
How would you describe the team culture in a few short words?
What is it like to work here, in your honest opinion today?
Do you think I would be a good fit for this team?
optionExplain: Right: it is specific and its answer reveals building versus fire-fighting.
Vague questions tend to get vague answers.
It is broad, and likely to get a general reply.
It asks the interviewer to judge you, which does not tell you about the job.
questions.explain: Specific questions reveal real conditions. The card next explains what several questions show.
questions.rule: Specific questions, revealing answers.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Match each question to what its answer can reveal.
pairs: How are technical decisions made on the team?
How much autonomy or micromanagement there is
What kind of support does the team get to be successful?
Whether management gives the team what it needs
What tools or processes do you wish you could change?
Whether there are pain points and a willingness to address them
questions.explain: Each question is built to expose a feature of the team's working life beyond what the job posting says.
questions.rule: Questions that expose conditions.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wants to know whether the team is trusted to make its own technical choices. Which question fits?
options: What technologies does the team use, and which version of each?
How many people are on the team, and how long have they worked together?
What was the most exciting project the team has finished this year alone?
How are technical decisions made, and who has the final say?
optionExplain: Technology versions say nothing about who decides.
Size and tenure are different topics.
A favourite project does not reveal the decision process.
Right: it targets how decisions are made, which shows autonomy or micromanagement.
questions.explain: To learn about autonomy, ask about decisions.
questions.rule: Ask how decisions are made.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Sort each question: does it draw out real information or invite a stock reply?

items.t: What tools or processes do you wish you could change?
How often do you ship features versus address technical debt?
What kind of support does the team get to be successful?
What is great about working here?
How is the team culture?
Do you enjoy working here?

questions.explain: The three under 'Draws out real information' are specific and ask for facts or frustrations. The others are broad and invite polished, positive answers.
questions.rule: Specific gets real.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: True or false: If a team mostly fixes technical debt rather than shipping features, the candidate may be putting out fires more than building.
questions.explain: The authors say the answer indicates whether you will spend more time building or putting out fires.
questions.rule: The ratio tells you the work.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate knows the team released something last month. How could she show research and learn something real?
options: Ask when the next release is planned and whether she can join the work
Say she saw the launch and ask what the team learned from it
Say the launch was good but could have had better design
Ask the engineer to list all the features of the new release
optionExplain: That asks about the schedule and does not show interest in the team's experience.
Right: the authors suggest asking what the team learned from the launch, which shows research and invites a good story.
Unasked criticism risks offending the people who built it.
Asking for a feature list adds nothing she could not read herself.
questions.explain: The authors say asking what the team learned from a recent launch impresses because it shows specific research, and people like talking about launches, especially successful ones.
questions.rule: Ask about a launch.
questions.teaches: If you know the team released something recently, asking what it learned from the launch shows you researched their work, and people enjoy talking about recent launches, especially successful ones.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Which question to a hiring manager will tell you the most about the team's immediate priorities?
options: How would you describe your own management style in brief?
What do you like most about working at this company?
Do you think the company will be successful in coming years?
If I were hired today, what would you assign me to?
optionExplain: It is about the manager, not the team's current priorities.
It asks for a general opinion with a predictable answer.
It asks for a prediction that tells little about the role.
Right: it asks for a concrete near-term assignment.
questions.explain: A concrete assignment reveals the real priorities. The card next lists more.
questions.rule: Ask for the first assignment.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Asking what you would be assigned if hired today reveals the manager's immediate ____.
questions.explain: The authors say the answer reveals the manager's immediate priorities.
questions.rule: Assignments reveal priorities.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wants to know whether the company supports new hires. Which question fits?
options: How many new hires has the team made over the last year?
What does onboarding look like, and how long is the ramp-up?
How many hours a week do people typically work on the team here?
How soon could I be considered for promotion on this team after joining?
optionExplain: Hire counts say nothing about how they are supported.
Right: it asks directly about onboarding, which shows investment in new hires.
Working hours is a separate topic.
Promotion timing is a different question and may look premature.
questions.explain: Onboarding and ramp-up questions show how the team treats newcomers.
questions.rule: Ask about onboarding.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Sort each question: is it a good fit for a hiring manager?
groups: Good fit for a hiring manager

items.t: If I were hired today, what would you assign me to?
What does your onboarding process look like?
How long have most team members been here?
What is the salary range for this role?
Can you walk me through the benefits package?
Which text editor does the team prefer?

questions.explain: Priorities, onboarding and team stability suit a manager. Pay and benefits go to recruiters, and tool preferences go to the team.
questions.rule: Managers: direction, onboarding, stability.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate learns the role has been open for a very long time. According to the authors, how might she read that?
options: As proof that the company is selective and that the team is excellent
As a sign that the role must be paid more than similar jobs
As a sign of urgency, and possibly a red flag if it is long
As evidence that nobody else has applied for the position
optionExplain: Selectivity is one explanation, but the authors point to urgency and a possible warning.
Pay is not suggested by the length of time.
Right: the authors say a long-open role may be a red flag.
The duration does not tell you the number of applicants.
questions.explain: The authors say the answer to how long the role has been open indicates urgency, and a position open for a long time may raise a red flag.
questions.rule: A long-open role may be a warning.
questions.teaches: How long the role has been open indicates the manager's urgency, and a position that has been open for a long time may be a red flag.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wants to judge team stability without asking about turnover directly. Which question fits the authors' advice?
options: How long have most team members been with the team?
Why did the last two people on this team leave the company?
Is the team stable, and does anyone plan to leave soon?
How many people have quit since the beginning of this year?
optionExplain: Right: it probes stability without being too direct about turnover.
That asks about turnover directly and may put the manager on the defensive.
That asks about private plans, which the manager cannot answer.
That is a direct turnover question.
questions.explain: The authors present this question as a way to understand how stable the team is without being too direct about turnover.
questions.rule: Probe stability indirectly.
questions.teaches: Asking how long most team members have been there is a way to understand the team's stability without being too direct about turnover.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A product manager is interviewing you. Which question tells you most about how engineering and product actually work together?
options: How does your team collaborate with Engineering?
What do you enjoy most about working at the company?
Do you think engineers are generally easy to work with?
What is the product's biggest strength compared with its rivals?
optionExplain: Right: it asks directly about the working relationship.
It invites a stock answer about enjoyment.
It asks for a generalisation rather than a description of this team.
It asks about the product, not the collaboration.
questions.explain: Partners are the best source on collaboration. The card next lists what else to ask.
questions.rule: Ask about collaboration.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A question about collaboration shows whether engineering has a true partnership or is only order-____.
questions.explain: The authors say the answer shows whether there is a true partnership or an order-taking relationship.
questions.rule: Partnership versus order-taking.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wants to know whether the product team has a clear strategy. Which question fits?
options: How many features did you release last year?
Which feature do you personally like the most?
How do you decide which features to prioritize?
Who decides the names of new features?
optionExplain: A count does not reveal how they decide.
A favourite feature is a personal view.
Right: the answer will suggest a clear strategy or chaos.
Naming is a minor issue.
questions.explain: Priority questions expose the logic behind decisions.
questions.rule: Ask how they prioritize.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Sort each answer by what it would suggest to the candidate.

items.t: Engineers join planning from the start and challenge the plan
Priorities follow a clear strategy that is shared with the team
The roadmap process is open and explained to everyone
Engineering receives a finished list of tasks to carry out
Priorities change from week to week with no explanation
Nobody can explain how features are chosen

questions.explain: Partnership, strategy and an open process are healthy. Order-taking, chaos and an unexplained process are warning signs.
questions.rule: Listen for partnership and strategy.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: True or false: If a partner answers what has been harder than expected with specifics, the candidate learns honest challenges she could face.
questions.explain: The authors say this question gets honest insight about the challenges you could expect to face.
questions.rule: This question invites candor.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate has used the company's product and wondered why one feature works as it does. How could she ask a partner about it?
options: Tell the partner that the feature seems badly designed to her and why
Ask if a technical constraint or user feedback drove that design
Ask whether the partner uses the product on a regular basis herself
Ask the partner to promise that the feature will be changed soon
optionExplain: Unsolicited criticism may offend people who built the feature.
Right: it shows genuine curiosity and research, and invites the reasoning.
That asks about the partner's habits, not about the decision.
That asks for a commitment the partner cannot make.
questions.explain: The authors suggest questions about functionality you are genuinely curious about, such as what drove a decision, and say they impress when you have really used the product.
questions.rule: Ask about decisions you noticed.
questions.teaches: If the company has a customer-facing product, ask specific questions about functionality you are genuinely curious about, such as whether a technical constraint or user feedback drove a decision; this impresses when you have really used the product.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Which question is the weakest choice to ask a member of the team at the end of an interview?
options: What has been harder than you expected in this role?
How are technical decisions made on this team?
What did the team learn from its last launch?
What does your company do for its customers?
optionExplain: This invites an honest account.
This asks about the decision process.
This shows research and invites a story.
Right: the answer is on the About page and has probably been covered already.
questions.explain: Questions should add information the interviewer can supply. The card next lists what to avoid.
questions.rule: Ask what cannot be found easily.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Sort each question: should it be avoided, or is it a good question?

items.t: What does your company do?
How did I do?
Where do you see the company in ten years?
What has been harder than you expected?
What tools or processes do you wish you could change?
What did the team learn from its last launch?

questions.explain: Easily found answers, requests for a verdict and distant hypotheticals are on the avoid list. Specific questions about real experience are good.
questions.rule: Avoid the easy, the anxious and the distant.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate planned to ask an engineer about the company's vacation policy. What should she do?
options: Ask it anyway, because engineers know the policy better than recruiters
Swap it for a work question, and ask the recruiter about vacation
Ask it twice, to be sure that the answer is the same for everyone
Drop questions altogether, so that she cannot make a mistake
optionExplain: Engineers may read it as a sign that she cares about perks.
Right: perks go to recruiters; the engineer gets work questions.
Repeating does not remove the problem of audience.
Dropping questions wastes the opportunity.
questions.explain: The authors say asking team members about salary, benefits or perks should be saved for recruiters.
questions.rule: Perks are for recruiters.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wants honest information about the work. Which version is better?
options: What is great about working here, in your experience?
What would you say is the best part of the company culture?
How would you describe the company to a friend you like?
What has been harder than expected since you joined?
optionExplain: It invites a promotional answer.
It invites praise, which the interviewer will likely provide.
It asks for a friendly pitch and not a candid account.
Right: it invites an honest, specific answer and not a marketing line.
questions.explain: The authors advise swapping marketing-bait questions for ones that are more likely to produce real answers.
questions.rule: Ask for the harder truth.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: True or false: If a candidate asks how many other candidates are being interviewed, she is likely to come across as confident.
questions.explain: The authors list this among the questions that show desperation, together with How did I do? and What are my chances?
questions.rule: Do not ask for reassurance.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wants to ask a manager about the company's future. Which question avoids the pitfall the authors name?
options: What are the team's main goals for the next year?
Where do you see the company in ten years?
Will this company still exist in ten years?
What will the industry look like a decade from now?
optionExplain: Right: it is concrete and near-term, and the manager can answer it.
That is the distant hypothetical the authors warn about.
That is also distant, and it may sound negative.
That is another distant speculation.
questions.explain: The authors list hypothetical questions about the distant future, such as where the company will be in 10 years, among those to avoid.
questions.rule: Keep questions concrete.
questions.teaches: Hypothetical questions about the distant future, such as where the company will be in ten years, are on the authors' list of questions to avoid.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: You have a final-round interview tomorrow. How should you prepare your closing questions?
options: Prepare one general question and leave the rest to inspiration on the day
Prepare the same questions you asked in your first interview
Prepare several specific questions on how you would contribute
Prepare no questions, since the process is almost complete by then
optionExplain: One general question leaves you exposed if it is answered.
The first-round questions are likely to be too shallow now.
Right: later rounds call for deeper questions, and several are better than one.
The final round is the time to show how you would contribute.
questions.explain: Preparation depends on how many and what stage. The card next gives the numbers.
questions.rule: Prepare several, fit the stage.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Prepare five to ____ questions before the interview.
questions.explain: The authors recommend preparing five to seven questions.
questions.rule: Five to seven.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate must choose between asking how is the team culture or how often the team ships features versus fixes debt. Which fits the advice?
options: The first, because culture is the most important thing to learn
The first, because a short question is easier for the interviewer
The second, because a direct question gets a specific answer
The second, but only if the interviewer is a recruiter
optionExplain: Culture matters, but a vague question gets a vague answer.
Short is not the same as direct.
Right: the more direct the question, the more revealing the answer.
The question suits a team member, not a recruiter.
questions.explain: The authors contrast a vague culture question with a specific one about features versus technical debt.
questions.rule: Direct questions, revealing answers.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: Match each interview stage to the focus of the questions.
questions.explain: The authors suggest moving from role and team questions to deeper ones, and in the final round to ones that show you have thought about contributing.
questions.rule: Go deeper as the stages go on.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: True or false: If a candidate asks how is the team culture, the authors expect an answer as vague as the question.
questions.explain: The authors say a vague question deserves a vague answer, while a specific one gets a specific answer.
questions.rule: Vague in, vague out.

questions.section: 4.4 Do You Have Any Questions for Me?
questions.q: A candidate wonders why she should prepare seven questions when she will ask only two or three. What reason do the authors give?
options: Some will be answered during the talk, so backups cover her
Interviewers score candidates by the number of questions that they ask
Asking seven questions shows the interviewer that she is a thorough person
The questions are meant to fill the time that is left over
optionExplain: Right: the authors say some will be answered along the way.
The authors do not say interviewers count questions.
Asking too many would not be the aim; preparing many is.
The purpose is information and interest, not filling time.
questions.explain: The authors explain that some questions will be answered during the conversation, so backups mean you are not caught empty-handed.
questions.rule: Prepare extra as a safety margin.
questions.teaches: Some of your prepared questions will be answered during the conversation, so having backups ready means you will not be caught empty-handed at the end.

questions.q: Why do interviewers ask candidates about their biggest weakness?
options: To find a flaw serious enough to justify rejecting the candidate outright
To test whether the candidate can think of a clever-sounding reply quickly
To learn which skills the candidate dislikes using in her daily work
To see how candidates judge themselves and work to improve
optionExplain: It is not a search for grounds to reject; a sensible answer is welcome.
A polished disguise is what interviewers see through.
Dislikes are not the aim; improvement is.
Right: it is about self-awareness, honesty and improvement.
questions.explain: The question probes character as much as skill. The card next lists what interviewers want.
questions.rule: It tests self-awareness and honesty.

questions.q: The weakness question assesses your self-awareness, your honesty and your willingness to ____.
questions.explain: The authors name these three things as the purpose of the question.
questions.rule: Self-awareness, honesty, improvement.

questions.q: A candidate must answer the weakness question. Which approach matches the purpose of the question?
options: Name a weakness that is really a strength so that it sounds impressive
Name a real weakness honestly and show what she is doing about it
Say she has no weaknesses that affect her work in any meaningful way
List every weakness she can think of so that nothing is concealed
optionExplain: Disguising a strength is a humblebrag that interviewers see through.
Right: honesty and improvement are exactly what is tested.
Claiming none fails the honesty and self-awareness tests.
Listing everything shows no judgement and invites doubt.
questions.explain: A real weakness plus action serves all three purposes.
questions.rule: Honest and improving.

questions.q: Which reply best shows self-awareness?
options: I work too hard and I care too much about quality in everything I do
I have a few areas to develop, but nothing worth mentioning here today
I am a perfectionist, which I think is a good thing in my kind of work overall
I dive too deep into problems, and last quarter it delayed a release
optionExplain: This is a humblebrag that disguises a strength.
This avoids naming anything, so it shows no self-awareness.
This is a cliché and presents the flaw as an advantage.
Right: it names a real tendency and a real cost.
questions.explain: Self-awareness shows in specifics, not in disguises.
questions.rule: Specific cost, honest tone.

questions.q: True or false: If a candidate claims to have no real weakness, the interviewer is likely to read that as strong self-awareness.
questions.explain: The question exists to test self-awareness and honesty, so a refusal to name anything fails the test.
questions.rule: No weakness reads as no insight.

questions.q: A candidate dreads the weakness question because it has a reputation for catching people off guard. What do the authors suggest?
options: Improvise on the day, because a rehearsed answer will sound fake to anyone
Think it through beforehand, since unprepared candidates get tripped up
Ask the interviewer to skip the question since it is badly out of date
Give the shortest answer possible so that very little can go wrong in it
optionExplain: Preparation does not make an honest answer fake.
Right: the authors say candidates who have not thought through these questions can be tripped up.
Declining the question wastes the opportunity and looks evasive.
A very short answer leaves out the improvement that matters most.
questions.explain: The authors note that the question has a reputation for catching candidates off guard, which is why thinking it through helps.
questions.rule: Prepare so it does not catch you off guard.
questions.teaches: The weakness question has a reputation for catching candidates off guard, so think it through before the interview.

questions.q: You are asked about your biggest weakness. Which answer plan gives the most complete reply?
options: Name two or three weaknesses briefly and then move on to your strengths again
Describe one weakness in detail and explain at length why it matters to you
Name a real weakness, give a short example, then say what you are doing
Give a weakness, then explain why it is actually not a problem for you at all
optionExplain: Listing several weaknesses shows no depth and no action.
Dwelling on the weakness leaves out what you are doing about it.
Right: weakness, example and improvement make a complete answer.
Minimising it fails the honesty test.
questions.explain: A good answer has three parts. The card next adds how much time each deserves.
questions.rule: Weakness, example, action.

questions.q: Put the three parts of the weakness answer in order.
items: Select a real weakness
Give a specific context in which it affected you
Describe your active improvement
questions.explain: The answer names the weakness, shows it was real with a short example, and spends the rest on improvement.
questions.rule: Weakness, context, improvement.

questions.q: Match each sentence of one candidate's answer to its part.
pairs: I sometimes hold on to work I should hand off
Last month this left two teammates waiting on me for days
Now I hand off anything a colleague can do at 80 percent of my level
questions.explain: The first names the weakness, the second ties it to a real event, and the third gives a concrete rule for improving.
questions.rule: Each sentence has one job.

questions.q: Sort each element: is it part of the three-part structure or not?

items.t: A real weakness that has affected work
A brief example of when it caused a problem
Concrete steps being taken now
A claim that the weakness is secretly a strength
An apology for having the weakness
A promise that the weakness will be gone by next year

questions.explain: The structure needs a real weakness, an example and concrete action. Disguises, apologies and promises are not part of it.
questions.rule: Real, specific, active.

questions.q: True or false: If a candidate spends most of her answer on the weakness and one sentence on improvement, the answer is out of balance.
questions.explain: The authors say the improvement should form the bulk of the answer, because what you are doing now matters more than the weakness itself.
questions.rule: Weight the answer toward action.

questions.q: A candidate has a vivid story about a mistake and wants to retell the whole incident in detail. What do the authors suggest?
options: Keep the incident brief and spend the time on what she is doing
Tell the whole story, since a detailed account shows honesty and candour
Tell the story but leave out the lesson, to avoid sounding rehearsed or neat
Skip the story and describe only the lessons that she has learned from it
optionExplain: Right: the improvement should form the bulk of the answer.
Detail on the problem takes the time from the improvement that matters more.
The lesson and action are the parts that matter most.
The brief example is needed to prove the weakness is real.
questions.explain: The authors say that what you are doing now matters more than the weakness itself, so the improvement should be the bulk of the answer.
questions.rule: Spend time on the improvement.
questions.teaches: The improvement should form the bulk of the answer, because what you are doing now matters more than the weakness itself.

questions.q: A candidate for a backend role must choose a weakness to share. Which choice is best?
options: Visual design, which she has worked on but the job barely needs
Writing reliable code, which she finds hard to get right in practice
Working with other engineers, which she finds hard to really enjoy
Learning new technologies, which she tries to avoid whenever possible
optionExplain: Right: it is a real weakness that is unlikely to disqualify her.
This is a core requirement of the job and would be a deal-breaker.
Collaboration is central to engineering work, so this raises concern.
Learning is central to the role, so avoidance is serious.
questions.explain: The best weakness is real but not central to the job. The card next explains the choice.
questions.rule: Honest but not disqualifying.

questions.q: Pick an honest weakness, but not one so severe that it ____ you.
questions.explain: The authors tell candidates to choose something real that is not a deal-breaker for the role.
questions.rule: Real, not fatal.

questions.q: A candidate for a senior lead role is deciding between two weaknesses. Which should she share?
options: Delegating work, which she rarely does and often regrets later
Setting priorities, which she finds hard to do for the whole team
Presenting to large groups, which she is working on with a coach
Mentoring junior colleagues, which she has never had time to try
optionExplain: Delegation is a core duty of a lead, so it is a poor choice.
Prioritising for a team is central to the lead role.
Right: it is real but not central to a lead's core duties.
Mentoring is a core expectation of a senior or lead position.
questions.explain: The same weakness can be acceptable at one level and a concern at another.
questions.rule: Check it against the level.

questions.q: Sort each weakness: is it acceptable for the role named, or a concern?

items.t: Backend engineer: struggles with visual design
Junior engineer: not yet strong at delegating
Backend engineer: occasionally nervous in large presentations
Frontend engineer: struggles with visual design
Senior lead: not good at delegating
Developer: dislikes coding

questions.explain: A weakness is acceptable when the role does not rest on it. The same weakness may be a concern when it is a core requirement.
questions.rule: Role decides.

questions.q: A candidate weak at delegation moves from applying to a junior role to applying to a senior role. What changes?
options: The weakness becomes less relevant, because seniors rarely need to delegate
The weakness becomes more problematic, as senior work involves delegating
The weakness stays equally acceptable, since weaknesses do not depend on role
The weakness becomes a strength, because seniors are expected to be hands-on
optionExplain: Seniors and leads need delegation more, not less.
Right: the authors say it is acceptable for junior individual contributors but a problem for senior or lead roles.
Acceptability does depend on what the role needs.
Being hands-on in place of delegating is exactly the concern.
questions.explain: The role's requirements set what counts as an acceptable weakness.
questions.rule: Same weakness, different level, different weight.

questions.q: A candidate wants to know what kinds of weakness are typically worth sharing. Which is on the authors' list?
options: A weakness that could be seen as an advantage in every possible kind of role
A trait of a colleague that makes work difficult for her whole team
A weakness in a skill that the job description requires on day one
A strength taken too far, such as attention to detail turning into perfectionism
optionExplain: An advantage in disguise is the humblebrag the authors warn against.
The question is about her own weakness, not about a colleague.
A skill the job requires on day one risks being a deal-breaker.
Right: the authors list strengths taken too far among the best categories.
questions.explain: The authors list working style issues, communication gaps, skill development areas and strengths taken too far as the best categories.
questions.rule: Four good categories.
questions.teaches: The best weaknesses to share fall into categories such as working style issues, communication gaps, skill development areas and strengths taken too far.

questions.q: Which statement best proves that a candidate's weakness is real?
options: Sometimes I spend too long on things that do not really need it at all
Last quarter I spent three days on an optimization that delayed a launch
I think my attention to detail can sometimes be a problem for others
People have occasionally said that I take my time over some tasks
optionExplain: This is general and cannot be checked.
Right: a dated, concrete event with a cost.
This is vague and offers no example.
This relies on unnamed people and gives no event.
questions.explain: Specifics prove it is real. The card next explains how much to say.
questions.rule: Name the event.

questions.q: True or false: The context part of the weakness answer should fill most of it, with the improvement kept to a sentence.
questions.explain: The authors say the context only needs to prove the weakness is real; the improvement should form the bulk of the answer.
questions.rule: Short example, then improvement.

questions.q: A candidate's weakness is not updating teammates. Which example fits the advice?
options: I sometimes forget to keep people informed about changes that affect them all
I once had a long project during which the team had many difficulties and delays
I have a tendency to go quiet when things are busy, which is a flaw of mine
Last month a designer rebuilt a screen because I had not told her of a change
optionExplain: It restates the weakness without an event.
It describes a project but says nothing about her part.
It is a general tendency and offers no specific case.
Right: it names a real event with a cost to a colleague.
questions.explain: A good example names a time, a result and its cost.
questions.rule: Event plus cost.

questions.q: Sort each example: does it follow the advice or break it?

items.t: It names a recent, real situation
It takes one or two sentences
It shows a cost such as a delay or extra work
It runs for several minutes of detail
It describes the weakness only in general terms
It blames a teammate for what went wrong

questions.explain: A good example is real, brief and shows a cost. Long accounts, vague statements and blame all fail.
questions.rule: Real, brief, costly.

questions.q: True or false: If a candidate describes the context at length, the improvement section is likely to be squeezed.
questions.explain: The authors want the improvement to form the bulk of the answer, so a long example takes time from it.
questions.rule: Long context shrinks the improvement.

questions.q: A candidate wants to find a convincing example of a weakness. Which questions do the authors suggest she ask herself?
options: Did I miss a deadline over quality, or create extra work by not sharing updates?
Which colleague has annoyed me the most in the last year or so?
Which of my strengths do I think the interviewer will like the best?
Which weakness will be least likely to prompt a follow-up question later?
optionExplain: Right: the authors suggest looking at real situations with a cost.
That invites blame and not self-assessment.
That points toward a disguised strength.
That aims to avoid scrutiny, which defeats the purpose.
questions.explain: The authors prompt candidates to recall a time the weakness caused a missed deadline or extra work for others.
questions.rule: Look for a real cost.
questions.teaches: To find an example, ask whether the weakness made you miss a deadline because you focused too much on quality, or created extra work for others because you did not share updates proactively.

questions.q: A candidate's weakness is that she over-engineers solutions. Which improvement is most convincing?
options: She tries harder to remember that simple solutions are usually better ones
She hopes that experience will gradually correct the habit over time
She sets time limits for each task and checks her estimates
She has decided to be more careful about this in the future from now on
optionExplain: Good intentions without a mechanism are weak.
Hoping for change is not a step.
Right: it is a concrete system with measurement.
A future resolution is not an action taken now.
questions.explain: Concrete steps beat intentions. The card next lists the kinds of steps.
questions.rule: Concrete steps, not intentions.

questions.q: Match each kind of improvement to an example.
pairs: I now set time boxes for exploration
I asked peers to call me out when I get too deep in details
I created a checklist for code reviews
I took a technical writing course
I track how long I spend on tasks
questions.explain: The authors name these five kinds of improvement step, each with examples.
questions.rule: Five kinds of step.

questions.q: A candidate's weakness is nervousness when presenting. Which improvement is best?
options: She plans to attend a presentation course at some point later this year
She reads about presentation skills whenever she has some spare time at home
She joined a speaking club, volunteers to present, and her last two talks went better
She avoids presenting whenever possible to prevent a bad outcome for herself
optionExplain: A plan for later is not current action.
Reading without practice is not strong evidence.
Right: it combines action, practice and recent progress.
Avoidance is the opposite of improvement.
questions.explain: Action plus progress shows a trajectory.
questions.rule: Action plus progress.

questions.q: Sort each statement: is it concrete improvement or only intention?

items.t: I track my estimates against actuals in a spreadsheet
My last three estimates were within 10 percent of actual time
I now send weekly status updates to everyone affected
I am trying to be better about this
I plan to improve at some point
I will work harder on it in future

questions.explain: Concrete improvement names an action or a measured result. Intentions name neither.
questions.rule: Name the action or the result.

questions.q: True or false: If a candidate can show recent progress, such as a document that earned positive feedback on clarity, the improvement is more convincing.
questions.explain: The authors say to show recent progress if you can, since it proves the steps are working.
questions.rule: Progress proves the steps.

questions.q: A candidate has spent one sentence on her weakness and four on her improvement. How does this ratio compare with the authors' advice?
options: It matches: the improvement should run two to three times longer
It is too heavy, since the improvement should be shorter than the weakness
It is too light, since the improvement should be ten times longer
It does not matter, since the authors give no guidance on length
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the improvement should be two to three times the length.
The authors want the opposite balance.
Ten times would crowd out the weakness altogether.
The authors do give a ratio of two to three times.
questions.explain: The authors say that the improvement section should be two to three times longer than the description of the weakness.
questions.rule: Improvement runs two to three times longer.
questions.teaches: The improvement section should be two to three times longer than the description of the weakness.

questions.q: A candidate says her weakness is that she is too thorough. What makes the answer honest rather than a boast?
options: She explains that thoroughness is a quality every employer wants to see
She adds that she receives praise from her colleagues for it all the time
She says she works on it by trying to be thorough about fewer things overall
She describes a case where thoroughness cost time or a deadline
optionExplain: Defending the trait turns the answer into a boast.
Praise confirms the strength, not the weakness.
Being thorough about fewer things is a vague fix, not a real problem.
Right: a real problem with a specific cost makes it honest.
questions.explain: A strength counts as a weakness only when it caused a real problem. The card next gives the authors' examples.
questions.rule: Show the problem.

questions.q: Match each strength to the weakness it can turn into when taken too far.
pairs: Losing sight of timelines or the bigger picture
questions.explain: The authors give these three pairs as good examples of the approach.
questions.rule: Each strength has its overextension.

questions.q: A candidate who prides herself on being collaborative wants to use the approach. Which version is honest?
options: I am so collaborative that the team often says that I am the best part of the group
I seek so much input that decisions slow, and last month it delayed a release
I love collaborating so much that I can never say no to anyone's idea at all
I care so much about everyone's views that I am a very good manager of people
optionExplain: This is a boast with no problem.
Right: it names the overextension and gives a concrete cost.
It states an absolute and gives no specific case or cost.
This is a humblebrag that praises a management skill.
questions.explain: A real problem in a specific case makes the approach work.
questions.rule: Overextension plus cost.

questions.q: Sort each answer: is it a good strength-as-weakness answer or a poor one?

items.t: I make snap decisions and sometimes act before I research
I get lost in details and lose sight of timelines at times
I over-engineer and have shipped late because of it
I care too much
I am too dedicated
I hold people to high standards

questions.explain: The three under 'Good answer' name a trait that backfires and a real consequence. The three under 'Poor answer' are humblebrags or describe a management skill.
questions.rule: Real backfire, not a boast.

questions.q: True or false: If a candidate says I care too much, the interviewer is likely to see it as a humblebrag, not a real weakness.
questions.explain: The authors list this as a poor example because it is just a way to disguise a strength.
questions.rule: Disguise is easy to see.

questions.q: A candidate with a methodical style wants to avoid the humblebrag trap. What should she do?
options: Say that being methodical is her only flaw and that she is working on it hard
Say that she has a very high standard that most people cannot meet
Say that her methodical style makes her slower than anyone else she knows
Give the circumstances, such as three days spent on a tiny gain, and the problem
optionExplain: Naming a single flaw adds no specifics.
Boasting about standards is a humblebrag.
An exaggerated claim without an example is not credible.
Right: specific circumstances and problems make the answer real.
questions.explain: The authors give the example of spending three days squeezing 0.01 percent more efficiency when 99.99 percent of the benefit had been delivered in one day.
questions.rule: Describe the circumstances and the cost.
questions.teaches: A real example of thoroughness taken too far is spending three days squeezing out 0.01 percent more efficiency when 99.99 percent of the benefit arrived in one day.

questions.q: A candidate answers the weakness question with: I work too hard. How would an interviewer likely react?
options: They would admire her dedication and move on with the rest of the interview
They would see a disguised strength and begin to doubt her honesty overall
They would worry that she is likely to burn out and leave the company soon
They would be unable to judge, and ask the same question again in other words
optionExplain: Interviewers recognise this move and do not treat it as admiration.
Right: it is a humblebrag and reads as dishonest.
Burn-out is a different concern from honesty.
They will understand it, which is the problem.
questions.explain: A strength dressed up as a weakness fails the honesty test. The card next names four such failures.
questions.rule: Do not disguise a strength.

questions.q: Match each weak answer to the reason it fails.
pairs: Disguises a strength and reads as dishonest
A cliché that is vague and shows no awareness
Gives no sign that you take growth seriously
Raises the question of why you are applying
questions.explain: The authors give a reason for each: dishonesty, cliché, lack of growth, and unsuitability.
questions.rule: Each failure has its own reason.

questions.q: A candidate says: I struggle with communication sometimes. What is missing?
options: A statement that communication is the most important skill in the whole field
A list of all the other skills that she believes she has in full measure
Which kind of communication, in what situations, and what she does about it
A promise to communicate better when the interviewer next asks her
optionExplain: Importance does not add specifics or action.
Listing strengths changes the subject.
Right: the authors say it needs specifics and action.
A promise for later is not current action.
questions.explain: Vague weaknesses with no action suggest she does not take growth seriously.
questions.rule: Be specific and show action.

questions.q: Sort each answer by the kind of failure it shows.

items.t: I work too hard
I care too much about quality
I'm a perfectionist
I struggle with communication sometimes
I hate coding
I'm not good with people (for a management role)

questions.explain: The three under 'Humblebrag or cliché' disguise a strength or repeat a cliché. The others are too vague to mean anything or fatal for the role.
questions.rule: Disguised, vague or fatal.

questions.q: True or false: If a developer says her biggest weakness is that she hates coding, the interviewer is likely to wonder why she applied.
questions.explain: The authors use this as an example of a disqualifying weakness: if that is your weakness, why are you applying?
questions.rule: Some weaknesses disqualify.

questions.q: A candidate wants a weakness she is actively working on, with no cliché or boast. Which pro tip from the authors guides her?
options: Show self-awareness without self-deprecation, and focus on the improvement journey
Pick the weakness that sounds least harmful to the interviewer, and keep the answer short
Apologize for the weakness so that the interviewer knows that she takes it seriously
Pick a weakness from the job description so that she appears relevant
optionExplain: Right: honesty without self-deprecation, with the focus on progress.
Avoiding substance is the failing the authors warn about.
Apologies add self-deprecation and shift attention away from progress.
Copying the job description would not be an honest weakness.
questions.explain: The authors advise choosing something you are actively working on, showing self-awareness without self-deprecation or humblebragging, and focusing on the improvement journey.
questions.rule: Honest, not self-deprecating.
questions.teaches: Choose something you are actively working to improve, and show self-awareness without self-deprecation or humblebragging.

questions.q: A candidate cannot think of any weakness to mention. Where is the best place to look?
options: Constructive feedback given in her recent performance reviews at work
The list of strengths in her resume, to find one that she can turn around
The job description, to find something that she can claim as a gap
The weaknesses that other candidates are likely to name in this interview
optionExplain: Right: reviews contain real feedback, with patterns she can address.
That would produce a disguise, not a real weakness.
A made-up gap is not honest.
Other candidates' answers do not describe her.
questions.explain: Real feedback is the best source. The card next lists five.
questions.rule: Look at real feedback.

questions.q: Match each source to what it can tell you.
pairs: What led to something going wrong
Where others find something easy that you do not
Where you feel you are not performing at your best
questions.explain: The authors give five sources of insight, each pointing to a different kind of weakness.
questions.rule: Five sources.

questions.q: Three different reviewers told a candidate that her code needs more comments. How can she use this?
options: Ignore it, since three people could be mistaken about her code and style
Mention it only if the interviewer asks about code quality directly and in detail
Name it as her weakness, and describe a checklist and a peer check
Say she has been commenting more but do not mention the feedback she was given
optionExplain: Feedback from several people is the pattern the authors say is worth addressing.
Waiting to be asked wastes a good example.
Right: repeated feedback is a real pattern, and she can show action and results.
Leaving out the feedback hides the evidence that makes it believable.
questions.explain: Repeated feedback plus a concrete fix and a check is a model answer.
questions.rule: Quote the feedback, show the fix.

questions.q: Sort each description: is it a weakness drawn from a source in the list, or not?

items.t: My manager said I should communicate more proactively
I tested only on desktop and broke the mobile app
Everyone else presents well, and I get nervous
I'm the best at everything but sometimes impatient with slower colleagues
I wish the company had better tools
I lose track of my emails

questions.explain: The three under 'Drawn from a listed source' come from reviews, a mistake, and colleagues' skills. The others are boasts, complaints about the company, or have no evidence behind them.
questions.rule: Draw from real evidence.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate who describes a mistake and a checklist now covering testing on all platforms gives a realistic way to show improvement.
questions.explain: The authors use this example: a checklist confirming testing on all platforms, with six months free of platform-specific bugs.
questions.rule: A mistake plus a fix is credible.

questions.q: A candidate consistently under-estimates how long projects take. Which source in the authors' list fits, and how can she show progress?
options: A colleague's skill, shown by copying how a colleague estimates
Her own frustration, shown by tracking estimates against actuals
A single mistake, shown by describing the one project that ran late
A performance review, shown by quoting the manager's comment on timelines
optionExplain: It is not about a colleague's skill she lacks.
Right: the authors give this frustration example with an estimates-versus-actuals spreadsheet.
It is a repeated pattern and not a single mistake.
No review is mentioned in her case.
questions.explain: The authors' example tracks estimates against actuals in a spreadsheet and adds a buffer for unknowns, resulting in estimates within 10 percent of the actual time instead of being off by 100 percent.
questions.rule: Measure estimates against actuals.
questions.teaches: A frustration with being over-optimistic about timelines can be addressed by tracking estimates against actuals in a spreadsheet and adding a buffer for unknowns; in the authors' example the last three estimates came within 10 percent of the actual time.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate's last job ended badly. The interviewer asks why she left. What is the best approach?
options: Explain in full what went wrong so that the interviewer hears her side
List everything the previous employer did wrong so the facts are clear
Refuse to discuss it and ask the interviewer to move on to another topic
Keep it short and professional, and turn to what she wants next
optionExplain: Full detail invites doubts and may sound defensive or bitter.
Criticism of a former employer is a red flag in itself.
Refusing to answer is itself a warning sign to the interviewer.
Right: brief, professional and forward-looking.
questions.explain: You do not owe the interviewer the whole story. The card next gives the authors' reasoning.
questions.rule: Brief, professional, forward-looking.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Keep your answers brief, professional and ____.
questions.explain: The authors say to keep answers brief, professional and forward-looking.
questions.rule: Brief, professional, forward-looking.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: An interviewer asks a candidate why she left her previous job, which ended after a dispute with her manager. Which reply follows the advice?
options: My manager was unreasonable, and I had no choice but to leave the team
It wasn't the right fit; I'm looking for a role with clearer technical direction
It's a long story involving several incidents, and I can go through each one
I would rather not discuss that part of my career if it is all the same
optionExplain: Blaming a manager is a red flag.
Right: brief, neutral, and moving to what she wants.
Offering a long story volunteers exactly the detail she need not share.
Refusing to discuss it draws more attention to it.
questions.explain: A short neutral reply plus a forward-looking point is enough.
questions.rule: Neutral, then forward.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Sort each element of an answer about leaving: does it follow the advice or break it?

items.t: It stays brief and professional
It focuses on what the candidate wants next
It describes the former employer neutrally
It lists the manager's mistakes in detail
It explains at length that the candidate was blamed unfairly
It fills a silence with extra explanation

questions.explain: Brief, neutral and forward-looking answers fit the advice. Blame, long explanations and filling silence do not.
questions.rule: Say little, look ahead.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: True or false: If a candidate criticises a previous employer, the interviewer is likely to take it as honesty rather than a red flag.
questions.explain: The authors list badmouthing previous employers as a red flag, along with fleeing problems you created.
questions.rule: Badmouthing is a red flag.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate wonders which other patterns, besides fleeing problems and badmouthing, make interviewers suspicious. What do the authors list?
options: A resume that shows only one employer for many years in a row
A candidate who gives a short, simple answer without extra detail
A candidate who mentions what she hopes to learn in the next role
Patterns of instability in the resume, or a story that does not add up
optionExplain: Long tenure is not named as a red flag.
The authors recommend brief answers, not warn against them.
Looking forward is what the authors want.
Right: the authors name instability patterns and inconsistent stories.
questions.explain: The authors list four red flags: fleeing problems you created, badmouthing past employers, patterns of instability, and a story that does not add up.
questions.rule: Four red flags.
questions.teaches: Besides fleeing problems you created and badmouthing employers, interviewers treat patterns of instability in a resume and a story that does not add up as red flags.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate is leaving a job because the team is chaotic. How should she explain her move?
options: By describing the growth and structure she wants in her next role
By explaining how disorganized the team was and why it was hard to work there
By saying the company was not worth staying at and that she is relieved to go
By saying she had nothing in particular to say about the reason for the move
optionExplain: Right: she frames it around what she is moving toward.
That is a description of what she is leaving behind, which the authors advise against.
That is criticism, which the authors say not to do.
That avoids the question and may seem evasive.
questions.explain: Voluntary moves are best explained in terms of the future. The card next gives the structure.
questions.rule: Toward, not away.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Put the parts of an answer about looking for a new role in order.
items: Brief context, if needed
What you are looking for
Why this opportunity fits
questions.explain: The authors suggest a simple structure: brief context, what you want, and why this role provides it.
questions.rule: Context, goal, fit.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate at a startup wants to move to a larger company. Which answer fits the advice?
options: I'm leaving because the startup has no processes and everything is a mess
I'm leaving because the founders make poor decisions and ignore the engineers
I've learned a lot at a startup, and I'm ready for a place with more established processes
I'm leaving because the pay is too low and the hours are far too long
optionExplain: It focuses on what is wrong with the old place.
It criticizes the founders, which the authors advise against.
Right: it gives a positive view of the past and a forward-looking reason.
Pay and hours are complaints, not an opportunity.
questions.explain: Company stage is one of the good reasons the authors give, framed positively.
questions.rule: Frame the stage change positively.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Match each good reason for moving to an example of how to say it.
pairs: I want more technical challenges and responsibility
I want to work with distributed systems at scale
I want more direct user impact
I'm looking for a stronger engineering culture
questions.explain: The authors list these reasons, all of which look forward to what the candidate wants.
questions.rule: Reasons that point forward.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: True or false: Describing a current employer negatively is likely to be seen as a warning sign, even if the criticism is accurate.
questions.explain: The authors say not to trash your employer, even if the workplace is terrible, because it raises doubts about you.
questions.rule: Even true criticism can hurt.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate is leaving a toxic workplace. What wording do the authors suggest?
options: Say the old workplace was toxic and that she is relieved to have left it
Say she cannot discuss why she is leaving because of a confidentiality rule
