Say she wants to work for a company proud of its supportive culture, and has heard good things about this one
Say that her old employer treated people badly and that she hopes yours does not
optionExplain: This describes the toxicity directly, which the authors advise against.
Inventing a confidentiality rule would be untrue and suspicious.
Right: the authors give a positive, future-facing phrase like this.
This criticizes the old employer and implies a comparison with yours.
questions.explain: The authors give the example: I want to work for a company that is proud of their supportive culture, and I've heard good things about yours, and add that the answer should take 30 seconds to a minute.
questions.rule: Say what you want, not what you fled.
questions.teaches: Even when leaving a toxic workplace, frame the reason positively and look forward, for example by saying you want to work for a company proud of its supportive culture; keep the whole answer to 30 seconds to a minute.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate was laid off when her whole team was cut. How should she say so?
options: State it plainly, add a line of context, and move on to what she wants
Apologize first, then explain in detail why her team was the one cut
Describe how unfair the decision was and how much the company lost
Avoid the subject by talking about how much she enjoyed the old job
optionExplain: Right: direct, factual and forward-looking.
An apology treats the layoff as her fault.
Complaint about fairness sounds defensive.
Avoiding the subject makes it look as if she has something to hide.
questions.explain: A layoff is a fact, not a flaw. The card next gives the tone.
questions.rule: Plain, brief, forward.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, someone who was laid off should explain at length and be ready to defend herself.
questions.explain: The authors say a layoff is not your fault and needs no defensiveness or over-explanation.
questions.rule: No shame, no defensiveness.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Which sentence fits the authors' advice for explaining a layoff?
options: I was let go, but it was not really my fault, and I can explain exactly why that is
My company was badly run, and it was clear from the start that cuts would come
I was laid off, which has been very difficult, and I hope you will understand
My company cut the whole data team in a restructuring; I'm now looking for a team that invests in data long term
optionExplain: It sounds defensive and invites a detailed discussion of blame.
It criticizes the company and implies she saw it coming.
It appeals for sympathy and focuses on feelings.
Right: factual, brief and forward-looking.
questions.explain: State the fact, add context, pivot.
questions.rule: State it, then pivot.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Sort each reply to a question about a layoff: does it match the advice or not?

items.t: I was laid off in March when the team was cut
Since then I've been selective about my next move
I want a team investing in infrastructure for the long term
I can't believe they let me go after everything I did
I should have seen it coming and I apologize
Let me explain in detail why it wasn't my fault

questions.explain: Direct statements, brief context and forward-looking aims match the advice. Resentment, apology and long explanations do not.
questions.rule: Matter-of-fact, then move on.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate worries that a layoff will look bad. What context does the authors' advice add about the industry?
options: Layoffs are rare in tech, so she should explain the reason in detail
Layoffs are common in tech, so the interviewer is unlikely to judge her for it
Layoffs are common, so interviewers prefer candidates who have never had one
Layoffs matter only for senior candidates, who are expected to see them coming
optionExplain: The authors say they are common, not rare.
Right: the authors note that layoffs are common in tech.
Commonness works in her favor and does not create a preference.
The authors do not limit this to senior candidates.
questions.explain: The authors say that being laid off is not your fault and carries no shame, especially in tech, where it is common.
questions.rule: Common in tech.
questions.teaches: Being laid off carries no shame, especially in tech, where layoffs are common.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate was put on a performance improvement plan and then left. What is the authors' advice for her interview?
options: Explain the plan in full so that the interviewer hears it from her first
Invent another reason for leaving that sounds better to the interviewer
Apologize at length for the poor performance and promise to do better
Say it wasn't a good fit and move on, without volunteering the plan
optionExplain: Volunteering details gives the interviewer something to worry about.
Inventing a reason is dishonest and can be exposed.
Over-apologizing draws attention to the problem.
Right: it is true and enough.
questions.explain: A short true phrase protects you without lying. The card next gives the rest.
questions.rule: It wasn't a good fit.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: If you were fired or asked to leave, tell them, it wasn't a good ____.
questions.explain: The authors recommend the phrase it wasn't a good fit.
questions.rule: The phrase is: not a good fit.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: The interviewer presses for more detail on why it was not a good fit. Which reply follows the advice?
options: I would rather not say, and I hope you will respect that and leave it there for now
I learned I work best with clear direction and mentorship, which is why this team appeals
My manager and I disagreed about almost everything, and it got worse over time
I was not given enough support, and the other engineers did not help me when I asked
optionExplain: Refusing to answer invites suspicion.
Right: one sentence on what she learned, linked to this opportunity.
It adds blame and detail, which the authors advise against.
It blames others and does not show what she learned.
questions.explain: If pressed, add one sentence of learning and link it to the new role.
questions.rule: One sentence of learning.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Sort each element of an answer about a job that ended badly.

items.t: It says the role wasn't a good fit
It adds one sentence about what was learned only when pressed
It connects the lesson to the current opportunity
It volunteers that she was fired
It explains why it wasn't a good fit without being asked
It blames the manager for the outcome

questions.explain: Say the short phrase, add one sentence only if pressed, and tie it to the new role. Volunteering details or blaming does not follow the advice.
questions.rule: Short phrase; one sentence if pressed.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: True or false: A candidate who volunteers that she was on a performance improvement plan gives the interviewer less to worry about.
questions.explain: The authors say you do not need to disclose a performance improvement plan and should not volunteer information; volunteering it gives the interviewer more to worry about.
questions.rule: Do not volunteer.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate left because of tension with colleagues. Which neutral phrase do the authors suggest instead of blame?
options: A toxic group of colleagues
Colleagues who were not competent
Differences in working style
Management that did not listen
optionExplain: That assigns blame.
That is an insult and a red flag.
Right: the authors suggest neutral phrases such as differences in working style or different approaches to problem-solving.
That blames management.
questions.explain: The authors suggest neutral phrases that acknowledge the mismatch without assigning blame.
questions.rule: Neutral phrases, no blame.
questions.teaches: If you had issues with management or colleagues, neutral phrases such as differences in working style or different approaches to problem-solving acknowledge the mismatch without assigning blame.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate has a six-month gap after a layoff. How much should she say?
options: A sentence or two about the reason, then a statement about what she wants now
A long explanation of the job market and every application she made
An apology for the gap and a promise that it will not happen again
Nothing, hoping the interviewer will not notice the gap at all
optionExplain: Right: brief, then forward-looking.
A long account over-explains something that is not a problem.
An apology treats it as a fault.
The interviewer has seen the resume, so silence draws attention.
questions.explain: Gaps need a short answer. The card next shows the pattern.
questions.rule: One or two sentences.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: True or false: The authors suggest spending several minutes explaining a gap in your resume before moving on.
questions.explain: They advise addressing the gap briefly, in one or two sentences, and then moving on to what you are looking for.
questions.rule: Brief, then move on.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate took a year to retrain as a developer. Which answer follows the pattern?
options: I spent a year retraining from teaching to development, and I'm ready to apply that now
I know it looks odd, and I apologize for the year; I can explain everything
I took time off but would rather not go into the reasons, if that is acceptable
I had personal reasons, a number of which were quite difficult and complicated
optionExplain: Right: reason, what she did, and a forward-looking point.
Apologizing for the gap treats it as a problem.
Refusing to explain draws attention to the gap.
Vague references to personal difficulty invite probing.
questions.explain: The pattern is reason, optional current activity, forward look.
questions.rule: Reason, activity, look ahead.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Sort each element of a gap explanation: does it follow the pattern or break it?

items.t: One sentence stating the reason
An optional sentence on staying current
A forward-looking closing statement
A long apology for the time away
Details nobody asked about
A defensive tone about the gap

questions.explain: The pattern has one sentence of reason, an optional note on staying current, and a look ahead. Apology, extra detail and defensiveness break it.
questions.rule: Reason, optional activity, forward look.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate worries that she should apologize for a short gap on her resume. What do the authors say?
options: Apologize first, since the interviewer expects an acknowledgment of fault
Apologize only if the gap is longer than six months in total
Do not apologize excessively, since the company already saw the gap and still invited her
Apologize only to the recruiter, who has the most contact with her
optionExplain: Expectation of fault is not what the authors describe.
Length of the gap is not the test.
Right: the interview invitation shows the gap was not disqualifying.
The recruiter is not the target of the advice.
questions.explain: The authors point out that if you are being interviewed, the gaps or short tenures were not disqualifying, so you should not apologize excessively or volunteer unnecessary details.
questions.rule: The invitation shows the gap was acceptable.
questions.teaches: If you made it to an interview, the company has already seen your gaps and short tenures and was not put off, so do not apologize excessively or volunteer unnecessary details.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate has three jobs of under two years each. How should she explain them?
options: As proof that she is adaptable and enjoys frequent change in her work
As different circumstances, each with its own reason, ending with a wish for stability
As the result of bad managers at each company she worked for
As too complicated to explain briefly, so she will skip the details
optionExplain: That may suggest she will leave again, which is the interviewer's concern.
Right: different reasons show a sequence, not a repeated mistake.
Blaming all three managers sounds like a pattern of her own.
Skipping the details leaves the doubt unanswered.
questions.explain: Multiple short stints need more explanation. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Different situations, not the same mistake.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Frame multiple short stints as a sequence of circumstances, not a pattern of ____.
questions.explain: The authors tell candidates to show the moves came from different situations and not from the same mistake repeated.
questions.rule: Circumstances, not a pattern.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate left one job after eight months because the work was mostly maintenance. Which explanation follows the advice?
options: It was a bad job with a boring manager, and I left as soon as I could
I was not told the truth about the job, and the company misled me from the start
I left because I was bored, which I know is a problem I have in general
It wasn't a good fit; I learned I want to build, and that is why this role appeals
optionExplain: It criticizes the old job and the manager.
It blames the company and could sound like an excuse.
It presents the reason as a general flaw.
Right: a short phrase, a lesson and a link to this role.
questions.explain: A single short stint is easy to explain with a lesson.
questions.rule: Fit, lesson, link.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Sort each part of an explanation of multiple short stints.

items.t: A different legitimate reason for each move
A learning from the first move
A clear wish for a long-term role now
The same reason repeated for every move
A claim that every employer was at fault
A suggestion that she enjoys changing jobs often

questions.explain: Different reasons, learning and a wish for stability help. Repeating a reason, blaming everyone or enjoying change hurts.
questions.rule: Different reasons plus stability.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: True or false: Giving the same reason for every short stint is likely to look like a pattern, not a series of circumstances.
questions.explain: The authors say the key is to show the moves resulted from different situations, not the same mistake repeated.
questions.rule: Repeated reasons look like a pattern.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate has one eight-month stint and worries it is a red flag. What do the authors say?
options: One short stint is a serious red flag and needs a long explanation
A single short stint is easy to explain and is not a red flag
One short stint is fine only if the candidate was laid off
One short stint should be left off the resume to avoid questions
optionExplain: The authors contrast a single stint with multiple stints.
Right: the authors say one short stint is not a red flag.
The reason is not restricted to layoffs.
Leaving it off would risk looking like concealment.
questions.explain: The authors say a single short stint is easy to explain and not a red flag; it wasn't a good fit works perfectly, with a lesson.
questions.rule: One short stint is fine.
questions.teaches: A single short stint is easy to explain and is not a red flag.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: True or false: Because you need not share every detail, it is acceptable to make up a more flattering reason for leaving.
questions.explain: Leaving things out is allowed, but fabricating is not, and it can be exposed by references. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Omit if you like; never invent.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Your account of leaving must be consistent with what ____ might say, so do not fabricate.
questions.explain: The authors tie the account to what references could report, which is why inventing a reason is risky.
questions.rule: Match what references would say.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Interviewers on the same loop each ask why a candidate left. What should she do?
options: Give each a different version to keep the conversation fresh
Give the first a short version and the rest a much more detailed one
Give the strongest reason to the manager and none to the rest of the panel
Give each of them the same account of the facts, in her own natural words
optionExplain: Different versions risk contradictions that raise red flags.
Changing the detail between interviewers risks inconsistency.
Withholding the reason from some of them will look odd when they compare notes.
Right: one story, kept consistent.
questions.explain: Interviewers compare notes, so stay consistent.
questions.rule: One story for every interviewer.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Sort each practice: does it keep the story credible or put it at risk?

items.t: Preparing one account and using it in every interview
Leaving out details she does not owe anyone
Saying what she learned and linking it to this role
Inventing a reason that sounds more impressive
Giving different reasons to different interviewers
Contradicting what a former manager would say

questions.explain: A consistent, true, selective account is credible. Fabrication, shifting versions and contradictions invite red flags.
questions.rule: True, selective, consistent.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate wants to show growth when explaining a departure. What do the authors suggest she say?
options: A statement such as I learned I need a particular environment, linked to this role
A statement that she has no regrets and would do exactly the same again today
A statement that the departure was entirely caused by circumstances beyond her control
A statement that she is still angry about it but is trying to move on
optionExplain: Right: statements like I learned I need X show growth.
Having no learning gives the interviewer nothing to see growth in.
Blaming circumstances does not show what she gained.
Showing anger is a risk, not a sign of growth.
questions.explain: The authors say statements like I learned I need X show growth, and the answer should end by connecting to this opportunity.
questions.rule: State a lesson and link it.
questions.teaches: Statements like I learned I need X show growth; end by connecting to this opportunity and explaining why the role fits what you want.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: A candidate still feels angry at her old employer. How should she prepare for the question about leaving?
options: Hide the feelings by memorising the wording as exactly as she can
Let the anger show a little, since it proves that she is honest
Work through those feelings first, so that the answer comes out neutral
Avoid thinking about it until the question comes up in the interview
optionExplain: Negativity can leak through tone and body language despite the words.
Anger can look like the red flag the interviewer fears.
Right: the authors advise processing the feelings before interviewing.
Avoiding the issue leaves the feelings unresolved.
questions.explain: Bitterness can show through professional words. The card next explains the advice.
questions.rule: Process first, then prepare.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Keep your answer about leaving to 30 to ____ seconds.
questions.explain: The authors recommend 30 to 60 seconds.
questions.rule: Thirty to sixty seconds.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: After giving a good short answer, a candidate feels a silence. What should she do?
options: Fill the silence by adding more detail about what went wrong
Apologize for the brevity and ask whether she should explain more
Stay with the short answer and let the interviewer move on
Ask the interviewer whether the answer was satisfactory to them
optionExplain: More detail volunteers what she need not share.
Apologizing invites more questions.
Right: she does not need to fill the silence.
Asking for approval signals anxiety.
questions.explain: Get comfortable with brevity.
questions.rule: Do not fill the silence.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Sort each habit: does it help a neutral, brief answer or hurt it?

items.t: Practising a brief answer until it feels natural
Using neutral phrases for any mismatch
Working through bitter feelings beforehand
Adding detail to fill a silence
Letting frustration colour the tone
Telling the story differently in each round

questions.explain: Practice, neutral wording and processed feelings help. Padding, leaked frustration and shifting versions hurt.
questions.rule: Brief, neutral, steady.

questions.section: 4.6 Why Are You Looking? / Why Did You Leave? / Resume Gaps
questions.q: Where do the authors suggest a candidate work through leftover bitterness?
options: With friends or a therapist, before the interview
With the interviewer, by being open about it in the meeting
With her former manager, by sending a message beforehand
On a public review site, so that others can see her point of view
optionExplain: Right: the authors suggest friends or a therapist.
Telling the interviewer shows the bitterness they want to avoid.
Contacting the manager could make matters worse.
Public posts are the kind of badmouthing the authors warn against.
questions.explain: The authors say to process those feelings with friends or a therapist first, so you can discuss the situation neutrally.
questions.rule: Process feelings in private first.
questions.teaches: Process lingering bitterness with friends or a therapist before the interview, so you can discuss the situation neutrally.

questions.section: 5.1 What Does It Mean To Take Initiative?
questions.q: A developer notices a slow test suite that nobody has complained about. Which response is closest to taking initiative?
options: Mention the slowness at standup and then leave it for the team to decide
Look into why it is slow and propose a fix, though no one asked her to
Keep working around the slowness, as the whole team has been doing for months
Log a ticket about it and then return to the assigned sprint work as planned
optionExplain: Sharing the problem feels responsible, but it passes the choice to act to someone else.
This is the move the book calls initiative: she chooses to act on a problem nobody handed her.
Working around it is common and feels practical, but it accepts the problem instead of acting on it.
A ticket is a reasonable record, but it leaves the problem unaddressed by her.
questions.explain: The book lists ignoring, logging, mentioning or working around a problem as the usual responses, and sets them against choosing to fix it. The card next gives the full definition.
questions.rule: Initiative is choosing to act on what nobody assigned.

questions.section: 5.1 What Does It Mean To Take Initiative?
questions.q: Taking initiative means identifying problems or opportunities on your own and acting without explicit ____.
questions.explain: The card defines initiative as acting on a self-spotted problem without explicit direction from anyone.
questions.rule: No direction, no assignment: you spot it and you act.

questions.section: 5.1 What Does It Mean To Take Initiative?
questions.q: Sort each case by whether it shows taking initiative as the card defines it.

items.t: A support agent notices the same refund question every day and drafts a help-page fix unasked
A designer finds an unreadable colour pair in shared components and proposes a fix before any complaint
A tester studies a pattern in flaky results that no one asked about and starts tracing its cause
A developer completes each assigned ticket on schedule
An engineer starts building only after a manager sends a written spec
A tester runs the test plan she was given and reports the results

questions.explain: The three cases under 'Shows initiative' each involve self-spotted work with no instruction; the three under 'Does not show initiative' are work that was handed over.
questions.rule: Self-spotted and self-started is initiative; handed over is not.

questions.section: 5.1 What Does It Mean To Take Initiative?
questions.q: True or false: an engineer who fixes a shared-code bottleneck on her own, before anyone assigns it, has acted on initiative.
questions.explain: Nobody directed it, so the choice was hers. The card defines initiative as acting without explicit direction, before the problem hits.
questions.rule: Self-started work is initiative; assigned work is not.

questions.section: 5.1 What Does It Mean To Take Initiative?
questions.q: A candidate says she noticed an error, did exactly what her lead told her to do, and calls that initiative. What is wrong?
options: She should have ignored the error until it caused a real incident for users later
Noticing a problem alone can never be counted as initiative in any story
She should have fixed it quietly without telling her lead or any teammate at all
The action followed direction instead of coming from her own decision to act
optionExplain: Waiting for an incident is the opposite of the early action the book describes.
Noticing is part of the idea; the gap is that the action was assigned.
The book does not ask for secrecy; acting without direction is different from hiding the work.
Right: noticing was hers, but the doing was directed, so the story misses the core of initiative.
questions.explain: The card's test is who chose the action. Here the choice belonged to her lead.
questions.rule: Ask who decided to act; if it was someone else, it is not initiative.

questions.section: 5.1 What Does It Mean To Take Initiative?
questions.q: A retail analyst sees holiday forecasts failing and fears waiting for complete data will cost sales. What does the card suggest?
options: Start investigating now, since waiting for perfect information can mean missed chances
Wait for the full data set first so that any fix she proposes is certain to be correct
Wait until a manager formally asks for a forecast review before starting any investigation
Hand the problem to another team, because forecasts are shared work across the whole company
optionExplain: This applies the card's reasoning that waiting for perfect information can lose opportunities.
Certainty feels careful, but the card says waiting for perfect information is itself a cost.
Waiting for a request is exactly the direction-dependence the card contrasts with initiative.
Handing it over is possible, but it does not show her acting on the opportunity she spotted.
questions.explain: The card says waiting for direction or perfect information can lead to missed opportunities, so starting now fits the idea.
questions.rule: Do not let missing information or missing instructions be the reason nothing happens.
questions.teaches: The book says Amazon calls this Bias for Action, valuing speed and acting despite ambiguous information; Netflix expects decisions without waiting for approval; Stripe looks for people who move with urgency and focus.

questions.q: Your team has worked around a flaky build step for months, and fixing it is nobody's job. What defines whether you show initiative?
options: Whether you complain about it more loudly than your teammates
Whether you finish your assigned work before anyone else does
Whether you decide to fix it even though you did not have to
Whether you describe the problem accurately in a standup update
optionExplain: Complaining is visible, but it is talk, not the choice to act.
Speed on assigned work is performance, a different thing from choosing extra work.
The book places initiative in the choice to go beyond your assignment.
A good report helps, but describing is not the same as deciding to fix it.
questions.explain: The book says the choice you make next defines initiative. The card next explains the choice.
questions.rule: The choice to fix what is not yours is the heart of initiative.

questions.q: Initiative lives in the choice to extend beyond your assigned ____.
questions.explain: The card says initiative is the choice to go beyond what you were assigned when you see something broken that is not yours.
questions.rule: Initiative sits in the choice to go beyond your assignment.

questions.q: Sort each reaction to a broken shared template by whether it is the choice the card describes.
groups: The choice to extend beyond scope

items.t: She rewrites the shared onboarding template herself after seeing new hires stumble
He starts repairing the department's stale price list, which no one owns
She builds a small checker that catches the template's errors, although nobody requested it
He posts a message saying the template is out of date and moves on
She adds the problem to her notes for the next retrospective and does nothing else
He keeps using the old template and corrects each copy by hand

questions.explain: The three under 'The choice to extend beyond scope' involve deciding to do work beyond the person's scope; the three under 'Not that choice' leave the problem in place by reporting or working around it.
questions.rule: Fixing it yourself is the choice; reporting or working around it is not.

questions.q: True or false: if a team has tolerated a problem for years, fixing it still counts as initiative.
questions.explain: The card says the choice defines initiative, and it notes the problem may have been worked around for weeks, months or years. Age of the problem does not change the choice.
questions.rule: A long-tolerated problem is still a problem you can choose to fix.

questions.q: A colleague says: I saw the bug, wrote the ticket and mentioned it at standup, so I showed initiative. What does the card say?
options: Writing a ticket is the strongest form of initiative that the card describes at all
Mentioning a bug at standup counts as initiative once the manager replies to it
Those are usual reactions; initiative is the decision to fix it with no obligation
Initiative requires fixing the bug in secret without telling a single teammate
optionExplain: A ticket is useful but the card names it among the usual responses.
The manager's reply is not the test; the test is the colleague's own decision.
The card lists logging and mentioning as ordinary reactions set against the choice to fix.
The card sets no secrecy rule; later ideas say initiative works best with communication.
questions.explain: The card separates raising a problem from deciding to fix it.
questions.rule: Raising a problem is not the same as choosing to solve it.

questions.q: An office manager sees visitors wander lost each day. Signage belongs to facilities. Which choice is what the card calls initiative?
options: She drafts clearer signage and offers it to facilities, having seen the problem
She tells each new visitor to ask at reception and takes no further step herself
She waits for the facilities team to schedule a review of the signage later
She mentions the problem in her weekly report and then waits for a reply
optionExplain: She goes beyond her scope by acting on a problem she chose to take on.
Telling visitors to ask works around the problem rather than addressing it.
Waiting for facilities leaves the choice to someone else.
A report helps, but she would then be waiting rather than acting.
questions.explain: The pattern holds outside tech: a self-spotted problem outside her role, with a decision to act.
questions.rule: The choice can happen in any job, not only in engineering.
questions.teaches: The book says the choice counts regardless of the scale of impact: even automating a tedious task that saves only 30 minutes a week is initiative.

questions.q: A teammate wants to rewrite an outdated shared logging library nobody asked her to touch. Which view is closest to the book's?
options: She should start the rewrite at once, because asking for approval only slows the company
She should ask permission before every single step, so that nothing happens without sign-off
She should leave the library alone, because shared code is never an individual's concern
She should judge whether acting alone is acceptable here or asking first is better
optionExplain: Speed is attractive, but the book warns that uncoordinated fixes lead to chaos.
Caution is attractive, but the book warns that universal permission-seeking leads to stagnation.
Staying out is safe, but the book wants people who solve problems, within boundaries.
The book frames the matter as a judgment between acting independently and seeking permission.
questions.explain: Both extremes fail in the book's picture. The card next explains why a judgment is needed.
questions.rule: Neither blind action nor blind permission-seeking works; judge.

questions.q: Match each situation to the result the book expects.
pairs: Everyone fixes what they think is broken, with no coordination
Everybody waits for permission before doing anything
You discern which problems to solve alone while respecting boundaries
questions.explain: The book describes chaos at one extreme, stagnation at the other, and discerning judgment as good initiative.
questions.rule: Good initiative sits between chaos and stagnation.

questions.q: Sort each change by whether acting alone is reasonable or coordinating first is wiser. This is our reading of the book's stress on boundaries.

items.t: Fixing a typo on your own team's internal page
Tidying a helper script that only your own project uses
Renaming a folder where only you keep drafts
Changing a form that three departments fill in
Editing a database layout that several teams read
Switching a company-wide alert threshold

questions.explain: Our reading: the book gives no list, but its call to respect boundaries and priorities suggests that changes touching other people's work deserve coordination.
questions.rule: The wider the effect on others, the more reason to coordinate.

questions.q: Suppose every member of a team fixed whatever they believed was broken and told no one. What would the book expect?
options: Faster progress, because nobody would lose time waiting for others
Chaos, since uncoordinated fixes would collide with one another
Stagnation, because unreported work would never be reviewed by anyone
Better quality, because each person knows their own area of the code best
optionExplain: Speed looks like a gain, but the book expects collisions rather than progress.
The book pictures this exact scene as the way initiative without judgment leads to chaos.
Stagnation is the book's result of universal permission-seeking, the opposite case.
Local knowledge helps, but it does not remove the need for coordination.
questions.explain: Initiative without judgment leads to chaos in the book.
questions.rule: Uncoordinated action is a risk, not a virtue.

questions.q: A candidate says that the whole point of initiative is acting alone and not checking with anyone. What does the card say is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because acting alone is the only real form of initiative there is
The mistake is acting at all before a manager has approved the plan in writing
The mistake is judging a problem's size and reach before deciding whether to act
Good initiative includes judging when to act alone and when to respect boundaries
optionExplain: This reads initiative as pure independence, which the card calls chaos without judgment.
Requiring approval first is the stagnation case the card warns about.
Weighing the situation is the judgment the card asks for, not a mistake.
The card defines good initiative as discerning what to solve alone while respecting boundaries.
questions.explain: Initiative without judgment leads to chaos.
questions.rule: Independence without judgment is not good initiative.

questions.q: A school librarian wants to change how overdue books are tracked; the front office uses the same system. What does the judgment ask her to weigh?
options: Whether the change is large enough to justify dropping her regular library duties
Whether she can act alone here or should check with the front office
Whether to wait until the head teacher personally asks her for the change
Whether any change to the shared systems can be left to a vendor to decide
optionExplain: Her duties are not the issue; the issue is who else the change touches.
The same tension appears outside tech: a self-spotted fix that touches another group's work.
Waiting for a request is the stagnation extreme.
Handing it off wholesale skips the judgment the card asks her to make.
questions.explain: The card asks for judgment about independent action against permission, in any field.
questions.rule: Weigh who else the change touches before choosing.
questions.teaches: The book says interviewers ask about this on purpose: questions about deciding independently and telling the manager afterward probe your judgment about when to act alone versus seek guidance.

questions.q: True or false: in every culture, doing work beyond what you were explicitly asked is read as a sign of commitment.
questions.explain: Views differ. In some places the same behavior can look like overstepping. The card next explains the book's advice.
questions.rule: Cultures differ on whether extra work is welcome.

questions.q: According to the book, in some countries doing more than you were asked can be seen as what?
options: A sign of outstanding loyalty to the company
A neutral habit that interviewers ignore entirely
Overstepping, or disrespect toward authority
Proof of strong ownership of assigned projects
optionExplain: Loyalty is how other settings may read it, but the book says some read it as the opposite.
The book says cultural background does affect how the behavior is viewed.
This is the book's description of how some cultures view extra work.
Ownership concerns assigned scope; the book does not link it to this cultural point.
questions.explain: The book says that in some countries it can be seen as overstepping or disrespectful to authority.
questions.rule: Extra work can read as disrespect in some cultures.

questions.q: Sort each story by whether it is an initiative story or a story to reframe as Delivery or Problem-Solving.

items.t: She noticed that exports were slow for another team and began fixing them unasked
He saw nobody documented the release steps and wrote a guide on his own
She proposed and built a small tool that nobody had requested
He shipped the assigned migration on time after a key dependency was blocked
She diagnosed the memory leak her lead had assigned and found the cause
He kept the assigned service running through a vendor outage

questions.explain: The three under 'Initiative story' are self-chosen work; the three under 'Reframe as Delivery or Problem-Solving' show value inside assigned work, the territory of Delivery and Problem-Solving.
questions.rule: Assigned work done well belongs under Delivery or Problem-Solving.

questions.q: A candidate who prefers following instructions needs a story. Which approach matches the book?
options: Present a delivery under pressure as Delivery, showing value in assigned work
Invent an unassigned side project so that the story sounds like real initiative
Decline to answer, since initiative questions only suit some cultures of work at all
Call the long hours on assigned work initiative, because the effort was so large
optionExplain: The book suggests reframing through competencies such as Delivery that fit assigned work.
Inventing a story is dishonest and the book never suggests it.
Declining wastes the chance; the book offers a reframing instead.
Effort on assigned tasks is diligence, which a later red flag names as a mistake.
questions.explain: The book's route is a reframe, not an invention or an avoidance.
questions.rule: Reframe truthfully; do not invent.

questions.q: True or false: the book advises candidates from a culture that values following instructions to reframe that experience through Delivery or Problem-Solving.
questions.explain: The book advises reframing the experience through competencies such as Delivery or Problem-Solving, not hiding the background.
questions.rule: Reframe the experience; do not conceal the background.

questions.q: A hospital administrator, trained to follow protocol exactly, is asked about going beyond her job. Her best story is a protocol-based rescue of a failed discharge schedule. What fits?
options: Present it as Problem-Solving or Delivery, since it shows value within her job
Present it as initiative, since the rescue demanded effort beyond her normal working day
Leave it out, since stories about following protocol never help in an interview
Rewrite it to claim she volunteered for the rescue, so that the story matches the question
optionExplain: Her best story is assigned work done well, which the card says to reframe through these competencies.
Effort on assigned work is not initiative; she would be mislabelling the story.
The card says such stories do have value under the right competency.
Claiming she volunteered would be untrue and risks the credibility of the whole answer.
questions.explain: The same reframing works in any field where the best story sits inside assigned work.
questions.rule: Match the label to what actually happened.
questions.teaches: The book adds that organizations differ too: some companies see initiative as essential, while others prefer employees to stay within defined boundaries, so such a reframed story can suit the employer.

questions.q: A candidate has no initiative stories at all. At which type of company would the book call that a red flag?
options: A regulated bank or insurer with strict review rules
A large traditional enterprise with a slow change process
A startup or high-growth company, where it is expected
A consultancy with fixed client-scoped deliverables only
optionExplain: Regulated firms want proper channels, but the book does not call a missing story a red flag there.
Traditional enterprises are careful with change, not hungry for it.
The book says initiative is expected at startups, so the lack of it is a red flag there.
Consultancies value extras beyond the brief, but the book singles out startups for the red flag.
questions.explain: Startups and high-growth firms expect it. The card next sets the four settings side by side.
questions.rule: Startups expect initiative from everyone.

questions.q: Match each setting to what its culture prizes in initiative.
pairs: Fixing blockers imperfectly rather than leaving them broken
Improving things without breaking what already works
Proposing change through proper channels with low risk
Adding value beyond the stated scope
questions.explain: Each setting has its own emphasis in the book: speed, care for ownership, risk reduction and extra value.
questions.rule: Different settings prize different shapes of initiative.

questions.q: Sort each initiative story by the setting it suits best. This is our reading of the book's descriptions.

items.t: She patched the broken deploy script overnight and refined it later
He took on customer support and fixed a billing bug in one week
She shipped a rough fix first, since the bug blocked all signups
He wrote a formal proposal and ran a small proof-of-concept first
She piloted the change on a test system and reported results to the risk team
He submitted the improvement through the change board before any rollout

questions.explain: Our reading: speed with imperfect fixes suits startups; formal proposals and proofs-of-concept match the careful, low-risk approach of regulated settings.
questions.rule: Match the style of initiative to the setting's risk tolerance.

questions.q: An engineer pushes an unreviewed fix into a bank's critical payment system. What would the book's priority for such firms lead you to expect?
options: Praise, since speed to fix a problem is the top priority in every kind of firm
Concern, since the priority there is reducing risk and protecting critical systems
Indifference, since an engineer's initiative is private to their own team
Approval, since regulated firms expect staff to skip all review steps for urgent fixes
optionExplain: Praise fits startups; the book gives regulated firms a different priority.
The book says traditional and regulated firms prioritize reducing risk and protecting critical systems.
A fix to a critical system touches many people, so it is not private.
Regulated firms ask for proper channels, not for skipped review.
questions.explain: Risk reduction is the first priority in the book's description of regulated settings.
questions.rule: In regulated settings, risk comes before speed.

questions.q: Which statement best separates initiative at a large tech company from initiative at a startup?
options: Startups ask for permission for every step while large firms do not
Large tech firms do not value initiative, while startups require it
Startups value fixing blockers imperfectly while large firms expect perfection before any change
Large tech asks you to weigh consensus against going alone and respect ownership
optionExplain: It is reversed: startups expect people to act without waiting for permission.
The book says large tech companies do value initiative, with added care for ownership.
The book does not ask large firms for perfection; it asks for improvement without breaking what works.
The book's large-tech description centers on knowing when to build consensus and when to go alone.
questions.explain: The difference is the judgment about ownership, not whether initiative counts.
questions.rule: Large tech adds the judgment about consensus and ownership.

questions.q: A designer at an agency finishes a client's brand pack on time. Which extra step fits the consultancy view of initiative?
options: Redesign the client's whole product line without being asked, to show enthusiasm for the account
Document the design patterns so the client can reuse them after the work ends
Stop at the brief exactly, since extra work would exceed the agreed scope
Pitch the client a new engagement before the current work has even been delivered
optionExplain: Redesigning everything is beyond scope but not a targeted, helpful extra.
The consultancy view is adding value beyond the stated scope in a useful, targeted way.
Stopping at the brief is the opposite of the consultancy emphasis.
Selling more work is about the agency's revenue, not value to the client.
questions.explain: Extras that help the client later fit the consultancy description.
questions.rule: At an agency, extra value for the client is the initiative.
questions.teaches: The book's consultancy examples are delivering more than expected in targeted areas, documenting patterns that help the client after you leave, and building tools that make their future work easier.

questions.q: True or false: the book tells candidates to hide any habit of regular overtime, because every company dislikes it.
questions.explain: Some companies value intense dedication, others do not. The book says to be honest about your style. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Whether overtime helps you depends on the company's culture.

questions.q: Match each work style to the framing the book suggests.
pairs: Regularly works extra hours and sees it as a strength
State it explicitly as a deliberate choice
Stress choosing high-impact problems that need no heroics
Works extra hours only in critical situations
Explain what made the situation critical
questions.explain: Each style has its own framing: own it, show efficiency instead of heroics, or explain the exception.
questions.rule: Frame extra hours to match what really happened.

questions.q: A candidate who values boundaries once worked a weekend during a genuine outage. How should she describe it?
options: As proof that she is available at any hour for any company, always
As a story she should hide, since weekend work counts against everyone
As her usual style, to match what most startups probably expect to hear
As a rare exception during a real crisis, not her regular pattern
optionExplain: That overstates her style and invites a mismatch the book warns about.
The book does not say to hide it; it says to frame it truthfully.
Claiming a style she does not have leads to the mismatch the book calls the worst outcome.
The book's advice for boundary-keepers is to call extra hours a rare exception in a genuine crisis.
questions.explain: Honest framing keeps her story true and lets the company judge the fit.
questions.rule: Describe extra hours as what they were.

questions.q: True or false: a boundary-keeping candidate who claims a heavy overtime habit to impress a startup, and is hired, is likely to end up in a poor match.
questions.explain: The book names accepting a role whose expectations do not fit your real work style as the worst outcome, and a false impression invites exactly that.
questions.rule: A false impression of your style leads to a mismatch.

questions.q: A coach tells every candidate to stress weekend work. What problem does the book point to?
options: Sustainable-work firms can read regular overtime as a red flag
Weekend work is never relevant to any initiative story at any company
Only senior candidates are allowed to mention extra hours in interviews
Interviewers rank weekend work below all other signals of initiative
optionExplain: The book says sustainable-work cultures may view regular overtime negatively.
The book says extra hours can matter, in the right culture.
The book sets no seniority rule on mentioning hours.
The book does not rank weekend work against other signals.
questions.explain: One framing does not fit every culture.
questions.rule: Advice that ignores culture can backfire.

questions.q: At a firm that prizes sustainable work, a pharmacy manager says she regularly fixes ordering errors at night. How might an interviewer read this?
options: As proof that she is the strongest candidate the firm could hope to meet
As a sign that she has no interest in unassigned work or improvement
As a possible sign of poor planning or trouble setting boundaries
As a sign that she dislikes sharing problems with her wider team
optionExplain: That reading fits a startup, not a firm that prizes sustainability.
Nothing in her answer says she avoids unassigned work.
In a sustainable-work culture, regular overtime is read with suspicion.
Nothing in her answer concerns teamwork.
questions.explain: The culture decides how the same fact is read.
questions.rule: Know how the company reads overtime before you stress it.
questions.teaches: The book says such companies may see regular overtime as a sign of poor planning, slow execution, or an inability to set boundaries.

questions.q: An engineer runs her assigned project flawlessly from start to finish. Which statement fits best?
options: She shows initiative, because ownership and initiative mean the same
She shows delivery only, because ownership never applies to projects
She shows strong ownership but not necessarily any initiative
She shows no skill at all, since she only did what was assigned
optionExplain: The two are often conflated, which is the confusion the book points out.
Ownership is exactly responsibility for assigned work, so it does apply.
Ownership covers outcomes in your assigned scope; initiative needs work outside it.
Doing assigned work well is good performance; the point is that it is not initiative.
questions.explain: Being excellent inside your scope is a different quality. The card next separates four related ideas.
questions.rule: Strong ownership alone is not initiative.

questions.q: Match each quality to its meaning in the book.
pairs: Responsibility for outcomes within your assigned scope
Choosing to do work outside your immediate area
Fixing complex issues through investigation and analysis
questions.explain: Each quality is defined by what it is about: scope, choice, obstacles, or analysis.
questions.rule: Four qualities, four different questions.

questions.q: Sort each story by whether it shows initiative or not.

items.t: She spotted that another team's nightly job slowed everyone and began fixing it
He noticed page speed was degrading and chose to investigate unasked
She built a shared template library after seeing teams repeat the same effort
He debugged the memory leak that his lead had assigned to him
She shipped the assigned release on time after a vendor's service failed
He kept his own assigned service healthy throughout the year

questions.explain: The three under 'Initiative' are unassigned problems chosen by the person; the three under 'Not initiative (assigned work done well)' are assigned work, valuable but not initiative.
questions.rule: Unassigned and chosen is initiative; assigned is not.

questions.q: Ana is assigned a performance bug and solves it with analysis. Ben notices slowdowns nobody mentioned and investigates. What fits?
options: Ana shows problem-solving on assigned work, while Ben shows initiative
Both show initiative, because a performance bug always needs some choice
Ana shows initiative, because solving a hard bug requires choosing a method
Neither shows any skill, because performance work is part of every job
optionExplain: What separates them is who picked the problem: Ana was handed hers, Ben chose his.
Choosing a method is not choosing the problem.
Hard analysis is problem-solving; the choice of problem is what makes initiative.
Both show real skill; the question is which quality each shows.
questions.explain: Assigned analysis is problem-solving; unassigned discovery is initiative.
questions.rule: Ask who chose the problem.

questions.q: A candidate says that owning her whole project end to end proves initiative. What is the error?
options: Owning a project is impossible without taking some initiative every day
Projects cannot be owned by one person, so ownership proves nothing at all
Ownership shows initiative only when the project is larger than average
Ownership covers assigned scope, while initiative needs work beyond it
optionExplain: The book says you can own your work perfectly and show no initiative.
The book defines ownership as responsibility for outcomes, which one person can hold.
Size does not change the scope test the book applies.
The book keeps them apart: ownership is within scope, initiative is beyond it.
questions.explain: Mislabelling ownership as initiative is a common confusion.
questions.rule: Scope decides which quality it is.

questions.q: A hospital data analyst sees readmissions rising, unasked investigates, then models the likely causes. Which description fits her story?
options: Ownership only, since the readmission data belongs to the hospital
Initiative in choosing to look, then problem-solving in the analysis
Delivery only, since she finished a report despite a lack of requests
Problem-solving only, since the choice to look was not hers to make
optionExplain: Ownership needs assigned scope, which the scene does not give.
She chose the unassigned problem, then applied analysis to it, so both qualities appear.
Delivery means finishing despite obstacles, which is not the main point here.
The choice was hers, so the story shows initiative as well.
questions.explain: Initiative can open the door that problem-solving then walks through.
questions.rule: Name each quality separately when a story shows two.
questions.teaches: The book notes that many stories combine both qualities: you take initiative to investigate a problem, then apply your skills to fix it.

questions.q: Interviewers ask about initiative from many angles. Where should a candidate's preparation focus first?
options: Covering one polished story for every question category in equal depth
Rehearsing answers about the long hours put in on assigned projects
Finding examples with the largest possible business impact for the firm
Spotting unassigned problems, then deciding to fix them where it fits
optionExplain: Even coverage feels thorough, but the book prioritizes two areas over breadth.
Hours on assigned work are diligence, not the core signals.
Impact matters later, but the book's two core areas are about spotting and choosing.
The book names these two as the core signals.
questions.explain: The book trims the target to two areas. The card next states them.
questions.rule: Two core areas carry the weight.

questions.q: The two core areas are identifying ____ problems and deciding to fix them if appropriate.
questions.explain: The card names the first core area as spotting problems nobody assigned to you.
questions.rule: Spot what is unassigned, then choose to act.

questions.q: Which story should a candidate with limited time prepare first for an initiative question?
options: Delivering an assigned migration flawlessly under a tight deadline for the whole department
Spotting a recurring outage nobody tracked and choosing to look into it first
Carrying out an improvement plan that a manager designed and assigned in fine detail
Working through a hard weekend to finish a project that the lead had assigned to her
optionExplain: It shows delivery on assigned work, not a self-chosen problem.
This story contains both core areas: a self-spotted problem and a judged decision to act.
The plan came from the manager, so the spotting and choosing are missing.
Effort on assigned work is not the core signal.
questions.explain: Choose the story that shows both spotting and choosing.
questions.rule: Lead with the story that shows both core areas.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate whose main story is strong on both core areas must also fit every other question category into the same story.
questions.explain: The book says the other categories support the core signals, but it is not essential to include them if the primary examples are strong.
questions.rule: Strong core stories do not need every other category.

questions.q: A story lists many achievements but does not say how she found the problem or why she chose to act. What is missing?
options: A longer list of the achievements that she had gathered over her career
A description of who assigned the work and how it was tracked afterwards
Both core signals: spotting an unassigned problem and choosing to act
A statement of how many hours she worked on the project in total
optionExplain: More achievements do not add the missing signals.
Assignment tracking points away from unassigned work.
The story skips the spotting and the choice, which are the two core areas.
Hours do not show spotting or choosing.
questions.explain: Build the story around how you found it and why you chose it.
questions.rule: Show how you found it and why you chose it.

questions.q: A community organizer has time to polish only one story. Which fits the book's priority?
options: Noticing volunteers quietly dropping out, then surveying them to fix the cause
Describing a year in which she led every assigned event without a single complaint
Listing every team award she has received since joining the organization
Explaining her tidy filing habits for the records she was given to keep
optionExplain: It shows spotting an unassigned problem and choosing to act, the two core areas.
Flawless assigned events show ownership, not the core signals.
Awards show recognition, not the two core areas.
Tidy filing of given records is assigned work.
questions.explain: The priority works in any field.
questions.rule: Pick the story with a self-found problem and a chosen action.
questions.teaches: The book lists the other angles interviewers use: going above and beyond, spotting problems early, making things better, acting independently, and taking smart risks.

questions.q: An interviewer asks about work you did that nobody asked for. What will they most want to hear?
options: What was assigned, what you chose to add, and why you chose it
How many hours the extra work took and how tired you were afterwards
Which senior leader praised the work most warmly once it was done
How the project's budget compared with the original estimate in total
optionExplain: The book says good stories are clear about assigned versus chosen work and the reason for the step.
Hours show effort, not choice.
Praise may follow, but it does not show the choice.
Budget is unrelated to the choice the interviewer is probing.
questions.explain: The line between assigned and chosen is what the interviewer needs. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Show the line between assigned and chosen.

questions.q: According to the book, what do above-and-beyond questions directly probe?
options: Whether you are able to finish assigned tasks sooner than your peers
Whether you can describe a project's technical details in full depth
Whether you choose to do more than required or only act when told
Whether you are willing to accept any extra assignment from a manager
optionExplain: Speed on assigned tasks is performance, not the choice probed.
Technical depth is useful but not the point of these questions.
The book frames these questions as probing choice beyond requirements.
Accepting assignments is being directed, the opposite of the point.
questions.explain: These questions look for choice.
questions.rule: The probe is whether you choose to do more.

questions.q: Sort each opening line by whether it keeps assigned and chosen work clear.

items.t: My role was to run weekly reports; nobody asked me to fix the data source, but I chose to
The ticket covered only the login page; I decided on my own to fix the shared error messages
I was hired for the front desk; I started a visitor guide because I kept answering the same question
We improved the whole pipeline together over a busy few months
There was a lot of extra work around the launch, and I was involved
The team pitched in on many things, including me, and it went well

questions.explain: The three under 'Clear about assigned versus chosen' state the assignment, the extra piece and the reason; the three under 'Blurs the two' leave the reader unable to tell what was chosen.
questions.rule: State the assignment, the extra work, and the reason.

questions.q: True or false: if a story describes only what the candidate did, with no mention of what was assigned, the interviewer can still see that she chose the work.
questions.explain: Without the assigned side the interviewer cannot tell whether she chose the work or was directed to it, so the choice stays invisible.
questions.rule: Without the assigned side, the chosen side means nothing.

questions.q: A candidate lists impressive launch results but does not say which part was her own idea. What is wrong?
options: Launch results should never appear in an above-and-beyond answer at all
It never separates the assigned work from the parts she chose herself
The story should name every colleague who worked on the launch with her
The story should end earlier, before the results are described in detail
optionExplain: Results can help; the gap is the missing split.
Without the split, the story cannot show whether she chose any of it.
Naming colleagues does not show her choice.
Length is not the problem; the content is.
questions.explain: Fix the story by marking where assigned work ends.
questions.rule: Mark where the assignment ended and your choice began.

questions.q: A nonprofit coordinator finished all her assigned grant tasks superbly. What would most improve her answer about going beyond her role?
options: More detail on how quickly she completed each of the assigned grant tasks
A longer list of the grants her organization had won in earlier years
A note that her manager rated her work as consistently excellent
A problem she found herself outside her tasks, and why she took it on
optionExplain: Speed on assigned tasks does not show choice.
The organization's earlier wins say nothing about her choice.
A rating of her assigned work is not unassigned work.
The question asks for work she chose, so she needs a self-found problem and her reason.
questions.explain: In any field, the missing piece is the chosen work and the reason.
questions.rule: Add the self-found problem and the why.
questions.teaches: The book says interviewers want to tell apart someone who works hard only on given tasks, which is good, from someone who also finds new problems to solve, which is even better.

questions.q: A candidate stopped a minor issue from becoming a major outage. Besides what she did, what do interviewers also want to learn?
options: How many of her coworkers had also failed to notice the issue earlier
How she balanced that work with her assigned responsibilities
Which tools she prefers for monitoring across all of her projects
Whether she informed customers about the outage she had prevented
optionExplain: Others' failures do not show her judgment.
The book says these questions also test how you balance the work with your assignments.
Tool preferences may come up but are not the stated aim.
Informing customers is unrelated to the balance.
questions.explain: Early action has a cost in time. The card next explains what interviewers weigh.
questions.rule: Early action must fit with assigned work.

questions.q: Interviewers want to see how you balance early-problem work with your assigned ____.
questions.explain: The book says they are testing how you balance such work with your assigned responsibilities.
questions.rule: Balance early fixes against assigned duties.

questions.q: A developer sees error rates creeping up on a batch job. Which opening shows spotting a problem early?
options: The system crashed on a Friday night, so I stayed until I had restored the service
My manager asked me to review error rates during the quarterly audit of the system
The error rate looked stable, so I kept monitoring it each morning without any change
Error rates doubled in three weeks, still under alert levels, so I investigated
optionExplain: A crash is a failure already visible to everyone.
A manager's request makes the work assigned.
Monitoring a stable rate does not show a problem found early.
She noticed a trend before it triggered any alert and chose to act.
questions.explain: Early means before others notice or before it becomes critical.
questions.rule: Early means before the problem is visible to others.

questions.q: True or false: if a candidate fixed a problem early but let assigned tasks slip, interviewers may count the slip against the story.
questions.explain: The book says interviewers also test how you balance early-problem work with your assigned responsibilities, so a slip weakens the story.
questions.rule: A good catch does not excuse neglected assignments.

questions.q: A story says, I noticed the issue only after customers complained, then fixed it quickly. What does it miss for this question category?
options: Spotting early, since customers were hurt before she noticed
Speed, since a quick fix is the only thing this category measures
Cost, since the book asks for a dollar figure in every such story
Teamwork, since early spotting must always come from a group effort
optionExplain: The category asks for noticing before others do; the complaint shows the notice came late.
Speed of the fix is not the measure of noticing early.
The book does not demand a dollar figure here.
The book does not say early spotting needs a group.
questions.explain: Early catches happen before harm shows.
questions.rule: Early means before the harm shows.

questions.q: A marketing analyst has a full sprint but spots a data error that will skew next month's reports. What suits the book's advice?
options: Stay silent and fix it secretly at night so that nobody is disturbed
Drop her assigned work for the week to give the error her full attention
Ask her manager for time, or fit a quick win into a lighter week
Report the error to the team and refuse to work on it herself
optionExplain: Secret overtime is not the book's example and the culture question arises.
Dropping assigned work fails the balance the interviewer tests.
The book's examples of good answers include negotiating capacity or choosing time-light quick wins.
Refusing to act gives up the initiative she has just shown.
questions.explain: Balance can be negotiated, not just absorbed.
questions.rule: Make room openly rather than quietly or by dropping duties.
questions.teaches: The book says good answers describe finding time during lighter sprint weeks, negotiating with your manager to allocate capacity, or identifying quick wins that need little time.

questions.q: A report generator works adequately but is slow and clumsy. Which person fits the improvement mindset the book describes?
options: One who leaves it alone because it produces correct reports each week
One who waits until the report breaks before looking at it at all
One who asks why it works that way and invests time to improve it
One who complains about it so that someone else will take it up
optionExplain: Leaving it alone is accepting the status quo, which the questions look for.
Waiting for a break is reacting, not improving something that works.
The book values questioning a working system and investing in something better.
Complaining hands the work to others instead of choosing to improve.
questions.explain: Improvement that nobody requested is the aim. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A working system can still be improved.

questions.q: Strong responses show you questioning ____ things work the way they do.
questions.explain: The card says strong responses show you asking why something works as it does before investing in a better version.
questions.rule: Ask why it works this way.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether it shows the improvement initiative the card describes.

items.t: She noticed the weekly invoice process worked but took three steps, and streamlined it unasked
He saw a spreadsheet would break at twice the customers and rebuilt it before growth arrived
She rewrote an adequate checklist after asking why each step existed
He fixed the invoice bug that the finance director assigned this sprint
She left the process alone because it was functional and nobody complained
He followed the improvement plan that his manager had drawn up in detail

questions.explain: The three under 'Improvement initiative' involve questioning something that worked and choosing to improve it; the three under 'Not improvement initiative' are assigned fixes or leaving things alone.
questions.rule: Improve what works, without being asked.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate who improves something that already worked adequately shows the improvement mindset these questions test.
questions.explain: The book's questions mention improving things even though they worked adequately; fixing only reported breakage does not show the mindset.
questions.rule: Look past what is already broken.

questions.q: A candidate says: the dashboard failed daily, my lead assigned me the repair, and I did it. Why does this not answer an improvement question?
options: It shows no questioning of a working system and no choice to improve it
Repairs are a different job from improvements and are never worth mentioning
Dashboards cannot be improved because they are owned by the data team
Her lead should have written the repair plan before assigning the work
optionExplain: The story is an assigned repair of something broken, so it misses the questioning and the choice.
Repairs have value, but not as an answer to this category.
The book sets no rule that dashboards cannot be improved.
Who wrote the plan is not the point; the choice was not hers.
questions.explain: An improvement story needs the questioning and the choice.
questions.rule: Show the question you asked and the choice you made.

questions.q: A bakery's order sheet copes with today's volume. The owner expects a holiday rush. Which action fits improvement-minded initiative?
options: Keep using the sheet unchanged until errors start appearing in orders
Ask the owner to hire more staff to cope with the expected rush
Praise the sheet to the owner for coping with the current volume
Redesign the order sheet before the rush, though it works today
optionExplain: Waiting for errors is the status quo approach.
More staff may help, but it is not an improvement she chose to make.
Praise does not improve anything.
She improves something functional in advance of a change she anticipates.
questions.explain: Anticipating growth is a form of improvement initiative.
questions.rule: Prepare for what is coming, not only for what has broken.
questions.teaches: The book lists other improvement prompts: anticipating future growth or change and preparing a solution, and fixing something before it becomes a problem.

questions.q: A developer starts improving a shared build script. Which approach is closest to what interviewers want to hear?
options: She asks permission before each step, so that no change ever surprises anyone
She acts, and tells the affected people what she is doing as she goes
She finishes in secret and presents the large change on the day of release
She waits until the manager assigns the build script as formal work to her
optionExplain: Permission at every step is the stagnation the book warns about.
The book wants action with stakeholders kept informed.
Secrecy surprises people, which the book says to avoid.
Waiting for assignment removes the independence the question probes.
questions.explain: Independence and transparency go together. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Act openly.

questions.q: Acting independently does not mean hiding what you are doing or making important decisions in ____.
questions.explain: The card says independent action should not mean working in secret or deciding major things alone.
questions.rule: Independent does not mean isolated.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether it fits acting independently with transparency.

items.t: She posts to the team channel: I am fixing the retry bug and will demo Friday
He starts a prototype and tells the affected team lead the same day
She fixes a small issue in her own module and mentions it at standup
He rebuilds a shared service over a month and reveals it at release
She quietly changes a team-wide setting and tells no one about it
He insists on a signed approval for every one-line change before making it

questions.explain: The three under 'Fits the book's advice' act and inform; the others either surprise people or stall waiting for approval at every step.
questions.rule: Tell people what you are doing while you do it.

questions.q: What if a candidate makes a major change in isolation and reveals it only at launch?
options: Interviewers will see a bold leader who needs no one else's agreement
Interviewers will see no issue, because the outcome was good for the company
Interviewers will prefer this, since asking questions slows every project down
They may see a trust risk, since the book warns against surprising people
optionExplain: The book describes boldness as including transparency.
Outcome does not remove the trust cost the book names.
The book does not treat asking or telling as a delay to avoid.
The book says strong answers do not surprise people with major changes.
questions.explain: Surprise erodes trust even when the change is good.
questions.rule: Do not surprise people with major changes.

questions.q: A candidate says that acting independently means keeping everyone out of the loop until the work is done. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because independence is shown by working with no discussion
Stakeholders should be kept informed, since good initiative builds trust
The mistake is starting before a written approval has been obtained in advance
The mistake is telling the manager after the work is finished and not before
optionExplain: That reads independence as secrecy, which the book rejects.
The book pairs independence with transparency.
A written approval is not what the book asks for.
Telling afterward is allowed in some cases; hiding major changes is the issue.
questions.explain: Independent work should be visible.
questions.rule: Independent and informed go together.

questions.q: A hospital pharmacist redesigns a shift handover form used by two wards. Which step best fits the book's advice?
options: Roll out the new form on all wards at once without telling the managers
Wait until the hospital board asks for a new form before starting any work
Tell both ward managers what she is changing as she makes the change
Ask both ward managers to approve each separate field of the new form
optionExplain: A surprise roll-out is the isolation the card warns against.
Waiting for the board gives up the independence the question probes.
She acts and keeps those affected informed.
Approving every field is permission at every step, which the book does not require.
questions.explain: Transparency applies in every field.
questions.rule: Name the affected people and tell them as you go.
questions.teaches: The book's sample prompts include starting a project without first receiving formal approval or resources, and taking action despite unclear requirements.

questions.q: Asked about an initiative that did not work out, what should a candidate show?
options: How she weighed the risk beforehand and what she learned afterwards
That she acts on hunches and does not need evidence to start work
That the failure was caused by factors that she could not have foreseen
That she will avoid unassigned work after this experience in the future
optionExplain: The book wants evidence of thinking through implications and learning from success and failure.
Hunches show no evaluation, which is what the question examines.
Blaming outside factors skips the learning the book wants to hear.
Avoiding unassigned work abandons the competency being assessed.
questions.explain: A failure story can still be a strong one. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Show the weighing and the learning.

questions.q: Interviewers want evidence that you think through the ____ before acting on unassigned work.
questions.explain: The card says interviewers want evidence you think through the implications before acting.
questions.rule: Think it through before acting.
