questions.q: A product manager prototyped an unrequested feature after weighing its cost, and it flopped. Which account fits what interviewers want?
options: She explains why the odds looked good, what happened, and what she changed
She hides the flop and describes only the prototype's design in detail to them
She blames the users for not understanding the feature she had prototyped
She says the risk was zero because nobody had assigned the work to anyone
optionExplain: It shows weighing the risk beforehand and learning from the outcome.
Hiding the flop loses the learning and invites distrust.
Blaming users shows no lesson taken.
Claiming zero risk skips the weighing the question examines.
questions.explain: A flop can be a good story if the thinking and the lesson are visible.
questions.rule: Own the result and the lesson.

questions.q: True or false: interviewers asking about smart risks accept an honest account of a setback, since they want learning from successes and failures.
questions.explain: The book says interviewers want to see you learn from both successes and failures, so an honest account of a setback can fit.
questions.rule: Failures can serve as evidence of learning.

questions.q: A candidate says: I started the side project on a hunch, so there is nothing to explain about why. What is wrong?
options: Hunches are fine because side projects need no justification to interviewers
The candidate should have chosen a project that was assigned instead
Interviewers examine how you judge the work, and a hunch shows none
The candidate should have reported only the successes of the project
optionExplain: The book wants the reasoning, not a bare hunch.
Assigned work would not answer an unassigned-work question.
These questions examine how you judged the opportunity, which the answer skips.
The book wants lessons from failures too, not only successes.
questions.explain: Explain how you decided.
questions.rule: Show the evaluation, not just the action.

questions.q: A teacher started an unrequested after-school reading club, and attendance fell after a month. Which interview account fits the book?
options: Describe the club as a total success so that the drop is not discussed at all
Explain why she judged the club worthwhile and what she changed
Say the club failed because the school did not support unrequested activities
Say she will now avoid starting activities that nobody has asked her for
optionExplain: Overstating success hides the learning.
It shows the decision, the risk, and the learning.
Blaming the school gives no lesson.
Avoiding future initiative undermines the point of the competency.
questions.explain: The same reasoning applies outside tech.
questions.rule: Judge, act, review, and report what you learned.
questions.teaches: The book's sample prompts include a calculated risk taken on unassigned work, a time your initiative did not work out as planned, and how you decide whether to pursue an opportunity nobody has asked for.

questions.q: Interviewers look for several signals of initiative. If you must choose, which kind of evidence matters most?
options: A long record of working beyond normal hours on assigned projects
A polished summary of the final results of your most recent project
A list of the teams that eventually adopted your finished solution
A clear moment when you chose to act, and open communication
optionExplain: Hours on assigned projects are diligence, not the critical signals.
Results are a supporting signal, not the top tier.
Adoption belongs to follow-through, the supporting tier.
The book names the decision to act and the communication during action as the critical signals.
questions.explain: The book ranks the signals in tiers. The card next sets them out.
questions.rule: Not all signals weigh the same.

questions.q: Put the signal tiers in order from the heaviest weight to the lightest, as the book ranks them.
items: Critical: the proactive decision and acting while communicating
Strong: seeing patterns others miss
Supporting: follow-through to impact
questions.explain: The book labels the decision and the communication as critical, pattern-spotting as strong, and follow-through as supporting.
questions.rule: Critical, then strong, then supporting.

questions.q: Sort each story element by whether it belongs to a critical signal or to a strong or supporting one.

items.t: I noticed the problem and decided, though it was not my job, to investigate
I told my manager the plan while already building the fix
I explained the moment when I chose to take it on
I noticed that three small incidents shared a hidden cause
I pushed the fix through to adoption and measured the results
I found a bottleneck in an adjacent team that could also benefit

questions.explain: The decision moment and the open communication are critical; pattern-spotting is strong and follow-through is supporting.
questions.rule: Decision and communication come first.

questions.q: True or false: a story with excellent follow-through but no clear decision to act misses the top-tier element of initiative.
questions.explain: The decision to act is a critical signal, and follow-through is a supporting one, so the story misses its top-tier element.
questions.rule: Follow-through cannot stand in for the decision.

questions.q: Which pair contains one critical signal and one supporting signal?
options: Acting while communicating and the proactive decision together
The proactive decision and follow-through to impact
Seeing patterns others miss and follow-through to impact
Seeing patterns others miss and acting while communicating
optionExplain: Both of these are critical.
The decision is critical and follow-through is supporting.
One is strong and one is supporting, with no critical signal.
One is strong and one is critical, with no supporting signal.
questions.explain: Know which tier each signal belongs to.
questions.rule: Two critical, one strong, one supporting.

questions.q: A candidate says the four signals all carry equal weight, so she gives each the same space. What does the book's labelling show?
options: The book orders them alphabetically, so the order carries no meaning at all
The book labels all four critical, so each deserves an equal share of the story
The book gives no ranking, leaving each candidate to choose how to weigh them
They are labelled critical, strong and supporting, so their weight differs
optionExplain: The tier labels are not alphabetical; they describe weight.
Only two are labelled critical.
The book ranks them explicitly.
The tier names tell the reader which signals matter more.
questions.explain: Give the heaviest signals the most space.
questions.rule: Weight your story by tier.

questions.q: A candidate with an hour left has these gaps: no decision moment, vague results, manager never informed. Which two matter most by tier?
options: The decision moment and the communication, as both are critical
The vague results and the decision moment, since results prove the story
The vague results and the communication, since results are the final proof
None of them, since a hidden pattern in the data would outrank all three
optionExplain: Both the decision and the communication are critical signals.
Results are a supporting signal and rank lower than communication.
The same: results rank below communication.
Patterns are strong, not above critical, and are not a gap here.
questions.explain: The decision moment and keeping her manager informed are the two critical signals. Results sit under follow-through, a supporting signal, and a hidden pattern is only a strong signal.
questions.rule: Fix the critical gaps first.
questions.teaches: The book says the strongest candidates show a pattern of finding opportunities and acting on them with good judgment, not a single isolated act.

questions.q: Which story opening best captures the moment the book calls the proactive decision?
options: My manager asked me to look at slow exports, and I finished the work within the week
I ended up helping with slow exports because nobody else was free to do it that day
I noticed slow exports hurting three teams and chose to look into it, off my brief
Slow exports were on our roadmap, so I delivered the planned fix right on schedule
optionExplain: Assigned work has no choice to show.
Being the only free person is circumstance, not choice.
It shows noticing, realizing consequences and choosing to act outside her job.
A planned roadmap item is assigned work.
questions.explain: The choice is the critical element. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Show the moment you chose.

questions.q: The critical element is showing you made a deliberate ____ to go beyond your assigned scope.
questions.explain: The card says the story must show a deliberate choice, not stumbling into extra work.
questions.rule: A deliberate choice, not an accident.

questions.q: Sort each story opening by whether it shows a proactive decision.

items.t: I saw the nightly backup silently failing and decided, though it was not my area, to find out why
I realized the signup form would collapse under launch traffic, so I chose to load-test it
Nobody owned the vendor list; I decided to audit it because stale entries would soon cause errors
My lead put me on the audit, and I did it thoroughly
I stumbled into the vendor list while helping a friend, so I fixed it
The team asked for a volunteer and I was nominated for the audit

questions.explain: The three under 'Shows the decision' describe noticing, a consequence and a choice; the three under 'Does not show it' are assigned, accidental or nominated.
questions.rule: No deliberate choice, no decision moment.

questions.q: True or false: describing an impressive fix is enough to show the proactive decision, even if the moment of choosing goes unmentioned.
questions.explain: The book says strong stories capture the decision point explicitly, because the critical element is the deliberate choice, not the fix.
questions.rule: The fix is not the decision.

questions.q: A candidate says: I got pulled into extra work on the migration and it went well. What is wrong?
options: It shows too little detail about the technology that the migration used
It shows that migrations are never suitable stories for initiative questions
It shows being drawn in, not a deliberate choice to go beyond her scope
It shows that she should have refused the extra work to protect her time
optionExplain: Detail is not the gap.
Migrations can be fine stories; the issue is the lack of choice.
The story lacks the deliberate choice the book calls critical.
Refusing extra work is not what the book advises.
questions.explain: Choice, not circumstance, shows initiative.
questions.rule: Show choosing, not drifting into work.

questions.q: A chef tells a cook to volunteer for weekend inventory, and he agrees. Does this show the proactive decision?
options: No: the choice was not his, because he was told to volunteer
Yes: he said yes, so the choice to act was entirely his own
Yes: inventory is outside a cook's role, so any such work is initiative
No: inventory is too routine to be used as a story in any interview
optionExplain: A deliberate choice is missing; the instruction came from the chef.
Agreeing to an instruction is compliance, not a chosen initiative.
Working outside a role is not enough if the work was directed.
Routine work can be initiative if chosen; the issue here is the instruction.
questions.explain: Being directed is not choosing, even when it is called volunteering.
questions.rule: Ask who decided.
questions.teaches: The book warns against being voluntold to help, meaning told to volunteer, which does not show a deliberate choice.

questions.q: You found a flaw in a shared deployment tool. Which message to your manager best fits the book?
options: Should I look into this flaw in the deployment tool, or would you rather I left it alone?
Nothing to report yet; I will present the finished fix once everything is complete next month
Could someone tell me whether the deployment tool is actually mine to fix at this stage?
A flaw is hurting two teams' releases; I am tracing it this week and will report Friday
optionExplain: Asking whether to look is permission-seeking at the first step.
Silence until completion is working in isolation.
Asking who owns it hands the choice to someone else.
It announces action in progress and a date to share results.
questions.explain: Announce, do not ask. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Announce what you are doing.

questions.q: Match each way of speaking to what it signals.
pairs: Asking: should I look into this?
Saying: I am investigating this week
Revealing a finished change at release
questions.explain: The book contrasts telling people your plan while acting with asking for permission or hiding the work.
questions.rule: Tell while you act.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it announces action in progress or does not.

items.t: I am rewriting the alert rules and will walk you through them on Thursday
I started a fix for the race condition and will demo it on Friday
I noticed an issue affecting billing and am digging into the root cause this week
May I please check whether the alert rules could possibly be rewritten?
I will surprise everyone with the new rules on launch day
Is it okay if I start on the race condition when I find some free time?

questions.explain: The three under 'Announces action in progress' tell people what is happening and when they will see it; the three under 'Asks first or hides' ask permission or plan a surprise.
questions.rule: State the action and when others will see it.

questions.q: What if a candidate describes asking permission before every action on a shared system?
options: It reads as the strongest possible example of building trust through transparency
It reads as seeking permission rather than showing initiative through action
It reads as work in isolation, since permission is not needed on shared systems
It reads as neutral, because the book has no view on how permission is sought
optionExplain: Transparency is telling, not asking at every step.
The book says initiative does not mean asking permission at every step.
Permission requests are not isolation.
The book does state a view on this point.
questions.explain: Constant permission-seeking dilutes the initiative.
questions.rule: Inform; do not keep asking.

questions.q: A candidate says telling people her plan would mean asking permission, so she told no one. What is the error?
options: Nothing is wrong, because telling people always slows initiative down
She should have waited until the work was done and then asked for approval
She should have asked every affected person to approve the plan first
Announcing a plan while acting is not asking permission; it builds trust
optionExplain: The book says telling people builds trust.
Waiting then asking is neither acting nor informing.
Approval from everyone is the permission-at-every-step the book rejects.
The book distinguishes informing during action from asking permission.
questions.explain: Informing is not asking.
questions.rule: Tell people; do not conceal and do not beg.

questions.q: A librarian plans to reorganize shelves used by two branches. Which statement to the branch heads fits the book?
options: May I reorganize the shared shelves, or should I wait for some later year?
I am reorganizing the shared shelves now and will show a layout Friday
I will reorganize everything quietly and you will see the result at opening
Please tell me whether the shared shelves are my responsibility to touch
optionExplain: Asking permission at the start gives up the initiative.
She states her action and a date for sharing the layout.
A silent reorganization surprises people who share the shelves.
Asking about responsibility hands the choice back to others.
questions.explain: The pattern works in any shared setting.
questions.rule: Say what you are doing, with a date.
questions.teaches: The book's contrast: telling a manager you are investigating a root cause this week shows initiative, while asking whether you should look into it does not.

questions.q: Three support tickets this month mention the same confusing error message. What is the pattern-minded reaction?
options: Answer each ticket politely and close it as soon as the user is satisfied
Wait for a fourth ticket so that the pattern is certain before saying anything
Ask whether one underlying cause links them and go looking for it
Ask the users to stop reporting the error message since it is already known
optionExplain: Handling each in isolation misses the link.
Waiting for more evidence delays the action the book values.
Looking for the cause behind repeated incidents is the book's pattern-seeing.
Silencing reports ignores the signal.
questions.explain: Repeats are clues. The card next sets out this signal.
questions.rule: Repeated pain points hide a cause.

questions.q: People with strong initiative look past the ____.
questions.explain: The card says strong initiative means looking past the obvious to find patterns others miss.
questions.rule: Look past the obvious.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it shows seeing patterns or reacting to a single incident.

items.t: She noticed the same three customers kept filing late-payment tickets and traced a flaw in the reminder emails
He saw that each approval delay added a day to every launch and mapped the queue
She realized the sales team's spreadsheet errors matched her team's and offered a shared fix
He fixed one failed upload and closed the ticket
She reset a user's password when asked and moved on
He restarted the stuck job each morning, as he was instructed to do

questions.explain: The three under 'Seeing a pattern' connect repeated or related events; the three under 'Reacting to one incident' deal with each event alone.
questions.rule: Connect the incidents.

questions.q: True or false: seeing patterns others miss is a strong signal, ranked below the two critical signals.
questions.explain: The book labels it a strong signal, below the two critical signals: the proactive decision and acting while communicating.
questions.rule: Strong ranks below critical.

questions.q: A candidate says: I handled all six tickets quickly, so I show strong pattern-spotting. What is the error?
options: She handled each incident singly and never asked what linked them
Six tickets are too few to show anything about a pattern at all
Handling tickets quickly is the opposite of the pattern-seeing skill
She should have waited for more tickets before she handled any of them
optionExplain: Speed on separate incidents is not the same as spotting what connects them.
The number is not the issue; the missing link-search is.
Speed is fine, but it is not the pattern skill.
Waiting is not the book's advice.
questions.explain: A pattern needs a link between incidents.
questions.rule: Look for the link.

questions.q: A warehouse picker notices the aisle with most mis-picks is restocked right before lunch each day. What does pattern-spotting suggest?
options: Check whether restocking time causes the errors and test a change
Tell pickers to work faster in that aisle, since mis-picks come from slowness
Ignore it, because mis-picks are the picker's own responsibility each shift
Wait for the manager to notice the mis-pick figures in the weekly report
optionExplain: She links a recurring error to a possible cause and investigates it.
Speed demands do not examine the cause.
Dismissing it overlooks a lead.
Waiting for the manager skips the initiative.
questions.explain: Recurrence points to a cause.
questions.rule: Test the link you spot.
questions.teaches: The book's examples: analyzing isolated incidents to find systemic issues, recognizing when small inefficiencies compound into major problems, and spotting opportunities in adjacent areas that could benefit your team.

questions.q: A tester notices a recurring bug, tells the team it needs fixing, and moves on. What would the book call missing?
options: Humility: she should have kept the discovery to herself and said nothing
Speed: she should have fixed the bug on the same day that she saw it
Follow-through: driving the problem to impact, not leaving it to others
Seniority: she should have waited for a more senior tester to raise it
optionExplain: Silence would be worse; the issue is stopping at the report.
The speed of the fix is not the point; completion is.
The book separates raising a problem from owning it through to impact.
Seniority is not part of the book's signal.
questions.explain: Raising is a start, not an end. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Raising a problem is not the same as solving it.

questions.q: Follow-through means you drive the initiative to ____ and do not only raise it as a question for others.
questions.explain: The card says you own the work through to impact instead of handing it on.
questions.rule: Finish what you start.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether it shows follow-through to impact.

items.t: He built the checker, got two teams to adopt it, and tracked bug counts afterward
She found budget for the pilot, ran it, and adjusted after feedback
He persuaded the data team to adopt his cleanup script without being their manager
She posted the problem on the forum and hoped someone would take it
He wrote a proposal and handed it to whoever was free
She built the tool and never checked whether anyone used it

questions.explain: The three under 'Shows follow-through' finish the work, win adoption and check results; the three under 'Stops short' leave the problem or the result unattended.
questions.rule: Adoption and measured results complete the story.

questions.q: What if a candidate builds a fix, nobody adopts it, and she does nothing further?
options: The story is complete, since building the fix was the hard part of the work
It lacks follow-through, since the book expects adoption and measured results
The story is strongest, since unused fixes prove she acted without being asked
The story is a critical failure, since follow-through is the top-tier signal
optionExplain: Building alone does not reach impact.
The book wants you to drive the initiative to impact and measure results.
Acting unasked is only part of the picture.
Follow-through is a supporting signal, not top tier.
questions.explain: Impact needs adoption and measurement.
questions.rule: Count the change, not just the build.

questions.q: A candidate says follow-through means doing every part of the work alone without help. What is the error?
options: Nothing is wrong, because the book forbids involving anyone else at all
Doing it alone is wrong because the book wants a committee to decide
Follow-through means handing the work over once the first version exists
The book allows involving others strategically while you own the result
optionExplain: The book does not forbid involving others.
A committee is not what the book asks for.
Handing it over is the opposite of owning it through.
Owning to impact does not exclude strategic help.
questions.explain: Own the result; involve others where it helps.
questions.rule: Own the outcome, not every task.

questions.q: A community-garden volunteer builds a shared watering rota. Which next step shows follow-through?
options: Post the rota on the notice board and assume that people will follow it
Get the other volunteers to use it, track missed days, and adjust the rota
Hand the rota to the garden committee and step back from the work
Draft a second rota for next season and never check the first rota's results
optionExplain: Posting and assuming leaves adoption to chance.
She drives adoption and measures results.
Handing it off ends her ownership.
A new rota without checking skips the measurement.
questions.explain: Follow-through applies to any initiative.
questions.rule: Adopt, measure, adjust.
questions.teaches: The book adds that you should be comfortable doing this without formal authority or assignment, influencing others to adopt your solution and iterating on feedback.

questions.q: A candidate describes working every weekend for two months to finish her assigned project. Which verdict fits the book?
options: Strong initiative, since she did a great deal more than anyone had asked her
A red flag only because she worked weekends at all, whatever the project was
Initiative, since a project that large and hard always calls for personal sacrifice
Real diligence and commitment, though not initiative, since the work was assigned
optionExplain: More effort is not more scope; the work was still assigned.
The weekends are not the flag; the confusion of hard work with initiative is.
The size of the project does not change who assigned it.
Effort on assigned work shows diligence, which the book separates from initiative.
questions.explain: The book treats this confusion as serious. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Effort on assigned work is not initiative.

questions.q: Doing assigned tasks really well is good performance, not ____.
questions.explain: The card says assigned work done well is good performance, which differs from initiative.
questions.rule: Good performance on assigned work is not initiative.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes initiative or hard work on assigned tasks.

items.t: I noticed nobody tracked flaky tests and built a dashboard in my spare time
I started a mentoring wiki because newcomers kept asking the same questions
I spotted a billing mismatch in another team's job and proposed a fix
I stayed late every night to hit the sprint goal that my manager set
I redid my assigned report four times until it was flawless
I worked through the weekend to finish my assigned feature early

questions.explain: The three under 'Initiative' are problems the person found and chose; the three under 'Hard work on assigned tasks' are assigned work done with great effort.
questions.rule: Chosen unassigned work is initiative; effort on assigned work is not.

questions.q: What if a candidate spent the same weekends on a problem she found herself and nobody had assigned?
options: It could be genuine initiative; the flag is about confusing the two
It would still be a red flag, since weekend work is always penalized
It would show only diligence, since time spent never separates the two
It would count as delivery only, because the problem was hard to solve
optionExplain: The flag targets the confusion, not extra hours as such.
The book says the flag is not about extra hours per se.
The book separates chosen unassigned work from assigned work, not by time.
Hardness of the problem is not what separates the qualities.
questions.explain: Chosen problems can be initiative whatever the hours.
questions.rule: The flag is about confusion, not hours.

questions.q: A candidate says: I worked nights and weekends on my project, which shows how much initiative I have. What is wrong?
options: It shows too few hours, since initiative is proved by long weeks of work
It shows initiative only if she also tells the interviewer about her salary
It shows diligence; initiative means fixing what nobody asked her to
It shows a lack of ownership, since projects should never need extra hours
optionExplain: Hours do not prove initiative.
Salary is unrelated.
The story confuses effort on assigned work with initiative.
Ownership is not the problem; the label is.
questions.explain: Match the label to the work.
questions.rule: Do not present diligence as initiative.

questions.q: A nurse manager regularly stays late to fix a scheduling problem nobody assigned to her. How should a candidate in her position see it?
options: As diligence only, since late hours always signal assigned work
As a red flag, since staying late shows poor planning in every setting
As initiative, with the late hours a separate matter of cultural fit
As ownership, since scheduling problems belong to nurse managers
optionExplain: Late hours do not decide whether the work was assigned.
Whether hours are a flag depends on the company's culture.
The problem was unassigned and chosen, so it is initiative; the hours are a fit question.
The scene says nobody assigned it to her.
questions.explain: Separate the quality of the work from the question of hours.
questions.rule: Treat chosen work as initiative and hours as a fit question.
questions.teaches: The book says whether unassigned work happens during regular or extra hours is a separate question of cultural fit, not part of the red flag.

questions.q: You notice a settings file nobody has touched for a year. What should you consider before changing it?
options: Why nobody has changed it yet, such as an owner or a higher priority
Whether the file looks old enough that nobody could still need it in practice
Whether changing it quickly will make your own work easier to do this week
Whether the change can be finished before anyone notices that you touched it
optionExplain: The book asks you to think about why the work has not been assigned before you act.
Age alone does not show that the file is unused.
Your own convenience is not a reason the book offers.
Hiding the change is the opposite of the transparency the book values.
questions.explain: Unassigned does not mean unowned. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Ask why it is still open.

questions.q: Tackling work without considering why it has not already been assigned suggests poor ____.
questions.explain: The card says acting without that thought suggests poor judgment.
questions.rule: Think before you take it on.

questions.q: Sort each opening by whether it shows thinking first or acting without thinking.

items.t: Before touching the billing job I asked who owned it and whether a rewrite was already planned
I asked my manager whether the slow query had been left alone on purpose
I checked the roadmap and found the cleanup deferred, so I proposed a smaller step
I rewrote the billing job overnight since nobody seemed to be working on it
I assumed the config was forgotten and changed it
I deleted the old reports module because it looked unused

questions.explain: The three under 'Shows thinking first' check ownership and priorities; the three under 'Acts without thinking' assume that unassigned means free to change.
questions.rule: Check ownership and priorities before acting.

questions.q: What if a candidate rebuilds another team's module without asking why it was left as is, and it breaks a nightly job?
options: The story shows strong initiative, since the candidate acted quickly on a problem
The story shows ownership, since the candidate took responsibility for the module
The story shows no weakness, since breaking a job is the other team's concern
It shows poor judgment about ownership and how organizations work
optionExplain: Speed without thought is the weakness the book names.
Ownership is responsibility within assigned scope, which this was not.
The break is a consequence of the unconsidered action.
The book warns that another team may own the work for good reasons.
questions.explain: Unthinking action shows weak judgment.
questions.rule: Think before you build.

questions.q: A candidate says: nobody had assigned it, so I assumed it was free to take. What is the error?
options: The error is believing that any work can ever be taken on without approval
Lack of assignment does not mean nobody owns it; there may be good reasons
The error is choosing work at all instead of waiting for a manager to assign it
The error is telling the story at all, because assumptions cannot be discussed
optionExplain: The book does not say all unassigned work needs approval.
The book warns that unassigned work may be left for good reasons.
Choosing work is initiative; the flaw is the lack of thought.
Assumptions can be discussed; the point is to test them.
questions.explain: Test your assumption before acting.
questions.rule: Unassigned is not the same as free.

questions.q: A new analyst finds a report nobody updates and wants to revive it. Which preparation fits the book?
options: Restart the report at once, since a lapsed report must be abandoned work
Leave the report alone since anything unassigned is not worth the effort
Revive it in secret so that nobody can object to the work in advance
Ask why the report lapsed and who owns it before starting
optionExplain: Assuming abandonment is the unthinking action the book warns about.
Leaving it alone gives up the initiative.
Secrecy increases the risk the book describes.
She tests the reasons for the gap before acting.
questions.explain: The check applies in every field.
questions.rule: Ask why it lapsed.
questions.teaches: The book adds that the work may also have needed context you do not have, which is another reason it was not already assigned.

questions.q: A candidate begins: I rebuilt the notification service in three weeks. What is missing from this opening?
options: The names of the engineers who attended the demonstration afterwards
Why she chose to act, which the interviewer needs to judge her
The full list of tools that she used while she rebuilt the service
The date on which her team first adopted the notification service
optionExplain: Names do not show why she acted.
The opening gives the action without the reason.
Tools do not show why she acted.
Adoption dates do not show why she acted.
questions.explain: The reason lets others assess judgment. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Lead with the why.

questions.q: Which three things does the book say to describe about why a problem caught your attention?
options: Why nobody else was addressing the problem
How many hours the whole project eventually took you
Which colleagues disagreed with your choice at the time
What would happen if you did not act
The patterns you saw
optionExplain: The book lists why nobody else was addressing it.
Hours are not part of the why.
Disagreement may arise, but it is not in the book's list.
The book lists what would happen if you did not act.
The book lists the patterns you saw.
questions.explain: The card lists the three: patterns, why unaddressed, and the cost of inaction.
questions.rule: Patterns, why unaddressed, cost of inaction.

questions.q: Sort each opening by whether it explains the why or only states what was done.

items.t: Our alerts fired at 3am from the same cause; nobody owned it and pages would worsen, so I investigated
Three teams copied one spreadsheet and nobody tracked its errors, so I took it on
Handover notes were missing and new staff would repeat old mistakes, so I wrote a template
I wrote a handover template
I built an alert dashboard last spring
I made a shared spreadsheet for three teams

questions.explain: The three under 'Explains the why' give the observation, the gap and the cost of leaving it; the three under 'States only what was done' only name the action.
questions.rule: Observation, gap, cost of inaction, then action.

questions.q: True or false: interviewers can assess your judgment about unassigned work even when you leave out what motivated it.
questions.explain: The book says interviewers cannot assess your judgment about unassigned work if they do not understand what motivated you.
questions.rule: No motive, no judgment to assess.

questions.q: A candidate skips the reason she acted, saying the reason is self-evident. What is the error?
options: Judgment about unassigned work cannot be assessed without the motive
Self-evident reasons are always weaker than reasons based on data from the team
Reasons belong in the closing line of a story rather than anywhere near its start
Reasons only matter for large projects and not for small improvements
optionExplain: The book says motive is needed for the interviewer to judge her choice.
The book does not rank reasons by their source.
The book says to explain the why first, not last.
The book does not limit the point to large projects.
questions.explain: State the reason even when it seems self-evident to you.
questions.rule: Do not assume the reason is understood.

questions.q: A chef describes revamping the prep list. Which opening best shows she chooses her battles wisely?
options: Prep shortages hit service twice weekly and nobody tracked why, so I looked in
I revamped the prep list in a week and the kitchen found it very helpful to use
I am the sort of person who always wants to improve every list in the kitchen
The owner asked me to revamp the prep list, and I completed it on time
optionExplain: She gives the observation, the gap and the cost of leaving it.
It states the action and a vague benefit with no reason.
A personality claim gives no reason about this problem.
An assigned task has no choice to explain.
questions.explain: A clear why shows selective choice, not random extra work.
questions.rule: Give the why behind this problem.
questions.teaches: The book says supplying this context shows you choose your battles wisely rather than randomly taking on extra work.

questions.q: A candidate says: I found the problem, designed the fix and rolled it out with nobody's help. How might interviewers read this?
options: As proof that she works well with others and shares credit with everyone
As the clearest sign of ownership of the problem and of her whole team
As a possible tendency to chase pet projects and ignore the firm
As unremarkable, since solving problems alone is how initiative is judged
optionExplain: A solo story gives no evidence about teamwork.
Ownership concerns assigned scope, and the story is about unassigned work.
The book says solo stories raise eyebrows and suggest pet projects.
The book says it is judged with concern, not as unremarkable.
questions.explain: Initiative that ignores others looks risky. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Initiative works with others.

questions.q: True or false: the book says even self-directed work needs buy-in from others.
questions.explain: The card says even self-directed work needs validation of the problem and input on solutions.
questions.rule: Even self-directed work needs buy-in.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it shows alignment with the organization or a lone-hero approach.

items.t: I checked with two users that the slowdown was real before building anything
I shared my prototype with the platform team and adopted their suggestions
I persuaded the support leads to try the macro before rolling it out
I decided what the team needed and shipped it without telling anyone
I solved it entirely myself and presented the finished tool as a surprise
I did not ask anyone whether the problem mattered to them

questions.explain: The three under 'Aligned with the organization' seek validation, input or support; the three under 'Lone-hero approach' work alone and assume the need.
questions.rule: Validate, ask, and win support.

questions.q: What if the candidate adds that she validated the problem with users and refined the design with colleagues' input?
options: The story becomes weaker, since sharing the work hides her own contribution
It looks aligned with what the firm needs and avoids the lone-hero flag
The story is unchanged, since only the final results matter to interviewers
The story turns into an assigned task, since colleagues were involved at all
optionExplain: The book wants her contribution plus alignment, not hidden contribution.
Validation and input are what the book asks for.
The book says buy-in matters, not only results.
Involving others does not make the work assigned.
questions.explain: Buy-in strengthens the story.
questions.rule: Show validation and input.

questions.q: A candidate reasons: to show initiative I should show I did everything myself. What is the error?
options: Showing the work as solitary is correct, since help weakens the idea of initiative
Initiative cannot be shown at all in a story that involves more than one person
Showing everything alone is correct provided the results were large enough
Initiative typically succeeds with validation, input and influence from others
optionExplain: The book says the opposite: solo stories raise concerns.
Stories with others can show initiative; the issue is sole credit.
Large results do not offset a pet-project impression.
The book says even self-directed work needs buy-in.
questions.explain: Others make initiative succeed.
questions.rule: Show others' input; it strengthens the story.

questions.q: A teacher starts a reading program for her whole school. Which account avoids the lone-hero flag?
options: She designed the whole program in secret and announced it at a staff meeting
She asked colleagues if the need was real, adapted the plan, won support
She credited herself with every idea so the head teacher would notice her
She ran it alone in her own classroom and never mentioned it to colleagues
optionExplain: A secret design then announcement skips buy-in.
She validated the need and used others' input.
Claiming all credit is the pattern the book flags.
Staying silent avoids organizational alignment.
questions.explain: Buy-in applies in any institution.
questions.rule: Win support for a self-started effort.
questions.teaches: The book adds that you may also need to influence others to adopt the solution you develop.

questions.q: Which closing line best supports an initiative story?
options: The work helped the team a great deal and everyone seemed to appreciate the result
I put a great deal of effort into it, and it was a very rewarding experience for me
It was a challenging project that taught me a lot about the codebase and its history
The checker caught 40 formatting errors in a month and two teams adopted it
optionExplain: Praise without numbers is vague.
Effort and feeling are about the candidate, not the value.
Learning for the candidate is not value for the organization.
Specific outcomes prove the work was worth doing.
questions.explain: Value is shown with evidence. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Prove value with results.

questions.q: True or false: saying your work helped the team leaves interviewers unsure whether it created real value.
questions.explain: The book says this leaves interviewers wondering whether the work created real value or only kept you busy.
questions.rule: Help claims need evidence.

questions.q: Sort each result statement by whether it is concrete or vague.

items.t: Support tickets about password resets fell by a third in two months
The script cut the monthly close from six hours to one
Three teams adopted the template within a quarter
It made things better for everyone
The team was happy with the result
It really helped us move faster

questions.explain: The three under 'Concrete' give a measurable change or adoption; the three under 'Vague' give impressions.
questions.rule: Numbers and adoption beat impressions.

questions.q: What if a candidate says only that her project helped the team?
options: Interviewers may wonder whether it created real value or only kept her busy
Interviewers will assume the value was large, since she did not boast about it
Interviewers will skip the point, since value is not part of how initiative is judged
Interviewers will count it as a strong signal, since modesty is a sign of judgment
optionExplain: The book states that exact doubt.
Absent evidence, interviewers do not assume large value.
The book includes outcomes among what justifies the initiative.
Modesty does not substitute for evidence.
questions.explain: Silence on value invites doubt.
questions.rule: State the value.

questions.q: A candidate says the hours she put in prove the value of her initiative. What is the error?
options: Hours worked are the only proof that interviewers are able to check themselves
Hours should be reported in place of outcomes so the story stays brief and modest
Effort is not an outcome; the book asks for time saved or errors avoided
Hours prove value only when they were worked at nights or at weekends
optionExplain: Outcomes are the checkable proof the book asks for.
The book asks for outcomes, not hours in their place.
Effort does not show that the work was worth doing.
Time of day does not turn effort into value.
questions.explain: Report outcomes, not effort.
questions.rule: Outcomes, not hours.

questions.q: A store clerk redesigned the shelf labels unasked. Which closing line best fits the book?
options: The new labels made the store look neater and customers seemed to like them
I spent three weekends on the labels and I am proud of how they turned out
The new labels halved restocking errors, and two other stores copied them
The labels were my own idea, and I think they were a good one for the store
optionExplain: Looks and impressions are not measured outcomes.
Weekends and pride are effort and feeling.
It states a measured change and adoption by others.
Ownership of the idea says nothing about its value.
questions.explain: Concrete results apply in any field.
questions.rule: Name the change you can show.
questions.teaches: The book suggests asking: how much time did you save by preventing future problems, what errors were avoided, and did your colleagues adopt your solution?

questions.q: In a four-part initiative answer, where would the final results and your lesson usually go?
options: At the end, in a landing giving the outcome and what you do differently
In the opening line only, with the rest of the answer leaving them unmentioned
In the first key point, before the problem has been described to the listener
In a note after the interview ends, sent by email once the panel has left
optionExplain: The book's examples close with a landing that gives results and the lesson.
The headline gives a brief result, but the full outcome comes at the close.
Results before the problem would not make sense to the listener.
Results belong in the answer, not in a later note.
questions.explain: The book's examples share a shape. The card next sets it out.
questions.rule: The landing closes with results and lesson.

questions.q: Put the parts of the book's example initiative stories in order, from first to last.
items: Headline
Key Point 1
Key Point 2
Key Point 3
Landing
questions.explain: Each example opens with a headline, moves through three key points and closes with a landing.
questions.rule: Headline, three key points, landing.

questions.q: Sort each sentence by whether it belongs in key point 1 or in the landing. This is our reading of the shape.

items.t: I noticed our releases needed three hours of manual checks
Although it was not my job, I decided to automate them
I realized the team was wasting effort a script could do
The tool saved twelve hours a week
I now scan for repetitive tasks on a regular basis
Deployments became less stressful and happened more often

questions.explain: Key point 1 holds the noticing and the choice; the landing holds the results and what you now do.
questions.rule: Notice and choose early; results and lesson at the end.

questions.q: True or false: a story that opens with a long list of steps and leaves the decision to act until the end matches the shape of the book's examples.
questions.explain: In the examples, the noticing and the decision come in the first key point, and the landing holds the results.
questions.rule: Put the decision near the start.

questions.q: A draft has a headline and a landing but no key point on how she judged whom to involve. What is missing?
options: The step-by-step technical detail of the build that the headline promised
A fourth key point to repeat the headline for any listener who was distracted
A list of every person on the team who ever touched the project
The judgment about others that each example's second key point shows
optionExplain: Technical detail is not what the examples use their second key point for.
The examples use three key points, not four.
A list of names is not judgment.
Each example's middle part shows judgment about whom to involve, which links to the acting-while-communicating signal.
questions.explain: The middle shows how you handled others.
questions.rule: Show how you judged whom to involve.

questions.q: A hospital pharmacist drafts a story about a new labeling check. Which opening line fits the examples' headline?
options: Last year I worked on many things at the hospital, including labeling and ordering
Last year I added a labeling check, and wrong-label errors fell by two thirds
I am a pharmacist who cares deeply about patient safety in every task I do
Our hospital has always had a labeling process, and it has served patients well
optionExplain: It names no action or result.
It states the action and the result in one sentence.
It is a self-description, not a headline.
It describes background without the action.
questions.explain: A headline states what you did and the result.
questions.rule: Open with the action and its result.
questions.teaches: The book's examples each begin by naming the interview question that the story answers, before the headline is given.

questions.q: How does the book say initiative stories differ between an entry-level and a staff-level engineer?
options: Only staff-level engineers are expected to have any initiative stories at all
Entry-level stories should avoid unassigned work, and staff stories should seek it
Staff-level stories need no follow-through because their scope is already broad
The scope grows with level, but the underlying pattern stays the same
optionExplain: The book gives an entry-level example, so it expects them.
The entry-level example is about unassigned work.
The staff example includes a rollout and results.
The book says the scope gets bigger but the pattern is unchanged.
questions.explain: Same pattern, bigger scope. The card next gives the four examples.
questions.rule: Same pattern at every level.

questions.q: The scope gets bigger as you go up, but the pattern is the ____.
questions.explain: The card says the pattern, spot something unassigned, choose to act and follow through, is the same at every level.
questions.rule: The pattern stays the same.

questions.q: Sort each initiative by the scope it fits. This is our reading of the book's examples.

items.t: Automating a manual check that your team takes turns doing
Writing a runbook for your own team's on-call issues
Cleaning duplicated test fixtures in your own service
Building retry defaults into a framework that twenty teams use
Proposing a shared logging standard after seeing the same failure across services
Partnering with a platform team to ship a library that removes a class of outages

questions.explain: The three under 'Team-level scope' stay within one team's work; the three under 'Platform-wide scope' change what many teams get by default.
questions.rule: Match the scope to your level.

questions.q: What if a staff-level candidate tells a story of huge scope that shows no moment of choosing to act?
options: It will be strong anyway, because scope compensates for a missing choice
It misses the core, since the choice to act is what makes it initiative
It will be judged only by the size of the impact and not by how it began
It will count as an entry-level story, because the choice is missing
optionExplain: Scope does not replace the pattern.
The pattern, not size, defines initiative at every level.
The book's pattern begins with choosing, so how it began matters.
Level is not decided by the missing choice.
questions.explain: Scale cannot replace the choice.
questions.rule: A big story still needs the choice.

questions.q: A senior engineer says only large-scale stories count as initiative. What is the error?
options: Large-scale stories never count unless they involve at least twenty teams
Only entry-level engineers can tell small-scale stories in interviews
Spotting, choosing and following through counts at every scale
Scale decides initiative, so stories of any size must name the headcount
optionExplain: No headcount threshold appears in the book.
The book does not restrict small stories to one level.
The book shows the same pattern at four different scales.
Initiative is defined by the pattern, not by headcount.
questions.explain: Scale changes; the pattern does not.
questions.rule: Judge by the pattern, not the size.

questions.q: A staff-level candidate closes with: we improved resilience a lot. Which rewrite fits the pattern the examples show?
options: Cascade failures fell by a third in six months and four teams adopted it
We did a great deal of resilience work, and I am proud of how the team did
The resilience work took three quarters and many late nights across the platform
We improved resilience far more than any other platform group in the company
optionExplain: It gives measured results and adoption.
It still gives no measure.
Time and nights are effort, not outcome.
A comparison with other groups is unmeasured.
questions.explain: Measured results close the story at any level.
questions.rule: Close with a measured outcome.
questions.teaches: The book's examples state outcomes in numbers: deployment time cut from 3 hours to 10 minutes, incident response time cut from 45 to about 15 minutes, and cascade failures down by about 80 percent.

questions.q: A candidate believes she has no initiative stories. Where does the book suggest she look?
options: At small moments when she improved something that worked or filled a gap
At her biggest assigned project, since large projects always show initiative
At her job description, since the duties listed there define her initiative
At her performance reviews, since praise there proves she took initiative
optionExplain: The book points to the margins of assigned work.
Size of an assigned project does not make it unassigned.
The job description lists assigned duties.
Praise on assigned work is not unassigned work.
questions.explain: Look in the margins. The card next gives examples.
questions.rule: Stories hide in small unassigned improvements.

questions.q: True or false: automating a task that was not broken but was inefficient can count as initiative, even if it saved only a little time.
questions.explain: The card says small improvements to adequate work count as initiative when nobody asked for them.
questions.rule: Small improvements count.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether it can serve as an initiative story.

items.t: Wrote a help page because I was tired of answering the same questions
Created a script for a tedious weekly export that worked but wasted time
Reworked a messy module while adding a feature, going beyond what the feature needed
Refactored exactly what the feature ticket required
Wrote the release documentation that my manager assigned
Finished my sprint tasks ahead of schedule

questions.explain: The three under 'Can be an initiative story' go beyond the assignment by choice; the three under 'Not an initiative story' stay within the assignment.
questions.rule: Beyond the requirement and chosen means initiative.

questions.q: What if she refactors code only as far as the feature requires?
options: That is initiative, since any refactoring shows a desire to improve code
That is delivery, since a refactor always finishes the feature quickly
That is part of the assigned work, so it is not initiative on its own
That is a red flag, since refactoring signals a lack of focus on features
optionExplain: Improving code within the assignment is still assigned work.
Delivery is about overcoming obstacles, not about refactor scope.
The book says a refactor counts when it goes beyond the feature's requirements.
The book does not call refactoring a flag.
questions.explain: Beyond the requirement is the test.
questions.rule: Check whether it went beyond the requirement.

questions.q: A candidate says: nothing at work was ever broken, so I have no initiative stories. What is the error?
options: Initiative can be shown only by fixing things that are broken and reported
Initiative includes improving what worked, not only fixing what is broken
Working systems are never worth improving, so she has no story to tell
She should have waited for something to break to create a story to tell
optionExplain: That restricts initiative to breakage, which the book does not.
The book says improving adequate things unasked is a good source of stories.
The book says improving working things counts.
Waiting for a break is the reactive stance initiative avoids.
questions.explain: You do not need a failure to have a story.
questions.rule: Look at what worked but could be better.

questions.q: A data steward made a checklist that helps new hires get set up faster, without being asked. Does it fit the book's idea of initiative?
options: No: onboarding help belongs to human resources and not to a steward
No: checklists are too small to be an initiative story in any interview
Yes, but only if she worked on it over several weekends of her own time
Yes: she made a resource that helps others work better, unasked
optionExplain: Nothing in the book assigns onboarding help to one department.
The book says small improvements count.
The book does not tie it to weekend work.
It is a self-chosen improvement that helps others.
questions.explain: Resources that help others onboard are within the book's examples.
questions.rule: Think of what you made for others without being asked.
questions.teaches: The book's reflection prompts also cover tools or templates for tedious tasks, streamlining communication between teams, and fixing data quality issues early, and it says two or three strong stories on different aspects are enough.

questions.q: Before an interview, which checklist best describes a strong initiative story?
options: The longest hours worked, the biggest project handled, the most colleagues helped, and a praise quote
A clear choice to act, thought about why, judgment about going alone, outcomes, learning
A technical summary, the tools used, the team's size, the budget, and the final launch date given
A list of awards, a stated passion for work, a promise to work late, and a link to a portfolio
optionExplain: Hours and praise are not on the list.
The book's takeaways list exactly these five elements.
Technical detail is not on the list.
Awards and promises are not on the list.
questions.explain: The chapter ends with a checklist. The card next gives it.
questions.rule: Five things belong in the story.

questions.q: Which three belong in a strong initiative story, according to the chapter's takeaways?
options: A record of the longest hours you worked on the project
Specific outcomes that justified taking on the unassigned work
A clear moment when you chose to act on something unassigned
A list of the senior leaders who praised the finished work
Evidence that you thought through why the work was not already assigned
optionExplain: Hours are not on the list.
The takeaways name specific outcomes.
The takeaways name the clear moment of choice.
Praise is not on the list.
The takeaways name the evidence of thinking it through.
questions.explain: The takeaways list the choice, the thinking, the judgment, the outcomes and the learning.
questions.rule: Choice, thinking, outcomes.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it is an element of a strong story or a trap.

items.t: At that point I decided, although it was not my job, to take it on
I checked why nobody had picked the work up before I began
Errors fell by a third within two months
I worked every weekend on my assigned project
I did everything myself and told no one
It helped the team a lot

questions.explain: The three under 'Element of a strong story' are elements of a strong story; the three under 'Trap to avoid' are the traps of hard work, lone action and vague value.
questions.rule: Choose, think, show outcomes.

questions.q: What if a story has every element of the checklist except specific outcomes?
options: It falls into the vague-value trap and weakens the case for the work
It stays fully strong, since outcomes are the least important element
It becomes a red flag, since missing outcomes are a serious issue
It becomes an assigned task, since outcomes are what separate the two
optionExplain: Missing outcomes leave the value unproven.
The book lists outcomes among the elements.
The book classes vagueness about value as a yellow flag.
Assignment is decided by who chose the work, not by outcomes.
questions.explain: Outcomes justify the choice.
questions.rule: Add outcomes to every story.

questions.q: A candidate lists her strengths: hard work, long hours, flawless assigned delivery. What does the checklist say is missing?
options: A higher number of hours worked each week on her assigned projects
A more detailed list of the assigned deliverables she completed on time
A clear moment when she chose to act on something unassigned
A statement of the salary band that she expects for the position
optionExplain: More hours on assigned work still misses the choice.
More detail on assigned deliverables still misses the choice.
All three strengths concern assigned work; none shows a self-chosen action.
Salary is unrelated.
questions.explain: Add the moment of choosing.
questions.rule: Include the choice.

questions.q: A candidate says her department's sales rose 20 percent in her first year, which shows initiative. What should she add?
options: A comparison of her department's growth with other departments' growth
A statement that sales growth is always caused by the person who joined
The choice she made and what it added beyond the natural trend
A list of the hours that she worked while the sales were rising
optionExplain: Comparisons show growth, not her choice.
That claim is unsupported.
Initiative is shown by a specific chosen action, not by growth around her.
Hours show effort, not contribution.
questions.explain: Show your contribution, not just the trend.
questions.rule: Show your specific contribution.
questions.teaches: The book lists one more trap: do not confuse natural growth with initiative, and show your specific contribution beyond what would have happened anyway.

questions.q: A product manager coordinates a launch across several teams. When does her work show delivery?
questions.explain: Delivery is judged by the outcome that reaches users. The card next sets out the definition.
options: When every team agrees that the launch plan reads well and looks thorough
When her meeting notes record each decision and the owner of every task
When the feature goes live on schedule and works for the people using it
When she spots the largest number of risks before the work has started
optionExplain: A well-liked plan feels like progress, but agreement alone ships nothing.
Good records help coordination, yet they are not the shipped result.
Right: delivery is measured by a working result in users' hands.
Spotting risks is useful, but delivery is judged on what finally ships.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?
questions.rule: Judge your work by whether a working solution reaches users, not by how clever it is.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, delivery means getting working solutions into the hands of users.
questions.explain: That is the author's opening definition: working solutions that reach users, not plans or prototypes kept inside the team.
questions.rule: Working and in users' hands.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: Sort these pieces of work: do they show delivery, or not yet?
questions.explain: The three under 'Shows delivery' end with something working for users. The three under 'Does not yet show delivery' describe effort that never gets into users' hands.
questions.rule: No users, no delivery.

items.t: A mobile developer releases a fixed checkout flow that customers use this week
A database engineer upgrades a live system without interrupting customers
A project lead gets four teams to launch a feature on the agreed date
A developer finishes a clever script that stays on her own laptop
An analyst writes a detailed plan for a dashboard that nobody starts to build
A tester studies code for weeks, but none of it reaches users

questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: Two ML engineers work at the same company. One trains models with impressive accuracy figures. The other deploys models reliably at scale. Who shows stronger delivery?
questions.explain: The author sets reliable deployment above training for impressive metrics when judging delivery.
questions.rule: Reliable use beats impressive numbers.
questions.teaches: The author says an ML engineer who deploys models reliably at scale shows stronger delivery than one who only trains models to impressive accuracy metrics.
options: The one deploying reliably at scale, because the work reaches users and keeps working
The one with impressive accuracy figures, because real skill is shown in the numbers she reports
Neither, because delivery is judged only on how fast each one finishes
Both equally, because training and deploying are the same competency
optionExplain: Right: the author gives this as an example of stronger delivery.
Accuracy is a real achievement, but a model that never serves users is not delivered.
Speed matters, yet the definition is about working solutions reaching users.
They overlap, but the author separates solving the problem from shipping it.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: A team ships on the agreed date, but the release crashes for many users every day. How does the definition rate this?
questions.explain: Applying the definition: a release that keeps failing does not give users a working solution, even on time.
questions.rule: On time and working.
options: It counts fully, because meeting the date is what delivery is about
It counts fully, since crashes are a support problem for another team and not a delivery one
It counts if the team promises a fix, since delivery is judged by intent
It falls short, because delivery needs a working solution, not only a release on the date
optionExplain: The date matters, but the definition names working software, not a date alone.
Passing the problem to support moves the work, but users still lack a working solution.
Intent is not mentioned; the definition looks at what users actually receive.
Right (Our reading): the definition asks for working solutions in users' hands.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: A school district must replace its attendance system before term starts, and the team keeps debating the perfect design. Which move fits delivery best?
questions.explain: Shipping one valuable piece first, shown working, turns debate into progress.
questions.rule: Ship a thin working slice first.
questions.teaches: In the opening story, a live demo and a detailed timeline won the team's go-ahead, and the incremental rollout caught problems that one big migration would have missed.
options: Finish the design debate so that the entire system can be moved in one go
Move one needed function first, prove it with a working demo and agree a short timeline
Start the new system at term start in every school with whatever parts are ready by then
Keep the old system for another year and write a thorough report on options
optionExplain: A full design feels safe, but it is the planning-into-failure pattern the story describes.
Right: a thin working slice with a visible plan is how the opening story won support.
Speed without a plan risks a broken start for everyone at once.
A report may help later, yet it puts nothing new into users' hands.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: A team can ship a reliable version next week or a flawless one in six months. Which would the companies the author cites prefer?
questions.explain: These companies lean towards early, reliable results. The card next gives their shared belief.
options: The flawless version, since a first impression cannot be repeated
The reliable version next week, then improve it from real feedback
Whichever version the most senior engineer personally prefers
Neither, until the team has researched what every rival is planning
optionExplain: It sounds careful, but waiting six months delays any value to users.
Right: they value reliable results that arrive in time over perfect ones that arrive late.
Seniority does not settle it; the stated belief is about results under constraints.
Research is fine, but it adds delay and does not put anything in users' hands.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?
questions.rule: Prefer a reliable result that arrives in time over a perfect one that arrives late or not at all.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, Meta, Spotify and Uber all prize fast delivery and share the belief that reliable results under real constraints beat perfect but late ones.
questions.explain: The author uses all three companies to show the same belief about shipping reliable results over late perfection.
questions.rule: Reliable and on time beats perfect and late.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: A bakery wants an online ordering page before the holiday rush. Which plan best matches the principle?
questions.explain: The principle asks for a reliable result in time. Two options delay too long and one gives up reliability.
questions.rule: Reliable now, polished later.
options: Hold the launch until every special case, from gift notes to allergies, is handled
Release a quick page that sometimes loses orders so that it is live sooner
Wait until a competitor launches and copy whatever turns out to work
Launch a simple page that takes orders reliably now, and add extras after the rush
optionExplain: Completeness feels responsible, but the rush would pass with nothing in place.
Speed without reliability breaks the principle, which asks for reliable results.
Waiting avoids risk, yet it delivers nothing during the window that matters.
Right: a working page in time beats a fuller page that misses the rush.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: Match each company to the culture the author describes.
questions.explain: Each company expresses fast delivery in its own way: a value, a build-and-tweak cycle, and a willingness to challenge the status quo.
questions.rule: Fast delivery has several company flavours.
questions.teaches: Spotify pairs rapid delivery with continuous iteration on user feedback, and Uber's toe-stepping means moving fast even if it means challenging the status quo.
pairs: Think it, build it, ship it, tweak it, with iteration based on user feedback
Toe-stepping: moving fast to deliver, even if it challenges the status quo
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: A manager reads the chapter and says: these companies show that delivering well means skipping quality. What does that reading miss?
questions.explain: The principle favours reliable results in time. It does not say quality can be dropped.
questions.rule: Fast, but reliable.
options: The author asks for reliable results, so speed is not a licence for poor work
The author says delivery is about building perfect solutions, which take as long as they take
The author says these companies move slowly to protect their brand
The author says quality only matters for engineers who work on security
optionExplain: Right: reliability is part of the claim.
The author argues the reverse: perfect solutions that arrive late matter less.
The companies are cited because they move fast.
No such limit is given; reliability is a general part of the claim.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: A volunteer group plans a flood-warning text service. A flawless system would take a year, and a basic reliable one four weeks, before storm season. What would the author's stance favour?
questions.explain: The principle applies at small scale too: what matters is a reliable result inside the window that counts.
questions.rule: Work that never arrives earns nothing.
questions.teaches: The author's reason is blunt: unused code helps no one, so work that never reaches users earns nothing however good it is.
options: Wait for the flawless system, since warnings must be perfect before anyone relies on them
Launch a rough service that sometimes fails silently, to be live by the next day
Launch the basic reliable service before the season and improve it afterwards
Skip the project, since a partial service might give residents false confidence
optionExplain: Perfection sounds right for warnings, yet a year-long wait leaves everyone unwarned.
Warnings that fail silently are not reliable, so this breaks the principle.
Right: unused work helps no one, and a late perfect system misses the season.
Avoiding all risk leaves residents with nothing in the meantime.
questions.section: 6.1 What Does it Mean to Deliver?

questions.q: A team has one week left. Which plan best balances speed and quality?
questions.explain: A good plan protects what matters and trims the rest. The card next names the tension.
options: Ship everything as fast as possible and fix whatever breaks once real users have found it
Move the date until every part of the product has been fully polished
Cut testing across the board so that the extra days go to new features
Ship the core feature on time, defer polish, and keep the parts users depend on dependable
optionExplain: It feels bold, but broken releases cost everyone time.
It feels safe, but a perfect result that is late is useless.
It saves time now, yet it gambles with the parts users depend on.
Right: it protects what matters and lets the rest wait.
questions.rule: Aim for valuable work shipped on time, and decide which shortcuts are safe and which quality you will not trade.

questions.q: A perfect solution delivered too ____ is useless.
questions.explain: The author calls a perfect solution that comes too late useless. The opposite failure is a quick solution that breaks.
questions.rule: Late is useless; broken is wasteful.

questions.q: A team must launch a customer app this week. Sort each item: a safe shortcut, or quality to protect?
questions.explain: Our reading: items that users will not notice or that can be repaired later are safe to cut. Anything that can harm customers or lose their data cannot be traded.
questions.rule: Cut what can wait; protect what harms if broken.

items.t: Leave a rarely used settings screen plain for the first release
Use a simple animation instead of a custom one on the home page
Do the monthly summary report by hand, to be automated later
Store customer passwords without any protection
Skip the backup of customer orders
Launch without checking that a payment is charged only once

questions.q: A team ships a quick release that breaks in production. What does the author say follows?
questions.explain: Speed that produces breakage costs time for everyone, which is why the sweet spot needs both.
questions.rule: Speed without quality is waste.
options: It is still good delivery, because the date was met and fixes can follow
It wastes everyone's time, so speed alone did not make it good delivery
It saves time overall, since problems are found faster by real users
It matters little, because users forgive a product that arrives early
optionExplain: Meeting the date helps, but breaking in production undoes the value.
Right: quick, poor-quality solutions that break are named as a waste.
The author does not defend breaking releases as a testing method.
The chapter does not say users forgive breakage in exchange for earliness.

questions.q: Priya says: with a tight deadline, good delivery means choosing speed every time. What does the card say she misses?
questions.explain: Priya fixes on one side of the tension. The author asks for valuable work on time, without creating excessive future problems.
questions.rule: Both sides of the tension count.
options: Deadlines are rarely tight in real jobs, so the situation she describes seldom arises at all
Speed should always be avoided, because quality is what gets noticed
Quick work that breaks in production wastes time, so speed is only half the balance
Only managers decide how fast to ship, not the people doing the work
optionExplain: Tight deadlines are the normal case in the chapter.
The author does not tell you to avoid speed; late perfection is useless.
Right: the sweet spot needs speed and protected quality.
Discerning safe shortcuts is described as part of the work itself.

questions.q: A clinic's booking tool must launch Monday. Which item should the team protect even if it delays other work?
questions.explain: Which quality is non-negotiable depends on the harm it prevents, and patient data is the clearest case here.
questions.rule: Protect reliability, integrity and security.
questions.teaches: The author names production reliability, data integrity and security as non-negotiable, while perfect code, over-testing and flawless documentation can get in the way of delivering.
options: Storing patient records correctly and securely
Matching the tool's colours to the clinic's brand
Writing polished help pages for every screen
Adding calendar sync with the receptionists' phones
optionExplain: Right: the author lists reliability, data integrity and security as non-negotiable.
Appearance matters to some, but it can wait for a later release.
Flawless documentation is one of the things the author says can get in the way of delivery.
Useful, yet an extra feature is the kind of nice-to-have that can follow.

questions.q: Two engineers meet their deadlines. One had a calm quarter. The other lost a teammate and had requirements change twice. Whose record says more about delivery?
questions.explain: Delivery shows most when conditions are difficult. The card next separates it from task completion.
options: The second engineer's, because she shipped despite changes and a missing teammate
The first engineer's, because a calm record proves she plans very well
Both are equal, because each one met the same deadline in the end
Neither, because a record of deadlines cannot be fairly compared between different people
optionExplain: Right: shipping through disruption shows delivery.
Planning is useful, but a smooth run tests little.
The date is the same, yet the conditions behind it differ greatly.
Comparison is possible; the conditions overcome are what the author weighs.
questions.rule: Show that you finish and ship even when requirements shift and obstacles appear.

questions.q: Match each term to what the author says about it.
questions.explain: Basic competence needs only a smooth run. Delivery is tested by shifting requirements and surprises, and the shipper adapts.
questions.rule: Smooth completion is competence; completion through trouble is delivery.
pairs: Completing assigned work on schedule when everything goes smoothly
Completion despite shifting requirements and unforeseen obstacles
Someone who turns ideas into working technology and adapts instead of giving up

questions.q: A lead finishes her assigned module on the due date during a quiet month. How would the author describe that?
questions.explain: The distinction turns on disruption. This lead completed work; she has not yet shown delivery.
questions.rule: Smooth is competence.
options: Strong delivery, because she met the date and so proved she can ship work to users
Weak work, because modules finished on time are usually too small
Basic competence; delivery shows when she still finishes after plans are disrupted
Irrelevant, because only work that nobody assigned counts as delivery
optionExplain: A smooth run does not test shipping under difficulty.
Size is not the author's measure; conditions are.
Right: on-schedule work in good conditions is competence, not yet delivery.
