That mixes up delivery with initiative, which the chapter treats separately.

questions.q: According to the author, which example describes a QA engineer showing delivery?
questions.explain: The author gives three examples of disruption: flaky SDK behaviour for a mobile engineer, conflicting partner demands for a program manager, and compressed timelines for QA.
questions.rule: Examples differ by role; the pattern is the same.
questions.teaches: The author's examples of delivery despite disruption include a mobile engineer shipping despite flaky SDK behaviour, a technical program manager balancing conflicting partner demands, and a QA engineer shipping despite compressed timelines.
options: Testing every feature fully, whatever the deadline, before any release goes out to users
Shipping quality releases despite compressed timelines and last-second feature requests
Writing a long test plan that all teams sign off before work begins
Reporting bugs found late so that developers can explain the cause
optionExplain: Thorough testing has value, but the example is about shipping through pressure.
Right: this is the author's example for a QA engineer.
Sign-off is not the example; the point is shipping despite changes.
Reporting helps, yet it is not the delivery example given.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, when plans fall apart, a shipper stops and waits until conditions improve.
questions.explain: The shipper does not give up but adapts to the conditions that arise. Waiting for ideal conditions is the opposite.
questions.rule: Adapt, do not wait.

questions.q: A wedding planner learns the venue has cancelled two weeks before the event. Which response matches a shipper?
questions.explain: A shipper treats the cancellation as terrain to work through and keeps the people affected informed.
questions.rule: Adapt and tell people early.
questions.teaches: A strong shipper communicates early to partners when plans have to change, rather than letting them find out late.
options: Wait for the old venue to refund the deposit, then restart the whole plan from scratch
Explain to the couple that the cancellation was the venue's fault
Hold the original plan and ask the guests to travel to the new place
Find a new venue, adjust the plan and tell the couple early what has changed
optionExplain: Waiting for a refund lets the date slip while nothing is rebuilt.
Explaining blame does not move the wedding forward.
Copying the plan unchanged ignores what the new conditions require.
Right: she adapts and keeps the partners informed.

questions.q: Your feature will land two weeks late because a dependency broke. What best protects people's trust in you?
questions.explain: Early, honest news with an option lets others adjust. The card next gives the author's reasoning.
options: Say nothing yet and work extra hours, hoping to recover the two weeks before anyone asks
Wait until the original date, then explain which dependency caused the delay
Tell the affected teams now and propose a smaller version that can still ship on time
Promise the original date again to keep everyone calm for the moment
optionExplain: It feels like protecting them, but a late surprise costs far more trust.
An explanation after the fact leaves partners no time to adjust their plans.
Right: early notice plus a valuable alternative keeps trust.
A promise you doubt buys calm now and a bigger loss of credibility later.
questions.rule: Tell partners early when a plan must change, and offer the most valuable alternative you can still ship.

questions.q: Strong delivery includes communicating to partners ____ when plans have to change.
questions.explain: The author puts timing first: partners who hear early can adjust.
questions.rule: Say it early.

questions.q: A freelance web developer sees she cannot finish all five pages by the client's launch date. Which action fits the principle?
questions.explain: Early notice with a workable alternative keeps the client able to decide. The others hide the issue or hand it over.
questions.rule: Early notice plus an option.
options: Tell the client this week, propose launching three key pages first, and add the rest later
Work through the weekend and deliver all five pages late without mentioning the problem to anyone
Launch all five pages on time, with the last two left unfinished and unmarked
Ask the client to move the launch date without offering any alternative
optionExplain: Right: she gives early notice and a valuable alternative.
A hidden slip surprises the client and shows no plan for the next one.
Hiding the gaps misleads the client and risks a visible failure.
A bare request leaves the client with a problem and no option.

questions.q: Dev reports a slipping project. Which lines break the author's advice? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Early notice and a valuable alternative are the author's advice. Waiting for certainty and clinging to the original scope work against it.
questions.rule: Do not wait, and do not cling.
options: Line 2: he waits for the final week so that the news comes with full facts
Line 1: he tells the partner teams as soon as the plan looks unworkable
Line 4: he insists the original scope be delivered, since changing it looks weak
Line 3: he offers a smaller version that would still move the organisation forward
optionExplain: Wrong: late news leaves partners no time to respond.
Fine: early notice is what the author recommends.
Wrong: the author accepts delivering something other than first envisioned if it is valuable.
Fine: a valuable alternative preserves credibility.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, if you deliver something different from what was first envisioned but still valuable, you can keep your credibility.
questions.explain: The author says that delivering a valuable alternative that moves the organisation forward maintains credibility.
questions.rule: Valuable alternatives keep credibility.

questions.q: A hospital IT lead must report a risky upgrade to leadership, and a rollback is not possible. What will leadership most value?
questions.explain: When risks are high and rollback is impossible, leaders need plain facts to choose well.
questions.rule: Clear facts let others decide.
questions.teaches: According to the author, when rollbacks are not possible or risks are high, stakeholders value someone who gives clear information that lets them make good decisions.
options: A reassuring summary that avoids alarming the leadership until the upgrade is already under way
A long technical report that shows how much work the team has already done
A promise that nothing will go wrong, to keep morale high before the upgrade
Clear information that lets them decide well, stated directly without softening the risks
optionExplain: It feels kind, but it removes the information they need to decide.
Effort shows commitment, yet it does not inform the decision.
A promise of no risk is not credible and cannot support a decision.
Right: the author says clear, direct information is what stakeholders value in such cases.

questions.q: A candidate has interviews at a start-up and at a bank. Should she describe her delivery the same way in both?
questions.explain: Organisations differ in what they value. The card next lists the five settings the author describes.
options: Yes, because delivery has one standard meaning that every employer uses
No, because each setting prizes a different mix of speed, reliability and compliance
Yes, because interviewers compare candidates and need one common story
No, because only the bank cares about delivery, while a start-up cares about ideas alone
optionExplain: A single standard feels fair, but the author says definitions vary by organisation.
Right: the same skill is valued differently by setting.
Comparison matters, but story emphasis can still fit the setting.
Both care about delivery; they weigh different aspects of it.
questions.rule: Learn what the organisation prizes before choosing which part of your delivery story to stress.

questions.q: Match each organisation type to what its delivery stresses.
questions.explain: Each setting puts its own pressure on delivery: speed, scale, predictability, compliance and client commitments.
questions.rule: Know the setting's emphasis.
pairs: Shipping fast and iterating on feedback
Delivery that scales reliably across millions of users and many teams
Predictable, stable delivery within established processes
Shipping within strict constraints while staying compliant
Meeting client deadlines and managing scope creep

questions.q: Sort each situation by what the setting mainly prizes in delivery.
questions.explain: The three settings under 'Speed and iteration first' favour shipping early and learning. The three under 'Predictability and compliance first' put approvals, compliance and fixed dates first.
questions.rule: Match your story to what the setting prizes.

items.t: A seed-stage app ships a bare-bones version in two weeks to test demand
A fast-growing team launches the core feature now and fixes edge cases later
A new company releases an early product to learn what users really want
A hospital software team must pass a privacy review before every release
An insurer's team moves a change through approval chains to a fixed date
A government project must show that each requirement is met before launch

questions.q: A firm succeeds by shipping quality work within fixed budgets and agreed timelines, and by managing scope creep. Which setting is this?
questions.explain: Fixed budgets, agreed timelines and scope creep are the agency pattern in the chapter.
questions.rule: Agency delivery is client-bound.
options: A high-growth startup choosing between many ideas
An agency or consultancy working for clients
A large tech company coordinating many internal teams
A government department managing public records
optionExplain: A startup stresses speed and iteration, not client budgets.
Right: client deadlines, fixed budgets and scope creep belong to this setting.
Large tech stresses scale and dependencies across teams.
Regulated work stresses compliance more than client scope.

questions.q: Alex prepares one story and plans to tell it unchanged to every employer, because delivery means the same everywhere. What does the card say he misses?
questions.explain: Alex treats delivery as one fixed thing. The author says what is valued shifts by organisation.
questions.rule: Same skill, different emphasis.
options: Companies do not ask about delivery, so any story will do
A story should be rewritten from scratch for every interview
Only large companies care about reliability, so only candidates applying to them need adapting
Organisations define and value delivery differently, so emphasis should fit the setting
optionExplain: The chapter is about interview questions on delivery, so they do ask.
The advice is to adjust emphasis, not to start over each time.
Every setting has its own emphasis; none is exempt.
Right: the author says the definition varies with priorities and constraints.

questions.q: A school fundraising committee has a fixed budget and an agreed event date, and parents keep adding requests. Which setting does it most resemble, and what helps?
questions.explain: Fixed budget, fixed date and rising requests are the agency pattern, where the answer is clear trade-off talk.
questions.rule: Under fixed limits, talk trade-offs and find value.
questions.teaches: In agencies and consultancies, success requires clear communication about trade-offs, and people who produce creative solutions that maximise value within budget and time are rewarded.
options: An agency: explain trade-offs plainly and find creative value within the budget
A startup: ship quickly, drop the budget and expect to iterate after the event
A regulated industry: delay all decisions until every rule has been checked
A traditional enterprise: refuse changes and follow the original plan exactly
optionExplain: Right: this matches the agency pattern the author describes.
A fixed budget and date do not allow startup-style open iteration.
No regulation is described, and delay would miss the date.
Refusing every change ignores the scope creep the committee faces.

questions.q: Which candidate story would a fast-moving startup most likely value?
questions.explain: Startups lean on speed and iteration. The card next gives the contrast with large companies.
options: Waiting several months to release one version that covered every possible edge case
Coordinating a release through four approval stages across six departments
Shipping a rough first version in days, then reshaping it from user feedback
Documenting a flawless process that no future change could disturb
optionExplain: A thorough release feels responsible but conflicts with startup speed.
Coordination is valuable, yet it is the large-company or enterprise emphasis.
Right: shipping fast and iterating is the startup emphasis.
Process polish suits other settings and slows a startup down.
questions.rule: At a startup, show you can ship a minimum viable product fast; at a large tech company, show you can ship reliably inside a system.

questions.q: Sort each trait by the setting where the author places it.
questions.explain: The three under 'Startup' describe the startup's speed and tolerance. The three under 'Large tech company' describe scale, dependencies and process.
questions.rule: Startup: speed. Large tech: scale and fit.

items.t: Shipping a minimum viable product quickly
Iterating on feedback as the default way of working
Accepting high risk because not shipping is worse than shipping imperfectly
Working through complex dependencies across teams
Making sure your work fits into larger systems and integrates smoothly
Keeping velocity while meeting quality bars and process requirements

questions.q: A candidate once rebuilt a payment screen used by millions, working with five dependent teams. Which interview is this story best for?
questions.explain: Coordination across teams at scale is the large-company strength. The story would need a different slant for a startup.
questions.rule: Pick the story the setting values.
options: A seed-stage startup, because it shows he can ship an early prototype
An agency, because it shows he can manage a single client's wishes
Any employer equally, since a large number of users is impressive everywhere
A large tech company, because it shows dependencies, integration and scale
optionExplain: A five-team, million-user rebuild is not a prototype story.
The story involves internal dependent teams, not client scope.
Scale impresses most where scale is the daily problem.
Right: it matches what large companies prize.

questions.q: A startup team insists on handling every edge case before the first release. What does the author's picture of startups suggest happens?
questions.explain: The author warns of getting bogged down in edge cases. Our reading connects this to delay in the startup setting.
questions.rule: Core value first, edge cases later.
options: The release gains trust, because startups reward thoroughness above speed
The team gets bogged down and the core value reaches users late
Nothing changes, because edge cases take no time compared to features
The investors step in and take over the release plan from the team
optionExplain: Startups reward speed and iteration, so thoroughness first is the opposite.
Right (Our reading): startups want the core value out without drowning in edge cases.
Edge cases can take large amounts of effort, which is the author's worry.
The chapter says nothing about investors acting this way.

questions.q: True or false: because large tech companies value reliable scale, a candidate there should avoid mentioning coordination across teams.
questions.explain: Coordination across teams and working through dependencies is what the author says large companies want to hear about.
questions.rule: Large tech: show coordination.

questions.q: A three-person team is testing a food-delivery pilot in one town. Which choice fits what the author says startups want?
questions.explain: Launching the core value and learning is the startup move, because not shipping is the greater risk.
questions.rule: Ship the core value; accept rough edges.
questions.teaches: Startups tolerate high risk because, in the author's words, not shipping is worse than shipping imperfectly, and they value people who find the core value proposition and deliver it.
options: Build a complete system for ten cities first, so that no rework is ever needed once it launches
Delay launch until each rough edge has been removed and tested twice
Identify the core value, launch only that, and accept a few rough edges to learn sooner
Hand the launch plan to a separate approvals group before starting any work
optionExplain: It aims at scale before the core value is proven.
Polishing first conflicts with the high risk tolerance startups show.
Right: it finds the core value proposition and accepts risk, as startups do.
That adds process steps typical of other settings.

questions.q: A bank's team needs approval from three review groups before any release. How should a strong deliverer treat this?
questions.explain: Strong deliverers in enterprises plan around the process. The card next gives the author's view.
options: As part of the terrain: learn the process and plan so approvals do not stall momentum
As an obstacle to avoid by shipping quietly before the review groups can catch up with it
As proof that the bank cannot deliver, so the project should be cancelled
As someone else's job, so the team waits for the reviewers to chase it
optionExplain: Right: the author says to work the system, not fight it.
It feels fast, but it breaks the rules the organisation depends on.
Approvals slow things; they do not make delivery impossible.
Waiting hands control of the pace to others and loses momentum.
questions.rule: Work with the system and tell real blockers from apparent ones, so you can move fast inside the rules.

questions.q: In a traditional enterprise, success comes from understanding how to work the ____ rather than fighting it.
questions.explain: The author advises working within established processes such as approval chains instead of resisting them.
questions.rule: Work the system.

questions.q: A health-app team learns that a law bars storing patient names in its error logs. Which response fits the author's advice?
questions.explain: Names are truly barred, but the debugging need can be met another way. The skill is finding the route inside the boundary.
questions.rule: Block the data, not the work.
options: Check whether replacing names with anonymous codes meets the law, keeping the error details
Stop all debugging until the legal team rewrites the rule for the team
Log the names anyway and delete them once each bug has been fixed
Drop error logging altogether, since it can never be made compliant
optionExplain: Right: it separates what truly blocks (names) from what can be adapted.
A pause treats the whole task as blocked when only one part is.
That breaks the law the moment the names are stored.
Removing logs loses the information needed to fix bugs and is not required.

questions.q: Mina says in an interview: regulation means we could not move fast. What does the author want her to show instead?
questions.explain: Mina presents regulation as the end of the story. The author treats it as a constraint to work through.
questions.rule: Constraint, not excuse.
options: How she persuaded regulators to relax the rules for her team
How she kept quality high by delivering at the pace the rules allowed
How she found ways to move quickly inside the regulatory boundaries
How she avoided regulated projects in favour of unregulated ones
optionExplain: The author does not describe changing the rules.
Following the rules matters, yet the point is finding speed within them.
Right: this is the major skill the author names for regulated work.
Avoidance does not show delivery in this setting.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a requirement that only appears to block a release may leave room for a faster route that still meets the rule.
questions.explain: The author contrasts requirements that truly block with those that only appear to, and values finding the route through the second kind.
questions.rule: Check whether the block is real.

questions.q: An app must show developers where errors happen, but privacy rules bar logging user identities. Which approach follows the author's own example?
questions.explain: Hashing keeps the pattern while removing the identity, so it meets the rule and unblocks the release.
questions.rule: Anonymise the data, keep the signal.
questions.teaches: The author's example: while barred from logging personally identifiable information for debugging, a team can likely unblock the release with a hashing strategy that anonymises the data but keeps the error patterns.
options: Collect identities in a private spreadsheet outside the product and promise to delete it later
Hash the identifiers so the data is anonymised while the error patterns remain usable
Ask users to describe their errors by email instead of using any logs
Release without any error tracking, since privacy rules take priority
optionExplain: That still stores identities, which the rule bars.
Right: this is the author's example of unblocking a release.
It avoids logging but loses the patterns needed to fix bugs quickly.
Dropping tracking removes the means to fix problems.

questions.q: A developer notices a slow report that annoys everyone and starts a fix on her own. What is missing before this counts as delivery?
questions.explain: She has shown initiative; delivery needs the fix to reach users. The card next separates the two.
options: Approval from a manager, because only assigned work can be delivered
More problems found of the same kind, to show she can notice patterns
A written proposal that explains each idea she considered along the way
The fix being shipped and working for the people who use the report
optionExplain: Approval is not the issue; self-started work can be delivered if it ships.
Noticing more problems shows initiative again and does not finish the fix.
A proposal records thinking and still leaves the report slow for users.
Right: delivery needs a working result in users' hands.
questions.rule: Take on unassigned work only if you can carry it through to something shipped.

questions.q: Initiative gets you started; delivery gets you ____.
questions.explain: The author's short version: initiative opens the work, delivery closes it with something shipped.
questions.rule: Start with initiative, close with delivery.

questions.q: Sort each action: is it initiative, or is it delivery?
questions.explain: Spotting, starting and volunteering are the front end of the work. Managing dependencies, deadlines and release belong to delivery.
questions.rule: Front end: initiative. Back end: delivery.

items.t: Notices a recurring failure that nobody owns
Starts a fix without anyone asking
Volunteers to look into a problem nobody has time for
Agrees a launch date with the team that depends on the fix
Sorts out a blocker with another team so the fix can be released
Rolls the fix out to live users and checks that it works

questions.q: A candidate's stories all describe problems she found and plans she began, but none says what shipped. What impression will an interviewer likely take?
questions.explain: Without a shipped result the stories show initiative only.
questions.rule: Say what shipped.
options: Strong delivery, because noticing problems is the hard part of shipping
Weak initiative, because none of the work was assigned to her
Strong initiative but weak evidence of delivery
Little at all, because interviewers ignore stories about unassigned work
optionExplain: Noticing is the front end, not the shipping.
Unassigned work is exactly what initiative looks like.
Right: the starts are clear and the finishes are missing.
They do not ignore them; they judge which competency is shown.

questions.q: A colleague is expert at spotting problems worth fixing but does not complete the projects she starts. How does the author treat her work?
questions.explain: Noticing is not enough on its own: even an expert at it has not delivered until working solutions ship.
questions.rule: Spotting is not shipping.
questions.teaches: The author says that even an expert at noticing problems worth fixing through initiative projects has not delivered if she cannot ship working solutions for them.
options: As not delivery, however well chosen the problems are, if she cannot ship working solutions
As delivery in progress, since choosing the right problems to fix is the harder skill of the two
As strong delivery, because noticing problems early prevents outages
As a sign she needs more problems, since delivery improves with volume
optionExplain: Right: spotting worthwhile problems does not count as delivery without a shipped fix.
The author says it is not delivery when you cannot ship the solutions.
Prevention is useful but is not shipping a working solution.
More starts without finishes only repeats the gap.

questions.q: An engineer designs an elegant caching strategy that would cut database load. What does delivery add to her work?
questions.explain: The design is the problem-solving part. The card next shows what delivery adds.
options: A better theory of caching, so that the design earns wide respect
A longer-term vision of how the company could treat all of its data
Permission from leaders to explore other uses of caching across several teams at once
Getting it implemented, tested, deployed and refined so the saving is real
optionExplain: More theory is problem-solving; it does not put the saving into production.
A broader vision is strategic thinking, a different competency.
Permission may help, yet it is not the work of taking the design live.
Right: delivery carries the idea into production and keeps improving it.
questions.rule: See delivery as the link between a good solution or vision and something running in production.

questions.q: Match each competency to its focus in the author's description.
questions.explain: Each competency covers a different stretch of the path from idea to result.
questions.rule: Approach, journey, direction.
pairs: Finding the right technical approach to a challenge
The whole journey from solution to production
Identifying long-term opportunities and driving organisational change

questions.q: A data lead has a vision for transforming how her company handles data. What should she do to show delivery rather than strategy?
questions.explain: Strategy sets direction; delivery shows up in the increments that were actually shipped.
questions.rule: Name what shipped toward the vision.
options: Describe how the vision would change the company over ten years
Describe the first incremental changes she shipped that moved the vision forward
Describe how many senior leaders agreed with the vision at the first planning meeting
Describe the best tools on the market for each part of the data stack
optionExplain: This restates the strategy and says nothing about shipping.
Right: shipped increments are how a vision is realised.
Agreement is support for the vision, not delivery of it.
A survey of tools is background, not shipped change.

questions.q: Put the stages the author lists after a solution is found in order, from first to last.
questions.explain: The author lists implementing, testing, deploying, monitoring and then refining on actual performance as what strong delivery ensures.
questions.rule: Delivery does not stop at deploy.
questions.teaches: The author's picture of delivery continues after deployment: the solution is monitored and refined based on actual performance.
items: Implemented
Tested
Deployed
Monitored
Refined based on actual performance

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a vision without delivery remains a vision.
questions.explain: The author says shipping the incremental changes is what turns a vision into something real.
questions.rule: No shipping, no change.

questions.q: A city planner has a clear aim to reduce traffic but ships only fixes for this month's jams. What risk does the author name for delivery without vision?
questions.explain: The author treats each competency as incomplete without the other.
questions.rule: Pair delivery with direction.
questions.teaches: The author warns that delivery without vision might solve today's problem but may miss tomorrow's opportunity.
options: It will slow the fixes down, because vision makes delivery faster
It may solve today's problem but miss tomorrow's opportunity
It will fail to reach residents, since quick fixes are never used
It will upset the planner's colleagues, who prefer longer plans
optionExplain: The author does not say vision speeds delivery; the gap is about direction.
Right: delivery with no direction can be short-sighted.
Quick fixes can be used; the risk is missing what comes next.
No such social risk is named in the chapter.

questions.q: An interviewer asks about a time you delivered despite major blockers. Which answer shape is strongest?
questions.explain: The question tests what you did when things went wrong. The card next separates constraints from obstacles.
options: Explain in detail why the blocker made the target impossible for anyone
Describe how hard you worked and how late you stayed during the weeks when you were blocked
Move quickly past the blocker and talk about the technology you used
Name the blocker, then explain how you changed the plan so something valuable still shipped
optionExplain: It feels honest, but it justifies the failure instead of showing delivery.
Effort matters, yet it is not the pivot and leaves out what shipped.
It skips the very part the question tests.
Right: it centres on the pivot and the outcome.
questions.rule: Tell stories about how you adapted to constraints and obstacles, not about why the project could not succeed.

questions.q: Match each term to the author's description.
questions.explain: Constraints are known upfront; obstacles arrive during the work; the strong story is about the pivot.
questions.rule: Known limit, surprise problem, pivot.
pairs: A limitation known from the start
An unexpected problem that emerges during execution
Focuses on the pivot that let something of value still ship

questions.q: Sort each item: is it a constraint, or an obstacle?
questions.explain: Constraints are limits that were known when the work began. Obstacles are problems that turned up during the work.
questions.rule: Known at the start: constraint. Appears later: obstacle.

items.t: A budget capped before the project began
A team of two engineers for the whole project
A launch date fixed at the kickoff meeting
A partner team's interface changes without warning in week five
The test data turns out to be corrupt just before release
A hosting provider fails the night before launch

questions.q: A candidate answers an obstacle question with: the requirements changed too quickly, so the target could not be met. What is wrong with this answer?
questions.explain: The author's weaker answers justify a stall. The better answer turns on what the candidate did next.
questions.rule: Pivot, not excuse.
options: It explains why the project stalled instead of how the plan was adjusted to ship value
It names a requirement change, which interviewers do not accept as a real obstacle in an answer
It is too brief, because every obstacle answer needs at least five minutes
It is dishonest, since a candidate should never admit that a target was missed
optionExplain: Right: the author says weak answers justify the failure and strong ones show the pivot.
Changing requirements are a typical obstacle; naming one is fine.
Length is not the author's complaint; the focus is.
The issue is the justification, not admitting a miss.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a candidate who treats obstacles as reasons to stop will come across as showing strong delivery.
questions.explain: The questions test whether you treat obstacles as problems to be solved or as valid reasons to stop; the second reading weakens the signal.
questions.rule: Problems to solve, not reasons to stop.

questions.q: Which question would a volunteer who ran a food drive with two helpers and no budget be best placed to answer?
questions.explain: Two helpers and no budget are limited people and money, so the limited-resources question fits.
questions.rule: Constraints: resources or time.
questions.teaches: The author says tight constraints typically means limited resources such as budget, people or technical skills, while challenging deadlines are about time not being on your side.
options: Describe an example of handling unexpected challenges that threatened a delivery deadline
Tell me about a time you communicated a delay to leadership
Give me an example of delivering something when the available resources were limited
Have you juggled several projects with conflicting deadlines
optionExplain: That question is about obstacles that appear mid-project, not limits known at the start.
A different theme, communicating risk, which the drive may not involve.
Right: tight constraints typically mean limited budget, people or technical skills.
A different theme, competing priorities, which the drive does not describe.

questions.q: Three teams each ask you to finish their work first. What is the strongest first step?
questions.explain: Good prioritising begins with judgment about what truly needs to ship first. The card next gives the author's view.
options: Start with the team whose manager is the most senior and works in the next room
Split your time evenly so that no team feels it has been put second
Work on the easiest request first so that at least one team is happy sooner
Find out what truly needs to ship first, then explain the order to everyone
optionExplain: Seniority is easy to apply, yet it does not tell you what matters most.
Even splits feel fair but delay every team and avoid a decision.
Ease is a poor ranking when other work matters more.
Right: judge what matters most, then communicate the choice.
questions.rule: When everything seems important, decide what truly ships first and tell people why.

questions.q: Interviewers want to see that you can assess what truly needs to ship ____ when everything seems important.
questions.explain: The questions test your judgment about what must ship first, and how you communicate the choice.
questions.rule: Judge first, then tell.

questions.q: A freelance designer has three clients, each with a deadline this Friday. One client's launch is public, one is internal, one is a draft. How should she act?
questions.explain: A ranking based on what matters, communicated to those affected, is what the interviewers want to hear.
questions.rule: Rank, then say so.
options: Work on all three together each day and reassure every client that their piece is on track
Rank them by what depends on each, do the public launch first, and tell the others when theirs follows
Finish the draft first because it is the quickest, then see how much time is left for the others
Ask the three clients to agree among themselves who goes first and then report back to her
optionExplain: It claims progress on everything and risks all three slipping.
Right: a clear ranking with communication shows the competency.
Speed of finishing is not the same as importance.
It hands the decision over instead of making and explaining it.

questions.q: Which answer to everything felt urgent shows prioritisation, rather than hard work alone?
questions.explain: Strong examples show a clear prioritisation and the right things delivered in the right order.
questions.rule: Order is the evidence.
options: I worked weekends for a month until every request on the whole list had finally been completed for everyone
I asked my manager which team shouted loudest and did their work first
I ranked the requests by impact, told each team the order and delivered in that sequence
I started everything at once so that no team was left waiting for a start
optionExplain: It shows effort; it does not show any ranking.
Reacting to volume is not a judgment about what matters.
Right: it shows ranking, communication and order.
Starting all of it is the opposite of choosing an order.

questions.q: True or false: If a candidate chooses the right priority but does not tell the other teams why, the author expects interviewers to be fully satisfied.
questions.explain: The interviewers check both the decision and how effectively you communicate the choice.
questions.rule: Decision plus communication.

questions.q: A platform lead faces twelve teams who each call their needs urgent. Which step does the author's staff-level story report as helpful?
questions.explain: Asking for must-haves makes teams separate what they need from what they want.
questions.rule: Ask for must-haves.
questions.teaches: In the author's staff-level story, asking each team to name its absolute must-haves worked because the must-haves shrank once the teams were on the hook for the first implementation.
options: Asking each team to name its must-haves, which shrank once it owned version one
Promising every team its own date, then adding people to meet all twelve
Refusing every request from the twelve teams until the platform was finished
Asking leadership to choose one team and then ignoring the other eleven
optionExplain: Right: this is the technique in the staff-level example.
The story's lead could not commit to everyone's timelines.
Teams escalated to leadership when the lead could not commit; refusal was not the technique.
The lead worked with each team rather than discarding eleven.

questions.q: You are asked to describe a time you decided what was good enough to ship. What is the best centre of your answer?
questions.explain: The question looks for judgment about the essential and the deferrable. The card next gives the author's view.
options: Which quality you protected, which you deferred and why that split suited users
How you refused to release anything until every single known defect had been fixed
How quickly you released by skipping the checks that slowed the team down
How the whole team felt about the decision after the product had gone live
optionExplain: Right: it shows a considered choice about minimum viable quality.
It sounds principled, but it shows inflexibility rather than judgment.
Speed alone looks like corner-cutting and gives no sign of judgment.
Feelings are not the evidence the question asks for.
questions.rule: Show a considered decision about minimum viable quality: protect what hits users, defer what can wait.

questions.q: Tell stories that highlight your considered decisions about minimum viable ____.
questions.explain: The phrase is minimum viable quality: the lowest level that still serves users well enough to ship.
questions.rule: Choose the minimum viable quality on purpose.

questions.q: A team ships a new ordering app. Sort each item: protect it now, or defer it?
questions.explain: Our reading: money, privacy and a blocked order directly harm users. Visual polish, internal pages and rare formats can wait.
questions.rule: Protect what harms users if broken.
groups: Protect now: it directly affects users

items.t: Charging the customer the right amount
Keeping saved delivery addresses private
An error that stops users from submitting an order
Rounded corners on the buttons
The layout of an internal reporting page
A rarely used export format

questions.q: Two candidates cut scope to ship on time. Which one shows minimum viable quality rather than reckless corner-cutting?
questions.explain: Considered cuts leave a protected core and a clear list of deferrals. Even cuts and blanket delays do not.
questions.rule: Cut with reasons.
options: Raj: skipped testing across the whole product because the date was close and the team was tired
Sam: kept every feature but shipped them all in a rough state to meet the date
Dana: dropped three nice-to-have screens, kept payments and data checks, listed what she cut
Lee: delayed the release by a month so no screen would look unfinished
optionExplain: Cutting everything evenly is not a considered choice.
A rough release across the board gives no protected core.
Right: she chose what to cut with reasons.
Delaying for polish ignores the deadline.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate who cuts corners but cannot say why those corners were safe will, in the author's view, risk appearing reckless.
questions.explain: The author names reckless corner-cutting as a weakness, and a considered reason is what separates a trade-off from carelessness.
questions.rule: No reason, no judgment.

questions.q: A candidate shipped a data export early by dropping a polished interface. What did the author's entry-level story do about its shortcuts?
questions.explain: Recording shortcuts and booking the clean-up shows the cuts were a decision, not a habit.
questions.rule: Write down what you deferred.
questions.teaches: In the author's entry-level story, the candidate documented all the shortcuts taken and created tickets for future cleanup, so the trade-off stayed visible.
options: Kept the shortcuts private so the users would not be worried
Documented every shortcut taken and made tickets for future clean-up
Promised the users a rewrite within a week to make up for them
Removed the shortcuts before the audit so that the code looked polished
optionExplain: Hiding shortcuts is the opposite of what the story reports.
Right: that is how the story kept the cuts honest.
No promise of this kind is reported.
The story shipped the basic version and improved it afterwards.

questions.q: You must tell a vice president that a launch will slip three weeks. Which approach does the author favour?
questions.explain: Direct, early news with options lets leaders act. The card next gives the author's reasoning.
options: Wait for the next planning meeting and mention it among the other routine updates
Describe the delay as a small timing issue to avoid worry at the top
Send a long report and let the vice president work out what it means
Say it directly now, state the impact and give options for how to proceed
optionExplain: Burying it in a routine meeting delays the decision and softens the news.
Softening the risk is the sugar-coating the author warns against.
A long report hides the key point and leaves the reader to find it.
Right: direct, early and with options.
questions.rule: Tell stakeholders about risks and delays early and plainly, without sugar-coating.

questions.q: Strong answers show you communicating difficult news directly without ____ the risks.
questions.explain: The author asks for directness without sugar-coating, because softened news does not help anyone decide.
questions.rule: Direct, not softened.

questions.q: A data engineer finds that a pipeline migration will miss its date because a vendor changed its interface. What should she tell the product head?
questions.explain: The message works when it contains the delay, the cause, the impact and the options.
questions.rule: Impact plus options.
options: That things are mostly fine and the team is still hopeful about hitting the original date
That the vendor caused the problem and that the delay is therefore not her fault
The date will slip about a week, the reason, what it affects and two ways to recover
Nothing until she has fixed the interface, so she can report only good news
optionExplain: Hope without facts sugar-coats the risk.
Blame explains nothing about impact or options.
Right: it is direct, specific and offers options.
Silence takes away the time others need to respond.

questions.q: A lead reports a risk to stakeholders. Which parts of her report go against the author's advice? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Early, plain reporting with options is the advice. Understating and omitting both remove what leaders need.
questions.rule: Do not understate or omit.
options: She leaves out the worst case so as not to cause alarm
She says the risks are minor although the team is worried
She states plainly what the options are and what each costs
She raises the risk as soon as she sees it
optionExplain: Wrong: stakeholders need information to decide well.
Wrong: understating the risk is sugar-coating.
Fine: clear options help stakeholders decide.
Fine: early notice is the advice.

questions.q: A new graduate hears that questions about managing stakeholder expectations are common. Why might she be asked fewer of them than a senior engineer?
questions.explain: These questions become more important at mid-level and above, because wider stakeholder work grows with seniority.
questions.rule: Scope of communication grows with level.
questions.teaches: According to the author, questions on managing delivery expectations become more important at mid-level and above, since entry-level engineers usually work within their teams.
options: They mostly work inside their teams, not managing wider stakeholder relationships
Entry-level engineers rarely meet delivery problems, so there is nothing to report
Interviewers assume graduates will sugar-coat risks and so do not ask them
Stakeholders prefer hearing bad news only from managers, never from engineers
optionExplain: Right: the author ties these questions to mid-level and above.
Delivery problems happen at every level; the point concerns responsibilities.
No such assumption is stated.
The author does not give a rule against engineers reporting news.

questions.q: A manager of a community centre plans a renovation and sees the budget may run out. According to the author's advice for strong answers, when should she set expectations?
questions.explain: Setting realistic expectations early is what keeps later bad news from being a surprise.
questions.rule: Set expectations at the start.
questions.teaches: The author says strong answers show you setting realistic expectations with stakeholders early in a project, not only reporting trouble once it arrives.
options: At the point when the budget is gone and nothing can change
Only if a trustee asks about the budget at a meeting
After the renovation, in a final report on what happened
Early in the project, before any problems appear
optionExplain: Too late to give anyone choices.
Waiting to be asked is not proactive.
A report afterwards cannot protect decisions made during the work.
Right: strong answers show realistic expectations set early.

questions.q: Which story contains the strongest delivery signal?
questions.explain: The strongest signal shows how you got past the blocker. The card next sets out the signal.
options: The project went to plan from kickoff to launch with no surprises at all
A key dependency broke, so I built a workaround and shipped by the date
A partner team blocked us, so the project was delayed until they were ready
I worked very long hours for weeks until the product was eventually ready
optionExplain: A smooth run shows little about trouble.
Right: it names an obstacle and a workaround that shipped.
Waiting for the blocker is the opposite of working around it.
Effort is not a workaround and says nothing about adapting the plan.
questions.rule: Make the story show a blocker named, a workaround found and something valuable shipped on time.

questions.q: Blockers may slow you down, but they won't ____ you.
questions.explain: The author states the signal as blockers slowing you without stopping you.
questions.rule: Slow, not stop.

questions.q: Sort each sentence from a candidate's story: strong or weak evidence of shipping despite obstacles?
questions.explain: Workarounds, scope negotiation and early recognition show the signal. Waiting, blaming a dependency and having no obstacles do not.
questions.rule: Name the obstacle, show the way round.

items.t: The vendor interface broke, so I built a small adapter and shipped on schedule
Requirements changed, so I negotiated a smaller scope and shipped that first
By week two I saw the plan could not work and switched routes
The other team was late, so our project missed its date
I waited for requirements to settle before starting again
Everything went exactly as planned until launch

questions.q: A candidate describes an obstacle and then says the team shipped nothing until it was cleared. What will the interviewer likely conclude?
questions.explain: A story that ends with waiting does not show the working-around the signal needs.
questions.rule: Show the way round.
options: That she was careful, which is the main thing delivery asks for
That blockers stopped her, so the critical signal is weak
That she shows strong delivery, because obstacles are easy to describe
That she should have put more of the blame on the blocker in her account
optionExplain: Care is useful, but it is not the signal.
Right: the signal needs a way round the blocker.
Describing is not working around.
Blame is a red flag in this chapter.

questions.q: Kai says: when the plan stopped working, I kept to it to show commitment. What does the card say about this?
questions.explain: The signal includes recognising an unworkable plan quickly and switching.
questions.rule: Recognise and switch.
options: It is the best response, because sticking to plans proves reliability
It is acceptable only if a manager has approved the original plan
It is wrong because plans should never be written in the first place
It misses that strong deliverers quickly see a plan is no longer workable and change course
optionExplain: Sticking to an unworkable plan is not shown as strength.
Approval is not the point; adapting is.
The chapter does not argue against planning.
Right: quick recognition and a change of route are the signal.

questions.q: A theatre director learns two weeks before opening that the lead actor is ill, and the cast and crew depend on her plan. According to the author, what should she do before switching approach?
questions.explain: Telling those affected before the switch keeps people aligned behind the new plan.
questions.rule: Inform, then switch.
questions.teaches: According to the author, strong deliverers loop in everyone affected before switching to a new approach.
options: Loop in everyone affected, then move to the new approach
Switch quietly and tell the cast on the opening night
Cancel the opening and start again from the beginning in a month
Ask the lead actor to perform anyway and hope no one notices
optionExplain: Right: the author says to inform those affected before switching.
Surprising people undoes the trust the work depends on.
Cancelling does not show a way round the problem.
It ignores the problem rather than working round it.

questions.q: A candidate tells of choosing which features to drop so that the product could ship useful value on time. Which kind of evidence is that?
questions.explain: Choosing between competing goods is the trade-off signal. The card next names all three tiers.
options: Maintaining momentum: catching issues before they become blockers
Initiative: starting work that nobody had assigned to her
Smart trade-offs: deciding what is essential and what can wait
Blame avoidance: keeping the story free of anyone else's mistakes
optionExplain: Related, but this is about early detection of problems.
Dropping features is not self-started work.
Right: this is the author's strong signal.
Not a signal in this chapter; the candidate is describing a decision.
questions.rule: Add evidence of smart trade-offs and steady momentum to your stories of shipping through trouble.

questions.q: Match each signal to its tier in the author's list.
questions.explain: The author ranks the three as critical, strong and supporting.
questions.rule: Critical, strong, supporting.

questions.q: Sort each line from a story: smart trade-off, or maintaining momentum?
questions.explain: The three under 'Smart trade-off' decide what to keep and what to cut. The three under 'Maintaining momentum' keep progress steady and catch issues early.
questions.rule: Trade-offs choose; momentum sustains.

items.t: I dropped the search filters and kept the checkout, which users needed most
I delayed the colour themes so the date could hold
I cut the second report format and kept the one finance used
In week two I spotted a failing test setup before it blocked anyone
I split the work so that something shipped every week
I sent partners a short update each Friday

questions.q: Which of these is the critical signal, rather than a strong or supporting one?
questions.explain: The critical signal is about continuing to ship through trouble; the other two are about choices and steady habits.
questions.rule: Critical is shipping through trouble.
options: The team cut nice-to-have features so a useful version could go out
The team caught small problems early so there were no last-minute scrambles
The team reported weekly to partners so no one was surprised
The team kept shipping after a dependency broke and requirements changed
optionExplain: That is the strong signal of smart trade-offs.
That is the supporting signal of momentum.
That also belongs to the supporting signal.
Right: shipping despite obstacles and changes is the critical signal.

questions.q: True or false: In the author's list, a candidate who shows only maintaining momentum, with no obstacle or trade-off in the story, has given the strongest evidence of delivery.
questions.explain: Maintaining momentum is the supporting signal; the critical signal is shipping despite obstacles.
questions.rule: Supporting evidence is not the top tier.

questions.q: Ravi says his story shows trade-offs because he cut the testing to meet the date. What does the author's description say?
questions.explain: A smart trade-off is judged by what it protects as well as what it cuts.
questions.rule: Protect the critical, drop the nice-to-have.
options: It is a good trade-off, because any cut that meets the date counts
Cutting alone is not enough; it must protect critical functionality
It is not a trade-off, because trade-offs only involve adding features
It is weak because trade-offs should be decided by the manager alone
optionExplain: The cut needs to protect critical functionality.
Right: the trade-off must keep what is essential.
Trade-offs include dropping the less important.
The author does not give this limit.

questions.q: A school-play organiser wants to show momentum. According to the author, which habit shows it?
questions.explain: Momentum means steady progress and no surprises for the people who depend on you.
questions.rule: Steady progress, no surprises.
questions.teaches: The author says momentum comes from structuring work to enable steady progress, so last-minute scrambles are avoided, and from keeping stakeholders in the loop so they have no surprises.
options: Leaving all the work until the last two weeks so that the effort is concentrated
Taking on extra tasks outside the play to show everyone how busy she is
Steady progress and keeping partners informed, so there are no last-minute surprises
Fixing each problem only after the cast and crew have noticed it exists
optionExplain: Last-minute work is the scramble momentum avoids.
Busyness is not momentum.
Right: this is how the author describes momentum.
Momentum means catching issues before they become blockers.

questions.q: A candidate's story about a missed deadline spends most of its time on how another team failed to deliver its part. What does an interviewer likely conclude?
questions.explain: Blame suggests the candidate would do the same at the new company. The card next explains the red flag.
options: That she may not take ownership when her own project is in trouble
That she has high standards for the colleagues she works with
That the other team is the real problem and she has been unlucky with them
That she is being open about the challenges the project faced
optionExplain: Right: blame signals not owning outcomes.
It can feel like standards, but the author reads it as blame.
Interviewers judge the candidate's behaviour, not the other team.
Openness is fine; the issue is where the weight of the story falls.
questions.rule: Tell the story through what you controlled, and treat obstacles as terrain, not as the reason for failure.

questions.q: Match each flag colour to the author's description.
questions.explain: The author uses red for serious damage and yellow for patterns that weaken examples; blaming others is a red flag.
questions.rule: Red hurts the candidacy; yellow weakens the example.
pairs: A serious issue that will significantly damage your candidacy
A concerning pattern that weakens your examples
Signals that you do not own outcomes

questions.q: Sort each sentence from a delivery story: ownership, or blame?
questions.explain: Ownership sentences state what the candidate did about the situation. Blame sentences place the cause outside her control.
questions.rule: Say what you did.

items.t: The partner team was late, so I rebuilt my part to run without them
I set up a daily check with the dependency owner to spot slips early
I changed the plan when the approval took longer than expected
The project failed because the product manager kept changing his mind
None of this was my fault, as the other team never answered our messages
Leadership gave us too little time, so nothing could have been done

questions.q: Which rewrite of this sentence follows the author's advice: The vendor was late, so we missed the date?
questions.explain: Keep the fact, change the focus: the rewrite shows what the candidate did about the delay.
questions.rule: Fact, then response.
options: The vendor was late, so I rescoped the release and shipped the core part on the date
The vendor was late and it is fair to say that it was entirely their failure, not ours
We missed the date but I had warned everyone that the vendor was a risk
The vendor was late, which proves that dependencies cannot be managed
optionExplain: Right: the blocker is named and the response is the centre.
It keeps the blame and adds nothing about the candidate's response.
Having warned people is fine, but the sentence is still a defence.
It generalises the excuse instead of showing a response.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, interviewers who hear a candidate blame others for delivery problems imagine the candidate doing the same on their project.
questions.explain: That is the author's stated reason the flag is serious: the interviewer projects the behaviour onto their own project.
questions.rule: They picture it on their project.

questions.q: A candidate says: I mentioned the blocker, and then showed how I rebuilt the plan. A coach says this is blaming. What is wrong with the coach's view?
questions.explain: The distinction is about emphasis: naming a cause supports the story, while defending yourself replaces it.
questions.rule: Name it briefly, then act.
options: Blockers should never be mentioned in a delivery story of any kind
Interviewers like blame provided the other team really was at fault and the candidate can show it
Naming a cause is not blame when the story's weight is on the candidate's response
The coach is right, because any mention of another team is blame
optionExplain: The author wants obstacles described, then worked around.
The author says blame signals not owning outcomes whoever was at fault.
Right (Our reading): the flag arises when the story is built to clear the candidate's name.
A factual mention is part of describing the obstacle.

questions.q: A candidate explains a failed event by listing late suppliers, a changing brief and a short timeline. What does the author say about such problems?
questions.explain: Because every project has them, the story that stands out shows how the candidate handled them.
questions.rule: Trouble is normal; your response is the story.
questions.teaches: The author says every project has blockers, difficult stakeholders and teams that do not deliver on time, because that is the normal operating environment.
options: They are rare in practice, which is why listing them proves the project was unusually hard for her
They are the normal operating environment of projects, so listing them does not set her apart
They are signs the employer chose the wrong projects for her
They are useful in an interview only if a manager confirms them
optionExplain: The author says they are normal, not rare.
Right: every project has blockers, difficult stakeholders and late teams.
No such claim appears in the chapter.
Confirmation is not mentioned.

questions.q: Every story a candidate tells includes weeks of 80-hour work to hit the date. What might an interviewer wonder?
questions.explain: Heroics as a pattern raise doubts about planning. The card next explains the yellow flag.
options: Whether she is the only person on her team who really cares about the product's success
Whether the company she left treated all of its staff unfairly
Whether she will refuse to work late in the future on any project
Whether she can estimate accurately or manage scope instead of relying on heroics
optionExplain: The author's concern is about estimation and scope.
The question is about her pattern, not her employer.
The worry is about a pattern of crunch, not a refusal.
Right: this is the author's concern.
questions.rule: Choose stories of realistic trouble handled by structure, and present any crunch as an exception.

questions.q: Match each yellow flag to what it signals.
questions.explain: Heroics as default and perfect conditions are the two yellow flags; a crisis crunch is acceptable if presented as an exception.
questions.rule: Crunch is an exception, not a style.
pairs: You may not estimate accurately or manage scope
Your story shows little about delivery under real constraints
Occasional crunch in a genuine crisis
Part of software delivery when framed as an exception

questions.q: Sort each line from a story: fine, or a yellow flag?
questions.explain: A crunch with a cause and a fix, and an adaptation to real trouble, are acceptable. Habitual heroics and trouble-free stories are the flags.
questions.rule: Exception with cause.

items.t: The outage forced a weekend of work, and afterwards I added alerts so it could not repeat
Late hours were rare, tied to a vendor failure, and I reported the cause
The project was hard, so I adjusted the scope when the timeline slipped
I worked 80 hours a week on every project to get it done
The project went smoothly from start to finish with no problems
My team always relies on me to rescue the final week

questions.q: A candidate is asked for a tough delivery and chooses a project that ran exactly to plan because it shows she can plan. What is the problem?
questions.explain: The author asks for stories with challenges that required adaptation.
questions.rule: Choose a story with challenge.
options: Planning is never part of delivery, so a story about planning is off topic for this question
Interviewers dislike projects that finished on time
A smooth project shows little, because it does not test how she adapts to trouble
It shows the candidate avoided hard work and is therefore lazy
optionExplain: Planning matters; the issue is the missing challenge.
On-time delivery is welcome; a trouble-free path is weak evidence.
Right: perfect conditions are hardly the norm and show little.
That is a stronger claim than the author makes.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a candidate who frames a crunch as an exception with a clear external cause weakens her delivery story.
questions.explain: The author advises exactly that framing, because it shows the crunch was not her default way of working.
questions.rule: Frame crunch as the exception.

questions.q: A candidate has one story with a crunch period. What does the author say strong stories show in place of constant heroics?
questions.explain: Structure that prevents emergencies is the alternative to heroics.
questions.rule: Structure over heroics.
questions.teaches: The author says strong delivery stories show how you structured work to ship reliably: decomposing ambiguity early, identifying risks before they became emergencies and adjusting scope when timelines shifted.
options: Early risk-spotting, scope adjustment and breaking down ambiguity
Staying later than everyone else, so the team notices the effort
Taking on more projects than the team can finish, to show ambition
Avoiding any mention of difficulty, so the story stays positive
optionExplain: Right: these show structure rather than heroics.
That is the heroics pattern.
Overloading is not named as a strength.
The author wants realistic trouble, handled.

questions.q: A candidate describes weeks of code reviews and design meetings and stops there. What is missing from the story?
questions.explain: The story shows activity but no landing. The card next explains the yellow flag.
options: More detail about each review, so that her workload is clear
A list of the tools the team used while the work was under way
A description of how she felt about the team during the work
What actually shipped to users and what difference it made
optionExplain: More effort detail adds to the pile of activity.
Tools are background, not outcome.
Feelings are not the result the interviewer needs.
Right: effort needs a confirmed outcome.
questions.rule: End each delivery story by saying what shipped, so the interviewer hears a result, not only activity.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, delivery means done and deployed, and development alone is not enough.
questions.explain: The author contrasts finished and deployed work with development alone.
questions.rule: Done and deployed.

questions.q: Which ending best fixes a story about a rebuilt login page?
questions.explain: The best ending names the release, the users and the value.
questions.rule: Release, users, value.
options: I wrote most of the new login page and the whole team liked my code
The new page went live in March; customers used it daily and sign-in failures dropped
It took six sprints and every task on the board was closed
I reviewed all the pull requests from the other developers on this project for several months running
optionExplain: It describes the work and the opinion, not the outcome.
Right: it says what shipped, who used it and what value it gave.
Closed tasks are activity, not a shipped result.
Reviewing is effort without a confirmed outcome.

questions.q: Sort each line: effort, or outcome?
questions.explain: Effort lines say what the candidate did. Outcome lines say what went live, who used it and what changed.
questions.rule: Effort is not outcome.

items.t: I spent eight weeks building the tool
I reviewed forty pull requests during the project
I attended every planning meeting for the release
The tool went to production in May
Two hundred staff now use it each week
Report errors fell by a third after release

questions.q: Two candidates tell the same project. One lists tasks. The other adds that it went to production and what users gained. Whose delivery signal is stronger?
questions.explain: The same work counts for more when its result is stated.
questions.rule: Result strengthens the signal.
options: The first, because a long task list shows more effort
The second, because it confirms the work shipped and had value
They are equal, because the same work was done by both
Neither, because the interviewer will check the facts later anyway
optionExplain: Effort alone is not what the signal measures.
Right: the confirmed outcome strengthens the signal.
The work is the same but the evidence is not.
The interviewer relies on what is said in the story.

questions.q: A nonprofit coordinator says she organised a training programme. What should she add so that the story shows delivery?
questions.explain: Stating the programme that ran, its audience and benefits gives the interviewer an outcome to credit.
questions.rule: Production, users, value.
questions.teaches: The author says to be explicit about what went to production, who used it and what value it delivered.
options: How many hours she spent organising it on her own time
Which colleagues deserve the thanks for helping with her plan
A description of the room, its location and the catering provided
What was run, who attended and what they gained
optionExplain: Hours are effort; they do not show the outcome.
Credit is kind but not the result.
Setting details are noise to the outcome.
Right: what went live, who used it and the value delivered.

questions.q: A candidate says she refused to ship until every part of the code, tests and documentation was perfect. How might an interviewer read this?
questions.explain: Refusing all compromise reads as inflexibility. The card next gives the author's view.
options: As inflexibility: she could not decide which quality mattered for this delivery
As a strength, since the best engineers never accept imperfect work
As honesty, because she admitted that she delayed the release
As a lack of skill, because she could not write correct code the first time round
optionExplain: Right: the author reads it as inflexibility, not high standards.
The author says the opposite for delivery contexts.
Candour is fine, but the pattern is the problem.
The issue is prioritising, not skill.
questions.rule: Show which quality you held firm on, which you let go, and why, so your standards read as judgment.

questions.q: Sort each item as the author does: non-negotiable, or can get in the way of delivery?
questions.explain: The author puts reliability, integrity and security beyond compromise and warns that perfect code, over-testing and flawless documentation can block shipping.
questions.rule: Three firm, three flexible.

items.t: Production reliability
Data integrity
Security
Perfect code
Over-testing
Flawless documentation

questions.q: Which sentence best presents a candidate's standards as judgment in a delivery story?
questions.explain: Judgment shows in the split between what was protected and what was relaxed.
questions.rule: Protect some, relax some.
options: I would not release until every page of the documentation was flawless
I always refuse to cut corners of any kind, whatever the pressure
I held firm on data checks and security, and shipped with plainer documentation to meet the date
I let the team decide quality, and I did not form a view on what mattered
optionExplain: It refuses compromise on a non-critical item.
It claims a blanket rule, which reads as inflexible.
Right: it names what was protected and what was let go.
It shows no judgment at all.

questions.q: Tom says his refusal to ship a release with minor documentation gaps shows high standards. What does the card say?
questions.explain: Documentation perfection is not among the non-negotiables, so refusing to ship over it looks inflexible.
questions.rule: Do not hold the release for polish.
options: He is right, because documentation is as critical to a release as security
He is wrong only because the interviewer was asking about speed
He is right so long as he explains his reasons calmly to the interviewer
Perfect documentation can block delivery, so it shows inflexibility
optionExplain: The author does not rank documentation with security.
The reason is given in the author's list, not the question.
Tone does not change what the example shows.
Right: documentation perfection is a delivery blocker in the author's list.

questions.q: True or false: the author treats protecting data integrity while relaxing code polish to meet a date as pragmatism, not perfectionism.
questions.explain: The author lists data integrity as non-negotiable and perfect code as something that can wait. Keeping the essentials and flexing the rest is the pragmatic pattern.
questions.rule: Firm on essentials, flexible on the rest.

questions.q: A candidate calls herself a perfectionist and says that is her high standard. What does the author say about this framing in delivery contexts?
questions.explain: In delivery contexts the label perfectionism points to weak prioritising rather than strong standards.
questions.rule: Prioritise; do not hide behind standards.
questions.teaches: The chapter's takeaways warn against disguising perfectionism as high standards, because in delivery contexts it signals an inability to prioritise effectively.
options: It is a safe answer, because every interviewer values perfectionism
It can signal an inability to prioritise, so do not disguise perfectionism as high standards
It is acceptable only when the candidate is senior enough to afford delay
It is a strength, provided the candidate adds a note about teamwork
optionExplain: The author says it is a trap in delivery contexts.
Right: the closing takeaway warns against this disguise.
No seniority condition is given.
The caveat does not address the prioritising problem.

questions.q: You have two minutes to tell a delivery story. Which plan would an interviewer find easiest to follow?
questions.explain: A clear frame helps the listener hold the story. The card next gives the author's version.
options: A full history of the project from its first meeting through to launch day
A list of every task you completed, in the order in which you did them
A one-sentence summary, three main points, then the result
A long description of the team and company before any mention of your work
optionExplain: A full history buries the key contributions.
A task list is activity, not a story.
Right: a short frame lets the listener capture each part.
Background first delays the point of the story.
questions.rule: Open with a headline, make three key points, close with a landing, and stop at about two minutes.

questions.q: Put the parts of the author's story shape in the order they are told.
questions.explain: The author's shape runs from the headline through three key points to a landing.
questions.rule: Headline, three points, landing.
items: Headline
Key Point 1
Key Point 2
Key Point 3
Landing

questions.q: Which is the best headline for a story about a data-migration project?
questions.explain: A headline names the delivery and its difficulty in one sentence.
questions.rule: Headline: what, when, what was hard.
options: Last spring I moved our billing data to a new system in six weeks, though the vendor's rules changed twice
I want to tell you about a big project that I was involved with some time ago
Our team is very proud of the billing project and of how well we all worked together
To explain the migration I first need to describe the history of our billing platform
optionExplain: Right: it names what was delivered, when and what made it hard.
It promises a story but says nothing about what was delivered.
It praises the team and has no content for the interviewer to hold.
It delays the story with background.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, after the first two minutes the interviewer's follow-up questions should lead the conversation.
questions.explain: The author says to let the conversation flow naturally after the focused core, led by the interviewer's follow-ups.
questions.rule: Core first, then follow-ups.

questions.q: Mia tells her delivery story for ten minutes without stopping, so the interviewer will have every detail. What does the author's advice say?
questions.explain: Mia loses the benefit of the focused core.
questions.rule: Two minutes, then follow-ups.
options: She should tell the focused core in about two minutes and let follow-up questions lead
She is right, since a complete account removes the need for questions
She should shorten it to thirty seconds so there is no risk of boring or confusing the interviewer
She should let the interviewer tell her which parts to leave out in advance
optionExplain: Right: the core is brief and the follow-ups lead.
The author recommends the opposite.
A very short story would lack the three key points.
The structure is chosen by the candidate in advance.

questions.q: A teacher moving into a project role wants to tell a story about a school timetable rebuild. Which plan follows the shape and keeps the interviewer in control afterwards?
questions.explain: The shape works in any field, and the pause lets the interviewer decide what to probe.
questions.rule: Frame, then hand over.
questions.teaches: After the two-minute core, the author wants the conversation to flow naturally, led by the interviewer's follow-up questions.
options: Tell the story in the order it happened and ask them to say out loud when they want to stop
Give the landing first and then explain nothing more unless they ask
Give a headline and three key points ending with a landing, then pause for their questions
Prepare four separate minutes so that the story can fill the whole slot
optionExplain: Chronological storytelling is not the structure described.
The three key points carry the contribution and are part of the core.
Right: the focused core followed by their follow-ups.
The core is meant to take about two minutes.

questions.q: A lead faces product, marketing and support teams who each say their need is most critical. What is the strongest way to decide?
questions.explain: A prioritisation backed by data persuades all sides. The card next gives the author's examples.
options: Give the decision to whichever team shouts loudest because it shows the greatest need
Look at the data on what hurts customers most and show it to all three teams
Split the work equally so that every team gets a share at the same time
Ask the vice president to pick one team without any information from the lead
optionExplain: Volume is not evidence of need.
Right: evidence settles competing claims.
Equal shares delay all three.
It hands over the decision without evidence.
questions.rule: Study each example for its central decision and how it was communicated, then find the same pattern in your own work.

questions.q: Match each example story to its central move.
questions.explain: Each story hangs on one decision that made delivery possible under pressure.
questions.rule: One decision carries each story.
pairs: Cut the interface to deliver accurate exports in half the time
Used ticket data to put transactional reliability first
Phased the migration with rollback points at each stage
Built a pluggable architecture so teams got minimum capabilities early

questions.q: A developer's reporting tool must meet an audit date that has been moved up by half. Which example story offers the closest pattern?
questions.explain: A halved timeline asks for the essential output first, as in the export story.
questions.rule: Match the squeeze to the move.
options: The database migration: plan for two weeks, with phased services and rollback points at each stage
The notification overhaul: analyse ticket data to pick which team goes first
The event platform: build pluggable architecture for twelve different teams
The admin export tool: cut the interface and ship the accurate core, after agreeing with the user
optionExplain: A phased migration suits a risky technical cutover, not a halved timeline.
Ranking competing teams is a different problem.
That addresses many teams' competing needs, not one halved date.
Right: a halved timeline met by cutting to the essential output.

questions.q: In the senior-level migration story, why did the lead choose scheduled read-only periods for each service?
questions.explain: The dry run exposed a consistency problem, so the plan changed before anything went live.
questions.rule: Test the plan, then change it early.
