questions.teaches: In the senior story, a staging dry run showed that replication would not keep data consistent during cutover, leaving a 30-minute period when reads and writes could hit different databases, so the lead switched to brief read-only windows per service.
options: The vice president asked for it before the project began
The partner teams requested it from the start because they disliked any live changes to services
A staging dry run showed replication could not keep data consistent during cutover
It was cheaper than keeping a second database cluster running
optionExplain: The change came from the dry run, after planning.
Several teams pushed back until the lead showed there was no alternative.
Right: reads and writes could hit different databases for about half an hour.
Cost is not given as the reason.

questions.q: True or false: In the notification story, putting transactional emails first left marketing's later campaigns with worse delivery rates.
questions.explain: Marketing thanked the lead because their campaigns had better delivery rates on the more reliable infrastructure.
questions.rule: A reliable base helped the deferred work.

questions.q: A candidate retells the staff-level story: I promised each of the twelve teams its own deadline. What is wrong with this?
questions.explain: The lead's central move was to avoid per-team promises and give teams early minimum capabilities.
questions.rule: Do not promise what you cannot deliver.
options: He could not promise every date, so he asked each team for its must-haves
Nothing, because staff-level leaders are expected to say yes to every team
The lead promised the dates but gave the work to a single junior developer
The lead refused all twelve teams and built the platform alone
optionExplain: Right: he did not promise every deadline.
The story is the opposite: he could not commit to all of them.
No such assignment appears in the story.
He worked with each team to find must-haves.

questions.q: A festival coordinator learns that a permit change adds six weeks of work and affects ten volunteer leads. Which action follows the staff-level story?
questions.explain: Immediate group notice, then individual conversations, then leadership backing made the change feel manageable.
questions.rule: Tell everyone, ask individuals, win backing.
questions.teaches: In the staff story, when a GDPR requirement pushed timelines back about six weeks, the lead told all 12 team leads immediately, held individual conversations to see who could flex, and then worked with product leadership to communicate the impact.
options: Tell the leads only after the new date is final so that nobody is worried
Decide alone which leads must move and announce the result on the day
Ask each lead to find their own solution and report back when they have one
Tell all leads at once, speak to each about flexing, then get leadership backing
optionExplain: The lead in the story communicated immediately.
The lead held individual conversations before reprioritising.
That leaves the coordinator without a view of who can flex.
Right: this matches the story's communication steps.

questions.q: A candidate thinks she has no impressive delivery story. What does the author suggest?
questions.explain: Ordinary projects often contain real obstacles. The card next explains how to find them.
options: Describe a project that went smoothly, since smooth projects show competence
Look for a project where several small obstacles were pushed through to ship
Say that she has no example and move quickly on to another topic
Invent a larger project so the story seems more impressive
optionExplain: Smooth projects are a yellow flag in this chapter.
Right: small snags together can make a compelling story.
The author tells you to look for stories, not to skip.
Inventing is dishonest, and the author does not suggest it.
questions.rule: Look for ordinary projects with several small snags and tell how you pushed through them to ship.

questions.q: Almost every project hits ____, and pushing through several of them can make a good story.
questions.explain: The author's point is that almost every project has snags worth telling about.
questions.rule: Small snags add up.

questions.q: A candidate once finished a feature while two requirements changed and a tester went on leave. How could she present it?
questions.explain: Two changes and a missing tester are obstacles; the shipped feature is the landing.
questions.rule: Several snags, one result.
options: As a project that nearly failed and was saved by luck
As delivery despite changing requirements and lost resources, ending with what shipped
As an unremarkable project that she should leave out of her interview preparation altogether
As a list of the tasks she did in each week of the project
optionExplain: Luck gives no evidence of how she delivered.
Right: several small obstacles and a shipped outcome.
Unremarkable projects with snags are the source the author recommends.
A list of tasks is effort without outcome.

questions.q: Match each situation to what it shows, according to the author.
questions.explain: The author lists several kinds of complication, each showing a different part of delivery.
questions.rule: Each snag shows a different strength.
questions.teaches: The author's examples of complications to mine: a key team member leaving (resource constraints), requirements changing repeatedly (adapting while keeping momentum) and a major re-org (keeping things moving through organisational chaos).
pairs: A key team member left halfway through
Requirements changed multiple times but the feature shipped
A major re-org hit, and the deadline was still met creatively
Keeping things moving despite organisational chaos

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a story about several small obstacles can be compelling even though each challenge on its own seems small.
questions.explain: The author says recounting how you pushed through several obstacles to ship often makes a compelling story, even if the individual challenges seem small.
questions.rule: Count the snags together.

questions.q: A nurse moving into healthcare IT wants to find a delivery story. Which reflection question from the chapter would best prompt one?
questions.explain: The chapter's reflection questions ask about delivery under interruptions and missing support, not about size or hours.
questions.rule: Ask where you shipped despite interruptions.
questions.teaches: The author's reflection questions include delivering while supporting teammates with their blockers and while handling production issues or other urgent demands.
options: What is the largest team that you have ever managed in one project
Which programming language did you enjoy using the most last year
How many hours did you work in your busiest week of the past year
When did you ship important work while handling production issues or other urgent demands
optionExplain: Team size is not what the questions probe.
Enjoyment of a tool does not surface a delivery story.
Hours are effort, not a delivery story.
Right: this is one of the author's reflection questions.

questions.q: Which description best fits what a strong delivery story contains?
questions.explain: The strong story shows how you got past trouble. The card next gives the list.
options: A specific blocker, how the plan changed, trade-offs made and how people were kept informed
A thorough account of the whole team, the tools it used and the project's full history, in order
A calm project that ran to plan, which shows the candidate plans well
A record of the long hours worked, which proves commitment
optionExplain: Right: these are the author's summary points.
Background fills time and hides the contribution.
Smooth projects show little.
Hours are effort, not the signals the author lists.
questions.rule: Build every delivery story from blockers, changed approach, trade-offs and trust, and avoid blame, smooth tales and activity without outcome.

questions.q: Sort each element: include it in a strong delivery story, or avoid it?
questions.explain: The author's summary pairs the elements to include with the traps to avoid.
questions.rule: Include blockers and trade-offs; avoid blame and smoothness.

items.t: A specific blocker and the workaround that got past it
A change of approach when the original plan failed
Trade-offs made between competing priorities
Explaining why a failure was other people's fault
A project in which everything went as planned
A long list of activity with no word on what shipped

questions.q: A candidate has four stories. Which should she choose for a delivery question, by the author's summary?
questions.explain: The story with the broken dependency, the changed plan, the partner update and the shipped date has the author's strong elements; the others contain traps.
questions.rule: Choose blocker, pivot, communication.
options: One where the project had no problems and she finished a week early
One where she worked every weekend, and the delay that remained was due to another team that let her down
One where a dependency broke, she changed the plan, told partners and shipped on the date
One where she completed many tasks and received praise from her manager
optionExplain: A problem-free project is a trap.
It mixes heroics and blame.
Right: it contains blocker, changed approach and communication.
It stresses activity and praise without a shipped result.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the traps the chapter's summary tells you to avoid?
questions.explain: The summary lists four traps, and disguised perfectionism is one of them.
questions.rule: Perfectionism is not a strength here.
options: Naming the blocker you faced
Describing a trade-off you made
Telling stakeholders about a risk as early as you can
Describing perfectionism as high standards
optionExplain: Naming obstacles is part of a strong story.
Trade-offs are a strong signal.
Proactive communication is encouraged.
Right: the summary warns against disguising perfectionism.

questions.q: A candidate's answer contains these statements. Which fall into traps from the summary? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The statements about a smooth, uneventful launch and about blaming another team match the traps of trouble-free stories and blame.
questions.rule: Blame and smoothness are traps.
options: Everything went smoothly and the launch was uneventful
We shipped in March, and about two hundred staff used it that week
The other team never gave us what we needed, so it was out of our hands
We changed approach in week three, because the first plan could not work
optionExplain: Wrong: it describes a project where all went as planned.
Fine: it states what shipped.
Wrong: it blames others.
Fine: a changed approach is a strong element.

questions.q: A candidate's story has an obstacle and a workaround but no statement of what the work achieved. What is the likely weakness?
questions.explain: The summary closes with delivering measurable value despite imperfect conditions.
questions.rule: End on measurable value.
options: It has too many details about the workaround
It lacks measurable value, one of the elements a strong story includes
It will be taken as a red flag for blaming others
It cannot be used at all in an interview, because outcomes are only optional extras
optionExplain: The weakness is the missing outcome, not an excess of detail.
Right: strong stories deliver measurable value despite imperfect conditions.
Nothing in the story blames anyone.
Outcomes are part of the list, so they are not optional.

questions.q: A charity worker prepares a story about a fundraising event run with half the volunteers expected. What should the story's ending include?
questions.explain: The summary's final element is the measurable value delivered despite imperfect conditions.
questions.rule: Close with measured value.
questions.teaches: One of the author's summary points for strong stories is delivering measurable value despite imperfect conditions.
options: A description of how tired the volunteers were by the end of the event
A thank-you list naming everyone who helped to run the evening
Measurable value delivered, such as money raised, despite the shortage
A promise that next year's event will be much larger and better staffed
optionExplain: Tiredness is effort, not value.
Credit is kind but not a measured result.
Right: strong stories deliver measurable value despite imperfect conditions.
Future plans do not show what was delivered.

questions.section: 7.1 What Does It Mean to Problem-Solve and Deep Dive?
questions.q: A web page keeps timing out, and a teammate suggests doubling the servers. Which question shows root-cause thinking?
options: How many more servers can we afford this quarter?
Why did response times get worse in the first place?
Who changed the page most recently and should repair it?
Can we restart the service on a schedule until later?
optionExplain: A reasonable budget question, but it assumes the fix and skips the cause.
Right: it looks for the cause rather than covering the symptom.
Finding a person is not the same as finding the cause of the slowdown.
A restart schedule hides the symptom and leaves the cause untouched.
questions.explain: Asking why something degraded is the first step towards a cause, while extra capacity only treats the symptom. The card next defines the terms.
questions.rule: Look for the root cause behind a failure, and go deeper than a working fix when the problem is likely to return.

questions.section: 7.1 What Does It Mean to Problem-Solve and Deep Dive?
questions.q: The chapter defines problem-solving as breaking challenges down to address root causes, not only ____.
questions.explain: The contrast is between the cause of a failure and the symptoms it produces.
questions.rule: Fix causes, not just symptoms.

questions.section: 7.1 What Does It Mean to Problem-Solve and Deep Dive?
questions.q: Sort each action into one that treats the symptom or one that pursues the root cause.

items.t: Restart the service every time the alert fires
Add servers each time the page slows down
Clean the bad rows by hand every Friday
Trace repeated bad records to the import step that makes them
Find out why latency crept up before choosing a fix
Study why one kind of crash keeps returning so it can be prevented

questions.explain: The three under 'Treats the symptom' make the trouble go away for now; the three under 'Pursues the root cause' ask why it happens, which is where a real fix starts.
questions.rule: Look for the root cause behind a failure, and go deeper than a working fix when the problem is likely to return.

questions.section: 7.1 What Does It Mean to Problem-Solve and Deep Dive?
questions.q: Which description fits deep diving, as opposed to ordinary problem-solving?
options: Restoring service quickly so that customers can carry on working
Breaking a challenge into parts to find and address its root causes
Handing a hard bug to a more senior colleague without looking at it
Seeking fuller understanding of a failure when a surface fix would do
optionExplain: That is a quick fix to restore service, not the extra understanding that deep diving adds.
This is how the chapter defines problem-solving itself; deep diving goes beyond it.
Delegating without looking involves no investigation at all.
Right: the chapter says deep diving goes further than the point where a patch suffices.
questions.explain: Problem-solving looks for root causes; deep diving continues to seek understanding when a fix would already do.
questions.rule: Look for the root cause behind a failure, and go deeper than a working fix when the problem is likely to return.

questions.section: 7.1 What Does It Mean to Problem-Solve and Deep Dive?
questions.q: A candidate says: the alerts stopped after we added servers, so the latency problem is solved. What is wrong with this?
options: Quiet alerts hide the symptom without explaining why it slowed
Nothing is wrong, since a fix that stops the alerts has solved the problem
Servers cannot affect latency, so the fix must have been an accident
Alerts should have been switched off earlier to avoid false confidence
optionExplain: Right: without knowing why it slowed, nothing prevents a repeat.
Stopped alerts are the symptom disappearing, which is not the same as the cause being found.
More capacity can help latency; the issue is that it was applied without a cause.
The alerts were useful signals; muting them would hide more, not less.
questions.explain: A quiet dashboard shows the symptom has gone, not that the cause was understood.
questions.rule: Quiet alerts are not a diagnosis.

questions.section: 7.1 What Does It Mean to Problem-Solve and Deep Dive?
questions.q: A family's basement floods in heavy rain, and they found where the water enters and sealed it. Which further step matches the chapter's opening story?
options: Keep a bucket and pump ready by the stairs in case the water comes back
Wait for the next big storm to find out whether the new seal holds
Document how the cause was found and add early-warning monitoring
Stop here, since the cause has been found and sealed and the floor is dry
optionExplain: Preparation for a repeat is sensible, but it plans for failure instead of capturing what was learned.
Waiting tests the fix but leaves nothing behind for the next person.
Right: this is how the opening engineer turned a fix into lasting knowledge.
Fixing it is the start; the opening story goes on to document and monitor.
questions.explain: The opening engineer patched a library bug, documented the investigation, added monitoring and wrote runbooks for memory leaks.
questions.teaches: In the chapter's opening story, the engineer documented her investigation, built monitoring and wrote runbooks, so a later team diagnosed a similar problem in hours rather than days.
questions.rule: Look for the root cause behind a failure, and go deeper than a working fix when the problem is likely to return.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: True or false: a good problem-solver investigates every issue as thoroughly as possible.
questions.explain: Investigating everything leads to analysis paralysis. The card next shows how to choose which problems deserve depth.
questions.rule: Spend depth where impact and the chance of recurrence are high, and move fast elsewhere.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Match each way of going wrong to the result the authors give for it.
pairs: Shipping quick patches without knowing why
Judging impact and likelihood of recurrence
Deciding which problems deserve a closer look
questions.explain: The tension runs between too little depth, which leaves problems recurring, and too much, which stalls progress.
questions.rule: Too shallow breeds repeats; too deep stalls.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: One bug garbles a total in an annual report read by one person. Another makes logins fail for every customer. How should depth be split?
options: Thorough diagnosis for the report glitch, quick fix for the login failures
Thorough diagnosis for both, so that no hidden fault is left to chance
Quick fix for both, since the team is short of time this week and both look small
Quick fix for the report glitch; deep diagnosis of the logins
optionExplain: This reverses the priorities: the wide, serious problem gets the shallow treatment.
Equal depth everywhere is the analysis-paralysis trap the chapter warns about.
Patching the login failures without knowing why risks technical debt and repeats.
Right: login failures have high impact and are likely to recur.
questions.explain: Impact and likelihood of recurrence decide the depth, so the broad, serious failure earns the investigation.
questions.rule: Spend depth where impact and the chance of recurrence are high, and move fast elsewhere.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: True or false: when the same leak moves from a rarely used feature into core infrastructure, the case for a thorough diagnosis gets stronger.
questions.explain: The leak is unchanged, but its impact has grown, and impact is one of the two things that set the depth of response.
questions.rule: When impact changes, depth should change.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A lead insists: before we ship anything, we trace the root cause of every failed test. What is wrong with this policy?
options: It invites analysis paralysis, since depth should follow impact
It is fine, because deep diving is always better than patching
It confuses root causes with symptoms and so cannot work
It will produce too little documentation to prevent repeats
optionExplain: Right: following every thread has a cost, so depth is chosen.
The chapter treats depth as a choice, not a rule that holds in every case.
The policy does look for causes; its flaw is applying that search to everything.
Documentation is not the problem; the effort per issue is.
questions.explain: Thorough investigation of every issue stalls delivery, so the authors want depth reserved for problems that merit it.
questions.rule: Spend depth where impact and the chance of recurrence are high, and move fast elsewhere.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A household has a dripping tap and a damp patch spreading on a load-bearing wall. Using the same logic, how should effort be split?
options: Inspect the tap thoroughly and cover the damp patch with paint
Treat both with a quick cosmetic fix and review them next year
Quick washer fix for the tap, thorough inspection of the wall
Hire a specialist to investigate every pipe and surface in the house
optionExplain: This puts depth on the minor problem and a cosmetic patch on the serious one.
A patch on the wall risks recurring and growing trouble.
Right: the low-stakes problem gets a quick fix, the high-stakes one a diagnosis.
Surveying everything is analysis paralysis for a small leak.
questions.explain: The authors add that each effort should produce knowledge that helps beyond the immediate fix, such as runbooks, tools or documented patterns.
questions.teaches: The authors expect each investigation to leave something behind beyond the fix, such as runbooks, tools or documented patterns that prevent similar issues.
questions.rule: Spend depth where impact and the chance of recurrence are high, and move fast elsewhere.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: You have worked on a legacy system for hours with no progress. What would a strong problem-solver most likely do?
options: Keep going alone, since asking would show a lack of ability
Judge whether someone with the context could answer sooner, and ask
Ask the first colleague who walks by without looking at anything
Restart the service and move on to the next ticket in the queue today
optionExplain: Self-reliance feels admirable but here it only prolongs the struggle.
Right: asking at the right moment is part of good judgment.
Asking early can help, but the strong version does some digging first.
That abandons the investigation instead of progressing it.
questions.explain: The skill is knowing when digging alone has stopped paying off. The card next gives the balance.
questions.rule: Do some digging first, and ask for help as soon as asking would get you to the answer faster.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Strong problem-solvers balance independence with ____.
questions.explain: Independence on its own can waste time; the balance is with how quickly the answer is reached.
questions.rule: Independence balanced with efficiency.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Sort each situation into one where you keep digging alone or one where you should ask for help.

items.t: You have not yet looked at the logs of the failing job
You have a fresh hypothesis you can test in ten minutes
The unfamiliar code is starting to make sense as you read it
The next step needs access that you have not been given
Only the original author knows the business rules involved
You keep repeating the same checks and learning nothing new

questions.explain: Dig while you are still learning; ask when the missing piece is context or access that someone else holds.
questions.rule: Do some digging first, and ask for help as soon as asking would get you to the answer faster.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A developer asks for help after five minutes, before opening a log or reading any code. What weakness does the balance point to?
options: Too little independent digging before asking
Too much independence, since help was needed sooner
Too little deference to the helper's schedule
Too much attention to access and permissions
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says to do some digging first.
Five minutes with nothing tried is the opposite of too much independence.
Courtesy to the helper is not what the balance is about.
Nothing in the case suggests an access problem.
questions.explain: The balance has two ends; asking before any digging misses the first half of it.
questions.rule: Do some digging first, and ask for help as soon as asking would get you to the answer faster.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Dana says: asking for help signals weakness, so I debug alone until I solve it. How does the chapter judge this?
options: It is the right approach, since ownership means doing it all yourself
It is fine as long as Dana writes a report afterwards
It ignores that knowing when to ask is part of the skill
It is wrong only when the problem touches production systems
optionExplain: The chapter wants independence balanced with efficiency, not absolute self-reliance.
A report does not recover the time spent spinning.
Right: the authors list asking for help at the right moment as a mark of maturity.
The chapter draws no such line.
questions.explain: Productive struggle ends when asking would be quicker, and recognizing that is itself a strength.
questions.rule: Do some digging first, and ask for help as soon as asking would get you to the answer faster.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: An accountant has chased a spreadsheet error for hours after checking all of her own formulas. What should she do, and what does the chapter's mid-level story add?
options: Rebuild the whole spreadsheet in case she missed something
Ask whoever built the model, as the story's engineer did
Wait a day in case the error disappears on its own
Replace the model with a simpler one nobody has audited
optionExplain: Rebuilding discards what she has learned instead of seeking missing knowledge.
Right: she has exhausted her own checks and someone else holds the missing context.
Waiting adds delay without new information.
A new unaudited model could multiply errors rather than explain this one.
questions.explain: In the mid-level story the engineer read code for three hours, brought in a distributed-systems specialist, and the cause was spotted within 30 minutes.
questions.teaches: In the mid-level story, after three hours of reading code the engineer pulled in a distributed-systems specialist, who spotted the failure mode within 30 minutes.
questions.rule: Do some digging first, and ask for help as soon as asking would get you to the answer faster.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Which kind of organization is most likely to reward understanding a failure fully even when a quick fix is available?
options: A startup racing to ship its next feature before the money runs out
An agency handed a client system for a short engagement
A team that measures success only by closed tickets
A research organization, where thorough analysis is the default
optionExplain: Startups lean towards fast resolutions, with depth aimed only at what blocks growth.
Agencies must build context quickly under tight time limits.
Closed tickets reward speed, not depth of understanding.
Right: research organizations value understanding every aspect of a problem.
questions.explain: Where thoroughness is the default, depth is valued even when quicker fixes exist. The card next maps each kind of organization.
questions.rule: Learn what the target organization values and calibrate how deep and how fast your stories go.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Match each kind of organization to what it values most in problem-solving.
pairs: Fast resolutions, with thorough analysis only on what blocks growth
Systematic work that scales across teams
Thorough analysis by default, even when quicker fixes exist
Quickly building a mental model of unfamiliar systems
Careful, documented work inside established procedures
questions.explain: Each organization's needs shape the depth it wants and the speed at which it wants it.
questions.rule: Depth follows the organization's needs.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Maya is interviewing at a consultancy. Which story from her past will fit best?
options: A year-long study of a single failure mode to advance her field
A long record of following the same approval steps on every change
How she quickly mapped an unfamiliar codebase and delivered a fix
A fast patch she shipped without examining why the problem arose
optionExplain: That suits a research organization more than a consultancy.
That suits a traditional enterprise that prizes established procedure.
Right: consultancies value rapid mental models of unfamiliar systems.
Speed matters here, but the consultancy still wants problems identified, not just masked.
questions.explain: Agencies and consultancies reward speed in understanding client systems followed by actionable solutions.
questions.rule: Learn what the target organization values and calibrate how deep and how fast your stories go.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Sort each expectation into one that leans to targeted speed or one that treats thoroughness as the default.

items.t: Separate what matters now from what can wait
Build a working picture of an unfamiliar system quickly
Aim thorough analysis at problems that block growth
Understand why a failure mode exists even if a quicker fix is possible
Find root causes while working within established procedures
Dig thoroughly enough to stop problems spreading across huge systems

questions.explain: Startups and agencies aim depth where time is short; research, traditional and large organizations expect thoroughness.
questions.rule: Learn what the target organization values and calibrate how deep and how fast your stories go.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: What would a hiring manager at a startup most likely think of a story about a month spent analysing a minor, non-blocking issue?
options: It shows admirable thoroughness that startups prize above speed
It shows poor targeting, as startups aim depth at what blocks growth
It shows a good fit, since all organizations default to depth
It shows nothing, since the length of an investigation is irrelevant to hiring
optionExplain: Startups value targeted analysis, not thoroughness for its own sake.
Right: the startup skill is separating what matters now from what can wait.
The chapter says organizations differ, so depth is not the default everywhere.
Duration and focus both feed the picture of your judgment.
questions.explain: Depth that does not serve the organization's priorities can read as weak judgment.
questions.rule: Learn what the target organization values and calibrate how deep and how fast your stories go.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A candidate for a large company tells a story where she fixed a hard bug and stopped. What would most strengthen it for that audience?
options: Adding more detail about how fast she restored service afterwards
Showing she avoided asking colleagues for any help with the bug
Stressing that she kept the investigation as short as possible
Showing the tool or guide she made that other teams went on to use
optionExplain: Speed of restoration is delivery and does not show reusable knowledge.
Independence alone is not what large companies prize.
Brevity is a startup value more than a large-company one.
Right: at large companies the expectation is that analysis produces reusable knowledge.
questions.explain: Problem-solving at large tech companies includes creating tools and generating documentation that help many other people.
questions.teaches: At large tech companies, problem-solving includes creating tools and documentation for many other people, so the expectation is that your analysis produces reusable knowledge.
questions.rule: Learn what the target organization values and calibrate how deep and how fast your stories go.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: At a firm that wants decisions backed by wide agreement, a new engineer has found a fix. What should she do first?
options: Present findings formally and build agreement before implementing
Deploy the fix right away to show her initiative to the team
Wait silently until a manager asks her about the problem
Rewrite the fix in a different language to impress the team
optionExplain: Right: in consensus-minded firms the route to action goes through agreement.
That could break the culture's expectation of agreement before action.
Silence adds no information for the people who must agree.
Novelty does nothing for consensus.
questions.explain: How findings travel matters as much as the findings. The card next sets out the cultural patterns.
questions.rule: Notice whether a culture runs on consensus, quick iteration or real-time teamwork, and carry solutions forward its way.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Match each cultural pattern to how a solution is carried forward.
pairs: Present findings through formal channels and build agreement first
Individuals implement after a quick consultation
Teams solve the problem together in real time
questions.explain: Each pattern sets a different path from analysis to action.
questions.rule: Fit the path to the culture.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Sort each action into one that fits a consensus-and-documentation culture or a rapid-iteration culture.

items.t: Circulate a written root-cause report and collect sign-off before changing code
Present findings through the formal review channel
Wait for stakeholders to agree before touching production
Make the fix after a quick chat with the owner and watch the result
Ship a small change yourself once the owner says go
Try a fix, measure and iterate within the same afternoon

questions.explain: The three under 'Consensus and documentation' build agreement before acting; the three under 'Rapid iteration' act quickly after minimal consultation.
questions.rule: Notice whether a culture runs on consensus, quick iteration or real-time teamwork, and carry solutions forward its way.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A candidate claims: the fastest route to a fix is right in every company. What does the chapter say against it?
options: Speed matters only in startups, so the claim is wrong everywhere else
Some cultures expect formal findings and agreement before implementation
Fast fixes are careless and a thoughtful engineer should avoid them
Companies decide by hierarchy alone, so fixes cannot be fast
optionExplain: That overstates the case; some cultures still prize rapid iteration.
Right: cultural values about risk and decision-making change what counts as right.
The chapter does not condemn speed; it asks you to match the culture.
The chapter also describes cultures that empower individuals to act quickly.
questions.explain: What counts as a good route from analysis to action depends on the company's values.
questions.rule: Notice whether a culture runs on consensus, quick iteration or real-time teamwork, and carry solutions forward its way.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: An engineer from a rapid-iteration culture joins a firm that builds consensus first. What is the likely friction?
options: Her root-cause skills will no longer be needed in the new firm at all
The firm will ask her to stop investigating problems altogether
Nothing, because culture does not affect problem-solving
Her habit of acting after quick consultation may clash with formal agreement
optionExplain: Root-cause skills travel; the friction is in process, not skill.
The firm still wants analysis; it just wants a different route to action.
The chapter says problem-solving approaches reflect cultural values.
Right: the two cultures have different paths to action.
questions.explain: Changing culture changes the expected process, so habits of one setting can misfire in another.
questions.rule: Notice whether a culture runs on consensus, quick iteration or real-time teamwork, and carry solutions forward its way.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A public agency expects a written analysis to circulate before any meeting. A new analyst has found a flaw in a process. What should she do?
options: Write the analysis up and circulate it before the discussion
Raise the flaw informally in the next meeting and write up later
Fix the process herself and report the result afterwards
Gather the team to solve it together live without any paperwork
optionExplain: Right: some organizations require detailed written analysis before discussions are held.
This reverses the order that the agency expects.
That suits an empowered, rapid-iteration culture, not this one.
Real-time collaboration is another pattern, and not the one this agency uses.
questions.explain: A written-first culture is a further pattern the chapter names alongside consensus, rapid iteration and real-time teamwork.
questions.teaches: Some organizations require detailed written analyses to be completed before any discussion is held.
questions.rule: Notice whether a culture runs on consensus, quick iteration or real-time teamwork, and carry solutions forward its way.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: An engineer restarts a crashed service within minutes and users recover. Which competency does that mostly show?
options: Deep problem-solving, because the system is working again
Taking initiative, because she acted without being asked
Delivery, because the aim was to restore service quickly
Learning and growth, because she handled a crash
optionExplain: Working again says nothing about whether the cause was found.
Nothing says the work was unassigned.
Right: shipping a quick fix to restore service is delivery.
No new capability was built by a restart.
questions.explain: Restoring service is delivery; finding why it crashed is problem-solving. The card next separates these.
questions.rule: Ask which competency a story proves: depth of cause analysis is problem-solving, speed of restoring service is delivery.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Match each competency to its focus.
pairs: Depth of analysis into underlying causes
Shipping a quick fix to restore service
Choosing to work on unassigned problems
questions.explain: Each competency answers a different question about the same work.
questions.rule: Same work, different focus.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: Sort each action into the competency it mainly shows.

items.t: Isolated why the queue stalls and removed the cause
Traced intermittent errors to a race condition
Found that a workflow gap was producing inconsistent data
Rolled back the release to restore service within the hour
Shipped a temporary setting so customers could keep working
Met the deadline by patching the visible error

questions.explain: Problem-solving is about causes; delivery is about getting things working or shipped.
questions.rule: Ask which competency a story proves: depth of cause analysis is problem-solving, speed of restoring service is delivery.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A manager assigns you a tricky bug. Separately, you spot slowness nobody asked about and dig in. How does the chapter label these?
options: Both are initiative, because each goes beyond the person's routine tasks
Both are problem-solving only, because initiative has no link to analysis
The first is delivery work and the second is learning and growth
Bug: problem-solving; the slowness dig: initiative leading into problem-solving
optionExplain: Only the unassigned slowness involved a decision to take it on.
Initiative can lead into problem-solving, as the unassigned slowness did.
Neither label fits: the first is analysis of an assigned bug, the second self-started analysis.
Right: initiative is about the decision to start, problem-solving about how thoroughly you examine.
questions.explain: Initiative shows in choosing to work on an unassigned problem; problem-solving shows in how deeply you examine it.
questions.rule: Ask which competency a story proves: depth of cause analysis is problem-solving, speed of restoring service is delivery.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A candidate says: I restored the service fast, which proves my root-cause skills. What is the flaw?
options: A quick restoration shows delivery; root-cause skill is addressing why it failed
Nothing, since restoring service always requires finding the cause
Speed never counts for anything in an interview
Root causes are found only by managers, not engineers
optionExplain: Right: the two competencies have different focuses.
A restart can restore service without any cause being found.
Delivery is a legitimate competency; it just proves something else.
The chapter expects engineers to find root causes.
questions.explain: Restoring service quickly shows delivery; the proof of problem-solving is in the cause you addressed.
questions.rule: Ask which competency a story proves: depth of cause analysis is problem-solving, speed of restoring service is delivery.

questions.section: 7.2 The Essence of Problem-Solving and Deep Diving
questions.q: A plumber uses well-known techniques to trace a hidden leak and learns nothing new on the job. Which statement fits the chapter?
options: She cannot count as a problem-solver without learning something new
She has shown initiative, because she found the leak
She can solve problems well without new skills, since the competencies differ
She has shown delivery only, since the leak was fixed
optionExplain: That merges the two competencies the chapter keeps apart.
Finding the leak says nothing about whether she chose to take it on.
Right: the chapter says problem-solving is about the process, whether or not you build new skills.
Fixing it is delivery, but tracing the cause is problem-solving too.
questions.explain: The authors note you can be an excellent problem-solver who applies known techniques well, just as you can be a strong learner without deeply examining every issue.
questions.teaches: You can be an excellent problem-solver using well-known techniques, just as you can be a strong learner without deeply examining every issue.
questions.rule: Ask which competency a story proves: depth of cause analysis is problem-solving, speed of restoring service is delivery.

questions.q: An interviewer asks whether you have debugged an issue that crossed team boundaries. What ability is mostly being probed?
options: Typing speed and fluency in a particular language under pressure
Solving problems beyond your own immediate domain
Whether you like to work with large teams in open offices
How quickly you can restore service after an unexpected outage
optionExplain: Coding fluency is judged in technical rounds, not by a boundary question.
Right: the question is about reaching past the parts you own.
Preference for team settings is not what this question measures.
Speed of restoring service is delivery, which this question does not target.
questions.explain: The question is about problems that sit beyond your own domain. The card next lists all four families.
questions.rule: Work out which of the four families a question belongs to, then answer with depth, not a patch.

questions.q: Match each interview question to its family.
pairs: Walk me through how you investigate a system failure
When did the real cause differ from the obvious one?
Tell me about a time you had to test several explanations
Describe a bug that crossed team lines
questions.explain: Each family targets a different part of how you work through a problem.
questions.rule: Work out which of the four families a question belongs to, then answer with depth, not a patch.

questions.q: A candidate's best story: three explanations for a billing error were tested one after another until the fourth held. Which family fits?
options: Testing and validating theories, because several were tried and dropped
Investigation methods, because every story concerns a method
Cross-system problem-solving, because billing touches many systems
Finding root causes, because the fourth explanation was the cause
optionExplain: Right: the story is about hypotheses tested and discarded.
All stories show some method, but this one is about the hypotheses specifically.
Nothing in the story says other teams or systems were involved.
The emphasis is on testing several theories, not on spotting that the obvious was wrong.
questions.explain: When the heart of a story is trying and discarding theories, it belongs to the testing family.
questions.rule: Work out which of the four families a question belongs to, then answer with depth, not a patch.

questions.q: True or false: a root-cause question asks about your investigation process, while a method question asks you to tell symptoms from causes.
questions.explain: The two are the other way round: method questions probe your process, and root-cause questions probe whether you can tell symptoms from causes.
questions.rule: Method asks how; root cause asks what lay beneath.

questions.q: Asked about a complex problem solved through investigation, a candidate says: I restarted the service and it worked. Why does this fall short?
options: It is too short to count as an answer in any interview round
It leaves out the names of the teammates who helped at that time
It shows no investigation and no gap between a fix and analysis
It hides a failure that the candidate should have confessed to
optionExplain: Length is not the issue; the content shows no analysis.
Naming people is not what these questions look for.
Right: a restart reveals nothing about how the problem was diagnosed.
The problem is lack of depth, not lack of confession.
questions.explain: These questions exist to see depth, and a restart is the very kind of surface fix they contrast with it.
questions.rule: Work out which of the four families a question belongs to, then answer with depth, not a patch.

questions.q: A product manager is asked about a churn hypothesis that proved wrong. What is the interviewer mainly assessing?
options: How much data the manager can recite from memory on demand
How the manager handles uncertainty and dead ends
Whether the manager avoids ever being wrong about forecasts
How well the manager avoids sharing bad news with senior staff
optionExplain: Recall of figures is not the point of a testing question.
Right: testing questions look at how you cope when a theory fails.
Being wrong is expected; the question is how it is handled.
Nothing in the family concerns concealing news.
questions.explain: The testing family asks how you handle uncertainty and dead ends, in any field.
questions.teaches: Testing-and-validating questions are meant to reveal how you handle uncertainty and dead ends.
questions.rule: Work out which of the four families a question belongs to, then answer with depth, not a patch.

questions.q: Asked how you investigate system failures, what should your answer mainly show?
options: A long list of tools and dashboards that you have used before
How quickly you reached a fix on your most urgent incident
How many colleagues you consulted before touching the system
An ordered way of collecting evidence and checking suspected causes
optionExplain: Tools matter less than the reasoning that links them.
Speed is delivery; this question is about method.
Consulting is a different signal and not the core of this question.
Right: the question probes whether you diagnose with structure.
questions.explain: Interviewers want to see how you work, not only what you used. The card next sets out the parts of a strong answer.
questions.rule: Describe your investigation as gathered data, formed hypotheses, tested theories and validated conclusions.

questions.q: Put the parts of a strong investigation phase in the order the book gives them.
items: Gather data
Form hypotheses
Test theories
Validate conclusions
questions.explain: The book lists the phase as gathering data, forming hypotheses, testing theories and validating conclusions.
questions.rule: Evidence, then theory, then test, then confirm.

questions.q: Which opening of an answer best fits a method question?
options: I tried several configuration changes until the errors finally went away for good
I asked a teammate who guessed the cause, and I applied the guess
I logged timings, suspected two causes, ruled one out by test, confirmed the other
I read the code until I felt which function was probably to blame
optionExplain: That is trial and error, the opposite of structure.
No evidence was gathered and no theory was tested.
Right: it shows data, hypotheses, testing and validation in order.
A feeling is not a tested hypothesis.
questions.explain: A structured answer links each step to evidence and shows how the conclusion was checked.
questions.rule: Describe your investigation as gathered data, formed hypotheses, tested theories and validated conclusions.

questions.q: True or false: a story that gives only the symptom and the final fix leaves interviewers without evidence of structured thinking.
questions.explain: The middle of the story, the investigation phase, is where a method shows. Without it the interviewer cannot tell a method from luck.
questions.rule: The method lives in the middle of the story.

questions.q: A candidate lists the data she gathered, then says: so it was the cache. Which part of the phase is missing?
options: Gathering data, because logs are not real evidence of any cause at all
Testing theories and validating the conclusion
Forming hypotheses, because every cause is known in advance
Nothing, since gathering data is the whole of an investigation
optionExplain: She did gather data; the gap lies after it.
Right: she jumps from data to verdict without a check.
The jump hides the hypotheses, but the key absence is a test.
The book lists four parts, and the later ones are missing.
questions.explain: Data on its own does not establish a cause; a theory has to be tested and the conclusion validated.
questions.rule: Describe your investigation as gathered data, formed hypotheses, tested theories and validated conclusions.

questions.q: A baker sees dense loaves on some days. Which approach resembles the opening story's engineer, who mapped a memory leak against every variable she could find?
options: Change the recipe and the oven at once, hoping the loaves improve overall
Blame the newest staff member and retrain them straight away
Wait for a good week and assume the problem has resolved itself
Record flour, oven, humidity and shift against each bad day
optionExplain: Changing everything together hides which variable mattered.
A guess at a person is not an investigation.
Waiting gathers no evidence at all.
Right: recording the variables against the problem is how she began.
questions.explain: In the opening story, the engineer tracked memory growth against request types, payload sizes, user segments and regions, then built custom profiling tools when standard ones were too coarse.
questions.teaches: In the opening story, the engineer mapped memory growth against request types, payload sizes, user segments and regions, and built custom profiling tools when the standard ones were not granular enough.
questions.rule: Describe your investigation as gathered data, formed hypotheses, tested theories and validated conclusions.

questions.q: Asked about a time the real problem differed from first appearances, which story is the strongest?
options: A slowdown blamed on load that proved to be a database lock
A server crash fixed within minutes by restarting the machine on the spot
A launch delivered a day early thanks to a carefully written plan
A long outage resolved after three senior managers joined the call
optionExplain: Right: the obvious explanation was wrong and the evidence pointed elsewhere.
A restart shows nothing about a real problem behind the appearance.
Good delivery, but no obvious explanation was overturned.
Escalation is not discovering a different underlying problem.
questions.explain: A strong story overturns the first explanation. The card next sets out how to tell it.
questions.rule: Tell the moment the obvious problem turned out not to be the real one, and what evidence turned you.

questions.q: Strong stories describe the moment you realized the obvious problem was not the ____ problem.
questions.explain: The moment of realization is the centre of a root-cause story.
questions.rule: Show the turn from obvious to real.

questions.q: Which statement shows a candidate questioning an initial assumption?
options: We assumed bad input, so I added stricter input checks and moved on to the next task
We assumed bad input, but data showed our parser dropped fields, so I followed that
We assumed bad input, and my manager agreed, so we went ahead with the plan
We assumed bad input, and I added a log line in case it came up again later
optionExplain: This acts on the assumption without testing it.
Right: the evidence replaced the assumption.
Agreement from a manager is not evidence.
A log line watches for a repeat but does not test the assumption.
questions.explain: Questioning an assumption means checking it against evidence and following the evidence where it leads.
questions.rule: Tell the moment the obvious problem turned out not to be the real one, and what evidence turned you.

questions.q: True or false: when the evidence contradicts your first expectation, a strong story leaves that moment out so that it sounds confident.
questions.explain: That moment is the best material for the story. The authors want you to question initial assumptions and follow the evidence even when it differs from expectations.
questions.rule: Show the revised assumption.

questions.q: A candidate answers a deeper-cause question with a patch that worked and no further story. What is missing?
options: A longer account of how quickly the team applied the patch itself
A list of the tools that were open on the screen at the time
A statement that the patch was approved by the project manager
Evidence that the obvious fix would have left the cause in place
optionExplain: More speed does not show a deeper cause.
Tools are not the point of this question.
Approval does not show what the real problem was.
Right: the question needs the contrast between the patch and the cause.
questions.explain: Without the gap between the obvious fix and the true cause, the story is just a patch.
questions.rule: Tell the moment the obvious problem turned out not to be the real one, and what evidence turned you.

questions.q: A clinic manager finds late starts, billing errors and patient complaints all stem from one scheduling rule. Why is this a strong story?
options: One cause explained several symptoms at once, which is valued even more
Complaints are the clearest possible evidence of any underlying problem
Billing errors prove that clinics should not use scheduling rules at all
The manager avoided consulting anyone outside the clinic itself
optionExplain: Right: the book says a cause that explains multiple symptoms is even better.
Complaints are one symptom here, not special evidence of cause.
The story concerns one rule, not scheduling in general.
Working alone is not what makes the story strong.
questions.explain: The authors add that a story in which one underlying issue explained multiple symptoms simultaneously is even better.
questions.teaches: Interviewers value even more a story where one underlying issue explained multiple symptoms at the same time.
questions.rule: Tell the moment the obvious problem turned out not to be the real one, and what evidence turned you.

questions.q: An interviewer asks about a theory of yours that proved incorrect. Which detail in a story is the most reassuring?
options: A statement that the theory was right in the end if viewed differently enough
A remark that the theory was suggested by someone more senior
A test that ruled the theory out, and how the next idea followed
A claim that you never form theories before the evidence is in
optionExplain: Defending a failed theory suggests the opposite of objectivity.
Who suggested it says nothing about how you tested it.
Right: the test and the follow-on show method.
Forming hypotheses is part of the process the authors want to see.
questions.explain: The reassuring detail is evidence of testing, not of being right. The card next sets out the elements.
questions.rule: Give each theory its own test, read the result honestly, and change course when it points elsewhere.

questions.q: Strong stories show you creating specific ____ for each theory.
questions.explain: Each theory gets its own check, so a result can be read against it.
questions.rule: One theory, one test.

questions.q: Sort each statement into one that shows objective testing or one that does not.

items.t: I wrote a check that would fail if my cache theory was right
The test contradicted my guess, so I dropped that theory
I designed a separate test for each of the three suspects
I only looked at the logs that matched my theory
I assumed the second server was fine and moved on
I kept my first idea because it felt right

questions.explain: Objective testing means a check that could prove you wrong, and honest handling of the result.
questions.rule: Give each theory its own test, read the result honestly, and change course when it points elsewhere.

questions.q: The first test of your theory comes back negative. What does a strong story do?
options: Repeat the same test until it finally supports the theory
Treat the test as faulty and keep the theory, since it fits the facts
Stop investigating, as one negative result ends any useful inquiry
Change the direction of inquiry according to what the result showed
optionExplain: Repeating a test until it agrees is not objective.
Dismissing a result that disagrees is the opposite of reading it objectively.
A negative result is information that helps choose the next step.
Right: the authors list changing direction based on what you learned.
questions.explain: A negative result is information, and the story is stronger for showing it steered the next step.
questions.rule: Give each theory its own test, read the result honestly, and change course when it points elsewhere.

questions.q: A candidate says: I was sure the database was at fault, so I skipped testing and tuned it. What is the flaw?
options: No test was designed, so the belief went unchecked
Tuning a database is never a legitimate response to a slow system
Candidates must always test the network before the database
The candidate should have asked a manager to approve the theory
optionExplain: Right: certainty replaced a test.
Tuning can be right; the flaw is acting without a check.
No fixed order of suspects is set by the chapter.
Approval is not a test.
questions.explain: A theory held with confidence still needs a test that could show it wrong.
questions.rule: Give each theory its own test, read the result honestly, and change course when it points elsewhere.

questions.q: A gardener thinks her roses wilt from too little water. A bed given extra water still wilts. Which next move matches a strong story?
options: Water the roses still more, since the first test must have been too weak
Replace every rose in the garden before checking anything else
Set the theory aside and test the next suspect, such as soil drainage
Decide the plants are unlucky and stop looking into it any further
optionExplain: Dismissing a negative result without evidence is not objective.
That abandons investigation for a drastic reset.
Right: the result changes the direction of inquiry.
Giving up leaves the cause unfound.
questions.explain: In the mid-level story, instrumenting the sync process showed the timeouts occurred on the engineer's own side and the requests never reached the warehouse APIs, which overturned the network theory.
questions.teaches: In the inventory story, timing data showed the timeouts were happening on the engineer's own side, because the requests never reached the external APIs, which overturned the network theory.
questions.rule: Give each theory its own test, read the result honestly, and change course when it points elsewhere.

questions.q: A payment fails only when three teams' services interact. Which first move best fits a strong cross-system approach?
options: Restart your own service and see whether the other two settle down after it
Map which services and teams the request passes through
Ask each team to confirm that their own service is working properly
Wait for the failures to stop appearing in the production monitoring
optionExplain: Restarting your own part treats the symptom in the part you own.
Right: dependencies have to be mapped before the failure can be placed.
Each team will probably answer yes; the problem lies between them.
Waiting leaves the cause where it is.
questions.explain: A failure between components calls for a picture of how they connect. The card next sets out what a strong story shows.
questions.rule: Map the dependencies, work across team lines, and combine what each part of the system tells you.

questions.q: Strong cross-system answers show you mapping ____, working across team lines and pulling information from different parts of the system.
questions.explain: Mapping dependencies is the first of three skills the authors list for these answers.
questions.rule: Map dependencies, cross team lines.

questions.q: A nurse manager traces late discharges through the ward, the pharmacy and billing, with a separate team in each. Which line shows cross-system skill?
options: I plotted each patient's waits in all three areas and compared notes
I reminded the ward to complete its own forms earlier each morning
I asked the pharmacy to speed up since it seemed to be the slowest place to me
I wrote a long report about the delays in the ward I managed
optionExplain: Right: she mapped the path across areas and gathered input from each.
That works only within the part she owned.
A guess about one area is not a view of the whole path.
A report limited to her own ward misses the other two areas.
questions.explain: The skill is seeing and following the whole path, including parts you do not own.
questions.rule: Map the dependencies, work across team lines, and combine what each part of the system tells you.

questions.q: True or false: a strong cross-system answer can be given even when you owned only one of the components involved.
questions.explain: These questions explicitly cover problems where you did not own all the components. The answer shows you gathering information from the other teams to see the whole problem.
questions.rule: Owning one part does not stop you pursuing the whole.

questions.q: A candidate says: I proved my component was fine, so I closed the ticket although users still saw failures. What is the flaw?
options: It should have been closed earlier to avoid wasting engineering time
It overlooked that proving a component fine needs a manager's signature
It stops at the edge of her own domain and does not follow the issue on
It relies too much on other teams to confirm whether she was right
optionExplain: Closing early abandons a problem still affecting users.
Sign-off is not the missing element.
Right: the problem lived between systems.
She did not involve other teams at all, which is the flaw.
questions.explain: A cross-system story shows you following the problem past your own boundary.
questions.rule: Map the dependencies, work across team lines, and combine what each part of the system tells you.

questions.q: An airline analyst pursues delayed baggage across the check-in, loading and customs teams. What does the book say interviewers want to see in such a story?
options: That you can finish the investigation faster than the other teams could manage
That you can manage organizational and technical complexity end to end
That you can take over the responsibilities of the other teams involved
That you avoid depending on other teams for any information at all today
optionExplain: Speed against other teams is not the point.
Right: end-to-end understanding is what these questions target.
Taking over is not the skill described.
The skill is combining information, not avoiding it.
questions.explain: The authors say these questions probe whether you can manage organizational and technical complexity to understand an issue end to end.
questions.teaches: Cross-system questions look for evidence that you can manage organizational and technical complexity to understand an issue end to end.
questions.rule: Map the dependencies, work across team lines, and combine what each part of the system tells you.

questions.q: Of the four signals interviewers look for, which one is treated as critical?
options: Asking for help as soon as a problem looks hard enough
Turning each investigation into a write-up for the whole team
Fixing the visible symptom as fast as the team can manage
Methodical investigation of the problem
optionExplain: Knowing when to ask is rated strong, not critical.
Learning from investigation is the supporting signal.
Quick fixes are what the signals are contrasted against.
Right: it is the signal the authors rank highest.
questions.explain: A guess here is fair; the card next gives all four and their weights.
questions.rule: Build each story around methodical investigation first, and let the other three signals add to it.

questions.q: Match each signal to the question it answers.
pairs: Do you use a repeatable method to gather evidence and test theories?
Can you trace a problem to its source?
Recognizing when to ask for help
Do you know productive struggle from wasted time?
Can you turn what you learned into knowledge others can use?
questions.explain: Each signal tests a different part of how you handle a problem.
questions.rule: Four signals, four questions.

questions.q: A candidate's story has insightful post-incident write-ups but no clear method of investigation. Which signal is weak, and how much does it matter?
options: Learning from investigation, the critical signal, so the gap matters most
Asking for help, a strong signal, so the gap matters moderately here
Methodical investigation, the critical signal, so the gap matters
Symptoms and causes, the supporting signal, so the gap matters little
optionExplain: Learning is the supporting signal, and the write-ups show it.
Nothing in the story concerns asking for help.
Right: write-ups are supporting evidence that cannot make up for a missing method.
That signal is rated strong, not supporting.
questions.explain: The critical signal is the method itself; strengths in a supporting signal do not replace it.
questions.rule: Build each story around methodical investigation first, and let the other three signals add to it.

questions.q: Which two signals do the authors rate as strong?
options: Methodical investigation
Distinguishing symptoms from causes
Recognizing when to ask for help
Learning from investigation
Speed of restoring service
optionExplain: This one is rated critical, a level above strong.
Right: it is one of the two strong signals.
Right: it is the other strong signal.
This one is rated supporting, a level below strong.
Speed of restoring service is not one of the four signals.
questions.explain: Two signals sit at the strong level: telling symptoms from causes, and recognizing when to ask for help.
questions.rule: Build each story around methodical investigation first, and let the other three signals add to it.

questions.q: A candidate says: the key to scoring well is writing great post-mortems. What does the ranking suggest?
options: It is correct, since learning from investigation is the critical signal here
Post-mortems are supporting; methodical investigation is the critical signal
It is wrong, since writing anything down counts against a candidate
It is correct, since the strong signals depend on documents more than on actions
optionExplain: The critical signal is methodical investigation.
Right: write-ups matter, but not as much as the method.
Writing up findings is explicitly part of the supporting signal.
No signal depends on documents more than on actions.
questions.explain: Post-mortems help, but the weight sits with how you investigated.
questions.rule: Build each story around methodical investigation first, and let the other three signals add to it.

questions.q: A lab technician wants to impress with an unexplained result. Which behaviour matches the critical signal?
options: A polished slide deck summarizing the surprising result for management teams
Quick replacement of the equipment that produced the odd reading in the lab
Frequent requests to senior staff for their opinion of the result
A repeatable way to collect evidence and test hypotheses
optionExplain: A summary is communication, not method.
Replacement is a quick fix with no evidence behind it.
Asking others is a separate strong signal, not the critical one.
Right: method is the critical signal in any field.
questions.explain: The authors say the strongest candidates show they can investigate issues methodically and build lasting solutions.
questions.teaches: The strongest candidates show interviewers that they can investigate issues methodically and build lasting solutions.
questions.rule: Build each story around methodical investigation first, and let the other three signals add to it.

questions.q: Which detail in a story best signals a repeatable approach to an unknown problem?
options: I changed one factor at a time to see which one mattered
I kept a calm manner while everyone around me was worried about it
I worked late for several days in a row until the problem went away
I tried whichever fix a colleague had used on a similar problem before
optionExplain: Right: changing one thing at a time is how variables are isolated.
Calm helps, but it is not a method of investigation.
Effort and hours say nothing about how the work was organized.
Copying a fix applies someone else's answer without investigating this case.
questions.explain: A method changes things in a controlled way so that results can be read. The card next names the elements.
questions.rule: Show a repeatable method: isolate variables, test with designed experiments, and build the picture step by step.

questions.q: Strong stories show you isolating variables, designing useful ____ and building your picture incrementally.
questions.explain: Designed experiments are the middle element: tests built to tell the possible causes apart.
questions.rule: Isolate, test, build up.

questions.q: Sort each statement into one that shows a repeatable method or one that shows guesswork.

items.t: I held traffic constant and changed only the cache size
I designed a test that would split the possible causes in two
I added one piece of evidence at a time until a pattern showed
I changed three settings at once and one of them helped
I followed a hunch that happened to work
I rebooted everything and the fault went away

questions.explain: A repeatable method controls what changes so that a result points to a cause.
questions.rule: Show a repeatable method: isolate variables, test with designed experiments, and build the picture step by step.

questions.q: You change three settings together and the fault disappears. What does the story now lack?
options: Any proof that the fault was ever present before the changes
Any way to tell which of the three changes made the difference
Any sign of effort, since three changes take little time to try
Any link to a result, since the fault is no longer being seen
optionExplain: The fault was observed; the gap lies in what fixed it.
Right: isolating variables is what lets a result point to one cause.
Effort is not the signal; control over what changed is.
The result is visible; the cause is what is unknown.
questions.explain: When several things change at once, a good result cannot be traced to one of them.
questions.rule: Show a repeatable method: isolate variables, test with designed experiments, and build the picture step by step.

questions.q: A candidate says: I trust my gut, so I do not write down what I try. How does this fit the critical signal?
options: It fits well, since instinct is faster than any written method
It fits well, since gut feel is a form of testing hypotheses
It fails only because the candidate has not been asked a question
It shows no evidence-based approach that anyone could repeat
optionExplain: Speed from instinct is not the signal the authors describe.
A hypothesis needs a test; a feeling is not one.
The question is the setting; the flaw is the missing method.
Right: a method has to be reproducible and rest on evidence.
questions.explain: The signal rewards a repeatable way of gathering evidence, which a gut-led approach cannot show.
questions.rule: Show a repeatable method: isolate variables, test with designed experiments, and build the picture step by step.

questions.q: A homeowner's heating cuts out. Logging each outage shows it happens at the same time every day. What does that regularity suggest?
options: A scheduled or timed cause, rather than a random fault
A fault in the thermostat, since thermostats always fail at set times
A random fault, since patterns only appear by chance in a log
A problem with the log itself, since logs create the patterns they show
optionExplain: Right: a fixed pattern points to something running on a timetable.
The regularity does not single out the thermostat.
A pattern repeating at one time of day argues against chance.
Nothing suggests the log is inventing the pattern.
questions.explain: In the entry-level story, logging every stage with timestamps showed records vanishing exactly two hours after import, which pointed to something scheduled rather than a random bug.
questions.teaches: In the entry-level story, timestamps on every stage showed that records disappeared exactly two hours after import, which pointed to something scheduled rather than a random bug.
questions.rule: Show a repeatable method: isolate variables, test with designed experiments, and build the picture step by step.

questions.q: Mismatched figures keep appearing in a monthly report. Which finding is closest to a source rather than a symptom?
options: The totals differ by a few percent each month in the report
Staff keep spending hours correcting the totals before each meeting
Two intake forms let different versions of the same record through
Managers complain that they cannot trust the figures in the report
optionExplain: That describes the symptom itself, not why it happens.
Correction effort is a workaround and does not explain the cause.
Right: it explains why the mismatches appear in the first place.
Complaints are another sign of the symptom.
questions.explain: A source explains why the symptom appears. The card next describes how to show it.
questions.rule: Name the symptom, show how you traced it to its source, and fix that.

questions.q: Interviewers want to hear about your ability to trace problems to their ____.
questions.explain: Tracing to the source is where the authors say real fixes begin.
questions.rule: Real fixes start at the source.

questions.q: Sort each item into a symptom or a source.

items.t: Intermittent checkout failures
Customers see mismatched totals
Pages load slowly in the evening
A nightly job that overwrites a table the day shift relies on
A setting copied wrongly into one region's configuration
A step in intake that lets duplicate records through

questions.explain: Symptoms are what people notice; sources are what produce them.
questions.rule: Name the symptom, show how you traced it to its source, and fix that.

questions.q: An obvious fix works for a week and then the failures return. What does that suggest?
options: The fix was correct but the weather changed the behaviour of the system
The failures are random and cannot be explained by any single cause
The fix should be applied again each week as routine maintenance
It treated a symptom, and the source is still in place
optionExplain: Nothing in the case points to outside conditions.
A pattern of return suggests a cause, not randomness.
Reapplying a fix on a timetable keeps treating the symptom.
Right: a returning problem points to an untouched cause.
questions.explain: If a problem returns, the fix probably addressed the surface, which is why the signal prizes tracing to source.
questions.rule: Name the symptom, show how you traced it to its source, and fix that.

questions.q: Describing a fix, a candidate says: the errors stopped, so we knew the cause. What is the flaw?
options: Errors stopping shows only that the symptom went away
Errors stopping is no sign of anything, since logs are unreliable
Candidates should never claim to know any cause with certainty
The candidate should have waited longer before looking for the cause
optionExplain: Right: the symptom can stop while the cause remains.
The flaw is the inference, not the reliability of logs.
The issue is the missing evidence, not claiming certainty.
Waiting is not what separates symptoms from causes.
questions.explain: Disappearance of a symptom is not evidence about its source.
questions.rule: Name the symptom, show how you traced it to its source, and fix that.

questions.q: A data team finds mismatched numbers whenever two departments key the same customer by hand. Which of the book's examples of a source does this match?
options: A race condition that causes intermittent failures
An architectural decision that creates a bottleneck
A workflow gap that produces data inconsistencies
A network fault that drops requests between two buildings
optionExplain: No timing conflict is described; two people enter the same data.
No design limit on throughput is described in this case.
Right: the gap between two hand-keyed processes produces the mismatches.
The case has no network element and the book does not list that example.
