questions.explain: The book gives three examples of sources: a race condition behind intermittent failures, an architectural decision behind performance bottlenecks, and a workflow gap behind data inconsistencies.
questions.teaches: The authors' examples of sources are a race condition causing intermittent failures, an architectural decision behind performance bottlenecks, and a workflow gap producing data inconsistencies.
questions.rule: Name the symptom, show how you traced it to its source, and fix that.

questions.q: In a story, which reason for asking for help is the most convincing?
options: I wanted someone else to share the blame if the fix turned out wrong
I needed business rules that only the original developer knew
My manager told me to ask someone, so I did without thinking further
I had another meeting and could not carry on working on the bug
optionExplain: That is about risk to yourself, not about unblocking the problem.
Right: it names a concrete gap that someone else could fill.
Following an instruction does not show your own judgment.
A scheduling clash does not explain why help was needed.
questions.explain: The convincing reason is a specific gap that someone else could close. The card next lists the reasons the book gives.
questions.rule: Say what stopped you, why someone else could unblock it, and who you went to.

questions.q: Which reasons does the chapter give for bringing in help?
options: You lacked access or permissions
You needed others' domain expertise
Your current approach hit a dead end
You wanted to finish before a holiday
A colleague asked to join the effort
optionExplain: Right: lacking access or permissions is one of the examples.
Right: calling on others' domain expertise is another.
Right: realizing the approach has hit a dead end is the third.
A holiday is a personal schedule matter, not a reason the chapter gives.
Being asked to join is not the kind of self-judgment the signal shows.
questions.explain: The chapter's three reasons all describe you recognizing a gap that someone else can fill.
questions.rule: Say what stopped you, why someone else could unblock it, and who you went to.

questions.q: A data analyst cannot see a restricted table. Which line shows this signal?
options: I lacked access, so I asked the table's owner for a view
I rebuilt an approximate table from the reports that I could still open
I waited until someone noticed that the analysis had not been finished
I assumed the table matched last year's figures and moved on to the rest
optionExplain: Right: it names the gap and the person who could close it.
Working around the gap avoids the question of who can help.
Waiting for others to notice shows no judgment.
An assumption fills the gap with a guess.
questions.explain: Naming the missing access and going to the person who holds it is the pattern the authors describe.
questions.rule: Say what stopped you, why someone else could unblock it, and who you went to.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate who tried several things for a while before asking for help shows the balance of independence and efficiency.
questions.explain: The signal contrasts productive struggle with wasted time, so some digging has to come before the ask.
questions.rule: Dig first, then ask.

questions.q: A candidate says: I asked nobody and solved it alone over a week, which shows independence. How does the chapter read this?
options: As the strongest possible example, since nobody else helped
As poor, only because the solution took more than one working day
A week alone may be wasted time; the balance is missing
As unhelpful, because no team members were mentioned in the story
optionExplain: The chapter wants balance, not isolation for its own sake.
The chapter sets no fixed time limit.
Right: independence has to be balanced with efficiency.
Mentioning people is not the issue; recognizing when help would have saved time is.
questions.explain: Independence for its own sake can be wasted time; the signal is knowing when asking is quicker.
questions.rule: Say what stopped you, why someone else could unblock it, and who you went to.

questions.q: A paralegal spent two hours with an old filing system. Which sentence follows the pattern of the book's sample line?
options: After two hours on the old filing system, I gave up and asked to be moved to another task
After two hours on the old filing system, I saw I needed its author's knowledge, so I found them
After two hours on the old filing system, I asked everyone in the office at the same time
After two hours on the old filing system, I decided to rebuild all of it from scratch
optionExplain: Quitting is not the same as bringing in the right expertise.
Right: it names the time spent, the gap and the person found.
Asking everyone shows no sense of who could actually help.
Rebuilding avoids the question of who understands the old design.
questions.explain: The book's sample says that after two hours debugging the legacy billing system, the engineer realized she needed someone who understood the business logic and found the original developer to explain the design decisions.
questions.teaches: In the book's sample line, after two hours debugging a legacy billing system the engineer realized she needed someone who understood the business logic, and found the original developer to explain the design decisions.
questions.rule: Say what stopped you, why someone else could unblock it, and who you went to.

questions.q: After fixing a rare bug, which extra step would most strengthen a story about it?
options: Fix the bug again quickly next time it appears in production
Keep the details private so competitors cannot copy the approach
Move on to the next task before the details start to fade from view
Share what was learned so that teammates can spot it sooner
optionExplain: Repeating a fix does not build team knowledge.
Hiding what you learned benefits no one on the team.
Moving on without a record loses what was learned.
Right: the knowledge then outlasts the single fix.
questions.explain: The strength comes from making the lesson reusable. The card next names three ways.
questions.rule: Leave something behind that the team can reuse: a write-up, a detection tool or a shared way of seeing the pattern.

questions.q: Match each way of sharing a lesson to what it gives the team.
pairs: A record of how the problem was solved
Building tools to detect similar issues
Faster detection of the same kind of problem
A way for others to recognize the pattern
questions.explain: Each route turns a private lesson into something the whole team can use.
questions.rule: Leave something behind that the team can reuse: a write-up, a detection tool or a shared way of seeing the pattern.

questions.q: Sort each action into one that shows learning from investigation or one that does not.

items.t: Added an alert that catches the same leak pattern early
Wrote a guide to the debugging steps and shared it with the team
Gave a short talk on how to recognize the pattern
Fixed the bug and told nobody how
Kept my notes in a private file
Restarted the service each time the leak returned

questions.explain: The signal needs the lesson to travel beyond you.
questions.rule: Leave something behind that the team can reuse: a write-up, a detection tool or a shared way of seeing the pattern.

questions.q: What separates this signal from having learned something yourself?
options: The lesson is stored in your head so you can answer questions on it
The lesson led you to ask for a new title or a larger area to own
The lesson is turned into knowledge that the whole team can use
The lesson took longer to learn than other issues you handled that year
optionExplain: Private knowledge does not help the rest of the team.
Seniority is not what this signal is about.
Right: sharing it makes it a team asset.
Duration of learning is not what makes it a team asset.
questions.explain: The signal is about shared knowledge, not private learning.
questions.rule: Leave something behind that the team can reuse: a write-up, a detection tool or a shared way of seeing the pattern.

questions.q: A candidate says: I learned a great deal from this bug myself, so I show this signal. What is missing?
options: Any sign the candidate felt proud of the result they had reached
Any sign the team gained, not only the candidate
Any mention of a certificate that records what the candidate learned
Any explanation of why the bug had been assigned to the candidate
optionExplain: Pride is a feeling and not a team benefit.
Right: the signal asks for knowledge others can use.
Certificates are not what the signal looks for.
Assignment is another matter, covered by initiative.
questions.explain: Personal learning is not enough; the signal looks for what others gained.
questions.rule: Leave something behind that the team can reuse: a write-up, a detection tool or a shared way of seeing the pattern.

questions.q: A vendor's update slowed eight services. Which follow-up best matches the senior-level story?
options: Ask each team to fix its own service and report back separately
Stop using the vendor's updates for the next financial year
Write a private note for the manager who first raised the issue
Set up a channel where teams share vendor discoveries
optionExplain: Separate fixes repeat work and share nothing.
A ban does not capture or share what was learned.
A private note helps one person, not the teams affected.
Right: it made later vendor problems quicker to deal with.
questions.explain: In the senior-level story, the channel proved valuable when two later vendor changes hit several teams, saving weeks of duplicated debugging.
questions.teaches: In the senior-level story, the cross-team channel for vendor issues proved valuable when a CDN provider's caching change and a database driver update each affected several teams, saving weeks of duplicated debugging.
questions.rule: Leave something behind that the team can reuse: a write-up, a detection tool or a shared way of seeing the pattern.

questions.q: Which sentence in a story would worry an interviewer the most?
options: I tried a cache flush, then a reboot, then a rollback, and the rollback worked
I suspected the cache because errors followed deploys, so I flushed it
I compared timings before and after the deploy and found the delay
I asked the on-call engineer which service had changed that morning
optionExplain: Right: it is a list of attempts with no reasoning behind them.
This gives a reason for the attempt, which is what is wanted.
This describes evidence-gathering rather than guessing.
This is a targeted question seeking evidence.
questions.explain: The worrying story is the one with no logic between steps. The card next names this the red flag.
questions.rule: Explain why you formed each hypothesis and what each experiment taught you, not just what finally worked.

questions.q: A story that tries fixes at random until one works shows a lack of ____ thinking.
questions.explain: The authors say random troubleshooting shows a lack of methodical thinking.
questions.rule: Reasoning, not luck.

questions.q: Which rewrite removes the flag from the story: I tried restarting, then clearing the queue, then rolling back, and rolling back worked?
options: I tried more fixes than anyone else on the team to be thorough about it
Errors began after a deploy, so I checked the queue, then the release
I rolled back first, since rolling back is the quickest fix to try
I tried everything on the checklist and the last one worked in the end
optionExplain: More attempts are still attempts without reasoning.
Right: each step has a reason and a lesson.
A single reason of speed does not explain the earlier steps.
Working through a checklist shows effort, not logic.
questions.explain: The rewrite supplies a hypothesis for each step and what the result taught.
questions.rule: Explain why you formed each hypothesis and what each experiment taught you, not just what finally worked.

questions.q: What if your story lists many attempts but names each hypothesis and what each experiment taught?
options: The flag applies in full, since a long list of attempts is always random
The flag applies more strongly, since many attempts suggest low skill
The flag becomes yellow, since naming hypotheses only weakens the story
The logic connecting the steps shows, so the story avoids the flag
optionExplain: The flag is about missing reasoning, not about the number of attempts.
Many attempts with reasons are a method and not a flaw.
The colours mark seriousness, not whether you named hypotheses.
Right: the authors ask for the reasoning behind each step.
questions.explain: Naming the hypothesis and the lesson of each step turns a list of attempts into a visible line of reasoning.
questions.rule: Reasons turn attempts into method.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate who says persistence is what matters, because they kept trying fixes until one worked, avoids the red flag.
questions.explain: Persistence without reasoned hypotheses shows no methodical thinking, which the authors call persistence without intelligence.
questions.rule: Persistence needs reasoning.

questions.q: A mechanic tried three parts in turn. Which description avoids the flag?
options: I started with the part the fault code named, then moved on after it failed
I replaced parts until the car ran, starting with whichever part came to hand first
I replaced all three parts together to be completely sure the fault was gone
I followed my usual routine because it has worked before on most of the cars
optionExplain: Right: each choice has a stated reason.
The order is arbitrary and unexplained.
Changing everything at once shows no reasoning about which mattered.
A routine is not a reason tied to this fault.
questions.explain: The book adds a condition: an I-tried-X-then-Y-then-Z story is acceptable when you can explain your reasoning for trying the solutions in that particular order.
questions.teaches: A story of trying X, then Y, then Z does not trigger the flag if you can explain your reasoning for trying those solutions in that particular order.
questions.rule: Explain why you formed each hypothesis and what each experiment taught you, not just what finally worked.

questions.q: A story ends: I increased the timeout and the errors stopped. How might an interviewer read it?
options: As proof that the candidate is willing to take bold decisions
As a sign that the candidate found the root cause immediately
As a hint that the candidate avoids hard debugging work
As a neutral detail that says nothing about the candidate's depth
optionExplain: Nothing in the story shows an investigation or a risk.
A longer timeout does not reveal a cause.
Right: the story stops at the surface.
Interviewers do read it as a sign of how far the candidate went.
questions.explain: Ending at the workaround leaves the interviewer wondering. The card next explains the yellow flag.
questions.rule: If you used a quick fix, show it was a stopgap that bought time for finding the cause.

questions.q: The book treats stopping at surface fixes as a ____ flag.
questions.explain: Surface fixes are a yellow flag: a concerning pattern that weakens a story.
questions.rule: Surface fixes weaken a story.

questions.q: Sort each story ending into one that stops at a surface fix or one that goes beyond it.

items.t: I restarted the service and the alerts stopped
I doubled the retry limit and the failures went away
I cleared the cache whenever the page stalled
I restarted it to buy time, then traced why it crashed
I added a temporary limit while I studied the cause of the overload
I found why the cache filled and removed the reason

questions.explain: A surface fix is acceptable as a first step; the flag is a story that ends there.
questions.rule: If you used a quick fix, show it was a stopgap that bought time for finding the cause.

questions.q: What if your quick fix was a deliberate stopgap while you investigated, and how would interviewers react?
options: It still counts as the flag, since any quick fix signals carelessness
It earns extra credit, since speed matters more than depth
It becomes a red flag, since a stopgap is always disguised random work
It can be fine, if you show it bought time for a proper investigation
optionExplain: The flag is about stopping there, not about using a stopgap.
The stopgap earns credit only because the investigation followed.
Nothing makes a deliberate stopgap into a red flag.
Right: the authors accept it when it was a temporary step.
questions.explain: A quick fix framed as temporary, followed by investigation, is the authors' recommended way to present it.
questions.rule: Say why the quick fix was temporary.

questions.q: A candidate ends: I restarted the service and it worked. There was nothing more to say. What is the flaw?
options: It leaves the cause unknown and sounds like avoiding hard work
It is too long, since a restart takes only a few seconds
It hides a weakness in the service that the candidate should have named
It should have mentioned the restart's date and time in the story
optionExplain: Right: restarting treats the symptom.
Length is not the issue; the missing cause is.
The weakness is in the story's depth, not in the service.
Timestamps do not supply a cause.
questions.explain: A story that ends at the restart shows nothing about why the service failed.
questions.rule: If you used a quick fix, show it was a stopgap that bought time for finding the cause.

questions.q: A facilities engineer resets a tripping breaker every night. Which move matches the opening story's engineer, who stared at the metrics at 2 AM?
options: Reset the breaker earlier each night so that no one at all is inconvenienced by it
Replace the breaker with a larger one so that it stops tripping, which settles the matter
Notice the trips fit no usual cycle and study the pattern before resetting
Ask the night staff to stop using the equipment at that hour of the night, then
optionExplain: That polishes the workaround and ignores the cause.
A larger breaker hides the symptom and may be unsafe.
Right: the opening engineer studied a pattern that did not fit.
Avoiding the trigger does not explain it.
questions.explain: In the opening story, restarting the service always worked, but the engineer noticed that the leak accelerated in time windows that did not match traffic, and kept investigating.
questions.teaches: In the opening story, the quick fix of restarting always worked, but the engineer noticed the leak accelerated in time windows that did not match traffic, and that unease started the deep dive.
questions.rule: If you used a quick fix, show it was a stopgap that bought time for finding the cause.

questions.q: A candidate spends most of the answer on clever profiling details and does not say what changed afterwards. What is the risk?
options: Interviewers will assume the candidate worked alone on the problem
Interviewers cannot see why the deep dive mattered
Interviewers will think the profiling tools were too basic for the task
Interviewers will think the problem was easier than it was described
optionExplain: Working alone or in a team is a separate question.
Right: the outcome is what justifies the depth.
The tools are not what is at issue.
The risk is not about difficulty but about missing outcomes.
questions.explain: Cleverness alone does not show value. The card next explains the yellow flag.
questions.rule: Tie every deep dive to what improved because of it, in addition to how you found it.

questions.q: Going deep is valuable only when it leads to meaningful ____.
questions.explain: Depth is justified by what it improves.
questions.rule: Depth must lead somewhere.

questions.q: Which closing line best ties a deep dive to impact?
options: After the fix, the nightly export stopped failing and support lost its Monday ticket queue
The profiler output covered nine separate layers, which took considerable skill
I enjoyed learning the internals of the scheduler during the investigation
The final patch changed forty lines across three different files in the codebase
optionExplain: Right: it names what changed for real people.
This restates the technical depth without any outcome.
Personal enjoyment is not an improvement for the business.
A count of changes is not an outcome.
questions.explain: Impact is expressed in changes to outcomes for users, the team or the business.
questions.rule: Tie every deep dive to what improved because of it, in addition to how you found it.

questions.q: The deep dive removed the cause of recurring outages, but the story does not mention it. What follows?
options: Interviewers will assume the outages continued after the work
Interviewers will treat the technical details as more impressive
Interviewers lose the main reason the work mattered
Interviewers will give extra credit for modesty about the result
optionExplain: They may assume little, which is the problem, not that outages continued.
Technical detail without outcome is the very flag described.
Right: removing the outages is the impact, and it has been left out.
Hiding the result does not earn credit.
questions.explain: An outcome that is not told cannot count for anything.
questions.rule: Tie every deep dive to what improved because of it, in addition to how you found it.

questions.q: A candidate says: talking only about the intricate debugging proves my depth. What is the flaw?
options: It shows too little detail for the interviewer to follow the story
It shows cleverness but not why the work mattered to anyone
It shows an interest in debugging, which the interviewers dislike
It shows the candidate has been avoiding talking about teamwork
optionExplain: The flag is about too little impact, not too little detail.
Right: the authors want the outcome as well.
Interest in debugging is not penalised.
Teamwork is a different matter from outcomes.
questions.explain: Depth has to be connected to results.
questions.rule: Tie every deep dive to what improved because of it, in addition to how you found it.

questions.q: A data analyst finished a deep dive into bad survey data. Which closing facts would show impact, following the book?
options: The cause of the faulty reports was removed
An estimate of the analyst hours saved each month
Evidence that the survey respondents' experience improved
The list of statistical packages used
The number of rows examined along the way
optionExplain: Right: removing the cause of the problem is one of the book's examples.
Right: an estimate of hours saved is another of its examples.
Right: evidence of improved experience for users is the third example.
Tools used describe the work and not what it achieved.
A row count describes effort, not an outcome.
questions.explain: The book suggests asking whether the work eliminated the problem, how many engineering hours it likely saved, and whether the user experience improved.
questions.teaches: The book's examples of impact are eliminating the problem behind outages, an estimate of the engineering hours the work should save, and evidence of an improved user experience.
questions.rule: Tie every deep dive to what improved because of it, in addition to how you found it.

questions.q: A candidate says: I kept digging for three weeks and reached no conclusion. Which flag does this raise?
options: Random troubleshooting, because many attempts were made over time
Stopping at surface fixes, because no fix was ever delivered
Technical depth without impact, because the details were too clever
Analysis paralysis, because the investigation produced no action
optionExplain: The weeks of digging are not random attempts.
The pattern is too much depth, not too little.
The issue here is the missing conclusion.
Right: endless investigation without conclusions is the pattern.
questions.explain: More investigation did not lead to a decision. The card next names this pattern.
questions.rule: Show the constraint you weighed and the point at which more digging would not have changed what you did.

questions.q: Match each flag pattern to its description.
pairs: Trying solutions without reasoning until one works
Getting the system working again without knowing why it broke
Intricate details not connected to meaningful outcomes
questions.explain: The four flags cover the ways a problem-solving story can go wrong, from too little reasoning to too much digging.
questions.rule: Show the constraint you weighed and the point at which more digging would not have changed what you did.

questions.q: Sort each statement into good stopping judgment or analysis paralysis.

items.t: More data would not have changed the fix, so I acted
I stopped once I could name the cause with enough confidence to act
I weighed the deadline against the value of a fuller picture
I wanted every possible cause ruled out before doing anything
I kept following new threads each week without a decision
I could not act until the picture was complete in every detail

questions.explain: Good judgment stops when more digging will not change the plan.
questions.rule: Show the constraint you weighed and the point at which more digging would not have changed what you did.

questions.q: More digging would not change how you solve the problem. What should the story show?
options: That you kept going to be absolutely certain of every detail
That you asked a manager to decide when you should stop
That you saw more digging would not help, and moved on
That you stopped because the allotted hours for the task had run out
optionExplain: Perfect certainty is the trap the flag describes.
Handing off the judgment is not what the authors describe.
Right: recognizing the point where more depth changes nothing is the skill.
Running out of time is not the same as judging that depth would not help.
questions.explain: The authors want the decision to stop to be a judgment about whether going deeper would alter your approach.
questions.rule: Show the constraint you weighed and the point at which more digging would not have changed what you did.

questions.q: A candidate says: I stop investigating only when every possible cause has been ruled out. What is the flaw?
options: It stops too early, since ruling out every cause takes only a few days
It ignores the test of whether going deeper would change your approach
It relies on other people to confirm each cause that gets ruled out
It treats ruling out causes as less useful than finding a single cause
optionExplain: The statement describes stopping too late, not too early.
Right: the stopping point is a judgment about what more digging would change.
Nothing in the statement involves other people.
Ruling out causes can be useful; the flaw is the stopping rule.
questions.explain: A sound stopping rule asks whether more digging would alter what you do, not whether every cause is eliminated.
questions.rule: Show the constraint you weighed and the point at which more digging would not have changed what you did.

questions.q: A planner delays a purchase until her data is perfect, and the vendor's offer expires. Which book observation applies?
options: Waiting longer is usually wise because decisions are hard to reverse
The planner should have asked a colleague to finish the data analysis
The planner was right, since incomplete data always leads to errors
It is not always necessary to achieve a complete picture, and it often is not economical
optionExplain: The authors argue for acting once enough is known.
Handing off the work does not address the judgment problem.
The authors do not accept that a complete picture is required.
Right: waiting for completeness has a cost.
questions.explain: The authors say it is not always necessary to achieve a complete picture of a problem, and it often is not economical to try.
questions.teaches: It is not always necessary to achieve a complete picture of a problem, and it often is not economical to try.
questions.rule: Show the constraint you weighed and the point at which more digging would not have changed what you did.

questions.q: How long should a headline, three key points and a landing take to tell?
options: About two minutes of focused telling
About ten seconds, a brief reply
About five minutes, covering each step
As long as the full detail takes
optionExplain: Right: it is long enough for substance and short enough to follow.
That is too short to carry three key points.
The book wants a focused core of about two minutes.
An open-ended telling loses the interviewer.
questions.explain: The authors keep the core short and let follow-ups lead. The card next shows the examples.
questions.rule: Tell the story as a headline, three key points and a landing in about two minutes, and let follow-ups lead after that.

questions.q: Match each level's example to the real problem it uncovered.
pairs: A deduplication service whose matching threshold was too low
A race condition that created duplicate sync jobs
A monitoring agent uploading metrics on every request
questions.explain: In every example the visible problem was a symptom of something less obvious.
questions.rule: Tell the story as a headline, three key points and a landing in about two minutes, and let follow-ups lead after that.

questions.q: Which is a headline in the book's style for a story about a flaky upload feature?
options: I am going to tell you about a project that I worked on last year
I traced upload failures that looked like network drops to a retry bug in our client
Uploads failed, so we kept trying different fixes until they worked
My team and I met every week to review the upload feature together
optionExplain: It announces a story but gives no content.
Right: it states the surface problem and the real cause in one sentence.
It describes random troubleshooting, which the book flags.
It names a routine and not a problem or a discovery.
questions.explain: A headline names the problem and the twist in one sentence.
questions.rule: Tell the story as a headline, three key points and a landing in about two minutes, and let follow-ups lead after that.

questions.q: What do all four example stories have in common?
options: Each one was solved without help from any other person at work
Each one ended with a quick restart that restored normal service
Each one involved a team of at least ten engineers across offices
The visible problem was a symptom of a different underlying cause
optionExplain: Several of the stories involve asking others for help.
Each ends with a root-cause fix.
Team size varies, and the entry-level story is one person's work.
Right: each uncovers a real cause beneath the first explanation.
questions.explain: The stories differ in scope but share the move from symptom to cause.
questions.rule: Tell the story as a headline, three key points and a landing in about two minutes, and let follow-ups lead after that.

questions.q: True or false: after the two-minute core, the book expects you to keep going until the story is finished before taking any question.
questions.explain: After two minutes the conversation flows naturally, led by the interviewer's follow-ups.
questions.rule: Core first, then follow-ups.

questions.q: A candidate gives eight minutes of unbroken detail with no landing. What is wrong by the book's shape?
options: It lacks a focused core and a landing, so key contributions are hard to capture
It has too many details about the customers who were affected
It is correct, since interviewers like to hear every step
It breaks the rule that a story must name three separate teams
optionExplain: Right: the structure exists to make contributions easy to capture.
Customer detail is not what the structure addresses.
The authors want a focused core of about two minutes.
No such rule exists in the chapter.
questions.explain: A long, shapeless telling buries the contributions the interviewer needs.
questions.rule: Tell the story as a headline, three key points and a landing in about two minutes, and let follow-ups lead after that.

questions.q: A hospital operations lead describes cutting failed discharges. Which landing best follows the staff-level story's pattern?
options: A reminder that the team worked very hard through many long weeks of the project
A list of the departments and staff who attended the final project meeting
A measured fall in failures, similar flaws found elsewhere, and an early-warning dashboard
A statement that the lead was glad to have been asked about the project at all
optionExplain: Effort is not a result.
Attendance does not show an outcome.
Right: result, wider discovery and lasting mechanism.
Gratitude is not a landing.
questions.explain: In the staff-level landing, failed orders fell from 50 a day to under 1 over eight months, the effort exposed 8 other workflows with similar flaws, and a system health dashboard was built to catch such issues early.
questions.teaches: The staff-level landing reports failed orders falling from about 50 a day to under 1 over eight months, 8 other workflows with similar flaws found, and a system health dashboard built to catch such issues early.
questions.rule: Tell the story as a headline, three key points and a landing in about two minutes, and let follow-ups lead after that.

questions.q: You cannot think of a problem-solving story. Where should you look first?
options: The project where you finished first and had the least trouble
The largest outage in the company, even if you only watched it
A task from your job description that you completed on schedule
A bug that stumped others or that you took well past the quick fix
optionExplain: Smooth work gives little to show about investigation.
A story needs your own investigation, not an event you observed.
Routine tasks rarely show depth.
Right: such investigations are the best raw material.
questions.explain: The stories come from confusing situations. The card next lists where to look.
questions.rule: Mine the confusing situations you worked through, and match each one to the signal it shows.

questions.q: Match each kind of memory to what it shows.
pairs: An intermittent bug that others had given up on
Finding the real issue differed from everyone's assumption
Creating tools or documentation to help others
questions.explain: Each kind of memory points to a different strength.
questions.rule: Mine the confusing situations you worked through, and match each one to the signal it shows.

questions.q: Which memory is the best raw material for a problem-solving story?
options: A flaky test nobody could reproduce, which you traced to a timing issue
A routine update that you applied to all servers on a quiet afternoon
A meeting at which you presented the quarterly plan to the director
A tool you installed after seeing it recommended by a colleague
optionExplain: Right: it is a confusing situation where you went deeper than the quick fix.
A routine update involves no investigation.
Presenting a plan is not an investigation.
Installing a tool shows no problem to dig into.
questions.explain: Pick the moment that required you to work out why.
questions.rule: Mine the confusing situations you worked through, and match each one to the signal it shows.

questions.q: True or false: a problem fixed with one quick change is stronger story material than an investigation that went well beyond a quick fix.
questions.explain: The authors say investigations that went well beyond quick fixes will often give you your best problem-solving stories.
questions.rule: Raw material needs a real investigation.

questions.q: A candidate says: I have no stories because no major outage ever happened to me. What is the flaw?
options: Stories can only come from outages in which the candidate led the response
Stories are not needed in problem-solving interviews at all
Stories come from confusing situations you worked through, not only from major outages
Stories must always come from a recent job rather than earlier ones
optionExplain: The chapter does not limit stories to outages.
The chapter says to prepare them.
Right: the chapter points to bugs and puzzles of all sizes.
The chapter sets no such limit.
questions.explain: A small but baffling bug can produce a strong story.
questions.rule: Mine the confusing situations you worked through, and match each one to the signal it shows.

questions.q: A candidate has solved problems only alone. Which of the book's reflection questions would help her find a new story?
options: When did you last finish a task before the deadline given to you?
When have you had to coordinate across teams to fully understand a problem?
Which tools in your editor have you customized most heavily so far?
How many hours do you usually spend on code review each week?
optionExplain: Deadlines are about delivery and not investigation.
Right: it is one of the book's prompts and opens up a different kind of story.
Editor customization is not a reflection prompt about problem-solving.
Review hours do not point to a story.
questions.explain: The book's prompts also ask about investigations done while juggling other urgent work, and documented investigation processes that became team standards.
questions.teaches: The book's reflection prompts also ask about investigations done while juggling other urgent work, and about investigation processes you documented that became team standards.
questions.rule: Mine the confusing situations you worked through, and match each one to the signal it shows.

questions.q: Which aim sits at the centre of strong problem-solving?
options: Seeking to understand root causes rather than only fixing symptoms
Fixing every reported problem as quickly as the team possibly can
Avoiding all risk by checking every possible cause before acting
Working alone so that nothing slows the investigation down at all
optionExplain: Right: it is the chapter's opening claim and its closing one.
Speed alone is the delivery habit the chapter contrasts it with.
That is the analysis-paralysis trap.
Isolation is itself one of the traps.
questions.explain: The centre is understanding causes. The card next sets out the full picture.
questions.rule: Show a method, the cause behind the symptom and a useful legacy, and avoid the traps of random attempts, surface fixes, impact-free detail, endless digging and isolation.

questions.q: Sort each item into something a strong story includes or a trap to avoid.

items.t: A clear investigation methodology
Tools or documentation that help others
A distinction between symptoms and root causes
Random attempts until something works
A surface fix with no reason given for stopping there
Technical detail with no link to impact

questions.explain: The traps are the mirror images of the strengths.
questions.rule: Show a method, the cause behind the symptom and a useful legacy, and avoid the traps of random attempts, surface fixes, impact-free detail, endless digging and isolation.

questions.q: Which closing best fits the takeaways?
options: I restarted the service each time and kept a log of how often it failed
I studied every part of the system for a month before making a decision
I traced it to a design flaw, fixed that, and wrote a guide so others can spot it
I tried many settings and one worked, so I left them all in place
optionExplain: A log of restarts treats the symptom.
That is endless investigation without a decision.
Right: cause, fix and a lasting legacy.
That is random attempts with no reasoning.
questions.explain: The takeaways combine root cause, practical action and shared knowledge.
questions.rule: Show a method, the cause behind the symptom and a useful legacy, and avoid the traps of random attempts, surface fixes, impact-free detail, endless digging and isolation.

questions.q: True or false: according to the takeaways, a quick fix is acceptable when you can explain why it was appropriate.
questions.explain: The authors allow a surface fix when you can explain why it was appropriate, for example to buy time for a deep dive.
questions.rule: A quick fix needs a reason.

questions.q: A candidate says: I investigated for a month so I could be certain before acting. Which trap is this?
options: Working in isolation when collaboration would have helped
Investigating endlessly without reaching actionable conclusions
Technical detail without a link to impact
Stopping at a surface fix with no reason given
optionExplain: The story does not mention how many people were involved.
Right: certainty at any cost is the trap.
The problem is the lack of a decision, not of impact.
The candidate went too deep, not too shallow.
questions.explain: A month of digging with no action is the endless investigation the chapter warns about.
questions.rule: Show a method, the cause behind the symptom and a useful legacy, and avoid the traps of random attempts, surface fixes, impact-free detail, endless digging and isolation.

questions.q: A school IT admin fixed a printer fault. Which closing is the strongest evidence of prevention?
options: The printer was repaired on the same day, as users had asked for
The admin wrote a long email describing the repair to the headteacher
The admin agreed to look at the printer again if it broke once more
The fault never came back, and a warning she set caught a similar one
optionExplain: A same-day repair is delivery and not prevention.
An email is communication, not evidence of prevention.
Agreeing to repeat the fix is the opposite of prevention.
Right: the problem no longer occurs and a developing one was stopped.
questions.explain: The authors want specific examples where deep knowledge prevented future problems, such as similar problems no longer occurring, or a problem you could see developing that never came about because of your solution.
questions.teaches: Strong stories give specific examples where deep knowledge prevented future problems, for instance similar problems no longer occurring, or a developing problem that never came about because your solution made sure of it.
questions.rule: Show a method, the cause behind the symptom and a useful legacy, and avoid the traps of random attempts, surface fixes, impact-free detail, endless digging and isolation.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: True or false: Earning trust and dealing with conflict are the same skill under two names.
questions.explain: The authors call them closely related but distinct skills. The card next shows how they differ.
questions.rule: Related is not the same as identical.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: Match each term to the way the authors describe it.
pairs: A proactive skill that builds over time
A reactive process that starts when a disagreement arises
Challenging ideas while respecting others' expertise
Build trust that lets them engage in healthy conflict
questions.explain: Trust is built ahead of time through consistent behavior, conflict handling responds to disagreement as it appears, and strong performers link the two.
questions.rule: Trust is proactive; conflict handling is reactive.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: Sort each action by the skill it mainly shows.

items.t: Delivering the feature you promised by the date you promised
Admitting quickly that a release bug was yours
Helping a teammate finish a task they were stuck on
Working through a clash over which database to choose
Challenging a design choice while respecting its author's expertise
Settling a disagreement between two teams about priorities

questions.explain: The first three are consistent behaviors that others learn to rely on. The last three respond to a disagreement that is already in the room.
questions.rule: Trust is what you do steadily; conflict handling is what you do when views clash.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: Which statement best separates earning trust from dealing with conflict?
options: Trust matters with peers and managers, while conflict handling matters only with outside partners and clients
Trust is built ahead of time by consistent behavior, while conflict handling responds once a disagreement appears
Trust is about being liked by colleagues, while conflict handling is about winning the argument at hand
Trust is a fixed personality trait, while conflict handling is a skill that a person can learn and improve
optionExplain: Both skills apply with peers, managers and partners, so audience does not separate them.
Right: the book calls trust proactive and slow, and conflict handling reactive.
Being liked is not the book's definition of trust, and winning is not its aim in conflict.
The book treats both as skills shown through behavior, not as fixed traits.
questions.explain: The authors describe trust as proactive and time-based, and conflict management as a reactive process that starts when disagreements arise.
questions.rule: Trust comes first in time; conflict handling responds.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: A candidate says conflict skills are only needed when trust has failed, so trust stories can be skipped. What is the flaw?
options: Trust stories matter most because interviewers rarely ask about conflict at all in behavioral interviews
Conflict skills matter most because trust cannot be shown through stories and only conflict can be
Nothing is wrong, since a team without trust problems has no use for conflict skills in practice
The two feed each other: trust allows open disagreement, and well-handled conflict strengthens trust
optionExplain: The book includes whole groups of interview questions about both, so neither is rare.
Trust can be shown through stories of consistent behavior; the book gives examples.
Disagreement arises in teams that trust each other too, and trust is what makes it healthy.
Right: the authors say strong performers build trust that allows healthy conflict and handle conflict in ways that keep trust.
questions.explain: In the authors' view the skills reinforce each other, so treating them as unrelated misses how they work in practice.
questions.rule: Trust enables healthy conflict; healthy conflict can deepen trust.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: A new lead joins two squads that already distrust each other and trade blame. What does her situation call for?
options: Both skills at once: building trust from nothing while helping the squads work through their dispute
Conflict skills first, with trust-building postponed until the blame between the two squads has ended for good
Trust skills alone, because the dispute will fade once the squads come to like their new lead
Neither skill, because a newcomer has no history with the squads and should stay out of it
optionExplain: Right: she has no earned trust to draw on, so she must build it while resolving the dispute.
Waiting for the blame to end leaves the dispute running and gives the squads no reason to trust her.
Being liked does not resolve a disagreement, and the authors want the dispute worked through.
A newcomer is exactly the case the authors describe, and staying out lets the distrust continue.
questions.explain: Without prior trust, she cannot lean on credibility she has not yet earned, so she builds it through her behavior as she works through the conflict.
questions.rule: A newcomer into a conflict needs both skills together.
questions.teaches: The book notes that a person may come fresh into a conflict where trust has to be built from a starting point of zero, so the two skills can be needed at the same moment.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: A company's website says it values trust. What is that statement most useful for when you prepare?
options: Supplying exact sentences to repeat back in your answers
Telling you which conflicts to leave out of your stories
Suggesting which behaviors to show in your stories
Replacing the need to have a story of your own at all
optionExplain: Echoing the wording shows you read the page but gives no evidence of how you act.
Conflict stories are often exactly what trust-focused questions ask for.
Right: a value points toward behavior you can demonstrate.
Interviewers ask for evidence, and a value statement cannot stand in for your own story.
questions.explain: A value statement is a clue to what the company hopes to see. The card next shows how the book's three examples work.
questions.rule: Values point to behaviors.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: Match each company to how the book describes its trust and conflict value.
pairs: Listen attentively, speak candidly, treat others respectfully
Understand different perspectives and build trust through care
A careful balance between rigor and trust
questions.explain: Each company states the value in its own terms, and each can be turned into behavior a candidate shows in a story.
questions.rule: Same topic, three phrasings.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: You prepare for a firm that values empathy. Which story detail shows that value best?
options: You won a design debate with benchmark data and the other engineer conceded the point
You finished a large project two weeks ahead of schedule without needing any help
You asked a frustrated support lead about his team's pressures before proposing a new process
You told the panel that you personally consider empathy the most important quality
optionExplain: Winning with data may be strong, but it does not show understanding of another view.
Early delivery shows reliability, not care for colleagues' perspectives.
Right: it shows you seeking another person's perspective, which is what the Slack value describes.
Declaring a value is not the same as showing it through an action.
questions.explain: Empathy as the book describes it means understanding different perspectives, so the best detail is an action that does that.
questions.rule: Show the value as an action.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: A candidate opens every answer by reciting the employer's trust value word for word. What is the weakness?
options: The borrowed wording gives the interviewer no evidence of what the candidate actually did
Interviewers prefer candidates who have never read the employer's published statement of values
A value should be recited only once at the very end of the whole interview, never in answers
Reciting works for one company's wording but fails for the wording of any other company
optionExplain: Right (our reading): a story shows behavior; a recited phrase only shows that you read the page.
Knowing the values is useful preparation; the problem is using them in place of evidence.
Where the phrase sits matters less than whether a story stands behind it.
The issue is not which company's wording it is but that no behavior is shown.
questions.explain: Our reading: stories are the evidence that interviewers ask for, so a recited value adds little by itself.
questions.rule: A value without a story is only words.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: True or false: A company that values both rigor and trust would expect candidates to avoid strong disagreement.
questions.explain: Stripe's description pairs rigor, which includes strong disagreement, with trust. A candidate who avoided all disagreement would not show the balance.
questions.rule: Rigor and trust are meant to work together.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: At a firm that prizes rigor and trust, a candidate describes a heated design debate. Which closing line fits that firm best?
options: We argued hard for a week, and afterwards I kept my distance from her to avoid more friction
We never really argued, so the question of rigor against trust did not come up on that team
I proved the design wrong with data, which settled the matter for good in my favor
We argued hard for a week, and I never doubted she wanted the best outcome for the product
optionExplain: Keeping distance after a debate shows the relationship did not survive the rigor.
Avoiding the argument skips the rigor half of the balance.
Winning with data shows rigor but leaves out any trust in the other person's intent.
Right: it combines strong disagreement with trust in the other person's intentions.
questions.explain: The firm's statement pairs hard challenge with confidence in each other's good faith, so the best line shows both.
questions.rule: Argue hard and trust intent.
questions.teaches: Stripe's statement adds that, no matter how strong the disagreement, people should firmly trust each other's intentions.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: Trust is mainly built through a few grand gestures at key moments.
questions.explain: The authors say trust builds through many small moments. The card next shows which kinds of moments count.
questions.rule: Small and repeated beats large and rare.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Trust accumulates through hundreds of small ____, such as admitting you do not know an answer.
questions.explain: The authors stress that trust is not built by grand gestures but by many small moments.
questions.rule: Trust is built in small moments.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each action by its likely effect on trust, according to the authors' view.

items.t: Telling your lead on Monday that a deadline will slip
Saying you do not know the answer and offering to find out
Disagreeing politely with a design during a review
Hiding a delay until the morning of the release
Posting in the team channel that the other team caused the outage
Letting a mistake of yours sit until someone else finds it

questions.explain: The first three are the book's small moments: admitting a gap, delivering bad news promptly and disagreeing respectfully. The others do the opposite.
questions.rule: Prompt and honest builds trust; hiding and blaming erode it.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: What if Raj had posted only the backend team's bugs and kept his own quiet? (Our reading; the book does not say.)
options: Tension would ease faster, because both teams would then see the mobile team as the victim
The calming effect would shrink, since he would be asking others for openness he did not offer
Nothing would change, because the weekly sessions alone carry all of the effect on trust between the teams
Trust would grow, because pointing at the other side shows confidence in your own code
optionExplain: Blaming one side reproduces the blame game that had already broken trust.
Right: Raj's own admission is part of what de-escalated the tension.
The book credits his open posting, including his own bug, with an immediate calming effect.
Pointing only at others is how the teams were already behaving.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book highlights that he posted his own bug too, which suggests the openness only works when it runs both ways.
questions.rule: Openness has to include your own errors.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A manager plans one large offsite to repair months of blame between two teams. What does the card suggest about that plan?
options: An offsite can work only for remote teams, which have not had the chance to meet in person
Trust cannot be rebuilt at all once two teams have started blaming each other for problems
The plan would work if the most senior leaders of both teams were present throughout
A single event cannot replace the many small honest actions that actually build trust
optionExplain: Nothing in the book ties grand gestures to remote teams; the point is about accumulation.
Raj's story shows blame-ridden teams rebuilding trust, so the book does not call it impossible.
Seniority is not what builds trust; repeated behavior is.
Right: the authors say trust is not built through grand gestures but through accumulated small moments.
questions.explain: A big event is the kind of grand gesture the authors say trust does not depend on. Steady small actions do the work.
questions.rule: No single event replaces a record of small moments.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Two hospital departments blame each other for late lab results and keep their data private. Which first move mirrors Raj's approach?
options: Ask each department for its data first, then decide whose process caused the delays and report it
Share your own department's findings, errors included, then invite both sides to review cases together without blame
Ask management to name one owner for lab results so that blame has a clear and permanent target
Wait until relations improve before starting joint reviews of the hardest cases on the list
optionExplain: Collecting data to assign fault repeats the blame game; neither side has agreed to share.
Right: it uses open sharing, including your own faults, and a judgment-free session for both sides.
Assigning a single blame target does not rebuild the relationship between the departments.
Waiting leaves the pattern in place; Raj's joint sessions were what improved relations.
questions.explain: Raj began by sharing openly, then created a regular judgment-free place for both teams, and the sharing became mutual.
questions.rule: Go first with openness, then make it shared.
questions.teaches: In Raj's case the change came in stages: about two weeks after the first session the other team began sharing its own discoveries, after three months the teams debugged together, and the crash rate dropped significantly.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You must tell a teammate their design has a serious flaw. Which approach fits best?
options: Soften the message until the flaw is barely mentioned and the mood stays pleasant
Say it bluntly so that nobody can miss how serious the flaw really is
State the problem plainly, explain its impact and show that you value their work
Wait for the formal review so that a group, not you, delivers the news
optionExplain: Softening so far that the flaw is lost leaves the teammate unaware of a real problem.
Bluntness makes the point but can damage the relationship, whatever its honesty.
Right: it is clear about the problem and respectful of the person.
Delaying through a group lets the problem grow and avoids owning the message.
questions.explain: Good delivery keeps both the truth and the relationship. The card next gives the authors' balance.
questions.rule: Keep the truth and the relationship.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Match each way of delivering a message to its effect, per the authors.
pairs: Doing what you say you will do
Adds further to the trust you earn
questions.explain: The book pairs each style with its effect: harshness damages relationships, empty diplomacy damages credibility, and clear, kind honesty plus consistency builds trust.
questions.rule: Harsh strains, vague erodes, clear and kind builds.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A manager's launch date cannot be met. Which message reflects the authors' balance?
options: I do not see us hitting that date, and here is why; here is what we could ship by then
The date may be a little tight, but I am sure the team will do everything it can to get there
This date is unrealistic and the plan behind it was badly made, so we should restart
I will raise concerns about the date after launch, when everyone is less stressed
optionExplain: Right: it states the problem clearly, gives a reason and offers a way forward.
It sounds kind but hides the real message, so the manager may not hear that the date is at risk.
It is honest but attacks the plan's makers, which strains the relationship.
Delaying the message until after launch withholds it when it is most needed.
questions.explain: The best message is direct about the problem, explains it and stays constructive toward the person.
questions.rule: Clear, reasoned and constructive.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each review comment by the weakness it shows.

items.t: You wrote this without thinking
This is the worst design I have seen
Everyone knows this module is a mess because of you
Great work, nothing at all to change
Maybe, if you like, consider looking at it at some point
I am sure it is fine, so let us not dig into it

questions.explain: The first three are honest-sounding but harsh and personal. The last three avoid the substance, even though a flaw exists.
questions.rule: Neither harshness nor vagueness works.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate says: my feedback was brutal but honest, so trust grew. What is the flaw?
options: The authors say a harshly delivered message strains a relationship, however honest it is
Brutal feedback is wrong only when it is given in public, and the candidate gave it in private
Honesty has no place in building trust, which depends mainly on warmth and agreeable manners
Trust can grow only through repeated praise, so any criticism at all would have harmed it
optionExplain: Right: honesty alone is not enough; delivery matters.
The book does not limit the harm to public delivery; it says the harsh delivery itself strains the relationship.
The authors say trust sometimes requires hard truths, so honesty has a place.
Trust comes from clear and empathetic messages, not from praise alone.
questions.explain: In the authors' view, a hard truth earns trust only when it is delivered with clarity and empathy.
questions.rule: Honest is not enough; kind and clear matters too.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A designer's concern is dismissed by an engineer who finds it annoying. Which response fits the authors' advice on conflict?
options: Rank the concern by how often the designer raises concerns, then decide how much weight it gets
Agree with the designer in the meeting, then quietly ignore the concern afterwards
Address the substance of the concern and look for a fix, without attacking the person who raised it
Reply that the designer lacks the technical background to judge the issue in question
optionExplain: Judging the person instead of the concern is the personality focus the authors warn against.
Agreeing without acting is diplomacy with no substance, which erodes credibility.
Right: it focuses on the idea and on solving a legitimate concern.
Questioning the person's background attacks the person rather than the idea.
questions.explain: The authors say good conflict resolvers focus on ideas and outcomes rather than personalities and find solutions to legitimate concerns.
questions.rule: Fix the concern; do not attack the person.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, someone good at resolving conflict focuses on ideas and outcomes rather than personalities, and finds solutions that address legitimate concerns without attacking the people who raise them.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: One teammate wants to skip code review to save a day. Another wants a different naming style for a helper. Which do you contest harder?
options: The naming style, because inconsistent names are a form of quality problem
Skipping code review, because it touches a quality standard
Neither, because contesting anything with teammates damages the working relationship
Both equally, because a firm stance is only believable when applied evenly
optionExplain: Naming is closer to an implementation detail that can be adjusted.
Right: a quality standard is the kind of core value worth defending.
Healthy conflict is expected; avoiding all of it is a pattern the book warns about.
Treating every point as equal makes it hard to see what you truly care about.
questions.explain: Some points are worth defending and others are not. The card next gives the authors' test.
questions.rule: Not every point deserves the same push.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Effective professionals pick their battles based on ethics and ____.
questions.explain: The authors give ethics and impact as the basis for choosing which battles to fight.
questions.rule: Choose battles by ethics and impact.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each issue into worth standing firm on, or worth flexing on.

items.t: Merging code without any review
Shipping a feature that exposes customers' private data
Skipping tests for core payment logic
Which of two clear names a helper function gets
The order of sections in a design document
Which of two equal libraries formats the dates

questions.explain: Quality standards and ethical risks are core values. Names, document order and an equal choice of library are details where adjusting costs little.
questions.rule: Core values firm; details flexible.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a lead who refuses to change any decision builds more trust through clear principles.
questions.explain: The authors say clear principles build trust, but too much inflexibility stifles collaboration. Our reading: refusing every change therefore costs more than it gains.
questions.rule: Firmness on everything is rigidity.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate says: I gave way on a data-handling standard to keep the peace, and that built trust. What is the flaw?
options: Giving way is always a mistake in a disagreement, whatever the issue under discussion
Peace in a team is not a valuable goal, since good teams argue about everything
Trust is built only through winning arguments, so giving way cannot build any trust
Trust comes from clear boundaries on core values, so giving way on one weakens it
optionExplain: The book endorses compromise on areas that are not core, so giving way is not wrong in itself.
The book values healthy teams and collaboration, and does not ask for argument on everything.
Winning is not how the book says trust is built.
Right: the authors say clear principles and boundaries build trust.
questions.explain: Compromise suits flexible areas; a core standard is where a clear boundary does the trust-building.
questions.rule: Compromise on details, not on core values.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A volunteer coordinator insists every helper gets a safety briefing, yet lets them choose their own shifts. What does this show?
options: Inconsistency, because a coordinator who trusts helpers would not require any briefing at all
Firmness on a core value and flexibility on a detail, which is the skill the authors describe
Over-rigidity, because a flexible coordinator would let helpers decide about safety as well
Avoidance of conflict, because letting people pick shifts means she cannot say no to them
optionExplain: Requiring a briefing is the boundary, not a sign of distrust.
Right: safety is the firm point and shifts are a flexible detail.
Safety is the core value here; flexing on it would remove the boundary that builds trust.
She does say no where it matters and bends where it does not.
questions.explain: The coordinator separates what must hold from what can move, which is the skill the authors describe.
questions.rule: Hold the safety line; flex the schedule.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, you also build trust by making it clear to others what truly matters to you and why.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A flawless record with no admitted mistakes builds more trust than admitting mistakes early.
questions.explain: The authors say that admitting mistakes before others find them builds more trust than perfect execution. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Early admission outweighs flawless-looking execution.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Admitting your mistakes before others find them will build more trust than perfect ____.
questions.explain: The authors state that early admission builds more trust than perfect execution.
questions.rule: Early admission beats a perfect appearance.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You find an error in your analysis that nobody has noticed yet. Which action matches the authors' advice?
options: Correct it quietly in the next version, because nobody has yet been affected by the error
Wait and see whether anyone notices before you decide whether it is worth raising with them
Mention it only if a senior colleague asks about the numbers, to avoid distracting the team
Tell the team now, explain the error and say when the corrected result will be ready
optionExplain: A quiet fix hides the error and loses the trust that early admission would have built.
Waiting to see if you are caught is the opposite of admitting a mistake before others find it.
Waiting for a question makes disclosure depend on being asked, not on your own openness.
Right: you name the mistake before others find it and show you will fix it.
questions.explain: Early, calm admission with a plan is the behavior the authors say builds trust and safety.
questions.rule: Say it first and say how you will fix it.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each behavior by its effect on psychological safety.

items.t: Saying I am not sure and asking for help
Admitting you were wrong about an approach
Changing your plan after hearing feedback
Defending an error until someone proves it
Mocking a colleague's question in a meeting
Hiding a mistake to look flawless

questions.explain: Uncertainty, help-seeking, admitting error and adapting to feedback make it safe for others to do the same. The other three teach people to hide.
questions.rule: Safety grows when you show your gaps.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, changing your approach based on feedback shows weakness.
questions.explain: The authors call changing your approach based on feedback a strength, and it is part of what creates psychological safety.
questions.rule: Changing course after feedback is a strength.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A manager admitted she does not know the new grading system and asked for help. Now two teachers sharply disagree with her plan. What does the card suggest?
options: Welcome the pushback calmly, since her openness has made it safe for teachers to speak up
Treat the pushback as proof that admitting a gap cost her the team's confidence in her
Defend the plan firmly to restore her authority, since the admission has already weakened her standing
Postpone the plan until nobody disagrees, because open conflict now would undo her earlier admission
optionExplain: Right: safety to admit gaps tends to make disagreement possible and useful.
The authors say such admissions create safety that enables better collaboration, not loss of confidence.
Defending for authority's sake treats honesty as a weakness, which the authors reject.
Waiting for agreement avoids the healthy conflict that safety makes possible.
questions.explain: Her admission set up conditions where people can speak up, so the disagreement is a resource.
questions.rule: Safety makes disagreement useful.
questions.teaches: The authors add that when you handle vulnerable moments professionally, potential conflicts become moments that build deeper trust.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Which way of handling disagreement do you expect a young startup to value most?
options: Slow and routed through formal management channels, to protect existing relationships
Indirect, with careful avoidance of challenging leadership decisions in front of others
Direct and immediate, because there is little time for politics
Staged and committee-led, so that each objection receives a written formal reply first
optionExplain: That describes a traditional enterprise rather than a startup.
A flat startup structure tends to invite open challenge to leadership.
Right: startups want people who raise disagreements directly and then keep collaborating.
Committee processes are slower than the book describes for startups.
questions.explain: Organizations differ, and the card next sets out three types.
questions.rule: Match the style to the setting.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Match each type of organization to how it builds trust, per the authors.
pairs: Intense collaboration and shipping together under pressure
Slowly, through formal processes and proven reliability
questions.explain: Each type has its own route to trust, shaped by speed, scale and structure.
questions.rule: Startup: shared pressure. Large tech: consistency. Traditional: process.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate is applying to a traditional enterprise. Which story theme fits best?
options: Publicly challenging a senior leader's decision during an all-hands meeting
Skipping the approval chain to ship a change quickly and prove the process slow
Working within established norms while gently pushing for a positive change
Escalating a dispute straight to the executive team before talking to the other party
optionExplain: That fits a flat startup better than a hierarchy that favors management channels.
Bypassing process undermines the formal reliability these organizations prize.
Right: it respects existing relationships and norms while still improving things.
Skipping direct conversation goes against respecting existing relationships.
questions.explain: Traditional enterprises value people who respect existing relationships and improve them gradually.
questions.rule: Gentle change inside the norms.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each behavior by the organization where the authors say it fits best.

items.t: Disagree directly and then collaborate the same afternoon
Challenge a leadership decision openly in a flat structure
Show trust by shipping together under pressure
Find win-win solutions that acknowledge different team goals
Work through competing incentives across organizational boundaries
Keep relationships healthy across several teams with competing priorities

questions.explain: Startups reward direct, fast, shared-pressure behavior. Large tech companies reward finesse across many stakeholders and boundaries.
questions.rule: Startup: speed and directness. Large tech: finesse across teams.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A story about openly challenging a senior leader in a team meeting is the best fit for a traditional enterprise.
questions.explain: Traditional enterprises tend to resolve conflict through management channels and prefer people who respect existing relationships, so open challenge is a weaker fit than in a startup.
questions.rule: Fit the story to the hierarchy.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A nurse manager moves from a large hospital to a twelve-person health startup. Which adjustment to her conflict style matches the book's startups?
options: Raising disagreements directly and early, then working together the same day
Routing disagreements through her director and waiting for a formal written decision
Holding back objections until trust has built up slowly through formal processes
Avoiding open challenge of leaders, so that existing relationships are protected
optionExplain: Right: startups value direct, immediate conflict followed by collaboration.
That is the traditional enterprise approach, which suits a hospital hierarchy.
Slow formal trust-building is the traditional route, and startups cannot wait for it.
That also describes a hierarchy; a small startup expects open challenge.
