questions.explain: The startup setting changes what interviewers and teammates value, so she adjusts.
questions.rule: Adjust the style to the setting.
questions.teaches: Startups want people who can disagree in the morning and collaborate in the afternoon, and their flat structure means you may feel empowered to challenge leadership decisions openly.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: In some cultures direct disagreement is read as disrespect. How might a candidate from such a background present conflict skills?
options: By pretending to be blunt, because interviews reward bluntness over every other style
By leaving conflict stories out entirely, since disagreement conflicts with those values
By arguing that disagreement should be avoided, since harmony outranks every other goal
As consensus-building and working within established structures
optionExplain: Pretending is not honest, and the authors advise framing your real skills.
Leaving conflict out removes the evidence interviewers look for.
Treating conflict as always avoidable is a flag in the book's red flags.
Right: it presents real strengths in terms interviewers can recognize.
questions.explain: Background shapes how skills are best described. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Frame real strengths in terms others can read.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: In remote-first organizations it is important to ____, which means erring on the side of more communication rather than less.
questions.explain: The authors advise overcommunicating so that people stay on the same page and tensions are addressed before they escalate.
questions.rule: Remote: overcommunicate.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate from a very direct culture is applying to a team with mixed norms. What do the authors suggest emphasizing?
options: That directness is a virtue and every team should adjust to her style over time
How she has learned to adapt her style for different contexts
That she avoids disagreement with colleagues from other cultures out of caution
That the interviewers should ask people from other backgrounds to be more direct
optionExplain: Insisting others adapt shows inflexibility rather than collaboration.
Right: it shows awareness and range.
Avoiding disagreement is a different trait and sends a poor signal.
It shifts responsibility to others instead of showing your own adaptability.
questions.explain: The authors suggest highlighting adaptation, not insisting that one style is right.
questions.rule: Show you can flex across contexts.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Match each setting to the framing the authors suggest.
pairs: How you adapted your style for different contexts
Calling out mistakes of people above you can be inappropriate
questions.explain: Each setting carries its own cue about how skills read to others.
questions.rule: Read the setting, then frame the story.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate assumes everyone from a harmony-focused background avoids conflict. What is the flaw? (Our reading.)
options: The book says that people from harmony-focused backgrounds are the most direct of all
The book claims that cultural background has no effect on views of conflict in any workplace
The book says that avoiding conflict is dishonest in every culture, whatever the background
The book describes how cultures shape views of conflict, not what each individual does
optionExplain: The book says the opposite about how such backgrounds view directness.
The book says culture shapes views of directness, conflict and hierarchy.
It says that in some cultures avoiding conflict seems dishonest, not in all.
Right (our reading): the book offers these as tendencies and gives advice for framing.
questions.explain: Our reading: cultural patterns are a starting point for framing, not a rule about any person.
questions.rule: Patterns are not people.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A volunteer group runs only on chat, and a terse message was read as hostile. What would the card advise?
options: Reply briefly to every message, so that nobody has time to read hostility into it, whatever the topic
Overcommunicate, watch the tone of written messages and build relationships on purpose, before tension grows
Move all disagreements into a single weekly video call and keep the chat for logistics and scheduling only
Wait to see whether the misunderstanding fades before sending any clarifying message
optionExplain: Brief replies are the cause of misreading, not a cure.
Right: it applies proactive communication, care with tone and deliberate relationship-building.
Postponing disagreement to a weekly call lets tension grow in between.
Waiting lets misunderstandings escalate, which the authors want addressed early.
questions.explain: Remote groups lack in-person cues, so the authors stress extra care and more communication.
questions.rule: Remote groups need more words, not fewer.
questions.teaches: The authors note that trust develops differently when you rarely meet in person, which is why remote-first organizations value proactive communication and deliberate relationship-building.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Why might a mentee ignore advice from a mentor?
options: Advice is weaker whenever it arrives in writing rather than in a face-to-face session
Mentees prefer advice from peers and rarely accept guidance from anyone more senior
People resist coaching from someone they do not trust
Coaching works only when it is part of a formal program with a written agreement
optionExplain: Format matters less than the relationship behind the advice.
Seniority is not the problem; trust is.
Right: trust is what makes coaching land.
A formal program is not what makes coaching effective in the book's account.
questions.explain: Coaching depends on a relationship. The card next gives the connection.
questions.rule: No trust, no coaching.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Match each link between trust and another competency.
pairs: People resist coaching from someone they do not trust
Investing in someone's growth shows care and deepens trust
It can arise where ownership is unclear
It gives you credibility before you act
questions.explain: The book describes a two-way link with developing others and a credibility link with initiative.
questions.rule: Trust underpins coaching and initiative.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A staff engineer wants to take over an unowned alert dashboard. What best prepares the ground?
options: Having built trust with the teams earlier, so her credibility exists before she acts
Announcing the takeover in a message and asking anyone who disagrees to speak up soon
Waiting until the dashboard fails so that the need for her action is plain to all
Taking over quietly and revealing it once the improvements are too visible to reverse
optionExplain: Right: earlier trust makes others accept her action.
An announcement with a deadline does not create credibility.
Waiting for a failure lets the damage happen first.
Acting quietly erodes trust and invites conflict over ownership.
questions.explain: People accept initiative more readily from someone they already trust.
questions.rule: Build credibility before you act.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each effect by the competency it connects to trust.

items.t: A coachee admits a gap in knowledge
A coachee accepts hard feedback
A disagreement in coaching strengthens the relationship
Teammates accept you stepping into unclear territory
Earlier credibility softens friction about ownership
Colleagues welcome a trusted person acting unasked

questions.explain: The first three are about the coaching relationship; the others are about acting where nobody owns the work.
questions.rule: Coaching needs trust in the relationship; initiative needs credibility.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A new hire who takes over a poorly owned system on day one will meet less resistance than a long-trusted colleague.
questions.explain: The authors say it is easier to accept a person you trust taking initiative than someone you do not, so a long-trusted colleague is likely to meet less resistance.
questions.rule: Trust smooths initiative.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.2 The Essence of Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A running coach notices athletes hide small injuries. What does the card's link between trust and growth suggest?
options: Building trust would help, since people need to feel secure to admit gaps
Stricter rules would help, since athletes hide injuries only when no penalty exists
Nothing, because injuries are physical and trust belongs to workplace relationships only
More public praise would help, since athletes hide injuries to avoid looking weak
optionExplain: Right: trust supplies the security that makes it possible to admit what you cannot do.
Penalties tend to increase hiding, not reduce it.
The link between trust and admitting gaps is not limited to offices.
Praise alone does not give people the security to admit a problem.
questions.explain: The chain is trust, then security, then honest admission, then growth.
questions.rule: Growth needs the security to admit gaps.
questions.teaches: The authors add that trust creates the psychological safety that growth requires, because people need to feel secure enough to admit gaps in their knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: An interviewer asks about a time you disagreed with your manager. What are they mainly assessing?
options: Whether you can win disagreements with people who have more authority than you
Whether you have worked for managers that you personally disliked in the past
Whether you can disagree respectfully and reach a constructive resolution
Whether you keep a list of technical decisions that you would have made differently
optionExplain: Winning is not the aim; the book prefers resolution through discussion.
The question is about handling a disagreement, not about whom you like.
Right: the focus is respectful, constructive handling.
A list of differences says nothing about how you handled them.
questions.explain: Interviewers use the story to see how you handle conflict. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: The test is how you disagree.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Strong answers show you standing firm on important issues when supported by data and ____.
questions.explain: The authors link standing firm to data and facts, combined with openness to other views.
questions.rule: Firm on facts, open to others.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Which story best answers a question about disagreeing with a colleague over a technical approach?
options: You stayed silent about your doubts, and the original plan went ahead exactly as instructed by the colleague
You raised load-test numbers, heard the colleague's reasons and agreed on a compromise
You repeated your position in every meeting until the colleague stopped objecting
You asked the director to overrule the colleague before discussing it with them
optionExplain: Silence skips the disagreement that the question asks about.
Right: facts, listening and a joint outcome.
Repetition forces a view instead of finding a resolution.
Going over the colleague's head avoids discussion.
questions.explain: The best story shows a disagreement and a discussion that reaches a resolution.
questions.rule: Facts plus listening plus a joint result.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each story detail by whether it shows resolution through discussion.

items.t: Compared data with the colleague and agreed an approach
Listened to the concern and revised your proposal
Held your position while staying open and found a middle path
Dropped your objection to avoid friction
Repeated your position until the other person gave up
Let the decision proceed without raising your doubts

questions.explain: Discussion means the views meet and change the outcome. Dropping an objection, wearing the other person down or staying silent do not.
questions.rule: Resolution needs two-way talk.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: If your story ends with the manager giving in after you pushed repeatedly, an interviewer will read it as a strong disagreement answer.
questions.explain: The authors want resolution through discussion with openness to other perspectives, so a story where one side simply wore the other down shows less of the signal.
questions.rule: Winning by pressure is not discussion.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Two co-organizers of a charity run disagree on the route. Which ending would an interviewer value most?
options: One gave way in silence, so the run went ahead without any tension between them
One insisted on the route until the other stopped raising the matter in meetings
They split the event into two separate routes, so that the disagreement never needed to be settled between them
They compared safety records and agreed on a route that kept the hill out of the final stretch
optionExplain: Silent giving-way avoids the conflict instead of resolving it.
Insisting forces a view.
Splitting avoids the decision rather than resolving it through talk.
Right: facts, discussion and a joint decision.
questions.explain: The interviewer is looking for resolution through discussion, and neither giving way nor forcing delivers it.
questions.rule: Resolve it together.
questions.teaches: The authors say you achieve resolution through discussion rather than by either avoiding conflict or forcing your view.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: An interviewer asks how you rebuilt trust with a teammate. Which detail do you expect them to value most?
options: A thorough account of the circumstances that made the original problem unavoidable
Specific steps you took, including honest acknowledgment of your own part
A statement that the relationship returned to normal soon after the incident
Proof that the teammate also made mistakes during the same difficult project
optionExplain: Circumstances may explain events, but they shift attention away from your role.
Right: steps and ownership are what the question probes.
A claim of quick normality gives no steps and nothing to check.
Pointing at the teammate's faults avoids ownership.
questions.explain: Interviewers want concrete evidence of repair. The card next lists what counts.
questions.rule: Steps plus ownership.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Effective examples acknowledge your own ____ in the relationship honestly.
questions.explain: The authors say effective examples show you acknowledging your role honestly.
questions.rule: Own your role.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You missed a handoff and let your team down. Which summary best fits the authors' advice?
options: I apologized once in the stand-up and we all moved on without ever discussing it again
I explained the circumstances that made the miss unavoidable and the team accepted the reasons
I took on extra work quietly so that nobody would need to mention the miss to management
I told the team that day, owned the miss, delivered a corrected handoff and checked in weekly for a month
optionExplain: A single apology gives no steps and no evidence the relationship improved.
Explaining circumstances sidesteps your own role in the miss.
Quiet extra work hides the issue rather than rebuilding the team's trust.
Right: it names specific steps, ownership and follow-through over time.
questions.explain: The answer should show actions, honest ownership and a relationship that strengthens.
questions.rule: Show what you did and what changed.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it shows ownership of the relationship.

items.t: I said what I had missed and what I would change
I asked the teammate what would help rebuild their confidence
I did what I promised on each milestone that followed
I explained that the miss was mostly the other team's fault
I waited for the teammate to bring the matter up first
I hoped the matter would fade with time

questions.explain: Ownership means naming the problem, asking what repairs it and following through. Blaming, waiting and hoping keep you at a distance.
questions.rule: Take the first step.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: What if your rebuilding story lists steps but leaves out your own role in the failure?
options: It would miss the honest acknowledgment of your role that the authors expect
It would gain strength, because steps alone give interviewers a clean and focused picture
It would be judged equal, because the order of the steps matters more than any mention of role
It would be judged better, because mentioning your role distracts from the solution you built
optionExplain: Right: ownership is part of what the question tests.
Without ownership the steps look like polishing a record rather than repair.
The authors list honest acknowledgment as a feature of effective examples.
Role acknowledgment is part of the solution, not a distraction.
questions.explain: Steps without ownership leave the central question unanswered.
questions.rule: Name your part.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Asked how you earned credibility when you joined a new team, which answer fits the authors' trust questions best?
options: I let my past title and reputation speak for me until the team had seen my results
I waited for the manager to introduce me to everyone so that credibility could be handed over to me in time
I delivered one small promised piece early, asked for feedback and reported my own slips at once
I avoided all disagreements for the first few months so that nobody could challenge my standing in the group
optionExplain: Reputation is borrowed credibility and the team has seen nothing yet.
Waiting for a handover leaves trust to chance.
Right: small reliable acts and openness establish credibility.
Avoiding disagreement for months builds none of the signals the book values.
questions.explain: Credibility in a new team comes from consistent actions and honesty, the same behaviors that repair trust.
questions.rule: Credibility is earned, not assigned.
questions.teaches: Trust questions also cover establishing credibility in a new team, not only repairing a relationship that has already broken down.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Asked about your most challenging stakeholder relationship, which element do you expect an interviewer to value most?
options: A detailed account of how unreasonable the stakeholder was and how often you were right
A statement that you stayed polite throughout and never raised the problem with anyone
Understanding the stakeholder's pressures and finding common ground
Evidence that you outranked the stakeholder and could decide the matter yourself
optionExplain: Detailing the other person's faults tells the interviewer little about your skill.
Politeness alone is basic courtesy, which the authors say is not enough.
Right: perspective and common ground are the signals.
Rank may settle a decision but is not a relationship skill.
questions.explain: The question probes relationship skill beyond politeness. The card next lists the signals.
questions.rule: Perspective, then common ground.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Strong stories show finding ____ ground with others despite tensions.
questions.explain: The authors say strong stories show finding common ground despite tensions.
questions.rule: Find common ground.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A supplier manager keeps moving delivery dates. Which story approach shows the skills the authors look for?
options: You asked about the pressures behind the changes, then agreed dates with a buffer that suited both sides
You logged every moved date and sent the manager a monthly report on the missed commitments
You stayed courteous and accepted each change without comment so that the relationship stayed calm
You asked your director to replace the supplier as soon as the second date had moved
optionExplain: Right: it shows understanding of a perspective and a workable shared solution.
Reports may record the problem but do not show understanding of the manager's side.
Courtesy without engagement is the basic politeness the authors say is not enough.
Replacing the supplier skips the relationship work the question is probing.
questions.explain: The skills are understanding the other side and finding a solution that works for both.
questions.rule: Understand, then agree something workable.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate says: I was courteous to the difficult colleague throughout, which shows my relationship skills. What is the flaw?
options: Courtesy is a sign of weakness and interviewers prefer candidates who confront colleagues
Courtesy shows skill only when the colleague returns it, which the candidate cannot show
Real relationship skills are demonstrated only through the outcome of the project itself
The authors want real relationship skills, with basic courtesy alone not enough
optionExplain: The book does not discourage courtesy; it says courtesy alone is insufficient.
Whether the other person returns courtesy is not the test the authors describe.
Outcomes matter, but the authors also look for how you understood and worked with others.
Right: courtesy is a baseline, not the evidence.
questions.explain: Understanding perspectives and finding common ground go beyond politeness.
questions.rule: Courtesy is the floor.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A story where you found common ground but the working relationship stayed strained for the whole project is the pattern the authors prefer.
questions.explain: The authors want strong stories to show positive working relationships maintained through challenging projects, not only common ground in one conversation.
questions.rule: Keep the relationship working through the project.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: An interviewer asks about handling competing priorities from different teams. Which answer fits the family of complex-relationship questions?
options: You chose the priorities of the team with the larger budget and told the other team why
You met both teams, learned their goals and agreed a sequence that served each of them
You followed the order in which requests arrived and ignored any later pressure from either team
You left the teams to resolve their priorities between themselves and reported the outcome
optionExplain: Choosing the stronger side does not show common ground.
Right: it shows understanding of both sides and a shared solution.
Arrival order is a rule, not relationship skill.
Leaving it to them avoids the skill the question probes.
questions.explain: Competing priorities put you between teams, so the skill is finding common ground between them.
questions.rule: Serve both goals where you can.
questions.teaches: A question about handling competing priorities from different teams belongs to this same family, since it sits where trust and conflict meet.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You are asked about a production incident in which people blamed each other. What should your answer centre on?
options: Who was responsible for the incident and how you showed it with the logs
How quickly the incident was closed, with no mention of the people involved
Why you stayed out of the discussion so that blame would not land on you
How you steered the discussion toward fixing the problem and keeping people working together
optionExplain: Assigning fault is the finger-pointing the authors warn about.
Speed matters, but this question is about relationships under pressure.
Staying out avoids the pressure the question tests.
Right: the question probes focus on solutions under stress.
questions.explain: The authors link these questions to behavior under stress. The card next shows what good looks like.
questions.rule: Solutions over blame.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: During crises, good responses focus on solutions rather than ____.
questions.explain: The authors say good responses show a focus on solutions rather than finger-pointing.
questions.rule: Solve, do not blame.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You must tell leadership a launch will slip. Which approach matches the authors' advice?
options: Wait until the date is only days away so that the team has time to recover the schedule
Say plainly that it will slip, give the cause and the options, and stay respectful of those affected
Present the slip as a small risk and keep the full cause for a later post-mortem
Tell your own team first and let them decide what leadership needs to know and when
optionExplain: The authors list sharing bad news early as part of direct, transparent communication; late news also leaves leadership fewer options (our reading).
Right: it is direct, careful and offers a way forward.
Softening the risk until later is the vague, indirect message the authors caution against.
Withholding from leadership avoids the hard conversation the question is about.
questions.explain: Direct but careful delivery is what the authors say good responses show.
questions.rule: Direct, careful and constructive.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each response in a crisis by its focus.

items.t: Gather the facts and agree who does what in the next hour
Set up a call to restore service before the review of causes
Ask what we need to stop the same fault repeating
Post the name of the team that caused the fault in the channel
Argue about whose fault it was while the service stays down
Document your own innocence before helping anyone else

questions.explain: Solution focus moves toward restoring service and preventing repeats. Naming, arguing and protecting yourself delay both.
questions.rule: Fix first, assign lessons later.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A calm story in which you said nothing about a risk you knew about would satisfy a question on delivering bad news.
questions.explain: These questions ask about delivering the news directly, so a story with no message delivered misses the point even if it stayed calm.
questions.rule: Calm must come with a clear message.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A site manager must push back on a client's unrealistic deadline. Which closing line fits the pressure questions best?
options: I accepted the deadline so that the client would not feel I was resisting their wishes
I told the client the deadline was foolish and that the team would be ignoring it when planning the work
I explained the risks, offered a realistic date and stayed firm on it while respecting their concerns
I handed the problem to my director and waited for a decision on whether to push back
optionExplain: Accepting an unrealistic deadline avoids the pushback altogether.
Calling it foolish is direct without being careful.
Right: it combines directness, firmness and respect.
Handing it up avoids the pushback the question asks about.
questions.explain: Holding a position respectfully while staying direct is the skill under pressure.
questions.rule: Firm and respectful.
questions.teaches: Good responses to pressure questions also show standing firm while respecting others.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Asked about the hardest feedback you have received, which answer element carries the most weight?
options: A specific change in how you now work, linked to the feedback
A description of how unfair the feedback was and how you defended yourself at the time
A statement that you had already thought of the issue before the feedback arrived
A comparison of the feedback with the praise you got from other colleagues
optionExplain: Right: the question tests whether feedback changes behavior.
Defending yourself shows resistance rather than growth.
Claiming you already knew shows no change in response to it.
Praise does not show how you acted on the criticism.
questions.explain: These questions look for growth. The card next lists what shows it.
questions.rule: Feedback should show up in behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Strong answers show genuine ____ and describe specific behavioral changes.
questions.explain: The authors say strong answers show genuine reflection on your part along with specific changes.
questions.rule: Reflect, then change.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A reviewer told you your pull requests were too large to review. Which answer fits the authors' advice?
options: I thought about why large changes hid problems, then began splitting work into small reviewable pieces
I explained that large changes were quicker for me and that reviewers should adapt
I accepted the comment and promised to do better with future pull requests
I asked another reviewer for a second opinion until someone agreed with my approach
optionExplain: Right: it shows reflection and a specific change.
Defending your habit shows no change.
A vague promise gives no specific behavior to examine.
Seeking agreement avoids the feedback instead of acting on it.
questions.explain: Reflection plus a concrete new practice is what the interviewer wants to hear.
questions.rule: Specific change shows growth.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each statement by the strength of the feedback story it tells.

items.t: I realised my updates left out risks, so I now list risks first
I asked for examples, then changed how I prepare reviews
I checked back a month later to see whether it had improved
I listened politely and carried on as before
I decided the reviewer did not understand my work
I said I would try to be better in general

questions.explain: Strong stories include reflection and a checkable change. Weak ones show no change, deflection or only a general intention.
questions.rule: Reflection plus a checkable change.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A story about criticism that ends with I felt hurt but eventually moved on shows the growth these questions test.
questions.explain: The authors want specific behavioral changes, so a story that ends in feelings without changed behavior does not show growth.
questions.rule: Feelings are not a change in behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Asked how a conflict with a colleague made you a better collaborator, which answer fits best?
options: The clash taught me that I work best alone, so I now take solo projects wherever I can
The colleague later apologized to me, which proved that I had been right about the issue from the beginning
After the clash I began checking assumptions with colleagues first, which has cut my rework since
I learned that it is better to avoid people who hold strong opinions on technical subjects, to keep the peace
optionExplain: Withdrawing from collaboration does not show you becoming a better collaborator.
Being proven right says nothing about how you changed.
Right: it names a changed behavior and its effect on collaboration.
Avoiding people is the opposite of better collaboration.
questions.explain: The point is a better way of working with others that you can describe and show.
questions.rule: Show how you became easier to work with.
questions.teaches: The authors say that if you have become a better person to work with as a result of challenging interactions, you should tell the interviewers and show them how.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Two senior engineers disagree sharply about a design. What would most strengthen your answer to a conflict question?
options: Showing that your design was chosen and the other engineer later left the team
Showing that the debate stayed about the design and the team remained cohesive
Showing that you kept quiet throughout the debate so that the team stayed calm and nobody was upset
Showing that you won the argument because you were the more senior engineer in the room that day
optionExplain: Winning at the cost of a colleague is not cohesion.
Right: strong conflict skills preserve cohesion.
Staying quiet is avoiding the conflict.
Seniority settles the point but shows no skill.
questions.explain: Conflict can be vigorous and still constructive. The card next sets out the signal.
questions.rule: Disagree about the decision, not the person.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Constructive conflict resolution is rated as a ____ signal, the highest of the three tiers.
questions.explain: The book ranks it as a critical signal, with direct and transparent communication.
questions.rule: Critical signal.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Your team is split about whether to rewrite a module. Which approach shows this signal?
options: Gather support from teammates before the meeting so that the vote favors your preferred rewrite
Argue for the rewrite on the basis of the author's lack of experience with the module
Agree with everyone in the meeting and settle the matter later through a private message
Compare error rates and costs with the other side and design a plan that addresses their main worry
optionExplain: Gathering votes treats it as a contest, not a search for a solution.
Attacking the author is the personal focus the signal rules out.
Agreeing and reversing later is avoidance.
Right: it uses data and solves for another party's concern.
questions.explain: The signal rewards data, outcomes and solutions that serve several parties.
questions.rule: Data, outcomes and shared concerns.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each action by whether it shows constructive conflict resolution.

items.t: Argue vigorously about the design while keeping the team intact
Cite error rates and drop personal remarks
Seek a fix that meets both teams' real concerns
Win the point by questioning the other person's judgment
Stay silent in the review and complain afterwards
Insist on your version without hearing alternatives

questions.explain: Constructive conflict stays on the decision and looks for a shared solution. The others make it personal, avoid it or close it down.
questions.rule: Keep it about outcomes.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: If you disagree vigorously but the team's cohesion breaks down as a result, interviewers would still rate this as strong constructive conflict resolution.
questions.explain: The signal asks for vigorous disagreement while preserving team cohesion, so broken cohesion would weaken the story.
questions.rule: Cohesion is part of the signal.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A community garden board voted against your layout proposal. Which response best matches this signal?
options: Withdraw from the board so that the layout cannot be blamed on your involvement
Accept the vote, help carry out the chosen layout and offer to review the results in a season
Keep arguing for your layout at every meeting until the board finally agrees to revisit the vote
Carry out the layout while telling other members privately that the board's decision was a mistake
optionExplain: Withdrawing leaves the team when cohesion matters most.
Right: you support the final decision while staying constructive.
Reopening the vote repeatedly refuses to accept the outcome.
Undermining privately damages cohesion.
questions.explain: Constructive conflict ends in support for the decision reached, even when it was not your choice.
questions.rule: Support the decision you did not choose.
questions.teaches: The authors say interviewers also check that you will support a final decision even if it was not your preference.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You suspect a vendor's interface will not be ready in time. When should you tell your lead?
options: After the failure is confirmed, so that the news is complete and certain when it arrives
At the next scheduled milestone review, so that the report fits the usual reporting rhythm
Once you have a workaround ready, so that the news never arrives without a ready fix
As soon as the concern is credible, with what you know and do not know
optionExplain: Waiting for certainty can leave no time to act.
Waiting for a scheduled review lets the problem grow in between.
Waiting for a fix delays information others could use now.
Right: early warning gives others time to respond.
questions.explain: Early honest signals are the heart of this expectation. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Early beats complete.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Direct and transparent communication means sharing bad news ____, before problems grow into crises.
questions.explain: The authors list sharing bad news early, admitting uncertainty and raising concerns before they become crises.
questions.rule: Share early.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You are unsure whether your estimate will hold. What does this signal suggest?
options: Say your confidence is low, explain what is unknown and say when you will know more
Give the estimate with full confidence and quietly revise it later if it proves to be wrong
Hold the estimate back until you have enough certainty, to avoid giving a misleading number
Give a very wide range and leave out the reasons, so that nobody can hold you to it
optionExplain: Right: it admits uncertainty openly and gives others a plan for it.
False confidence hides the uncertainty and costs trust when the estimate moves.
Withholding any number leaves others with nothing to plan on.
A wide range without reasons hides your uncertainty instead of sharing it.
questions.explain: Admitting uncertainty, with a clear next step, is part of the signal.
questions.rule: Share the uncertainty and the plan.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate says: I kept the bug quiet until I had a fix, so nobody worried. What is the flaw?
options: Nothing is wrong, because the signal is mainly about delivering a complete solution on time and within budget
Quiet fixing is fine, but the candidate should have thanked everyone who was kept informed along the way
Waiting removes others' chance to help, whereas the signal is to raise concerns before they become crises
The flaw is the bug itself, because strong candidates tell stories without any bugs in them at all
optionExplain: The signal is about early transparency, not only the finished fix.
Nobody was informed in this story, so there was nobody to thank.
Right: early disclosure is the behavior.
The book values how mistakes are handled, not stories without them.
questions.explain: Delay can feel considerate, but the signal is about giving others time to respond.
questions.rule: Do not wait for the perfect moment.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a story where you shared bad news early and asked for help shows this signal better than one where you quietly fixed the problem.
questions.explain: Sharing bad news early and raising concerns before they become crises are the behaviors the signal names; a quiet fix shows neither.
questions.rule: Early and open beats quiet and complete.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: In a club meeting, everyone sees the event budget will fail, but nobody speaks. What does this signal ask of you?
options: Wait until a more senior member raises it so that you do not appear to be criticizing them
Mention it afterwards in private messages so that the meeting stays positive for everyone
Say plainly that you see a budget risk, explain it with care and propose a next step
Offer to review the budget later, without saying why you think a review is needed
optionExplain: Waiting for someone senior to speak leaves the risk unspoken.
Private messages after the meeting delay the information from the group that needs it.
Right: you say what needs saying when others stay silent.
An unexplained review offer gives others nothing to act on.
questions.explain: The signal rewards the person who raises the issue clearly and kindly.
questions.rule: Be the one who says it.
questions.teaches: The authors describe this signal as being the person who says what needs to be said when others stay silent, and keeping transparency even when it would be easier to hide problems.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Which story detail shows reliability best?
options: Delivering what you promised, repeatedly, across several months of a project
Delivering one very large piece of work in a single weekend to save a release
Taking on every request that arrived so that nobody on the team was ever refused
Working long hours throughout the project so that the effort was visible to everyone
optionExplain: Right: reliability is a pattern.
One rescue shows capability but not a pattern.
Taking everything on makes promises you may not keep.
Hours measure effort, not kept commitments.
questions.explain: Reliability shows over time. The card next gives the signal.
questions.rule: Pattern, not a single act.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Reliable people deliver what they ____ and communicate early when problems arise.
questions.explain: The authors say reliable people deliver what they promise and communicate early when problems arise.
questions.rule: Deliver what you promise.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You will miss a promised date by two days. What does this signal suggest?
options: Work through the weekend and say nothing, so that nobody learns the date was at risk
Wait until the date arrives and explain the reasons in a thorough written report
Tell your manager only, and let your manager decide whether the others are informed
Tell the people who rely on you now, give the new date and meet it
optionExplain: Silent catching-up can still fail and denies others the chance to adjust.
Explaining after the date removes the chance to plan around the delay.
Passing the message upward leaves the people who rely on you uninformed.
Right: early communication plus keeping the revised promise.
questions.explain: The signal rewards early notice and a kept revised commitment.
questions.rule: Warn early; keep the new date.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each behavior by whether it shows reliability and accountability.

items.t: Delivered each promised item on the date given for months
Told the team on day two that a dependency was late
Owned a mistake and explained how to prevent it
Blamed the schedule for a missed commitment
Said yes to a request without checking capacity
Fixed a problem silently to protect an image

questions.explain: Reliability means consistent delivery, early warning and ownership. Blaming, over-promising and silent fixes weaken it.
questions.rule: Deliver, warn, own.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: If a story shows you completing a heroic one-off rescue but missing smaller promises that month, the reliability signal is weak.
questions.explain: The signal is about consistent trustworthy behavior over time, so a one-off rescue alongside missed promises shows a mixed pattern.
questions.rule: Consistency counts more than one big act.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A neighbor promised to water a friend's plants but fell ill. Which response shows accountability best?
options: Skip the watering and mention it on the friend's return, when the plants cannot be saved
Tell the friend straight away, arrange cover and take responsibility for the original promise
Ask the friend to understand, since illness is outside anyone's control and nobody is at fault
Water the plants only when well enough, without telling the friend about the gaps
optionExplain: Late disclosure hides the missed promise.
Right: early notice, a fix and ownership.
Illness may explain the miss but it does not replace ownership and a plan.
Silence about gaps leaves the friend unable to protect the plants.
questions.explain: Accountability is owning the promise and acting on it.
questions.rule: Own it and cover it.
questions.teaches: The authors add that accountability means owning your mistakes without trying to blame others.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Two teams argue about whose roadmap goes first, and you are on neither. What would strengthen your story?
options: Backing the team whose request has the higher business value and telling the other why
Staying out of it because the dispute is not yours and could spoil your own relationships
Asking your manager to rule on the order so that nobody blames you for the result
Helping each team see the other's constraints and the goal they share
optionExplain: Picking a side settles the order but not the relationship.
Staying out gives up the chance to help.
Handing it up avoids the work of bringing the teams together.
Right: bridging means helping others work through the dispute.
questions.explain: This signal is about helping others with their conflicts. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Help others across the gap.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Strong collaborators help teams see past territorial disputes to shared ____.
questions.explain: The authors describe helping teams see past territorial disputes to shared goals.
questions.rule: Look for the shared goal.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A designer and an engineer talk past each other about a deadline. How could you build a bridge?
options: Tell both of them to be more professional and to stick to the written specification from now on
Explain each person's concern in the other's terms and ask what each needs from the other
Take the engineer's side privately, since the schedule is the harder constraint to change of the two
Schedule a longer meeting in which each of them presents their case to the whole team
optionExplain: Telling people to be professional does not create understanding.
Right: translating between viewpoints is the core of bridging.
Taking a side deepens the divide.
Longer presentations may harden positions rather than translate them.
questions.explain: Translation between viewpoints is how the book describes the skill.
questions.rule: Translate, do not just referee.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Match each situation to the kind of skill it shows.
pairs: Resolving your own disagreement with a peer
Telling a non-technical team what an engineering limit means
Warning a lead early that a date will slip
questions.explain: Bridging is about helping others understand each other, while the other two skills are about your own conflict and your own messages.
questions.rule: Bridging helps other people connect.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A candidate who only describes resolving their own disagreements shows the building-bridges signal.
questions.explain: The signal is about helping others work through their conflicts, so stories about only your own disagreements do not show it.
questions.rule: Bridging looks beyond yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Two departments in a school keep a long feud about timetable slots. Which action best builds a bridge?
options: Publish a fixed timetable that favors the larger department and end the discussion for the year
Ask each head to write down their grievances and send them to the principal for a final judgment
Meet both heads, find what each needs from the timetable and propose a shared rule
Wait for one of the two heads to retire so that the feud ends with a change of people
optionExplain: Favoring one side leaves the feud in place.
Sending grievances up asks for judgment, not understanding.
Right: it surfaces needs on both sides and finds a shared rule.
Waiting for a change of people does not build understanding.
questions.explain: The skill is helping both sides see what the other needs and finding common ground.
questions.rule: Find the shared rule.
questions.teaches: The authors say that if you can show others that understanding different constraints and pressures helps everyone work better together, you should show your interviewers that ability.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A junior colleague makes a costly mistake. Which response builds the most psychological safety?
options: Asking what happened with curiosity and what support would help prevent it
Explaining firmly how the mistake could have been avoided and how it affects the team
Recording the mistake in the team report so that the lessons are formally captured
Telling them it is fine and moving on without discussing what went wrong in the work
optionExplain: Right: curiosity rather than judgment.
Firm explanations of what they should have done feel like judgment.
Formal capture may be useful but does not by itself make someone feel safe.
Skipping the discussion removes the chance to learn together.
questions.explain: Safety grows from how you respond. The card next lists the behaviors.
questions.rule: Curiosity before judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You respond to mistakes with ____ rather than judgment.
questions.explain: The authors say you respond to mistakes with curiosity rather than judgment.
questions.rule: Respond with curiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: In a design review, you realize you are unsure about the best approach. What builds safety?
options: Saying you are unsure and asking the room for other views before deciding
Presenting a firm choice and asking people to raise objections only if they are certain
Delaying the review until you are sure so that nobody sees you hesitate in front of them
Deferring to the most senior person so that nobody feels challenged by the process
optionExplain: Right: sharing uncertainty and inviting views.
Asking for objections only from the certain discourages hesitant voices.
Delaying until sure signals that uncertainty is not welcome.
Deferring by rank closes the door to other perspectives.
questions.explain: Sharing your uncertainty invites others to share theirs.
questions.rule: Show your uncertainty.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Match each signal to its tier in the book.
questions.explain: The book ranks conflict resolution and transparency as critical, reliability and building bridges as strong, and safe collaboration as supporting.
questions.rule: Two critical, two strong, one supporting.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: If colleagues are afraid to admit problems to you, the supporting signal of creating safe collaboration is likely to be weak.
questions.explain: The signal describes people feeling safe to disagree and to admit their problems, so fear of admitting problems is the opposite.
questions.rule: Safety shows in what people dare to tell you.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A volunteer leader wants new helpers to flag problems early. Which action builds the safety the book describes?
options: Reminding helpers that problems reflect badly on the whole group and need quick fixes
Setting a rule that every problem must be reported in writing within the same hour
Sharing her own recent mistake and thanking the first helper who reports a problem
Reviewing the team's error log each month and naming the helpers who made mistakes
optionExplain: Reminding helpers of the reputational cost makes them hide problems.
A rigid rule may produce reports but not a feeling of safety.
Right: she shows openness and rewards reporting.
Naming individuals publicly turns the log into judgment.
questions.explain: Modelling openness and welcoming reports builds safety.
questions.rule: Model it, then welcome it.
questions.teaches: The authors say the result is that people know it is safe to disagree with you and are not afraid to admit their problems.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Asked for a disagreement story, which reply would worry an interviewer most?
options: I questioned an assumption in a design review, and the plan was adjusted as a result
I get on with everyone, so I have never had a real disagreement
I disagreed mildly with my manager, and we talked it through to a workable compromise
I disagreed with a colleague, and after the debate they persuaded me I was wrong
optionExplain: That is a mild but real disagreement with a good outcome.
Right: it signals avoidance or lack of self-awareness.
A mild disagreement resolved by talking is what the book values.
Changing your mind after a real debate is an honest example of resolution.
questions.explain: The chapter treats this claim as a warning sign. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: No disagreement at all is the warning.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Avoiding all conflict is classed in the book as a ____ flag.
questions.explain: The book calls it a red flag, the serious category, and the other four patterns yellow flags.
questions.rule: Red flag: avoiding all conflict.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You have no dramatic conflicts to describe. Which example would the authors accept as productive conflict?
options: Agreeing with every proposal in a meeting and keeping your doubts for a later email
Complaining to a friend about a plan that you were told to carry out unchanged
Rewriting a colleague's code in private after the review without telling them
Questioning an assumption in a design review, which led to a better design
optionExplain: Agreeing and doubting privately is avoidance.
Complaining outside the team is not pushback.
Private rewriting skips the open challenge.
Right: even mild pushback counts.
questions.explain: The authors count small, open challenges as productive conflict.
questions.rule: Mild pushback counts.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each action by whether it counts as productive conflict.

items.t: Questioning an assumption in a design review
Suggesting an alternative approach to the lead
Advocating for a different priority in planning
Agreeing with every proposal to keep the peace
Complaining to friends about the plan afterwards
Quietly redoing a colleague's work

questions.explain: Productive conflict is open and respectful challenge of ideas, even if mild. Silent agreement, complaint and covert rework are not.
questions.rule: Open and respectful challenge.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A candidate whose stories contain no disagreement at all will be read as an especially good team player.
questions.explain: The authors say such stories make interviewers wonder whether the candidate avoids necessary conflicts or lacks strong opinions.
questions.rule: No disagreement is a warning, not a virtue.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A paramedic says that in ten years she has had no significant disagreement with colleagues. How will an interviewer likely read it?
options: As a sign of an unusually harmonious team where disagreement was not needed at all, which interviewers admire
As a red flag about self-awareness, since meaningful work always involves differing views
As evidence of strong patient outcomes, since no time was lost on arguing in her team over the years
As a neutral remark, since the interviewer is mainly interested in her clinical skills
optionExplain: The authors read it as a warning sign, not as harmony.
Right: the book hears this answer as a red flag.
Outcomes are not what the claim shows.
The authors treat the claim itself as telling.
questions.explain: A claim of no disagreements invites doubts about awareness and candor.
questions.rule: Find a real example, however small.
questions.teaches: The authors say that if you genuinely cannot recall disagreements, you are either not paying attention, not speaking up or not being honest with yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate ends a conflict story with: I was right, and my colleague eventually had to admit it. How will it likely land?
options: As confidence that shows the candidate will defend good engineering decisions every time
As honesty, since the candidate was open about winning the argument in the story
As neutral, since the correctness of the technical point is what the interviewer wants
As ego over collaboration, even if the technical point was correct
optionExplain: Confidence is not the issue; the framing around winning is.
Honesty about winning does not fix the damage to collaboration.
The authors say correctness alone is not success.
Right: the story centers on proving someone wrong.
questions.explain: The flag is about what the story emphasizes. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Winning is not the whole story.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Stories focused on proving others wrong show ego over ____.
questions.explain: The authors say that stories focused on proving others wrong show ego over collaboration.
questions.rule: Ego over collaboration is the flag.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You were technically right in a dispute. How should you shape the story?
options: Describe how you and the other person worked out a solution that used the strongest points of each
Describe the evidence that proved your position and showed exactly how the other person's argument was weak
Describe how the other person eventually conceded after the team lead reviewed all of the evidence
Leave out the dispute completely and describe only the technical result that came out of it
optionExplain: Right: it centers on a joint solution.
Emphasizing proof and weakness repeats the flagged pattern.
A concession story still centers on winning.
Leaving out the dispute removes the conflict evidence the question wants.
questions.explain: A joint solution turns a debate into collaboration evidence.
questions.rule: Find the solution together.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each story ending by what it shows.

items.t: We built a design that used both our ideas
We agreed on a test that would settle the question for both of us
He thanked me for pointing out the gap, and we fixed it together
I proved the whole team wrong in front of the director
I won the debate, and the others stopped speaking up
Everyone finally admitted that my approach was the only workable one

questions.explain: Collaboration endings keep the relationship intact and credit both sides. Ego endings celebrate the win and leave damage behind.
questions.rule: Prefer endings that keep the relationship.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, winning an argument technically still counts as success even if team dynamics are damaged.
questions.explain: The authors say that damaging team dynamics in the process of winning a debate is not success.
questions.rule: A win that costs the relationship is not a success.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A volunteer coordinator tells of proving a co-organizer's schedule wrong, after which the co-organizer left. How does the book view the story?
options: As proof that the coordinator was conscientious, since the schedule really was flawed
As a strength, since the coordinator took a stand against an incorrect plan
As poor judgment about what matters in the long term, since the win cost a colleague
As fair, provided the coordinator gave the co-organizer a chance to respond in public
optionExplain: The flaw in the schedule does not rescue the outcome.
Taking a stand is fine, but the cost to the relationship is the issue.
Right: winning by making enemies shows poor judgment.
A public chance to respond does not repair the damage.
questions.explain: The book weighs the long-term relationship, not only who was right.
questions.rule: Count the cost of the win.
questions.teaches: The authors add that winning arguments by making enemies shows poor judgment about what matters in the long term.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Which description of a difficult colleague is most believable to an interviewer?
options: He missed deadlines and ignored every reminder, while I did everything the process required
He was difficult, but I kept my temper and the project survived despite his behavior
He missed deadlines, and I also failed to raise it early; here is what I changed
He did not respond to messages, which meant I was forced to work around him alone
optionExplain: That blames him entirely.
Calm under difficulty does not show any self-reflection about my part.
Right: it balances his behavior and my part.
Being forced is a blaming frame.
questions.explain: Honest stories include your own part. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Two people, two parts.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Every relationship involves ____ people, so describe your own part too.
questions.explain: The authors say every relationship involves two people.
questions.rule: Two people in every relationship.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Your story is about a teammate who often cut meetings short. How should it be framed?
options: Say what he did, what you did that added to the problem and how you changed your own approach
Say what he did, how you stayed professional throughout and how the team eventually moved on without him
Say what he did, what the team said about him and what the manager did to address it
Say only what you did to fix the problem, without describing anything about the teammate
optionExplain: Right: it names your own contribution.
Staying professional is not acknowledging a contribution.
Other people's views are about him, not about your part.
Leaving him out hides the conflict and weakens the evidence.
questions.explain: Honest framing includes what you could have done differently.
questions.rule: Include your own part.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it shows self-awareness.

items.t: I should have raised the issue sooner
I assumed he knew what I needed and never said so
Looking back, my tone made it harder for him to respond
He simply refused to cooperate on anything
I was the only reasonable person in that group
There was nothing more I could have done

questions.explain: Self-awareness acknowledges what you could have done differently. Blaming describes only the other party.
questions.rule: Own your side of it.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: If all of a candidate's conflict stories cast the candidate as the reasonable one, interviewers will trust the stories more.
questions.explain: The authors say interviewers will suspect that they are hearing only half the story and that the candidate lacks self-awareness.
questions.rule: One-sided stories lose trust.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A tenants' association chair says every dispute in her building was caused by unreasonable neighbors. What would the book's reasoning suggest?
options: Listeners will conclude that the building has an unusually difficult group of people living in it
Listeners will admire her patience in putting up with so many difficult neighbors for years
Listeners will focus on the details of each dispute rather than her explanation of its causes
Listeners may suspect that she is telling only half the story
optionExplain: It is more likely that the story is one-sided.
Patience does not answer the question of her own role.
Listeners react to the pattern as well as the details.
Right: one-sided accounts invite suspicion.
questions.explain: A pattern of reasonable-me, unreasonable-them stories looks incomplete.
questions.rule: Tell both halves.
questions.teaches: The authors say that if all your conflict stories position you as the reasonable one dealing with unreasonable people, you are missing half the picture and interviewers will suspect you are telling only half the story.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A candidate says: I say yes to every request, so colleagues trust me. How might an interviewer read this?
options: As a reliable sign of the generosity that interviewers look for in good team players of any seniority
As accommodation without boundaries, which creates dependency rather than professional trust
As a strength, since colleagues who trust you in this way will then support your own requests later
As neutral, since saying yes is only a problem when the request is unreasonable
optionExplain: Generosity without limits becomes dependency.
Right: trust needs boundaries.
Trust and favours are different things.
The flag applies to a pattern of yielding, not only to unreasonable requests.
questions.explain: Healthy trust has limits. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A yes means more when a no is possible.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Professional trust requires healthy ____ and the ability to say no firmly but respectfully.
questions.explain: The authors say professional trust requires healthy boundaries and the ability to say no.
questions.rule: Trust needs boundaries.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A colleague repeatedly asks you to take over his reviews. How does a story show healthy boundaries?
options: You took all of the reviews and added them to your weekends so that no one would be let down
You ignored the requests until he stopped asking, and the pattern stopped after a few weeks
You reported him to the manager as soon as he asked for the second time without comment
You explained your workload, offered one agreed review and said no to the rest, courteously
optionExplain: Taking everything is the flagged accommodation.
Ignoring requests avoids the conversation.
Reporting him skips the direct, respectful no.
Right: a respectful, firm no with an alternative.
questions.explain: Boundaries are expressed directly and kindly.
questions.rule: Say no respectfully.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each behavior by whether it shows healthy boundaries.

items.t: Declined a request that conflicted with a commitment, with an alternative
Held a technical position and explained the reasons
Said no to extra work and told the manager what had to give
Took on every task to avoid disappointing anyone
Dropped an important technical point whenever someone objected
Kept concerns to yourself, to stay liked by the team

questions.explain: Healthy boundaries mean saying no, holding positions and being open about limits. The other three give way every time.
questions.rule: A boundary is a respectful no.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: A candidate whose stories show saying yes to every request will be seen as someone colleagues can safely depend on.
questions.explain: The authors say that endless accommodation creates dependency rather than professional trust.
questions.rule: Dependency is not trust.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A shop owner lets customers haggle and agrees to every discount asked. What does the book's reasoning suggest about her customers' trust?
options: Her customers will trust her more because she has shown she will give way to them
Her customers may like her, but liking differs from trusting her judgment
Her customers will trust her judgment because she has built a record of agreeable deals
Her customers will see her pricing as dependable, since every deal is open to review
optionExplain: Giving way every time is the pattern the book warns about.
Right: being liked is not being trusted.
Agreeable deals show accommodation, not judgment.
Prices that move every time are not dependable.
questions.explain: Unlimited accommodation does not make someone trusted.
questions.rule: Be trusted, not just liked.
questions.teaches: The authors say such stories suggest a tendency to confuse being liked with being trusted.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Which ending to a conflict story gives the interviewer the most to work with?
options: We talked it through and eventually worked it out between ourselves as a team
The relationship improved a lot after that and we got along well from then on
We agreed to a weekly check-in and a shared change log, and rework fell
Things were much better afterwards and everyone was happy with the way it ended
optionExplain: That claim gives no specifics.
Improvement without detail is the flagged pattern.
Right: it names practices and results.
General satisfaction is not evidence of change.
questions.explain: Specifics make the story believable. The card next lists what to include.
questions.rule: Name what changed.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Vague outcomes such as we worked it out make your ____ unclear.
questions.explain: The authors say vague outcomes make your impact unclear.
questions.rule: Say what changed.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: You resolved a long feud with a colleague. How should you end the story?
options: Describe the new practice you set up together and the difference it made to the team
Say that the relationship is now excellent and that you have no remaining difficulties
Say that you gradually learned to work together and now understand each other well
Say that the feud ended once both of you had cooled down and got on with the work
optionExplain: Right: a practice and an effect.
Excellent relationship is a claim without a detail.
Gradual understanding is general.
Cooling down describes feelings, not changed behavior.
questions.explain: The authors ask for changed communication and collaborative practices.
questions.rule: Practice plus outcome.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each ending by whether it is specific or vague.

items.t: We set a Monday check-in and the rework dropped
We wrote an agreement on who approves changes
He now sends a heads-up before changing anything
We worked it out in the end
The relationship got a lot better
We understand each other now

questions.explain: Specific endings describe a behavior or practice. Vague ones describe a feeling or a conclusion.
questions.rule: Behavior, not feeling.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: True or false: An interviewer is likely to rate we worked it out as strong evidence of conflict resolution skill.
questions.explain: Without specifics, the impact is unclear, which is why the authors flag it.
questions.rule: Claims need specifics.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A band member says: we sorted out our differences and the band is better for it. What would make this stronger?
options: Saying what changed, such as a rehearsal rule, and how the shows improved
Saying it again with more feeling, so that the improvement sounds more convincing
Adding that other band members agreed that the band was now better for it
Adding that the disagreement had been serious, so that the improvement seems larger
optionExplain: Right: specifics are what is missing.
Emphasis does not add information.
Other people's agreement is another claim.
Making the dispute sound larger does not show what changed.
questions.explain: Behavior change is what the authors look for.
questions.rule: Show the change.
questions.teaches: The authors say real trust shows in changed behavior, not just in a statement that you worked it out.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A senior colleague proposes an approach you think is risky. What is the most constructive first move?
options: State the risk as settled fact in the team meeting so that the group can judge for itself
Wait until the risk shows up and then show your notes that you had warned them earlier
Acknowledge their concern, then ask how to meet it without the risk
Write a full proposal for your own approach so that they can compare it with their own
optionExplain: Raising it as settled fact in public puts them on the defensive.
Waiting turns the disagreement into an I-told-you-so.
Right: it respects their goal and invites a shared solution.
A rival proposal can be useful but skips the conversation.
questions.explain: The entry-level story models one way. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: Start from their concern.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Put the entry-level story's events in order.
items: The tech lead asked the pipeline to keep running after failed records
The candidate worried that corrupt data would reach customer reports
The candidate raised the concern in a one-on-one and asked a how question
They agreed three error types: critical, warning and info
The candidate built monitoring for each category
questions.explain: The story moves from the lead's request through the candidate's worry and a direct conversation to a shared solution and its implementation.
questions.rule: Concern, conversation, solution.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A junior analyst thinks a manager's survey sampling will skew results. Which approach mirrors the story?
options: Send the manager an article on sampling bias and ask for a decision before the survey goes out
Say she understands the need for speed, ask how to keep speed while checking skew and bring a small example
Agree to the plan and mention the skew in the report once the results have been delivered
Rework the sampling on her own and show the corrected results at the next review meeting
optionExplain: An article without a conversation may feel like criticism.
Right: concern, how question and specifics.
Raising it afterwards misses the chance to improve the plan.
Reworking alone bypasses the manager.
questions.explain: The story shows respect for the other aim, a question and a shared outcome.
questions.rule: Respect, ask, build.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: Sort each move by whether it mirrors the entry-level story.

items.t: Opened with the lead's valid concern about uptime
Asked how to keep uptime without missing critical failures
Built a classification that both sides could accept
Waited quietly and let the pipeline run as asked
Argued the lead was wrong and refused to implement it
Escalated to the lead's manager before talking to the lead

questions.explain: The story engages directly, respects the lead's concern and builds a joint answer. Silence, refusal and going over the lead's head do not.
questions.rule: Direct, respectful, shared.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: What if the candidate had stayed quiet because the tech lead was senior?
options: The tech lead would have noticed the risk later on and would have thanked the candidate for deferring
The pipeline would have run without any incident, because senior judgment is usually right in such cases
The candidate would have earned trust by avoiding any friction at all with a more senior person
The data-quality risk would have gone unraised and no shared standard would have emerged
optionExplain: Nothing in the story suggests the lead would have spotted the risk alone.
The story treats the risk as real.
Avoiding friction is not how the story builds trust.
Right: in the story, staying quiet would have hurt product quality.
questions.explain: Silence loses both the risk signal and the chance to improve the plan.
questions.rule: Speak up with a question.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.q: A junior nurse thinks a handover form omits allergies. Which move best uses the story's lesson?
options: Add an allergies line to her own copy of the form and say nothing to anybody else
Bring a concrete case, acknowledge the need for brevity and ask how to cover allergies too
Tell the ward manager that the form is unsafe and ask for it to be replaced at once across the ward
Wait for a near miss to occur, then present it as hard evidence at the next ward safety meeting
optionExplain: Changing only her own copy leaves the form unchanged for others.
