Shipping is delivery, not proof that nurses benefit.
Waiting reacts late; the author describes monitoring behaviour after releases.
Other products do not show how these nurses' work changed.
questions.explain: The check does not end at launch. Following behaviour after each release shows whether the change helped and what to adjust.
questions.teaches: The book names task completion, goal achievement and user efficiency as what user-focused people measure, instead of technical system metrics alone.
questions.rule: Define success as the user would, then check it after release and adjust.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: You interview at a streaming service and at a workflow-software vendor. What most likely differs in how customer focus is judged?
options: Nothing, since customer focus is judged by the same kinds of stories at every company
The kind of understanding stressed: behaviour data at one, workflows at the other
Only the streaming service values customer focus
Only the vendor wants outcomes you can measure
optionExplain: The author says expression varies with business model and user relationships.
Right: the business model shapes the evidence.
Both value it; they express it differently.
Measured results matter at both; the author's contrast lies in what is understood.
questions.explain: The model of the business changes the evidence interviewers look for. The card next sets out the contrast.
questions.rule: Match your customer-focus story to the company's type: behaviour data for consumer products, workflows and stakeholders for enterprise.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: Sort each emphasis by the type of company where the author places it.

items.t: Obsessing over user experience and engagement metrics
Turning behaviour data into product improvements
Reading mass user patterns alongside individual journeys
Understanding complex business workflows
Weighing competing stakeholder needs
Turning business requirements into tools users can work effectively with

questions.explain: Consumer firms stress experience and engagement data; enterprise firms stress workflows and stakeholders.
questions.rule: Consumer: behaviour and engagement. Enterprise: workflows and stakeholders.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: You apply to a music-streaming company. Which story best shows customer focus in the way it values?
options: Mapping a client's purchase-approval chain before building a custom workflow
Moving old reports to cheaper storage tiers to reduce the company's monthly cloud bill
Rewriting a batch job so it runs in half the time
Reading listening data to find where new users drop out, then reworking onboarding
optionExplain: A good enterprise story, but it fits a vendor selling to organizations.
A cost story; it says nothing about what users needed.
A technical gain with no link to users.
Right: behaviour data turned into a product improvement.
questions.explain: A consumer company wants evidence that you read user behaviour and turned it into a better product.
questions.hint: Which story starts from how users behave?
questions.rule: Match your customer-focus story to the company's type: behaviour data for consumer products, workflows and stakeholders for enterprise.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: True or false: A candidate tells an enterprise interviewer only about engagement metrics, with nothing on workflows, and so covers what such firms look for.
questions.explain: Enterprise interviewers look for understanding of business workflows and competing stakeholders. The engagement story suits a consumer firm, so here it misses the point.
questions.rule: Fit the story to the company.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: Enterprise software has two kinds of people to serve. Which pair does the author name?
options: Developers who write plug-ins, and executives who approve the budget
End users who work in the software daily, and buyers who make the purchasing decision
Customers who pay for the product, and employees who build it
Power users who find bugs, and beginners who file tickets
optionExplain: These are plausible roles, but not the pair the author names.
Right: both count.
Employees are the team, not the second user group.
This is a split by ability, which the author uses elsewhere.
questions.explain: Customer focus here means managing both the daily users and the buyers, and turning business requirements into tools users can work well with.
questions.teaches: Enterprise customer focus means managing end users who use the software daily and buyers who make purchasing decisions.
questions.rule: Match your customer-focus story to the company's type: behaviour data for consumer products, workflows and stakeholders for enterprise.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: A fitness-app candidate shows only aggregate charts of daily activity. What would the author add?
options: More charts and dashboards, since consumer companies value the quantity of data they hold
A list of stakeholders and their approval roles
Individual user journeys beside mass patterns, balancing numbers with qualitative insight
A claim that individual users cannot be understood at scale
optionExplain: More of one kind does not give the balance the author names.
That belongs to enterprise settings.
Right: both halves.
The author asks for both mass patterns and individual journeys.
questions.explain: Understanding mass patterns and individual journeys together is the skill the author describes for consumer products.
questions.teaches: At consumer product companies the skill is balancing quantitative and qualitative data, understanding mass user patterns while also individual user journeys.
questions.rule: Match your customer-focus story to the company's type: behaviour data for consumer products, workflows and stakeholders for enterprise.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: A backend team serves a frontend team that serves shoppers. How could the backend team show customer focus?
options: Trace how its latency and reliability choices reach shoppers
Meet the frontend team's technical requirements and stop there
Treat shoppers as the product team's concern alone
Count how many tickets the frontend team files
optionExplain: Right: it follows its decisions down the chain.
Requirements are the starting point, not the end of the chain.
Distance from shoppers does not remove the effect of the backend.
Tickets show friction between teams, not impact on shoppers.
questions.explain: Even far from end users, you can follow the chain of effects. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Make the common path simple and the advanced path available; for backend work, follow your decision down to the end user.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: Match each kind of team to what customer focus means there, per the author.
pairs: Obsessing over experience and engagement metrics
Serving occasional users through to power users
Tracing decisions to their impact on end users
questions.explain: Each business model changes who the user is and how close they are.
questions.rule: Know your users and how far away they are.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: A cloud database vendor offers two hundred options, and most developers use a handful. Which change fits platform user focus?
options: Make the common tasks simple and keep the other options available for advanced use
Remove the rarely used options to keep the product clean
Show every option on the first screen so no one misses any
Require all new users to complete a full configuration wizard covering every available option
optionExplain: Right: both ends of the spectrum.
It fails the advanced users who need depth.
It overwhelms the typical user who needs only a few.
It treats every user as an advanced one.
questions.explain: Most users need a fraction of the features, so the common path should be simple while depth stays available.
questions.hint: Serve both the typical and the advanced user.
questions.rule: Make the common path simple and the advanced path available; for backend work, follow your decision down to the end user.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: True or false: A backend team that meets its technical requirements still needs to look at the full chain of impact on users.
questions.explain: The author asks backend teams to think beyond the immediate technical requirements and look at the full chain of impact on users.
questions.rule: Requirements met is not the same as users served.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: An SDK team hides all advanced options because most users do not need them. What is the flaw?
options: Nothing, since most users are better off with fewer options
It should have shown all options so users could choose
It should have asked each user to pick a skill level first
The author wants common tasks simple while still providing depth for advanced use cases
optionExplain: It is true that most need a fraction, but the advanced users would be shut out.
That treats everyone as a power user.
A gate is one tactic, but the author names the goal, not that method.
Right: serve the whole spectrum.
questions.explain: The error is in dropping depth altogether; the aim is a simple common path with depth behind it.
questions.rule: Simple for most; deep for some.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: A team supplies water-quality sensor data to a dispatch team that alerts residents. How does the author's idea apply?
options: Make sure the data feed matches the dispatch team's format and delivery times, then stop there
Look at the full chain from sensor data to residents' alerts, and judge choices by that impact
Leave resident concerns to the dispatch team entirely
Speed up the sensors regardless of how alerts are used
optionExplain: Format is a requirement; it is not the chain of impact.
Right: think beyond the immediate requirements.
The sensor team's choices still reach residents.
Optimizing without context is the trap the author warns about later.
questions.explain: A team far from end users still shapes what they receive, so its work is judged along the whole chain.
questions.teaches: In internal and backend contexts, success requires thinking beyond the immediate technical requirements and looking at the full chain of impact.
questions.rule: Make the common path simple and the advanced path available; for backend work, follow your decision down to the end user.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: Your background favours hints over direct statements. How could you use that in a customer-focus story?
options: Leave it out, since culture has no place in a story about customer focus or interviews
Say you wait until users ask for what they want
Show how you noticed needs users did not state, and what you did about them
Claim you never need to ask users questions
optionExplain: The author says culture shapes how people learn about customers.
Waiting for direct requests would hide the very strength.
Right: it turns a style into evidence.
Noticing the unsaid still needs checking against users.
questions.explain: Noticing what users do not say can be a strength. The card next shows how the author frames it.
questions.rule: Choose stories that show your natural strength, and cover the half your style might leave thin.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: Some cultures emphasize explicit communication and ____ feedback.
questions.explain: The author contrasts explicit communication and direct feedback with reading between the lines.
questions.rule: Cultures differ in how they learn about customers.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: Sort each story detail by whether it shows noticing the unsaid or probing past a surface request.

items.t: Our reading: I noticed no one mentioned the export step, so I watched them work
Our reading: I picked up hesitation on a call and followed up on it
Our reading: I asked three follow-up whys instead of taking the first answer
Our reading: I pushed past a polite first answer to the actual problem

questions.explain: Both moves reach the need behind the request: one by listening for what is missing, the other by asking more.
questions.rule: Unsaid needs and surface requests are two ways in.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: A candidate from a very direct culture says, I ask users what they want and build it. Which weakness does this risk?
options: It shows too little respect for users' own opinions
It may stop at surface requests instead of showing probing deeper
It proves the candidate cannot work with indirect colleagues
It breaks the rule that interviewers prefer indirect answers
optionExplain: Asking users is good; the risk is in stopping at the first answer.
Right: the author says to highlight probing deeper.
The author says nothing of the kind.
Interviewers look for depth, not for an indirect style.
questions.explain: Direct asking is valuable but incomplete; the story should show going past the surface request.
questions.rule: Show the probe, not only the ask.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: True or false: A background of indirect communication can help in a customer-focus interview, because you may notice what users do not say.
questions.explain: The author says it might make you excel at noticing what users do not say, which is the depth customer focus needs.
questions.rule: Indirect style can be an asset.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: A ward-software engineer from a very direct culture prepares a story. What should it highlight, per the author's advice?
options: How she learned to probe deeper than the surface requests nurses made
That she always states her own needs without hedging
That she avoids asking follow-up questions in order to save the nurses' valuable time
That her culture makes customer focus unnecessary
optionExplain: Right: the author's advice for a very direct background.
Directness in speaking is not the skill the author asks to show.
This keeps to surface requests.
The author treats customer focus as needed everywhere.
questions.explain: For a very direct background, the added step is to show that you learned to go beyond surface requests.
questions.teaches: If you come from a culture known to favour being very direct, highlight how you have learned to probe deeper than surface requests.
questions.rule: Choose stories that show your natural strength, and cover the half your style might leave thin.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: An engineer redesigns a confusing screen on her own, without asking users. Which quality is most missing?
options: Initiative, because she acted without being asked
Innovation, because the redesign was not original
Customer focus, which ties the initiative to what users need
Problem-solving, because confusing screens cannot be fixed without a full rewrite
optionExplain: She did show initiative; the gap is in what guided it.
Originality was not the problem.
Right: the action lacked the user's view.
Confusing screens can be fixed; the question is what users need fixed.
questions.explain: Initiative needs a direction. The card next shows how customer focus supplies it.
questions.rule: Check any innovation, initiative or problem-solving against what actually helps users.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: Match each competency to what the author says it involves.
pairs: Identifying opportunities for improvement and acting
Making sure solutions address real needs
questions.explain: The first three describe what you can do; customer focus checks that it matters to users.
questions.rule: Customer focus checks the others against real needs.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: A developer cuts a report's load time from forty seconds to five. Finance users still distrust the report because totals differ from the ledger. What was missing?
options: More initiative, since he should have fixed the totals unprompted
More innovation, since a new report format would have helped
Nothing, because load time was the reported problem
The users' view of the problem: accuracy mattered more to them than speed
optionExplain: He acted; the issue is what he chose to fix.
A new format would not reconcile the totals.
Fixing the reported problem can still miss what users value.
Right: problem-solving without customer focus.
questions.explain: He solved a speed problem while users cared more about accuracy. Customer focus gives the context for which problem matters.
questions.hint: What did the finance users care about most?
questions.rule: Check any innovation, initiative or problem-solving against what actually helps users.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: Which situation shows initiative without customer focus?
options: Redesigning a settings page unprompted, without checking how people use it
Interviewing users after a redesign to refine it
Inventing a new report layout after watching finance staff work through month-end close
Fixing a bug exactly as a customer reported it
optionExplain: Right: action without the users' view.
This adds the user's view; it shows customer focus.
Innovation informed by users.
Responding to a report is neither initiative nor deep customer focus.
questions.explain: Initiative alone identifies and acts; customer focus makes sure the action matters to users.
questions.rule: Initiative needs the users' view.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: True or false: Idris invents a new interface pattern and argues that its novelty alone shows users will like it, which is sound reasoning by the author's view.
questions.explain: A new pattern may not match users' mental models and could confuse them. Customer focus keeps innovation grounded in what helps users.
questions.rule: Novel is not the same as useful.

questions.section: 10.2 The Essence of Customer and User Focus
questions.q: A clinic team can fix only one of five issues in its booking tool this month. According to the author, what should decide?
options: Which problem is technically the most interesting to the engineers on the team
Which problem was reported first
Which problem is fastest to fix
Which problem has the biggest impact on users, from their view
optionExplain: This is optimizing for engineering satisfaction.
Order of arrival says nothing of impact.
Speed to fix is convenient, but not the same as impact.
Right: customer focus gives that context.
questions.explain: With limited time, the user's view of impact decides which problem to pick.
questions.teaches: Customer focus provides the context for deciding which problems will have the biggest impact for users.
questions.rule: Check any innovation, initiative or problem-solving against what actually helps users.

questions.q: An interviewer says: Describe a time you pushed back on a technical approach because of its effect on users. Which family is this?
options: Understanding user needs
Advocating for users
Measuring user success
Balancing technical and user needs
optionExplain: That family asks how you found out what users needed.
Right: it asks whether you champion users in a technical decision.
That family asks how you knew a solution helped.
It overlaps, but pushing back for users is the heart of advocacy.
questions.explain: Pushing back on behalf of users is advocacy. The card next lays out all four families.
questions.rule: Identify which of the four families a question belongs to, then tell the story that answers it.

questions.q: Match each question, in paraphrase, to its family.
pairs: Tell me how you worked out what users needed on a project
Describe a time you made trade-offs to serve users
How did you check that your solution helped users?
When did you influence a technical choice for users?
questions.explain: The four families ask about discovery, trade-offs, evidence and championing users.
questions.rule: Discovery, trade-offs, evidence, advocacy.

questions.q: You are asked: Tell me about a time you found users were not benefiting from a feature you built. Which should your story show first?
options: How you persuaded leadership to give you a bigger team
How elegant the original architecture was
How you detected the gap by looking at user outcomes
How many features the product had at launch
optionExplain: A different skill from the one this question tests.
Technical quality is not the point of the question.
Right: a measuring-success story starts with the evidence.
Feature count does not show users benefiting.
questions.explain: This question belongs to the measuring family, so the evidence of user outcomes comes first.
questions.rule: Identify which of the four families a question belongs to, then tell the story that answers it.

questions.q: A candidate answers an advocacy question with a story about choosing a tool the team preferred. What is missing?
options: Bringing the users' perspective into a technical discussion, even at extra cost
A longer explanation of the tool's features
A claim that the team agreed unanimously
An apology for the extra work the choice caused
optionExplain: Right: that is what advocacy questions probe.
More detail on the tool does not add the users' side.
Agreement is not the evidence sought.
The point is the advocacy, not an apology.
questions.explain: Advocacy questions test whether you bring the users' view into technical choices.
questions.rule: Advocacy brings users into the technical room.

questions.q: True or false: Interviewers ask these questions to see whether you care about what users actually need, or only do your job.
questions.explain: According to the author, they ask to see whether you care about what users actually need and can translate it into technical decisions.
questions.rule: They test your practice, not your phrasing.

questions.q: A restaurant manager is asked how she worked out what guests needed beyond what they ordered. Which family is this, and what does it test?
options: Advocating for users: whether she accepts extra work to get a better result for guests
Measuring user success: whether she tracks results with numbers
Understanding user needs: whether she digs into the true nature of the problem
Balancing needs: whether she can trade off kitchen and guest priorities
optionExplain: Advocacy asks about pushing for users in a decision.
Measurement asks how she knew the solution helped.
Right: discovery of the need behind the request.
That family asks about conflicts between technical and user needs.
questions.explain: Asking how needs were found beyond the request is the understanding-needs family. It assesses whether you dig deeper.
questions.teaches: Understanding-needs questions assess whether you will dig deeper to understand the true nature of user problems.
questions.rule: Identify which of the four families a question belongs to, then tell the story that answers it.

questions.q: An interviewer asks: Describe building something when the requirements were unclear. What do they most want to hear?
options: That you waited until the requirements were clarified
That you picked the most likely requirement and built it
That your manager decided what to build
The methods you used to find out what users needed
optionExplain: Waiting is the opposite of digging into the problem.
Guessing the need skips the discovery they ask about.
Handing off the decision does not show how you understood users.
Right: methods that uncover needs.
questions.explain: The question tests how you find needs, not how you cope with ambiguity passively. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Describe the methods you used to uncover the need, not only the request you received.

questions.q: Strong answers show you talking directly with users and ____ their actual behaviour when working.
questions.explain: Direct conversation and observation are the two methods the author names for uncovering needs.
questions.rule: Talk to users and watch them work.

questions.q: You built a booking tool from vague requirements. Which line in your story is strongest?
options: I asked the manager to write a clearer spec before I started
I shadowed three receptionists for a day and noted where they re-typed data
I built the most common booking features first and then waited for feedback to arrive
I emailed a survey asking which features the team wanted
optionExplain: It delegates the discovery instead of doing it.
Right: direct observation.
Waiting for feedback is slower than finding the need first.
A survey collects requests, the very thing to look beneath.
questions.explain: Shadowing shows what people actually do, which is where unstated needs appear.
questions.hint: Which line is about watching real work?
questions.rule: Describe the methods you used to uncover the need, not only the request you received.

questions.q: A candidate describes a project. Which lines weaken the story? Select all that apply.
options: The spec was thorough, so I never spoke with users
I watched two users work and noticed they exported data every day
I compared what users said they did with what I saw them do
A director gave me twelve features and I built all twelve
optionExplain: It avoids the direct contact the question tests.
Observation of real behaviour is a strength.
Comparing words with behaviour is a strength.
Building a list as handed over shows no discovery.
questions.explain: Lines that accept requests as given or avoid users weaken the story; observation and comparison strengthen it.
questions.rule: Show discovery, not delivery of a list.

questions.q: True or false: A story saying you accepted the feature requests as given answers an understanding-needs question well.
questions.explain: Interviewers want the methods you use to uncover needs rather than hearing that you accept feature requests without looking deeper.
questions.rule: Accepting requests is not understanding needs.

questions.q: A school-bus scheduler hears administrators ask for printable route lists. Which answer best fits an understanding-needs question?
options: I compared what they asked for with what I saw them do, then chose the solution that helped them most
I printed the lists as requested and confirmed they were pleased
I asked them to rank their requests by importance
I chose the printable format because it was the simplest to build
optionExplain: Right: separates what is said from what would work better.
It satisfies the request without looking at the need.
Ranking requests does not uncover the problem under them.
Ease of building drives the choice, not the users' needs.
questions.explain: The strongest answers separate what users say they want from what would be a more effective solution.
questions.teaches: Strong answers distinguish between what users say they want and what would be a more effective solution to help them succeed.
questions.rule: Describe the methods you used to uncover the need, not only the request you received.

questions.q: An interviewer asks: Tell me about a time user needs conflicted with technical best practices. Which opening fits best?
options: A case where I followed best practice because rules are rules
A case where I weighed both and protected the users without giving up integrity
A case where I gave users exactly what they wanted and ignored the architecture entirely
A case where my manager decided between the two
optionExplain: It ignores the user side of the conflict.
Right: a considered balance.
It drops the technical side.
It hides your own judgment.
questions.explain: The question asks how you weighed two legitimate priorities. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Weigh technical quality and user success together, and look for a solution that serves both.

questions.q: Balancing questions test well-considered ____ between competing priorities.
questions.explain: The author describes these questions as testing your ability to make well-considered trade-offs.
questions.rule: Make considered trade-offs.

questions.q: A team wants to cache account balances for five minutes, but customers need exact balances at checkout. Which story line shows a strong balance?
options: We cached everywhere because best practice says that caching reduces server cost for everyone
We removed caching from the whole app so users never saw old data
We cached the checkout balance as well and showed a note that it may be five minutes old
We cached for browsing but read live balances at checkout, protecting the critical step
optionExplain: Best practice wins, and the checkout user loses.
The technical side is dropped completely.
Customers need exact balances at checkout, so a stale figure there breaks the critical step even with a warning.
Right: protects the key experience and keeps the benefit.
questions.explain: Protecting the critical step while keeping the technical gain elsewhere is the pattern of a good balancing example.
questions.hint: Which keeps both sides intact where it counts?
questions.rule: Weigh technical quality and user success together, and look for a solution that serves both.

questions.q: Sort each story detail by whether it fits a strong balancing answer.

items.t: Kept the checkout fast and accepted a plainer code path elsewhere
Found a design meeting both the latency budget and the users' main task
Followed the coding standard exactly and noted that users disliked it
Gave users every request because they asked loudly
Skipped the trade-off discussion and let the lead choose
Protected the signup flow and documented what the team gave up

questions.explain: Strong answers weigh both sides and protect what matters most. Following rules blindly, giving in to volume or skipping the discussion do not.
questions.rule: Protect the critical experience; keep integrity.

questions.q: True or false: A balancing story is strongest when it finds a solution that achieves both technical quality and user success.
questions.explain: The author asks for creative solutions that achieve both technical quality and user success, not a win by one side.
questions.rule: Aim to serve both sides.

questions.q: A parks department asks for a QR code on every bench; the developer proposes a text-message option instead, since many visitors lack data plans. What does this show?
options: Ignoring the request because the developer prefers texting
Finding the cheapest way to meet the original request
Advocating for a different approach than requested because it serves users better, even at more work
Delaying the project until everyone agrees on one method
optionExplain: The change is justified by visitors' needs.
It adds work rather than cutting it.
Right: the author's second pattern.
No delay appears in the case; the point is the changed approach.
questions.explain: Pushing for a different technical approach than the one requested, because it serves users better, counts as a strong balancing example.
questions.teaches: Good balancing examples can show advocating for a technical approach different from what was requested because it would better serve user needs, even if it means more work.
questions.rule: Weigh technical quality and user success together, and look for a solution that serves both.

questions.q: An interviewer asks how you validate that your technical work improves user outcomes. Which answer fits best?
options: I confirmed that all the tests passed and that latency stayed within the agreed target
I defined what success meant for users, gathered usage feedback and adjusted
I counted tickets before and after the release
I asked my manager whether the release looked good
optionExplain: Both are technical checks, not user outcomes.
Right: defines success first, then checks it.
Tickets show friction; they do not show users reaching goals.
A manager's opinion is not user evidence.
questions.explain: Validation starts from the user's definition of success. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Say what success meant for the user, and how you found out whether it happened.

questions.q: The best measurement stories define what ____ looks like for the user.
questions.explain: The author puts defining success from the user's side first in strong measurement stories.
questions.rule: Define success first.

questions.q: You built an order-tracking page for a delivery app. Which story line best answers: Describe how you measured whether your solution helped users?
options: I set success as fewer where-is-my-order calls, gathered feedback and tuned the page
The page launched on schedule with zero reported defects and a clean, well-documented code review
Page views reached a million in the first week
The design review gave it top marks
optionExplain: Right: user-side goal, feedback, adjustment.
Delivery quality describes the team's work.
Views show traffic, not that users got what they needed.
Peers' approval is not the users' outcome.
questions.explain: A user-side goal, feedback and adjustment together make a measurement story.
questions.hint: Which line starts from what users wanted?
questions.rule: Say what success meant for the user, and how you found out whether it happened.

questions.q: A candidate says: Our dashboard load time improved thirty percent, so users benefited. What is missing, per the author?
options: A larger load-time improvement figure
A comparison with a competitor's dashboard
A user-side definition of success and evidence of user outcomes
A statement that load time is important to everyone
optionExplain: A bigger number is still a system metric.
Competitor speed does not show these users' outcomes.
Right: the claim jumps from a system metric to a user result.
Asserting importance is not evidence.
questions.explain: Faster loading may help, but the story does not show users reaching their goals.
questions.rule: Link the metric to the user's goal.

questions.q: True or false: If quantitative metrics look healthy, a measurement story needs no user feedback.
questions.explain: The best stories gather feedback and adjust based on user outcomes rather than only quantitative metrics.
questions.rule: Numbers alone are not enough.

questions.q: A city's tutoring-booking site has high sign-ups, but tutors say students rarely turn up. What fits the author's approach?
options: Treat the high sign-ups as proof of success and move on to the next project on the list
Remove the site, since sign-ups cannot predict attendance
Add more sign-up reminders without asking students anything
Gather feedback on why and adjust the approach, rather than rely on sign-up numbers
optionExplain: Sign-ups measure intent, not attendance.
It abandons the evidence instead of acting on it.
It adjusts without finding the reason.
Right: outcomes over a quantitative metric.
questions.explain: High sign-ups hide a failing outcome. Feedback explains it and guides the next change.
questions.teaches: The best measurement stories gather feedback about usage and adjust the approach based on user outcomes rather than only quantitative metrics.
questions.rule: Say what success meant for the user, and how you found out whether it happened.

questions.q: An interviewer asks: Give an example of influencing technical decisions to serve user needs. What are they probing?
options: Whether you are the most senior voice in the room
Whether you can win arguments with the product team and keep your preferred roadmap intact when challenged
Whether you bring the users' view into technical choices and help the team weigh it
Whether you prefer user-facing work to infrastructure
optionExplain: Influence here is about users, not rank.
Winning is not the aim; weighing user impact is.
Right: user perspective in the decision.
The question is about how you act, not your preferences.
questions.explain: Advocacy means giving users a voice in technical decisions. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Bring the user's perspective into the technical decision and help the team weigh it.

questions.q: Advocacy responses show you bringing the user's perspective to technical ____.
questions.explain: The author describes strong responses as bringing the user's perspective into technical discussions.
questions.rule: Give users a voice.

questions.q: Your team plans to cut a form's autosave to save server cost. Which action is advocacy?
options: Accept the cut because the budget is fixed
Argue against it as a matter of personal taste
Keep autosave on quietly without telling the team
Show session data on how many users would lose work, and propose a cheaper autosave
optionExplain: Silent acceptance gives users no voice.
Taste is not evidence of user impact.
It bypasses the discussion the author wants you to join.
Right: user impact brought to the decision.
questions.explain: Evidence of user impact plus an option that eases the cost helps the team weigh the trade-off.
questions.hint: Which action puts user impact in front of the team?
questions.rule: Bring the user's perspective into the technical decision and help the team weigh it.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it is advocacy for users.

items.t: Shared recordings of users struggling, to show the team the cost of a design
Argued for a simpler API shape because callers' tasks were simpler
Pushed back on a launch date because users could not complete checkout
Agreed in the meeting and raised no user concerns
Chose the approach that cost the team the least effort
Raised user concerns in private messages only after the decision

questions.explain: Advocacy brings user impact into the decision, at the time it is made. Silence, convenience and late comments do not.
questions.rule: Speak for users when the decision is made.

questions.q: Beyond skill, what do advocacy questions check about the candidate?
options: Whether you can convince other people on the team to take on the extra work instead of you
Whether you champion users even when it creates more work and inconvenience for you
Whether you avoid conflict with technical teams
Whether you can cut scope to protect the deadline
optionExplain: The extra work is yours in the author's description.
Right: the author's point.
Advocacy often involves pushing back.
Scope cutting is a different trade-off.
questions.explain: Advocacy has a cost to the advocate, and interviewers listen for whether you pay it.
questions.teaches: Advocacy questions probe whether you will champion user interests even when it creates more work and inconvenience for you.
questions.rule: Bring the user's perspective into the technical decision and help the team weigh it.

questions.q: A hospital kitchen supervisor wants to change a meal-ordering form for patients with allergies. Which response matches strong advocacy?
options: Show the staff what patients face and help them weigh patient and kitchen trade-offs
Insist that the form change right away, without discussing any of the kitchen's limits
Accept the current form to avoid disrupting the kitchen
Leave the decision to whoever has the most seniority
optionExplain: Right: perspective plus a shared weighing.
It brings the perspective but not the weighing of both sides.
It gives patients no voice.
It hands off the decision instead of helping the group weigh it.
questions.explain: Strong responses help teams consider technical and user trade-offs together.
questions.teaches: Advocacy questions probe whether you will champion user interests even when doing so creates more work and inconvenience for you.
questions.rule: Bring the user's perspective into the technical decision and help the team weigh it.

questions.q: Interviewers listening for the critical signal in a customer-focus story most want to hear what?
options: That you delivered on the original schedule
That you probed beyond requests to uncover needs, then built for them
That you used a well-known framework
That users thanked you at the end
optionExplain: Timeliness is not the signal here.
Right: user-centred decision-making.
A named method is not evidence of understanding users.
Thanks may follow, but the signal is in the decisions.
questions.explain: The strongest signal is decisions built on what users are trying to do. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Show that you probed past the request and built for what users were trying to do.

questions.q: The critical signal is user-centered ____-making.
questions.explain: The author names user-centered decision-making as the critical signal for customer focus.
questions.rule: Decisions start from the user's goal.

questions.q: Operations staff ask a platform engineer for a longer log-retention setting. Which story shows the critical signal?
options: She extended retention to ninety days as requested, confirmed the setting worked and closed the ticket
She wrote documentation explaining the retention policy
She shadowed an on-call shift, saw staff search by customer ID, and added that filter
She asked the staff to file a formal specification
optionExplain: It meets the request without checking the need.
Documentation does not change what the staff can do.
Right: observation led to a solution for the task.
It pushes discovery back onto the users.
questions.explain: Observation revealed the actual task, and the solution addressed it.
questions.hint: Which story starts from the staff's real work?
questions.rule: Show that you probed past the request and built for what users were trying to do.

questions.q: True or false: A story whose customers are other engineering teams can show user-centred decision-making by understanding their workflows.
questions.explain: The author says that for internal tools, platform and backend work, the customers can be other engineering teams, data scientists or operations staff, and the signal is shown by understanding their workflows.
questions.rule: Internal customers count.

questions.q: A candidate says: Users told me exactly what they wanted, so I built it. What is the weakness, per the author?
options: Users struggle to explain their real challenges, so the story lacks any probing
Asking users is never part of customer focus
The story should have named a competitor's product that already solves the same problem
Building quickly is a sign of poor planning
optionExplain: Right: the request was taken at face value.
Asking is fine; stopping there is the weakness.
Competitors do not address this gap.
Speed is not the issue raised.
questions.explain: The critical signal needs the probing step. Taking the request at face value skips it.
questions.rule: Probe before you build.

questions.q: A transit data engineer can rewrite a pipeline in a favourite new language or fix stale arrival times riders complain about. What does the author's idea suggest?
options: Rewrite the pipeline first, since cleaner code helps everyone eventually
Do both at once so neither group waits
Let the team vote on which task sounds more exciting
Fix the stale times first, since work is prioritized on user impact rather than technical interest
optionExplain: It follows technical interest, not user impact.
It avoids the decision about priority.
Excitement is not user impact.
Right: the author's prioritization point.
questions.explain: Interviewers want to see that you prioritize by what helps users, not what interests you technically.
questions.teaches: Show interviewers that you prioritize work based on user impact rather than your technical interests.
questions.rule: Show that you probed past the request and built for what users were trying to do.

questions.q: You maintain a search index that end users do not touch directly. How could you show you understand its user impact?
options: Report the index's uptime to your manager each month
Wait for the frontend team to complain about it
Track query latency against shoppers' waits, and talk to the team facing shoppers
Describe the index's data structures in detail
optionExplain: A system number with no tie to users.
Waiting is reactive and shows no understanding.
Right: connects your work to user experience.
Technical depth does not show user impact.
questions.explain: Even far from users, you can tie your system's behaviour to what they feel. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Find a way to see user effects, directly or through the people and metrics that stand between you and users.

questions.q: Match each technical measure to the user effect the author ties it to.
pairs: Determines whether users can complete their tasks
questions.explain: Each metric is a bridge from a technical property to something users notice.
questions.rule: Link each technical metric to a user effect.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it shows understanding of user impact.

items.t: A backend engineer meets weekly with the support lead to hear user complaints
A database engineer links slow queries to page-load time on checkout
A platform engineer checks whether outages stop users completing tasks
An engineer reports server CPU graphs with no link to users
A team treats the frontend team's tickets as the end of its duty
A developer says users are someone else's concern

questions.explain: The left column connects technical work to user effects; the right treats users as outside the job.
questions.rule: Connect your work to what users feel.

questions.q: True or false: A backend engineer can show this strong signal through dialogue with customer-facing teams and metrics tied to user outcomes.
questions.explain: The author describes ways to show it without direct contact: dialogue with customer-facing teams, metrics tied to user outcomes, and feedback from internal customers.
questions.rule: No direct contact does not rule out the signal.

questions.q: A backend candidate says: I do not speak to frontend or product people, as my API meets spec. What is the gap?
options: No dialogue with people who see users daily, and no link from the API to users
Meeting spec is a weakness in any engineering story
The API should have been faster than the spec required
The candidate should have contacted end users personally instead of working through other teams
optionExplain: Right: neither route to user impact is shown.
Meeting spec is fine; the gap is in what lies beyond it.
Speed alone is not the signal.
Direct contact is one route, not the only one.
questions.explain: The story stops at the specification. The signal needs a view of how the API affects users.
questions.rule: Look past spec to effect.

questions.q: A payroll team supports HR staff who answer employee questions. Which approach fits the author's strong examples?
options: Track only the payroll run time and report it monthly
Ask the HR staff regularly for feedback, trace how changes reach employees, and prioritize by downstream impact
Wait for HR to file defects and fix them in order
Ask employees directly and ignore the HR staff
optionExplain: A system metric with no user tie.
Right: all three habits.
Reactive and not impact-based.
The HR staff are the internal customers.
questions.explain: Internal customers, the cascade to end users and downstream impact are the elements the author names.
questions.teaches: Strong examples show you proactively gathering feedback from internal customers, seeing how technical decisions cascade to end users, and prioritizing work based on downstream impact.
questions.rule: Find a way to see user effects, directly or through the people and metrics that stand between you and users.

questions.q: Two candidates describe a new onboarding flow. Which shows the strong measurement signal?
options: I tracked how many lines of onboarding code I shipped
I tracked server error rates and response times on the onboarding endpoint each week
I tracked how many onboarding screens we had
I tracked how many new users finished their first task and how long it took
optionExplain: A volume-of-work measure.
A system health measure.
A count of features, not outcomes.
Right: user goals, measured.
questions.explain: Measures tied to users finishing what they came to do are the signal. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Instrument what users are trying to achieve, then iterate on what the numbers show.

questions.q: The signal is measuring real user ____.
questions.explain: The author names measuring real user outcomes as a strong signal.
questions.rule: Measure outcomes, not output.

questions.q: You shipped an invoicing tool. Which instrumented measure reflects user goals?
options: Share of invoices sent without needing a correction
Number of API requests handled per minute at peak traffic hours
Time the build pipeline takes to finish
Number of invoice templates available
optionExplain: Right: reflects the users' goal of invoices that work.
A load figure.
A team metric.
A feature count.
questions.explain: Invoices that need no correction show users getting what they wanted.
questions.hint: Which measure would the invoicing users themselves care about?
questions.rule: Instrument what users are trying to achieve, then iterate on what the numbers show.

questions.q: Sort each measure by whether it sits on the user side or the system side.

items.t: Share of users who reach their goal
Time a user needs to finish a task
Task completion rate
CPU utilization on the servers
Duration of the build
Number of deployments per week

questions.explain: User-side measures describe what users achieve; system-side ones describe the machines and the team.
questions.rule: Ask whose success the metric reports.

questions.q: According to the author, what does this signal separate?
options: Senior engineers from junior engineers
Quantitative engineers from qualitative ones
Feature-focused engineers from user-focused ones
Fast shippers from careful planners
optionExplain: Seniority is shown by other dimensions.
The signal asks for user-side definition, not a method split.
Right: the author's wording.
Speed is not what the signal separates.
questions.explain: Defining success from the user's perspective is what marks a user-focused engineer from a feature-focused one.
questions.teaches: Defining success from the user's perspective separates feature-focused engineers from user-focused ones.
questions.rule: Instrument what users are trying to achieve, then iterate on what the numbers show.

questions.q: A school-lunch ordering team reports, The order feature works. Which restatement follows the author's key?
options: The order feature has no known bugs
Students now get lunch faster with fewer wrong orders
The order feature was released on schedule and passed every acceptance test
The order feature uses a modern database
optionExplain: Still a system statement.
Right: success framed in what affects students.
Still a delivery statement.
A technology statement.
questions.explain: The key is to frame success in terms of what affects users.
questions.teaches: The key is framing success in terms of what affects users.
questions.rule: Instrument what users are trying to achieve, then iterate on what the numbers show.

questions.q: Your product has casual and expert users. Which statement best shows the supporting signal?
options: We built the same features for everyone
We followed the wishes of our largest customer because it brings in the most revenue
We let users pick their own plan
Experts went first this quarter for stated reasons; casual users kept simple flows
optionExplain: Ignores the differences.
Follows one voice, not the segments.
A packaging choice, not a prioritization decision.
Right: prioritized with reasons, protecting the other group.
questions.explain: A deliberate choice, with reasons and protection of the other segment, is the signal. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Name the segments you weighed, and show how you served them or chose between them.

questions.q: Match each ability to the signal it demonstrates.
pairs: Probing past requests and building for the real task
Watching users and asking questions that reveal underlying needs
Defining success by what users achieve
Explaining which group you served first
questions.explain: The four signals cover how you decide, see, measure and choose among users.
questions.rule: Four signals: decide, see, measure, balance.

questions.q: You improved the admin console before the guest portal. Which explanation best supports the signal?
options: Admins matter more than guests, which is self-evident
Both groups got the same fixes in the same week
The loudest requester asked for the console
Admins run every account change and guests rarely log in, so admin tools went first
optionExplain: Asserts a ranking without a reason.
Equal treatment, not a prioritization.
Volume is not a reason about segments.
Right: a reason tied to the segments' needs.
questions.explain: A stated reason grounded in how the segments use the product shows the signal.
questions.hint: Which answer gives a reason about the segments?
questions.rule: Name the segments you weighed, and show how you served them or chose between them.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate who picked beginners over experts because beginners are more pleasant to support has given a sound reason tied to the segments' needs.
questions.explain: The reason rests on the candidate's convenience, not on what either segment needs. A prioritization needs a reason rooted in users.
questions.rule: Give a user-based reason for your priority.

questions.q: Which tier does the author give the balancing signal among the four?
options: Critical, since the choice of whom to serve comes first
Supporting, below the critical signal and the two strong ones
Strong, alongside measuring outcomes
Optional, so it can be left out of any story
optionExplain: The critical signal is user-centred decision-making.
Right: the author's labels.
Strong is for understanding impact and measuring outcomes.
The author calls it supporting, not optional.
questions.explain: The four signals are one critical, two strong and one supporting.
questions.teaches: The author labels user-centred decision-making critical, understanding user impact and measuring real user outcomes strong, and balancing multiple user needs supporting.
questions.rule: Name the segments you weighed, and show how you served them or chose between them.

questions.q: A museum app serves school groups and solo adults, and budget covers one new feature. What does the author want in your explanation?
options: A clear reason why one group came first when both could not be served equally
A claim that both groups were served equally well
A list of every feature each group asked for
A statement that overall visitor numbers decide everything, whatever each group needs
optionExplain: Right: the articulation.
The budget stops that.
A list is not a reason.
Numbers can inform but need to be tied to needs.
questions.explain: The author asks you to say clearly why you prioritized one group when you could not serve everyone equally.
questions.teaches: Strong stories can clearly articulate why you prioritized one group over another when you could not serve everyone equally.
questions.rule: Name the segments you weighed, and show how you served them or chose between them.

questions.q: Which story opening would raise the most serious concern about customer focus?
options: I checked what users needed once, at kickoff
I made the queries twenty percent faster
The spec said to add a search box, so I added a search box
I treated all users as having the same needs and the same level of technical skill
optionExplain: A weakness, but some understanding is shown.
A technical gain; it does not show blind building.
Right: implementation with no sign of asking why.
A weakness of a different kind.
questions.explain: Building to the request with no thought about its use is the most serious pattern. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Do not let your story jump straight from request to implementation; show the discovery between them.

questions.q: True or false: The author reserves red flags for serious issues that significantly damage your candidacy.
questions.explain: Red flags are the serious category. Building features blindly is the red flag in this chapter.
questions.rule: Red flag means serious.

questions.q: Sort each story detail by whether it shows blind feature-building or understanding of why.

items.t: The story goes straight from ticket to implementation
Built the requested screen without asking how it would be used
Delivered exactly the fields listed in the request
Asked users what they hoped to do with the export before building
Showed what users were really trying to achieve
Changed the plan after watching people use a prototype

questions.explain: The left column stops at the request; the right shows discovery.
questions.rule: Show the discovery between request and build.

questions.q: A candidate adds detail about the technology stack to fix a story that jumps from request to build. Does this remove the flag?
options: Yes, because more detail always shows depth
Yes, since technology choices are customer focus
No, because the gap is missing thought about how users would use the result
No, because red flags cannot be fixed
optionExplain: Depth in the build is not depth about users.
They can serve users but do not show the thinking.
Right: more technical detail does not supply it.
They can be avoided by showing discovery.
questions.explain: The flag concerns understanding why, not how much technical detail is given.
questions.rule: Add the why, not more how.

questions.q: What does a story that jumps straight to implementation show, per the author?
options: Order-taking rather than problem-solving
Strong speed of execution
A careful respect for the user's specification
A preference for technical work over people work
optionExplain: Right: the author's wording.
Speed is not what the story shows.
Following the spec blindly is the problem.
The author names order-taking, not preference.
questions.explain: The story shows an order-taker rather than a problem-solver.
questions.teaches: A story that jumps straight to implementation without thinking about how it will be used shows order-taking rather than problem-solving.
questions.rule: Do not let your story jump straight from request to implementation; show the discovery between them.

questions.q: A carpenter's story: a client wanted bigger windows, and I built bigger windows without asking why. How does the author's scale rate this pattern?
options: As a yellow flag, a concerning pattern that weakens the example
As a strength, since the client got what they asked for
As neutral, since it is not about software
As a red flag, the serious kind that significantly damages candidacy
optionExplain: Yellow flags cover patterns like one-time research.
Meeting the request is not the test.
The principle is not specific to software.
Right: blind implementation.
questions.explain: Yellow flags are concerning patterns that weaken your examples; red flags significantly damage your candidacy. This pattern is the red kind.
questions.teaches: Yellow flags are concerning patterns that weaken your examples, while red flags are serious issues that significantly damage your candidacy.
questions.rule: Do not let your story jump straight from request to implementation; show the discovery between them.

questions.q: A candidate says: We interviewed users in week one, then built alone for six months. What would an interviewer note?
options: Admirable depth of up-front research, which sets a strong base for the project
User understanding looks like a one-time event
Too much contact with users
Unusual speed of delivery
optionExplain: The research is fine; the lack of later checks is the issue.
Right: no later checks are shown.
The story shows none after week one.
Speed is not the subject.
questions.explain: Research that stops early leaves later needs unseen. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Return to the users more than once, and show how what you learned changed the work.

questions.q: Strong customer focus is shown by testing whether your solution works as you build, not only at the beginning or ____.
questions.explain: The author asks for testing during the build, not only at the beginning or the end.
questions.rule: Test throughout, not only at the ends.

questions.q: You are building a tax-filing helper. Which plan avoids the yellow flag?
options: Interview filers in depth at kickoff, then freeze the requirements until launch day
Interview filers at kickoff, then test prototypes with new filers at each milestone
Test with filers only on launch day
Ask the team to predict what filers will want
optionExplain: A single check.
Right: repeated checks.
A single check at the end.
Guessing replaces contact.
questions.explain: Repeated contact keeps the picture of users current.
questions.hint: Which plan returns to users more than once?
questions.rule: Return to the users more than once, and show how what you learned changed the work.

questions.q: True or false: If research at kickoff found all the main use cases, no further checks are needed.
questions.explain: User needs evolve, and the initial research might have missed important use cases, so assumptions are validated at several points.
questions.rule: Keep checking.

questions.q: Why does the author say initial research alone is not enough?
options: Interviewers dislike early research
Users change their minds to impress researchers
Initial research might have missed important use cases
Requirements documents are always out of date
optionExplain: Early research is fine.
No such claim is made.
Right: and needs evolve.
The author gives other reasons.
questions.explain: Early findings are incomplete, and the world moves on. Later checks fill the gap.
questions.teaches: Your initial research might have missed important use cases, so you validate your assumptions at multiple points.
questions.rule: Return to the users more than once, and show how what you learned changed the work.

questions.q: City planners study cyclists once, then build a whole bike-lane network without further contact. What fits the author's view?
options: Trust the first study, since it was thorough
Wait until the network is finished, then ask riders
Ask only the planners' own staff
Check with riders at several points as lanes open, and adjust the plan
optionExplain: Thoroughness at one time point is not ongoing.
A single end check.
Staff are not the users.
Right: ongoing practice.
questions.explain: Collecting needs early and then building in isolation treats research as a checkbox, not as an ongoing practice.
questions.teaches: Stories that gather requirements early and then build in isolation suggest you treat user research as a checkbox and not an ongoing practice.
questions.rule: Return to the users more than once, and show how what you learned changed the work.

questions.q: A candidate says: I cut the nightly job from four hours to one. Which addition best fixes the weakness?
options: Who benefited from the job finishing sooner, and how
A chart of the job's CPU use and memory use before and after the change
More detail on the algorithm that sped it up
The server cost saved each month
optionExplain: Right: ties the gain to users.
More technical detail.
Another technical detail.
A business figure, but not a user benefit.
questions.explain: A technical gain needs a user-side reason. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Name the user who gains from each technical improvement, and say how.

questions.q: Improving technical metrics without connecting them to user ____ shows misplaced priorities.
questions.explain: The author asks you to connect technical improvements to user outcomes.
questions.rule: Connect the metric to the user.

questions.q: Sort each improvement by whether it is tied to a user benefit.

items.t: Cut page load so checkout finishes before shoppers give up
Shortened sync time so field nurses see updated charts at shift start
Trimmed query time because analysts waited on dashboards each morning
Halved the build time and mentioned no one who gains
Reduced memory use by thirty percent as a personal challenge
Made a job faster although no one was waiting on it

questions.explain: The left column names who gains; the right column only reports the technical change.
questions.rule: Say who gains.

questions.q: A team makes an internal tool three times faster, but users spend their time lost in a confusing menu. How does the author's logic rate the speed-up?
options: As a success, since faster software is better in itself and users will notice it
As a failure of the algorithm
It matters only if it helps users reach their goals, which this one may not
As neutral, since users do not notice speed
optionExplain: The author denies this when users' goals are not helped.
The algorithm may be fine; the priority is misplaced.
Right: speed is not an end in itself.
Users may notice; the point is that it needs a user link.
questions.explain: A faster tool in a confusing menu leaves users' goals unmet.
questions.rule: Speed counts only when it helps users.

questions.q: True or false: Adding more benchmark figures to an optimization story removes the yellow flag.
questions.explain: Benchmarks add technical evidence. The flag is about the missing link to a user benefit.
questions.rule: Add the user link, not more benchmarks.

questions.q: A mapping team shaves rendering time because it is an interesting puzzle. What does the author say this kind of optimization serves?
options: Engineering satisfaction rather than customer success
Customer success, since faster is better
Business revenue, whatever the users' view
Team morale, which is the real aim of engineering
optionExplain: Right: the author's phrase.
Only when users' goals benefit.
The author makes no such link.
Morale is not the author's concern here.
questions.explain: Optimization without a user reason serves the engineers' interest, not the customers'.
questions.teaches: If improvements do not translate to better user experiences, you are optimizing for engineering satisfaction rather than customer success.
questions.rule: Name the user who gains from each technical improvement, and say how.

questions.q: A candidate says: We built one dashboard for finance, sales and operations, since everyone wants the same numbers. What will interviewers likely hear?
options: Admirable simplicity in design
Strong evidence of measured outcomes
Careful balancing of competing groups of users
An assumption that users are all alike
optionExplain: Simplicity is good when it fits; here it was assumed.
No outcomes are mentioned.
No groups are weighed.
Right: the sameness was assumed.
questions.explain: Sameness assumed rather than checked weakens the story. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Name the user groups in your story and show how their needs shaped the solution.

questions.q: Sort each pattern by the flag the author gives it.

items.t: Building features blindly
Treating user understanding as a one-time event
Technical optimization without user context
One-size-fits-all solutions

questions.explain: Only building features blindly is red in this chapter; the other three are yellow.
questions.rule: One red flag, three yellow.

questions.q: Which story line best avoids the one-size-fits-all flag?
options: I designed for the average user across all roles
I split pilots from ground crew by their tasks and tuned the app for each
I gave every user the same interface and added a help page for those who struggle
I built what the largest customer's pilots asked for
optionExplain: An average is a single imagined user.
Right: groups identified, needs addressed.
Same treatment for different needs.
One voice stands for all.
questions.explain: Identifying the groups and fitting the solution to each avoids the flag.
questions.rule: Name the user groups in your story and show how their needs shaped the solution.

questions.q: Your tool serves one team of three people who do identical work. Does the one-size-fits-all flag apply? (Our reading.)
options: Only if you assumed they were alike without checking; showing you checked is what counts
Yes, because the author expects every solution to serve several distinct user groups
No, because a team that small cannot have different needs worth checking for
Yes, because the author bans any solution that treats its users as one group
optionExplain: Right: the flag is about unexamined sameness.
The author does not demand several groups.
Small teams can differ too; check.
The flag targets assumed sameness.
questions.explain: Our reading: the yellow flag is about not thinking about who uses the system, not about uniform audiences as such.
questions.rule: Check for sameness; do not assume it.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate who averaged survey answers from all users to decide a design has avoided treating users as one group.
questions.explain: Our reading: an average describes no group in particular, so averaging treats users as a single imagined user and hides the differences between them.
questions.rule: Look at groups, not averages.

questions.q: A museum guide's story assumes every visitor reads English text panels. What would the author say this suggests?
options: That he values clear writing
That he has not thought deeply about who his visitors are
That he focuses on measured outcomes for each kind of visitor
That he knows his visitors very well
optionExplain: Clarity does not address the assumption.
Right: the author's reading of such stories.
No outcomes are described.
The assumption suggests the opposite.
questions.explain: Stories that assume users are all the same suggest you do not think deeply about who uses your systems.
questions.teaches: Stories that assume users are all the same suggest you do not think deeply about who uses your systems.
questions.rule: Name the user groups in your story and show how their needs shaped the solution.

questions.q: Logs show a dashboard feature is used by 20 percent of its audience. Which first step best reveals why?
options: Run a training session for the audience
Add more filters to the dashboard
Ask the audience's managers to require its use of every team member from next week
Sit with a few users during their normal routine and watch what they do
optionExplain: Assumes the cause is a lack of training.
Adds more of what is not used.
Compels use without learning why.
Right: observation of real use.
questions.explain: Watching shows what people do, which the logs cannot. The card next shows the book's example.
questions.rule: When use is low, observe real sessions before you decide what is wrong.

questions.q: In the entry-level story, the sales team was barely using the analytics ____ that the engineer had built.
questions.explain: The headline names the dashboard the sales team was barely using.
questions.rule: The surprise goes in the headline.

questions.q: Your team's travel-booking widget has low usage. Which action follows the story's pattern?
options: Send coordinators a reminder to use the widget
Add new booking options to the widget
Watch a few travel coordinators book trips and note where they leave
Wait a month to see whether usage rises
optionExplain: Pushes use without learning the cause.
More features before understanding.
Right: observe real sessions.
Waiting teaches nothing about the cause.
questions.explain: Observing real use reveals what the logs cannot.
questions.rule: When use is low, observe real sessions before you decide what is wrong.

questions.q: True or false: A teammate who sees 20 percent adoption and proposes a training session has found the cause of the low use.
questions.explain: Training treats a guessed cause. In the story, watching users showed a mismatch between the desktop design and the way reps worked on their phones.
questions.rule: Find the cause before choosing the cure.

questions.q: How did the engineer answer the manager's doubts about spending time on mobile?
options: The engineer promised to finish the requested filters first
The engineer argued that mobile is the future of all software and that the team should follow it
The engineer showed that 70 percent of sessions were on mobile and lasted under 30 seconds
The engineer asked the sales director to overrule her
optionExplain: Not what the story reports.
A general claim, not evidence.
Right: usage data.
The story used data, not authority.
questions.explain: Evidence from the logs turned a doubtful request into a justified one.
questions.teaches: The engineer persuaded a skeptical manager with evidence: 70 percent of dashboard sessions were on mobile devices and lasted under 30 seconds.
questions.rule: When use is low, observe real sessions before you decide what is wrong.

questions.q: A hospital developer's landing line for a similar story should turn the lesson into what, following the entry-level example?
options: A habit: check device analytics and watch real sessions before building
A rule that every tool must be mobile-first
A claim that users do not know what they want, so research is of little use
A promise to build every request faster
optionExplain: Right: the story's landing.
Too broad; the landing is a method.
Not the lesson.
Speed is not the lesson.
questions.explain: The landing names a repeatable practice, which saved the engineer from building desktop-only features for phone-first teams.
questions.teaches: The landing was a habit: check device analytics and observe a few real usage sessions, which prevented building desktop-optimized features for phone-first teams.
questions.rule: When use is low, observe real sessions before you decide what is wrong.

questions.q: Engineers say a single-page checkout means messier code, but data suggests customers leave between steps. What is the best response?
options: Ship to all customers, since revenue matters most
Keep the clean design, since engineers know best
Let the engineers vote on the final design
Test it on a slice of traffic and document the technical costs
optionExplain: Skips the test and the cost.
Ignores the customer data.
A vote does not test the effect.
Right: evidence plus open accounting.
questions.explain: Evidence and openness beat both sides' certainty. The card next shows the book's example.
questions.rule: Test the trade-off, record the technical cost, and let user results settle the argument.

questions.q: The mid-level story answers a question about when user needs ____ with technical best practices.
questions.explain: The question the story answers is about user needs conflicting with technical best practices.
questions.rule: Best practice can conflict with user needs.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it matches the mid-level story's approach.

items.t: Tested the new flow on a small share of traffic
Recorded the extra page-load time and added complexity
Documented the trade-offs for the team
Declared best practice must win without checking customer data
Shipped to everyone untested and dismissed the engineers' objections
Kept the code complexity quiet from the team

questions.explain: The story tests, measures the technical cost and discloses it.
questions.rule: Test, measure and disclose.

questions.q: True or false: In the mid-level story, the engineers' technical objections were mistaken.
questions.explain: The story says they were right from a technical perspective; the user results settled the matter anyway.
questions.rule: Respect the technical objection and weigh it.

questions.q: What settled the argument in the mid-level story?
options: The designer's preference for a single page
A 10 percent traffic test cut abandonment from 30 to 25 percent, worth about $50,000 monthly
The manager's decision to side with the revenue team over the engineering team's technical concerns
The new page loading faster than the old one
optionExplain: The designer helped but did not settle it.
Right: the A/B result.
The test settled it.
Load time rose by about 250 milliseconds.
questions.explain: A controlled test showed a clear user and revenue gain, even though load time and code complexity got worse.
questions.teaches: An A/B test on 10 percent of traffic cut abandonment from 30 to 25 percent, worth roughly $50,000 a month, while page load time increased by 250 milliseconds.
questions.rule: Test the trade-off, record the technical cost, and let user results settle the argument.

questions.q: A clinic's booking form went to one long page after a test showed gains, though the code got more complex. What does the mid-level story suggest next?
options: Schedule clean-up of the code while keeping the improved form
Revert to the clean multi-step form to protect the code and the engineers' time
Leave the complexity as it is, since results are good
Run the test again until the code improves
optionExplain: Right: the story's follow-up.
Throws away the user gain.
Skips the repayment of the technical cost.
Tests do not repair code.
questions.explain: The team spent the next sprint cleaning up the implementation while keeping the improved checkout intact.
questions.teaches: After the evidence convinced the skeptics, the team spent the next sprint cleaning up the implementation while keeping the improved checkout intact.
questions.rule: Test the trade-off, record the technical cost, and let user results settle the argument.

questions.q: Product wants new advanced features, but most users cannot finish the basic task. What would a senior engineer do first?
options: Quietly build the features and fix the basics later
Refuse the features until the basics are perfect
Ask users to vote on the roadmap
Gather evidence of where users fail the basic task and show it to the team
optionExplain: Avoids the conflict, but not the problem.
Blocks without offering evidence.
A vote does not show where they fail.
Right: evidence for advocacy.
questions.explain: Making the struggle visible comes before arguing. The card next shows the book's example.
questions.rule: Make users' struggle visible to those who decide, then offer a concrete alternative.

questions.q: Match each story detail to what it shows.
pairs: 65 percent could not book an appointment
The basic task was failing for most patients
The team saw the struggle first-hand
A highlight reel of the sessions
The struggle was made hard to dismiss
Users were working around the portal
questions.explain: Each detail adds evidence that the basics, not the advanced features, were the priority.
questions.rule: Stack evidence people can see.

questions.q: A senior engineer wants to pause roadmap work to fix a confusing tax-form wizard. Which step most resembles the story?
options: Send leadership a long memo explaining why the wizard is poorly designed and hard to use
Have engineers watch real filers struggle with the wizard, then show leadership clips
Fix the wizard in spare time without telling anyone
Ask the product team to explain their roadmap again
optionExplain: Opinion without evidence.
Right: makes the struggle visible.
Skips the persuasion.
Does not bring in user evidence.
questions.explain: Seeing is more persuasive than describing.
questions.hint: Which step lets decision-makers see the users?
