questions.rule: Make users' struggle visible to those who decide, then offer a concrete alternative.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it is advocacy for users, as in the story, or blocking the product team.

items.t: Showed session clips and proposed a plain-language redesign
Presented support-call data with a plan to pause advanced features
Tested the new wording with real patients before rollout
Refused every new feature without showing evidence
Said the roadmap was wrong without showing any users
Withheld work until the plan was dropped

questions.explain: Advocacy brings evidence and a way forward; blocking offers only a no.
questions.rule: Bring evidence and an alternative.

questions.q: In the senior-level story, why was every terminology change A/B tested with real patients?
options: To confirm that the simpler wording was clearer to the patients who would use it
To show the product team that advanced features were no longer worth building
To let the support team choose the wording they found easiest to explain
To meet a leadership rule that every interface change must be tested first
optionExplain: Right: the story says the key was testing every change with real patients to ensure the simpler language was indeed clearer to them.
The testing was about wording; the feature question was already settled when leadership paused feature work.
Support calls informed the diagnosis, but the story tests wording with patients, not with support staff.
The story gives no such rule; the engineer chose to test.
questions.explain: Plain language was the goal, so each change was tested with real patients to confirm it was clearer to them.
questions.teaches: A/B testing each terminology change with real patients showed surprises: Book Appointment tested better than Book a Visit with younger patients.
questions.rule: Make users' struggle visible to those who decide, then offer a concrete alternative.

questions.q: A city permit portal gets requests for map layers, yet most applicants cannot find the application form. What might advocacy mean here, per the senior-level lesson?
options: Adding the map layers quickly to please the requesters
Removing the map idea from consideration forever
Waiting for applicants to complain louder
Protecting users from feature creep by fixing the basic path first
optionExplain: Feeds the creep.
The lesson is about priority, not permanent refusal.
Passive waiting is not advocacy.
Right: the story's landing.
questions.explain: User advocacy sometimes means protecting users from feature creep.
questions.teaches: Advocating for users sometimes means protecting them from feature creep, and terminology changes should be tested with real users before broad rollout.
questions.rule: Make users' struggle visible to those who decide, then offer a concrete alternative.

questions.q: Each team's app metrics look healthy, yet users who use two devices are leaving. What should a staff-level leader do first?
options: Ask each team to improve its own metrics further until the churn figures drop
Measure the cross-device journey to see whether it is the cause
Wait for churn to reach a larger share of users
Remove the features that cross devices
optionExplain: Local metrics are already healthy.
Right: look at the whole journey.
Delays learning the cause.
Removes the symptom and some of the value.
questions.explain: When parts look healthy, the problem may sit between them. The card next shows the book's example.
questions.rule: If every part looks fine but users are leaving, measure the whole journey and change the measure of success.

questions.q: Success on individual platforms had ____ how badly the app was failing users who expected a unified experience.
questions.explain: Each platform's success hid the failure of the cross-platform experience.
questions.rule: Local success can mask a shared failure.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it is an organization-level change or a local fix.

items.t: Evaluating teams on cross-platform retention
Requiring consistency fixes before new feature work
Building unified data models and calculation methods
Renaming one label on the watch app
Fixing one crash on the web app
Adding a social feature to the mobile app

questions.explain: The left column changes how teams work and are judged; the right column changes one product.
questions.rule: Change the measure, not only the product.

questions.q: A candidate says: I unified the calculations in the code, so the problem was solved. What does the staff story show is missing?
options: A change in what teams are measured on, so silos stop causing inconsistencies
A larger engineering team to maintain the unified code and the new data models
More features on the smartwatch app
A written apology to users
optionExplain: Right: the metric change.
Not the point of the story.
Features were not the issue.
Users needed consistent data, not apologies.
questions.explain: Code changes alone could drift apart again. The new measure of success kept the teams aligned.
questions.rule: Align incentives with the user journey.

questions.q: What rule enforced the new measure of success in the staff-level story?
options: Every team had to share one code repository
Only the watch team could ship new features
A team that broke cross-platform consistency had to fix it before moving on to new work
Teams were paid bonuses for each new feature
optionExplain: Not what the story describes.
Not part of the story.
Right: no exceptions.
The story evaluates cross-platform retention instead.
questions.explain: The mobile team had to delay new social features a week to align its calorie calculations, and word spread quickly.
questions.teaches: Teams were evaluated on cross-platform user retention, and any team that broke cross-platform consistency had to make fixing it its top priority before new work, with no exceptions.
questions.rule: If every part looks fine but users are leaving, measure the whole journey and change the measure of success.

questions.q: A hospital group's three clinics each hit their own targets, yet patients who move between clinics get conflicting records. Which move parallels the staff story?
options: Reward each clinic for exceeding its own target and let each keep its own record format as before
Tell patients to use one clinic only
Judge clinics on a shared cross-clinic measure and fix inconsistencies before new projects
Hire more records staff at each clinic
optionExplain: Strengthens the silos.
Moves the burden to users.
Right: same structure.
Adds local effort, not a shared measure.
questions.explain: Changing the measure of success transformed siloed platform teams into a unified product organization.
questions.teaches: Changing the measure of success transformed the siloed platform teams into a unified product organization.
questions.rule: If every part looks fine but users are leaving, measure the whole journey and change the measure of success.

questions.q: You cannot think of a customer-focus story. Which memory is worth checking first?
options: A time you finished a large project well ahead of schedule and under budget
A time you refactored code for readability
A time you won a hackathon
A time you changed your technical approach after learning how users worked
optionExplain: Speed is not customer focus.
A technical improvement without a user link.
Winning does not show user insight.
Right: a clear match.
questions.explain: The best material links your work to what users did or needed. The card next lists three kinds.
questions.rule: Search your history for moments when users changed what you built.

questions.q: Match each kind of experience to what it shows, per the author.
pairs: Changed a technical approach after seeing how users really worked
Translating user needs into technical decisions
Found users struggling with something nobody had reported
Advocated for users even though it meant more work
questions.explain: Each kind of experience shows a different part of customer focus.
questions.rule: Three kinds of experience to mine.

questions.q: Sort each memory by whether it is worth developing into a customer-focus story.

items.t: Noticed in logs that users abandoned a form nobody had complained about
Rebuilt a flow after watching users work around it
Argued to keep an accessible control although it cost the team extra days
Wrote clean code that passed review
Delivered a feature in the sprint it was assigned
Updated a library version

questions.explain: Worthwhile memories link your decisions to users; the others describe routine work.
questions.rule: Look for the user link.

questions.q: A candidate rejects a memory of fixing a problem users had not reported, since there was no ticket. What is wrong?
options: Finding unreported struggle shows early awareness of user needs
Fixes without tickets are against policy
A story needs a ticket to be believable
Unreported problems are not real problems
optionExplain: Right: the author counts it.
No such claim.
The author does not require one.
They are real and unseen.
questions.explain: Spotting what nobody reported is itself the skill.
questions.rule: Unreported struggle counts.

questions.q: Which of these is among the author's reflection questions?
options: Have you reduced the number of meetings your team holds each week for its members?
Have you helped non-technical teams better understand what users need?
Have you mentored colleagues on code style?
Have you migrated systems to a new cloud provider?
optionExplain: Not a customer-focus prompt.
Right: one of the author's prompts.
Not a customer-focus prompt.
Not a customer-focus prompt.
questions.explain: The prompts also cover simplifying complex features after learning user workflows and solving user problems not stated in any requirements.
questions.teaches: The author's reflection prompts also include simplifying complex features after understanding workflows, solving user problems that no requirement stated, and gathering user feedback during regular development.
questions.rule: Search your history for moments when users changed what you built.

questions.q: A hospital pharmacist redesigned medicine-label wording after seeing patients misread doses. Does this count as material, by the author's logic?
options: Yes, because she changed her approach once she understood how patients used labels
No, because pharmacy is not a technical field
No, because she did not write software
Yes, but only if patients praised her work afterward and later asked for more redesigns elsewhere
optionExplain: Right: it connects work to outcomes.
The logic is about users, not the field.
Customer focus is not limited to software.
Praise is not required.
questions.explain: A deeper knowledge of users that changed her whole approach is the kind of experience the reflection questions look for.
questions.teaches: A deeper knowledge of users that changed your entire approach is one of the experiences the author's reflection questions look for.
questions.rule: Search your history for moments when users changed what you built.

questions.q: Which story is most likely to read as strong customer focus?
options: Delivered every requested feature ahead of schedule
Cut latency by thirty percent across services
Interviewed users once and shipped the plan
Observed users, tied findings to a decision, accepted extra work for them, and measured outcomes
optionExplain: Delivery without discovery.
A technical metric with no user link.
A one-time event.
Right: discovery, decision, trade-off and result.
questions.explain: A strong story links discovery to decision to measured result. The card next sums up the chapter.
questions.rule: Show discovery, a decision, a trade-off, and a measured result for users, and avoid the five traps.

questions.q: Which are elements of a strong customer-focus story, per the author? Select all that apply.
options: A long list of shipped features
Measurement of actual user outcomes
Recognition of different user segments
Direct user research or observation
Benchmarks of technical speed gains
optionExplain: Features alone are not outcomes.
Named by the author.
Named by the author.
Named by the author.
Technical metrics are a named trap.
questions.explain: Strong stories include research, a link to decisions, advocacy with trade-offs, measured outcomes and recognized segments.
questions.rule: Research, decision, trade-off, outcome, segments.

questions.q: Sort each story element by whether it is a strength or a trap.

items.t: Watched users do the task before designing
Measured whether users reached their goals after launch
Gave a reason for serving one segment first
Assumed we knew what users wanted
Reported only server speed gains
Treated all users as alike

questions.explain: Strengths show evidence from users; traps replace it with assumption or technical numbers.
questions.rule: Evidence from users beats assumption.

questions.q: A draft story: researched thoroughly, built what was found, and closed with: It shipped on time. What does the chapter say is missing?
options: A longer description of the schedule
A claim that users were satisfied, with no evidence beyond the team's own impression
Measurement of actual user outcomes, not only delivery
Fewer details of the research
optionExplain: More about delivery, not about users.
Needs evidence of outcomes.
Right: the result for users.
The research is a strength.
questions.explain: Delivery is not the same as benefit; the story must show that users gained.
questions.rule: Show the user result.

questions.q: Which trap does the chapter warn against about describing features?
options: Describing features by their names in the story rather than by the numbers behind them
Describing building features without confirming they have helped users
Mentioning features at all in a customer-focus story
Describing features that the team did not build
optionExplain: No such trap.
Right: delivery is not proof.
Features can appear if the benefit is shown.
Not the trap named.
questions.explain: A feature in your story needs evidence that it helped the people it was for.
questions.teaches: Do not describe building features without confirming they have helped users.
questions.rule: Show discovery, a decision, a trade-off, and a measured result for users, and avoid the five traps.

questions.q: A school IT lead summarizes her work for a panel. Which sentence matches the chapter's summary of customer focus?
options: I deliver every requested feature on time and keep the system fast
I look for needs beyond stated requests, weigh the conflicting needs of groups, and judge success from users' side
I treat every student and teacher the same so no one is favored
I decide what users need from my own experience
optionExplain: Delivery and speed, not user outcomes.
Right: all three elements.
Treats users as uniform.
An assumption, the first trap.
questions.explain: Customer focus also requires carefully balancing the conflicting needs of different user segments.
questions.teaches: Customer focus requires carefully balancing the conflicting needs of different user segments.
questions.rule: Show discovery, a decision, a trade-off, and a measured result for users, and avoid the five traps.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A warehouse team keeps sending out pick lists with mistakes. Which response goes beyond improving the current method?
options: Have a second person proofread every pick list before it goes out
Redesign the picking so that a wrong item cannot be recorded as picked
Train the pickers to read the lists more slowly and with more care
Print the pick lists in a larger font so errors are easier to see
optionExplain: Proofreading feels thorough, but it still catches mistakes after they exist in the old process.
It changes how the problem is handled, so the mistake cannot happen, instead of checking for it afterwards.
Training raises care within the same method, so it improves the old way of working.
A larger font polishes the existing list without altering how errors arise.
questions.explain: Three of these make the current process work a little better; one changes the process itself. The card next names the difference.
questions.rule: Ask whether the fix reshapes the method or tunes it.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: Innovation means inventing new ways to solve problems, rather than only ____ existing methods.
questions.explain: The card defines innovation as a new way of solving the problem, which is more than making existing methods better.
questions.rule: A new way, not a better old way.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: Sort each project by whether it invents a new approach or improves an existing one.

items.t: Library staff install shelf sensors so loans are recorded as books leave, with no manual checkout
A clinic lets patients describe symptoms in plain speech and builds the intake record from it, replacing the paper form
A designer builds buttons that cannot be given text too faint to read
A school office buys a faster printer for its weekly timetables
A bakery shortens the proofing time in its standard recipe by five minutes
A team moves its database to a larger server to answer queries sooner

questions.explain: The first three change how the task is done; the last three keep the same method and make it quicker or stronger.
questions.rule: New method means innovation; same method, better results means improvement.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: an analyst who builds a system where users ask questions in plain conversation, so they no longer need SQL, has invented a new approach.
questions.explain: Users no longer work the old way, so the problem is handled differently. This matches the card's contrast with a better version of what came before.
questions.rule: A changed way of working is a new approach.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: according to the book, a new approach is a strong innovation story even if it solves no real problem and nobody adopts it.
questions.explain: The book says newness alone is not sufficient: interviewers want an approach that was the best way to solve a real problem and that changed how people work.
questions.rule: New is necessary, not sufficient.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A payment service crashes on holiday traffic spikes. Which design fits the idea of innovation for this problem?
options: Let the service drop optional features automatically when busy, instead of failing
Add alerts that page engineers earlier when the spike begins to build
Buy more servers ahead of each holiday season to carry the larger load
Rewrite the slowest functions so each request finishes a little sooner
optionExplain: It changes what happens under load, so the failure itself is removed rather than managed.
Earlier alerts help people react but leave the failure in place.
More servers is a known solution that scales the old design.
Faster functions improve the old design without changing how it behaves under strain.
questions.explain: The pattern holds outside the examples on the card: change how the system behaves, instead of strengthening what exists.
questions.rule: Look for the design that removes the failure mode.
questions.teaches: The book's third example is an infrastructure engineer whose services automatically reduce functionality under load instead of failing, which eliminates the need for most monitoring alerts.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A candidate for a large tech firm worries she has not built a revolutionary product. What would the book tell her?
options: Only breakthrough products count, so she should talk about a different kind of strength
She should describe a product she admires instead, to show that she understands innovation
Innovative thinking at the scale of her role counts, for instance a new tool for her own team
She should wait to interview until she has led a project that changed her whole industry
optionExplain: This feels realistic given famous products, but the book rejects breakthrough products as the entry price.
Admiring someone else's work shows taste, not that she has invented anything herself.
The book says these companies want innovative thinking at whatever scale the role allows.
Waiting is cautious, but the book says smaller-scale tools and solutions already qualify.
questions.explain: Big names make innovation sound enormous. The card next sets out what the book actually asks for.
questions.rule: Match the scale of your story to the scale of your role.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: Google explicitly evaluates ____ in its hiring process and looks for people who invent novel solutions to complex challenges.
questions.explain: The card says Google evaluates innovation explicitly when it hires.
questions.rule: These companies hire for invented solutions, not only for applied ones.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: Sort each story by whether it fits what these companies look for, as the card describes.

items.t: A support lead builds a tool that ends a recurring chore for her own team
An engineer designs a solution adopted across her whole organization
A developer questions the status quo in a way that opens a new approach for a neighbouring team
An analyst follows a documented vendor procedure step by step each month
An engineer copies a rival product's feature without any change
An analyst reuses last year's report template and changes only the figures

questions.explain: The first three show invention at some scale; the last three apply a known method or throw away a story that is the right size.
questions.rule: Invention at any scale fits; routine application does not.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: these companies see more long-term value in inventing new solutions and simplifying problems than in only applying and refining existing approaches.
questions.explain: The book says these companies understand that inventing new solutions and simplifying problems generates more long-term value than just applying and improving what exists.
questions.rule: Invention is where their long-term value lies.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: because companies accept innovation at the scale of your role, a senior candidate is judged on the same scale as an entry-level candidate.
questions.explain: The book says expectations scale with level across scope, adoption and impact, so a senior story is expected to reach further than a personal one.
questions.rule: Flexible in scale, but expectations still rise with level.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A firm's stated mission is to make clean water available everywhere. How should a candidate frame an innovation story for it?
options: Show how the new approach advanced a goal the firm itself states
Avoid mentioning the mission, since stories should stay strictly technical
Claim the work solved water shortages worldwide, to match the firm's scale
Describe only the tools used, so the story can fit any employer
optionExplain: Linking the invention to the firm's own purpose shows why it matters to them.
Staying technical feels safe, but it leaves out why the invention matters to this employer.
Inflating the scale is tempting, but the book asks for innovation at the scale of your role.
A tools-only story could suit anyone, which makes it a weaker fit for this one.
questions.explain: The book shows companies tying innovation to their purpose. A candidate can do the same with a story.
questions.rule: Tie your invention to what the company says it exists to do.
questions.teaches: The book says that for Tesla, constantly innovate is core to its mission of accelerating the use of sustainable energy.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A support team's ticket queue is slow. Which change would a careful reader call optimization rather than innovation?
options: Replacing the queue with a system where common requests resolve before a ticket exists
Inventing a routing method that sends each request to its answer without a queue at all
Designing a self-service flow that removes the need for most tickets from the start
Sorting the same queue faster by adding a quick-filter shortcut
optionExplain: This removes the need for the queue, so it is a new approach.
This replaces the queue's logic with a different method.
This changes the problem so that most tickets never arise.
A shortcut makes the existing queue work better, while the other three do away with the need for the queue.
questions.explain: The right one keeps the queue and speeds it up. The card next gives the book's test for telling them apart.
questions.rule: Keeping the structure and speeding it up is optimization.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: The book's test asks: could someone else have achieved similar results by ____ what already existed?
questions.explain: The card states the test as whether similar results were reachable by refining the existing thing.
questions.rule: If refining could have got there, it is probably optimization.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: Sort each change by the book's test: reachable by refining what existed, or not.

items.t: Adding an index to a slow lookup
Raising the cache size on an existing cache
Compressing images on an existing page so it loads sooner
Redesigning how data is accessed so the slow lookups are not needed
Replacing manual approvals with a rule that makes bad requests impossible to submit
Inventing a way to validate input at entry so that a separate review step is not needed

questions.explain: The first three keep the structure and tune it; the last three build something that refining could not have reached.
questions.rule: Could refining have reached it? Yes suggests optimization.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: if the data access layer is redesigned so the slow queries disappear, refining the old queries could not have reached the same result.
questions.explain: Removing the need for the queries is a new approach. Refining the queries leaves them in place, which is the card's contrast.
questions.rule: A redesign that removes the problem is beyond refinement.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: according to the book, if someone else could have reached your result by refining what already existed, your work is certainly optimization.
questions.explain: The book words it as a likelihood: if the answer is yes, the work is likely optimization. The test guides your judgment and does not prove the case.
questions.rule: Treat the refine-it test as a strong hint, not a proof.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A bakery cuts its waste by 30 percent. Which description gives the strongest case for innovation?
options: It trimmed each day's batch sizes slightly until the waste figures fell
It asked staff to be more careful when stacking trays in the display
It moved the leftover table nearer the door so more items got sold
It replaced daily guessing with a new method that no refinement of the old guessing could have produced
optionExplain: Trimming batches is refinement of the same guessing method.
Care in stacking is effort inside the same process.
Moving a table is a tweak to the same selling process.
Only this describes a method that refining the old one could not have reached.
questions.explain: The test works outside software: ask whether the old approach could have been refined to the result.
questions.rule: Use the refine-it test in any field.
questions.teaches: The book adds that innovation means a new method that others could not have reached by incrementally improving the old approach.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: You have tuned a process three times and the same problem keeps coming back. What is the most sensible next question?
options: Which setting you have not yet adjusted in the process
Whether more tuning can ever fix it, or whether a new approach is needed
Whether a colleague could tune it a little further than you did
How long you can keep adjusting the process before anyone notices that it has failed again
optionExplain: Another setting feels like progress but keeps you inside the same approach.
After repeated tuning fails, the useful question is whether tuning can ever solve it.
A colleague's tuning would be refinement of the same method.
Hiding the failure avoids the real problem.
questions.explain: The book describes a moment when improvement runs out. The card next gives its examples.
questions.rule: Ask whether refinement can reach the goal at all.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: In the caching example, adding a standard caching layer is ____ because it applies a well-known pattern.
questions.explain: The card calls a standard caching layer optimization; inventing a new predictive strategy would be innovation.
questions.rule: A well-known pattern applied is optimization.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A team fights spam. Put these steps in the order that shows optimization turning into innovation.
items: Add more rules to the existing spam filter
Notice that spammers adapt faster than rules can be added
Decide that adding rules cannot solve the problem
Invent a method that scores senders by their behavior over time
questions.explain: The work starts as tuning, hits a limit, and shifts to invention, as in the card's pattern.
questions.rule: Tune, hit the limit, shift, invent.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: if the standard caching layer had kept up with the access patterns, the book would still call the work innovation.
questions.explain: A standard caching layer is a well-known pattern, so keeping it is optimization. The shift to innovation came only because it failed.
questions.rule: No limit reached, no shift to invention.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: a project that began as optimization counts as an innovation story even if nothing new was invented after the shift.
questions.explain: Our reading: in the caching example the work becomes innovation only because a new strategy is invented once ordinary caching fails. Without that invention it stays optimization.
questions.rule: The shift counts only if something new follows it.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A teacher keeps rewriting the same quiz to cut cheating and still sees it. She then changes how the class is assessed. What does this show?
options: A shift from improvement to invention after refinement failed
Only an improvement, because assessment is the same activity as before
A failure of nerve, since she should have kept refining the quiz
An optimization, since any change in a classroom counts as one
optionExplain: Refinement could not fix the cheating, and she moved to a different approach.
It feels like the same activity, but the approach differs.
Persisting feels virtuous, but the book describes moving on once refinement cannot work.
Changing the method is the opposite of tuning.
questions.explain: The story pattern fits any field: tune, hit the wall, change the approach.
questions.rule: The shift is recognizing that more of the same will not work.
questions.teaches: The book's opening story is a QA engineer who could have kept tweaking retry logic and timeouts but instead built a test architecture that made flaky tests structurally impossible; flaky failures dropped to zero and other teams adopted it.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: You are choosing between two projects for an innovation question. What should decide it?
options: Whether you created something different or only made the existing thing work better
Which project had the larger percentage improvement on its main number
Which project took more months of work from the whole team
Which project uses the most advanced tools from the latest conference
optionExplain: For an innovation question, the key is whether the work created something new.
Big percentages feel convincing, but they can come from either kind of work.
Longer effort suggests importance, but not novelty.
Advanced tools are not the same as a new approach.
questions.explain: The numbers and tools can mislead. The card next gives the book's question.
questions.rule: Choose by the kind of work, not by its size.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: The differentiator is usually whether you built something new that others could ____.
questions.explain: The card says the differentiator is building something new that others could adopt.
questions.rule: New and adoptable is the sign.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: Sort each way of cutting production bugs by the card's distinction.

items.t: Writing more unit tests for the existing modules
Adding a stricter review checklist for existing pull requests
Increasing the number of manual test passes before each release
Introducing a framework that makes a whole category of bug impossible to write
Designing an interface that rejects invalid states so they cannot be created
Building a generator that produces the risky code so it cannot be mistyped

questions.explain: More effort inside the old process is optimization; a new framework that prevents categories of bugs is innovation.
questions.rule: More of the same is optimization; a new structure is innovation.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: if teams adopt your method because it opens new possibilities, you have likely crossed into innovation.
questions.explain: The book ties the crossing to adoption for new possibilities, as opposed to adoption for making things work faster.
questions.rule: Adoption for new possibilities points to innovation.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: True or false: the book treats other teams adopting your method as proof that your work was innovation.
questions.explain: The book says that when teams adopt a method because it opens new possibilities, you have likely crossed into innovation. It is a sign, not proof.
questions.rule: Adoption points toward innovation; it does not prove it.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: A nurse reduces patient wait time by adding more staff at peak hours. Another builds a triage method that sends minor cases elsewhere. How should each frame it?
options: Both as innovation, since both cut the wait time
The first as optimization, the second as a candidate for innovation
The first as innovation, since adding more staff is a big and costly change for a hospital
Both as optimization, since hospitals already triage patients
optionExplain: Both cut waits, but the second changed the approach.
The first scales the existing process; the second changes how cases flow.
Adding people grows what exists.
Triage exists, but a new method of it can still be new.
questions.explain: The question to ask your own work works in any field.
questions.rule: Ask: better, or different?
questions.teaches: The book says that a 10x improvement from a better algorithm could be either kind: it depends on whether you applied a well-known algorithm or made a twist on it for your situation.

questions.q: A designer proposes a brilliant scheduling system that needs hardware the company will not buy. What is the main weakness?
options: It is too creative, and creativity is a weakness in a candidate
It is not new enough, since scheduling systems already exist somewhere
It relies on hardware, and hardware has no place in an innovation
It ignores the real constraints, so it is not workable as proposed
optionExplain: Creativity itself is what the book wants; the trouble is the missing practicality.
Novelty is not the problem here; workability is.
Hardware is allowed; the issue is that this one is unavailable.
A good idea that cannot be built under real constraints fails the practicality side.
questions.explain: The card next names this pull between new and workable.
questions.rule: A good idea must also be possible to build.

questions.q: The critical tension in innovation lies in balancing novelty with ____.
questions.explain: The card names novelty versus practicality as the critical tension.
questions.rule: New, and workable.

questions.q: Sort each remark by which side of the tension it risks: too little practicality, or too much focus on feasibility.

items.t: The design needs a team ten times our size and no deadline
The plan assumes the vendor will rebuild its product for us for free
The prototype only works if every user changes habits overnight
Reject any idea that cannot ship in the next two weeks
Never try anything the old system did not already do
Drop every proposal that has not been used successfully elsewhere

questions.explain: The first three ignore real limits; the last three let caution kill new ideas before they can be tested.
questions.rule: Constraints without ideas, or ideas without constraints, both fail.

questions.q: True or false: if a team removes every constraint from its brainstorm, the book expects the result to be more practical.
questions.explain: The book says creativity without constraints produces impractical solutions, so removing them makes the result less workable.
questions.rule: Take away the constraints and the practicality goes first.

questions.q: True or false: the book gives a formula for how much practicality to trade for novelty in each project.
questions.explain: The book names the tension and says each extreme costs something, but it gives no formula. Our reading: the balance is a judgment made case by case.
questions.rule: The balance is a judgment, not a formula.

questions.q: A city's buses run late at rush hour. Which proposal shows the balance the card describes?
options: Replace the whole network with an untested system in a single weekend
Add more buses to every line, which is the standard response whenever the buses keep running late
Cancel the idea because routes have been planned this way for decades
Test a new routing approach on one line first, using the current fleet and drivers
optionExplain: Bold, but ignores the real limits of time and risk.
This is the known solution, which applies what exists and is not new.
This treats feasibility as final and leaves nothing to invent.
It is a new approach, tried within real limits on a small scale.
questions.explain: The balance appears outside tech: a new method, tested within limits.
questions.rule: Try the new idea at a size the constraints allow.
questions.teaches: The book's own contrast is that fixing performance by adding more servers uses a known solution, horizontal scaling, while creating a new architecture that eliminates the bottlenecks shows innovation.

questions.q: A form is rejected by users because it has forty fields. Which fix reflects the idea that innovation often simplifies?
options: Ask why each field exists, and remove the need for most of them
Add a progress bar, a help panel and a save-for-later feature to the form
Put the forty fields in a smaller font so the form looks shorter
Add a training video showing users how to fill in each field
optionExplain: It questions why the complexity exists and designs it away.
More layers manage the problem but do not remove it.
A smaller font hides the complexity without changing it.
Training places the burden on users, leaving the form unchanged.
questions.explain: The book prefers removing a problem over managing it. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: Ask why it exists before deciding how to handle it.

questions.q: Innovators will often design solutions that ____ rather than manage complexity.
questions.explain: The card says innovators tend to eliminate complexity instead of managing it.
questions.rule: Eliminate, do not manage.

questions.q: Sort each response to a clumsy approval process by whether it eliminates or manages the complexity.

items.t: Remove the approval step for requests that cannot cause harm
Replace three overlapping forms with one that asks only what is needed
Rebuild the process so the checks the old steps did are automatic
Add a dashboard showing where requests are stuck in the steps
Hire a coordinator to chase approvals through the steps
Write a guide to explain the order of the steps

questions.explain: The first three remove the cause; the last three leave the steps and add effort or tools around them.
questions.rule: Removing the cause beats managing the symptoms.

questions.q: True or false: if a team adds features or layers to control a problem without careful thought, the book says things often get worse.
questions.explain: The book says adding features or layers without careful consideration often makes things worse.
questions.rule: Careless layers often make things worse.

questions.q: True or false: the book says that adding features or layers to manage a problem is wrong in every case.
questions.explain: The book says adding features or layers without careful consideration often makes things worse. It warns against careless additions, not against every addition.
questions.rule: Be careful with additions; do not treat them as forbidden.

questions.q: A family's shared calendar keeps falling out of sync across five apps. Which response uses the habit the card describes?
options: Install a sixth app to copy events between the other five
Set a weekly reminder to compare all five calendars by hand
Ask why five apps exist and move everyone to one source
Buy a bigger wall calendar to record the events twice
optionExplain: A sixth app adds a layer that must itself be maintained.
A weekly check manages the symptom and keeps the cause.
It asks why the problem exists and removes the cause.
A paper copy adds more places to keep up to date.
questions.explain: Outside work, the same move applies: question why the mess exists.
questions.rule: Ask why first; build second.
questions.teaches: The book says innovators break problems down to their most basic truths and build solutions from there, often in radical new directions.

questions.q: Your first prototype of a new tool fails in testing. What is the most useful way to see that failure?
options: As information about why the approach did not work, to shape the next try
As proof that the idea was weak and should be dropped at once
As a mistake to hide so that the second try looks like the first
As bad luck that will not repeat if you try the same version again
optionExplain: The book treats failures as data that guide later attempts.
Dropping it feels sensible, but it throws away what the attempt revealed.
Hiding it avoids embarrassment but also the learning.
Retrying unchanged assumes the cause was chance, not design.
questions.explain: The card next explains how failures feed the next attempt.
questions.rule: A failure is evidence, not a verdict.

questions.q: Effective innovators treat failures as ____ to understand why previous attempts did not work.
questions.explain: The card says failures are treated as data.
questions.rule: Failures are data.

questions.q: Sort each reaction to a failed experiment by whether it treats the failure as data.

items.t: Records which assumption the test disproved and changes the next design to avoid it
Compares the failed run with the passing one to see what differed
Asks users what made the prototype unusable and rebuilds around the answers
Reruns the identical test until it happens to pass
Deletes the results and starts a different project
Blames the testers and keeps the design as it was

questions.explain: The first three extract lessons to steer the next attempt; the last three ignore or discard what the failure showed.
questions.rule: Use the failure to decide the next version.

questions.q: True or false: if a first attempt at a new solution does not work, the book treats this as expected rather than as a reason to give up.
questions.explain: The book says inventing new solutions rarely succeeds on the first try, and that failures are used as data to guide later attempts.
questions.rule: Expect to fail first; learn from it.

questions.q: Which describes persistence as the book means it, rather than stubbornness?
options: Repeating the same design with more and more effort until it finally succeeds at last
Refusing to listen to any feedback so the vision stays pure
Switching to a new problem each time something goes wrong
Keeping at the problem while using each failure to change the next attempt
optionExplain: More effort on the same design repeats the failure.
Ignoring feedback discards the data the book values.
Switching constantly never lets any attempt teach anything.
Persistence includes learning; stubbornness repeats the same thing.
questions.explain: The difference lies in whether the next attempt changes because of what was learned.
questions.rule: Persist with the goal; change the method.

questions.q: A community garden volunteer tries a new watering scheme that fails in a heat wave. Which next step fits the card?
options: Drop watering schemes in favour of the old hose-and-can routine
Study why it failed in the heat and design the next version with that in mind
Run the same scheme again next summer and hope for cooler weather
Tell the others the scheme was perfect and that the weather alone was to blame for the loss
optionExplain: Going back avoids the experiment instead of learning from it.
It uses the failure as data to guide the next attempt.
Hoping for luck changes nothing in the design.
Blaming the weather ignores what the failure showed.
questions.explain: The habit works in any field where something new is tried.
questions.rule: Turn each failure into a design input.
questions.teaches: The book says these professionals balance confidence in their vision with flexibility in implementation.

questions.q: You are interviewing at a tiny startup with almost no budget. Which story should you lead with?
options: A new framework that took two years and a large team to roll out across the whole company
A careful improvement to a mature system with plenty of resources
A research idea whose practical use is still unknown
A new way you got a result despite severe limits on time and money
optionExplain: A big long program does not fit a small startup's limits.
Improving a mature system shows optimization, and it does not fit a lean setting.
Open-ended research fits a research organization, not a company fighting to survive.
Startups value inventing in the face of resource limits.
questions.explain: Different employers want different things from the same skill. The card next sets out two of them.
questions.rule: Fit the story to the employer's situation.

questions.q: Startups value people who can identify which constraints to accept and which ones to ____ through innovative thinking.
questions.explain: The card says the key startup skill is identifying which constraints to accept and which to challenge.
questions.rule: Accept some constraints; challenge others.

questions.q: Sort each story detail by the type of company it would impress more.

items.t: I built the first version in a week with one contractor and a tiny budget
I chose which limits to accept and which to push back on
We shipped before the next funding round because the product could not wait
I designed it so five other teams could adopt it without rewriting their systems
It plugged into our platform and was run by teams who had not built it
I handled the challenges of getting a big organization to take it up

questions.explain: The first three show invention under tight limits; the last three show scale, integration and adoption.
questions.rule: Constraint for startups; scale and integration for big companies.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate at a large tech company who designs a new solution that scales and fits with existing systems matches the book's expectation.
questions.explain: Large tech companies want new solutions that scale and integrate with existing systems, while considering the challenges of adoption.
questions.rule: At a large company, scale and integration count.

questions.q: True or false: a startup that depends on innovation to survive wants candidates to accept every constraint the company faces.
questions.explain: The book says the key skill for startups is identifying which constraints to accept and which to challenge through innovative thinking.
questions.rule: Accept some constraints and challenge others.

questions.q: A candidate built a framework that other teams could extend to make their own advances. Which employer type is this story best suited to?
options: A one-room startup, which values only solo building
A traditional factory, which values keeping every one of its processes exactly as they were before
A large tech company, which often values platforms that let others innovate
A research lab, which values only unfinished ideas
optionExplain: Startups value invention under limits, not extensible frameworks as such.
Traditional industries value respectful, incremental change, though they do modernize.
A platform that lets others innovate matches what large companies value.
Research labs value exploring fundamentals, not products that others extend.
questions.explain: The same story can be told differently to suit the employer.
questions.rule: Describe your story in the terms the employer values.
questions.teaches: The book says that at large tech companies innovation often means creating platforms or frameworks that enable others to innovate, and that success requires balancing breakthrough thinking with being practical.

questions.q: You apply to a research lab. Which approach to your innovation story is likely to fit best?
options: Show how you explored a fundamental question even though its use was not yet clear
Show how you delivered a feature the day before launch to meet sales targets
Show how you kept every old process unchanged during the whole project
Show how you copied a competitor's design to reduce all risk to the company
optionExplain: Research organizations value exploring new approaches without immediate commercial limits.
Commercial deadlines are the opposite of what the lab rewards.
Leaving processes unchanged suits the cautious side of a traditional setting.
Copying is the opposite of a new approach.
questions.explain: The card next describes two more kinds of employer.
questions.rule: Research rewards exploration; traditional industries reward respectful change.

questions.q: Traditional industries value those who can respect existing ____ while finding creative ways to transform operations.
questions.explain: The card says traditional industries want respect for existing processes alongside creative transformation.
questions.rule: Respect what exists while transforming it.

questions.q: Sort each detail by the setting where the book says it matters most.

items.t: I explained why the question was worth exploring before any use was known
I had structured reasons for choosing the direction of the study
I pushed past what was thought possible without a product deadline
I respected the existing process while replacing the slowest step
I showed value in small stages so people trusted a larger change
I was patient while the factory modernized one line at a time

questions.explain: The first three show unconstrained exploration with reasons; the last three show respectful, staged modernization.
questions.rule: Explore with reasons in research; change with patience in tradition.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, traditional industries want candidates who push large changes through before their value is proven.
questions.explain: The book says change in traditional industries must prove its value incrementally on the way towards a larger transformation.
questions.rule: Respect for what exists is part of the expectation.

questions.q: True or false: the book says research organizations judge innovation by how soon it earns money.
questions.explain: The book says research organizations reward people who push boundaries without immediate commercial constraints, even when practical applications are not yet clear.
questions.rule: Research rewards exploration with reasons, not quick revenue.

questions.q: A candidate for an old family manufacturer replaced a paper ordering step with a tablet form. How should the story be told?
options: As proof that the old process was wasteful and should have been scrapped years ago
As a wholesale overhaul done in a weekend so that nobody could resist it
As a change that respected the existing process and proved its value in stages
As an experiment whose only goal was curiosity about tablets
optionExplain: Criticizing the past conflicts with the respect the book mentions.
A rushed overhaul does not fit incremental proof.
It fits a traditional setting that respects the past and proves value step by step.
Pure curiosity suits a research setting more.
questions.explain: Present the invention the way the employer wants change to arrive.
questions.rule: In traditional settings, change that earns trust step by step.
questions.teaches: The book says that in a traditional industry, changes must prove their value incrementally on the way towards a larger transformation.

questions.q: You are applying to a company that favors steady, incremental improvement. How should you shape an innovation story?
options: Leave out every story involving a new approach, in order to appear as safe as possible to them
Show how you tempered your urge to innovate with practical constraints
Stress how you ignored the rules to force a radical change through
Say you have no interest in anything but incremental changes
optionExplain: Dropping new approaches is too much; the book keeps them and adds restraint.
The book advises showing that you balance the impulse to innovate against practical limits.
Ignoring rules clashes with an incremental culture.
Denying interest is dishonest and not what the book suggests.
questions.explain: The card next explains the thinking.
questions.rule: Adapt the emphasis, not the truth.

questions.q: If your target company favors incremental improvement, show how you have learned to ____ your impulse toward innovation with practical constraints.
questions.explain: The card says to temper the impulse to innovate with practical constraints.
questions.rule: Temper, not abandon.

questions.q: Sort each detail by the culture where the book's advice says it belongs.

items.t: How I learned to hold back a big idea until the practical limits were clear
How I worked within existing methods and improved them in steady steps
How I weighed risk against the constraints before changing anything
The moment I saw that the whole approach needed fundamental change
How I argued for dropping the old method completely
How I took a bold step to rebuild the foundation

questions.explain: The first three suit a culture that defaults to existing approaches; the last three suit one that welcomes radical change.
questions.rule: Match your emphasis to the culture.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate who chooses which true story to emphasize to suit the company's culture is following the book's advice.
questions.explain: The book says cultures view innovation and risk differently, and that you should tailor how you show your ability to innovate.
questions.rule: Tailor the emphasis; keep the story true.

questions.q: Taya was told a company prefers steady improvements, yet she presents herself as someone who overturns established methods whenever she can. What is the issue?
options: She should have invented a story to match the culture exactly
Cultural fit has no place in a behavioral interview answer
Overturning methods is a sign that she lacks any skills
She is not adapting to a culture that defaults to existing approaches
optionExplain: Fabricating a story is dishonest and not what the book says.
The book treats culture as a factor in how to present innovation.
Overturning methods is not itself a defect.
The book says to adjust your emphasis; inventing is not part of the advice.
questions.explain: She can stay truthful and still choose the examples that fit.
questions.rule: Choose among true stories; do not invent.

questions.q: You are applying to a company known for radical thinking. Which of your true experiences should you highlight?
options: Times when you waited for permission before changing anything
Times when you recognized the need for a fundamental change
Times when you chose the safest option every single time
Times when you left the old approach untouched on purpose
optionExplain: Waiting for permission is the incremental style.
A culture that encourages radical thinking responds to stories of recognizing the need for fundamental change.
Always choosing the safest option shows restraint.
Leaving the old approach in place shows restraint, which is for another culture.
questions.explain: This is the other end of the range; the decision is still yours.
questions.rule: Highlight true stories that fit the culture.
questions.teaches: The book advises that if you target a work culture that encourages radical thinking, you should highlight the times when you recognized the need for fundamental change.

questions.q: An engineer traces an outage to its cause using the usual debugging methods. Which competency does that show most directly?
options: Innovation, since any fix of a problem is a new invention
Initiative, since all troubleshooting is done unprompted
Optimization, since finding causes makes things run faster
Problem-solving: investigating and fixing a problem with established methods
optionExplain: Fixes can be done with known methods, which is not invention.
Initiative is about choosing unassigned problems; an outage may well be assigned.
Finding a cause does not necessarily speed anything up.
Using established methods to investigate and fix an issue is how the book describes problem-solving.
questions.explain: The card next separates three related competencies.
questions.rule: Fixing with known methods is problem-solving.

questions.q: Problem-solving focuses on investigating and fixing issues, often using ____ methods.
questions.explain: The card contrasts problem-solving with established methods against innovation when those methods fall short.
questions.rule: Problem-solving uses established methods; innovation steps in when they are not enough.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it is mainly problem-solving or mainly innovation.

items.t: A cook finds why the sauce splits and corrects the temperature using a standard technique
A technician locates a faulty cable by testing each connection in turn
An analyst works out why a figure is wrong by checking the usual sources
A cook devises a new cooking method that removes the risk of splitting
A technician designs a monitor that detects faults that used to be invisible
An analyst invents a way to catch bad figures before they enter the report

questions.explain: The first three investigate and fix with known methods; the last three invent a new approach.
questions.rule: Fix with the known; invent where the known is not enough.

questions.q: True or false: if an engineer debugs a failure with careful analysis and then invents a new monitor for silent failures, the story shows both competencies.
questions.explain: The book gives this exact pairing: analysis for the failure is problem-solving, and the new monitoring approach is innovation.
questions.rule: The best candidates show both.

questions.q: True or false: a story showing only problem-solving with established methods answers an innovation question as well as a story showing a new approach.
questions.explain: Problem-solving uses established methods, whereas innovation is a new approach when those methods are not enough. The book values both, but only the second answers an innovation question.
questions.rule: Fixing with known methods is not yet innovating.

questions.q: A school secretary notices that parents keep missing notices and, unasked, devises a new way of sending them that parents cannot overlook. Which combination is this?
options: Only problem-solving, because the notices were a problem
Only optimization, because notices were already being sent
Initiative in choosing the problem, and innovation in the new solution
Neither, because school offices are not the right place for this sort of work to be done
optionExplain: Problem-solving covers fixing with known methods, but she invented a new one.
The notices were sent before, but her method is new, not just faster.
She picked an unassigned problem and invented a new approach.
The book's pairs are not limited to engineering.
questions.explain: The combination in the book's strongest stories shows up outside tech as well.
questions.rule: The strongest stories combine choosing the problem and inventing the solution.
questions.teaches: The book's example is a slow mobile app launch that nobody has surfaced: deciding on your own to improve it shows initiative, and inventing a novel approach to surgically lazy-load resources is innovation.

questions.q: An interviewer says: Tell me about the most innovative thing you have done. Which answer plan gives the most signal?
options: The list of tools you used and the number of hours you worked on the project in total
A summary of the praise your manager gave you at the review
Why existing approaches would not work, what you invented, and why it was new
A description of how the team normally handled the problem
optionExplain: Tools and hours say nothing about novelty.
Praise is second-hand and tells little about what was new.
It lets the interviewer see both the problem and the novelty.
The team's usual way is the thing you were supposed to go beyond.
questions.explain: The book names three things strong answers cover. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Show why, what and how it was new.

questions.q: Strong answers explain why existing approaches wouldn't have worked, describe what you invented, and show how your ideas were ____.
questions.explain: The card lists these three parts: why old approaches fail, what you invented, and what made it novel.
questions.rule: Why, what, and novel.

questions.q: Put these parts of a strong answer to a creating-new-solutions question in a sensible order.
items: Say why the existing approaches would not have worked
Describe what you invented
Show what made your idea novel
questions.explain: The need comes first, then the invention, then what made it new.
questions.rule: Need, invention, novelty.

questions.q: True or false: if a candidate describes only the tool built and does not say why existing approaches were inadequate, the interviewer can fully judge the novelty.
questions.explain: Without the reason existing methods fell short, the interviewer cannot tell whether the solution was needed or new.
questions.rule: Skipping the why hides the novelty.

questions.q: Asked whether he built something new to his company, Cam describes a tool copying a known open-source product. What is the gap?
options: He does not show what was novel about it compared with the known product
He should have described the product's price in much more detail for the interviewer
He should not have mentioned any open-source tool at all
He should have said it was invented by a team of strangers
optionExplain: The question asks for something new, and the answer does not show what was new.
Price is not what the question asks about.
Mentioning open-source tools is allowed if you show what you added.
Claiming a stranger's invention is not an answer.
questions.explain: The question probes novelty, so the answer must locate it.
questions.rule: Say what was new, not only what was built.

questions.q: A teacher is asked about a completely new solution she created. Which part of her story best shows she saw that small changes would not work?
options: She admired a method used at another school and brought it in
She worked harder than before on the old method for a term
She asked her manager which method to use and followed the answer
She tried three tweaks to the old method, saw each fail for the same reason, and then built something different
optionExplain: Importing a method may be fine, but it does not show the incremental failure.
More effort on the old method is optimization.
Following an instruction does not show recognition of the limit.
It shows incremental changes failing and a move to something new.
questions.explain: The signal is the moment you see that tweaks will not be enough.
questions.rule: Show the point where tweaks stopped being an option.
questions.teaches: The book says strong answers describe you recognizing when incremental changes were not going to work and then building something completely new.

questions.q: You are asked: Tell me about a time you improved something that was already working fine. Which example fits best if you have both kinds?
options: The time you made the existing process a little faster for the whole team to use
The time you created a process that removed the original bottleneck
The time you were asked to repeat last quarter's fix
The time you waited for a manager to approve the new schedule
optionExplain: A speed-up is a solid answer but not the standout one.
A new approach that removes the cause stands out over a speed-up.
Repeating an old fix is not a new approach.
Waiting for approval shows nothing about the improvement itself.
questions.explain: The card next names the contrast.
questions.rule: Prefer the example with a new approach.

questions.q: Questions about improving something can be answered with optimization or innovation examples, but answers that refer to ____ will stand out.
questions.explain: The card says innovation answers stand out even for improvement questions.
questions.rule: Both are welcome; innovation stands out.

questions.q: Sort each answer to an improved something question by whether it is the standout innovation kind or a solid optimization kind.

items.t: I removed the weekly manual export by letting the two systems share data directly
I designed an intake form that stops bad requests from ever reaching the queue
I created a method so reports build themselves and no one assembles them
I cut the weekly export time from two hours to one
I shortened the queue's review step by adding a checklist
I made the report template load faster

questions.explain: The first three eliminate the original bottleneck with a new approach; the last three make the existing process faster.
questions.rule: Eliminate beats speed up.

questions.q: True or false: if you have only an optimization example, the book still calls it a solid answer to an improved something question.
questions.explain: The book says the former, making the existing process faster, is a solid answer, though the innovation answer stands out.
questions.rule: A solid answer is still an answer.

questions.q: Which pair of words in a question should make you check whether you have an innovation example?
options: Team and manager, which show who was involved in the work
Deadline and budget, which show the limits placed on the work
Learned and mistake, which show a story about a failure
Improved and better
optionExplain: These words describe the setting, not the improvement cue.
These describe constraints, which may appear in any story.
These words point to a different kind of question about learning from failure.
The card says the words improved or better are the cue.
questions.explain: Questions that sound modest can still call for an innovation example.
questions.rule: Hear improved or better and ask whether you invented something.

questions.q: A restaurant manager is asked about improving something that already worked. Which answer shows the stand-out kind?
options: She trained servers to write tickets more neatly
She replaced paper tickets with a system where orders reach the kitchen as guests place them
She bought a better pen for the servers
She asked servers to hurry when writing tickets
optionExplain: Neater writing is the same process, only improved.
It creates a process that removes the original delay.
A better pen is a minor aid to the same process.
Asking for speed pushes the same process harder.
questions.explain: The same distinction works in any field.
questions.rule: Look for the example that changed the method.
questions.teaches: The book says the former, making the existing process faster, is a solid answer, but the latter, a process that eliminated the original bottleneck entirely, demonstrates innovation.

questions.q: An interviewer asks you to describe turning an innovative idea into a working solution. What are they testing?
options: Whether you can think of more ideas than other candidates
Whether you can describe a theory in the most detail
Whether you can build and prove a new approach within real constraints
Whether you prefer working alone on difficult projects
optionExplain: Quantity of ideas is not the focus.
Theory detail does not show implementation.
These questions test moving from idea to implementation.
Working alone is not what the question asks about.
questions.explain: The card next sets out the book's reading of these questions.
questions.rule: Test of making the idea work.

questions.q: Interviewers use these questions to evaluate whether you are comfortable moving from new ideas to ____ them.
questions.explain: The card says these questions check that you can move from ideas to implementing them.
questions.rule: The test is implementation.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it is a strong implementation signal or a weak one.

items.t: I ran the new method on one team first to show it worked in practice
I made it usable by people who had not built it
I fit it to our real deadline and staffing
I had a detailed idea that never left my notes
I described the concept but not how it ran
I assumed it would work and never tried it

questions.explain: The first three show the idea working under real conditions; the last three leave it untested.
questions.rule: Show it working.

questions.q: True or false: an implementation story is complete once the candidate explains how clever the idea was.
questions.explain: The book says strong stories show the approach proven in practice, usable by others, and managed against resistance.
questions.rule: Clever alone is not complete.

questions.q: True or false: a story that proves a new approach in practice answers an implementation question fully even if it does not say what the problem was.
questions.explain: Our reading: an implementation story still needs the problem and the reason existing methods fell short, which the earlier ideas describe. Proof of working is only one part.
questions.rule: Implementation proof does not replace the problem statement.

questions.q: A nonprofit coordinator introduced a new method for volunteer sign-ups and some volunteers resisted it. Which detail best supports an implementation story?
options: How she addressed their concerns and showed the method working in practice
How much she personally liked the new method, and how often she told people about it
How rarely she needed to discuss it with anyone
How the old method had been in use for years
optionExplain: It shows managing resistance and proving the approach in practice.
Liking the method is personal, not evidence.
Avoiding discussion is the opposite of managing resistance.
The old method's age does not show implementation.
questions.explain: The same two proofs matter in any field: it worked, and people took it up.
questions.rule: Prove it works and bring people along.
questions.teaches: The book says strong implementation stories include managing organizational resistance to new ideas.

questions.q: You are asked how you test whether a new idea is worth pursuing. What should the answer show?
options: A strong belief in the idea that you kept despite the results
Trying many ideas in turn until one of them happened to work
Experiments aimed at the key assumptions, and changes made from what you learned
Waiting for management to decide which idea to back
optionExplain: Belief despite results ignores validation.
Throwing ideas at problems is what the book contrasts with systematic thinking.
Systematic testing of assumptions and adapting is what the book wants.
Waiting for a decision shows nothing about your own method.
questions.explain: The card next explains what these questions probe.
questions.rule: Method behind the creativity.

questions.q: Interviewers want evidence of systematic thinking, rather than throwing ideas at ____.
questions.explain: The card quotes systematic thinking as opposed to throwing ideas at problems.
questions.rule: Systematic, not scattershot.

questions.q: Put these steps of a validation story in a sensible order.
items: Name the key assumption the idea depends on
Design a small experiment to test that assumption
Run the experiment
Adapt the approach based on what the data shows
questions.explain: Assumption, experiment, results, adaptation is the sequence the card describes.
questions.rule: Test the assumption before you build further.

questions.q: True or false: if the first version of an innovation fails, a candidate who explains what the failure taught and what changed is answering the question well.
questions.explain: The questions ask about approaches that did not work out and about evolving based on feedback, and strong responses show adaptation.
questions.rule: A failure with learning is a good answer.

questions.q: True or false: a story about a brilliant invention with no testing step answers a validating question well.
questions.explain: According to the book, these questions probe systematic thinking, such as designing experiments and adapting to what you learn. A story with no testing step does not show that.
questions.rule: Validation questions need a test in the story.

questions.q: A teacher tries a new homework method and asks students for feedback each week, changing it based on their answers. Which question does her story answer best?
options: Have you built something that did not exist before?
Describe a time you convinced others to try it
Tell me about the most innovative thing you have done in your career so far
Give an example of evolving an innovation based on feedback
optionExplain: That question is about novelty.
That question is about persuasion.
That question is about your single best invention.
It centres on adapting from feedback.
questions.explain: The same story could answer several questions; choose the one it fits.
questions.rule: Match the story to the question's focus.
questions.teaches: The book says strong responses also show gathering data to test whether innovations lead to measurable improvements.

questions.q: An interviewer is judging an innovation story. Which result would they value most?
options: A clever design that nobody had any use for, which still shows how clever its maker was
A new approach that became the way people work because it was more effective
A long explanation of how hard the work was
An improvement to an existing process of a few percent
optionExplain: Cleverness without use falls short of what interviewers want.
It is a new approach with real value and adoption.
Difficulty is not the same as value.
A small improvement is optimization.
questions.explain: The card next sets out how the book ranks signals.
questions.rule: New, best for a real problem, and adopted.

questions.q: Match each signal tier to the signal the book assigns it.
questions.explain: The book labels inventing new approaches critical, simplifying and practical innovation strong, and learning from past work supporting.
questions.rule: Critical, strong, supporting.

questions.q: Sort each phrase by whether it builds the critical signal or weakens it.

items.t: I saw that the current method could not handle the load, so I built a different one
I questioned why everyone assumed the data had to be copied nightly
Other teams adopted my method because it worked better for them
I made something clever that nobody ended up needing
I made the existing method run a little faster
I built what I found interesting without asking what the problem was

questions.explain: The first three show limits recognized, assumptions questioned and a method others adopted; the last three show novelty without value or no new approach.
questions.rule: New, valuable and adopted.

questions.q: True or false: a new approach that solves a real problem and changes how people work shows the critical signal.
questions.explain: The book says it is not enough to invent something clever; it asks whether you created something valuable that changed how people work.
questions.rule: Value that changes how people work completes the signal.

questions.q: True or false: a new approach that is clever but is not the best way to solve a real problem fully shows the critical signal.
questions.explain: The book says newness alone is not sufficient: interviewers want to hear that the new approach was the best way to solve a real problem.
questions.rule: Clever and new is not the whole signal.

questions.q: A nurse invented a handover checklist method that a hospital then adopted widely. Which parts make her story strong on the critical signal?
options: It addressed a real problem, was adopted widely and changed how handovers were done
It was a checklist, a format that hospitals already trust and value for its simplicity
It was her own idea, which made it original by its nature
It took her a year, which shows how much effort she gave it
optionExplain: She shows a valuable method that changed how people work.
A checklist is only innovative if it is a new approach that solves a problem.
Ownership of an idea does not make it valuable.
Duration does not decide it.
questions.explain: The signal travels to any field.
questions.rule: Look for real problem and real adoption.
questions.teaches: The book says strong stories describe you creating methods that others adopt because they are more effective.

questions.q: Which story best shows an innovation that simplifies?
