options: Six manual approval steps became twelve, each with a dashboard
Six manual approval steps stayed, with a guide added on how to use them
Six manual approval steps were replaced by one automatic check
Six manual approval steps were moved to a new system without change
optionExplain: Twelve steps is more complexity.
A guide manages complexity; it does not remove it.
It removes complexity instead of rearranging or adding to it.
Moving unchanged steps does nothing about the complexity.
questions.explain: The card next names simplification as a strong signal.
questions.rule: Less afterwards than before.

questions.q: Innovators find ways to drastically ____ or eliminate complexity rather than manage it.
questions.explain: The card says strong innovators simplify or eliminate complexity.
questions.rule: Simplify or eliminate.

questions.q: Sort each result by whether it simplifies or adds complexity.

items.t: Four overlapping spreadsheets became a single shared view
A nightly reconciliation job was no longer needed
Three approval emails collapsed into a single click
A new layer was added to translate between two layers
A monitoring tool was added to watch the other monitoring tools
Extra settings were introduced to cover each special case

questions.explain: The first three remove things; the last three add parts to manage a problem.
questions.rule: Count what disappeared.

questions.q: True or false: a story that adds new components, layers and processes to manage a problem would be a strong example of the simplifying signal.
questions.explain: That story adds complexity, which is the opposite of the simplifying signal.
questions.rule: More parts rarely means simpler.

questions.q: A candidate says her new system is simple because its screen is clean, though the steps behind it tripled. What is wrong?
options: A clean screen is a sign that no real innovation took place
A system with many steps cannot have a clean screen at all
The complexity behind the screen grew, so nothing was removed
Simplicity is a quality that interviewers do not look for in stories
optionExplain: A clean screen is fine; the point is that it hides added complexity.
Screens and steps are separate matters; the issue is what was removed.
The signal is about eliminating complexity, not covering it.
The book names simplifying as a strong signal.
questions.explain: Tripling the steps adds complexity however the screen looks.
questions.rule: Measure the complexity that remains, not the front that shows.

questions.q: A public library merges three overlapping membership cards into one. How would you frame this as a strong signal?
options: As a clean solution to a messy problem that removed the need for two of the cards
As a large project whose strength was the number of staff meetings it needed
As an upgrade of each card's printing quality to look more professional
As a new database to manage all three cards in their separate forms
optionExplain: It removes complexity for members and staff.
Meetings measure effort, not simplicity.
Printing quality changes none of the structure.
A database manages the three cards instead of removing two.
questions.explain: The signal works outside technology as well.
questions.rule: Present what the solution took away.
questions.teaches: The book says good examples may have felt obvious in hindsight but required creative leaps to discover.

questions.q: Which statement best captures why practicality matters to an innovation story?
options: Practical ideas are better than creative ideas in every setting, so creativity adds little to a story
Interviewers care only about cost and time, not about the ideas
Practical work means choosing the easiest option at every step
An invention that is not built, or is built but not valued, is imagination or waste
optionExplain: The book wants both, balanced, not practicality over creativity.
Cost and time are two of the limits, not the only measure.
Practical does not mean easy.
The book says innovation without implementation is imagination, and without value is waste.
questions.explain: The card next details the signal.
questions.rule: Built and valuable.

questions.q: Innovation without implementation is only ____.
questions.explain: The book says innovation without implementation is just imagination.
questions.rule: Without implementation, it is imagination.

questions.q: Sort each remark by whether it shows practical innovation or a gap in practicality.

items.t: We checked the idea against our deadline and staffing before building it
It fixed a problem our support staff hit every day
We timed the rollout to when the teams were ready for it
It was brilliant but needed three times our budget
It was elegant but solved a problem nobody had
It worked in the lab but no team was ready to adopt it

questions.explain: The first three consider feasibility, real problems and readiness; the last three ignore them.
questions.rule: Feasible, useful, ready.

questions.q: True or false: a creative solution that considered feasibility from the start and that others adopted would be a good example of practical innovation.
questions.explain: The book says good examples consider feasibility from the start, solve real problems, and are adopted because they improved people's work.
questions.rule: Feasible, useful and adopted.

questions.q: Which story is the better example of balancing vision and reality?
options: A bold design that ignored all limits because limits spoil vision
A bold design shaped to fit the team's time, tools and readiness to adopt it
A safe design chosen because it asked nothing new of anyone and carried no risk at all
A design adopted only after everything was perfectly certain
optionExplain: Ignoring limits gives up practicality.
It keeps the vision and respects the limits.
A safe design gives up novelty.
Waiting for certainty is not how the book describes practical work.
questions.explain: Practical innovation holds both ends.
questions.rule: Keep the vision; fit the reality.

questions.q: A volunteer group designs a new sign-up app. Which detail would show the strongest practicality?
options: The app has more features than any competing app on the market and a longer feature list
The app was built in a language that was new to the group
The app was announced at the group's annual dinner with applause
Members stopped using paper sheets because the app saved them time each week
optionExplain: Features are not use.
A new language is novelty, not practicality.
Applause does not show use.
It shows adoption because it improved their work.
questions.explain: Others adopting because it improved their work is the sign.
questions.rule: Evidence of use beats evidence of effort.
questions.teaches: The book says the best stories describe how others adopted your solution because it genuinely improved their work.

questions.q: Which detail best shows a person treating a past project as an experiment?
options: She followed the plan exactly as first drawn up from start to finish
She challenged a core assumption early and changed the plan when results arrived
She waited until the end of the project to ask what had gone wrong
She repeated the first approach in the next project without change
optionExplain: Following the plan exactly leaves no room for learning.
It shows an early test of assumptions and adaptation.
Asking at the end is late and not an experiment.
Repeating without change ignores results.
questions.explain: The card next describes this signal.
questions.rule: Learn as you go.

questions.q: Match each element of learning from past innovation work to what it looks like in a story.
pairs: Pushing back on core assumptions at the start
Changing the approach based on preliminary results
Knowing when to persist or try something completely different
questions.explain: The card lists these three behaviors.
questions.rule: Challenge, adapt, judge.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it shows learning from past work or not.

items.t: After the pilot, I dropped the feature users ignored and doubled the one they loved
I questioned the sizing assumption in week one and tested it
I decided to stop after two failures because the data pointed elsewhere
I carried on with the original plan regardless of the pilot
I never looked back at the results once the project shipped
I assumed the design was right and skipped the early test

questions.explain: The first three use evidence to steer; the last three ignore it.
questions.rule: Evidence changes the plan.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate who changed direction after early results is showing the behavior the supporting signal looks for.
questions.explain: Adapting based on preliminary results is exactly what the supporting signal looks for.
questions.rule: Adapting is a strength.

questions.q: True or false: a story made only of learning from past projects, with no new approach, would earn the top signal.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book ranks inventing new approaches as the critical signal and learning from past work as a supporting one, so learning alone does not reach the top tier.
questions.rule: A supporting signal supports; it does not replace the critical one.

questions.q: A gardener tries a new composting method and, after a poor first season, changes the mix but keeps the method. What does this show?
options: Knowing when to persist in a direction while adapting the details
Giving up too soon on the original method after a single poor season of results
A failure to learn anything from the first season
A decision to try a completely different approach altogether
optionExplain: She stayed with the approach and adjusted using results.
She did not give up on the method.
She did learn, since she changed the mix.
She kept the method, so she did not change entirely.
questions.explain: Persisting and adapting can go together.
questions.rule: Persist when the data supports it; change when it does not.
questions.teaches: The book says the supporting signal includes knowing when to persist in one direction or try completely different approaches.

questions.q: A candidate describes a latency fix and a bug patch as her most innovative work. What does the interviewer likely conclude?
options: That she does not understand the difference between improving and inventing
That she is modest about her real achievements and holds back from claiming them
That she values reliability above everything else in engineering
That she has solved problems nobody else could have solved
optionExplain: The book says this shows you do not understand the distinction.
Nothing in her answer suggests modesty.
Her labeling of fixes as innovation points to a misunderstanding, not a preference.
Ordinary fixes do not show unique problem-solving.
questions.explain: The card next explains how serious this flag is.
questions.rule: Know what you are calling innovation.

questions.q: The book uses Red Flags for ____ issues that will significantly damage your candidacy, and Yellow Flags for patterns that weaken your examples.
questions.explain: The card defines red flags as serious issues and yellow flags as concerning patterns that weaken examples.
questions.rule: Red is serious; yellow weakens.

questions.q: Sort each claim by whether it is honest about the kind of work or falls into the red flag.

items.t: I made the checkout page 40 percent faster by tuning queries
I fixed a rare crash in the upload code
I improved reliability by adding retries to the existing job
My most innovative work was fixing a rare crash in the upload code
I invented a new approach by adding indexes to slow queries
My innovation was patching bugs faster than anyone before

questions.explain: Calling a fix a fix is honest; labelling fixes and tuning as innovation is the red flag.
questions.rule: Name the work for what it is.

questions.q: True or false: an interviewer who hears bug fixes called innovation would take this as a serious red flag.
questions.explain: The book classes this as the red flag, a serious issue that significantly damages the candidacy.
questions.rule: This one is serious.

questions.q: Quin says: A bug fix is not worth mentioning anywhere, since it is not innovation. What does the book say?
options: Bug fixes should be hidden from interviewers in every case
Bug fixes count as innovation when they are large enough to be noticed by the whole company
Making something faster or more reliable is valuable, only not innovative on its own
Bug fixes are valuable only if they are also new inventions
optionExplain: Hiding them is not recommended.
Size does not change the category.
The book values the work and rejects only the label.
Value does not depend on invention.
questions.explain: The flag is about the label, not about the work.
questions.rule: Value it; do not mislabel it.

questions.q: A shop manager tells an interviewer that rearranging the shelves was her innovation. She only moved items to better places. What is the better framing?
options: A revolutionary breakthrough in shop design for the whole sector
A sensible improvement to how the shop runs, not an invented approach
A failure, because moving items shows no value to customers
A secret to hide because small changes cannot be discussed
optionExplain: Exaggerating invites the red flag.
The honest framing keeps the credit and avoids the flag.
Moving items can be valuable.
Small changes are fine to describe.
questions.explain: The red flag applies to any field.
questions.rule: Use honest labels.
questions.teaches: The book says to avoid this red flag by focusing your answers on times you did new things, because innovation opens new possibilities.

questions.q: You begin your story with the new tool you built. What is the risk the book describes?
options: The interviewer will assume that the tool was really built by someone else on the team
The interviewer will think the tool is too simple to discuss
The interviewer will ask about unrelated tools in other teams
The interviewer cannot see why the tool was needed or how hard the problem was
optionExplain: Authorship is not the issue.
Simplicity is a strength in the book.
The risk is about missing context, not other teams.
Without the problem, the interviewer cannot judge the work.
questions.explain: The card next describes this yellow flag.
questions.rule: Problem before solution.

questions.q: Jumping straight into your creative solution without first explaining why existing approaches were ____ misses the point.
questions.explain: The card says you should first establish why existing solutions were inadequate.
questions.rule: Show the gap before the fix.

questions.q: Put the parts of a story in the order the card recommends.
items: Say what the problem was and why existing solutions were not enough
Describe the new approach you created
Report what changed because of it
questions.explain: The card puts the problem before the solution, and the result last.
questions.rule: Problem, solution, result.

questions.q: True or false: if a candidate explains the existing constraints before the solution, the interviewer is better able to assess the candidate's ability.
questions.explain: The book says missing this context prevents interviewers from fully assessing your ability, so adding it helps.
questions.rule: Context lets them judge.

questions.q: True or false: the longer you describe the background before the solution, the stronger the story becomes.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book asks for enough context to show why existing solutions fell short, not for as much as possible. A very long setup could bury the solution.
questions.rule: Give enough context to judge the work, then move on.

questions.q: A teacher says: I invented a new seating plan. A listener learns nothing about why. Which added sentence would fix the story?
options: Everyone loved the new plan on the first day of term
It was the best plan any teacher in the school had tried
It involved a diagram drawn on a large sheet of paper
Noisy groups had made every earlier arrangement fail, and the room allowed few options
optionExplain: Approval says nothing of the problem.
Praise does not explain the need.
A diagram describes the solution, not the problem.
It states why existing arrangements failed and the constraints.
questions.explain: Context turns a clever idea into a solved problem.
questions.rule: Say why the old ways failed.
questions.teaches: The book says you should also establish the existing constraints that made the problem a challenge to solve.

questions.q: Your best project added many layers and needs ten minutes to explain. What might interviewers conclude?
options: That you may have over-engineered rather than innovated
That you are the strongest candidate for the role
That you are too modest to boast about the project
That you dislike teamwork in complex settings
optionExplain: The book says interviewers are likely to question whether you were truly innovating.
Complexity does not signal strength.
Nothing suggests modesty.
Teamwork is not in question.
questions.explain: The card next describes this yellow flag.
questions.rule: Complex is a warning.

questions.q: If your example added multiple new components, layers and processes, you may have been guilty of ____.
questions.explain: The card says the pattern may reveal over-engineering.
questions.rule: Over-engineering is the suspicion.

questions.q: Sort each project summary by whether it fits the yellow flag or is a better example.

items.t: Six new services, three queues and a custom scheduler to run one report
A new rule engine with four layers that needs a long talk to explain
A system with many moving parts that took the team weeks to learn
One simple rule that replaced three steps and a review meeting
A single check that made the old approval chain unnecessary
A small tool that removed a whole class of manual rework

questions.explain: The first three add complexity and need long explanations; the last three make things simpler.
questions.rule: Prefer stories that end simpler.

questions.q: True or false: an interviewer who sees a long list of components in your story will likely assume the solution was elegantly simple.
questions.explain: The book says they will likely question whether you were truly innovating.
questions.rule: Long component lists raise questions.

questions.q: True or false: the book says a complicated solution cannot be an innovation.
questions.explain: The book says complicated solutions do not always make the best example and may draw questions, and it advises choosing a story that shows simplification. It does not rule complex solutions out.
questions.rule: Complex is a warning sign, not a disqualifier.

questions.q: A hospital administrator describes a new scheduling scheme with five forms and a long guide. Which change would improve the story?
options: Add a sixth form to show more thoroughness in the design and more care in the planning
Describe the guide in more detail to show how complete it was
Show how the scheme replaced old paperwork and made scheduling easier for staff
Make the story longer so that every form is covered
optionExplain: More forms add complexity.
More guide detail adds explanation.
It shows the simplification.
A longer story adds more of what weakens it.
questions.explain: Choose the example that ends simpler.
questions.rule: Show how things got simpler.
questions.teaches: The book says interviewers will likely question whether you were truly innovating if your example requires an extensive explanation, and you may have been guilty of over-engineering.

questions.q: You built a clever internal tool and nobody used it. How should this affect which story you tell?
options: Consider another story where others benefited, since unused tools show little value
Tell it anyway, since the cleverness is what matters most
Tell it and say that the users were not smart enough to use it
Tell it and add that you plan to promote it one day
optionExplain: The book says innovation delivers value only when others benefit.
Cleverness without use is innovation for its own sake.
Blaming users does not provide evidence of value.
A future plan is not a result.
questions.explain: The card next sets out the book's reasoning.
questions.rule: Value means others benefit.

questions.q: Building creative solutions that nobody uses suggests innovation for its own ____.
questions.explain: The card uses the phrase innovation for its own sake.
questions.rule: Use is what proves value.

questions.q: Sort each ending by whether it supplies adoption evidence or leaves it out.

items.t: Two other teams adopted it and cut their weekly effort by half
New hires now use it on their first day
Support staff say it saves them an hour each week
It is technically elegant and I am proud of it
It won an internal award for creativity
I built it over a quarter and presented it once

questions.explain: The first three show others benefiting; the last three give pride or process but no adoption.
questions.rule: Show who benefited.

questions.q: True or false: a story that includes the effects of your approach and how others benefited is stronger than one about cleverness alone.
questions.explain: The book says stories should include the effects of your approach and how others benefited, because innovation delivers value only when others benefit.
questions.rule: Show who benefited.

questions.q: True or false: a story with wide adoption but no new approach and no stated problem would be a strong innovation story.
questions.explain: Our reading: adoption is one of several features the chapter lists. Without a new approach and the problem it solved, the story would still lack the core of innovation.
questions.rule: Adoption supports the story; it does not make it innovation.

questions.q: A junior analyst has recently joined and built a helpful spreadsheet for herself that nobody else has used yet. How does the book treat her story?
options: It must be hidden because adoption evidence is required from all
Adoption evidence is not expected from an entry-level engineer in the same way
It should be inflated by claiming that the whole company already uses the spreadsheet today
It is equal to a staff-level story since the spreadsheet is useful
optionExplain: The exception exists.
The book makes an exception at entry level.
Inflating the claim is dishonest.
Levels still differ in expected scope and adoption.
questions.explain: Expectations rise with level.
questions.rule: Adoption expectations scale with level.
questions.teaches: The book's takeaways say to avoid claiming innovation without providing evidence that others adopted your approach, unless you are an entry-level engineer.

questions.q: You have one idea you did not build and one you built that failed. Which makes the stronger interview story?
options: The untried idea, since it cannot be shown to have failed
Neither story, since both lack a successful result at the end
The untried idea, since it shows more imagination than the other idea that was actually built
The failed attempt that taught you something, since you moved from concept to action
optionExplain: An untried idea avoids failure but also avoids evidence.
Success is not required.
Imagination is not enough without action.
The book says a failed attempt with lessons beats a whiteboard idea.
questions.explain: The card next sets out the book's reasoning.
questions.rule: Action beats theory.

questions.q: Describing ideas that you have not implemented will weaken your ____ in an interview.
questions.explain: The card says untried ideas weaken credibility.
questions.rule: Credibility comes from action.

questions.q: Sort each story by whether it shows concept to action or an idea stuck on the whiteboard.

items.t: I built a prototype, tested it on two teams and learned it was too slow
I shipped a small version and changed it after users complained
I ran a one-week trial and wrote down what failed
I had a design in mind but never began the work
I proposed an idea and never built or tested it
I sketched a plan in a meeting and moved on to other things

questions.explain: The first three show building and testing; the last three never left the page.
questions.rule: Build and test.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate whose attempt failed but who learned something valuable can tell a stronger story than one with an untried theoretical idea.
questions.explain: The book says a failed attempt that taught something valuable is far stronger than a theoretical idea that stayed on the whiteboard.
questions.rule: Failure with learning beats theory.

questions.q: True or false: any failed attempt makes a strong story, whatever it taught.
questions.explain: The book praises failed attempts that taught something valuable. Our reading: a failure with no lesson gives the interviewer little to use.
questions.rule: The lesson is what makes the failure useful.

questions.q: A designer's first prototype of a new booking flow failed in a user test. Which opening makes the best use of that failure?
options: I do not like to talk about prototypes that fail, so I will describe a plan that I have for later on
My idea was a good one that the testers failed to understand in time
I built a prototype and tested it; it failed, and here is what it taught me about the next version
I did not get as far as building anything because I wanted it to be perfect
optionExplain: Retreating to a plan puts the idea back on the whiteboard.
Blaming the testers hides the lesson.
It shows action, testing and learning, which the card says carry more weight than an untried idea.
Waiting for perfection is an idea without action.
questions.explain: The failed attempt is the strength of this story.
questions.rule: Lead with the build, the test and the lesson.
questions.teaches: The book says the initiative to build and test an idea matters more to interviewers than whether it succeeded on the first try.

questions.q: Which story shows innovation at the senior level rather than the entry level?
options: A solution built on purpose for a problem the whole team shared, adopted as a team standard
A tool built for your own chores that no one else saw
A small script that you wrote for yourself and kept private for several years without telling anyone about it
A fix to your own code that sped up your tests alone
optionExplain: Senior-level innovation targets shared problems and becomes a team standard.
Own-chore tools are entry-level.
Keeping a script private is also entry-level.
Fixes to your own code are entry-level.
questions.explain: The card next lays out all five levels.
questions.rule: Level changes the scope of the story.

questions.q: Match each level to the innovation scope the book gives it.
pairs: Solves problems in your own work
Helps immediate teammates who adopt it
Addresses a shared problem and becomes a team standard
Crosses team boundaries and becomes an organizational pattern
Transforms how significant parts of the organization or industry operate
questions.explain: The five levels widen from personal to team to cross-team to organization or industry.
questions.rule: Own work, teammates, team standard, many teams, industry.

questions.q: Sort each story by the level of innovation it fits best.

items.t: A script that ended my own weekly chore
A helper my teammates picked up after seeing me use it
A fix for something that slowed only my own work
A pattern now used by five different teams
An approach that became the reference design for the whole organization
A method that changed how companies in our field handle a task

questions.explain: The first three stay within me or my teammates; the last three cross team boundaries or reach the industry.
questions.rule: Count how far it spread.

questions.q: True or false: a mid-level candidate whose solution spread from herself to her teammates fits the book's mid-level description.
questions.explain: The card says mid-level innovation starts for yourself and spreads to teammates who face the same challenges.
questions.rule: Mid level spreads to teammates.

questions.q: How does senior-level innovation differ from mid-level innovation in the book's account?
options: Seniors set out to solve a shared problem for the group, rather than building for themselves and sharing later
Seniors work on bigger machines, whereas mids work on smaller ones
Seniors do not build for themselves, whereas mids do
Seniors invent only industry-wide standards, whereas mids invent tools
optionExplain: Mid starts with your own problem; senior starts with the group's.
Size of machines is not the difference.
The book says mid builds for self first; no absolute rule is given.
Industry-wide standards belong to principal level.
questions.explain: Intent differs: shared problem from the start.
questions.rule: Senior aims at the shared problem.

questions.q: A junior candidate is asked about innovation at the organizational level. What should she do, according to the book?
options: Refuse to answer, because she has not worked at that level and has no experience of any kind to draw upon
Invent a story about leading the whole company's strategy
Be ready to answer, because interviewers sometimes ask harder questions to see how she thinks
Say her level makes the question irrelevant to her interview
optionExplain: Refusing wastes the chance to show thinking.
Inventing a story is dishonest.
Prepare for questions above your level.
The book says to be prepared regardless of level.
questions.explain: Preparation should cover questions beyond your own experience.
questions.rule: Prepare above your level.
questions.teaches: The book says entry- and mid-level candidates more often face questions about the personal or team level, senior and above about inter-team and organizational levels, yet interviewers sometimes ask more advanced questions to see how you think.

questions.q: In a strong innovation answer, what usually comes right before the description of the new invention?
options: A list of awards the candidate has won in previous roles
An explanation of why standard solutions could not handle the problem
A summary of what the team plans to do in the next quarter and in the year after it
A comparison of the candidate's salary with the market
optionExplain: Awards are not part of the pattern.
Samples all start with the limits of standard solutions.
Future plans come after, not before.
Salary is unrelated.
questions.explain: The card next walks through the four samples.
questions.rule: Show the gap, then the invention.

questions.q: Match each sample story to its new approach.
pairs: Scenario requests such as a user with purchase history that create all related data
Declarative data profiles that reshape responses to what each client needs
Syncing user actions as immutable events instead of data states
AI-proposed remediation plans that run only inside enforced guardrails
questions.explain: Each story's new approach is named in its key points.
questions.rule: Match the story to its method.

questions.q: Sort each detail by whether it comes from the problem and limits side or the learning and results side of a sample story.
groups: How the work improved or was adopted

items.t: Firebase and AppSync required data models we could not adopt
Static seeders created the same data that no longer matched real use
Existing self-healing tools were only automated runbooks
The first version tried to be too smart, so I added an approval mode
The first version synced every interaction, so I synced only business-meaningful events
Three other teams adopted the same pattern

questions.explain: The first three describe limits of existing options; the last three describe iteration and adoption.
questions.rule: Limits first; learning and adoption after.

questions.q: True or false: in the senior sample, the engineer synced user actions as events instead of syncing data states.
questions.explain: The sample syncs user actions as immutable events, which removes the need for complex conflict resolution.
questions.rule: The change from state to events is the invention.

questions.q: True or false: the entry-level sample reports other teams adopting the test data generator.
questions.explain: Its landing reports the author's own time saved and that the tool was extensible so others could add scenario templates. The mid, senior and staff samples report others adopting the work.
questions.rule: Adoption evidence grows with level.

questions.q: You want to try a new approach in a risky area of your company. Which way of building it follows the mid-level sample?
options: As a complete replacement that goes live everywhere on the same day
As a layer that enhances what already exists, so it can be adopted without a full rebuild
As a private prototype kept on one laptop and not shown to others
As a copy of the standard tool with a new name and a new logo
optionExplain: A full replacement carries exactly the risk the sample avoided.
The mid sample built on top of existing APIs rather than replacing them outright.
A private prototype has no path to adoption.
A renamed copy invents nothing.
questions.explain: A new approach can be introduced in a way that limits risk.
questions.rule: Limit the risk of the invention without dropping it.
questions.teaches: In the mid sample the engineer designed the gateway as a proxy layer that enhanced the existing APIs, because building a completely new gateway would have been risky.

questions.q: You built a script because a weekly chore annoyed you, and you did not call it innovation. What does the book suggest?
options: It is not worth mentioning, since innovation must feel exciting and important while you are doing the work
It counts only if you had planned to be innovative from the start
It counts only if the script was made by a larger group of people
It may be an innovation story, since you built something new because existing options did not fit
optionExplain: Excitement is not part of the test.
The book says the people did not set out to be innovative.
Group size is not a criterion.
The book says innovation often does not feel innovative; it comes from solving a frustrating problem.
questions.explain: The card next shows how to look for these stories.
questions.rule: Frustration can be the start of invention.

questions.q: Look for times when you thought, There has to be a better ____, and then built it.
questions.explain: The card names this thought as the cue for finding innovation stories.
questions.rule: There has to be a better way.

questions.q: Sort each memory by whether it is a good candidate for an innovation story or probably not.

items.t: I built a small checker because no tool fit how our team reviews contracts
I combined two existing services in a way nobody on the team had tried
I replaced a long manual approval everyone accepted as necessary
I worked through my usual list of tasks without changing anything
I followed the vendor's instructions for setting up a standard tool
I trained a new colleague on our existing process

questions.explain: The first three involve building or combining something new for a need; the last three apply or teach an existing method.
questions.rule: Look for the better way you built.

questions.q: True or false: if you felt irritated by a problem and built a tool others adopted, the book says your story can still be an innovation story.
questions.explain: The book's samples came from frustration, not from a plan to be innovative.
questions.rule: Irritation can be where innovation starts.

questions.q: True or false: building a tool because a problem frustrated you is enough, by itself, to make your story an innovation story.
questions.explain: The book says the key is that you built something new to solve a problem more effectively than the existing method. Frustration is where it starts, not what qualifies it.
questions.rule: Frustration starts the story; the new approach qualifies it.

questions.q: A hospital pharmacist applies a method from airline scheduling to arrange shifts, which had not been done there before. How does the book treat such a case?
options: As a failure, since the method was not invented for pharmacies
As optimization, since both fields already have schedules
As an innovative application of a technique from one field to a problem in another
As irrelevant, since only inventions of new concepts count
optionExplain: Origin of the method does not decide.
A new method for her setting is not tuning.
Applying a technique from one domain to another counts.
The book says new concepts are not required.
questions.explain: The same logic as the event-sourcing example.
questions.rule: Fresh application counts.
questions.teaches: The book says most innovations combine existing ideas in new ways or apply techniques from one domain to another, such as using event sourcing for offline mobile sync, which does not mean inventing event sourcing.

questions.q: Your first innovation attempt failed. When might it make a stronger interview story than a smooth success?
options: When it failed so badly that no one else could repeat the attempt or learn anything from it
When you can show that the failure was somebody else's fault
When it shows how you thought through the problem and adapted after being proved wrong
When you left out why the existing solutions had not been enough
optionExplain: Severity of failure is not the value.
Blame hides the lesson.
The book says the value lies in how you think and adapt.
Omitting the context is a flagged weakness.
questions.explain: The card next lists what to focus on.
questions.rule: The lesson is the story.

questions.q: Put these focus points for telling a failed innovation in the order the card gives.
items: What you were trying to achieve and why existing solutions were no longer adequate
The innovation you attempted and why you thought it would work
What you learned when it did not work as expected
How the learning shaped your next attempt or pivot
Whether the failure taught the team valuable lessons
questions.explain: The card lists the five points in this order, from goal to wider lessons.
questions.rule: Goal, attempt, lesson, next step, team lesson.

questions.q: Sort each line by whether it belongs in a strong failed-attempt story or weakens it.

items.t: The prototype broke under real traffic, which taught me our test load was wrong
After the failure I changed the design to match what the data showed
The team later reused my notes on what did not work
It failed because the testers did not understand it
It did not work and there was nothing to learn from it
I hid the failure and described the second version as my first

questions.explain: The first three give lessons and a changed next step; the last three blame others, report no learning or conceal the failure.
questions.rule: Show the lesson and the change.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate who describes a failed innovation with a clear lesson and a better second version can tell a stronger story than one who reports a smooth success.
questions.explain: The book says failed attempts that led to learning often make stronger stories than smooth successes.
questions.rule: Learning from failure can beat smooth success.

questions.q: Sol describes a failed tool but does not say what he learned. What is the gap?
options: The story lacks the lessons he drew and how they changed his next step
The story omits the names of the teammates who worked on the tool
The story omits how much time and budget the tool used up
The story omits how many people tried the tool before it was dropped
optionExplain: Right: a failure story is strong when it says what was learned and what changed next.
Names are detail, not the lesson the failure was meant to teach.
Cost is context; the book asks for the lesson and the next step.
Usage figures are detail; the missing piece is the lesson.
questions.explain: A failure without a lesson is just a failure.
questions.rule: State the lesson.

questions.q: A chef tried a new batching method that produced uneven results, then redesigned it to keep cooks in charge of the final check. Which lesson fits the book's pattern?
options: The method failed because cooks dislike any change in how the kitchen is run each day
The method should have been hidden from the customers
The method proved that experiments are not worth the effort
The method needed to support human judgment rather than replace it
optionExplain: Cooks' dislike is not what the failure showed.
Hiding is unrelated.
The book values experiments.
It mirrors the book's deployment example: a failure showed that human judgment was needed.
questions.explain: A failure can point to a better design.
questions.rule: Let the failure shape the next design.
questions.teaches: The book's example is an AI system for predicting deployment windows that teams could not trust; the lesson was to enhance human judgment rather than replace it, and the redesigned version, which suggested windows while teams made the final decision, was widely adopted.

questions.q: Your job is mostly maintenance and you have built nothing new. Where might you still find an innovation story?
options: Nowhere, since maintenance roles have no innovation stories at all
In a debugging approach your team now uses, or a tool that improved its workflow
In the products of other teams that you only heard about secondhand
In a project you imagine but would not mean to build
optionExplain: The book says you can still find stories.
The book lists these less obvious places.
Secondhand stories are not yours.
Imaginary projects are ideas without action.
questions.explain: The card next lists more places to look.
questions.rule: Look in less obvious places.

questions.q: The person who automates a painful manual process that no one asked them to automate demonstrates ____.
questions.explain: The card gives this as an example of innovation outside your formal responsibilities.
questions.rule: Unasked automation can be innovation.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is a place to look for a story or a poor source.

items.t: A workaround for a limit in my environment that became a method others use
A helper I built for my team's daily workflow
A new onboarding process I created without being asked
A job description listing my formal duties
A famous product made by a company far away
A task I completed exactly as assigned with no change

questions.explain: The first three are things you built; the last three are not your own inventions.
questions.rule: Look for what you built, not what you were assigned.

questions.q: True or false: if you honestly have no story, the book says you can prepare how you would approach innovation.
questions.explain: The book says this preparation helps you discuss how you would approach innovation, which is valuable even without a complete story.
questions.rule: Show how you would approach it.

questions.q: Neil says an onboarding process he designed on his own does not count because nobody assigned it. What is wrong?
options: Only work that was formally assigned by a manager can appear in an interview answer
Onboarding processes are not examples of anything
Work done on one's own time is unreliable
Problems solved outside formal responsibilities are a good source of stories
optionExplain: The book says the opposite.
The book names this as an invention.
The book does not ban such work.
The card lists onboarding improvements as an example.
questions.explain: Being unassigned is part of what makes it a story.
questions.rule: Unassigned work counts.

questions.q: A school receptionist, unasked, builds a booking sheet that changes how teachers reserve rooms. Does her role rule out an innovation story?
options: Yes, since reception is not a role in which innovation is expected
No: unassigned work that changes how others work can count as innovation
Yes, since only projects assigned by a manager can be described
No, but only if the booking sheet was built with specialist software
optionExplain: Role does not set the limit; what she built does.
The card says problems solved outside formal responsibilities are a source of stories.
The book counts unassigned work, such as automating a process nobody requested.
The tools used do not decide it; the new approach and its effect do.
questions.explain: Her role gave few obvious openings, yet she found one by looking beyond her duties.
questions.rule: Look for what you built that changed how others work.
questions.teaches: The book's example of the analyst who built a dashboard that changed how teams made decisions is innovation around information access, and it adds that interviewers understand roles offer unequal opportunities but want you to recognize where innovation could help.

questions.q: You have one minute to check an innovation story before an interview. Which question is the most useful?
options: Does it use the largest number of technical terms I know?
Does it run longer than my other stories in the answer?
Does it show a new approach that others adopted, and why the old ways fell short?
Does it avoid every mention of what went wrong?
optionExplain: Terms are not evidence of invention.
Length is not value.
It tests the core of the chapter.
Hiding problems conflicts with the iteration the book values.
questions.explain: The card next gives the full check.
questions.rule: Use the checklist.

questions.q: Match each trap to the mistake it describes.
pairs: Calling an improvement a new approach
Using more parts when simplicity would have worked
Describing the invention without the problem it solved
Presenting an idea you did not implement
questions.explain: The first four traps in the chapter's list are paired with their mistakes.
questions.rule: Know the traps.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether a strong story includes it or it is a trap.

items.t: The old tool could not handle our scale, so I designed a different method
Two other teams adopted it because it worked better
After feedback I changed the design and kept it practical
I made the old process run faster and called it innovation
The system had many new layers but needed a long explanation
I have a great idea I have not tried yet

questions.explain: The first three match the chapter's list of strong features; the last three match its traps.
questions.rule: Include; avoid.

questions.q: True or false: a story that shows a new approach, the problem it solved and others adopting it matches the chapter's list of strong features.
questions.explain: The list includes explaining why existing solutions were insufficient, creating a new approach, and others adopting it.
questions.rule: Gap, new approach and adoption.

questions.q: Which self-check has an error in it?
options: My story is innovative because the project took the whole team a year
My story explains why existing solutions were not enough
My story shows evidence that others adopted the new approach
My story shows that I iterated on the design based on the feedback of the people who used it
optionExplain: Length of effort says nothing about innovation.
Explaining why existing solutions were not enough is on the chapter's list of strong features.
Evidence that others adopted the new approach is on the list of strong features.
Iterating based on feedback is on the list of strong features.
questions.explain: Effort is not one of the strong features.
questions.rule: Check the content, not the effort.

questions.q: A volunteer coordinator says she has an idea for a new rota system that her organization does not allow her to try. Is her story a trap?
options: Not necessarily, because the book excuses untried ideas where implementing innovations is not possible
Yes, because untried ideas are a trap in every case with no exceptions that the book would ever allow for
No, because untried ideas are the best kind of story
Yes, because volunteers cannot innovate in any case
optionExplain: The book gives an exception for environments where implementing is impossible.
The book names the exception.
Untried ideas are not best.
Volunteers can innovate.
questions.explain: The trap has a stated condition.
questions.rule: Know the condition.
questions.teaches: The book's trap list says to avoid presenting ideas you never actually tried to implement, unless you work in an environment where implementing innovations is not possible.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: A capable engineer froze in their first live incident. Which first move would you try today?
options: Send them a reading list on debugging and check in after a month
Handle every incident yourself until they say they feel ready
Invite them to sit with you on the next real incident
Book a classroom session on incident theory for the whole team
optionExplain: Reading helps, but it does not rehearse the pressure of a live incident.
This protects the system now, but they never get the practice that builds confidence.
Right: working beside you on real work gives practice with the actual pressure.
A class gives theory in a calm setting, away from the real work where the freeze happened.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows how the story handled it.
questions.rule: Learning sticks best where the practice is real.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: Toshi presented his invitation as needing a second pair of ____ rather than as training for Ian.
questions.explain: He asked Ian to sit with him because he could use a second pair of eyes, which kept the focus on shared work.
questions.rule: Frame the invitation around the shared work.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: A head baker notices a new hire panics when orders back up. Which step fits teaching through the work?
options: Give her a printed guide on rush-hour baking and test her next week
Ask her to stand beside you and explain your choices aloud
Take over the oven line during rushes until she asks for a turn
Praise her speed in quiet hours and let rushes sort themselves out
optionExplain: A guide may help, but it moves the learning away from the real work.
Right: it uses the real rush and shows the thinking, as Toshi did.
She stays safe, but sees only results, not the reasoning, and gets no practice.
Praise does not touch the actual gap, which is handling pressure.
questions.explain: Standing beside an expert on the real rush shows the reasoning in context, and later turns can hand over the lead.
questions.rule: Show your thinking aloud during real work.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: A lead says: join me on call, since you froze last time and need training. What is likely to be lost, by the story's reasoning?
options: Nothing, because honesty about the gap is always the strongest motivator
The practical value of the on-call shift, which is the same either way
The chance for the learner to lead investigations later on
The learner may feel singled out as the problem
optionExplain: Honesty has value, but the story chose a framing that avoided pointing at the learner.
The shift is the same, but how it is presented affects how the learner receives it.
Leading comes from the stepwise handover, which the framing does not change.
Right: the story's framing put the need on the mentor, not on the learner.
questions.explain: This is our reading of why the story stresses framing: the same pairing lands differently when the learner is not cast as the problem.
questions.rule: How you frame an invitation shapes how it is received.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: True or false: In the story, guiding questions were the only support Toshi gave Ian once Ian led investigations.
questions.explain: When Ian got stuck, Toshi also shared his mental models for different failure patterns, which helped Ian recognise common issues more swiftly.
questions.rule: Guide with questions; share your mental models when the learner is stuck.
questions.teaches: When the learner is stuck, share your mental models of common failure patterns so they can recognise them faster.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: Dana has paired with a call-centre supervisor for six weeks. Which observation would best show it is working, in the story's way of judging?
options: She escalates far less and colleagues now ask her questions
She says she feels far more confident when she speaks to customers
She has listened to every one of the supervisor's calls in full
The supervisor now handles fewer calls than before the pairing began
optionExplain: Right: Toshi judged progress by observed changes in Ian's behaviour, such as fewer escalations and fielding teammates' questions.
Confidence matters, but the story tracked what Ian did differently, not what he said he felt.
Time spent shadowing shows exposure, not a change in what she can do.
A lighter load for the mentor could mean many things; it does not show Dana's skill grew.
questions.explain: Toshi tracked Ian's progress through changes he saw: Ian no longer escalated every complex issue and began answering teammates' questions.
questions.rule: Judge progress by what the learner now does differently.
questions.teaches: Track a learner's progress through observed changes in behaviour, such as escalating less and fielding colleagues' questions.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: Which description best fits developing a colleague?
options: Solving their problem quickly so they stay productive today
Helping them build skills for handling future problems alone
Giving them extra tasks so they pick up experience by volume
Sharing everything you know in one long session after a mistake
optionExplain: This helps them now, but leaves the same gap next time.
Right: lasting skill, not a one-off fix, is the point.
Practice helps only when it is shaped to build a particular skill.
This transfers information in bulk but does not build the habit of solving problems.
questions.explain: A fair guess either way. The card next separates helping from developing.
questions.rule: Aim to leave the person able to solve the next similar problem without you.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: Match each role to the way the chapter says it develops others.
pairs: Reviews code so teammates grasp design principles
Creates opportunities that build judgment on system trade-offs
Structures projects to stretch skills, not only to finish efficiently
questions.explain: Each role develops people through its usual work: reviews, trade-off decisions and project design.
questions.rule: Development happens through the work each role already does.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: Sort each action by whether it develops the person or only helps them.

items.t: A data analyst walks a colleague through why she chose a join so he can pick joins himself
A manager rewrites an intern's slides overnight so they are ready by morning
A nurse lead has a new nurse draft the handover notes, then explains her edits
A developer pastes the exact fix into a teammate's pull request
A tech lead assigns a junior a feature slightly beyond their skill and offers to review a first draft
A colleague sends the same ready-made query whenever someone asks for the monthly report

questions.explain: Explaining the reasoning, having the person do the work and stretching them build ability. Doing the work for them solves the problem and leaves the skill unchanged.
questions.rule: Ask what the person can do afterwards that they could not do before.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: A team lead plans every project purely for fastest completion and does not stretch anyone. What outcome fits the chapter?
options: Skills grow anyway, since repetition builds every ability
Output falls, because efficient planning removes motivation
Tasks get done, but the team gains few new skills over time
People become independent, as nobody interferes with their work
optionExplain: Repetition builds familiarity, but the chapter treats stretch as a deliberate choice.
Efficiency does not reduce output; the loss is in growth, not speed.
Right: the chapter contrasts stretching people with always only completing tasks efficiently (our reading of the outcome).
Independence comes from stretching and teaching, not from being left alone.
questions.explain: The chapter says team leads should structure work to stretch capabilities, not always only to finish efficiently. Without stretch, little new skill is built.
questions.rule: Efficiency alone does not build capability.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, the goal of developing others is helpfulness.
questions.explain: The chapter's takeaways say the goal is independence, not helpfulness. Helping is a means, and independence is the measure.
questions.rule: The goal is independence, not helpfulness.
questions.teaches: The chapter's closing takeaway: the goal is independence, not helpfulness.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: A parent cooks every school-night dinner to save time. Which change applies the idea to a household?
options: Let the teenager cook weekly with your guidance, then step back
Keep cooking, but post the recipes on the fridge for the teenager to read
Hand the teenager a weekly takeaway budget so dinner is never a problem
Cook faster so there is more time for the teenager's homework help
optionExplain: Right: stretch plus explanation, then less support, builds a skill they can reuse.
Recipes are exposure only; the teenager still never practises cooking.
This solves dinner without building any cooking ability.
Speed helps the parent's schedule but passes on no skill.
questions.explain: The chapter measures success by whether people handle later similar challenges on their own. A teen who has cooked with guidance can do so again.
questions.rule: Success is people handling similar challenges alone.
questions.teaches: Success means people can handle subsequent similar challenges on their own.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: A candidate describes top personal output and says nothing about helping teammates. How might a company like Microsoft read this?
options: As ideal, since output is the clearest measure of value
As neutral, since helping others is a manager's job only
As risky, since helping others distracts from deadlines
As incomplete, since output alone is not enough
optionExplain: Output matters, but these employers treat it as only part of the picture.
The chapter notes some firms delegate development, but the named companies expect it of engineers.
The chapter argues the opposite: helping others creates longer-term value.
Right: Microsoft counts contributing to others' success as a core expectation.
questions.explain: This is a fair guess. The card next shows what these employers expect.
questions.rule: Show that your performance includes helping others grow, since leading employers count that as part of the work.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: Microsoft builds contributing to the ____ of others into its core expectations.
questions.explain: The chapter says Microsoft puts contributing to the success of others in its core expectations.
questions.rule: Contributing to others' success is a core expectation.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: A candidate has two stories: shipping a feature alone, or shipping it and teaching two peers the pattern. Which better fits these companies?
options: The first, since a fast solo launch shows the strongest delivery
Neither, since teaching peers is outside an engineer's role
The second, since it shows value beyond own output
Both equally, since the feature shipped in each case
optionExplain: Speed is useful, but the stated expectation goes further than personal delivery.
The chapter names engineers as people employers expect to help others.
Right: helping others grow creates more long-term value, per the author.
The shipped feature is shared, but the second story adds growth in others.
questions.explain: Both stories deliver, but only the second shows the extra long-term value employers look for.
questions.rule: Add what others gained to what you delivered.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: Two engineers have equal output. One also helps teammates grow. Whose work does the author expect to create more long-term value?
options: The one who focuses entirely on personal output
The one who also helps teammates grow
Neither, because equal output means equal value
The one with fewer teammates around them to help
optionExplain: Focus feels efficient, but the author says helpers create more long-term value.
Right: the author says helpers create more long-term value than those focused only on their own output.
Output is equal, but the effect on others differs, and that is where the extra value sits.
Team size is not the author's point; helping others grow is.
questions.explain: With output held equal, the difference is the growth passed on to others, which the author values.
questions.rule: Equal output plus growth in others beats output alone.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: Which practices does the chapter cite for how Google embeds peer development? Select all that apply.
options: A yearly ranking that scores engineers on mentees' promotions
A norm that senior engineers teach through code review instead of only approving
Design doc feedback
A rule that managers alone run all mentoring
Readability reviews
optionExplain: This sounds plausible for a rewards system, but the chapter does not mention it.
Right: this is the third item the chapter names.
Right: it is another practice the chapter lists.
The chapter presents Google as embedding it in peer culture, not leaving it to managers.
Right: the chapter lists them as a Google practice.
questions.explain: Google's peer development appears in readability reviews, design doc feedback and a norm that senior engineers teach in code review.
questions.rule: Culture shows up in routine reviews, not only formal programmes.
questions.teaches: Google embeds peer development through readability reviews, design doc feedback, and a norm that senior engineers teach in code review rather than just approve.

questions.section: 12.1 What Does It Mean to Develop Others?
questions.q: A senior engineer's old firm left mentoring to managers. Her new firm treats development as everyone's job. What should she expect?
options: To keep leaving mentoring to managers, as at her old firm
To be judged only on output, since culture talk is decoration
To be asked to mentor only new hires, once a year
To be asked to help peers grow, not only deliver tasks
optionExplain: Firms differ, and the new one does not follow the old model.
Employers like Microsoft write it into core expectations, so it is more than decoration.
Nothing in the chapter limits mentoring to new hires or to a yearly event.
Right: where development is everyone's job, senior people share it.
questions.explain: The chapter says some companies see development as everyone's responsibility while others delegate it solely to managers, so it pays to learn which model applies.
questions.rule: Learn how the employer divides responsibility for development.
questions.teaches: Companies differ: some see development as everyone's responsibility and others delegate it solely to managers.

questions.q: A colleague asks you a question an hour before a release. Which response fits best?
options: Answer quickly now and offer to explain after the release
Turn it into a full lesson on the topic, since teaching is always good
Tell them to work it out alone so they build resilience
Point them to the documentation and return to your own work
optionExplain: Right: the deadline favours a quick answer, and the lesson can wait.
This ignores the deadline and may slow the team down.
Struggle helps when time allows, but a deadline hour is a poor moment.
This avoids the cost of an answer but gives neither speed nor teaching.
questions.explain: A fair guess either way. The card next sets out how the chapter balances the two.
questions.rule: Choose between a quick answer and a lesson case by case, and weigh the deadline each time.

questions.q: The chapter says the core challenge is balancing immediate needs with the benefit of long-term ____ in others.
questions.explain: The core challenge is balancing immediate needs with long-term growth in others.
questions.rule: Weigh immediate needs against long-term growth.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether quick guidance or teaching the thinking fits better.

items.t: Production is down and the on-call engineer needs one config flag name now
A teammate asks about a recurring design pattern and the review is a week away
A demo starts in ten minutes and a colleague asks where the logo file lives
A new hire repeats a mistake during a quiet sprint week
A colleague asks how you would choose between two data stores, and planning is next month
The deadline is tomorrow and a colleague needs the command to export a report

questions.explain: The chapter gives the principle, not these cases; our reading is that tight deadlines favour quick guidance and slack time favours teaching.
questions.rule: Deadlines tilt the choice toward quick answers.

questions.q: A lead says: every question is a teaching moment, so I do not give plain answers, even on release day. What is the flaw?
options: Teaching moments exist only in training sessions, not in daily work
Experts should never explain their reasoning to the team
Release days are the best time to teach, since stakes are high
Teaching everything can slow the team down when deadlines loom
optionExplain: The chapter locates teaching moments in everyday questions to an expert.
The chapter says the pause to explain multiplies an expert's impact.
High stakes raise the cost of delay; the chapter treats that as a reason to be quick.
Right: the chapter warns that treating all as teaching can delay a team under deadline.
questions.explain: The lead has swung to the other extreme. Teaching suits some moments; deadlines call for quick guidance.
questions.rule: Do not make every moment a lesson.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter lists pushing people beyond their comfort zones among the things good development avoids.
questions.explain: It names a time to push people beyond their comfort zones, alongside the choices between quick and thorough teaching and between stepping in and letting people wrestle.
questions.rule: Include stretch among your choices.
questions.teaches: Good development includes a time to push people beyond their comfort zones.

questions.q: A sous-chef answers each cook's question in a few words and moves on. What does the chapter say about the impact of pausing to explain the thinking?
options: It lowers her impact, because each explanation costs service time
It leaves her impact unchanged, since cooks learn by watching anyway
It multiplies her impact, since the group learns the reasoning
It raises impact only for the first cook, who hears it
optionExplain: Time is a real cost, but the chapter says the pause multiplies impact.
The chapter does not assume people absorb the thinking by watching.
Right: the chapter says the pause to invest in others' growth multiplies the expert's impact.
The point is that the group understands the thinking behind the answer.
questions.explain: The chapter says the pause to recognise a teaching moment and help the group see the reasoning multiplies significantly the expert's impact.
questions.rule: A pause to teach multiplies impact.
questions.teaches: An expert's pause to recognise a teaching moment and explain the thinking multiplies significantly the expert's impact.

questions.q: Two new hires need the same skill. One prefers a written guide and the other prefers live pairing. What would you do?
options: Offer each the format that suits them and check how it goes
Use live pairing for both, since it is the fastest way to teach
Use the written guide for both, so the outcome is consistent
Let each find their own way, since adults learn independently
optionExplain: Right: matching the format to the person is the idea.
Pairing is excellent for some, but one method does not fit everyone.
Consistency of method does not give consistent learning.
Some thrive alone, but others need structured help.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next covers how the chapter treats differences.
questions.rule: Ask how someone prefers to learn, then change course when it is not working.

questions.q: The chapter says adapting often starts with asking how someone ____ to learn.
questions.explain: It suggests starting by asking how a person prefers to learn.
questions.rule: Ask first, then adapt.

questions.q: A pottery teacher's adult learner freezes in group demonstrations but works well from printed step cards. What fits the idea?
options: Keep the group demonstrations, since the class needs one pace
Offer step cards and one-to-one practice, then review
Move the learner to a beginner class to build confidence first
Tell the learner to push through the demonstrations
optionExplain: Keeping one format ignores the evidence of what helps this learner.
Right: it adapts the format to the person and stays open to change (our reading).
This assumes a skill gap, while the evidence points to a format mismatch.
Pushing harder is the opposite of adapting your approach.
questions.explain: The learner's pattern shows a preference for written steps and a quieter setting. Adapting the format matches support to the person.
questions.rule: Match the format to the learner.

questions.q: A teammate said she likes written guides, but after two weeks of guides nothing changes. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Keep using guides, since it is her stated preference
Conclude she lacks the ability and stop helping
Ask her manager to switch her to another task
Stay flexible and try a different approach
optionExplain: A stated preference can still fail in practice.
The chapter looks to your approach first, and fit only after varied approaches have failed.
Escalation is a later step, not a first response to one stalled method.
Right: the chapter says to stay flexible when the approach is not working.
questions.explain: A preference is a starting point. The chapter pairs it with flexibility when the approach does not work.
questions.rule: Treat a stated preference as a starting point.

questions.q: True or false: Differences in how people learn come only from personal style and have nothing to do with culture.
questions.explain: The chapter notes that cultural differences in communication affect how people process information.
questions.rule: Culture shapes how people take in teaching.
questions.teaches: Cultural differences in communication affect how people process information, so teaching can miss when you ignore them.

questions.q: Mina, an experienced nurse, tends to wave off advice from colleagues with fewer years. A newer colleague spots a charting gap. Which move fits?
options: Adapt how you offer, since the caution is about the helper
Insist on the correction, since the gap affects patient records
Say nothing, since experienced nurses never need help
Report Mina's attitude to her manager right away
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says some people are cautious about help from peers or those with fewer years.
The gap matters, but forcing help on a wary person is likely to be refused.
Experience does not remove the need, and the chapter says people differ in how they take help.
Escalation is premature when other ways of offering help have not been tried.
questions.explain: The chapter says some people are cautious accepting help from peers or those with fewer years of experience, while others take any help whatever the level.
questions.rule: Notice who is offering and how, not only what is offered.
questions.teaches: Some people are cautious about accepting help from peers or from those with fewer years of experience; others take any help regardless of level.

questions.q: A mentee's code-review pass rate rose from 40 to 55 percent in a month, still below the team average. How should you read it?
options: Wait until they reach the team average before praising anything
Credit the upward trend and keep supporting them
Decide the match is poor, since they remain below average
Switch your time to a stronger performer who is easier to polish
optionExplain: Withholding recognition ignores progress that is real.
Right: direction over time matters more than a single comparison.
One month of growth is no evidence of poor fit.
This chases the easier job, not the higher-value one.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains the chapter's view of trajectory.
questions.rule: Judge growth by its direction over time, and question the fit only when varied methods and genuine effort have both failed.

questions.q: People who excel at developing others focus on ____ rather than absolute performance.
questions.explain: The chapter says they focus on trajectory rather than absolute performance.
questions.rule: Look at direction, not only level.

questions.q: A piano student plays two bars cleanly that she could not play last month, but is behind classmates. What response fits?
options: Hold praise until she can play the whole piece without errors
Suggest piano suits her less than another instrument
Name the gain, keep the lessons and set a small next target
Skip to harder pieces, so she catches up with the class
optionExplain: This delays recognition of progress that is already happening.
A month of improvement is no basis for that conclusion.
Right: celebrate incremental progress and stay patient.
Jumping ahead ignores her current level and may shake her confidence.
questions.explain: Small wins show the direction of growth. Naming them and setting a next target keeps the learner moving.
questions.rule: Recognise small wins and set the next step.

questions.q: Which situation most suggests a fit problem rather than a slow pace?
options: Progress is slow, but each month shows some gain
Progress stalled this week after a hard stretch assignment
No movement at all despite varied methods and real effort
The learner is slower than peers but celebrates each win with you
optionExplain: Slow gains are growth at a different rate, which calls for patience.
A short stall after a stretch is not yet evidence of poor fit.
Right: this matches the chapter's description of when fit may be the issue.
Engagement and visible wins point to a pace difference, not a fit problem.
questions.explain: The chapter ties fit to the absence of any movement despite varied approaches and genuine effort on both sides.
questions.rule: No movement after varied methods and real effort points to fit.

questions.q: Which backfires does the chapter name when trying to develop someone? Select all that apply.
options: The mentor loses interest in technical work
Feedback triggers a defensive roadblock
The learner quickly outgrows the mentor and leaves the team
A person's confidence crumbles during a stretch assignment
optionExplain: Not named; the chapter's backfires concern the learner's reaction.
Right: the chapter gives this as one way an attempt can backfire.
Not named; the chapter talks about stalls, not about learners outgrowing mentors.
Right: this is the second backfire the chapter gives.
questions.explain: The chapter's examples are feedback that triggers defensiveness and confidence that crumbles under a stretch assignment.
questions.rule: When an approach backfires, vary your methods.
questions.teaches: Attempts can backfire when feedback triggers a defensive roadblock or confidence crumbles during a stretch assignment, so vary your methods.

questions.q: A running coach has tried three training plans with a runner who is committed, yet times have not moved in months. What could the chapter's logic suggest?
options: Consider that the coach-runner fit may be the issue
Try a fourth plan, because the right method will eventually work
Blame the runner's commitment, since results come from effort
Conclude the coach has failed and stop coaching altogether
optionExplain: Right: with genuine effort and varied approaches, the chapter says fit may be the problem.
More variety is sensible, but after varied approaches the chapter points to fit.
The scenario says effort is genuine, so the chapter looks elsewhere.
The chapter says recognising you are not the right person is not failure.
questions.explain: The chapter says sometimes you are not the right person to help someone, and recognising that is not failure.
questions.rule: Not being the right helper is not failure.
questions.teaches: Sometimes you are not the right person to help someone, and recognising that fact is not failure.

questions.q: At a fast-growing startup, which story about helping a new hire would likely land best?
options: Pointing the hire to the documentation and checking in at the end of the month
Pairing on a real feature while the team still shipped on schedule
Running a three-week training course before the hire touched real code
Setting up a formal yearly mentoring plan with a fixed curriculum
optionExplain: Pointing people to docs is the opposite of teaching through the work.
Right: it shows development inside the work, without slowing delivery.
A long course delays contribution, which a fast-moving company counts against it.
Formal structures suit some companies, but speed is the priority here.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next shows how company type changes what a good story emphasises.
questions.rule: Match your story to the company's stage: speed with growth at startups, scalable systems at large firms.

questions.q: Sort each story detail by the company type it fits better.

items.t: Pair a new hire on a real feature instead of sending them to the docs
Build an onboarding programme used across many departments
Help a junior with a production issue while shipping the fix on time
Run technical workshops that many teams attend
Show the team got faster because you invested in people
Balance individual mentoring with systems that scale

questions.explain: High-growth firms want development woven into fast delivery; large firms want development that scales across the organisation.
questions.rule: Fast firms want teaching in the work; large firms want it at scale.

questions.q: A candidate is applying to a 30-person scale-up. Which opening best frames her story?
options: I wrote a company-wide curriculum that took six months to launch
I ran a series of lectures after hours to share my knowledge
I referred a junior colleague to the official training catalogue
I brought a new engineer up to speed by pairing on live work
optionExplain: A large programme fits a large firm better than a scale-up that cannot wait.
Lectures outside the work do not show how the team got faster.
Pointing to resources shows little about growth you caused.
Right: it shows speed and teaching through the work.
questions.explain: At a scale-up there is no time for people to catch up alone, so stories about pairing inside live work fit best.
questions.rule: At startups, teach through the work itself.
