questions.q: True or false: At a large tech company, a story about excellent one-to-one mentoring with no resource others could use leaves a gap the interviewer may notice.
questions.explain: The chapter says large firms look for people who mentor individuals and also create resources that develop many people at once, so the scalable element is missing.
questions.rule: At large firms, pair mentoring with scalable systems.

questions.q: A consulting firm needs people upskilled quickly for new client engagements. Which story fits the chapter's picture of consulting?
options: Juniors learned by doing on real engagements
A research project that kept a senior expert away from clients for a year
A career ladder document that listed every skill by grade
A weekly newsletter of reading recommendations for the firm
optionExplain: Right: the chapter describes apprenticeship models where juniors learn by doing.
Consulting values quick upskilling for engagements, not long detached study.
A document may help, but the chapter stresses learning by doing.
Reading recommendations are exposure, and do not match apprenticeship by doing.
questions.explain: In consulting, development directly affects business success, so the chapter points to apprenticeship models and to skills that let the team take on more complex engagements.
questions.rule: In consulting, juniors learn by doing and the team's capacity grows.
questions.teaches: Consulting firms develop people through apprenticeship models where junior members learn by doing, and success means more ability to take on complex engagements.

questions.q: A hospital runs a formal mentoring scheme with defined career paths. A nurse joins it and also notices other growth chances. Which description fits the chapter?
options: She ignores the scheme and builds her own approach from scratch
She waits for the scheme to assign every development step to her
She uses the scheme and also finds extra growth chances
She skips the scheme because informal mentoring works faster
optionExplain: The chapter says traditional organisations value working within established programmes.
Passivity misses the chapter's call to identify extra growth opportunities.
Right: traditional organisations value people who do both.
Speed may suit a startup; traditional firms value the formal structures.
questions.explain: The chapter says traditional organisations follow formal structures and defined career paths, and value people who use established mentoring programmes while finding additional growth opportunities.
questions.rule: In traditional firms, use the programme and add to it.
questions.teaches: Traditional organisations value people who work within established mentoring programmes while also identifying additional growth opportunities.

questions.q: You are preparing a story about mentoring a junior. The company blog praises pairing and shared ownership. How do you shape it?
options: Stress the formal mentoring hours you scheduled with the junior
Leave the story as it is, since facts do not depend on the audience
Swap the story for one about your own technical output
Stress how you helped peers grow through shared work
optionExplain: Formal hours fit a structured model, but the blog points the other way.
The facts stay, but emphasis can be chosen to match the company's model.
That drops the development theme the interview is probing.
Right: it matches the collaborative model the blog signals.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next shows how the chapter suggests framing a story.
questions.rule: Learn the company's model before the interview and frame your story to fit it.

questions.q: The chapter lists job postings, engineering blogs and ____ reviews as places that signal which development model a company favours.
questions.explain: Job postings, engineering blogs and Glassdoor reviews can all signal the model a company favours.
questions.rule: Read the company's own signals first.

questions.q: The posting for your target company stresses shared ownership. Which sentence best frames your mentoring story?
options: I set weekly one-to-one lessons for a junior and graded each one
I helped two peers grow by sharing ownership of a service
I wrote a guide and told teammates to follow it for any problem
I increased my own commit count to set an example for the team
optionExplain: Graded lessons suggest a structured senior-to-junior model.
Right: it highlights peer growth through shared work.
A decree from above does not show peers growing together.
Personal output does not show growth in others.
questions.explain: When a company values collaborative development, the chapter says to emphasise helping peers grow through shared work.
questions.rule: Frame your story in the company's own terms.

questions.q: What if you tell a story about running structured mentoring sessions to a company that values peer-to-peer growth?
options: It will impress, since structure is valued everywhere
It will be ignored, since interviewers listen only to results
It will help, since formal mentoring replaces peer growth
It may not appear to fit how the company already operates
optionExplain: Companies differ, so structure alone does not impress everyone.
The chapter says interviewers weigh the fit of your approach.
The chapter treats the two models as different, not as replacements.
Right: the point of framing is to show that your approach fits their model (our reading of the risk).
questions.explain: The chapter's advice is to show that your approach fits how the company already operates. A mismatch weakens that fit.
questions.rule: Show that your approach fits how they already work.

questions.q: Which does the chapter name as forms of peer-to-peer growth? Select all that apply.
options: A senior's assigned reading list
Code review
Shared ownership
Annual performance ranking
Pairing
optionExplain: A reading list is top-down, not peer-to-peer.
Right: it is a listed form.
Right: it is a listed form.
A ranking system is not named as peer growth.
Right: it is a listed form.
questions.explain: The chapter lists code review, pairing and shared ownership as ways peers grow each other.
questions.rule: Peer growth runs through shared work.
questions.teaches: Peer-to-peer growth happens through code review, pairing and shared ownership.

questions.q: A charity trains newcomers through a year-long programme led by senior volunteers. What should an applicant's mentoring story highlight?
options: How she and her peers shared tasks without any senior involved
How fast she completed her own assigned volunteer shifts
Clear learning paths she created and the progress she tracked
How she avoided formal programmes to keep things flexible
optionExplain: That story suits a peer-to-peer culture, not a structured one.
Speed in her own shifts says little about developing others.
Right: for structured mentoring the chapter says to highlight clear learning paths and tracked progress.
Avoiding structure runs against a company that values it.
questions.explain: The chapter says that if a company values structured mentoring, you should highlight how you created clear learning paths and tracked progress.
questions.rule: For structured mentoring, show learning paths and tracked progress.
questions.teaches: If a company values structured mentoring, highlight how you created clear learning paths and tracked progress.

questions.q: A brilliant engineer knows the billing system better than anyone but explains nothing to others. What risk does this create?
options: The billing system will run better, because fewer people touch it
The team depends on her, as the knowledge stays with her
She will learn faster, because she is never interrupted
Nothing, because documentation is optional for experts
optionExplain: Fewer people touching it may reduce edits but makes the team fragile.
Right: knowledge no one else holds becomes a silo.
Her own learning may not suffer, but the team's benefit is lost.
Optional documentation does not remove the dependency on one person.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next names this risk and its counterpart.
questions.rule: Pass on what you learn, and earn trust before you coach.

questions.q: A person with a lot of knowledge but no ability to teach becomes a knowledge ____.
questions.explain: The chapter calls such a person a knowledge silo.
questions.rule: Learning is worth more when passed on.

questions.q: You are new on a team and see a flaw in a colleague's design. What does the chapter say should come before coaching?
options: Show you care about their success first
Write a detailed review of the flaw and send it to the team
Wait until the next promotion cycle to bring it up
Ask your manager to assign them a course on the topic
optionExplain: Right: trust forms the foundation for development.
A public critique before trust is likely to meet resistance.
Delay does not build trust; showing care does.
That bypasses the relationship and the trust it needs.
questions.explain: Most people resist coaching from someone they do not trust. Showing you care about their success comes first.
questions.rule: Trust comes before coaching.

questions.q: Which statement best matches the chapter's view of trust and development?
options: Trust is the foundation that makes coaching effective
Trust is a reward you receive after you have developed someone
Trust matters only when you manage the person you coach
Trust is optional when the advice itself is technically correct
optionExplain: Right: the chapter calls trust the foundation for effective development.
Trust comes first; it enables development rather than following it.
The chapter treats trust as needed for coaching generally.
Correct advice is resisted if it comes from someone untrusted.
questions.explain: The chapter places trust at the base: without it, coaching meets resistance.
questions.rule: Build trust first.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, trust matters partly because it lets people admit what they do not know and admit mistakes while learning.
questions.explain: The chapter says trust enables the vulnerability growth needs: people must feel safe admitting what they do not know and making mistakes while learning.
questions.rule: Safety to admit gaps comes from trust.
questions.teaches: Trust enables the vulnerability growth needs: people must feel safe admitting what they do not know and making mistakes while learning.

questions.q: A veteran accountant has not studied new tax rules for four years but trains juniors. What does the chapter suggest about her position?
options: Experience alone is enough, so her teaching is already complete
Teaching is separate from learning and needs no current knowledge
Keep learning to stay current while helping others grow
Juniors should learn from each other, not from her
optionExplain: The chapter pairs teaching with continuing to learn.
This sounds efficient, but the chapter links teaching to continued learning, since stale knowledge helps no one.
Right: learning and developing others go together.
The chapter does not move teaching away from experienced people.
questions.explain: The chapter says the best professionals constantly learn to stay current while also helping others grow alongside them.
questions.rule: Keep learning while you teach.
questions.teaches: The best professionals constantly learn to stay up to date while also helping others grow alongside them.

questions.q: A peer on another team keeps shipping slow queries. You cannot assign them training. What is your best lever?
options: Ask their manager to order them to attend a performance class
Offer useful help in a way they can accept
Rewrite their queries quietly so the slowdowns disappear
Send them a long email listing everything they should change
optionExplain: That relies on authority you do not hold and may harm the relationship.
Right: influence rests on invitation and usefulness.
This solves the symptom and builds no skill.
Unsolicited advice usually earns a polite nod and no change.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next lists the chapter's five strategies.
questions.rule: Without authority, develop people through influence using five strategies.

questions.q: Match each strategy to its core move.
pairs: Offer help as a choice the other person can decline
Solve a real problem with them before lecturing
Give partners only the context their decisions need
Frame mentoring as both people learning from each other
Write guides and talks so many can learn without you
questions.explain: Each strategy removes a barrier that authority would normally overcome: consent, credibility, relevance, status and reach.
questions.rule: Each strategy replaces something authority would give you.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it develops others through influence or relies on authority.

items.t: Assigns a mandatory training course to a colleague
Offers to think a problem through together, free to decline
Writes a guide answering the common questions teammates asked
Orders a colleague on another team to change their approach
Fixes a partner's bug while explaining the cause as they watch
Adds a required learning goal to someone's performance review

questions.explain: Influence works by invitation, usefulness and shared resources. Assigning, ordering and requiring need formal power.
questions.rule: No authority means no ordering: invite, help and share.

questions.q: You move teams and no longer manage the people you used to coach. What must change in your approach?
options: Nothing, because coaching works the same with or without authority
You should stop coaching, because only managers can develop people
You should coach harder, so that results arrive without a mandate
You must create conditions where they want to learn
optionExplain: The chapter says it requires a different approach.
The chapter says you can and should, through influence.
Pushing harder is the move that breaks the relationship.
Right: without formal power you can only create conditions that make learning attractive.
questions.explain: The chapter says you cannot require anyone to learn from you; you can only create conditions where they want to.
questions.rule: Create conditions; do not mandate.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, engineers who develop others only through formal authority will see their impact keep growing without limit.
questions.explain: The chapter says engineers who can develop others only through formal authority will hit a ceiling, while those who grow people through influence and shared resources multiply their impact.
questions.rule: Influence lifts the ceiling that authority sets.
questions.teaches: Engineers who can develop others only through formal authority will hit a ceiling; influence and shared resources multiply impact.

questions.q: A community-garden volunteer with no authority wants a fellow volunteer to learn composting. Which opening fits the five strategies?
options: Tell them the garden rules require a composting course
Post a list of composting mistakes on the shed noticeboard
Compost their bins yourself while they are away
Ask if they would like a hand with their bins
optionExplain: That appeals to authority she does not have.
A public list can read as criticism and invites resistance.
This helps once and builds no skill or trust.
Right: it asks permission and offers shared work.
questions.explain: The chapter counts guiding teammates who report to someone else as growth without authority, and the same approach applies: ask, help, learn together.
questions.rule: Invite and share; do not impose.
questions.teaches: Developing people who report to someone else counts as growing others without authority.

questions.q: A peer mentions struggling with database migrations and you know the topic well. What do you say?
options: Walk them through everything you know about schema versioning on the spot
Tell them migrations are easy once you have done a few
Ask if they would like to hear what went wrong for you last time
Send them a long document without any explanation
optionExplain: A full unrequested lesson usually earns a polite nod and no change.
This may sound dismissive and offers no real help.
Right: it offers experience as a choice.
Unrequested documents land like criticism.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next shows why asking comes first.
questions.rule: Offer help as a choice the other person is free to decline.

questions.q: The chapter says unsolicited teaching usually gets a polite nod and no ____ change.
questions.explain: Unsolicited teaching usually gets a polite nod and no behavior change.
questions.rule: Unasked advice rarely changes behaviour.

questions.q: A colleague keeps double-booking meeting rooms. Which opener best follows the idea?
options: Would a second opinion on your bookings help?
You should use the shared calendar like everyone else
I have fixed your bookings so they stop clashing
Let me teach you how calendars work
optionExplain: Right: it asks and leaves the choice with them.
A should-statement sounds like criticism.
This helps once and leaves their method unchanged.
An unrequested lesson positions you as the expert and invites resistance.
questions.explain: A question like this respects the colleague's agency and makes help easy to accept or decline.
questions.rule: Ask, then help.

questions.q: True or false: A peer nods after you tell them you should do it this way, so the nod shows your advice has changed their behaviour.
questions.explain: The chapter says unsolicited teaching usually earns a polite nod and no change, and a should-statement sounds like criticism; sharing what worked for you sounds like experience.
questions.rule: A nod is not a change in behaviour.

questions.q: Someone has not asked for help but plainly needs it. What does the chapter advise?
options: Wait until they ask, even if the problem grows
Start the conversation, but still ask permission first
Offer help directly, since their need removes the question of consent
Tell their manager so that help arrives from authority
optionExplain: The chapter says to watch for need and initiate.
Right: you can initiate, with their consent still needed.
The chapter says you still need permission.
Escalation is not the chapter's first step for peers.
questions.explain: The chapter says to watch for people who need help and to start the conversation by saying what you noticed and asking whether it would help to talk through approaches.
questions.rule: Initiate the conversation, not the lesson.
questions.teaches: You can initiate the conversation with someone who needs help, but you still need their permission.

questions.q: A neighbour declines your offer to help plan their vegetable patch. What does the idea suggest you do?
options: Keep offering until they give in, since you know it will help
Accept it, since forcing help on them rarely works
Plant the vegetables yourself to prove the plan works
Ask other neighbours to talk to them about it
optionExplain: Persistence against a refusal repeats the mistake the card warns about.
Right: the chapter says declining is fine.
This ignores their refusal and builds no goodwill.
This turns a refusal into social pressure.
questions.explain: The chapter says they can decline your offer, and that is fine, because forcing yourself on an unwilling recipient rarely works.
questions.rule: A refusal is an answer; accept it.
questions.teaches: People can decline your offer and that is fine, because forcing yourself on an unwilling recipient rarely works.

questions.q: You barely know a teammate whose ranking changes keep degrading other results. What is the best first move?
options: Offer a course on how search relevance works
Tell the team lead their changes are the cause of the damage
Offer to dig into the bug hurting their metrics
Review their next change quietly and correct it
optionExplain: A lecture opens with your expertise before they trust it.
That damages trust before you have helped.
Right: helping with a real problem shows your value.
Quiet corrections solve a case and build no relationship or skill.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains the idea.
questions.rule: Help solve their real problem first and teach inside that help.

questions.q: Opening with a lecture to someone who barely knows you will come across as ____.
questions.explain: The chapter says it will come across as condescending.
questions.rule: Do not lead with a lecture.

questions.q: An analyst sees a marketing manager's forecasts keep missing, but they have met only in weekly calls. Which move fits?
options: Offer to run a full workshop on forecasting methods for her team
Email her a list of the mistakes in her last three forecasts
Wait until a quarter-end review to raise the pattern
Help rebuild this week's forecast, explaining as you go
optionExplain: A workshop starts with expertise she has not yet seen.
This lands like criticism from someone she barely knows.
Waiting wastes the chance to help and build credibility.
Right: it is useful now and teaches inside the work.
questions.explain: Helping with the live forecast shows value, and narrating the method transfers knowledge naturally.
questions.rule: Teach while you help.

questions.q: True or false: After you have helped a teammate on a real problem, the chapter expects them to be far more likely to accept an offer to learn.
questions.explain: Showing your value through the work earns the invitation, so a later offer to go through the method is far more likely to be accepted.
questions.rule: Value shown first makes the offer welcome.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say cross-functional partners such as product managers and designers respond well to this approach?
options: They are eager to learn what helps them ship
They prefer to be taught by managers rather than peers
They are paid to study the system's internals in depth
They dislike pair work and prefer reading documents
optionExplain: Right: teaching tied to their work suits them.
The chapter does not suggest a preference for managers.
The chapter says they do not need deep internals.
The approach relies on working alongside them.
questions.explain: Partners usually want no lecture, but learn eagerly when relevant concepts come up while you help them ship.
questions.rule: Teach partners what their work needs.
questions.teaches: Cross-functional partners rarely want technical lectures but are eager to learn concepts relevant to shipping their features.

questions.q: A new volunteer treasurer at a charity struggles with the accounts. You want to teach her bookkeeping. What does the idea suggest, and what would you add while working?
options: Help close this month's accounts, saying why as you go
Hand her a bookkeeping textbook and test her at the next meeting
Redo the accounts overnight and present the finished set
Ask the chair to schedule a mandatory training evening
optionExplain: Right: help on the real task and explain your reasons aloud.
A textbook shifts learning away from the real problem.
This solves the problem but removes the learning.
This uses authority, and the learning is detached from her real task.
questions.explain: The chapter shows explaining your reasoning while you work, such as checking two measures separately because one overall figure can hide problems.
questions.rule: Say why as you work.
questions.teaches: While pairing, explain your reasoning aloud, such as checking recall and precision separately because overall accuracy can hide problems.

questions.q: A product manager asks why the recommendation engine is slow. Which reply helps most?
options: It comes from how our cache eviction policy and index selectivity interact
It is complicated, and engineering will handle it without any need for input
It slows as users add items, and the fix needs two weeks
It depends on the query planner, and I can send the design doc to read
optionExplain: Accurate, but it hands over mechanism she cannot use for decisions.
This withholds what she needs to plan around the delay.
Right: it gives the cause that matters and the cost to their plan.
A design doc passes the work of translating back to her.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains what partners actually need.
questions.rule: Translate the matter into the decision it affects, in the listener's own terms.

questions.q: The chapter says partners need to understand why a technical matter matters for their ____, not how it works.
questions.explain: Partners need the why-it-matters for their decisions, not the mechanism.
questions.rule: Explain what matters for their decisions.

questions.q: A finance lead asks why the overnight forecast run failed. As the data scientist, what do you say?
options: A memory error in the third pipeline stage killed the job after batch ten
It failed on one bad feed, so today's figures are a day old until tomorrow
It is a known problem with the scheduler and I would rather not go into detail
The model could not converge, so I am rerunning with a smaller learning rate
optionExplain: Technically precise, but she cannot act on stage and batch numbers.
Right: cause in plain terms plus what it means for her use.
This offers no usable consequence and invites worry.
Jargon about the model does not tell her how to treat today's numbers.
questions.explain: The finance lead's decision is how far to trust the figures. A plain cause and the effect on today's numbers serve that decision.
questions.rule: Lead with the practical effect.

questions.q: True or false: A security engineer who explains hashing algorithms to a call-centre lead answers the lead's question about whether to ask callers for a PIN.
questions.explain: The lead needs the practical implication for her call process, such as what to ask for and what to avoid. The algorithm does not answer her decision.
questions.rule: Answer the decision, not the mechanism.

questions.q: A designer asks about rate limiting. Which answer follows the chapter's approach?
options: We use a token bucket algorithm that refills at a steady rate
It is an infrastructure matter that you do not need to think about
Read the API documentation on throttling before our next meeting
Users get ten tries a minute, so design an error state
optionExplain: This explains the mechanism but gives no design consequence.
This hides a constraint she must design for.
This hands her the translation work.
Right: it states the constraint and what to design around.
questions.explain: The chapter's own example translates rate limiting into a limit the designer can design around, with an error state for when users hit it.
questions.rule: Turn the constraint into a design consequence.
questions.teaches: For a designer asking about rate limiting, say users can only do the action ten times a minute, so the design needs an error state.

questions.q: A structural engineer must tell a client why a retaining wall needs weeks to cure. Which approach follows the chapter's logic about people who do not write code?
options: Teach the client the chemistry of curing so he can check the work himself
Give the client a short date and skip the reason to avoid confusion
Build only the understanding his scheduling decisions need
Ask the client to trust the process since he is not a specialist
optionExplain: Full technical understanding is not the goal for non-specialists.
A date without a reason leaves decisions poorly informed.
Right: aim at the decisions, not at full technical understanding.
Trust-me answers withhold what supports his decisions.
questions.explain: The chapter says that at senior levels you need to build only a certain level of technical understanding in people who will never write code but whose decisions affect system quality.
questions.rule: Build only the understanding their decisions need.
questions.teaches: Build only a certain level of technical understanding in people who will never write code but whose decisions affect quality.

questions.q: You want to help a peer with system design. Which opener works best?
options: Want to work through this together? I am curious how you see it
Let me teach you how system design works so you can avoid mistakes
You should follow the same design pattern I used on my last project
Send me your design and I will mark the errors for you to fix
optionExplain: Right: it frames the work as shared exploration.
This positions you as the expert and invites resistance.
A should-statement sounds like criticism and gives them no say.
Marking errors keeps you as examiner and them as pupil.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains why this framing matters.
questions.rule: Make mentoring a two-way exchange: share your own mistakes and learn from their strengths.

questions.q: One-way teaching can feel condescending to peers because it positions you as the ____.
questions.explain: It casts you as the expert and them as less knowledgeable.
questions.rule: Do not cast yourself as the expert.

questions.q: Sort each line by whether it frames mentoring as mutual or as one-way teaching.

items.t: Want to work through this together? I am curious how you see it
Let me explain how this works
I got this wrong on my last project, so here is what I learned
You should follow this pattern from now on
I am still working out the best approach here; want to compare notes?
Sit down and I will show you the right way

questions.explain: Mutual lines invite, admit limits and share mistakes. One-way lines position the speaker as the expert.
questions.rule: Invite, admit limits, share mistakes.

questions.q: True or false: A peer may resist expert-to-novice teaching even when the guidance is correct.
questions.explain: The chapter says one-way teaching can lead to resistance even if you are the expert and your guidance is solid.
questions.rule: Correct advice can still be resisted.

questions.q: You are helping a mid-level engineer with architecture, and she knows the product domain far better than you. What might the chapter suggest?
options: Set the domain aside so the sessions stay focused on architecture
Learn her user workflows while teaching technical patterns
Ask her manager for a domain briefing in place of her input
Suggest she read your architecture notes before each session
optionExplain: This wastes a strength and keeps the exchange one-way.
Right: ask for her expertise in something she is strong at.
This skips the person who is the expert.
This keeps teaching one-directional.
questions.explain: The chapter suggests asking peers for expertise in their strong areas; the designer you help with constraints might teach you about user research.
questions.rule: Ask for their expertise in what they do well.
questions.teaches: Ask them for their expertise in something they are strong at: you teach technical patterns and learn about user workflows.

questions.q: In a design collective with many people at the same level, you want to help a colleague improve her presentations. What does the chapter say about the mutual approach in such settings?
options: It works only where a clear mentor-mentee hierarchy already exists
It is a weaker choice there, since nobody has authority to assign it
It works only when both people have identical skills
It works especially well in flat organisations
optionExplain: The chapter says neither person is the mentor or mentee.
Flat settings are where the chapter says it works especially well.
The mutual approach relies on different strengths.
Right: reciprocal relationships suit flat structures.
questions.explain: The chapter says reciprocal teaching and learning works especially well in flat organisations with many people at a similar level.
questions.rule: Mutual learning suits flat settings.
questions.teaches: Reciprocal learning works especially well in flat organisations with many people at a similar level.

questions.q: You helped five engineers with observability and thirty others could use the same help. What is the best next step?
options: Write guides from what the five asked and share them widely
Offer to pair with each of the thirty others one after another
Tell the thirty to ask the five engineers whatever they need
Wait for the other teams to request help before doing anything
optionExplain: Right: one resource reaches many people.
Pairing helps, but one-to-one time cannot reach thirty more people.
This shifts the load to the five and leaves quality uncontrolled.
Waiting leaves the need unmet and relies on each team noticing it.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next gives the chapter's reasoning.
questions.rule: Capture what you teach once as a resource so many people can learn without your time.

questions.q: The chapter says that if three people ask about the same topic, you should ____ it.
questions.explain: Three people asking about the same topic is the signal to document it.
questions.rule: Repeated questions are material for a resource.

questions.q: Eight colleagues have asked a spreadsheet lead the same pivot-table question this month. What fits the idea?
options: Answer each colleague by message as they ask, each time
Write a short guide with worked examples from your own sheets
Ask each colleague to try the problem alone before asking again
Schedule a one-hour session for each of the eight colleagues
optionExplain: Individual answers repeat the work and do not scale.
Right: a guide with real examples answers the repeat question once.
This slows them and gives no shared resource.
That multiplies your time instead of reducing it.
questions.explain: Repeated questions are a sign that a resource would pay off. A guide with real examples serves all eight and later askers.
questions.rule: Repeated questions call for a resource.

questions.q: A guide is written and shared, then left unchanged as new questions come in. What does the chapter's advice suggest happens?
options: It keeps its value, because the first version covered the basics
It improves by itself as readers add comments
It stops answering what people ask, and its value fades
It turns into a bottleneck, because every reader needs help
optionExplain: The chapter says to keep it up to date and add repeated answers.
Nothing in the chapter says it improves without the author's upkeep.
Right: the chapter says to keep resources current and add repeated questions (our reading of the effect).
The risk is staleness, not a bottleneck.
questions.explain: The chapter advises keeping the resource up to date and adding answers to questions you keep hearing; a static guide falls behind.
questions.rule: Maintain what you share.

questions.q: Which community-building actions does the chapter name for learning without being the bottleneck? Select all that apply.
options: Code review sessions where the team learns together
A yearly exam that every engineer must pass
A rota where only the expert answers every question
A chat channel for architecture questions
A weekly discussion where engineers share war stories
optionExplain: Right: it is a named example.
No such exam is mentioned; it would add pressure, not shared learning.
That makes the expert the bottleneck the chapter wants to avoid.
Right: it is a named example.
Right: it is a named example.
questions.explain: The chapter lists a weekly war-stories discussion, a channel for architecture questions and team code review sessions.
questions.rule: Build communities, not only documents.
questions.teaches: Build communities that encourage people to learn from each other: a weekly war-stories discussion, a chat channel for architecture questions, and code review sessions.

questions.q: A staff engineer spends every week mentoring individuals and feels her impact has hit a limit. Which direction does the chapter point to?
options: Mentor more individuals at the same time to raise the total
Stop mentoring and focus on her own technical work
Hand her mentees over to a manager and step back
Build resources that help many people grow at once
optionExplain: One-to-one mentoring alone cannot give sufficient impact.
The chapter wants her to keep developing others, at scale.
The chapter does not suggest handing development to managers.
Right: at senior and staff levels, scalable approaches are required.
questions.explain: The chapter says that at senior and staff levels a scalable approach is required, because one-to-one mentoring alone cannot give sufficient impact.
questions.rule: At senior levels, scale is required.
questions.teaches: At senior and staff levels the scalable approach is required: one-to-one mentoring alone cannot give sufficient impact.

questions.q: A remote engineer in another time zone seems quiet. Where do you start?
options: Start sending daily technical tips so they learn faster
Watch their commits and step in when quality drops
Build a connection through regular one-to-ones
Wait until they raise problems on their own initiative
optionExplain: Teaching before connection tends to land flat at a distance.
Watching output is not the same as knowing how they are doing.
Right: connection comes before teaching at a distance.
Remote people often struggle without saying so.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next covers the chapter's approach.
questions.rule: Build the connection first, then teach through scheduled contact and asynchronous materials.

questions.q: Match each remote-work problem to the response the chapter points toward.
pairs: You cannot see someone struggling at their desk
Trust develops more slowly at a distance
You are not available in real time
Record explanations they can watch on their schedule
People do not overhear other sessions
questions.explain: Each response replaces a contact that proximity gave for free.
questions.rule: Replace chance contact with structure.

questions.q: You tutor a student in another time zone. Which plan fits the idea?
options: Hold all sessions in your daytime and ask them to adjust
Send long written notes and skip live contact entirely
Check only their finished work and give grades by email
Agree talk times and record short walk-throughs
optionExplain: This ignores when they are available.
Notes alone skip the connection that must come first.
Output alone shows nothing about how they are coping.
Right: connection plus asynchronous material.
questions.explain: Ask about timing and communication preferences, then use recordings so teaching does not depend on shared hours.
questions.rule: Plan around their schedule.

questions.q: A lead holds weekly one-to-ones with a remote report but spends all of them reviewing project status. What is the flaw?
options: One-to-ones should also focus on the person
Weekly meetings are too frequent for remote reports
Status should be reviewed by email instead of live
The lead should spend time only on code review comments
optionExplain: Right: the chapter asks for one-to-ones focused on the remote worker.
The chapter asks for regular contact.
The issue is the focus, not the channel.
Code review is a different tool, not a replacement for the one-to-one.
questions.explain: The chapter says one-to-ones should be about the remote workers themselves, not just their projects.
questions.rule: Make the one-to-one about the person.

questions.q: True or false: Remote team members generally tell you promptly when they are struggling.
questions.explain: The chapter warns that they may struggle without admitting it, to avoid seeming unable to handle remote work, so check on how they are doing and not only what they deliver.
questions.rule: Ask how they are doing, not only what they delivered.
questions.teaches: Remote team members may struggle through problems without admitting it, so check in on how they are doing, not just what they deliver.

questions.q: A freelance editor mentors a junior editor by email. Which habit fits the chapter's ideas for async teaching?
options: Corrected files returned with all changes accepted silently
Margin comments that explain principles
A list of the junior's ten most common errors each month
A monthly call where the editor reviews the junior's totals
optionExplain: Silent fixes show what changed but teach nothing.
Right: comments that start conversations teach principles, not just fix issues.
A list points out issues and does not build understanding.
A call about totals is status, not teaching.
questions.explain: The chapter suggests detailed review comments that start conversations so you teach principles, and shared documentation that captures your thinking.
questions.rule: Teach principles in the margins.
questions.teaches: Write detailed review comments that start conversations, and shared documentation that captures your thinking process.

questions.q: Which idea links asking permission, being useful first and mutual learning?
options: They are ways to make learning mandatory for the other person
They are techniques to speed up teaching to save your time
They are ways to earn the right to help someone grow
They are rules for people who manage the learner
optionExplain: Mandating is exactly what you cannot do without authority.
They aim at the relationship, not at saving time.
Right: all three build the standing to help.
The chapter presents them for people you do not manage.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next states the thread.
questions.rule: Earn the right to help by being useful, by asking, and by making learning mutual.

questions.q: Which does the chapter name as ways of earning the right to help? Select all that apply.
options: Sending frequent reminders about what they should learn
Making the learning mutual
Pointing out your seniority
Asking rather than assuming
Being useful first
optionExplain: Reminders push, and do not earn willingness.
Right: it is the third.
Rank is a form of authority and does not earn the right.
Right: it is the second.
Right: it is the first way named.
questions.explain: The chapter names three ways: being useful first, asking rather than assuming, and making learning mutual.
questions.rule: Useful, asking, mutual.

questions.q: Sort each behaviour by whether it earns the right to help or assumes it.

items.t: Fixes a stuck colleague's bug alongside them before suggesting a lesson
Starts a lecture on best practice at the first sign of a mistake
Asks whether the person would like a second opinion
Tells a peer from another team what they should learn this quarter
Shares a past mistake and asks how the other person sees the problem
Sends a reading list to a colleague who did not ask for one

questions.explain: Earning the right means usefulness, asking and mutuality. Assuming it means teaching without invitation or credibility.
questions.rule: Earn first, then teach.

questions.q: Which statement best fits the chapter's view of influence-based development?
options: You create conditions where people want to learn
You persuade people until they agree to learn from you
You wait until a manager assigns people to learn from you
You teach whoever is willing and ignore everyone else
optionExplain: Right: you cannot require it.
Persuasion pressure is not the chapter's method.
That relies on authority you do not need to build influence.
The chapter is about building willingness, not ignoring the unwilling.
questions.explain: Influence works by shaping conditions: being useful, asking and sharing resources.
questions.rule: Shape the conditions.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, at senior and staff levels most of an engineer's impact comes through helping people they do not manage.
questions.explain: The chapter says that at senior and staff levels this skill becomes essential because most impact comes through people you do not manage.
questions.rule: At senior levels, influence is where impact comes from.
questions.teaches: At senior and staff levels the skill becomes essential, because most impact comes from helping people you do not manage.

questions.q: A clinic volunteer helps a new volunteer on another rota learn the booking system, and the new volunteer becomes the go-to person for it. Which description fits the chapter?
options: A failure, since the volunteer was not formally assigned to teach
Growth across teams through influence and shared resources
A shortcut, since the new volunteer should have asked a manager
A one-off favour that carries no lasting value to the clinic
optionExplain: The chapter treats unassigned help as the typical case.
Right: this is the chapter's picture of impact without authority.
Nothing in the chapter says asking a manager is the proper route.
The chapter values lasting capability across the organisation.
questions.explain: The chapter says those who grow peers and people across teams through influence and shared resources will multiply their impact across the organisation.
questions.rule: Influence across teams multiplies impact.
questions.teaches: Growing peers, partners and people across teams through influence and shared resources multiplies impact across the organisation.

questions.q: A colleague makes excuses when you coach them and starts avoiding you. What do you do?
options: Schedule extra coaching so they see you care about their growth
Give the same feedback in writing so they cannot dismiss it
Tell their manager they are refusing support
Step back and rebuild trust through small acts of help
optionExplain: More coaching is the move that created the problem.
Written feedback adds to the feeling of criticism.
Escalation damages trust further.
Right: recovery begins with stopping.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next gives the chapter's recovery path.
questions.rule: When coaching meets resistance, step back and rebuild trust before you coach again.

questions.q: Which does the chapter give as a reason for resistance to coaching? Select all that apply.
options: Your timing was off
You praised their work too often
Your delivery felt like criticism
You spent too little time coaching them
You had not earned the right to coach
optionExplain: Right: it is the second.
Praise can feel awkward to receive, but the chapter does not list it as a cause of resistance.
Right: it is the third.
The chapter does not blame too little coaching.
Right: it is the first cause given.
questions.explain: The chapter names three: the right was not earned, timing was off, and delivery felt like criticism.
questions.rule: Check your standing, timing and delivery.

questions.q: Put the chapter's recovery steps in order.
items: Step back from coaching entirely
Let the tension fade
Rebuild trust with small acts such as answering a question
Revisit coaching only once they are comfortable, and ask first
questions.explain: The chapter says recovery starts with stopping, then letting tension dissipate, then rebuilding through low-stakes help, and only later cautiously revisiting coaching.
questions.rule: Stop, wait, rebuild, then ask.

questions.q: After a colleague starts avoiding you, you book extra coaching sessions to repair things. What is the flaw?
options: Extra sessions are too expensive for a team to afford
Mentoring harder is what broke the relationship
Coaching should always be done in writing instead
They should have been coached by a more senior person
optionExplain: Cost is not the chapter's concern.
Right: the chapter says not to repair it that way.
Writing may feel safer, but the problem is trust, timing and delivery, which a written format does not solve.
The issue is trust, not seniority.
questions.explain: The chapter warns against trying to fix the relationship by mentoring harder. Step back first.
questions.rule: Do not repair coaching with more coaching.

questions.q: In interviews, how does the chapter say showing recovery from a mentoring setback is read?
options: As a sign that your coaching skills are weak
As a distraction from the story's outcomes
As emotional intelligence and adaptability
As irrelevant unless the person later improved
optionExplain: The chapter treats recovery as a strength.
The chapter says interviewers view it favourably.
Right: recovering shows you adjust when the approach fails.
The chapter values the recovery for what it shows about you.
questions.explain: The chapter says showing you know how to recover from setbacks shows emotional intelligence and adaptability, and that strong candidates adjust instead of pushing harder.
questions.rule: Setbacks you recovered from strengthen a story.
questions.teaches: Showing recovery from a setback demonstrates emotional intelligence and adaptability; strong candidates adjust instead of pushing harder.

questions.q: A colleague from a team where feedback is given indirectly goes quiet after your blunt comments. Which cause does the chapter allow for?
options: Cultural differences in giving and receiving feedback
A lack of technical ability that blunt feedback exposed
Poor timing alone, with the style of delivery irrelevant
An attempt to avoid work that comes with feedback
optionExplain: Right: the chapter lists them as a possible cause of resistance.
The chapter does not trace resistance to ability here.
Delivery matters, and cultural expectations shape how it lands.
The chapter does not assume the person is avoiding work.
questions.explain: The chapter says cultural differences in how people give and receive feedback can create resistance.
questions.rule: Check cultural expectations about feedback.
questions.teaches: Cultural differences in how people give and receive feedback can also create resistance.

questions.q: A teammate asks nearly the same question each day and you answer it every time. What might that show?
options: They value your expertise highly and are learning fast
They are testing whether your answers stay consistent
They need a more senior person to answer instead
A dependency may have formed through your answers
optionExplain: Repeating the same question suggests the opposite.
The chapter reads it as dependence, not testing.
Seniority is not the issue; the learning method is.
Right: repeated help without new skill builds dependence.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Teach the approach instead of the answer, and widen the gaps between check-ins.

questions.q: Instead of giving the answer, ask them for their ____ and how they would test it.
questions.explain: The chapter suggests asking what their hypothesis is and how they would test it.
questions.rule: Ask for the hypothesis.

questions.q: Sort each response by whether it builds independence or dependency.

items.t: Gives the exact command whenever the learner asks
Asks what the learner thinks is causing the fault and how to test it
Leaves a few days between check-ins so the learner can struggle productively
Steps in the moment the learner hits any snag
Writes up the troubleshooting steps for the learner to reuse
Answers instantly each time because it is faster

questions.explain: Questions, space and documented frameworks build the learner's own approach. Instant answers and early rescue remove the struggle that builds it.
questions.rule: Give frameworks and space, not answers.

questions.q: A learner makes an independent attempt that is imperfect. What does the chapter advise?
options: Celebrate the attempt itself
Correct it at once and show the right way to do it
Say nothing and wait for a better attempt
Take over the task so the result is perfect
optionExplain: Right: celebrate independent attempts even when imperfect.
Immediate correction takes back the problem.
Waiting for perfection seems rigorous, but silence gives the learner no reason to try again alone.
Taking over is the behaviour that creates dependency.
questions.explain: Celebrating independent attempts, even imperfect ones, encourages the learner to keep trying alone.
questions.rule: Celebrate independent attempts.

questions.q: Why do mentors fall into the dependency trap, according to the chapter?
options: They want credit for the learner's results later on
They lack the technical knowledge to explain the reasoning
They give answers for speed, or end struggle too early
They are asked questions too rarely to build good habits
optionExplain: The chapter does not name credit-seeking here.
The cause is the choice to answer, not lack of knowledge.
Right: both are named causes.
The pattern is too many repeat questions, not too few.
questions.explain: The chapter says you may give answers because it is faster, or remove the productive struggle too early and prevent the learner building problem-solving ability.
questions.rule: Speed and rescue breed dependency.
questions.teaches: Mentors may give answers because it is faster, or remove the productive struggle too early.

questions.q: A help-desk team rates itself by how many colleague tickets it closes. What does the chapter's view of success suggest instead?
options: Whether tickets are closed faster each month than the last
Whether colleagues thank the team more often than before
Whether the team handles a wider range of problem types
Whether colleagues stop needing help with the same type of problem
optionExplain: Faster closing can mean answering more, which builds dependence.
Thanks can follow rescue without any growth.
Breadth of coverage says nothing about colleagues' independence.
Right: independence, not how often people seek help, is the measure.
questions.explain: The chapter says independence is the measure of success, not how often people seek your help.
questions.rule: Independence is the measure.
questions.teaches: Independence is the measure of success, not how often people seek your help.

questions.q: For months most of your mentoring time has gone to one teammate with little progress. What is sensible?
options: Raise the hours, because the effort so far must pay off soon
Set milestones and treat missing progress as data
Quietly reduce all your help without telling the teammate
Ask the rest of the team to cover your other work
optionExplain: That is the sunk-cost reasoning that keeps the spiral going.
Right: it keeps the investment honest.
Silent withdrawal avoids the hard conversation the situation needs.
This hides the cost without addressing the imbalance.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains the pattern.
questions.rule: Set milestones in advance and treat missed progress after fair effort as data, not as a reason to give more time.

questions.q: Which does the chapter list as ways to avoid the over-investment spiral? Select all that apply.
options: Add an extra weekly session for the person who is struggling
Wait for the team to complain before changing course
Involve others as a support network
Set timelines with clear milestones
Know when to escalate for performance conversations
optionExplain: More time feels caring, but it deepens the imbalance the spiral describes.
The chapter wants you to act earlier.
Right: you should not be the single point of dependency.
Right: it is the first listed.
Right: it is listed.
questions.explain: The chapter lists milestones, a support network, tracking the return on time, and escalation when needed.
questions.rule: Milestones, support, escalation.

questions.q: A choir director spends every rehearsal break with one struggling singer, and her own sheet music preparation is slipping. Which step fits?
options: Add a Saturday session to help the singer faster
Stop all help, as the singer should work it out alone
Agree a milestone and ask a section leader to help
Hold off until the next concert to decide anything
optionExplain: It deepens the investment and leaves the imbalance in place.
It removes support without a diagnosis or conversation.
Right: a milestone plus a support network.
Waiting seems calm, but while you wait the imbalance and your slipping preparation both grow.
questions.explain: A milestone gives a way to read progress as data, and a section leader shares the load so the director is not the single point of dependency.
questions.rule: Add milestones and share the load.

questions.q: A mentor says: I have put in so much already that one more month of daily help will make it pay off. What is the flaw?
options: It shows too little confidence in the mentor's own skill
It is sunk-cost thinking that clouds judgment
It asks the learner to put in more than the mentor
It ignores the likelihood that the team will lose interest
optionExplain: Confidence is not the issue; the reasoning is.
Right: past time is not evidence of future results.
The flaw concerns judgment, not who works harder.
Team interest is one cost, but the flaw is the sunk-cost logic.
questions.explain: The chapter names the sunk cost fallacy as what drives the spiral: past investment makes you expect more investment to pay off.
questions.rule: Past effort is not evidence of future progress.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, helping one person very well gives the same benefit as building scalable talent development systems.
questions.explain: The chapter says that helping just one person well helps one person, while creating scalable talent development systems helps many.
questions.rule: One person well helped is still one person.
questions.teaches: Helping just one person well helps one person; scalable talent development systems help many people.

questions.q: A candidate describes a long effort to coach one weak colleague. Which addition would the chapter say strengthens the story?
options: A longer account of how many hours she gave the colleague
A line saying she never gave up on anyone
A comparison of the colleague with the best performer
How she balanced that person's needs with the team's
optionExplain: Hours alone feed the picture of over-investment.
Persistence without balance sounds like the spiral.
Comparison with a star says nothing about judgment.
Right: strong candidates show balance between individual and broader needs.
questions.explain: The chapter says that structuring your support shows judgment about resource allocation, and strong candidates describe how they balance individual and organisational needs.
questions.rule: Show how you balanced individual and team needs.
questions.teaches: Strong candidates describe how they balance the needs of individuals with broader team and organisational needs.

questions.q: Your usual walkthrough has worked for six teammates, but the seventh is not improving despite effort. What first?
options: Ask how they learn best
Repeat the walkthrough more slowly and with more detail
Compare them with the six who succeeded to motivate them
Move them off the task to avoid further frustration
optionExplain: Right: ask the learner directly.
Slower repetition keeps the method that is not working.
Comparison blames the learner and ignores method.
This avoids the issue and gives them nothing new to try.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next gives the chapter's approach.
questions.rule: When your method fails, ask the learner, change approach, or connect them with someone better suited.

questions.q: Some learners want theory first, while others need hands-on ____ before concepts make sense to them.
questions.explain: The chapter says some want theory first and others need hands-on practice first.
questions.rule: Learners differ in what comes first.

questions.q: Sort each response by whether it adapts to the learner or expects the learner to adapt.

items.t: Asks how the learner likes to take in new ideas
Repeats the same lecture again, more slowly
Switches from slides to a hands-on exercise after slides failed
Tells the learner that others had no trouble with this method
Introduces a colleague whose style may suit the learner better
Assumes the learner is not trying hard enough

questions.explain: Adapting means asking, changing the approach and finding a better match. Expecting the learner to adapt keeps your method fixed.
questions.rule: Change the method, not the learner.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says that connecting a learner with someone else can sometimes be the right move.
questions.explain: When your style does not suit the person, the chapter says the right move can be connecting them with someone else.
questions.rule: Handing on can be good teaching.

questions.q: In a style-mismatch story, what do interviewers hope to see from you?
options: Proof that your original method worked for most learners
Self-awareness and creativity in adapting your methods
A record showing the learner finally adopted your method
A plan that standardises one method for the whole team
optionExplain: Success with others is not the point of this story.
Right: adapting to individuals, not expecting all to learn your way.
The story shows you adapting, not the learner conforming.
The chapter wants flexibility, not one standard method.
questions.explain: The chapter says interviewers like to see self-awareness, creativity, and adapting methods to individuals instead of expecting everyone to learn your way.
questions.rule: Show self-awareness and adaptability.
questions.teaches: Interviewers like to see self-awareness and creativity, and that you adapt your methods to suit individuals.

questions.q: A driving instructor's usual method is not working for one learner after several lessons. Which step fits the chapter's last line of advice?
options: Repeat the lessons until the learner finally gets used to them
Tell the learner to practise more on their own at home
Admit she may not be the best fit; arrange another instructor
Skip the learner's next test to save everyone embarrassment
optionExplain: Repetition keeps the method that is not working.
It shifts the burden to the learner.
Right: be honest about fit and connect them with someone else.
It avoids the issue without helping.
questions.explain: The chapter says to be honest if you think you might not be the best fit, since sometimes the right move is to connect the person with someone else.
questions.rule: Be honest about fit.
questions.teaches: Be honest if you think you might not be the best fit for them; sometimes the right move is to connect them with someone else.

questions.q: Your mentee has asked about the same topic five times, is quieter in sessions, and you are spending more hours. What do you do?
options: Pause and diagnose before investing more
Schedule a longer weekly session to cover the topic fully
Wait another month to see if things settle
Hand the mentee a reading list and step back
optionExplain: Right: the signs call for a check, not more of the same.
More time repeats what is not working.
Waiting delays diagnosis while the signs accumulate.
It ends the relationship without finding the cause.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next lists the signs.
questions.rule: Pause and diagnose when the warning signs appear, before giving more time.

questions.q: Which does the chapter list as warning signs that development is not working? Select all that apply.
options: The person seeming to humour you
Decreasing engagement in conversations
Repeated questions about the same topics
The person thanks you often
The person asks for harder tasks
optionExplain: Right: it is the last.
Right: it is the second.
Right: it is the first sign.
Thanks may seem like engagement, but the chapter does not list it, and it says nothing about behaviour change.
Seeking challenge is not a warning sign.
questions.explain: The chapter lists repeated questions, falling engagement, no observable change, rising time without progress, and the person seeming to humour you.
questions.rule: Look for repetition, withdrawal and no change.

questions.q: Sort each observation by whether it is a warning sign or not.

items.t: The learner asks the same kind of question for the fifth time
The learner raises a new kind of question each week
Months of review have not changed how the learner's code behaves
The learner starts answering a peer's question without help
You spend more hours each month with no visible change
The learner nods in sessions but seems to be humouring you

questions.explain: Repetition, no behaviour change, rising time without progress and humouring are the chapter's signs. New questions and independent answers show growth.
questions.rule: Look for repetition and no change.

questions.q: A mentor notices several warning signs and responds by adding two more sessions a week. What is the flaw?
options: Two sessions a week is too few for a struggling learner
Extra sessions should be run by the person's manager
Warning signs should wait until the review cycle
It adds time before diagnosing the cause
optionExplain: The number is not the point; diagnosis is.
The chapter does not move the sessions to the manager.
Waiting delays the diagnosis the chapter asks for.
Right: the chapter says to pause and diagnose first.
questions.explain: The chapter says to pause and diagnose before investing more time.
questions.rule: Diagnose before adding effort.

questions.q: The chapter says the best recovery may sometimes be which of these?
options: Admitting your approach is failing and regrouping
Doubling the effort until the approach finally works
Reporting the person's lack of progress to the team
Waiting quietly until the person leaves the team
optionExplain: Right: honesty about a failing approach is the recovery.
More of the same is what the signs warn against.
Reporting is not the recovery the chapter describes.
Doing nothing avoids conflict, but it is passivity and does not repair or improve anything.
questions.explain: The chapter says the best recovery may be admitting that your current approach is not working, and regrouping.
questions.rule: Admit and regroup.
questions.teaches: The best recovery may be admitting that your current approach is not working, and regrouping.

questions.q: A candidate wants to show maturity in a story about a mentoring effort that stalled. What does the chapter say the best stories include?
options: Only the successes, since failures weaken the story
Only the final result, kept short to hold attention
A list of the learner's faults that caused the stall
Both successes and thoughtful recoveries
optionExplain: The chapter says recoveries strengthen it.
A short story feels crisp, but a bare result leaves out the noticing and adjusting that show maturity.
Blame does not show adaptability.
Right: describing how you noticed and adjusted shows maturity and adaptability.
questions.explain: The chapter says the best stories include successes and thoughtful recoveries, and that describing how you spotted a problem and adjusted shows maturity and adaptability.
questions.rule: Include the recovery.
questions.teaches: The best stories include both successes and thoughtful recoveries, showing maturity and adaptability.

questions.q: You are asked about helping someone who was not meeting expectations. Which opening shows what interviewers want first?
options: I told him that his results had to improve by Friday
I first looked into why the results were slipping
I moved his tasks to a stronger teammate straight away
I reminded him that the whole team relied on his work
optionExplain: A firm deadline without diagnosis skips the first step.
Right: diagnosis comes before action.
It avoids the problem and teaches nothing.
It may feel motivating, but pressure is not a diagnosis, so it skips the root-cause step.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next lists what interviewers look for.
questions.rule: Diagnose first, give feedback with empathy, set measurable milestones and be patient with the pace.

questions.q: Which elements do strong answers about underperformers show? Select all that apply.
options: Keeping the issue from management
Clear feedback given with empathy
A quick decision to replace the person
Looking for root causes
A plan with measurable milestones
optionExplain: The chapter includes knowing when to escalate.
Right: it is a listed element.
Replacement skips the diagnosis.
Right: diagnosis before action.
Right: it is a listed element.
questions.explain: Strong answers show diagnosis, clear and empathic feedback, tailored plans with measurable milestones and patience.
questions.rule: Diagnose, feedback, milestones, patience.

questions.q: A junior accountant's reports keep containing errors. Which story would best fit what interviewers want?
options: I reviewed every report myself until the errors stopped
I told her to be more careful and checked back in a month
I found unclear expectations, then set weekly targets
I asked her manager to move her to another team
optionExplain: It solves the output and teaches no skill.
It assumes carelessness without diagnosing.
Right: diagnosis, plan and milestones.
It skips the support the question probes.
questions.explain: The story diagnoses first, finds an expectations gap, and sets milestones that make progress measurable.
questions.rule: Diagnose, then plan with milestones.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate who assumed her colleague was unmotivated and told him to try harder showed the diagnosis interviewers want.
questions.explain: Interviewers want to see that you sought root causes rather than assuming there is a problem with motivation.
questions.rule: Do not assume motivation is the cause.

questions.q: According to the chapter, underperformance often signals which of these? Select all that apply.
options: Personal challenges
Low natural intelligence
Missing skills
A poor attitude to the team
Unclear expectations
optionExplain: Right: it is the third.
Some people assume ability is the cause, but the chapter lists missing skills, unclear expectations and personal challenges.
Right: it is the first named.
The chapter warns against assuming a motivation problem.
Right: it is the second.
questions.explain: The chapter says underperformance often signals missing skills, unclear expectations or personal challenges rather than a lack of effort.
questions.rule: Look for skills, expectations and circumstances.
questions.teaches: Underperformance often signals missing skills, unclear expectations or personal challenges, not a lack of effort.

questions.q: A warehouse supervisor set milestones and gave support for eight weeks, but a picker's errors have not improved. What does the chapter say interviewers also ask about?
options: Whether you replaced the picker without telling anyone
Whether you know when to escalate to management
Whether you extended the plan for another year
Whether you kept the problem within your team
optionExplain: Quiet replacement is not what interviewers want.
Right: it is part of what interviewers probe.
Open-ended extension fits the over-investment trap.
The chapter includes escalation when needed.
questions.explain: The chapter asks whether you know when performance issues require management escalation.
questions.rule: Know when to escalate.
questions.teaches: Interviewers also ask whether you know when performance issues require management escalation.

questions.q: You are asked for feedback that helped someone improve. Which answer is strongest?
options: Specific, actionable feedback adapted to the person
Praise for the person's overall attitude and effort
A written summary of everything that went wrong that quarter
An account of how often you gave feedback in a year
optionExplain: Right: specific and fitted to the person.
General praise does not change specific behaviour.
A long list of faults is not specific guidance.
Frequency says nothing about whether it worked.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next lists what interviewers want.
questions.rule: Show you found a growth area, stretched the person, tracked progress and gave specific feedback fitted to them.

questions.q: Match each question to the quality a strong answer should show.
pairs: Specific growth areas, stretch opportunities and tracked progress
Specific, actionable guidance fitted to the person
Support that goes beyond immediate project needs
questions.explain: Growth questions look for structure and stretch, feedback questions look for specific and adapted guidance, and long-term questions look for investment beyond the project.
questions.rule: Match the quality to the question.

questions.q: Sort each description by whether it shows a structured or an ad-hoc approach to someone's growth.

items.t: I identified three skill gaps, set a stretch project and met monthly to review progress
I answered his questions whenever he came by my desk
I assigned a task slightly beyond her level and tracked what changed
I mentioned a few tips in passing during meetings
I agreed learning goals and checked them every quarter
I shared articles I thought might be useful when I found them

questions.explain: Identified gaps, stretch assignments and tracked progress mark a structured approach. Passing tips and occasional answers are ad hoc.
questions.rule: Name the gap, stretch the person, track progress.

questions.q: A candidate says: I told her the report needed more polish. What is wrong with that as feedback?
options: It is too negative to be heard by a colleague
It should have been delivered in a team meeting
It is not specific or actionable
It leaves out praise for the work she already did
optionExplain: Tone is not the flaw; vagueness is.
A public setting does not make feedback more actionable.
Right: vague feedback gives nothing to act on.
Praise is fine, but the flaw is missing specifics.
questions.explain: Good examples show specific, actionable feedback, which more polish is not.
questions.rule: Make feedback specific and actionable.

questions.q: The chapter says good feedback examples show you did what after giving the feedback?
options: Waited for the person to ask for more feedback
Repeated the same feedback until it was heard
Passed the feedback to the person's manager
Followed through to confirm improvement
optionExplain: Waiting leaves improvement to chance.
Repetition is not follow-through on change.
The chapter asks for your own follow-through.
Right: follow-through completes the example.
questions.explain: Good examples show specific feedback, adjusting coaching to individual needs, and following through to ensure there is improvement.
questions.rule: Follow through.
questions.teaches: Good feedback examples show you following through to ensure there is improvement.

questions.q: A volunteer coach explains how she mentored a junior referee. Which approach does the chapter say interviewers prefer in such stories?
options: A casual approach that responded to whatever came up
A single long talk covering everything at once
A structured approach, not ad-hoc mentoring
A fixed schedule imposed regardless of the referee's needs
optionExplain: That is the ad-hoc approach the chapter contrasts.
One talk is not a structured approach.
Right: interviewers want structured approaches to helping others advance.
Structure is not rigidity, and the chapter wants needs identified.
questions.explain: The chapter says interviewers want to see structured approaches to helping others advance, instead of ad-hoc mentoring.
questions.rule: Prefer structure to ad-hoc help.
questions.teaches: Interviewers want to see structured approaches to helping others advance, instead of ad-hoc mentoring.

questions.q: An interviewer asks how you developed team members across time zones. What do strong answers show?
options: A habit of replying quickly to every message at any hour
A plan to bring everyone to one office for training
A record of how many calls you held in a month
Intentional practices such as scheduled check-ins
optionExplain: Speed of reply is not a deliberate development practice.
It dodges the question about remote development.
Call volume is activity, not development.
Right: deliberate structure replaces proximity.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next covers the four families.
questions.rule: Match your story to the question family: translation, intentional distance practices, team-level systems or persistence.

questions.q: Match each question family to what strong answers show.
pairs: Scheduled check-ins, documentation and async tools
Structures and practices that spread knowledge
Trying different methods when one has stalled
questions.explain: Each family targets a particular skill: translation, intentional distance practice, team-level design and persistence.
questions.rule: Each family probes one skill.

questions.q: Sort each story detail by whether it suits a cross-functional answer or a remote answer.

items.t: I explained the feature without jargon, using an everyday analogy
I set a weekly one-to-one and kept written notes for each
I focused on how the designer could use the knowledge in her work
I recorded explanations so people in other time zones could watch later
I gave the sales lead only what she needed to answer customers
I used an async review thread so no one needed to be online together

questions.explain: Cross-functional answers emphasise translation for practical use. Remote answers emphasise deliberate structure and async tools.
questions.rule: Translation versus structure.

questions.q: Which story best suits a question about building stronger teams?
options: Designing a review practice that spread knowledge
Coaching one engineer through a promotion
Explaining a database trade-off to a product manager
Recovering after one mentee stopped responding
optionExplain: Right: team-level structures that spread knowledge.
A single mentoring story suits a growth question.
It suits a cross-functional question.
This is a good story, but it answers a hard-case question, not a question about building stronger teams.
questions.explain: Team questions look for practices that spread knowledge, not single mentoring cases.
questions.rule: Match story scale to the question.

questions.q: Which example does the chapter give of developing a non-engineer?
options: Helping a designer pick up a new programming language for the web team
Telling a product manager why machine learning needs weeks of data
Teaching an ops team to rewrite deployment scripts for the platform
Training a sales team to run database migrations in production safely
optionExplain: The chapter's designer example is about cost per user.
Right: it is the chapter's first example.
The ops example is about reading dashboards.
This is plausible as an example, but the chapter gives no such case; its examples are a product manager, a designer and an ops team.
questions.explain: The chapter's examples include a product manager learning why machine-learning features need weeks of training data, so launch timelines are realistic.
questions.rule: Teach the part that improves their decisions.
questions.teaches: A product manager can be helped to understand why machine-learning features need weeks of training data before they are useful, so they set realistic launch timelines.

questions.q: A candidate's remote-mentoring story covers only technical teaching. Which addition does the chapter say interviewers look for?
options: Awareness of remote challenges such as isolation
A statement that remote work removes the need for trust
The number of tools used in the programme
A claim that time zones make coaching impossible
optionExplain: Right: beyond technical work.
Trust matters more at a distance.
Tools matter less than relationships.
The chapter describes ways to work across them.
questions.explain: The chapter says interviewers want to see that you build relationships and trust before developing people remotely, and understand the challenges remote people face such as isolation, beyond their technical work.
questions.rule: Include the human side of remote work.
questions.teaches: Interviewers want to see that you understand the challenges remote people face, such as isolation, beyond their technical work.
