questions.q: You mentor an analyst who struggles with SQL. Which plan builds capability best?
options: Give her the hardest report and offer help if she asks
Share all your best queries in one session for later reference
Start with simple queries and add harder ones as she is ready
Review her queries and fix errors each week, without discussion
optionExplain: Too big a jump can shake confidence.
Information without steps does not build skill.
Right: increasing complexity from her level.
Fixing for her removes the learning.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next states the critical signal.
questions.rule: Break the skill into steps, start where the person is, and raise the complexity as confidence grows.

questions.q: The chapter's critical signal is building capabilities step by ____.
questions.explain: The critical signal is building capabilities step by step.
questions.rule: Build skill in steps.

questions.q: A new cook can chop and sauté but has not yet run a station. Which plan matches the signal?
options: Put her on the busiest station on Saturday night
Have her watch the line for a month before cooking
Hand her the full menu and a stopwatch
Give one dish at a time, then add dishes as service goes well
optionExplain: Throwing her in feels like fast learning, but a big jump risks confidence, and the signal is about rising difficulty.
Watching feels safe, but watching alone gives no practice, so skill and confidence build slowly.
Pressure without steps teaches little.
Right: levelled challenges that grow.
questions.explain: A station built up one dish at a time increases complexity as confidence grows.
questions.rule: Raise difficulty gradually.

questions.q: Which description matches the critical signal, rather than occasional knowledge sharing?
options: Answering questions whenever a teammate asks them
Planned challenges of rising difficulty that suit the person's level
Posting useful articles in the team chat each week
Giving a one-off talk to the whole team on a topic
optionExplain: Answering is useful, but it is the occasional sharing the chapter contrasts with structured development.
Right: a structured progression.
Sharing information is not building capability.
A single talk is not a progression.
questions.explain: The signal is a structured progression of challenges, not scattered sharing.
questions.rule: Structure beats scattered sharing.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, the strongest candidates show lasting growth in individuals and teams.
questions.explain: The chapter says the strongest candidates show that they create lasting growth in individuals and teams.
questions.rule: Show lasting growth.
questions.teaches: The strongest candidates show they create lasting growth in individuals and teams.

questions.q: A swim coach plans to teach butterfly to a mixed group. According to the chapter, what should come first?
options: Teach the full stroke at race speed to all swimmers
Let swimmers practise freely and watch for problems
Find out where each swimmer is starting from
Give each swimmer the same drill sheet
optionExplain: It looks efficient, but it ignores where each swimmer begins and so skips the first step.
Free practice gives freedom, but it lacks designed challenges suited to each swimmer's level.
Right: identify the starting point before designing challenges.
One drill ignores differing starting points.
questions.explain: The chapter says strong stories show you identifying where a person is starting from, designing challenges for their level and helping them progress.
questions.rule: Start from where the person is.
questions.teaches: Strong stories show you identifying where a person is starting from before designing challenges for their level.

questions.q: Which sentence in a story best shows you noticing who needs help?
options: I attended every one of his design reviews for two months
I told him I was available whenever he wanted to talk about anything
I praised his work in front of the whole team every single Friday
I noticed he kept asking the same type of question about race conditions
optionExplain: Attending shows presence, but does not show that you spotted a particular gap or acted on it.
Availability waits for the person to come to you, while this signal is about noticing a need first.
Praise may help morale, but it does not show you saw a gap in his skills.
Right: a pattern in someone's questions points to a gap that needs more than answers.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next names the strong signals.
questions.rule: Show that you spotted the need early and fitted your teaching to each person.

questions.q: Match each signal to a sentence that could evidence it in a story.
pairs: I started the conversation before the gap became a limitation
When my first explanation failed, I tried a different one
I raised the difficulty as her confidence grew
questions.explain: Each sentence shows one signal: early initiative, flexible explanations and stepwise growth.
questions.rule: Match the evidence to the signal.

questions.q: A kitchen manager describes training two new cooks. Which detail best shows teaching different people differently?
options: Both followed the same recipe binder for the first three weeks
One used written prep cards, the other worked beside a senior cook
Both were assessed with the same end-of-month practical test
Both shadowed the manager on the same shifts for a month
optionExplain: A shared binder is easy to run and feels fair, but it is one method for both people.
Right: the methods were chosen to suit each learner.
A common test measures both, but it says nothing about how each was taught.
Shadowing can teach a lot, but identical shadowing is again a single method.
questions.explain: Tailoring the learning method to each person is what the signal looks for.
questions.rule: Vary the method by person.

questions.q: A story says: I waited until she asked for help, then explained it the way I explain to everyone. Which signals does it lack?
options: Noticing the need early, and adapting the explanation
Building capabilities step by step with rising difficulty
Reducing support gradually as the person gains confidence
Creating reusable resources for the wider team to use
optionExplain: Right: waiting to be asked and using a standard explanation miss both strong signals.
That signal is separate, and the story gives no clue about step-by-step progress either way.
The story never reaches that stage, so it is not the gap this story shows.
Resources are valuable, but the flaw in this story is about timing and fit, not scale.
questions.explain: Waiting to be asked shows no early initiative, and a standard explanation shows no adaptation.
questions.rule: Notice early; adapt.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says strong stories can include helping people see possibilities they had not considered for themselves.
questions.explain: It lists initiating conversations, identifying the need before it becomes a limit, and helping people see possibilities they had not considered.
questions.rule: Help people see further than they do.
questions.teaches: Good examples show you helping people see possibilities they hadn't considered for themselves.

questions.q: A scout leader works with one shy scout and one outgoing scout. Which approach matches the chapter's idea of varied learning?
options: Give both scouts the same group challenge each week of term
Create different learning experiences to suit each personality
Let the outgoing scout lead while the shy scout watches and learns
Set the pace to the shy scout's comfort for the whole troop
optionExplain: Fairness suggests identical tasks, but the shy scout may withdraw while the outgoing one thrives.
Right: varied experiences are what the signal describes.
This seems efficient, but it leaves the shy scout with no suitable challenge of their own.
One pace for both avoids discomfort, yet ignores how differently the two learn.
questions.explain: The chapter says strong examples show you creating varied learning experiences to suit different personalities.
questions.rule: Vary the experience.
questions.teaches: Strong examples show you creating varied learning experiences to suit different personalities.

questions.q: A learner repeats exactly what you taught on the same kind of task. Is that enough to call them independent?
options: Not yet; independence means solving new problems without you
Yes, since correct repetition proves they understood the method
Yes, since they have stopped asking you questions about it
Not yet, because a manager must formally approve independence
optionExplain: Right: new problems are the test.
Repetition may show memory of the steps and nothing about handling a different case.
Silence may mean they avoid asking, not that they can solve unfamiliar problems.
No approval step is described; the test is what they can do alone.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next states the signal.
questions.rule: Teach people how to think about problems so they can handle new ones alone.

questions.q: Put the chapter's four key signals in the order the chapter presents them.
items: Building capabilities step by step
Identifying who needs help
Teaching different people differently
Building independence
questions.explain: The chapter presents the critical signal first, then the two strong signals, then the supporting signal.
questions.rule: Step by step, notice, adapt, independence.

questions.q: A language tutor wants evidence that a student can use grammar on her own. Which test fits?
options: Ask her to repeat the dialogue from last week's lesson
Ask her to translate the sentences you wrote for her
Ask her whether she feels ready for a real conversation
Ask her to handle a situation you never practised
optionExplain: A replay checks recall of what was taught, not whether she can use it elsewhere.
These are tasks she has seen modelled, so success may reflect memory.
Self-report is easy to collect but weaker than watching her handle something new.
Right: a new problem shows independence.
questions.explain: Independence shows when she can handle a case you did not teach.
questions.rule: Test with something new.

questions.q: Which pair of descriptions separates independence from repetition?
options: Solving a problem quickly, versus solving it slowly and carefully
Asking for help once on a task, versus asking for help twice
Solving a new problem alone, versus reproducing a taught solution
Working on a problem with a team, versus working on it in private
optionExplain: Speed varies with skill and temperament, and does not separate the two.
The count of requests is a weak sign, and neither case shows a new problem solved.
Right: new versus taught is the line the chapter draws.
Setting does not decide independence; what matters is whether the problem was new.
questions.explain: The chapter measures success by new problems solved without you.
questions.rule: New problems are the measure.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, you should gradually reduce your support as people become more capable and confident.
questions.explain: The chapter says you should be able to show that you gradually reduce your support as people become more capable and confident.
questions.rule: Withdraw support gradually.
questions.teaches: Show that you gradually reduce your support as people become more capable and confident.

questions.q: How does the chapter classify building independence among its key signals?
options: As the critical signal, since it is the final goal of development
As a strong signal, equal to noticing needs and adapting methods
As a supporting signal, below the critical and strong signals
As a red flag when learners reach it within a month or two
optionExplain: It is the goal, but the chapter labels stepwise capability as critical.
Those two are the strong signals; independence is listed after them as supporting.
Right: it comes last in the chapter's ranking.
No time limit is given, and independence is a success signal, not a flag.
questions.explain: The chapter labels it a supporting signal, below the critical signal and the two strong ones.
questions.rule: Independence is supporting.
questions.teaches: The chapter labels building independence a supporting signal, below the critical and strong signals.

questions.q: A candidate says: every time he got stuck, I solved it for him. How does the chapter label this?
options: Strong development, since each problem was solved quickly
Neutral, since results are what an interviewer measures
A minor yellow flag, since solving problems is common
Helpfulness, not talent development
optionExplain: Solved problems feel like results, but the person is no more capable than before.
The chapter says the story misses the development interviewers want to see.
The chapter gives this one the more serious red-flag label.
Right: it is the red flag.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next names this red flag.
questions.rule: Describe the approach you taught, not only the answers you gave.

questions.q: The chapter says solving problems for people is helpfulness, not talent ____.
questions.explain: It is helpfulness, not talent development.
questions.rule: Helpfulness is not development.

questions.q: Sort each story line by whether it reads as development or as helpfulness only.

items.t: I gave him a method for finding the cause, and he later used it alone
Whenever she asked, I sent her the exact fix
I wrote a short checklist so the team could triage on their own
I stayed late to fix each ticket myself
I asked what he thought was wrong and how he could test it
I answered her questions faster than anyone else on the team

questions.explain: Frameworks, questions and checklists build skill. Fast answers and fixes solve the problem but leave the person where they were.
questions.rule: Tell the teaching story.

questions.q: A candidate says: she asked me the same question weekly, which shows how much she trusted me. What is the flaw?
options: Repeat questions suggest dependence, not development
Trust is irrelevant to development stories, so it should be left out
A weekly rate of questions is too low to count as a pattern
She should have asked her manager instead of asking a colleague
optionExplain: Right: the chapter reads them as dependence.
Trust matters elsewhere in the chapter; the flaw is the reading of repeat questions.
The rate is not the issue; the same type of question returning is.
The flaw is dependence on the helper, not who she asked.
questions.explain: Repeated questions of the same type signal that you are creating dependence.
questions.rule: Repeat questions signal dependence.

questions.q: How does the chapter distinguish red flags from yellow flags?
options: Red flags concern technical skill; yellow flags concern interpersonal skill
Red flags seriously damage a candidacy; yellow flags weaken examples
Red flags apply to senior candidates; yellow flags apply to junior ones
Red flags can be corrected by practice; yellow flags cannot be corrected
optionExplain: This sounds like a topic split, but the chapter splits by how serious the damage is.
Right: the difference is severity.
Levels appear elsewhere in the chapter, but they do not define the flag colours.
The chapter makes no claim about correcting either kind.
questions.explain: The chapter says red flags are serious issues that significantly damage your candidacy, and yellow flags are concerning patterns that weaken your examples.
questions.rule: Red damages; yellow weakens.
questions.teaches: Red flags are serious issues that significantly damage your candidacy; yellow flags are concerning patterns that weaken your examples.

questions.q: A candidate says she mentored a junior baker by correcting every loaf before it went out. According to the chapter, what do many candidates confuse?
options: Mentoring with managing, because both involve overseeing people
Quality control with leadership, because both involve checking work
Helping people with developing talent
Teaching with learning, because both involve passing on knowledge
optionExplain: They can feel alike, but the chapter does not name this confusion.
The baker's story is quality control, but the confusion the chapter names is different.
Right: they confuse helping with developing.
The chapter compares learning and developing others elsewhere, not here.
questions.explain: The chapter says many candidates confuse helping people with developing talent, which undermines their stories.
questions.rule: Help is not development.
questions.teaches: Many candidates confuse helping people with developing talent, which undermines their stories.

questions.q: A candidate ran a monthly lunch talk series and shared the slides afterwards. What would the chapter ask for next?
options: The number of people who attended each of the talks
A list of the topics that were covered over the year
A recording of the best talk to show how well it went
Evidence that people improved afterwards
optionExplain: Attendance shows reach, but not whether anyone developed a skill.
Topics show coverage, which is exposure again rather than improvement.
A recording shows the talk, not what changed for the listeners.
Right: exposure is not the same as growth.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Tie development to a real need and show evidence that people improved.

questions.q: Match each flag to the fix the chapter suggests.
pairs: Connect it to specific problems the team needed to solve
Giving answers instead of building skills
Tell the story of the approach you taught
questions.explain: Each flag has a matching remedy: relevance, evidence and approach.
questions.rule: Each flag has a remedy.

questions.q: A candidate wrote an onboarding guide. Which detail adds the evidence the chapter wants?
options: Two new hires shipped their first service unaided within a month
The guide runs to forty pages and comes with a full index
The guide was praised by several people in a team meeting
The guide was linked from every team's wiki page across the firm
optionExplain: Right: it is observable capability.
Length shows effort and care, but not that anyone learned from it.
Praise shows the guide was liked, which is not the same as improved skill.
Wide linking shows reach, but not that people could do more afterwards.
questions.explain: Evidence of growth is people doing something they could not do before.
questions.rule: Show capability, not reach.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate who taught a team a language that none of its systems use is open to the charge of development without business context.
questions.explain: Teaching skills unrelated to a person's actual work suggests you prioritise learning for its own sake over results.
questions.rule: Teach what the work needs.

questions.q: What evidence does the chapter say shows that training sessions developed skills and did not only share information?
options: People could now solve new problems, take on new responsibilities or produce better work
Attendance was high and the sessions were rated well by everyone present
Slides and documentation were shared with the whole team after each session
The sessions covered every topic on the team's skills list in order
optionExplain: Right: the chapter asks for evidence that people improved, such as new problems solved, new responsibilities taken and better quality of work.
Attendance and ratings show exposure, which the chapter says is not the same as developing skills.
Sharing documents is the surface teaching the yellow flag describes.
Coverage of topics says nothing about whether capability grew.
questions.explain: The chapter says exposure to information is not the same as developing skills, so a story needs evidence that people improved.
questions.rule: Link development to results.
questions.teaches: The chapter suggests asking whether people could solve new problems, took on new responsibilities and improved the quality of their work.

questions.q: A manager has two spare hours a week. The team lacks incident-triage skills, and a colleague suggests an interesting course on an unused language. What does the chapter's reasoning suggest?
options: Take the language course, because variety is good for a team
Split the hours evenly so that both suggestions get a fair hearing
Skip both and let people learn independently in their own time
Spend the hours on triage, since development time is limited
optionExplain: Variety sounds healthy, but it spends scarce time on a skill the team does not need.
Splitting avoids a choice, yet halves the time spent on the real gap.
This abandons development, though the team has a clear gap to close.
Right: limited time goes to real challenges.
questions.explain: The chapter says talent development bandwidth is limited, so it should be applied to the real challenges teams face.
questions.rule: Use limited time on real needs.
questions.teaches: Talent development bandwidth is limited, so it should be applied to the real challenges teams face.

questions.q: A junior's code quality improved over a year while you reviewed their work. How should you tell the story?
options: Say what your reviews specifically changed
Say the junior improved because of your mentoring over the year
Say the junior improved because of time spent on the job
Say that you cannot tell why the junior improved at all
optionExplain: Right: name your contribution.
This claims all of the growth, including what experience would have brought anyway.
This gives away your contribution and leaves the story without a role for you.
This is honest but gives the interviewer no sign of what you did.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Claim only the growth your specific contribution caused.

questions.q: People ____ improve with experience, so your story must show more than that.
questions.explain: The chapter says people naturally improve with experience.
questions.rule: Experience improves people anyway.

questions.q: Sort each line by whether it shows a specific contribution or claims natural growth.

items.t: After I paired on her first outage, she led the next one alone
He got much better at design over his first year with us
My template review changed how the team wrote tests
She has grown a lot since I mentored her
The breakthrough came when I asked her to explain the cause aloud
His reports improve every quarter

questions.explain: Specific moments you caused show contribution. General improvement over time may have come anyway.
questions.rule: Name the moment you made a difference.

questions.q: A candidate claims all of a mentee's growth, and the interviewer asks what the candidate did that went beyond experience. What is likely?
options: The answer lands well, since confidence tends to impress interviewers
Credibility weakens if no specific contribution can be named
The interviewer drops the question because it is an unfair one to ask
The mentee's growth is ignored and the story is judged on nothing else
optionExplain: Confidence helps delivery, but it cannot replace a specific contribution.
Right: the claim is hard to support.
The question is a fair test of the claim.
The growth stays in the story; it is the claim of credit that weakens.
questions.explain: The chapter says such claims weaken credibility, so the contribution needs to be specific.
questions.rule: Be ready to name your contribution.

questions.q: What does the chapter say to focus your stories on?
options: The total hours the mentee spent working with you over the period
The mentee's rank or title at the end of the period you describe
Breakthrough moments you facilitated, or abilities you helped develop
Praise that other managers gave the mentee for the same period
optionExplain: Hours show effort given, not what changed because of it.
Rank may have risen through experience, which is the very thing you must separate out.
Right: specific facilitation.
Praise from others is not about your specific contribution.
questions.explain: The chapter points to breakthrough moments you facilitated and abilities developed as a consequence of your specific intervention.
questions.rule: Show breakthroughs you caused.
questions.teaches: Focus on breakthrough moments you facilitated and abilities that people developed as a consequence of your specific intervention.

questions.q: A football coach says a player improved all season and credits his own coaching, but offers no specific moment. Which flag is this in the chapter's terms?
options: A red flag, a serious issue that significantly damages a candidacy
No flag at all, since the player did in fact improve
A yellow flag, a pattern that weakens examples
A strength, since confidence in your own influence is valued
optionExplain: It sounds serious, but the chapter lists it among the yellow flags.
The improvement is real, but the flag concerns the unsupported claim of credit.
Right: taking credit for natural growth is a yellow flag.
Unsupported credit weakens credibility and so counts against the story.
questions.explain: The chapter lists taking credit for natural growth among the yellow flags: concerning patterns that weaken examples.
questions.rule: Unsupported credit is a yellow flag.
questions.teaches: Taking credit for natural growth is a yellow flag, a concerning pattern that weakens examples.

questions.q: A candidate says: I noticed a new hire kept asking the same kind of question about debugging. What does that open?
options: Evidence that he was not well suited to the team
A reason to write a long reference document for him
A reason to hand his debugging tasks to someone else
Seeing that he needed a skill, not only answers
optionExplain: A pattern in questions is a sign of a skill gap, not a verdict on fit.
A document is one possible response, but the noticing is about the skill need.
This avoids the need and would not build any capability.
Right: it frames a development story.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next shows the example.
questions.rule: Show the pattern you noticed, the steps of rising complexity and the independent result.

questions.q: Put the problems in the order the example's learner worked through them.
items: Single-threaded calculation errors
Race conditions
Complex state corruption problems
questions.explain: The example moved from single-threaded errors to race conditions to complex state corruption, with complexity rising as confidence grew.
questions.rule: Raise complexity as confidence grows.

questions.q: Sort each action from the example by whether it teaches the approach or hands over a solution.

items.t: Asks what his hypothesis is and how he would test it
Tells him which line caused the bug
Thinks aloud while debugging so he can follow the reasoning
Fixes the race condition and sends him the patch
Has him do the debugging while the mentor asks guiding questions
Answers each question as it arrives, without discussion

questions.explain: The approach-teaching actions build how he thinks. The solution-handing actions solve cases and leave him dependent.
questions.rule: Teach how to think.

questions.q: A candidate says: I answered each of his questions about race conditions as they came. Which part of the example's story is missing?
options: Teaching him how to approach such problems himself
A reference to how many questions he asked in total
A mention of the team's tight delivery deadlines
A line about his strong coding skills before he joined
optionExplain: Right: the example's mentor taught the approach.
Counting questions would add detail, but it is not what the example's mentor did differently.
Deadlines are context, and the gap is in how the mentor responded to the questions.
His strengths set the scene, but they are not what the answering story lacks.
questions.explain: Answering each question is helpfulness. The example taught how to approach problems.
questions.rule: Teach the approach.

questions.q: Which techniques did the example's mentor show the learner?
options: Writing performance benchmarks and sizing databases for load
Thread sanitizers, stack traces and common concurrency bugs
Running load tests and reading network traces from production
Planning releases and negotiating deadlines with stakeholders
optionExplain: These sound like senior engineering skills, but they are not what the mentor taught here.
Right: these are the taught patterns.
Plausible for a trading system, but the example names different techniques.
These are planning skills, while the example concerns debugging concurrent code.
questions.explain: The mentor showed him how to use thread sanitizers, interpret stack traces and recognise common concurrent programming bugs.
questions.rule: Show concrete patterns.
questions.teaches: The mentor taught thread sanitizers, interpreting stack traces and recognising common concurrent programming bugs.

questions.q: A candidate for a hospital IT role writes the ending of a story about teaching a nurse informatics skills. Which ending is strongest, by the example's model?
options: She now thanks me warmly whenever we happen to meet in the corridor
She enjoyed every one of the sessions we ran together over the spring
Months later she diagnosed a subtle fault behind weeks of errors
She asks me noticeably fewer questions than she did before we started
optionExplain: Gratitude is pleasant, but it shows no new capability.
Enjoyment says how she felt, not what she could do afterwards.
Right: a concrete result on a new problem.
Fewer questions is a hint, but vague next to a concrete problem solved alone.
questions.explain: The example's landing is that five months later he diagnosed a subtle race condition that had caused intermittent trading discrepancies for weeks.
questions.rule: End on a concrete independent result.
questions.teaches: A strong ending shows the learner solving a hard new problem alone, such as diagnosing a subtle fault that had persisted for weeks.

questions.q: The data team cannot hire its way out of a backlog of routine requests from product teams. What would a staff engineer do?
options: Ask product teams to stop sending routine requests to the data team
Work extra hours to clear the backlog personally this quarter
Hire contractors to answer the routine requests as they arrive
Enable product teams to meet their own data needs
optionExplain: This sounds like a fair boundary, but it refuses a real need and builds no capability elsewhere.
Effort clears today's queue, yet the backlog returns because the underlying skills gap remains.
Hiring is a natural idea, but the example says the company could not hire its way out.
Right: build their capability.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next shows the staff-level example.
questions.rule: Build a staged programme with several routes and real work so teams can meet their own needs.

questions.q: Match each kind of team or learner in the example to the path it was given.
pairs: Backend teams who understood distributed systems
Building streaming pipelines with familiar patterns
Learners who learn best through problems
Data quality challenges based on real incidents
Sessions on slowly changing dimensions and warehouse patterns
questions.explain: Each path started from the learner's existing strength or style, so each team reached the same capabilities by a different route.
questions.rule: Start from the learner's strength.

questions.q: A staff security engineer wants product teams to handle basic threat modelling. Which design echoes the example?
options: One lecture series for every team, followed by a final quiz
Staged learning paths using each team's own systems, with peer reviews
A shared wiki page of security rules for every team to read
A request that the security team reviews every design before release
optionExplain: A single series is easy to run, but it gives every team the same route whatever their background.
Right: tailored, staged and practical.
Documentation scales, but it is exposure without staged practice on the team's own work.
Review catches problems, yet it makes the specialist team the bottleneck the example avoided.
questions.explain: The example's programme used paths tailored to teams, progressive stages, real work on their own problems and peer review.
questions.rule: Tailor, stage and use real work.

questions.q: True or false: If the programme had used generic exercises instead of each team's own data, the learning would have connected less closely to their work.
questions.explain: In the example every stage included real work on the team's own data problems. Generic exercises would lose that link (our reading).
questions.rule: Use the learners' own work.

questions.q: Which result did the staff example report?
options: Data request backlogs fell by 65% and teams caught quality issues during development
Backlogs vanished completely and the data team was then disbanded
Backlogs were unchanged although morale in the teams improved
Backlogs fell by 6.5% over the following year of the programme
optionExplain: Right: both were reported.
A dramatic result sounds appealing, but the data team stayed and moved to platform work.
Morale gains are plausible, but the example reports a clear drop in backlogs.
The figure looks close, but the example reports 65%.
questions.explain: The example reports eight teams building capability, backlogs down 65%, the data team freed for platform work, and quality issues caught during development.
questions.rule: Report concrete results.
questions.teaches: Data request backlogs dropped by 65% and product teams caught data quality issues during development instead of in production reports.

questions.q: A staff engineer in a finance firm ran a programme to improve spreadsheet quality. Which sign best shows the lasting effect the example describes?
options: Teams still share patterns with each other after the programme ended
Every team attended all of the sessions during the programme
The engineer was asked to repeat the programme for other departments
The firm printed the programme slides and filed them in the library
optionExplain: Right: the peer network continues.
Full attendance shows participation, but not that anything lasted after the programme ended.
Demand is encouraging, but it does not show the original teams kept improving by themselves.
Stored slides are material, not evidence that anyone kept using the skills.
questions.explain: The example ends with the peer review network continuing today, with teams sharing data modelling patterns and pipeline solutions.
questions.rule: Look for self-sustaining sharing.
questions.teaches: The peer review network continues today, with teams sharing patterns and solutions.

questions.q: You see strong individual contributors who cannot lead cross-team work. What is the first step to win investment in a programme?
options: Start a voluntary reading group and see who chooses to join it
Promote the strongest contributors into lead roles straight away
Document the impact and present it to an executive sponsor
Wait for the annual planning cycle before proposing any changes
optionExplain: A group could help some people, but it leaves the case for investment unmade.
Promotion rewards ability, but it puts people in roles without building the skill.
Right: make the case with evidence.
Waiting feels orderly, but the problem keeps growing while the case goes unmade.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next shows the principal-level example.
questions.rule: Make the evidence-based case, secure sponsorship and build a programme with several learning routes.

questions.q: What evidence of the problem did the principal-level candidate document? Select all that apply.
options: Senior engineers leaving because they saw no pathways for growth
Low scores in customer surveys
Failed cross-team projects
Repeated architectural mistakes
Slow hiring of junior engineers
optionExplain: Right: it is named.
Customer scores sound like a business signal, but the candidate documented internal problems, not survey results.
Right: it is named.
Right: it is named.
Hiring speed could be a scaling issue, but the candidate's evidence was about leadership gaps, not hiring.
questions.explain: The candidate documented failed cross-team projects, repeated architectural mistakes and senior engineers leaving for lack of growth paths.
questions.rule: Back the case with evidence.

questions.q: A principal at a hospital wants a clinical-leadership programme. Which design echoes the example?
options: A textbook course on leadership for all of the senior nurses
Case studies from the hospital's own decisions, with a coach for those who need one
A single annual conference featuring a few outside speakers
Promotion into leadership posts for the best clinicians on the staff
optionExplain: A course is simple to run, but it uses generic material instead of real decisions.
Right: real cases plus targeted support.
Conferences inspire, but a one-off event builds little lasting capability.
Promotion rewards skill, but it skips the development the programme exists to provide.
questions.explain: The example used the company's real decisions as teaching material and brought in an external coach for one-to-one work.
questions.rule: Use real decisions as cases.

questions.q: A candidate says: I built a leadership programme using only generic textbook cases. Compared with the example, what is the weakness?
options: It uses case studies at all, which tend to be too abstract
It runs for too long, since six months is far more than needed
It involves more than one senior engineer in the design work
It does not use the organisation's own decisions as teaching material
optionExplain: Cases can feel abstract, but the example also used them, with real material.
Length could be a concern, but the example ran six months and the weakness here is different.
More than one contributor is normal; the example brought in several principal engineers.
Right: the example used real decisions.
questions.explain: The example used the company's actual technical decisions as teaching material.
questions.rule: Teach from real decisions.

questions.q: True or false: In the principal-level example, the fellowship's impact ended when its first cohort finished.
questions.explain: The example ends with fellowship alumni running scaled-down versions of the programme within their sub-organizations, multiplying the impact.
questions.rule: Aim for programmes that propagate.
questions.teaches: Fellowship alumni now run scaled-down versions of the programme within their sub-organisations, multiplying the impact.

questions.q: A law firm's associate struggles with client-facing skills. Which step echoes how the example handled a specific gap?
options: Send her to a general presentation course run outside the firm
Ask her to practise alone using a set of training videos
Assign her to the largest client as soon as possible
Pair her with a partner who made the same transition earlier
optionExplain: A course may help a little, but it is generic and not matched to her particular gap.
Videos are flexible, but practising alone removes the example of someone who has made the move.
Stretch can help, but with no support it risks overloading her instead of closing the gap.
Right: pair with a leader who overcame a similar gap.
questions.explain: When fellows had specific gaps, the example connected them with leaders who had overcome similar challenges, such as pairing an infrastructure engineer struggling with product thinking with a leader who had made that move.
questions.rule: Match gaps to leaders who overcame them.
questions.teaches: When fellows had specific gaps, they were connected with leaders who had overcome similar challenges.

questions.q: You have not managed anyone. Do you have material for development stories?
options: No, because development stories require having direct reports
Probably, from times you helped teammates grow
Only if you once led a formal training session for others
Only if a manager formally recognised the help you gave
optionExplain: This sounds reasonable, but the chapter says you do not need a manager title.
Right: everyday help can qualify.
Formal sessions are one source, but the chapter points to everyday help as well.
Recognition is nice, but the chapter does not make it a condition for a story.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains where to look.
questions.rule: Look for moments where you helped someone become independent, not for a title.

questions.q: Which does the chapter give as possible sources of a story? Select all that apply.
options: Helping a teammate finally understand a concept
Winning an internal award for your own work
Explaining something differently for the fifth time before it clicked
Finishing your own tasks ahead of schedule
Creating documentation that became the team's onboarding resource
optionExplain: Right: it is named.
An achievement, but it is about you, not about someone else's growth.
Right: it is named.
Good work, but it is your own delivery, so it is not a development story.
Right: it is named.
questions.explain: The chapter points to helping with a concept, onboarding documentation and patient re-explaining.
questions.rule: Look at everyday help.

questions.q: Sort each memory by whether it could support a development story.

items.t: You taught a colleague the release process and she now runs it alone
You shipped your own project two weeks early
You wrote a guide that new starters use in their first week
You reviewed your own code carefully before merging
You reframed an explanation until a struggling teammate understood
You attended a conference and took notes

questions.explain: Stories about someone else's growth through your help fit. Your own delivery and learning do not.
questions.rule: The story is about someone else's growth.

questions.q: True or false: Not having managed anyone is a sound reason to conclude that you have no development stories.
questions.explain: The chapter says you do not need manager in your title; informal help with a concept or documentation counts.
questions.rule: A title is not required.

questions.q: Which is among the reflection questions the chapter asks?
options: Have you helped people work through confidence issues or imposter syndrome?
Have you met your own performance targets in every quarter?
Have you been promoted faster than most of your peers?
Have you written more code than anyone else on your team?
optionExplain: Right: it is listed.
Targets matter at work, but the chapter's reflection questions are about helping others.
Promotion speed is a career question, not one of the reflection questions about developing others.
Output is a personal measure and is not among the reflection questions.
questions.explain: The reflection questions include helping people with confidence issues or imposter syndrome.
questions.rule: Use the reflection questions.
questions.teaches: One reflection question asks whether you have helped people work through confidence issues or imposter syndrome.

questions.q: A candidate describes mentoring a colleague without letting her own project work slip. Which reflection question does her story answer?
options: When have you turned your expertise into teachable frameworks?
When did you identify opportunities for growth that others hadn't recognized in themselves?
What development have you provided while managing your own deliverables?
What systems or resources have you created that have helped multiple people learn?
optionExplain: A real reflection question, but it concerns frameworks, not development alongside your own deliverables.
A real reflection question, but it is about spotting growth, not about balancing your own work.
Right: it is listed.
A real reflection question, but it concerns systems that scale, not balance with your own deliverables.
questions.explain: The reflection list includes a question about development provided while managing your own deliverables.
questions.rule: Balance development with your own work.
questions.teaches: The chapter's closing list of traps says not to develop others at the expense of your own deliverables.

questions.q: Which of these would strengthen a developing-others story? Select all that apply.
options: A count of how many questions you answered
Examples of adapting your approach for different people
Evidence that people became independent where they once struggled
A statement that you treated everyone the same way
optionExplain: A high count looks like effort, but it shows helpfulness, not whether anyone became independent.
Right: it shows flexibility.
Right: that is the goal.
It is the one-size-fits-all trap.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next lists the five elements.
questions.rule: Strong stories show independence and adaptation.

questions.q: Match each element to a line that could show it.
pairs: He now resolves outages that used to need me
I used written guides for one person and pairing for another
Each month's task was harder than the last
I wrote a guide the whole team now uses
questions.explain: Each line shows one element: independence, adaptation, progression and reusable resources.
questions.rule: Match line to element.

questions.q: Sort each change to a story by whether it strengthens or weakens it.

items.t: Add what the learner could do alone after six months
Remove the part about adapting to the learner's style
Add the guide you wrote for later newcomers
Replace the stepwise plan with the single fix you made
Add how you split time between mentoring and a team-wide workshop
Add a claim that the growth came entirely from you

questions.explain: The five elements strengthen a story; removing them, or claiming credit for natural growth, weakens it.
questions.rule: Add elements; do not strip them.

questions.q: A story shows independence, adaptation and progression. Which element is still missing?
options: Evidence that the learner became independent in the area
Reusable resources, and balance between mentoring and scaling
Adapting the approach to suit the person being helped
Clear progression shown over a period of time
optionExplain: The story already has this, so it cannot be the missing element.
Right: the last two elements.
The story already has this, so it cannot be the missing element.
The story already has this, so it cannot be the missing element.
questions.explain: The five elements include reusable resources and balance between individual mentoring and scaling.
questions.rule: Check for resources and scale.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, what works for one person may confuse another.
questions.explain: The takeaways say effective development requires adapting to individual styles and needs, since what works for one person may confuse another.
questions.rule: Adapt to the person.
questions.teaches: What works for one person may confuse another, so adapt to individual learning styles and needs.

questions.q: A candidate's story says she taught everything in depth, even in the days before a launch. Which takeaway does it contradict?
options: Discerning when to solve problems quickly and when to invest in teaching
Building independence in people who once struggled
Creating reusable learning resources that others can use
Showing a clear progression of growth over time
optionExplain: Right: the chapter asks for that judgment.
The story concerns depth of teaching, not independence, so this takeaway is not contradicted.
Resources are not mentioned in the story, so this takeaway is not contradicted.
The story does not speak to progression, so this takeaway is not contradicted.
questions.explain: The takeaways ask you to balance immediate efficiency with long-term team growth, discerning when to solve problems quickly and when to invest in teaching.
questions.rule: Show judgment about when to teach.
questions.teaches: Balance immediate efficiency with long-term growth, discerning when to solve problems quickly and when to invest in teaching.

questions.q: Which of these weaken a developing-others story? Select all that apply.
options: Describing only the answers you gave
Using one approach for everyone
Adapting your approach for different people
Creating learning resources others reuse
optionExplain: Right: it is a trap.
Right: it is a trap.
It is easy to misread, but adapting to individuals is a strength, so it would not weaken a story.
It is easy to misread, but reusable resources are a strength the chapter values, not a trap.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next names the traps.
questions.rule: Avoid giving answers and one-size-fits-all.

questions.q: Match each trap to the stronger version of the story.
pairs: Describe the approach and frameworks you taught
Show how you adapted for different people
Name the specific breakthrough you facilitated
questions.explain: Each trap has a stronger counterpart: approach, adaptation and specific contribution.
questions.rule: Turn each trap around.

questions.q: Sort each story line by whether it falls into a trap or avoids it.

items.t: I always answered her questions straight away
I changed how I explained it when the first way did not work
He improved a lot while I was his mentor
I wrote down the debugging method so he could reuse it
I used the same weekly session for every new hire
I named the moment that changed how she approached reviews

questions.explain: Instant answers, vague credit and uniform sessions are traps. Reusable method, adapted explanations and named moments avoid them.
questions.rule: Replace each trap with its counterpart.

questions.q: A candidate says: I helped every junior in exactly the same way, because consistency is fair. Which trap is this?
options: Claiming credit for natural growth that would have occurred anyway
Developing others at the expense of her own deliverables
A one-size-fits-all approach
Focusing only on star performers while ignoring those who struggle
optionExplain: No credit claim appears in the statement, so this is not the trap it shows.
The statement mentions no deliverables, so this is not the trap it shows.
Right: it ignores individual needs.
The statement mentions no star performers, so this is not the trap it shows.
questions.explain: The chapter warns against one-size-fits-all approaches, since what works for one may confuse another.
questions.rule: Adapt to the person.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter lists focusing only on star performers while ignoring struggling team members as a trap.
questions.explain: The takeaways include not focusing only on star performers while ignoring struggling team members.
questions.rule: Do not neglect those who struggle.
questions.teaches: Do not focus only on star performers while ignoring struggling team members.

questions.q: A team lead cancels her own project work every week to coach a colleague. Which trap does the chapter's list name for this?
options: Describing only the giving of answers to colleagues
Using one approach for everyone on the team
Claiming credit for natural growth that would have occurred anyway
Developing others at the expense of your own deliverables
optionExplain: She coaches the colleague, so answer-giving is not what this story shows.
The story gives no sign of a uniform method.
The story contains no credit claim.
Right: the fifth trap.
questions.explain: The takeaways include not developing others at the expense of your own deliverables, which links to the over-investment spiral.
questions.rule: Protect your own deliverables.
questions.teaches: Do not develop others at the expense of your own deliverables.

questions.q: True or false: With no deadline pressure, the chapter's balance moves toward teaching the thinking behind an answer.
questions.explain: The chapter warns that treating everything as a lesson slows teams when deadlines loom. Without that pressure, teaching costs less (our reading).
questions.rule: Deadline pressure tips the balance toward quick answers.

questions.q: True or false: A learner who makes steady small gains but is still below their peers is, by the chapter, a sign of poor fit.
questions.explain: The chapter tells you to judge trajectory over absolute performance. Fit is questioned only when there is no movement despite varied methods and genuine effort.
questions.rule: Steady gains call for patience, not a fit verdict.

questions.q: True or false: A colleague who does not trust you will accept your coaching if the advice is technically correct.
questions.explain: The chapter says most people resist coaching from someone they do not trust, however sound the advice.
questions.rule: Trust comes before coaching.

questions.q: True or false: If a peer declines your offer of help, the chapter says to keep pressing because they need it.
questions.explain: The chapter says they can decline and that is fine, because forcing yourself on an unwilling recipient rarely works.
questions.rule: A refusal is an answer.

questions.q: True or false: If the person asking changes from a product manager to a fellow engineer, the same answer with no internals is still the best one.
questions.explain: The chapter says cross-functional partners need different explanations from what you would give engineers, so a change of audience changes the answer.
questions.rule: Match the explanation to the listener.

questions.q: True or false: If a remote teammate delivers on time and says everything is fine, you can stop checking on how they are doing.
questions.explain: The chapter warns that remote people may struggle without admitting it, so check in on how they are doing, not just what they deliver.
questions.rule: Check on the person, not only the output.

questions.q: True or false: A colleague you do not manage can be required to learn from you once you have shown your expertise.
questions.explain: The chapter says you cannot require anyone to learn from you when you do not manage them. You can only create conditions where they want to.
questions.rule: Without authority you can only invite.

questions.q: True or false: Once the tension has faded and a colleague is comfortable working with you again, you may cautiously revisit coaching, asking first.
questions.explain: The chapter says to return to any coaching dynamic only after they are comfortable, and even then to ask first.
questions.rule: Return to coaching slowly, and ask first.

questions.q: True or false: If a mentee shows no progress after reasonable investment against clear milestones, the chapter treats that as data that may call for escalation.
questions.explain: The chapter says no progress after reasonable investment is data, and to know when to escalate for performance conversations.
questions.rule: Missed milestones are data.

questions.q: True or false: If you notice only one of the warning signs, the chapter still advises pausing to diagnose before investing more time.
questions.explain: The chapter says that when you notice any of these signs, pause and diagnose before investing more time.
questions.rule: Any sign is a prompt to diagnose.

questions.q: True or false: If the cause of weak results turns out to be unclear expectations, the chapter's reasoning points to clarifying expectations over pushing for more effort.
questions.explain: The chapter says underperformance often signals missing skills, unclear expectations or personal challenges rather than lack of effort, so the response should fit the cause (our reading).
questions.rule: Treat the cause, not the symptom.

questions.q: True or false: Feedback that was specific and actionable but not checked afterwards would still lack follow-through in the chapter's terms.
questions.explain: The chapter's good examples include following through to confirm there was improvement, not only giving the feedback.
questions.rule: Check that the feedback worked.

questions.q: True or false: If you are early in your career, the chapter says questions about building stronger teams are typically aimed at you.
questions.explain: The chapter says those questions are typically targeted at seniors and above, so they matter less at earlier levels.
questions.rule: Team-building questions target senior levels.

questions.q: True or false: If a learner is starting from a higher level than you assumed, the same easy first challenges still suit them.
questions.explain: The signal is to design challenges appropriate to the person's level, so a higher starting point calls for harder first steps (our reading).
questions.rule: Start where the person is.

questions.q: True or false: Repeating a failed explanation more slowly counts as adapting your approach in the chapter's terms.
questions.explain: The chapter's signal is trying different explanations when someone does not understand, not repeating the same one.
questions.rule: Change the explanation, not the speed.

questions.q: True or false: Withdrawing all your support on the first day matches the chapter's idea of building independence.
questions.explain: The chapter says to reduce your support gradually as people become more capable and confident.
questions.rule: Withdraw support gradually.

questions.q: True or false: If your story shows you taught the approach and the person later handled similar issues alone, the red flag no longer applies.
questions.explain: The red flag concerns presenting answers as development. Teaching the approach, with independence as the result, is what the chapter wants (our reading).
questions.rule: Show the approach and the independence.

questions.q: True or false: For a staff-level interview, the senior example alone is the model for the story.
questions.explain: The chapter gives separate examples by level, and the staff example is about building capability across teams (our reading of why one model does not fit all).
questions.rule: Choose the example that matches your level.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says every principal-level story needs a fellowship of twelve engineers.
questions.explain: The fellowship is one example. The chapter does not make its size or form a requirement (our reading).
questions.rule: The example is a model, not a quota.

questions.q: True or false: Having no manager title but explaining something differently for the fifth time before it clicked can count as material for a story.
questions.explain: The chapter says you do not need manager in your title, and names patient re-explaining as possibly exactly the example you need.
questions.rule: Everyday patience can be a story.

questions.q: True or false: A story that lacks one of the five elements is, by the chapter, unusable.
questions.explain: The chapter lists what strong stories include and does not say that a missing element rules a story out (our reading).
questions.rule: Use the list as a check, not a gate.

questions.q: True or false: If a mentee's growth would have happened anyway but the outcome was good, claiming credit for it avoids the traps.
questions.explain: The chapter lists claiming credit for growth that would have happened anyway as a trap, whatever the outcome.
questions.rule: A good outcome does not justify unearned credit.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Three teams each built a system that decides who sees a new feature. What would you check first?
options: Which of the three systems has the fewest bugs, so the others can copy it
Whether leadership would back a company-wide order to merge them
How quickly each team could rewrite its system from scratch this quarter
Whether all three are answering the same underlying question
optionExplain: Quality matters later, but it says nothing about whether the problems match.
Backing is useful later, yet a mandate for a problem not understood is premature.
Rewrite speed measures effort, not whether the three solve the same need.
Right: the shared question shows whether the three really are one problem.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows what the opening story did.
questions.rule: Start from the question behind the solutions.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Under their different names, the three systems all answered how to test changes safely and ____ their impacts.
questions.explain: The story states the shared question as how to safely test changes and measure their impacts.
questions.rule: Name the shared question in plain words.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Three hospital wards each built their own bedside alert tool. Which finding best suggests one underlying problem?
options: All three tools answer how to warn staff fast when a patient's condition changes
Each ward's tool has a different name and screen layout
All three wards report to the same director on the organisation chart and share one budget line
Every ward says it is happy with the tool it built
optionExplain: Right: the same underlying question, as with the three testing systems.
Different looks are the surface; Ethan's case also had different names.
A shared manager does not show that the tools solve the same need.
Satisfaction shows the tool works locally, not that the problem is shared.
questions.explain: Matching the question behind the tools, not their looks, is what separates one problem from three.
questions.rule: Compare the problems the tools solve.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: True or false: the teams had valid reasons for their custom solutions, yet their choices could not combine.
questions.explain: The chapter says the teams had valid reasons, since each system was built at a different time. The trouble was that their architectural choices could not combine.
questions.rule: Separate solutions can each be reasonable and still fit badly together.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Per the chapter, how did Ethan win adoption of the shared platform?
options: He required each team to retire its tool by a date set by leadership
He built an architecture that absorbed each team's best ideas and showed how sharing would speed them up
He chose the strongest of the three systems and asked the others to migrate
He left the three systems as they were and added a common reporting layer above them, so no team had to change anything
optionExplain: The chapter says he did not force teams to abandon their existing solutions.
Right: he did not force teams to drop their work.
The platform took in ideas from all three, not one winner.
The result was a unified platform, not a layer over separate ones.
questions.explain: He worked with engineering leadership and team leads for eight months and focused on how shared infrastructure would help each team move faster.
questions.rule: Show teams what a shared solution gives them, instead of ordering them to give theirs up.
questions.teaches: Ethan did not force teams to abandon their systems; the platform absorbed the best ideas of each, and he showed how sharing would help them move faster.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: A company merges three overlapping reporting tools. Which payoff is the sort Ethan's platform produced?
options: The company pays for one licence in place of three
Each team holds fewer meetings about its own reporting tool
Teams can run an analysis across all products together that no single tool allowed
Every team keeps its current tool and reports exactly as before, only with a shared logo on the dashboards
optionExplain: Cost saving is real but is a tidier setup, not a new capability.
Fewer meetings help, but they do not change what the company can do.
Right: a new capability, as with experiments that span mobile, web and data.
Nothing changes in what the company can learn.
questions.explain: After the platform, a pricing test that took three teams two weeks took one team a day, and the chapter says Ethan gave the company a capability it did not know it lacked.
questions.rule: Judge a consolidation by the new capability it creates, not only by fewer tools.
questions.teaches: After Ethan's platform, a pricing test that once took three teams two weeks took one team a single day; the chapter says he gave the company a capability it did not know it lacked.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: A teammate says strategic leadership and thinking big are one skill. How would you respond today?
options: They are the same, since both mean proposing large projects
Thinking big covers both, because leading is only talking about the idea
They are different: one is how you lead change, the other is how ambitious the change is
Strategic leadership covers both, because ambition is only a matter of tone and tone is what leaders are judged on
optionExplain: Large proposals show ambition only; leading others is a separate skill.
Leading means connecting problems and gathering people, which is more than talk.
Right: the card separates the how from the how-big.
Ambition is the scale of the aim, not the tone used.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next separates the two.
questions.rule: Keep the two skills apart in your head.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Match each idea to what the chapter says about it.
pairs: How you lead change: see how problems connect and get people working together
How ambitious the change is, such as rebuilding instead of patching
Well-executed work that does not move the needle
questions.explain: The first two are definitions; the last two are what goes wrong when only one skill is present.
questions.rule: Each skill alone leaves a gap.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Sort each action by the skill it mainly shows.

items.t: Choosing to rebuild an ageing billing system instead of patching it
Noticing that two separate complaints trace back to one cause
Creating a new capability instead of tuning an existing tool
Working out which teams must act together on a shared problem
Aiming to replace a process outright, not to speed it up slightly
Seeing why several teams' recurring delays are linked

questions.explain: Ambition about scale or approach is thinking big; seeing links and bringing people together is strategic leadership.
questions.rule: Ask whether an action is about the size of the aim or about leading others to it.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: A leader has bold ideas but cannot gather the teams involved. By the chapter, what results?
options: Well-executed work that does not move the needle
Big ideas that never ship
A chain of small wins that builds trust quietly
Steady adoption driven by the idea's own quality
optionExplain: That describes the reverse case: good leadership with a small aim.
Right: thinking big without strategic leadership.
The chapter describes this as a way to spread change, not as the outcome of missing leadership.
Without someone leading, a good idea does not adopt itself.
questions.explain: Ambition alone does not move people; leading change does.
questions.rule: Ambition needs leadership to ship.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: A director reports a flawless but modest upgrade and says this proves both skills. Which diagnosis fits the chapter?
options: Thinking big without strategic leadership, since the upgrade was an ambitious idea
Both skills present, since good execution proves ambition
Neither skill, since only company-wide changes count at all
Strong leadership without thinking big: good execution that does not move the needle
optionExplain: The upgrade was modest, so it does not show ambition.
Execution quality and the size of the aim are separate things.
The case shows good leadership of change; it lacks only ambition.
Right: flawless delivery of a modest aim shows only one of the two skills.
questions.explain: Our reading: the result is well-run but small, which matches the chapter's second case.
questions.rule: Quality of execution does not prove ambition.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: A city officer sees four departments digging up the same street in turn. Whose approach does the chapter rate as creating the most value?
options: The one who spots the clash and gets departments to plan the street together
The one who makes her own department's digging ten percent faster
The one who writes a detailed report on the clash and files it
The one who asks each department to carry on and hopes they will coordinate by themselves
optionExplain: Right: cross-cutting problems and rallying others create far more value.
Optimising within her own area helps only that area.
A report without anyone rallied changes nothing.
Hoping leaves the cross-cutting problem unowned.
questions.explain: The chapter says people who spot cross-cutting problems and rally others create far more value than those who optimise only within their own areas.
questions.rule: Look for the problem that crosses departments.
questions.teaches: People who spot cross-cutting problems and rally others create far more value than those who optimise only within their own areas.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Five teams run five similar deployment pipelines. Which step is the bold, thinking-big step?
options: Noticing that the five pipelines do roughly the same thing
Working out why the duplication costs the company
Proposing one shared platform that replaces all five
Tidying each team's pipeline so it runs a little faster
optionExplain: Spotting the pattern is the seeing half.
Understanding the cost is also part of seeing the problem.
Right: choosing the ambitious path over the safe one.
A modest fix to each is the safe, incremental path.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next splits the two halves.
questions.rule: Separate the insight from the bold choice.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Put the steps of the chapter's five-pipelines example in order.
items: Notice that five teams built five similar pipelines
Understand why the duplication costs the company
Propose one shared platform replacing all five
Win agreement from each team lead
questions.explain: The example moves from noticing the pattern, to its cost, to the ambitious proposal and the buy-in it needs.
questions.rule: Insight first, bold proposal after.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Sort each action by the half of the pair it shows.

items.t: Noticing that six teams each wrote their own onboarding email tool
Explaining why six tools cost the company in support time
Proposing one shared tool to replace all six
Choosing a company-wide rebuild over a patch to one tool
Realising two teams' on-call rotas collide every launch week
Aiming for one shared rota system instead of a swap schedule

questions.explain: Noticing and explaining the cost is the seeing half; replacing, not patching, is the bold half.
questions.rule: Ask whether an action finds the problem or picks the scale of the answer.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: A candidate only describes noticing duplicated tools and their cost, then stops. Which half is missing?
options: The ambitious proposal that goes beyond patching
The pattern-spotting, since cost was explained
Nothing, because seeing a problem is the whole competency
The routine fix to each tool, which every story needs
optionExplain: Right: the story shows seeing the problem but not choosing the bold path.
Spotting and costing the pattern was done.
The chapter says thinking big is a separate half.
Small fixes are the safe path the chapter contrasts with bold ones.
questions.explain: Both halves matter; this story stops after the first.
questions.rule: A strong story shows both halves.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: True or false: a story about patching five pipelines one by one, each a little faster, shows thinking big.
questions.explain: Patching each pipeline is the safe, incremental path. The chapter ties thinking big to replacing them with one shared platform.
questions.rule: Thinking big means the ambitious path, not the incremental one.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: In the pipelines example, what accompanies the proposal to replace all five pipelines?
options: A mandate issued to all five teams from the top
A pause on all work until the five agree
A report listing the weakest team's mistakes
Getting buy-in from each team lead
optionExplain: The chapter pairs the proposal with buy-in, not a mandate.
No pause is described.
Blame is not part of the example.
Right: the proposal comes with winning each lead over.
questions.explain: The chapter describes proposing the shared platform and then getting buy-in from each team lead, so the bold step needs people on board.
questions.rule: A bold proposal needs the leads' agreement to count.
questions.teaches: In the pipelines example, the proposal to replace all five pipelines comes with getting buy-in from each team lead.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Why might a company care whether a senior hire sees beyond their own team's scope?
options: Senior staff are mainly hired to supervise more junior people
People who spot cross-cutting problems create more value than those optimising their own area
Looking beyond your team shows you dislike your own team's work
Wider scope guarantees that projects finish faster, with fewer people, and with fewer meetings overall
optionExplain: The chapter's reasoning concerns value from cross-cutting insight, not supervision.
Right: that is the reasoning the chapter gives.
Scope is not a verdict on current work.
No such guarantee is claimed.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next gives the companies' examples.
questions.rule: Senior roles are judged on reach.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Match each company to what the chapter says it expects.
pairs: Its Think Big principle asks whether leaders see opportunities beyond their scope
Its culture rewards people who find leverage points
Its staff-level and above promotion criteria expect technical direction well beyond one's team
questions.explain: Each company is tied to a different way of asking for the same wide view.
questions.rule: Wide reach is the shared thread.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Which story best fits Stripe's idea of a leverage point?
options: A weekend rewrite that made one busy service twenty percent faster for all its users
A new meeting format that made one team's planning calmer
A new hire guide that cut one team's ramp-up by a week
A single schema change that fixed slowdowns in four services at once
optionExplain: That improves one system, not several.
Helpful, but limited to one team.
Valuable, but again within a single team.
Right: one change improving multiple systems.
questions.explain: A leverage point is a place where one change improves several systems together.
questions.rule: Look for one change with many beneficiaries.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: True or false: a leverage point is any improvement that makes one team's own work faster.
questions.explain: A leverage point is where one change improves multiple systems at once, which a single team's gain does not meet.
questions.rule: A leverage point serves several systems.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: A candidate says: because Amazon asks for Think Big, every company wants the same story. What is wrong?
options: The chapter later says companies differ in how they expect strategic change
Think Big describes what Amazon wants from junior candidates, not from senior ones
Stripe and Google describe the same Think Big idea, so all three want one story
Amazon's principle was written for interviews, so every interviewer applies it the same way
optionExplain: Right: the Think Big evidence does not prove identical expectations.
The chapter ties these skills to senior roles, not junior ones.
Stripe's and Google's examples are different ideas (leverage points, technical direction), not one shared story.
The chapter gives Think Big as one company's principle, not as an interview rule.
questions.explain: Section 13.2.1 shows companies value consensus or boldness differently, so one example does not set one story for all.
questions.rule: Match the story to the company.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: Reading Google's staff-and-above criteria, what should a staff candidate be ready to show?
options: They finished every ticket they were assigned ahead of schedule for four quarters running
They became the top expert in one narrow tool
They drove technical direction that shaped work well beyond their own teams
They managed the largest number of direct reports
optionExplain: Delivery matters, but it is not the criterion named.
Depth in one area is not the stated expectation.
Right: that is the criterion the chapter names.
Headcount is not the named test.
questions.explain: The chapter says Google's promotion criteria at staff level and above expect candidates to have driven technical direction that shaped work beyond their teams.
questions.rule: Show direction-setting beyond your own team.
questions.teaches: Google's promotion criteria at staff level and above expect candidates to have driven technical direction that shaped work well beyond their own teams.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Five teams each report recurring failures in their own area. What does a strategic leader do first?
options: Fix the worst symptom well, so the other teams can copy the fix
Look for a shared root cause behind the five symptoms
Ask every team to put in ten percent more effort
Wait to see which team's failures grow before acting at all
optionExplain: A good fix to one symptom still leaves the cause in place.
Right: the leader asks what the problems have in common.
More effort treats symptoms and adds to the waste the chapter describes.
Waiting delays the search for the cause and keeps each team blind to the rest.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next explains the shared-cause idea.
questions.rule: Look for what the symptoms share.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Each team sees only its own ____, so nobody notices the shared root cause.
questions.explain: The chapter says the cause goes unspotted because each team sees only its own symptom.
questions.rule: Each team sees a symptom; the cause is shared.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Four stores report late deliveries, each blaming its own driver rota. What is the strategic move?
