options: Replace the drivers at the store with the worst delivery record and review their routes
Add a spare driver to every store's rota
Check whether all four share one cause, such as the depot's loading schedule
Ask each store to apologise to customers faster
optionExplain: That treats one store's symptom and leaves any shared cause.
A spare driver per store patches each symptom separately.
Right: look past each store's symptom to what they share.
Apologising faster does not touch why the deliveries are late.
questions.explain: Late deliveries in four places that each blame local rotas suggest a cause none of them can see alone.
questions.rule: Compare the symptoms before treating any.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: True or false: according to the chapter, fixing each team's symptom separately wastes energy because the real problem is deeper.
questions.explain: The chapter calls fixing symptoms a waste of energy because the real problem is somewhere deeper.
questions.rule: Symptom fixes do not remove the cause.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A team can speed up its release checklist by ten percent, or move every team to automated releases. Which does thinking big favour?
options: The ten percent speed-up, since it is certain to work and needs no other team's help
The move to shared automated releases, a different approach
Neither, because both change how teams work
The speed-up, since automation hides the real work
optionExplain: Certainty is the safe path the chapter warns against relying on alone.
Right: the chapter contrasts a different approach with a ten percent gain.
Changing how teams work is what strategic change is for.
Nothing in the chapter treats automation as hiding work.
questions.explain: Thinking big means proposing a different approach, not shaving a little off the old one.
questions.rule: Prefer a different approach to a marginal gain.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A leader finds one cause behind five clinics' missed appointments and proposes a shared system. What else does the chapter expect of her?
options: Build the whole system alone so nobody has to be persuaded
Present a detailed forecast of savings and leave the rest of the work to the clinics
Wait until all five clinics ask for the change themselves
Make the vision feel urgent and achievable to the people who must help build it
optionExplain: The chapter stresses getting other people excited to help build it.
A forecast alone does not make the work feel urgent or achievable.
Waiting is the opposite of acting as a catalyst.
Right: the best strategic leaders are catalysts.
questions.explain: The chapter says the best strategic leaders do not just have the vision; they are catalysts who make it feel urgent and achievable to everyone around them.
questions.rule: Insight needs a catalyst to become action.
questions.teaches: The best strategic leaders are catalysts who make the vision feel urgent and achievable to everyone around them.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A leader has a clear picture of a better future. What else does the chapter say is needed?
options: Knowing how to get there: dependencies, whom to convince first, and blockers
Nothing more, since a clear vision convinces people by itself once it is well presented
Doing only what is certain to work, to avoid mistakes
A longer vision document with more detail on the end state
optionExplain: Right: the getting-there part is the hard skill.
A clear picture alone is called daydreaming.
Playing safe means you never change anything important.
More detail on the destination does not supply the path to it.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next gives the chapter's answer.
questions.rule: A vision needs a route.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Which three belong to the getting-there skill, according to the chapter?
options: Mapping dependencies between teams that nobody has mapped
Understanding which blockers would kill momentum
Knowing which team to convince first
Avoiding all cross-team disagreement
Writing the longest possible vision statement
optionExplain: Right: seeing these dependencies is named.
Right: blockers are named.
Right: the order of persuasion matters.
The chapter expects to manage conflict, not avoid it.
Length is not part of the skill.
questions.explain: Dependencies, who to convince first and momentum-killing blockers are the three the chapter lists here.
questions.rule: Name dependencies, order and blockers.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Sort each action by whether it is the vision or the getting-there skill.

items.t: Describing a world where every clinic books appointments online
Finding which department's budget cycle would block the rollout
Painting a clear picture of the shared platform two years out
Deciding to convince the busiest clinic first
Mapping which teams' systems depend on the old scheduler
Naming a goal so clear that people can repeat it

questions.explain: Describing the destination is vision; dependencies, order and blockers are the route.
questions.rule: Ask whether an action describes the destination or the path.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A leader only does what is sure to work. What does the chapter expect?
options: Small safe gains that add up to a major change
Nothing important changes
Faster change than a bold leader would achieve
Strong support from teams who like low risk
optionExplain: The chapter does not say safe play adds up to change that matters.
Right: playing safe means you never change anything important.
Safe play is described as the cause of no important change.
Support is not the issue; the chapter says nothing important changes.
questions.explain: Doing only what is certain keeps the organisation where it is.
questions.rule: Safe play changes nothing important.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: True or false: a candidate whose story ends with a polished strategy presentation has shown the full competency.
questions.explain: The chapter says vision without execution is just daydreaming; a presentation is not a change in how the organisation works.
questions.rule: End the story with a real change.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A parent group wants every school club to use one booking system. What should it expect, per the chapter's cross-organisation point?
options: Clubs will adopt it quickly once the system is shown to work, so no extra planning is needed
Only technical blockers matter, so politics can be ignored
Politics will come with the change, so managing it is part of getting there
The change needs no one to be convinced first
optionExplain: The chapter expects obstacles even when the idea is good.
The chapter names politics as part of the hard skill.
Right: managing politics comes with any cross-organisation change.
Knowing whom to convince first is named as part of the skill.
questions.explain: The chapter lists managing the politics that come with any cross-organisation change among the hard parts of getting there.
questions.rule: Plan for politics as well as technology.
questions.teaches: Managing the politics that come with any cross-organisation change is part of the hard skill of getting there.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: You must move six departments to a new expense system. How would you choose where to start?
options: Pick a department that can show an early win and build momentum for harder ones
Start with the hardest department, so the rest look easy by comparison once it is done
Announce it to all six on one day and let them organise themselves
Start alphabetically, since fairness avoids arguments about order
optionExplain: Right: sequence to build momentum.
Starting hardest can burn momentum before it exists.
A single announcement leaves order and resistance to chance.
Fairness has value, but the order should be chosen for adoption.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next gives the chapter's questions about order.
questions.rule: Choose the first step for momentum.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Seeing the right ____ is not enough, because you also need to know what changes to make in the right order.
questions.explain: The chapter says seeing the right destination is not enough without the right sequence of changes.
questions.rule: A destination needs an order of steps.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A hospital will retire three old record systems. Which question is a sequencing question in the chapter's sense?
options: What should the new system be called?
How many nurses use the old systems on a typical day, and on which wards do they work?
When did the old systems first go live?
Which ward should move first, so its success helps win over the others?
optionExplain: Naming is not about the order of changes.
A headcount is information, not an order of steps.
History does not decide the order of the move.
Right: it asks which team to bring on board first.
questions.explain: Sequencing asks which team comes first, which early win builds momentum, and what could fail loudly.
questions.rule: Ask which comes first and why.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Our reading: a leader skips the item likely to fail loudly and starts with an easy win. What is the likely effect?
options: The loud failure can hit later and damage the momentum the win built
Nothing, since easy wins always outweigh later failures
The failure goes away because the team is more confident after its early win
Teams resist less because the failure was announced
optionExplain: Right: that is why the chapter asks what to address before everything else.
A loud failure can undo an early win.
Confidence does not remove a known failure point.
Nothing in the chapter suggests announcing failure lowers resistance.
questions.explain: The chapter lists the loudly failing item as something to address before everything else, so skipping it risks the whole effort.
questions.rule: Deal with the loudest risk before it surfaces.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: True or false: a to-do list with an owner and a deadline for every task is a strategic sequence by itself.
questions.explain: Owners and deadlines can appear in any list. The chapter's test is that the order was chosen to maximise adoption and minimise resistance.
questions.rule: Choose the order for its effect on adoption.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Two objections arise in a platform migration: one about a dashboard colour, one that the move would break billing. What does the chapter's view of fights suggest?
options: Fight both equally to show the plan is firm
Skip both and move ahead to protect momentum
Let the objecting team decide which fights count and follow its view on each
Choose which fights matter, concede the colour, and settle billing first
optionExplain: The chapter says to pick fights, not fight all.
Skipping a billing failure risks a loud failure later.
Choosing fights is part of the leader's judgement.
Right: strategic leaders know which fights matter and which ones to skip.
questions.explain: The chapter says strategic leaders know which fights matter and which to skip; here the billing risk matters more than the colour (our reading).
questions.rule: Pick the fights that matter.
questions.teaches: Strategic leaders know which fights matter and which ones to skip.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Many teams resist a cross-team change. What is your first move?
options: Announce the change to all teams and set a firm start date
Find the team hurting most and help it succeed visibly
Wait until every team is persuaded in principle before starting
Ask senior leaders to order every team to comply this quarter
optionExplain: One announcement leaves each team to resist on its own.
Right: its success becomes the proof point for the next team.
Waiting for total agreement can stall the change indefinitely.
Ordering compliance does not build the belief that makes change last.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next shows the chapter's approach.
questions.rule: Start where the pain is.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Put the chapter's spread-of-change steps in order.
items: Find the team hurting enough to try something different
Help that team succeed visibly
Use its success story to bring the next team along
Repeat until opting in is the obvious choice
questions.explain: The chain starts with the team in pain and grows through each visible success.
questions.rule: One visible success leads to the next.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Sort each action by whether it follows the proof-point approach or bulldozing.

items.t: Pilot the new tool with the team drowning in support tickets
Order all teams to switch on the same day
Share one team's before-and-after results with its neighbours
Treat each objection as stubbornness to be overruled
Back the first adopter until its win is visible
Escalate to a senior leader as soon as one team says no

questions.explain: Proof points rely on visible wins that persuade; bulldozing relies on orders and overruling.
questions.rule: Ask whether the action builds belief or forces compliance.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Team A, in real pain, adopts a new tool and succeeds visibly. What should the leader do next?
options: Announce that the matter is closed and everyone must follow Team A
Wait quietly in case the other teams notice by themselves
Use that success story to bring the next team along
Declare the change complete and move on to a new project
optionExplain: A decree skips the persuasion the chain relies on.
The chapter has the leader carry the story forward.
Right: the chain grows from proof.
One team's win is not an organisation-wide change.
questions.explain: A visible win is the story you use to persuade the next team.
questions.rule: Carry each win to the next team.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: True or false: the chapter says strategic leaders neither take resistance personally nor try to bulldoze through it.
questions.explain: The chapter says strategic leaders do not take resistance personally and do not try to bulldoze through it.
questions.rule: Treat resistance as information, not an attack.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A team lead says the new tool would push her quarterly roadmap back. How should the leader read this, per the chapter?
options: As proof that the lead dislikes change in general and will keep blocking every future step
As noise that fades once a deadline is announced
As one of the real reasons teams push back, to be addressed with a visible win
As a sign the whole change should be dropped
optionExplain: The chapter says teams have real reasons, not mere dislike.
A deadline does not remove a real reason.
Right: the chapter lists threats to a roadmap as a real reason.
Resistance is expected; it does not mean the change is wrong.
questions.explain: The chapter says people have real reasons to push back: the initiative threatens their roadmap, adds migration work, or forces them to learn something new.
questions.rule: Take the reason seriously and answer it.
questions.teaches: Teams have real reasons to push back: the initiative threatens their roadmap, adds migration work, or forces them to learn something new.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: You are interviewing at a fast-growing startup. Which strategic story fits best?
options: Coordinating a billion-dollar rollout across hundreds of teams
Building a foundation for ten times today's size while still fixing today's problems
Proving value in small steps to a sceptical, stable organisation that prizes caution over many years
Writing a detailed process for every stage of the company's work
optionExplain: That scale of coordination fits a tech giant.
Right: the startup values this view.
That fits a traditional company in transformation.
Heavy process risks constricting innovation at a startup.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next sets out the company types.
questions.rule: Match your story to the company type.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Match each setting to its strategic challenge, as the chapter describes.
pairs: Balancing bold ambition with coordinating across huge organisations
Knowing which processes to formalise and which flexibility to preserve
Strategies teams can execute while keeping coherent company-wide direction
Structures that enable growth without constricting innovation
questions.explain: Each setting has its own challenge and its own mark of success.
questions.rule: Know the challenge of the setting.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Sort each situation by the setting where it is the typical strategic work.

items.t: Changing a service that millions of users rely on, across many teams
Choosing which two processes to write down now and which to leave loose
Planning a data layer that will still work at ten times today's load
Pitching an effort that could shift billions in revenue
Keeping a growing team fast while adding the first real structure
Making the plan something hundreds of teams can each carry out

questions.explain: Huge scale and coordination mark the giant; foundations with agility mark the startup.
questions.rule: Ask which scale and constraint the situation has.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A startup leader formalises every process in detail. What does the chapter's description of success suggest?
options: Growth will speed up, because everything is predictable and written down
Nothing changes, because processes never affect agility
The company will need fewer leaders to run its work
Structures may constrict innovation and cost the company its agility
optionExplain: Predictability is not the success the chapter names.
The chapter treats the choice of what to formalise as the challenge.
Headcount is not part of the chapter's point.
Right: success means growth without constricting innovation.
questions.explain: The chapter's success test for startups is structure that supports growth without constricting innovation.
questions.rule: Formalise only what growth needs.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A candidate for a platform company talks only about a clever fix to one team's bug. What is missing?
options: The scale of the opportunity and coordination across a huge organisation
A more detailed description of the bug's code and of how the team found it
A statement that the fix was done quickly
A note that the team preferred the old design
optionExplain: Right: the setting values impact on millions of users.
More detail on the bug does not widen the scope.
Speed alone does not show strategic scale.
Team preference is not what the setting values.
questions.explain: A platform company wants evidence of opportunities touching millions of users and the skill to coordinate them.
questions.rule: Show scale and coordination.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A large retailer's leader writes a data-sharing policy. Which result fits the chapter's skill for a tech giant?
options: Individual teams can run the policy themselves while the company keeps one direction
Every team writes its own policy to suit its local needs and reports back on it yearly
Head office runs every data request to keep control
The policy is kept short so no one has to read it
optionExplain: Right: the giant's skill is strategies teams can execute within coherent direction.
That gives up coherent company-wide direction.
That removes the teams' ability to execute.
Brevity is not the skill described.
questions.explain: The chapter says the skill at tech giants is creating strategies that individual teams can execute while maintaining coherent company-wide direction.
questions.rule: Make a strategy both executable by teams and coherent overall.
questions.teaches: At tech giants the skill is creating strategies that individual teams can execute while maintaining coherent company-wide direction.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: You interview at an old, stable company that is modernising. Which story fits best?
options: A story of replacing every old system in one bold move before the sceptics could object
A story of ignoring objections to protect the schedule
A story of ten-times scaling for a young startup
A change plan that honoured existing strengths and brought sceptics along
optionExplain: A bold sweep ignores the strengths the setting values.
The setting values bringing sceptics along.
That belongs to a startup scaling up, not a traditional firm.
Right: this setting values respect for what works.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next gives the setting's view.
questions.rule: Fit the story to the organisation's values.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Match each setting to what it values in a strategic leader.
pairs: Understanding existing strengths and bringing even sceptics along
Connecting technical work to broader impact
Patient leadership that proves value step by step
Inspiring others with possibility while building practical paths forward
questions.explain: Traditional firms want respect and patience; mission-driven groups want a clear tie to impact.
questions.rule: Know what each setting values.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Sort each story element by the setting where it would land best.

items.t: Showing that the plan kept the billing system that already worked well
Explaining how a new tool lets the charity reach more families
Proving value in one department before asking the next to change
Linking an engineering rewrite to the organisation's stated purpose
Winning over a sceptical long-serving team with early results
Describing how a data change promotes the mission

questions.explain: Traditional audiences value respect and incremental proof; mission-driven audiences value a link to the mission.
questions.rule: Ask what the setting cares about most.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A leader at a mission-driven group presents a change purely as a cost saving, with no tie to the mission. What is the likely reception?
options: Strong approval, since savings always win support
No reaction, since missions do not affect decisions
The change may seem unconnected to what the group values
Excitement at the technical detail of the plan
optionExplain: The chapter says the setting values the link to the mission.
Mission-driven groups treat the mission as central.
Right: the setting values stating how changes promote the mission.
Technical detail is not what the setting is said to value.
questions.explain: Our reading: without the link, the case leaves out what the group prizes most.
questions.rule: State how the change serves the mission.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: True or false: a traditional company transforming rewards leaders who understand its existing strengths while driving needed change.
questions.explain: The chapter says such organisations value people who understand existing strengths and respect what works while driving necessary change.
questions.rule: Build on strengths while changing.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A nonprofit's engineer proposes a new data system. What does the chapter say success looks like there?
options: Keeping idealism aside while handling real constraints one at a time, in order of cost
Inspiring others with possibility while building practical paths forward
Using the strongest technical argument only
Moving quickly before staff can object
optionExplain: The chapter wants both idealism and constraints handled.
Right: success is idealism together with practical routes.
A technical case alone does not inspire.
Speed before agreement is not the aim here.
questions.explain: The chapter says success in mission-driven environments comes from inspiring others with possibility while building practical paths forward, keeping idealism while navigating real constraints.
questions.rule: Pair idealism with practical paths.
questions.teaches: In mission-driven organisations, success comes from inspiring others with possibility while building practical paths forward.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Before an interview you learn the company prizes broad agreement at each step. What do you stress?
options: How fast you drove adoption before anyone agreed
How you ignored objections to hit the date
How you built alignment across the people involved
How you worked alone to avoid delays
optionExplain: That suits a company that rewards speed.
That signals poor alignment skills.
Right: a consensus-valuing company wants to hear it.
Working alone does not show alignment.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next sets out the chapter's advice.
questions.rule: Match emphasis to the company.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Match each company culture to the part of your story to stress.
pairs: The ambition of your vision and how quickly you drove adoption
Fit your stories to how the company operates
questions.explain: Alignment for consensus cultures; ambition and speed for fast ones; research first.
questions.rule: Research, then emphasise.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Sort each story detail by the culture where it would help most.

items.t: You met each team in turn and adjusted the plan to their concerns
You launched the pilot within a week, before every group had signed off
You proposed the change in stages with agreement at each stage
You set an ambitious target and drove adoption in a quarter
You kept a log of who had agreed to what at each step
You moved first and brought the sceptics along afterwards

questions.explain: Alignment and staging suit consensus cultures; boldness and pace suit fast ones.
questions.rule: Choose the detail the culture values.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A candidate rewrites their personality for each employer. What does the chapter say about this?
options: The goal is to match stories to how the company operates, not to change who you are
It is wise, since employers hire only people who fit their culture exactly as it stands
It is needed only for startups
It matters only after being hired
optionExplain: Right: match the story, not the self.
The chapter rejects changing who you are.
No such restriction is stated.
The advice is about the interview.
questions.explain: The chapter ends its advice by saying to match your stories to the company's way of operating, not to change who you are.
questions.rule: Adjust emphasis, keep your identity.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: You emphasise how fast you moved before anyone agreed, in a company that values consensus. What is the likely result?
options: They will see it as proof of ambition and be impressed
It may suggest you skip the alignment they value
The emphasis will not matter to them either way
They will assume you also built alignment
optionExplain: Ambition suits fast cultures, not consensus ones.
Right: the emphasis clashes with that culture. (Our reading)
The chapter says to match stories to culture.
The story gives no sign of it.
questions.explain: The chapter ties each emphasis to a culture; a mismatch leaves out what the company values.
questions.rule: Stress what the culture values.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Which description fits a consensus-valuing culture's way of proposing big change, per the chapter?
options: Big changes are announced once and acted on at once
Big changes begin before anyone has seen the plan
Big changes are left to the most senior person to decide on behalf of everyone
Big changes get proposed gradually, with broad buy-in at each step
optionExplain: That sounds like a speed-and-boldness culture.
Starting early before agreement fits the fast culture.
Authority-led decisions skip the consensus-building.
Right: that is the example given.
questions.explain: The chapter's example of consensus culture is that big changes get proposed gradually with broad buy-in at each step.
questions.rule: Tell the sequence of agreement in such cultures.
questions.teaches: In consensus cultures, big changes get proposed gradually, with broad buy-in at each step.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A colleague invented a clever caching technique. What would make it a strategic-leadership story?
options: Showing the technique is more novel than any rival design that has been published
Shipping the technique to production before the deadline
Writing a clear technical paper about how it works
Seeing how it could change how the whole company works and driving that change
optionExplain: Novelty is innovation, not strategy.
Shipping is delivery.
A paper shares the idea but does not lead change.
Right: strategy recognises which innovations reshape the organisation.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next separates the three skills.
questions.rule: Strategy adds the company-wide change.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Match each skill to the chapter's description.
pairs: Creating novel solutions to specific problems
Shipping work despite the presence of obstacles
Ensuring teams deliver the right things in the right sequence
questions.explain: Each skill has its own focus, and delivery alone gives motion without progress.
questions.rule: Name each skill's focus.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: Sort each action by whether it is strategic leadership or innovation or delivery alone.

items.t: Inventing a new caching technique for one service
Judging which of three new techniques would reshape how all teams work, and rallying support
Shipping a late project despite a vendor outage
Choosing which projects will move the company toward its vision
Building a clever prototype that no other team adopts
Making sure teams deliver the right things in the right sequence

questions.explain: Choosing, sequencing and building support is strategic; inventing or shipping alone is not.
questions.rule: Ask whether the action chooses and rallies, or only creates or ships.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A team ships everything on time, yet none of the projects moves the company toward its vision. What does the chapter call the result?
options: Strategic leadership at its best
Motion without progress
Pure innovation with no delivery
Progress that takes time to show
optionExplain: Strategy would pick projects that move toward the vision.
Right: delivery without strategy.
The team did deliver.
The chapter says the work lacks direction.
questions.explain: Delivery without strategy keeps people busy without moving the company forward.
questions.rule: Delivery needs direction.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: True or false: a candidate who says delivery skills are unnecessary for strategic leadership is right.
questions.explain: The chapter says you need delivery skills to complete projects, though strategic leadership decides which projects matter.
questions.rule: You still need to deliver.

questions.section: 13.2 The Essence of Strategic Leadership and Thinking Big
questions.q: A VP proposes visionary programmes, but none of her teams ever finishes one. How does the chapter label this kind of leader?
options: A dreamer
A catalyst
An innovator
A strategist
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says leaders who cannot deliver are dreamers.
Catalysts make the vision feel urgent and achievable, which needs delivery.
Innovation is a different skill from leading delivery.
Size alone is not strategy.
questions.explain: The chapter says leaders who cannot deliver are dreamers.
questions.rule: Strategy needs delivery behind it.
questions.teaches: Delivery without strategy creates motion without progress: you need delivery skills to complete projects, but strategic leadership decides which projects move the company toward its vision.

questions.q: An interviewer says: describe a pattern you identified across teams. What are they most likely testing?
options: Whether you can write clear documentation for your own team and keep it current
Whether you finish tasks faster than your colleagues
Whether you see when separate issues point to a bigger opportunity
Whether you prefer working across many teams or alone
optionExplain: Documentation is not what the question probes.
Speed of task completion is not the point.
Right: this is a big-picture question.
Preference is not the target; evidence of seeing patterns is.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next explains the question groups.
questions.rule: Read the question for its skill.

questions.q: Match each question group to what the chapter says it probes.
pairs: Pattern recognition beyond your or your team's scope
Turning vision into reality through leadership
questions.explain: The two groups probe different skills, and each has its own mark of a strong answer.
questions.rule: Pair the group with its skill.

questions.q: Sort each interview question by the group it belongs to.

items.t: Tell me about spotting that three teams' bugs shared a cause
Tell me about getting four teams to adopt one API style
Tell me about connecting two unrelated complaints to one opportunity
Describe setting a direction other teams followed
Give an example of a company-wide pattern others missed
Tell me about keeping momentum through a hard rollout

questions.explain: Questions about noticing patterns fit the big picture; questions about aligning and driving fit leading change.
questions.rule: Ask whether the question is about noticing or about driving.

questions.q: A candidate answers a leading-change question by describing a pattern they noticed, with no teams aligned. What is the gap?
options: The pattern was too small to count as an example
The story shows seeing, not building support or carrying the change out
The candidate should have named more teams and more of the people involved in the story
Nothing; noticing a pattern fully answers the question
optionExplain: Size is not the gap; the missing action is.
Right: the question probes turning vision into reality.
More names do not supply the missing leadership.
That answers a big-picture question, not this one.
questions.explain: A leading-change question needs evidence of alignment and execution, not only insight.
questions.rule: Match the story to what is probed.

questions.q: A candidate answers a big-picture question with a story of leading a change through one team only. What is the likely concern?
options: The story is too large for the question
The story has too much detail on leadership
The story shows no pattern recognition beyond their own scope
The interviewer wants a story about failure instead of one about leading change
optionExplain: Scale is not the concern.
Leadership detail is not penalised, but it misses the target.
Right: the big-picture group looks past one's team.
Nothing in the chapter suggests a failure-only story.
questions.explain: Our reading: the question asks for connections beyond the team, which a one-team story cannot show.
questions.rule: Show patterns beyond your scope.

questions.q: You are asked to describe aligning several teams on a technical direction. Which detail would a strong answer include?
options: What each team's leaders cared about and how the case for change was built around it
The exact number of hours spent in alignment meetings
A statement that the direction was the best technical option and the cheapest one available
A list of the teams that disagreed with you at the start
optionExplain: Right: good examples show understanding of what different teams and leaders care about.
Hours spent do not show understanding of others.
Asserting the idea was best skips how support was built.
A list of opponents is not the answer's strength.
questions.explain: The chapter says good leading-change examples show understanding of what different teams and leaders care about, strong cases for change, and momentum through hard implementation.
questions.rule: Show what others cared about, not only what you wanted.
questions.teaches: Good leading-change examples show you understanding what different teams and leaders care about and building strong cases for change.

questions.q: An interviewer asks about an organisation-wide effect of your technical decision. What do they want to see?
options: A detailed account of how long the project took
Proof that your own team's metrics improved
A statement that leadership approved of the decision
Impact that scales beyond one project and lasts
optionExplain: Duration is not the target.
Team-level gains are narrower than the question.
Approval is not the same as lasting reach.
Right: broad-impact questions look for lasting company-wide value.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next covers these two question groups.
questions.rule: Show reach and lasting effect.

questions.q: Match each question group to what a strong answer shows.
pairs: Transformation that outlasts your direct involvement
Weighing readiness, resource limits and competing priorities
Approaches adopted because they work better
questions.explain: Impact answers show reach and endurance; trade-off answers show weighing.
questions.rule: Pair each group with its evidence.

questions.q: Sort each detail by the question group it would best support.

items.t: Five other teams still use the practice two years after you left
You compared two initiatives against the available engineers and picked one
A shared library you built now saves several teams weeks each quarter
You waited on a transformation because the company was not ready for it
Teams adopted your method because it was better than the old one
You balanced a short-term deadline against a long-term vision

questions.explain: Lasting spread is impact; choosing between options under limits is a trade-off.
questions.rule: Ask whether the detail shows reach or choice.

questions.q: A candidate describes a change that vanished the week they left the project. How does this fare against a broad-impact question?
options: Well, since the change worked while they were present and the whole team saw the benefits
Neutrally, since impact is judged only by size
Well, since leaving shows they trained others
Poorly, since the question looks for transformation that outlasts your involvement
optionExplain: Working only while present is the weakness.
The chapter names durability as a feature.
The change vanished, so little was passed on.
Right: durability is a mark of the strong answer.
questions.explain: Our reading: if the change did not outlast the candidate, it does not meet the chapter's description of effective stories.
questions.rule: Show impact that lasts.

questions.q: True or false: a trade-off question mainly probes your judgement about what and when to pursue.
questions.explain: Trade-off questions probe judgement about what and when to pursue, not how far an idea spread.
questions.rule: Trade-offs test judgement.

questions.q: You are asked about a valuable transformation you chose not to pursue. What does the chapter's question list suggest about this?
options: It cannot be asked, since strategy is only about doing things and not about choosing to hold back
It is a legitimate question about timing or approach, so be ready to explain the call
It signals failure, so avoid the topic
It is a technical question about code quality
optionExplain: The question list includes exactly this case.
Right: the list includes deciding not to pursue because the timing or approach was not right.
The chapter treats it as judgement.
It concerns timing and approach, not code.
questions.explain: One sample trade-off question asks for a time when you decided not to pursue a potentially valuable transformation because the timing or approach was not right.
questions.rule: A well-argued decision not to act can show judgement.
questions.teaches: A sample trade-off question asks about deciding not to pursue a potentially valuable transformation because the timing or approach was not right.

questions.q: Which kind of problem does a strategic leader most want to spot?
options: One that a single team already owns and is fixing
One that is easiest to fix quickly
One that cuts across teams and that nobody owns
One that senior leaders have already named
optionExplain: An owned problem is less likely to be a missed opportunity.
Ease is not the signal.
Right: problems in the gaps between groups.
A problem already named is not something others missed.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next sets out the signal.
questions.rule: Look in the gaps between groups.

questions.q: Strategic leaders spot problems that nobody owns because they live in the ____ between groups.
questions.explain: The chapter says these problems live in the gaps between groups.
questions.rule: Cross-team problems sit in the gaps.

questions.q: Which story element best shows the critical signal?
options: You linked outages in three teams to one shared cause and got them to fix it
You wrote a thorough post-mortem for your own team's outage
You proposed a new alerting tool and presented it to your manager and her peers
You led a quick fix that cut your team's alerts by half
optionExplain: Right: a cross-team cause, teams moved, real change.
A strong post-mortem stays within one team.
A proposal without teams moved is not the signal.
A local fix does not show cross-team insight.
questions.explain: The signal needs something others missed, teams you did not control, and a real change.
questions.rule: Show cause, teams and change.

questions.q: A story ends with a well-received proposal and a presentation. How does it measure against the signal?
options: It falls short, since the signal needs a real change, not a proposal or presentation
It meets the signal, since the insight was valuable
It exceeds the signal, since a presentation given to many people reaches a very wide audience
It cannot be judged without knowing the audience size
optionExplain: Right: the chapter requires an actual change in how the organisation worked.
Insight alone is not enough.
Reach of a talk is not change.
The chapter's test is about change, not audience.
questions.explain: The chapter says to show a real change in how the organisation worked, not just a proposal or a presentation.
questions.rule: End the story with real change.

questions.q: True or false: a candidate who says they patched each team's symptom one at a time has shown this signal.
questions.explain: The signal is arguing that fixing the root cause is worth more than patching each symptom separately.
questions.rule: Make the case for the root cause.

questions.q: A candidate shows that she saw a cross-team problem but ends with a proposal deck. What is missing, per the critical signal?
options: A longer list of the technologies that the proposal would replace across teams
More detail about how many weeks she spent preparing the proposal deck
A real change in how the organisation worked, not only a proposal
A statement of which team was most to blame for the original problem
optionExplain: Tools are detail; the signal asks for changed organisation.
Effort is not the evidence the signal asks for.
Right: the chapter says the result must be a real change in how the organisation worked, not only a proposal or a presentation.
Blame is not part of the signal.
questions.explain: The signal wants a real change in how the organisation worked, not only a proposal or a presentation.
questions.rule: Pair technical depth with business stakes.
questions.teaches: Your credibility on this signal comes from showing you understand both the technical details and the business stakes.

questions.q: Which is part of a compelling vision, as a strong signal?
options: A detailed list of tasks with owners and dates for next quarter
A narrative connecting present pain to future possibilities
A guarantee that the change will cost nothing
A single announcement of the final decision
optionExplain: A task list is a plan, not a vision narrative.
Right: it makes the direction something people can follow.
No such guarantee is part of the signal.
Announcement alone does not build a coalition.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next sets out the two strong signals.
questions.rule: A vision connects pain to possibility.

questions.q: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows.
pairs: Building things that keep working after you move on
questions.explain: The first two are marks of a compelling vision; the last two are marks of sustainable change.
questions.rule: Pair each piece of evidence with what it shows.

questions.q: Sort each story detail by the strong signal it supports.

items.t: You explained how today's delays would turn into a faster release path
You set up checks so new services followed the pattern without you
You gathered leads from four teams behind one picture of the platform
You staged the rollout so each team could adopt at its own pace
You kept the message clear as details changed over the project
You built tooling that kept the new approach working after you moved on

questions.explain: Direction and coalition are vision; staging and self-sustaining systems are sustainable change.
questions.rule: Ask whether the detail shows direction or durability.

questions.q: A story has a vivid vision but no sign anything lasted after the candidate moved on. How does it measure up?
options: It meets both signals, since vision is the harder one to build and carries most of the story
It exceeds both signals, since vision inspires
It misses the sustainable-change signal, since the work should keep going without you
It is judged only on the quality of the slides
optionExplain: Neither signal is said to be harder.
Inspiration without durability is incomplete.
Right: durability is part of that signal.
The chapter judges what lasted.
questions.explain: The chapter says effective examples show building things that keep working after you move on.
questions.rule: Make the change outlast you.

questions.q: True or false: the chapter lists coalitions around a shared vision under compelling vision, not under sustainable change.
questions.explain: The chapter lists coalitions under compelling vision; sustainable change covers sequencing, reinforcing systems and lasting results.
questions.rule: Coalitions belong to vision.

questions.q: A team lead introduces a new review practice and adds a template and checklist so new joiners follow it unprompted. What does the chapter's list say this shows?
options: Building a coalition around a shared vision
Spotting a problem nobody owns
Anticipating ripple effects across teams
Building systems that reinforce new approaches
optionExplain: The case describes tooling, not coalition-building.
The case shows follow-through, not discovery.
No cross-team effect is described.
Right: the template and checklist make the practice stick.
questions.explain: The chapter says effective sustainable-change examples show building systems that reinforce new approaches.
questions.rule: Embed the change in systems.
questions.teaches: Sustainable change includes building systems that reinforce new approaches.

questions.q: Before a change that touches shared infrastructure, what would a systems thinker do first?
options: Make the change and wait for the affected teams to report any problems
Map the dependencies and likely ripple effects across teams
Optimise the part your own team owns and move on
Ask a manager for a deadline before anything else
optionExplain: That reacts to ripples rather than anticipating them.
Right: mapping dependencies before changing is named.
Local optimising is what systems thinking avoids.
A deadline is not mapping the effects.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next sets out the signal.
questions.rule: Map before you change.

questions.q: Strategic thinkers are skilled at seeing the second- and third-____ effects of changes.
questions.explain: The chapter refers to second- and third-order effects.
questions.rule: Think past the first effect.

questions.q: A team will move its database to a new region. Which question is a systems-thinking question?
options: How long will the move take our team?
Who will present the migration results?
Which other teams' services call this database, and what happens to them?
Is the new region cheaper this month?
optionExplain: That is local planning.
Presentation is not about effects.
Right: it maps dependencies and ripple effects.
Cost looks at one factor, not ripples.
questions.explain: Dependencies and ripple effects across teams are what the signal looks for.
questions.rule: Ask who else is affected.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it shows systems thinking or local optimisation.

items.t: We mapped three downstream teams' dependencies and changed the rollout order to avoid breaking them
We cut our own build time in half
We checked how our API change would ripple into two partner teams before shipping
We moved faster than any other team that quarter
We redesigned the shared queue so every consumer benefited, not only us
We tuned our own service and left the neighbours to cope

questions.explain: Mapping dependencies and ripple effects marks systems thinking; gains confined to one team mark local optimisation.
questions.rule: Look for effects beyond your team.

questions.q: A team speeds up its own service but triples the load on a neighbour's database. What does a systems thinker conclude?
options: The change optimised locally and pushed cost to the whole system
The change is a success because the team met its own goal and stayed on schedule
The neighbour should scale up its database to absorb the extra load
Second-order effects only matter in very large firms
optionExplain: Right: the whole system did not improve.
Meeting a local goal ignores the ripple.
That treats the ripple as the neighbour's problem.
The case shows them in two teams.
questions.explain: Our reading: the gain came with a ripple that harmed another team, which systems thinking tries to foresee.
questions.rule: Check where the load goes.

questions.q: How does the chapter rank thinking in systems among the key signals?
options: As the critical signal, above all others
As a supporting signal, below the critical and strong ones
As a strong signal, equal in weight to building a compelling vision
As a red flag when overdone
optionExplain: The critical signal is spotting opportunities for transformation.
Right: it is the supporting signal.
Vision and sustainable change are the two strong signals.
It is not listed as a flag.
questions.explain: The chapter names spotting opportunities critical, vision and sustainable change strong, and thinking in systems supporting.
questions.rule: Know the ranking of signals.
questions.teaches: The chapter ranks spotting opportunities for transformation as critical, compelling vision and sustainable change as strong, and thinking in systems as supporting.

questions.q: You redesigned your own team's stand-up routine, and it worked well. How do you use it in a strategic leadership question?
options: Describe it as strategic, since it improved results for the whole team
Stress how it could in theory spread to others
Choose a different story with impact across multiple teams
Say nothing about its scope and let them assume
optionExplain: The chapter calls this dressing up local work.
A hypothetical spread is not impact.
Right: team-only changes do not show the competency.
Hiding scope risks the red flag.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next explains the flag.
questions.rule: Pick a story that crossed teams.

questions.q: True or false: the red flag is dressing local improvements up as something bigger, not the improvements themselves.
questions.explain: The chapter says local improvements are good; the flag is dressing them up as something bigger.
questions.rule: The flaw is mislabelling, not the work.

questions.q: Sort each example by whether it fits a strategic leadership story.

items.t: You shortened your own team's sprint planning meeting
You got five teams to use one shared incident process
You automated your team's test setup
You aligned three groups on a common data format
You wrote a style guide used only by your squad
You changed how several systems shared configuration

questions.explain: Impact across several teams or systems fits; changes inside one team do not.
questions.rule: Count the teams the change reached.

questions.q: A candidate says: my team's new release process is strategic, because it was a great improvement. What is the error?
options: The release process was probably not great at all
Release processes cannot be strategic in any setting, however many teams use them
The candidate should have used a longer story
Quality does not make it strategic; the change stayed within the team
optionExplain: The chapter says even a great local change does not count.
A release process can be strategic if it crosses teams.
Length is not the issue.
Right: scope across teams is the test.
questions.explain: A change that stayed inside the team's boundaries does not demonstrate the competency, however good.
questions.rule: Scope decides, not quality.

questions.q: A candidate calls a team-only fix strategic and the interviewer probes the scope. What is the likely result?
options: The label is exposed, which hurts the candidate
The interviewer admires the confidence
The scope question is dropped
The story is accepted as a good local example of a team's own work
optionExplain: Right: calling it strategic will hurt you.
The chapter says the label damages you.
Interviewers can tell the difference.
It would be accepted only if honestly labelled.
questions.explain: The chapter says interviewers can tell team-level improvements from organisational change.
questions.rule: Honesty about scope protects you.

questions.q: A candidate cut her own team's build time by half and offers it as her strategic leadership story. What does the chapter say?
options: Own that it stayed within her team and choose a story that crossed teams
Keep the story, since a result that large shows strategy at any scope
Keep it, and add that other teams might one day copy the build setup
Cut the numbers so the story sounds less like a purely local improvement
optionExplain: Right: the red flag is dressing local work up as strategy, so own the scope and pick a story that crossed teams.
A great local result still does not show impact across multiple teams or systems.
A hope that others might copy it is not impact across teams.
Hiding the numbers hides evidence without changing the scope.
questions.explain: The chapter says a change that stayed within your team's boundaries, even a great one, does not demonstrate strategic leadership.
questions.rule: Know how severe each flag is.
questions.teaches: Calling every improvement 'strategic' dilutes the meaning of the word, and interviewers can tell team-level improvements from organizational change.

questions.q: Your story ends when management approved your plan. What would strengthen it?
options: Add more detail about how good the plan was and who has approved it so far
Add how the plan became a change in how teams actually worked
Add a note that approval took months
Leave it, since approval shows leadership
optionExplain: More plan detail leaves the gap in place.
Right: show implementation.
Delay is not the same as implementation.
Approval is not the same as realised change.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next explains the yellow flag.
questions.rule: Show what happened after the plan.

questions.q: Anyone can imagine better futures, but strategic leaders make them ____.
questions.explain: The chapter says strategic leaders make better futures happen.
questions.rule: Leaders make it happen.

questions.q: Which ending best avoids this yellow flag?
options: The plan was presented to the engineering council and received a standing ovation
The proposal was praised by several directors
Five teams now follow the design-review practice, and rework has nearly gone
A roadmap was drafted for the following year
optionExplain: A presentation is not implementation.
Praise is not a change.
Right: an implemented change with a result.
A roadmap is still a plan.
questions.explain: A strong ending says what changed in the organisation.
questions.rule: End with the change.

questions.q: True or false: a story that ends with a strong presentation shows strategic leadership in full.
questions.explain: The chapter says stories that end with proposals or presentations show strategic thinking without leadership.
questions.rule: A presentation is not a result.

questions.q: A candidate's three examples all end at the proposal stage. What do interviewers conclude?
options: Full strategic leadership, with consistent examples
Strong delivery skills, since proposals are written well
Nothing in particular, since proposals are enough
Strategic thinking is shown but leadership is not
optionExplain: Consistency of unfinished stories does not complete the arc.
Delivery requires finished work.
The chapter calls this a yellow flag.
Right: incomplete strategic leadership.
questions.explain: The chapter says stories ending with proposals show strategic thinking without leadership.
questions.rule: Close the loop on every story.

questions.q: In a story about adopting a new testing approach, which sentence best repairs the vision-without-implementation flag?
options: I wrote a detailed memo on the benefits of the approach
I discussed the idea with several senior engineers who all said they liked it very much
I added the approach to the team wiki
I got three teams to adopt it and tracked defects falling over two quarters
optionExplain: A memo is still a proposal.
Liking the idea is not adoption.
A wiki page records the idea without showing change.
Right: adoption and result.
questions.explain: The chapter wants you to tell interviewers how you turned the vision into organisational reality, with stories that end in implemented changes.
questions.rule: Say how the vision became real.
questions.teaches: Effective examples show sequencing changes for maximum adoption, building systems that reinforce new approaches, and building things that keep working after you move on.

questions.q: Your story centres on a mandate you issued as the senior engineer. What would make it stronger?
options: Stress how quickly everyone complied
Show how you helped people see the value so they believed in it
Stress that you had the authority to do it and used it without delay
Stress that nobody objected
optionExplain: Compliance speed is the flagged pattern.
Right: the chapter wants genuine buy-in.
Authority is the flagged source.
No objections could mean no one dared.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next explains the flag.
questions.rule: Aim for belief, not compliance.

questions.q: True or false: sustainable transformation needs people to believe in new approaches, not only comply.
questions.explain: That is the chapter's reasoning for the flag.
questions.rule: Belief lasts longer than compliance.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether it builds buy-in or relies on authority.

items.t: Show each team how the change cuts its own support load
Announce that the new standard is mandatory from Monday
Invite sceptics to shape the migration plan
Tell teams the decision is final and not open to discussion
Pilot with a willing team and share their results
Cite your job title when someone raises a concern

questions.explain: Showing value and inviting input builds buy-in; mandates and titles rely on authority.
questions.rule: Ask whether people are persuaded or told.

questions.q: A leader mandates a new tool and everyone complies on paper. What does the chapter suggest about the change?
options: It may not be sustainable, since people complied without believing in it
It will last, since the mandate is clear
It will spread faster than a persuaded change
It will be judged by interviewers as a strong signal of your influence over others
optionExplain: Right: sustainable change needs belief.
Clear mandates do not create belief.
The chapter does not claim faster spread.
It signals the opposite.
questions.explain: Compliance without belief is shallow, so the change may not hold.
questions.rule: Compliance is not buy-in.

questions.q: A candidate compares Ethan's platform story with a mandate. Which Ethan action fits the flag's advice?
options: He ordered all three teams to migrate by a date
He asked leadership to cancel the teams' projects
He showed teams how shared infrastructure would help them move faster
He built the platform quietly and switched teams over one by one without notice
optionExplain: That is the mandate pattern.
Cancelling is authority again.
Right: he built buy-in.
Quiet switching skips belief.
questions.explain: Ethan worked with leaders and team leads for months and showed teams how sharing would help them, which is influence, not authority.
questions.rule: Win people by showing value.

questions.q: A candidate says: I forced the change through because I had the authority, and it worked. What may the interviewer infer?
options: That they are an expert at fast execution under pressure
That they may be unable to create real alignment
That they enjoy strong cross-team trust
That they avoid conflict wherever possible
optionExplain: Speed is not the inference.
Right: stories about mandating suggest this.
A forced change does not show trust.
Forcing is not conflict avoidance.
questions.explain: The chapter says stories that focus on mandating changes suggest the candidate may not be able to create real alignment.
questions.rule: Show alignment, not orders.
questions.teaches: Stories focused on mandating changes suggest to interviewers that you may not be able to create real alignment.

questions.q: You explain your strategy using a named framework and many technical terms. What risk does the chapter see?
options: It can obscure rather than illuminate the vision
It will make the story sound too short
It will make you seem too junior
It will make interviewers doubt your delivery speed
optionExplain: Right: jargon and frameworks cloud the message.
Length is not the concern.
Seniority is not the concern.
Speed is not the concern.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next explains the two flags.
questions.rule: Clear beats clever.

questions.q: Great leaders make complex changes feel simple and ____.
questions.explain: The chapter says great leaders make complex changes feel simple and intuitive.
questions.rule: Aim for simple and intuitive.

questions.q: Sort each way of explaining a plan by whether it is clear or complexity without clarity.

items.t: Describe the change in two sentences anyone on the team could repeat
Open with a framework acronym and five jargon terms
Say what changes for each team in plain words
Need a long background briefing before the idea makes sense
Tell people what to do differently on Monday
Rely on several diagrams to explain the logic

questions.explain: Plain, repeatable explanations are clear; heavy background and many diagrams signal the opposite.
questions.rule: Ask whether a listener could act on it.

questions.q: Which candidate statement is the loose-label flag rather than the complexity flag?
options: Our approach used a four-layer alignment framework with custom terms
The plan needed three diagrams and a glossary
My vision was hard to summarise even for me
Every improvement my team made last year was a strategic win
optionExplain: That is complexity without clarity.
Also complexity.
A vague vision is a clarity problem.
Right: calling everything strategic dilutes the word.
questions.explain: The flags differ: one is about how you explain, the other about what you call strategic.
questions.rule: Tell the two yellow flags apart.

questions.q: A candidate calls a renamed team meeting a strategic initiative. What happens to the word, per the chapter?
options: It gains weight from the candidate's confidence
It stays unchanged, since labels do not matter
It is diluted, and interviewers see through it
It shows modesty about the work
optionExplain: Confidence does not add meaning.
The chapter says they do.
Right: the chapter says labels dilute the meaning.
The chapter reads it as overclaiming.
questions.explain: Calling every improvement strategic dilutes the meaning of the word.
questions.rule: Save the word for real change.

questions.q: A candidate needs ten minutes of background and four diagrams to explain their plan. What does the chapter conclude?
options: They have shown unusual depth of analysis
They have met the red flag on local optimisation
They have shown thinking in systems
They have not achieved strategic clarity
optionExplain: Depth without clarity is the flagged pattern.
That flag is about scope, not explanation.
Systems thinking is not judged by diagram count.
Right: needing extensive background or multiple diagrams signals this.
questions.explain: The chapter says needing extensive background or multiple diagrams to explain a strategy means you have not achieved strategic clarity.
questions.rule: Test your story by explaining it simply.
questions.teaches: If you need extensive background or multiple diagrams to explain your strategy, you have not achieved strategic clarity.

questions.q: Developers keep finding design flaws only at code review. What is the best first move for a senior engineer?
options: Ask reviewers to be gentler in code review
Analyse recent projects to find the pattern behind the rework
Add more reviewers to each pull request
Tell developers to write less code per request and to submit more often
optionExplain: Tone does not address timing.
Right: the story starts by measuring the pattern.
More reviewers repeat the late feedback.
Smaller requests do not move design earlier.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next retells the story.
questions.rule: Find the pattern first.

questions.q: The senior engineer found that the issue was not code quality but ____, because architecture was discussed after implementation.
questions.explain: The story says the issue was timing: architecture discussions came after implementation instead of before.
questions.rule: The cause was when, not what.

questions.q: A support team keeps discovering policy errors only after customer replies are sent. Which move mirrors the story?
options: Add a second proofreader after replies are sent
Retrain everyone on policy over one long weekend and test them the following Monday
Add a brief policy check before drafting replies and trial it on one team
Ask customers to flag policy errors in surveys
optionExplain: That still reviews after the fact.
Training alone does not change when checks happen.
Right: move the review earlier, small first.
That finds errors even later.
questions.explain: The story moved design review ahead of code and trialled it on one team for a month.
questions.rule: Move the check earlier, then pilot.

questions.q: In the story, how did the practice spread beyond the senior's own team?
options: Adjacent teams noticed the improved velocity and asked about the process
A company policy required every team to adopt it
The senior personally rewrote the other teams' design documents to a common format
The practice stayed with one team throughout
optionExplain: Right: the practice drew others in.
The story describes teams asking, not a mandate.
The senior helped teams adapt, not rewrite.
It reached five teams within a quarter.
questions.explain: Adjacent teams noticed, and the senior helped three neighbours adapt the format to their needs.
questions.rule: Let results pull others in.

questions.q: True or false: the senior-level story succeeds mainly because it forced all teams to use one rigid template.
questions.explain: The story had each neighbouring team adapt the format to its needs.
questions.rule: Let teams adapt the format.

questions.q: In the story, how did the senior handle engineers who struggled with written design docs?
options: Excused them from writing design docs
Paired them with stronger writers and gave templates and examples of good docs
Had senior developers write the docs for them to save everyone's time on each project
Dropped the practice for those engineers
optionExplain: The story supports them rather than excusing them.
Right: skill-building supported the change.
The aim was to build their skill.
The practice continued with support.
questions.explain: The story pairs weaker writers with stronger ones and offers templates and examples, and notes junior developers grew their writing skills.
questions.rule: Support those who find the change hard.
questions.teaches: The senior paired engineers who struggled with writing with stronger writers and gave templates and examples, so skills grew alongside the practice.

questions.q: Every team's APIs behave differently, and partner integrations are coming. How would you start?
options: Order every team to adopt one API style this month and report on progress weekly
Write a style guide and wait for teams to read it
Map the inconsistencies and tie them to the coming partner launch
Let partners deal with each team's quirks
optionExplain: Sudden standardisation disrupts every roadmap.
A guide alone does not make anyone change.
Right: show why the mess becomes a blocker.
The inconsistencies would block the partner programme.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next retells the story.
questions.rule: Tie the mess to a business need.

questions.q: Put the staff engineer's phases in order.
items: Map the inconsistencies and link them to the partner programme
Phase one: make new APIs follow consistent patterns
Phase two: migrate existing APIs, prioritising those with many consumers
Add API review checkpoints to catch new inconsistencies
questions.explain: The story maps first, then phases new APIs, then migrates existing ones, and adds checkpoints.
questions.rule: Map, phase, then lock in.

questions.q: Sort each choice by whether it matches the story or contradicts it.

items.t: Standards focus on behaviour and developer experience
All teams must migrate in the first month
Migration starts with APIs that many consumers use
Technical uniformity is required across all protocols
Migration tools automate the tedious work
Teams with no integration pain go first

questions.explain: The story kept protocols flexible, phased the work, automated tedious parts and began with teams in pain.
questions.rule: Check each choice against the story's design.

questions.q: Why did early adopters become champions in the story?
options: They were drowning in integration questions and standardisation cut the burden
They were ordered to praise the project
They were paid extra for adopting early
They had spare time on their roadmaps and nothing else important to do that quarter
optionExplain: Right: it solved their own pain.
Nothing says they were ordered.
No payment is described.
The story says teams had full roadmaps.
questions.explain: The engineer started with teams hurting from integration support questions, so the change helped them directly.
questions.rule: Start where the change helps most.

questions.q: Which was the engineer's approach to teams' packed roadmaps?
options: Asking teams to work extra hours on the project without any recognition in planning
Skipping teams that raised roadmap concerns
Waiting for roadmaps to empty before starting
Getting API consistency recognised in quarterly planning so participation counted
optionExplain: The story gave recognition.
The campaign addressed concerns.
The change was phased around them.
Right: it gave teams a reason to take part.
questions.explain: The engineer worked with leadership to get consistency recognised in planning, so teams could point to cross-organisation impact.
questions.rule: Give participants a reason to take part.

questions.q: What was the real breakthrough sign, according to the story?
options: The last team finished its migration
Leadership praised the campaign in a company-wide meeting after the final migration
The number of APIs reached a round figure
The first external partner integrated without asking a single question
optionExplain: Not the sign given.
Praise is not the sign given.
The count was a result, not the breakthrough.
Right: consistency made integration self-explanatory.
questions.explain: The story calls the first partner integrating without asking a single question the real breakthrough, and the 18-month campaign reached over 200 APIs.
questions.rule: Look for self-service as proof.
questions.teaches: The real breakthrough was the first external partner integrating without asking a single question, and the 18-month campaign reached over 200 APIs.

questions.q: Ten-year-old in-house tools slow hiring and drive experienced people away. What drives a good first step?
options: Show why the tools hurt hiring and retention, and propose industry standards
Order a quick tool swap before the next quarter and retire the old tools at once
Wait for the tools to fail and then react
Add more training for the current tools
optionExplain: Right: the story begins with the talent problem.
Rushing a swap skips trust-building.
Waiting lets the talent loss continue.
Training does not fix non-transferable skills.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next retells the story.
questions.rule: Make the talent cost visible.

questions.q: Match each audience to the benefit the principal stressed.
pairs: Career growth and learning from widely used tools
Onboarding time falling from three months to three weeks
A shared picture where all saw personal and technical benefits
questions.explain: The vision was tailored to what each group cared about.
questions.rule: Tailor the benefit to the audience.

questions.q: You propose a platform change for 300 engineers. Which message follows the story's tailoring?
options: Send one identical announcement to everyone in the organisation, explaining the technical case
Tell engineers about career growth, leaders about speed, and leads about onboarding
Brief leaders only and let them pass it on
Stress technical elegance to every audience
optionExplain: That ignores differing interests.
Right: one vision, three framings.
The story spoke to each group.
Elegance did not address each group's stake.
questions.explain: The principal showed engineers, leadership and team leads the benefits each cared about.
questions.rule: Tailor the case to the audience.

questions.q: Why did senior engineers take ownership of their teams' migrations?
options: They were assigned their migrations by a top-down mandate from the engineering leadership
The principal handed them the hardest parts
They saw the principal solving the hardest problems first and trusted the effort
They had no other work at the time
optionExplain: The story credits trust, not mandate.
The principal took those personally.
Right: credibility from hands-on work.
Nothing says so.
questions.explain: Seeing the principal debug build cache issues at midnight and write tools that preserved workflows built trust.
questions.rule: Take the scariest problem yourself.

questions.q: True or false: the principal's approach was to leave the hardest technical problems for teams to solve.
questions.explain: The principal personally led migration of the most complex build components, dealing with the gnarliest edge cases.
questions.rule: Hard problems first, by you.

questions.q: Which result does the story give for engineering attrition after the migration?
options: It stayed about the same, though productivity rose steadily after the new tools arrived
It doubled during the migration year
It nearly halved, and exit interviews no longer cited the legacy toolchain
It fell to zero
optionExplain: Attrition fell.
No such rise is described.
Right: attrition dropped by nearly half.
It nearly halved.
questions.explain: The story says attrition dropped by nearly half and none of the leavers cited the legacy toolchain as a factor anymore.
questions.rule: Use results that show the people impact.
questions.teaches: Engineering attrition dropped by nearly half, and none of those who left cited the legacy toolchain as a factor anymore.

questions.q: You have not led a company-wide project. How should you search for a strategic example?
options: Look for times you influenced beyond your immediate scope
Look for your largest budget or headcount
Look for projects you finished well ahead of schedule and under budget
Wait until a company-wide project comes along
optionExplain: Right: scope beyond your team is the test.
Size of budget is not the test.
Delivery speed is not the test.
The chapter says you need not wait.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair. The card next gives the chapter's guidance.
questions.rule: Scope beyond your team is the key.

questions.q: Match each kind of evidence to what it shows.
pairs: Built consensus for changes affecting multiple groups
Envisioned possibilities others could not see and helped make them real
questions.explain: Each prompt in the chapter points to a different competency.
questions.rule: Read each prompt as evidence.

questions.q: Sort each memory by whether it is a promising strategic example.

items.t: You noticed three teams solving one problem three ways and proposed one shared tool
You tidied your own team's backlog labels
You saw a small design choice would cause trouble months later and persuaded others to change course
You sped up your personal build script
You got two neighbouring groups to agree on one release calendar
You finished your own tickets before the sprint ended
