questions.q: Beyond saving time, why do check-ins matter for the shape of the conversation?
options: They guarantee that the interviewer will approve of your answers
They prove to the interviewer that you have memorised a story outline
They create natural breakpoints and turn monologues into dialogues
They let you steer the interview toward whichever topic you prefer
optionExplain: Nothing guarantees approval.
They have nothing to do with memorisation.
They change the structure of the talk.
The aim is collaboration, not control.
questions.explain: The author says check-ins create natural breakpoints in your stories and convert monologues into dialogues.
questions.rule: Check-ins create breakpoints.
questions.teaches: Check-ins create natural breakpoints in your stories and convert monologues into dialogues.

questions.q: How often should you check in with the interviewer?
options: After every sentence, to be sure they are following you
Only when they look confused or bored while you speak
Not at all, since a well-built story needs no confirmation
At natural breaks between the major parts of your story
optionExplain: It signals uncertainty.
Reading faces is unreliable.
Check-ins keep it collaborative.
Breaks are where a check-in helps.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows what the author recommends.
questions.rule: Check in at breaks.

questions.q: Checking in after every sentence will make you appear ____.
questions.explain: Overuse of check-ins signals uncertainty.
questions.rule: Do not overdo check-ins.

questions.q: Eva has finished the problem section and is about to move into implementation. What should she do?

Dive straight into the implementation, since she prepared that part most
Ask whether they follow every sentence she has said so far
Skip the implementation altogether to be safe and move to the result
optionExplain: It is a natural transition point.
It risks overexplaining.
It is excessive and signals uncertainty.
It decides for them what they want to hear.

questions.q: True or false: The more often you check in, the more confident you appear.

questions.rule: Frequent checking looks uncertain.

options: After every sentence you say
After explaining a complex technical concept
Whenever you pause to take a breath
Before diving into implementation details
At the very start, before you have said anything
optionExplain: It makes you appear uncertain.
A check on understanding fits here.
A breath is not a transition between sections.
A check on interest fits here.
There is nothing to check yet.

questions.rule: Check at transitions.

questions.q: Wei sees the interviewer writing busily while he explains a design. What does the author suggest?

Keep going and let the interviewer catch up whenever they can
Pause and check whether the interviewer needs any clarification
Ask the interviewer to stop writing and listen to the explanation
optionExplain: It makes note-taking harder.
It risks losing them.
Note-taking is a cue for a check-in.
It disrupts their method.
questions.explain: The author lists the interviewer taking notes as a moment to pause and check whether they need clarification.
questions.rule: Note-taking is a cue.
questions.teaches: When you see the interviewer taking notes, pause and check whether they need any clarification.

questions.q: You are asked about conflict with your manager, but you only have a story about a team disagreement. What do you do?
options: Present the team story as if it were a manager conflict, changing a few details
Say you have not had that exact situation, share the team story, and link it to the question
Say you have no answer and ask to move quickly on to the next question

It leaves them to rescue you.

questions.q: When using a related story, explicitly ____ it to the original question.

questions.rule: Connect the story.

Tell it as if the new hire had been a struggling teammate all along
Say it is not the identical situation, share the onboarding story, and explain how it shows the same coaching skills

questions.rule: Acknowledge and explain the link.

questions.q: How do most interviewers react when a candidate acknowledges the mismatch and links a related story?
options: They mark it down because it did not match the question they asked
They ignore the acknowledgement and wait for the real story to begin
They end the topic and move on to the next question without comment or any follow-up
They appreciate the honesty and accept it, or adjust what they are looking for
optionExplain: The author describes an appreciative response.
The acknowledgement matters to them.
Follow-ups often follow a good related story.

questions.explain: The author says most interviewers will appreciate the honesty and will either accept the related story or adjust what they are looking for.
questions.rule: Honesty is appreciated.

questions.q: Sort these into strong and weak use of a related story.

items.t: Naming the mismatch openly
Explaining why the example shows the same skills
Keeping the lead-in short and moving on to the story
Passing the story off as a perfect match
Leaving the link to the question unstated
Using a story from an unrelated competency and hoping it passes

questions.q: Lin has no story about influencing executives and considers telling one about fixing an office printer. What does the author's view imply?
options: It will likely fail, since forcing an unrelated story never works; she should use it only if she can explain how it shows the same skills

optionExplain: Interviewers can tell when a story is forced.

questions.rule: Forced links fail.
questions.teaches: Forcing an unrelated story never works because interviewers can tell, but if you can clearly explain why your example shows the skills they want, most will accept it.

questions.q: Asked about a situation you have not faced, which answer shows the most judgment?

Describe a story from a friend's career as though it were your own

optionExplain: It is too general to show any real thinking.
It shows how you think.
It breaks the rule of truthfulness.
It misses the chance to show judgment.

questions.rule: Show your reasoning.

questions.q: A hypothetical answer is not an invented story; it explains how you ____ handle the situation.
questions.explain: The author frames it as how you would approach the situation, not as an invented past event.
questions.rule: Say what you would do.

questions.q: Dee has not yet disagreed with a manager. Which answer follows the advice?

I would stay professional and communicate well throughout the process
My manager and I once clashed over a deadline, though it was mostly a misunderstanding

optionExplain: It is specific and grounded in experience.
It is polite but too general to be useful.
It invents a past event.
It abandons the chance to show judgment.

questions.rule: Specific steps, honest framing.

questions.q: True or false: A hypothetical approach works best when you have no related experience to draw on at all.
questions.explain: The author says it works best when you have some related experience to draw from.
questions.rule: Ground it in experience.

questions.q: Sort these into specific enough and too vague.

I would write down the options and the cost of each before the meeting
I would ask each person which outcome matters most to them
I would handle it professionally
I would find a way to keep everybody happy
I would use good judgment

questions.rule: Name the steps.

questions.q: Which phrasing does the author hold up as showing real thinking?
options: I would communicate openly with everyone on the team
I would listen to all views and aim for a good outcome
I would try hard to find common ground quickly
I would document the trade-offs in a shared doc and ask each person to rank their priorities
optionExplain: The author says this tells the interviewer nothing.
It is a general virtue.
It states a hope, not a step.
It names specific steps.
questions.explain: The author contrasts a vague line, I would communicate clearly, which tells the interviewer nothing, with a specific line about documenting trade-offs and asking each person to rank priorities.

questions.q: You have no recent work example of leading through conflict, but you led a student club through one. What do you do?

Share it, say it is not recent professional experience, and show how it displays the skill
Skip it, because only recent professional examples can count
Describe the club in detail at length before mentioning the conflict
optionExplain: It misrepresents the setting.
Framing it openly keeps it credible.
Distant examples are an option the author gives.
Too much background hides the skill.

questions.q: When using a distant example, quickly establish its ____ and then focus on the competency.

questions.rule: Relevance first.

questions.q: Asked about organising a team under pressure, Ola has only run a volunteer food drive. What should she do?
options: Describe the food drive as a company project to make it fit the role
Skip the example and say that she has no experience to talk about
Say it was volunteer work rather than a job, link it to the question, and focus on how she organised people
Spend the answer describing the charity and its history in detail
optionExplain: It misstates the setting.
She has a real example she can use.
She frames it and then shows the skill.
It buries the skill in context.
questions.explain: The author says to establish relevance quickly and focus on the competency.
questions.rule: Frame briefly, focus on skill.

questions.q: True or false: Admitting that a distant example is not recent professional experience will weaken your answer.

questions.rule: Framing helps.

questions.q: Sort these into well framed and poorly framed distant examples.

items.t: This is not recent professional experience, but it shows how I handle conflict
A brief statement of why it is relevant, then straight to the skill
Naming that it was volunteer work and why it fits
Opening with ten minutes of background about the club
Passing a college project off as a recent job
Leaving out why it relates to the question

questions.rule: Frame honestly, then focus.

questions.q: In a distant example, what matters more to the interviewer: the setting or the skill shown?
options: The setting, because a prestigious setting is more impressive to most interviewers
Both equally, so the setting needs as much time as the skill
The skill shown, because the context matters less than showing you possess it
Neither, because distant examples are not weighed at all
optionExplain: The author puts the skill first.
The author says to establish relevance quickly.
The question asks about a skill.
The author recommends using them.
questions.explain: The author says the context matters less than showing that you possess the skill in question.

questions.teaches: In a distant example the context matters less than showing that you possess the skill the question asks about.

questions.q: Asked about a situation you honestly have not faced, with no related story either, what protects your credibility best?
options: Stretch a weak example until it seems to fit the question
Say plainly that you do not have an example
Make up a believable story, since nobody can check it on the spot
Talk around the question without ever saying you lack an example
optionExplain: It invites probing that exposes the stretch.
Honesty keeps your credibility intact.
Deep-dive questions can expose it.
It looks evasive.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows what the author recommends.
questions.rule: Say it plainly.

questions.q: Match each option for handling the unexpected to its description.
pairs: Adapt a story from a related competency
Explain how you would handle the situation
Reach back to college or volunteer work
Say plainly that you have no example

questions.q: Dee has no work example of influencing without authority, but once persuaded unmanaged student volunteers to change a robotics-club strategy. Which option fits best?
options: A hypothetical approach, since she has no real story to tell
Honest acknowledgment, because there is no work example to give
An unrelated story from her current job, with no link to the question
A distant example, framed as not recent professional experience
optionExplain: She does have a real story, so a hypothetical is weaker.
A real example is available, so she need not stop there.
Forcing an unrelated story never works, because interviewers can tell.

questions.q: Sort these responses to a question you cannot answer into honest and risky.

items.t: Say you have no example, then show interest in theirs
Adapt a related story and connect it
Describe how you would approach it with specific steps
Embellish a thin example until it sounds impressive

questions.q: An interviewer asks how you handled rollback. What should your first sentence do?

Describe the whole mechanism step by step in full technical detail
Ask what level of detail they want before you say anything else

Brief expansion in three or four sentences

Full detail

State the choice and its main reason in one sentence, then ask if they want more detail
Walk through the decision timeline starting from the project kickoff

It builds up before reaching the answer.

questions.q: Sort these into following the pyramid and breaking it.

items.t: Opening with the answer in one sentence
Expanding to three or four sentences only when invited
Checking before going into technical specifics
Building up context before stating the answer
Launching into full detail for a simple question
Giving all three levels every time regardless of interest

Another one-sentence summary of what you already said before
A fresh unrelated story about a different project they may like more
An apology for how long the explanation has already become

It adds nothing and undermines confidence.

questions.teaches: Level 3 holds complete technical details, implementation specifics or broader context, such as the flag-management tool, per-feature error tracking, alerts and a dashboard.

questions.q: Most follow-up questions need only one or ____ levels of the pyramid.

Stop there and be ready for the next question
Repeat her Level 1 sentence in case it was missed earlier

It ignores the signal.

questions.rule: Do not offer all three by habit.

questions.q: Sort these signals into ready to move on and wants more depth.

items.t: Leaning back and saying Got it, thanks

Asking for more specifics on one point
Following up on a detail you mentioned

questions.q: The interviewer's face stays serious through your whole answer. What is the most reliable reading?

The author does not list this as a likely meaning.

It is another listed meaning.

questions.q: Which is the most useful sign that an interviewer is engaged?

Her confidence keeps growing, and her positive energy helps make her a great hire
She will no longer need to prepare her key points in advance of interviews
Her delivery will become more scripted as she gets used to telling them
optionExplain: The stories remain the vehicle.
The author links ease, confidence and energy.
The structure is still the foundation.
The author expects it to become more natural.
questions.explain: The author says the investment in delivery pays off immediately: each interview gets easier, confidence grows, stories become natural and positive energy becomes part of what makes you a great hire.
questions.rule: Delivery practice compounds.
questions.teaches: You start to enjoy discussing your work with people who understand it.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which statement best describes how the book's parts relate to the work of preparing?
options: The parts give tools in order, while the pillars name three areas that all need strength
Each part matches one pillar exactly, so a reader can drop the parts that do not match theirs
The pillars apply only to Part I, and the other parts are separate material for later study
The parts are for first-time candidates, and the pillars are for people changing level or company
optionExplain: The parts are the tools; the pillars say which of them must all end up strong.
It treats the two cuts as identical; the pillars cut across the parts.
It confines the pillars to one part, although Part II and Chapter 14 also serve them.
It splits readers by experience, which the book does not do.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows how the two cuts meet.
questions.rule: Parts are tools; pillars are goals.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Part II covers ____ competencies, one in each chapter from Chapter 5 to Chapter 13.
questions.explain: Chapters 5 to 13 are nine chapters, one competency each.
questions.rule: Part II is nine competencies.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Dev has an interview in a week and has not begun. Which route does the book suggest first?
options: All of Part II from Chapter 5 onward, then the framework chapters if time remains
Chapters 3 and 4, then a skim of the nearest Part II chapters, then Chapter 14
Chapter 14 first, since delivery matters most when time is short, then whatever is left
Chapter 2 in full, then every Part II chapter in order, leaving the essentials for later
optionExplain: It starts with reference chapters before he has a method for using them.
It builds the story method and essentials first, then checks competencies and delivery.
It puts delivery before there are any prepared stories to deliver.
It spends the week on background and reads all of Part II, which a week cannot hold.
questions.explain: For a one-week timeline the book suggests Chapters 3 and 4, a skim of the closest competency chapters at his level, then Chapter 14.
questions.rule: Short on time: framework, essentials, nearest competencies, delivery.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each section of the book to its job.
pairs: Teaches how to identify, structure and deliver stories, and ends with the essential questions
Covers the behaviors companies assess, with level examples and cultural variations
Covers delivery techniques and how to handle the unexpected
Offers perspective on applying the skills across a career
questions.explain: Each section has its own job, and together they run from method to evidence to delivery.
questions.rule: Method, evidence, delivery.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate has well-built stories, all at entry level, and applies for a senior role. What do the pillars predict?
options: A senior offer is likely, because clear structure makes the level of a story easy to see
The company's values will decide, since level only matters when values already match
The stories will be read as mid level, because interviewers round up for good delivery
A senior offer is unlikely, since strong building cannot cover weak strength
optionExplain: It treats good building as a substitute for the right level.
It makes level depend on fit, but the two are separate readings.
It assumes delivery quality raises the level, which the authors deny.
Strength in one pillar does not make up for another.
questions.explain: The authors say junior-level stories do not get senior-level offers, however well told, and that all three pillars must be strong.
questions.rule: A weak pillar is not covered by a strong one.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Mina is interviewing at three companies this month. According to the authors, what should she do with her stories?
options: Build one story set for the company she likes best and reuse it unchanged at the other two
Skip Part I because three companies means she needs reference chapters, not a method
Work through Part I, use Part II per company, and note which stories suit which company type
Write three separate banks from scratch, one per company, with no shared stories
optionExplain: It ignores that company values differ, which the second pillar warns about.
It drops the framework at the point she needs the most stories.
It builds one framework, then matches stories to each company.
It wastes the overlap between companies that a shared bank gives.
questions.explain: For several companies the authors suggest working through Part I, using Part II as a reference for each company's values, and keeping notes on which stories work for which company type.
questions.rule: One bank, tagged by company type.
questions.teaches: For several companies at once, the authors say to keep notes on which stories work best for which company types.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Why can an excellent, well-told story still fail to win a senior-level offer?
options: Senior interviewers prefer short stories, and polished ones tend to run long
Level is decided by years of experience, and no story can change that number
Telling skill cannot lift material whose scope and difficulty sit below the target level
Only the company's values decide offers, and level is set by the recruiter afterwards
optionExplain: It invents a length preference; the issue is the content's level.
It makes level a matter of tenure, not of what stories show.
Delivery cannot change what the story shows about level.
It splits fit from level wrongly; interviewers read both from stories.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows the two readings.
questions.rule: Telling well does not lift a story's level.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Behavioral interviews help decide whether you fit the role and company and, if you do, at what ____.
questions.explain: The two questions are fit and level.
questions.rule: Fit, then level.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each problem by the pillar it mainly breaks.

items.t: Offers a story about tuning one query alone for a senior role
Describes a fast, rough launch to a company that prizes careful consensus
Says we throughout, so the interviewer cannot see her own part
Stresses weeks of solo work at a company built on pairing
Offers single-team ownership for a staff role that needs cross-team change
Shows decisions made by instinct at a company that expects data

questions.explain: Level problems hide or lower the scope, contribution, impact or difficulty; fit problems mismatch the company's way of working.
questions.rule: Level: what it shows. Fit: how it works.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Amara's stories sit at mid level and match the company's values well. She applies for a senior role. What follows?
options: A good fit reading but a level reading below target, so down-leveling is likely
A senior offer, because strong fit usually moves a mid-level candidate up a level
No effect, because senior roles are filled on fit and level is settled after the offer
Rejection only for lack of fit, since mid-level stories are never read for level
optionExplain: Fit and level are separate, and the weak one decides.
It lets fit raise the level, but the readings are separate.
It treats level as an afterthought, but interviewers read it from stories.
It has the readings reversed; level is read from every story.
questions.explain: Fit does not raise level. A wrong level reading means down-leveling or rejection as underqualified.
questions.rule: Check level separately from fit.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: If each of your stories passes both checks, your story bank is complete for any company.
questions.explain: The two checks test single stories. The bank also needs enough stories for the essential questions and for the competencies and level you target.
questions.rule: Good stories are not yet a full bank.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Jon's stories all show fast shipping. He moves from a startup to a firm that values process and consensus. What is the book's view of the difference?
options: The startup rewarded real skill and the firm rewards procedure, so he should expect a lower level
Fast shipping is a universal strength, so the same stories will fit every company type
He should drop shipping stories and invent consensus-building ones to suit the firm
Neither is better; they reward different approaches, so he needs stories that fit
optionExplain: It ranks one environment above the other, which the authors decline to do.
It assumes values never differ, against the matching pillar.
It swaps real stories for invented ones, which the book rules out.
It treats the gap as a difference to bridge, not a ranking.
questions.explain: The authors say neither a small company nor an enterprise is inherently better; they are different environments that reward different approaches.
questions.rule: Different environments, different emphasis.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, neither a small company nor an enterprise is inherently better: they are different environments that reward different approaches.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate lists six major projects. How many usable stories can she expect from them?
options: Exactly six, because each project can give only one story that is honest and complete
More than six, because each project can hold several separate behavioral moments
Fewer than six, since projects that ran for weeks have too little detail to retell
As many as the months the projects lasted, since longer work gives more material
optionExplain: It equates a story with a project, the approach the authors move away from.
A story is a moment, and projects contain many moments.
It treats long projects as hard to retell, but they hold the most moments.
It counts duration, but the authors count key moments, not time.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows the count rule.
questions.rule: Count moments, not projects.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A single strong story can answer an essential question, cover several ____ and show the right scope for your level.
questions.explain: The three sources overlap, so one story can serve all of them.
questions.rule: One story can serve three sources.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Leo has one story about rescuing a late payment-system launch. Which use fits the overlap idea?
options: Keep it for delivery questions only, since a story belongs to one competency
Retell it for every question in the interview, changing the opening line each time
Use it for the proudest project, then check it against delivery and his level
Set it aside until he has a story for each competency, then pick the best of them
optionExplain: It confines the story to one need, wasting the overlap.
It overuses one story, which leaves the rest of the bank empty.
It makes one story serve three needs at once.
It delays using a strong story while the gaps remain unfilled.
questions.explain: The authors say a single strong story can answer an essential question, cover several competencies and show the scope of the level.
questions.rule: Check a strong story against all three needs.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Because one story can serve three needs, three or four well-built stories can cover any company's interview.
questions.explain: Overlap reduces the count but does not remove it: the essential questions, the company's competencies and your level still ask for varied moments and gap-filling.
questions.rule: Overlap reduces the count; it does not reduce it to a handful.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Jo applies for a mid-level role at a product company. How many competencies does the book suggest she cover?
options: Four to six, the same as an entry-level candidate, with the same core competencies
Five to seven, adding initiative and trust-and-conflict to an entry-level core
Seven to ten, because a product company expects every competency at any level
Exactly two, her best, because depth in a few stories beats breadth in many
optionExplain: It copies the entry-level range, which the book raises for mid level.
It matches the book's mid-level range and additions.
It applies the senior range to a mid-level role.
It contradicts the book's ranges, which grow with level.
questions.explain: The authors give entry level four to six competencies, mid level five to seven, and senior level and beyond seven to ten.
questions.rule: More competencies as the level rises.
questions.teaches: The book sizes the competency list by level: four to six at entry level, five to seven at mid level (adding initiative and trust and conflict) and seven to ten at senior level and beyond.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A company prizes speed. How should a candidate with a well-run six-month project prepare?
options: Pick the true parts of the project that show fast, iterative delivery and lead with them
Describe the project as faster than it was, since the company will reward the speed claim
Tell the project in strict time order, since speed is shown by how long each month took
Leave the project out, because a long project cannot show speed to a fast-moving company
optionExplain: It chooses true material that matches the company.
It inflates the facts to match, which breaks the truth boundary entirely.
It confuses a timeline with the emphasis the company values.
It drops a real project instead of choosing which part to tell.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows what research can and cannot change.
questions.rule: Research picks the emphasis.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Research can change the emphasis of a story, but it cannot change the ____ of what you did.
questions.explain: Emphasis is a choice among true aspects; the facts stay as they were.
questions.rule: Emphasis flexes; facts do not.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Ana ran a checkout redesign with strong tests and a record-fast launch. The company prizes technical rigour. How should she tell it?
options: Claim she designed the underlying architecture, which a colleague owned, to sound more rigorous
Tell the same speed-first version, since the launch was the most impressive part of the project
Pick a different project she did not lead but knows well, since it sounds more rigorous
Lead with the testing decisions she really made and mention the fast launch as a result
optionExplain: It claims a contribution that was not hers, which is fabrication.
It ignores the research, wasting the chance to match the company.
It borrows a story that is not hers, which is not honest.
She emphasises what the company values, using true material.
questions.explain: The book says to select which experiences to share and which aspects to emphasise; it does not allow claiming work that was not yours.
questions.rule: Re-order the true material; do not add.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each move into honest emphasis or fabrication.

items.t: Opening with customer impact for a customer-obsessed company
Choosing the cross-team story over a solo one for a collaborative culture
Leaving out a technical tangent to keep to the company's priorities
Saying she led a team she joined only late in the project
Adding a made-up metric to suit a data-driven culture
Describing an experience she never had, in the company's own value words

questions.explain: Choosing what to tell and in what order is emphasis; adding what did not happen is fabrication.
questions.rule: Select and order, never invent.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: After research, Dana finds none of her experience matches what a company values. What does the author say this tells her?
options: It is useful information: gain such experience, choose another role or seek another culture
It shows her stories are weak, so she should rework the facts until they match the company's values
It shows the company is wrong for everyone, so she should stop researching companies of this type
It shows she should hide the mismatch and answer in the company's words, as a way to adapt
optionExplain: It treats a mismatch as a signal to act on, not a verdict.
It treats a mismatch as a flaw in her stories to be repaired by changing them.
It generalises from one company to a whole type of company.
It conceals a mismatch the authors say is worth knowing early.
questions.explain: The authors say a mismatch is useful information: maybe this is not the right role, maybe she needs to acquire those experiences, or maybe she needs a different culture.
questions.rule: A mismatch is information.
questions.teaches: If your experiences do not match what a company values, the authors call that useful information: you may need to gain those experiences, pick another role or look for a different culture.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: How do interviewers mostly decide the level a story shows?
options: From the job title the candidate held, which sets the level of every story told
From the pattern of scope, contribution, impact and difficulty across the story
From how long the project ran, since longer projects always show higher levels
From how confident the candidate sounds, since confident delivery signals seniority
optionExplain: It reads level from a title, but stories can be above or below a title.
Level is read from the content, across several dimensions.
It uses duration as a proxy, which does not measure what the person did.
It reads delivery style as level, although telling does not raise level.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows the pattern.
questions.rule: Level is a pattern across dimensions.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Make sure at least two or three stories sit solidly at your ____ level, and lead with them.
questions.explain: Mixed levels are normal, so lead with the stories at the level you want.
questions.rule: Lead with stories at your target.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Tom targets a staff role. His best story: he owned one team's deployment pipeline, and one other team adopted it. What does the book flag?
options: A staff-level story, because a pipeline another team adopted already crosses team lines
A story with unearned scope, because pipelines are never owned by one person
A story with no difficulty, because deployment pipelines are routine work at any level
A mid-level story: single-team ownership, where staff roles need cross-team consensus
optionExplain: It counts one adoption as cross-team leadership at staff level.
It misreads the flag; the problem is level, not false ownership.
It dismisses the work, but the issue is the scope of ownership.
The scope stops at one team, short of the staff pattern.
questions.explain: The authors give this example of mid-level stories for staff roles: single-team ownership when the role needs cross-team leadership.
questions.rule: Match scope to the level.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Rosa has three mid-level stories and plans senior-sounding headlines for them. What is wrong with the plan?
options: Nothing, since headlines set the level and the rest of the story is only supporting detail
Headlines should be left out, because the authors say a story needs no opening sentence
Framing cannot change the real scope, contribution, impact or difficulty
Senior-sounding words would be fine if she used them in the core instead of the headline
optionExplain: It gives the headline the power to set the level, which it does not have.
It misstates the book, which asks for a headline on every story.
It identifies that framing cannot change what the story shows.
It moves the same inflation to another place in the story.
questions.explain: The authors warn that three mid-level stories with senior-level framing is not enough; the stories need to show the target level.
questions.rule: Framing cannot raise the dimensions.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors call mixed levels within a story set normal, provided two or three stories sit solidly at the target.
questions.explain: Mixed levels are expected; what matters is that enough stories sit solidly at the target level and lead the set.
questions.rule: Mixed levels are normal.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sam describes a project he led as something he only took part in, to sound modest. What risk do the authors point to?
options: Rejection for overreaching, since modest phrasing hides how much he claimed to lead
No risk, since interviewers always probe and will find the real scope by themselves
Loss of credibility only, since vague phrasing is read as a form of exaggeration
Down-leveling, because he has not communicated what he can do
optionExplain: It swaps the risks; overreaching is the opposite error.
It assumes the interviewer will repair a vague account, which is not guaranteed.
It treats understatement as exaggeration, which are different errors.
Under-communicating capability costs a level.
questions.explain: The authors say getting this wrong means being rejected for overreaching or down-leveled for not communicating capabilities properly.
questions.rule: Both over- and under-claiming cost you.
questions.teaches: The authors name two costs of mis-framing: rejection for overreaching, or down-leveling for not properly communicating your capabilities.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Why build an answer as headline, core and base instead of telling events in order?
options: So the behaviors reach the interviewer's notes and the detail waits until it is asked for
So the story is shorter than a minute, which is the longest an interviewer will listen to
So the candidate can skip the result, which interviewers can work out from the actions
So every candidate sounds the same, which makes the interviewers' comparison easier
optionExplain: The layers put behaviors up front and keep detail ready.
It invents a time limit; the core runs about two minutes.
It drops the result, which belongs in the core.
It confuses a shared structure with a scripted, identical answer.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows the reasoning.
questions.rule: Behaviors first, detail on request.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put these steps in order, from raw experience to what the interviewer hears.
items: Pick one story-worthy moment from a larger project
Write a one-sentence headline that previews it
Build a core of about two minutes with your thinking, actions and result
Hold the technical and team detail in the base until asked
questions.explain: The moment comes first, then the headline, the core and finally the held-back base.
questions.rule: Moment, headline, core, base.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A clinic coordinator tells a story about cutting patient waits. Sort each detail into core or base.

items.t: How she noticed the pattern in the daily queue data
Why she chose to act before anyone assigned it to her
The result: waits fell by about a third
Which scheduling software the clinic bought years earlier
The two alternatives she considered and set aside
How the night shift reacted when the change began

questions.explain: The core carries signals of how she noticed, decided and what resulted; background and side detail wait in the base.
questions.rule: Signal in the core, detail in the base.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate converts her STAR story by relabelling Situation as the headline and Task as the core. What did she miss?
options: Nothing; the STAR parts map one to one onto headline, core and base in order
She should have deleted the Result, since the pyramid leaves outcomes for the base
Conversion is a rewrite: shrink the setup, expand Action, move Result into the core
She should have kept Situation long, since context is what makes the action understandable
optionExplain: It treats the pyramid as STAR with new names.
It misplaces the result, which belongs in the core.
It rebuilds the story, not only its labels.
It keeps the setup-heavy shape that the pyramid replaces.
questions.explain: The authors move the highlights to the headline, expand the Action in the core, shrink Situation and Task, and put the Result in the core and the Learning in the base.
questions.rule: Convert by rewriting, not relabelling.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Midway through, the interviewer asks how the night shift reacted. Which layer supplies the answer?
options: The headline, repeated word for word, since the interviewer is asking about the main point
The base, which she prepared and held back, so she answers from prepared detail
The core, which she must now extend by retelling the story from the start
None; she should say the detail is not relevant and move straight to her next story
optionExplain: The headline previews the story and does not hold side detail.
The base exists to answer follow-ups like this one.
It restarts the core for a question that the base can answer.
It dismisses a follow-up the base was built to answer.
questions.explain: Team reactions are base-layer material, kept ready for exactly this kind of question.
questions.rule: Follow-ups are answered from the base.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Lena spends five minutes on her company's history before reaching her actions. What cost do the authors point to?
options: Interviewers cannot write down any history, so the five minutes are lost to their notes
History is confidential, so mentioning a company's past can breach the candidate's contract
The interviewer will assume the actions came from the history and credit it, not her
The interview has about 45 minutes, so heavy context takes time from other stories
optionExplain: It gives a note-taking reason, but the cost is time across answers.
It invents a legal risk that the book does not raise.
It guesses at credit, although the cost named is lost time.
The time limit makes context costly across the whole interview.
questions.explain: The authors note that a behavioral interview has about 45 minutes to cover several questions through different stories, so five minutes on context for one story limits what you can show.
questions.rule: Time spent on context is time taken from other stories.
questions.teaches: A behavioral interview has about 45 minutes to cover several questions through different stories, so five minutes of context on one story limits what you can showcase.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate explains a missed deadline by listing other teams' delays. What impression is she most likely to give?
options: Someone who does not own outcomes and may blame others when this project runs into trouble
Someone realistic, since naming the real causes of a delay shows clear and honest analysis
Someone loyal, since explaining a team's delays shows care for the people she works with
Someone cautious, since pointing to outside risks shows she plans for what could go wrong
optionExplain: The authors say interviewers imagine the same blame later.
It credits the list as honesty, but the story names no action of hers.
It reads the list as loyalty, but it shifts focus from her own part.
It reads blame as planning, though no plan or action is described.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows what the flags have in common.
questions.rule: Own what you controlled.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each flag to what it makes the interviewer conclude.
pairs: Your credibility is damaged, and later claims become doubtful
You may not own outcomes when a project hits trouble
They cannot tell what you did, so cannot judge your level
You may not estimate or manage scope well
questions.explain: Each flag costs a different kind of trust: credibility, ownership, assessability or planning.
questions.rule: Each flag has its own cost.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Mei reports that we cut load time by 80 percent, but her own part was one query. How should she revise it?
options: Keep we and add the team's size, since a bigger team makes the result look more credible
Say I cut load time by 80 percent, since the result is what interviewers are listening for
Say what she decided and did on the query, and what her teammates did on the rest
Drop the number and say the team helped users, since figures invite hard follow-up questions
optionExplain: It adds a number but leaves her part hidden.
It claims the whole result, which turns vagueness into exaggeration.
It separates her contribution from the team's.
It removes the evidence and still hides her part.
questions.explain: The authors want the line between what you did and what the team did to be clear, without claiming the team's work as yours.
questions.rule: Separate your part from the team's.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which version repairs the blame in 'QA kept rejecting my build, which is why we shipped late'?
options: QA were only doing their job, but they still held up the release by rejecting two builds
QA found issues in two builds, so I added a pre-release check; the third passed
We shipped late because of testing problems that came up during the later stages of the release
I take the full blame for the delay, since I should have caught every issue before QA saw it
optionExplain: It softens the blame but still explains the delay by what others did.
It names what she controlled and did.
It removes the name but keeps the excuse and stays vague.
It over-owns without describing any action she took.
questions.explain: The repair keeps the facts but moves the story to what she controlled and did about the obstacle.
questions.rule: Obstacle first, your action second.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Rounding a figure you cannot recall exactly counts as the exaggeration flag.
questions.explain: The rule is against inflating a claim. The authors say rough figures are fine when you cannot recall exact ones; false precision is the problem.
questions.rule: Rough is fine; inflated is not.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Ben is tempted to say he led a migration he joined late. What do the authors say may follow?
options: Little, because interviewers rarely check details so long as the headline is strong
A mild penalty, since a small exaggeration is a normal part of how candidates present
It can be exposed, with consequences from rejection to career-ending termination
A better outcome, since a bolder claim can lift the level the interviewer assigns
optionExplain: It assumes interviewers do not probe, but deep follow-ups are standard.
It treats exaggeration as normal, against the book's strongest advice.
Fabrications get exposed, and the costs can be severe.
It gambles that exaggeration raises level, though it risks credibility.
questions.explain: The authors say fabrications get exposed, and the consequences range from immediate rejection to career-ending termination.
questions.rule: Fabrications get exposed.
questions.teaches: The authors warn that fabrications get exposed, with consequences that range from immediate rejection to career-ending termination.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which essential question most calls for a headline-and-core story?
options: Tell me about yourself and your career so far
Tell me about a project you are proud of
Tell me why you left your last job
Tell me why you want to work at this company
optionExplain: It is a personal summary, not a behavioral story.
It asks for evidence of behavior in a real project.
It calls for a brief, forward-looking answer, not a full account.
It calls for research and fit in a short answer.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows which questions get which form.
questions.rule: Pyramid for the project question.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each question by the form of answer it calls for.

items.t: Tell me about yourself
Why do you want to work at this company?
Why did you leave your last role?
Tell me about the project you are proudest of
Describe the most technically complex project you worked on
Tell me about the most challenging project you handled

questions.explain: The personal essentials get brief answers; the three project variants get the pyramid.
questions.rule: Personal essentials short; project question pyramid.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Jo is asked for her most complex project. She has an impact-heavy story and a deep-design story. What should she do?
options: Pick the impact-heavy story, since results are what interviewers weigh most in every variant
Tell both stories in a row so the interviewer can choose which one counts as the answer
Write a new core from scratch, because each variant needs different actions and decisions
Pick the deep-design story, with a headline that stresses complexity
optionExplain: It ignores that complexity is what this variant asks for.
It doubles the length where one headline-and-core is wanted.
It rebuilds the core, though only the headline changes much.
It matches the question variant with the headline.
questions.explain: The authors suggest a different headline for each variant while the behavioral core stays largely the same, and a complex-project answer should stress technical depth and scope.
questions.rule: New headline, same core.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Dana answers a question about leaving her last job with three minutes on what went wrong. What is the main fault?
options: It is far too long and detailed; the answer should be brief, neutral and forward-looking
It is too short, since the interviewer needs the whole story to understand the decision
It should have been told as a pyramid story, with a headline and a behavioral core
It names the wrong person, since the authors say to give the manager's name first
optionExplain: The question calls for a short answer without a full account.
It reverses the fault; the authors say she need not explain everything.
It treats a personal essential as a project question.
It invents a rule; the authors advise against badmouthing anyone.
questions.explain: The authors suggest 30 to 60 seconds, without explaining everything that went wrong or filling the silence.
questions.rule: Brief, neutral, forward.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: If the interviewer asks for the most challenging project instead of the most complex, the part to rewrite is mainly the ____.
questions.explain: A different headline for each variant, with the core largely the same, is the authors' advice.
questions.rule: Variant changes the headline.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Chen has a high-impact, simple-build story and a thorny-design, modest-impact story. Per the authors, which fits 'proudest project'?
options: The thorny-design story, because interviewers usually look for technical difficulty
Whichever he finds simpler to tell, because all variants are judged on delivery
Neither, because proud projects are personal and belong with the short answers
The high-impact story, because the proud variant is about the impact of the work
optionExplain: It matches the complex variant, not the proud one.
It drops the variant matching the authors recommend.
It files the project question with the short answers.
It matches the choice of project to the question variant.
questions.explain: According to the authors, match the project to the variant: the proud story should emphasise impact, the complex story technical depth and scope, the challenging story overcoming obstacles.
questions.rule: Choose the project to fit the variant.
questions.teaches: The authors match the project to the variant: proud emphasises impact, complex emphasises technical depth and scope, and challenging emphasises overcoming obstacles.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate has one story for a delivery question. How should she decide what to emphasise?
options: Give equal time to every signal the chapter lists, so the story covers the whole competency
Show the strongest evidence for the competency's top-ranked signal, then add lower-ranked evidence
Lead with whichever detail is most impressive, since interviewers weigh the most striking detail
Start with the lowest-ranked signal, which is the easiest for the interviewer to understand
optionExplain: It spreads the story thinly instead of weighting it.
The tiers rank evidence, so the top tier leads.
It uses impressiveness, not the competency's ranking.
It reverses the ranking the book gives.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows how the chapters rank signals.
questions.rule: Critical signal first.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each competency to its critical signal.
questions.explain: Each competency has its own top-tier signal, and the nine chapters share the tier structure.
questions.rule: Each competency has its own critical signal.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Elena noticed a failing nightly job, chose to fix it although it was unassigned, and told the team as she worked. Which tier is this evidence?
options: Critical for initiative: the proactive decision and acting while communicating
Strong for initiative: it shows she noticed a pattern others had missed in the job's failures
Supporting for initiative: it shows she followed her work through to a measured impact
None, because fixing a failing job is assigned work for any engineer on the team
optionExplain: Both critical signals of the initiative chapter appear.
It treats the decision as the pattern-spotting signal, which ranks lower.
It treats it as follow-through, which the story does not mention.
It ignores that the job was unassigned and she chose to act.
questions.explain: Initiative has two critical signals, the proactive decision and acting while communicating, and Elena's story shows both.
questions.rule: Match evidence to the right tier.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In the problem-solving chapter, which signal sits in the supporting tier?
options: Methodical investigation, the repeatable way of gathering evidence and testing theories
Distinguishing symptoms from causes, tracing a problem to its source before fixing it
Learning from investigation, leaving something the team can reuse
Recognizing when to ask for help, telling productive struggle from wasted time
optionExplain: It is the critical signal, the top tier for this chapter.
It is a strong signal, in the middle tier.
It is the supporting signal that adds value after the investigation.
It is also a strong signal, not a supporting one.
questions.explain: In the problem-solving chapter, methodical investigation is critical, symptoms versus causes and asking for help are strong, and learning from investigation is supporting.
questions.rule: Learning from investigation is supporting.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The chapters ask you to build a story around the top-tier signal rather than to cram in every signal listed.
questions.explain: The chapters rank the signals and ask you to build around the top tier; they do not require all of them in one story.
questions.rule: Rank, not checklist.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate offers hard work on her assigned project as an initiative story. How do the authors class that?
options: As a yellow flag, a concerning pattern that weakens the example but does not damage it
As a red flag, a serious issue that significantly damages the candidacy
As a supporting signal, because extra effort always adds some evidence of initiative
As a strong signal, since long hours on assigned work show commitment to the team
optionExplain: It uses the lower category, but the book ranks this as red.
Mistaking hard work for initiative is a red flag.
It counts effort as initiative, which is the confusion the flag names.
It rewards the confusion the chapter warns against.
questions.explain: The authors use Red Flags for serious issues that significantly damage a candidacy and Yellow Flags for concerning patterns that weaken examples; hard work on assigned tasks is a red flag for initiative.
questions.rule: Red flags damage; yellow flags weaken.
questions.teaches: In the book a Red Flag is a serious issue that significantly damages your candidacy, and a Yellow Flag is a concerning pattern that weakens your examples.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate tells how she restored a failing service within an hour. Which competency does the speed of restoring service mainly show?
options: Problem-solving, since any fix of a failure is evidence of depth in finding the cause
Innovation, since restoring a service in an hour needs a new approach to the problem
Initiative, since she acted fast on a problem without waiting for anyone to tell her to
Delivery, which is about getting working solutions to users despite obstacles
optionExplain: It treats a fast fix as depth, but problem-solving is about causes.
It assumes speed needs a new method, which is not claimed.
It assumes the problem was unassigned, which is not stated.
Speed of restoring service is the delivery side.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows the deciding question for each competency.
questions.rule: Ask which question the story answers.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
