questions.q: Match each red flag to the competency it imitates.
questions.explain: Each chapter names a red flag, and several of them are look-alikes of the competency.
questions.rule: Each chapter has a named red flag.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each example by whether it shows initiative.

items.t: Noticed unowned flaky tests and chose to fix them
Spotted a risk before it became critical and proposed an unrequested fix
Fixed a recurring error nobody had asked her to look at
Worked weekends to finish the assigned release
Completed every task assigned in the sprint
Stayed late to meet a deadline her manager had set

questions.explain: Initiative is choosing to act on a problem nobody assigned; effort on assigned work is diligence.
questions.rule: Who chose the problem?

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Hana's monitoring tool uses a known approach but halves false alerts. Does the book count it as innovation?
options: Probably not, since similar results from refining an existing method point to optimization
Yes, since halving false alerts is an improvement that opens new possibilities for the team
Yes, since any tool that someone builds is a new way of solving a problem at the company
Only if the alerts were halved in under a month, since speed is what marks an innovation
optionExplain: A known approach with better results is optimization.
It treats the size of the improvement as newness.
It treats building as inventing, ignoring the approach.
It adds a time condition the book does not set.
questions.explain: The book says that making something faster or more reliable is valuable, but it is innovative only if you used a new approach.
questions.rule: Innovation needs a new approach.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: One story can honestly serve two competencies if you tell the part of it that proves each.
questions.explain: The authors say competencies overlap and that the best candidates show more than one; the labels are for emphasis.
questions.rule: Overlap is allowed; mislabelling is not.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Leo debugs a complex system failure and then invents a new monitoring approach for failures nobody saw. What does the book say about such a candidate?
options: He should present only one competency, since a story that shows two cannot be graded
He should call all of it innovation, since the new monitoring approach is the larger part
He shows both: problem-solving by analysis and innovation by the new approach
He should call all of it problem-solving, since the failure was what began the work
optionExplain: It assumes a story can prove only one competency.
It folds the careful analysis into the innovation label.
The book's own example pairs the two.
It folds the new approach into problem-solving.
questions.explain: The authors give this exact pairing: debugging a failure by careful analysis is problem-solving, inventing a new monitoring approach is innovation, and the best candidates show both.
questions.rule: Show both where both are true.
questions.teaches: The book's example pairs the two: debugging a complex failure through careful analysis is problem-solving, then inventing a new monitoring approach for silent failures is innovation, and the best candidates show both.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate ends by saying she learned a lot about communication. What does the interviewer still lack?
options: A longer list of the tools she used, since tools show how deeply she worked on it
A concrete result: what changed, for whom, and how she knows
A statement of who was to blame for the problems, so the story has a clear cause
A repeat of the headline, so the story ends where it began for easier note-taking
optionExplain: It asks for more activity detail when the gap is the result.
The ending offers a feeling, not an outcome.
It asks for blame, which is a red flag.
It repeats the opening, adding no result.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows what the chapters ask for.
questions.rule: End on what changed.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Close each story on a specific ____: what shipped, who used it and what changed.
questions.explain: The chapters repeatedly ask for a concrete outcome as the close of a story.
questions.rule: Close on a result.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each weak ending to what it needs to add.
pairs: I put in long hours and finished every task
What actually shipped and who used it
I traced the bug through five layers of the system
What improved because of that deep dive
I built a clever new internal tool
Who adopted it and what they gained
I proposed an ambitious plan for the platform
We worked it out and the relationship improved
What specifically changed in how you work
questions.explain: Each weak ending names effort or an idea and stops; each fix adds the result that the matching chapter asks for.
questions.rule: Add the result each chapter asks for.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Omar cannot recall the exact figure for his result. What do the authors suggest?
options: Leave the number out, since an inexact figure is worse than a result with no number at all
Pick an exact-sounding number, since precision shows that he measured the result carefully
Give a rough baseline and an informal relative measure, without claiming false accuracy
Say the result cannot be measured, so the interviewer does not expect any figure at all
optionExplain: It removes the evidence, although rough figures are acceptable.
It invents false precision, which sounds suspicious.
Rough numbers convey scale honestly.
It claims the result is unmeasurable and still gives no outcome.
questions.explain: The authors say precision matters less than a sense of impact, and advise rough baselines and informal relative measures that convey scale.
questions.rule: Rough and honest beats precise and invented.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Mina has a failed prototype that taught her a lot, and a polished design that was not built. Which does the book favour?
options: The failed prototype, because building and testing beats an idea left on the whiteboard
The polished design, because a finished plan shows more thinking than an unfinished build
Neither, because a story without a successful result cannot be used in an interview
Both, merged into one story so the polish of the design hides the prototype's failure
optionExplain: She moved from concept to action.
It rewards the plan, but the authors want action.
It rejects failure, but a failed attempt that taught something can be used.
It blends the two and conceals the failure.
questions.explain: The authors say a failed attempt that taught something valuable is far stronger than a theoretical idea that stayed on the whiteboard.
questions.rule: Action beats an untested idea.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, even a story about a failed attempt that taught you something valuable is far stronger than a theoretical idea that stayed on the whiteboard.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: How should a well-prepared candidate treat a prepared story during the interview?
options: As a script, recited in the same words each time so that nothing important is left out
As a loose idea, improvised afresh in each answer so that it sounds spontaneous
As a document, handed over in outline so that the interviewer can read the details
As the start of a conversation, with fixed key points and flexible wording
optionExplain: It makes delivery a performance, which the book warns against.
It drops the structure that the preparation provides.
It treats the story as a handout, not a conversation.
It combines the foundation and the flexibility.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. The card next shows how structure and conversation combine.
questions.rule: Structure plus conversation.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Your stories should be the start of a conversation, not a memorized ____.
questions.explain: The authors say natural delivery adapts to follow-ups and to the interviewer's interest.
questions.rule: A conversation, not a monologue.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Halfway through her core, Ines is asked how her team tested the change. What fits the combined approach?
options: Answer directly, check whether more is wanted, then bridge back to her key points
Say she will cover testing at the end, and carry on exactly as she had planned the story
Drop the story and improvise a new one about testing from the beginning of her notes
Give a very long answer on testing and then end the story there, as it has been interrupted
optionExplain: It follows the question and keeps the structure.
It postpones the interviewer's interest, which is the conversation.
It abandons the structure instead of answering within it.
It lets the interruption end the story without a bridge back.
questions.explain: Answering the interruption fully and then bridging back combines responsiveness with structure.
questions.rule: Answer, check, bridge back.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each element into what you hold fixed and what can flex.

items.t: The facts and figures of the story
The key points you want to land
The truth of your account of what you did
The exact wording of each sentence
The order in which you reach your key points
How deep you go on a given point

questions.explain: The substance is prepared and held; the wording, order and depth follow the conversation.
questions.rule: Hold the substance; flex the route.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which reading of natural delivery goes wrong?
options: Natural means following the interviewer's lead while still landing the key points
Natural means answering a follow-up with the headline first and expanding if asked
Natural means telling the same true story in different words on different days
Natural means improvising without prepared key points, so preparation is not needed
optionExplain: It follows the conversation and keeps the structure.
It applies the pyramid to a follow-up.
It lets wording vary while the facts stay put.
It drops the foundation; natural delivery rests on preparation.
questions.explain: The authors balance structure with flexibility; without structure there is nothing for the conversation to rest on.
questions.rule: No structure, no foundation.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Asked about leading a company-wide change, Ola has no such story. Which answer fits the book?
options: Describe a company-wide change she watched from the side as though she had led it
Answer with a different question's story and never mention that it was not what was asked
Say so, then adapt a related, smaller story honestly and tie it to the question
Say that she cannot answer, then stop speaking until the interviewer asks something else
optionExplain: It fabricates a role, which the book rules out.
It dodges the question without saying so.
It follows the book's related-story option.
It gives no related story, hypothetical or honest framing at all.
questions.explain: The authors give four options for the unexpected: adapt a related story, describe how you would approach it, reach for a distant example, or honestly say you have no example.
questions.rule: Adapt honestly; never invent.
questions.teaches: The authors give four options when no story fits: adapt a related story, describe how you would approach it, reach back to a distant example, or honestly say you have no example.

questions.section: 2.4 Reading and Calibrating Your Own Level
questions.q: In the worked row, ratings differ by column yet one overall level is entered. What does that show about how a level is read?
options: The highest-rated column decides the level, here the senior contribution
The most common column rating decides the level, here mid
The level comes from the pattern across all columns, so it can sit between two labels
The scope column decides the level, since it is the first one scored
questions.explain: The row mixes mid and senior ratings and records mid-senior overall, so no single column decided it. A level is read as a pattern across all four dimensions.
optionExplain: Rejected: the highest rating is senior, but the overall entry is mid-senior, not senior.
Rejected: mid appears most often, yet the overall entry is mid-senior, not mid.
Correct: the overall cell blends the four columns into a level between two labels.
Rejected: scope is rated mid, but the overall entry is mid-senior, so scope alone did not decide it.
questions.rule: Read a story's level as a pattern across all four dimensions, not from any single one.

media.alt: A blank scoring table with columns for story topic, scope, contribution, impact, difficulty and overall level, each with a guiding question. One worked row, about repairing a deployment process, rates scope mid, contribution senior, impact mid, difficulty mid or senior, and overall mid-senior. Two empty rows follow.

questions.section: 11.1.1 Innovation vs. Optimization: Understanding the Difference
questions.q: Suppose refining the old method could not match a result, yet nothing new was created. Where does the flowchart end?
options: Still optimization, because no new approach or rule was created
Innovation, because refining the old method could not match the result
Optimization, because refining the old method would have reached the result
Neither, because the flowchart has no branch for this case
questions.explain: The first question sends the case down the no branch, and the second asks whether a new approach or rule was created. Without one, the flowchart ends at still optimization.
optionExplain: Correct: the second question gets a no, which the flowchart labels still optimization.
Rejected: the second question must also be answered yes before the flowchart says innovation.
Rejected: the scenario says refining could not match the result, so the first question was answered no.
Rejected: the second question has a no branch that ends in still optimization.
questions.rule: Count work as innovation only when it created a new approach, not merely when refining fell short.

media.alt: A decision flowchart. First question: could someone get a similar result by refining the existing approach? Yes leads to optimization. No leads to a second question: did this require creating a new approach or rule? Yes leads to innovation, no leads to still optimization.

questions.unitTitle: Earning Trust and Dealing with Conflict
questions.section: 8.1 What Does It Mean to Earn Trust and Deal With Conflict?
questions.q: In the comparison, which remarks challenge the idea rather than the person? Select all that apply.
options: Telling the author that they designed the system badly
Saying the design will fail once traffic grows
Telling a colleague that they do not understand the topic
Saying you think one assumption in the design is risky
questions.explain: The right-hand remarks aim at the design and an assumption, which keeps respect for the person who made it. The left-hand remarks judge the person.
optionExplain: Wrong: this judges the author, not the design's behavior.
Right: it targets how the design behaves, not who made it.
Wrong: this judges the colleague's understanding.
Right: it names a specific assumption as a risk and leaves the person out.
questions.rule: Challenge the idea and respect the expertise of the person who holds it.

media.alt: A vertical line splits two columns of speech bubbles. On the left, marked with a cross, one speaker criticises the designer and the reply attacks the other person's understanding. On the right, marked with a check, the remarks say the design breaks under heavy use and flag a risky assumption.

questions.q: True or false: in the diagram's flow, delivery is complete at the build stage, before the solution reaches users.
questions.explain: The arrows run from idea through build and ship to users, and delivery means a working solution reaches them. A built feature held back by a failed dependency has not been delivered.
questions.rule: Judge delivery by whether the working solution reaches users, not by whether the build is done.

media.alt: A left-to-right flow of four labelled stages joined by arrows: idea (light bulb), build (checklist with gear), ship (box with check mark) and users (group of people). A smiling man with open hands stands beneath, under a caption about shipping valuable solutions to users.

questions.section: 2.2 The Four Dimensions That Determine Your Level
questions.q: A mid-level engineer already owns whole solutions for her team. In the staircase, what must her stories add to read as the next level?
options: The same ownership, completed more quickly
Impact driven across several teams
Systems shaped across the whole organization
Work led at the level of a team
questions.explain: The step above owning full solutions is leading team-level work. Cross-team impact and organization-wide systems sit two and three steps higher.
optionExplain: Rejected: speed does not move a story up a step; the steps differ in the kind of work.
Rejected: cross-team impact is two steps above mid, not the next one.
Rejected: shaping organization-wide systems is the top step, three above mid.
Correct: the step directly above owning full solutions is leading team-level work.
questions.rule: Move up one level by changing the kind of ownership and reach, not just the speed.

media.alt: A staircase of five steps rising left to right, each labelled with a level and its main job: entry executes small pieces, mid owns full solutions, senior leads team work, staff drives cross-team impact, principal shapes organization-wide systems. A cartoon man runs up the steps.

questions.section: 13.1 What Does It Mean to Lead Strategically and Think Big?
questions.q: What does the direction of the arrows in the diagram show about the platform and the three teams?
options: Each team feeds its own tool into the platform, which merges them later
The platform serves all three teams as shared infrastructure they use
The platform reports to the data team, which informs the other two
The platform is built for the data team, with arrows showing reporting lines
questions.explain: The arrows start at the platform and end at all three teams, so one shared capability serves them in place of separate systems.
optionExplain: Rejected: the arrows point out of the platform toward the teams, not into it.
Correct: one platform sits at the source of arrows reaching every team.
Rejected: arrows reach the mobile and web teams directly, not through the data team.
